# The Jar on the Porch

Every morning, Mrs. Callahan walked to the store. She walked slowly. She liked to count her steps and smell the rain if it was wet.

One Tuesday, she came home with a heavy bag of peaches. They were red and soft and sweet. She set them on the counter and smiled.

She made jam. She did this every year. The kitchen filled with a thick, warm smell. The pot bubbled. She stirred and stirred and stirred.

When it was done, she filled eight jars. Seven went into her pantry. The eighth, she set on the small table by the door.

The next morning, she saw Mr. Oren from across the street. He was thin and quiet. He usually sat in his chair and did not say much to anyone. He was watching the jar.

He walked over. He picked it up. He looked at her and said, "I do not know what to say."

She said, "You do not have to say anything. Just eat a spoonful over toast. That is all."

He nodded. He carried the jar inside like it was made of glass and feathers, all at once.

The next day, there was a small paper bag on her porch. Inside was a single cookie, still warm. There was no note.

She ate it at the kitchen table. She did not need a spoon.

The week after that, Mr. Oren was in his garden. It was small, but it was green. He was pulling weeds. He looked up when he saw her.

"Mrs. Callahan," he said. "Would you like a cucumber?"

She said, "I would love a cucumber."

And he gave her one. A long, cool, bumpy one.

They did not become the closest of friends. They did not need to. They simply kept giving small, sweet things to each other, one morning at a time.

And that was enough.

# The Lantern

Mara found the lantern on the fourth morning of her walk.

It sat in the tall grass beside the trail, half-buried, green with age. The glass was cracked. The little door on top was stuck. But when she pried it open, a single wick still curled inside, dry and waiting.

She set it on her lap and kept walking.

The trail wound down through birch trees, then over a hill, then along a ridge where the grass grew thin. Below her, the whole valley opened up. The river cut a silver line through the green. Far off, the sea sat flat and gray, patient as a dog.

Mara had been walking for four days. She had left the city on a Tuesday and told no one why. She didn't need to. She needed to put one foot in front of the other, and then the next, and then the next.

She sat down on the ridge. She pulled the lantern out. She struck a match.

The flame caught. It flickered. It held.

Light spilled out over the grass. It touched her hands. It warmed the air around her face, small and golden and steady.

She sat there for a long time. The light swayed. The river moved. The birds went on their business.

When the light faded, she put the lantern back on her lap and stood up.

She kept walking.

She found the sea by afternoon. She walked along the wet sand for an hour, letting the water touch her shoes. Then she turned around.

The trail up the ridge was quiet. The birch trees were quiet. The lantern in her hands was quiet, and warm.

She walked home by nightfall.

She set the lantern on the windowsill.

And she left it there.

Mara found the book on a rainy Tuesday.

She had stopped at the little shop on Maple Street because the sky was doing its worst and her shoes were not waterproof. The shop was warm and smelled like old paper and coffee. She browsed the shelves for an hour, and her fingers kept returning to a thin blue book on a lower shelf.

She pulled it out.

The handwriting was small and careful. It read:

*To the person who opens this book next. I hope the rain outside sounds like music tonight. I hope you are in a warm place. I hope you read the cat poem. I did, a hundred times, and I always needed it.*

She read it twice.

And then she sat in the warm room, with the rain on the glass, and she let herself be still for a long, long while.

# The One Tulip

The garden had gone quiet by March. Just bare dirt and brown twigs and the low, gray sky pressing down on everything.

Marta walked the path each morning with her cup of coffee. She'd do it for thirty years. Same route. Same quiet. Same nothing to see.

Until the morning she stopped.

One single tulip. Small. Pink. Pushing up through the cracks in the stone path like it had been waiting for a long time. Its petals were still tight, folded around each other like a fist that had just decided to open.

She set the coffee down on a stone and just stood there.

"Hello, little thing," she said. Out loud. To the flower.

She knelt. The damp grass cold against her knees. She pulled back a tangle of dead leaves and found the soil beneath, dark and soft. She pressed her thumb into it. Still cool. Still alive underneath.

She didn't dig. Didn't move it. Didn't take a picture.

She just sat beside it for a while, sipping her coffee, watching the tip of the petal catch a thin line of sun that had finally broken through the clouds.

By the next morning, the tulip had opened a little more. And beside it, in the same crack, a second one. Smaller. Green, barely there. Just a hint.

Marta looked at them both.

"Okay," she said. "Okay, you two. I'll be back tomorrow."

She poured the rest of her coffee into the soil. The cold ground drank it fast.

She walked the rest of the path, and for the first time in a long while, her footsteps sounded a little lighter. The sky was still gray. The garden was still mostly brown. But the path was no longer empty.

And the coffee cup sat on its stone, waiting, as if it knew the morning was not quite over yet.

# The Extra Loaf

Every morning, before the sun cleared the rooftops, Elara pulled the bread from the oven.

Rye for the morning. Sourdough for the afternoon. And on Fridays, when the dough was rich and the kitchen smelled like honey, she baked one extra loaf.

She never ate it. She never sold it. She'd wrap it in a clean cloth and set it on the step outside her shop door, where the old bench sat.

People asked her why.

"Someone's always cold," she'd say, and move on to the next task.

Years went by. The loaf appeared every Friday. Rain, shine, the long grey stretch of winter. She never missed.

One November morning, the bench was not empty.

A man sat there, thin as a reed, his coat too thin for the season. He was eating the bread slowly, the way you eat something you're not sure is real. He looked up when Elara stepped outside, and his eyes were wide.

"It's for you," she said.

"I didn't— I mean, I can pay—"

"It's for whoever's cold," she said. "You're cold. Eat your bread."

He ate. He talked a little. He lived in a room above the shuttered bookshop two streets over. He was a former teacher, she guessed, from the way he held his bread and the careful, round shape of his words.

He came back the next Friday. And the one after.

By December, he was helping her knead the dough before dawn. By spring, he was writing the day's specials on the little chalkboard by the door. His handwriting was neat and proud.

Elara never thanked him. She didn't have to.

The bench held the bread. The bread held the morning together. And on the coldest Fridays, two people sat side by side, eating in the blue half-light, saying very little, needing nothing more.

That was the whole of it.

That was the whole of the thing.

And it was enough.

# The Blue Scarf

The morning air was cold and thin. Nora pulled her coat tighter and walked down the same street she always walked. Same bakery. Same corner. Same small window where the cat slept.

She liked the small things. The small things stayed.

Then she saw the scarf.

It was blue. Just blue. No pattern, no trim. It had slipped off a railing outside the post office and landed on the wet sidewalk. A little mud on one end. A little rain in the folds.

Nora knelt down.

"Nobody's claiming you," she said to it, and laughed at herself.

She folded the scarf into a square. Then she carried it home.

That evening, her granddaughter came over. Little Lily, seven years old, with a gap between her front teeth and socks covered in crayon marks. She dropped her bag by the door and ran to the kitchen.

"Grandma! What's that?"

Nora held up the blue scarf. "I found it this morning. On the sidewalk."

Lily took it. She held it up to the window. The late sun went through the blue cloth and made a soft, watery glow on the table.

"I'm going to wear it," Lily said. She was already sliding it around her neck, already running for the stairs. "It's the color of the sky right before it gets dark!"

The door swung shut behind her.

Nora stood in the kitchen for a long moment. The scarf was just a scarf. The mud was still on one end. The rain had dried into a faint stain near the corner.

But it made a glow on the table.

She smiled. She poured herself a cup of tea. And she let the evening be small, and quiet, and enough.

Outside, the sky turned that exact blue.

And then the dark came, gentle as a hand, and covered the town in the soft, even way that only night can.

But the scarf was safe inside.

And that was the whole story.

Old Man Pell baked bread every morning. Not just any bread. The kind that smelled like butter and honey and the kind of sunshine that sneaks in through your kitchen window in July.

# The Jar by the Door

Every morning, old Tom set two cups on the little wooden table by his front door. One was for him. One was for the bird.

He never knew which bird. A wren, maybe. A sparrow. Sometimes a blue jay with a loud voice and a proud tail. It didn't matter. The cup always held fresh water, and the bird always drank.

Tom had lived on that street for thirty-one years. The house was small. The yard was smaller. But the garden out back was his pride. Tomatoes. Herbs. A tangle of roses that never did quite what he asked them to do. He didn't mind. He liked the way they wandered.

One Tuesday in June, Tom set the cups as usual. But when he came back to his window, the table was empty. No bird. No cups. Just a small glass jar sitting where the cups had been.

Tom put on his shoes. He walked to the door. He picked up the jar.

Inside, there was a single white flower. Tiny. Perfect. It had a little note tucked under the petals. He unfolded it.

*Thank you for the water. — S.*

Tom stood on the porch for a long time. The jar sat in his palm, light as a whisper. He looked up at the eaves of his roof. At the bare branches. At the wide, open sky.

Then he smiled.

He carried the jar inside and set it on the kitchen windowsill. The morning sun came through the glass and caught the petals. They glowed, soft and pink.

The next morning, Tom set out the two cups again. And a third one, a little smaller, with a single petal resting at the bottom.

The bird came that afternoon. It looked at the cups. It drank from the small one. Then it tilted its head, as if to say, *What's this?*

Tom just watched from the window and smiled.

He set the cups out every day after that. Three cups. One for him. One for the bird. And one, just in case someone else stopped by and needed a drink.

And sometimes, in the morning, the third cup was empty.

And sometimes, there was a note.

Tom never complained. He liked the way things wandered.

# The Long Way Home

Every evening, Mara walked home from school by the same path. Past the bakery. Past the old oak. Past the creek where the stones clicked under her shoes.

But on a Tuesday in late October, she stopped.

A snail sat in the middle of the path. Small and gray and slow, it had only made it a hand's width past the bakery.

Mara knelt down. She tilted her head. The snail tilted its head, too, or seemed to.

"You have a long way to go," she said.

And just like that, she was walking beside it. Not the path. The grass at the edge of it, where the snail could keep its steady, sliding pace.

They passed the old oak. The snail took a minute under the tree, pausing to stretch. Mara waited.

They reached the creek. The stones were dry on this side, but the air was cool and wet. The snail made it across in a slow, shining line.

By the time they reached the garden at the end of the lane, the sun was low and orange. The sky went pink, then soft blue, then the color of a bruise healing.

The snail stopped at the edge of a hedge. It curled, just a little. Like it was settling in.

Mara stood there a moment, breathing the cold, sweet air of the garden.

She had missed the bakery. Missed the oak. Missed the clicking stones. And she had taken an hour instead of ten minutes.

But the evening felt long and golden and entirely her own.

She walked the rest of the way home, quiet, with the smell of leaves in her hair.

And that was enough.

```python
def word_histogram(s):
    # Convert to lowercase and remove punctuation
    s = s.lower()
    s = s.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
```

3. **Split & count** – `split()` breaks the cleaned string on whitespace, then we tally each word in a plain dict.

The lighthouse sat at the edge of the cliff like a tall, white finger pointing at the sky. For thirty years, Elias had climbed the stairs. For thirty years, he had polished the glass, trimmed the wick, and watched the dark water turn silver at dawn.

"Hello," she said. Her voice was small and tired.

"Hello," Elias said. He knelt beside her. "You're cold."

"I'm scared," she said. And then, quieter, "I don't remember how I got here."

Elias didn't ask again. He lifted her into his arms — she was lighter than he expected, like holding a bundle of wet bread — and he walked back up the cliff.

One hundred and twelve steps. He climbed them slow.

The lighthouse beam swept out over the water. Round and round. Round and round. A slow, steady promise in the dark.

"Is that your job?" she asked. "The light?"

"Keeping it on," he said. "So nobody gets lost."

She nodded. She took a sip of cocoa. And for the first time, she smiled.

Outside, the wind came back. The waves found their rhythm again. And the light kept turning, slow and sure, over all the dark water, saying *here, here, here* to anyone who needed to find their way home.

# Word Histogram Function

Here's a clean solution using `re.findall` to extract words (ignoring punctuation) and `collections.Counter` for frequency counting:

```python
import re
from collections import Counter

def word_histogram(text):
    # Convert to lowercase and extract only alphabetic words
    words = re.findall(r'[a-z]+', text.lower())
    return dict(Counter(words))
```

## How it works:

1. **`text.lower()`** — converts the entire string to lowercase so "Hello", "HELLO", and "hello" are all treated the same.
2. **`re.findall(r'[a-z]+', ...)`** — finds all sequences of lowercase letters, effectively stripping out any punctuation (commas, periods, exclamation marks, etc.) and non-letter characters.
3. **`Counter(words)`** — tallies up the occurrences of each word.
4. **`dict(...)`** — converts the Counter to a plain dictionary (as the tests expect).

## Verification against the tests:

```python

assert word_histogram("Python is great. Python is fun!") == {"python": 2, "is": 2, "great": 1, "fun": 1}
assert word_histogram("Test, test, TEST.") == {"test": 3}
```

All three pass. The regex approach handles edge cases well — it naturally discards punctuation regardless of where it appears (mid-word, at boundaries, etc.) and treats hyphenated or apostrophe-containing tokens as separate words, which keeps the behavior predictable.

# The Old Tree on Maple Street

Every morning, before the sun got high, Mr. Finch walked his little red dog to the corner of Maple Street.

Then they stopped.

The dog, Biscuit, sniffed the air. She tilted her head. Mr. Finch stood beside her, hands in his coat pockets, and he looked up.

The big oak tree was in bloom.

He hadn't noticed it happening. One day it had been bare and brown, all tangled branches against the gray sky. The next morning, it was full of small white flowers, soft as breath, heavy on every limb.

"Good morning, old friend," he said.

Biscuit barked, like she agreed.

He sat down on the low brick wall at the corner. Biscuit curled at his feet. The flowers dropped, one by one, like slow snow. They landed on his hat. They landed on the dog. One landed, very gently, on his hand.

He turned it over, looking at it from every side. It was small. It was white. It smelled like nothing, or maybe like everything.

He thought about his wife, Clara. She'd loved that tree. She used to press the leaves in her books, the ones with the wide, deep veins. *You can hold a whole season in your hand*, she used to say. *And it still lasts.*

Clara had been gone three years now. But the tree kept blooming. Every spring, without fail, it opened its arms and filled the whole corner with that quiet white softness.

Mr. Finch stood up. His knees crackled. Biscuit stood up too, stretched her front paws, and looked at him with those round, dark, expectant eyes.

"Alright, girl," he said. "Let's go home."

They walked on, slow and steady. Biscuit's little paws tapped the pavement. *Tap, tap, tap.* Mr. Finch hummed a song he couldn't quite remember the words to.

Behind them, the old oak kept dropping its flowers. The whole corner was white. The whole corner smelled like a spring that hadn't started yet, or maybe a spring that was just beginning to end.

And the tree just stood there, in the morning light, giving it all away.

Not because anyone was watching.

Just because it could.

# The Lamp and the Cat

Every evening, old Thomas walked up the spiral stairs of the lighthouse. One step. Two steps. Three steps. One hundred and twelve steps in all. His knees ached. His boots rang against the stone. But he never skipped a night. Not once. Not in thirty years.

At the top, he lit the great lamp. He wiped the glass. He oiled the wick. Then he sat in his chair, wrapped in his woolen blanket, and watched the sea turn black.

On the night of the autumn storm, a small gray shape appeared at the base of the tower. It was a cat. It was soaked through, shivering, and meowing like it was asking a question it couldn't find the words for.

Thomas looked at the rain. He looked at the cat. He looked at the rain again.

"Right then," he said.

He carried the cat up all one hundred and twelve steps.

The cat dried by the lamp's warm glow. It purred so loud it rattled the oil can. Thomas poured a little cream into a chipped mug, and the cat drank it all in one long, slow slurp.

That night, Thomas did not sit alone.

The cat did not leave the next morning. Or the morning after that. It walked up the stairs behind him. It sat on the glass shelf and watched the boats come and go. It stretched, yawned, and slept in a circle right under his chair.

The fishermen called him "Tommy the Cat Man" for a while, which made him grin behind his weathered hands.

Years passed. The lamp kept turning. The sea kept rolling. And every evening, two sets of footfalls rang up the spiral stone. One slow and heavy. One small and soft.

When Thomas finally grew too tired for the stairs, the cat walked up to the top, lay down in his chair, and waited.

The light still turned. The sea was still there.

And nobody ever left the lamp dark.

# The Maple Tree on Hill Street

Every morning, the same woman walked the same three blocks.

Her name was Ruth, and she carried a thermos of coffee and a small notebook. She was a teacher, though she had retired two years ago. But she still liked to walk. The world felt wider when she moved through it on her own two feet.

On the corner of Hill Street and the old elm, there was an empty space. A patch of bare dirt between two parking spots. No one paid it any mind. The city had no use for it.

But Ruth did.

One April, after a soft rain, she went to the garden shop at the end of the street. She bought a small maple sapling. It cost eleven dollars and a little change. She wrapped it in burlap and carried it home.

That weekend, she dug a hole in the bare dirt. The soil was hard and full of old brick. She dug for an hour. Then another. Her back ached. The neighbors looked out their windows. Some nodded. Most went back inside.

She set the little tree in the ground. She patted the soil flat. She poured water from her thermos, because that was all she had, and she walked home.

The next morning, she came back. And the morning after that. And the morning after that.

Spring turned to summer. The little tree grew two new leaves. Then four. Then a dozen.

A boy from the apartment above started pressing his face against the window to watch it grow. A dog from three doors down began to nap in its small circle of shade. An old man with a paintbrush showed up one Saturday and gave the tree a little red stripe at the base. "For luck," he said. And he left.

By the second summer, the shade was wide enough for the boy to sit under it with his book. By the third, the branches brushed the upper window.

Ruth still walked the three blocks. She still carried her thermos and her notebook. But now she paused. She looked up. She watched the leaves turn gold in October, watched them fall like little coins in the wind.

She never planted another tree.

She never needed to.

The one was enough. The one was everything.

And every morning, for as long as she walked, there was a small green place on Hill Street that was waiting for her. Just a little taller. Just a little wider. Just a little more like a home.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald

**Published:** 1925 | **Pages:** ~180

Few novels have become as synonymous with a single phrase—"the American Dream"—as *The Great Gatsby* has. Yet to reduce Fitzgerald's masterpiece to a parable about wealth and ambition is to miss just how layered, elegiac, and quietly devastating it truly is.

## The Story

Told by the reserved, observant Nick Carraway in the summer of 1922, the novel follows his neighbor, the enigmatic millionaire Jay Gatsby, and his obsessive pursuit of the golden, married Daisy Buchanan. Set against the glittering backdrop of Long Island, New York, the story unfolds through Gatsby's lavish parties, a slow unraveling of his past, and a crescendo of violence and disillusionment that arrives with the swiftness of a summer storm.

## What Works Brilliantly

**Fitzgerald's prose is the book's most undeniable triumph.** Sentences glow with a lyricism that feels almost baroque—opulent, warm, a little overheated—and then cut to ice. The famous final line, *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past,"* is a perfect distillation of the entire novel: beautiful, doomed, and inescapably human.

**The themes are deceptively simple.** At its core, the book asks whether the past can be recaptured, whether love can survive the architecture of class, and whether the dream of self-reinvention has a price tag written in human destruction. Gatsby's green light across the bay is one of literature's great symbols—simultaneously a single person and an entire mythology of possibility.

**Nick Carraway as narrator is a stroke of genius.** He is sympathetic and judgmental, a participant and a ghost. His unreliability forces the reader to question every scene, to wonder what he's withholding and what he's美化-ing. The story is never quite the story he tells.

## Where It Stumbles (If It Stumbles At All)

For modern readers, the novel's short length (~180 pages) and its compression of time can feel slightly underdeveloped in its middle chapters. Characters like Tom and Jordan Buchanan, while functionally essential as antagonists and satirical targets, remain somewhat two-dimensional. But this may be Fitzgerald's intent: they are types, social forces, not fully realized people. Gatsby is the novel's beating heart; everyone else exists in relation to him.

## Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is not a long novel. It's not a sprawling epic. It's a tightly coiled spring of a story—maybe 400,000 words that fit the shape of a single summer—and it hits with the force of something much larger. It is a book you can read at eighteen and recognize as beautiful, and read again at forty and recognize as a wound. Fitzgerald captures the specific, electric, terrible energy of the Jazz Age while building something far more permanent: a meditation on how we construct the people we want to be, how we love across the gaps class and time have dug, and how the past is never actually past.

**Rating: 4.5 / 5**

A novel that earns its place on every "required reading" list, not because it's easy, but because it rewards every reread with a new shiver.

# The Quiet Clock

Old Marcus kept a clock shop on the corner of Elm and Fifth. For thirty years, he fixed them. Spring clocks, pendulum clocks, little tin clocks that chimed at the hour. His hands knew every gear. His ears could hear a tick from across the room.

On a Tuesday in November, a young girl walked in. She set a small brass clock on the counter. It was no bigger than a teacup.

"It doesn't tick," she said.

Marcus lifted it to his ear. Silence. Not the silence of a stopped clock, which he had heard a thousand times. This was a different quiet. A full, round, peaceful quiet. Like the space between waves.

"Can I fix it?" she asked.

He turned it over in his palms. He looked inside through the little glass back. The hands were frozen at two o'clock. The gears were perfect. The spring was wound tight. Everything was in order. And yet. Nothing moved.

"I don't know," he said. And then, softly, he laughed. "In thirty years, I have never said that about a clock."

The girl smiled. "Then just leave it on the shelf. I'll come back next week."

He set it on a high shelf, between a cuckoo clock and a grandfather clock.

For six days, it sat there. Silent. Still. He walked past it each morning and each evening, and each time, the room felt a little more still. The other clocks ticked, but their ticking sounded kinder, somehow. Less hurried.

On the seventh day, the girl came back. She looked at the shelf. The hands still read two o'clock.

"It's still quiet," she said.

"Is that bad?" Marcus asked.

She shook her head. "No. I just wanted you to know that it's quiet for a reason. My grandfather made it. He stopped making clocks the day my grandmother died. He said, 'The world still has enough noise. I'm going to make one quiet thing.'"

She took it from the shelf. She tucked it under her arm. She walked to the door.

"Thank you for not breaking it, Mr. Marcus."

The door closed. The shop was full of ticking again, a hundred small hearts beating in brass and wood. But Marcus stood for a long time in the quiet space where the clock had been. And the ticking, he decided, was just right. Not too much. Not too little.

He picked up his tools. He went back to work.

# The Dog at the Lighthouse

Every evening at six, the light turned.

Round and round it went, slow and steady, painting the dark water in long silver strokes. And every evening at six, the keeper, Mr. Alden, climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the top.

One hundred and twelve. He never counted wrong. He had counted them every day for thirty years.

But on the morning of a cold Tuesday in November, Mr. Alden was not at the bottom of the stairs. He was in the kitchen, holding a cup of coffee that was too hot, and listening to a sound he had not heard in a long time.

*Thump. Thump. Thump.*

Something was tapping against the door.

He opened it.

A dog stood in the rain. A big, muddy, shaggy dog with one ear that flopped down and one eye that was a pale, friendly green. The dog looked up at him. The dog looked down at his own paws. The dog looked back up.

"Well," said Mr. Alden. "Well, well, well."

He let the dog in.

The dog's name, he decided, was Thursday. Because she had come on a Tuesday, and that felt wrong, so he gave her a name after a better day.

Thursday was not a good dog, exactly. She knocked over a pot of soup. She chewed the leg of a chair. She howled at the radio every time it played a song.

But she was a *good* dog in the ways that mattered. She warmed his feet by the stove. She fell asleep on the bottom step of the one hundred and twelve, right where his boot would land. And when the wind howled so loud it sounded like the world was ending, she pressed her big muddy head against his ankle and breathed, slow and steady, like a small engine.

The village at the bottom of the cliff heard about the dog. A woman brought a plate of meatloaf. A boy brought a ball that Thursday destroyed in four minutes flat. An old man brought nothing, just sat on the porch and said, "Good for you, Alden. You needed that."

Mr. Alden did not argue.

Spring came. The rain stopped. The light still turned every evening at six, round and round, slow and steady. And the one hundred and twelve steps still had to be climbed.

But now, on the first step, a shaggy tail wagged up and down.

And the climb felt a little shorter.

# The Great Gatsby – A Review

**By F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is a novel that has endured nearly a century not merely as a literary classic, but as a cultural touchstone—a shorthand for the seductive, ultimately hollow pursuit of the American Dream. At just over 180 pages, it reads like a glass of champagne: sparkling, intoxicating, and leaving a faint bitter aftertaste.

Set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island's East and West Egg, the story is filtered through Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest who rents a modest cottage next to the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Gatsby throws legendary parties, courts the distant green light across the bay—Daisy Buchanan's dock—and is consumed by a romantic fantasy he has been nursing since a wartime separation five years prior. Nick, the reader's moral compass, drifts between admiration for Gatsby's audacity and revulsion at the casual cruelty of the "old money" world of Daisy and her husband, Tom.

What makes the novel so powerful is Fitzgerald's prose, which operates on two registers simultaneously. The language is lush, almost baroque in its descriptions of parties, dresses, and the glittering excess of the Jazz Age—yet it is consistently undercut by a cooler, more elegiac awareness. The famous opening line ("In my younger and more vulnerable years…") sets a tone of retrospective sorrow that lingers over every page. The ending, with its meditation on boats, green lights, and the impossibility of recapturing the past, is among the most quietly devastating passages in American literature.

Fitzgerald is at his sharpest with his satirical targets. Tom Buchanan's brute racism and class entitlement, Daisy's beautiful emptiness, the way wealth converts human beings into disposable décor—these observations remain uncomfortably contemporary. The novel's central argument is that the American Dream, as a promise of self-creation through merit, quietly corrupts itself into a story about status, possession, and the refusal to let the past die. Gatsby's tragedy is that he mistook Daisy for the dream, and the dream for something real.

If one fault must be named, it is that the plot machinery is lean and somewhat predictable for readers familiar with the broad strokes of Gatsby's backstory. The novel is ultimately a mood and a meditation more than a story of twists. But that is a minor quibble in a book whose sentences carry so much weight.

*The Great Gatsby* is the kind of novel that rewards rereading at every stage of life. The teenager sees drama and glamour; the adult sees the machinery of class and the loneliness underneath the party lights. It is short, gorgeous, and quietly devastating. A must-read, and one of the very few novels where the adjective "American" doesn't feel like a genre limitation but a true descriptor.

**Rating: 5 / 5**

# The Small Green Thing

Every morning, before the sun fully climbed the kitchen window, Maeve put on her rubber boots and stepped into the garden.

It was a small garden. Not the kind you'd see in a magazine, with neat rows and perfect shapes. Hers was a tangle of tomato vines and overgrown herbs and a few stubborn rose bushes that bloomed late, just for her. She'd had it for twenty-two years, and it knew the shape of her hands.

She'd water the plants. She'd pull the weeds. She'd stand in the middle of it all, with dirt on her knees, and breathe.

That Tuesday in late June, she noticed something near the back wall. A small green shoot, pushing up through a crack in the old stone. Maybe two inches tall. Three leaves, soft and bright.

She knelt down. She didn't know what it was. It wasn't a weed, exactly. It didn't look like anything she'd planted.

She didn't pull it.

The next morning, it was a little taller. She didn't pull it.

By the end of the week, it had four leaves. Then five. It grew in a slow, quiet way, like it wasn't in a hurry. Maeve found herself checking on it before the tomatoes, before the roses, before anything else.

One evening, she was sitting on the low stone wall, wiping her hands on a rag, when her neighbor Dale waved from across the fence.

"What's the big secret?" he called over. "You've been over here smiling at the ground."

Maeve pointed down. "Look. That little thing. I don't know where it came from."

Dale leaned over the fence. He squinted. He tilted his head.

"Hmm," he said. "Might be a dandelion. Or a little wild parsnip. Can't tell yet."

"That's all right," Maeve said. "I like that I don't know."

A few more weeks passed. The little plant stretched up, thin and reaching, until one morning she saw a small white flower at its top, no bigger than a thumbnail.

She stood looking at it for a long time.

It didn't need her. It wasn't growing for her. It was just there, in the crack in the stone, doing its quiet work in the sun.

She went back to her tomatoes. But she smiled the whole way through.

# The Small Dog in the Rain

Mara heard it before she saw it. A small sound, just above the rain. A thin, quiet cry coming from behind the fence at the end of the yard.

She stepped outside in her socks. The water was cold on her feet. She pulled her jacket tight and walked to the fence.

There, under the old oak tree, was a dog. Small. So small. A patch of muddy brown fur, no bigger than a loaf of bread. It shook and shivered, and its eyes were wide and bright and afraid.

"Oh, you poor thing," Mara said.

The dog did not run. It just looked up at her. It wanted to come close, but it was too cold, too tired. It lay down in a wet patch of grass and closed its eyes.

Mara lifted the fence gate. It creaked, loud in the quiet rain. She crouched down and held out her hand. The dog sniffed her fingers. Then, slowly, it walked up and pressed its small nose against her palm.

Mara scooped it up. It was so light. It fit right in her arms, under her jacket, where it was warm. It stopped shaking. It sighed, a long, slow sound, like it was letting go of all its worry at once.

She carried it inside. She found a towel. She dried the dog gently, finger by finger, through the tangled fur. Under the mud, the coat was soft and golden. A little white mark on its chest, shaped like a star.

"Okay, little star," she whispered. "Okay."

She set a bowl of water on the floor. The dog lapped at it quickly, then lay down beside her feet, curled into a tight circle. Its tail gave one small thump against the wood.

Then it slept.

Mara sat on the floor beside it and watched the rain tap at the window. The house was quiet. The dog breathed in slow, steady little pulls. In and out. In and out.

She did not know where it had come from. She did not know if its person was out there, looking. But for now, the little star was safe. It was warm. It was here.

And that was enough.

# The Small Whale

Old Man Hale kept the lighthouse on the end of the cliff. Every night, he climbed the narrow stairs, polished the great glass, and lit the flame. And every morning, he came back down and made his coffee and walked the long, long path to the village for his bread.

It was a Tuesday in October when he saw her.

He was walking the path, and the fog was thick and soft, and the sea was the color of pewter. He looked down at the water near the rocks, and there, just under the surface, a small whale was swimming in slow, tired circles.

She was tiny. No bigger than a rowboat.

"Hello, little one," he said.

She made a low sound, like a cello plucked once. Then she sank.

Old Man Hale stood at the edge of the cliff for a long time. The fog rolled in and out. The gulls cried up above him. He thought: *I cannot swim. I cannot pull a whale from the sea. What can I do?*

Then he went back up the stairs. He lit the light. He made it burn twice as bright.

He stayed awake all night, watching.

And at dawn, the fog lifted, and the sea turned gold, and a large whale surfaced just beyond the small one. She sang a long, low note. The little whale swam toward it. She turned. She looked, almost, up at the cliff.

Then she followed her mother out past the headland, where the water runs deep and the whales belong.

Old Man Hale watched until they were gone.

He went back down the stairs. He made his coffee. He walked the long path to the village.

And the baker gave him his bread, just as always, and he said, "Fine morning, Hale," and he said, "Fine morning, Tom," and they both went on with their day.

The light kept turning that night, and the next, and the next.

And out past the headland, in the deep and wide water, a small whale grew.

# The Bread at the Door

Every morning, before the sun cleared the rooftops, the baker set a warm loaf on a small wooden tray. He tied a strip of red cloth around it, like a little bow. And he walked the two blocks to the house at the end of the street, and he set the loaf on the old neighbor's doorstep.

Then he walked back. And he went on with his day.

Morning after morning. Rain or shine. The bread was always there. Warm. Soft on the top. Golden in the light.

The old neighbor, a thin woman named June, would find it there every morning. She would lift the tray, carry it in, and peel off the red cloth. She would cut a slice. She would eat it, standing at the kitchen window, watching the yard.

She never knocked on his door. He never knocked on hers. They had lived next to each other for twenty years, and they had never once spoken more than a few words. "Morning, Mr. Dale." "Morning, June." That was all. That was always enough.

But one Tuesday, the bread did not come.

June looked at the doorstep. Nothing. She looked again. Still nothing. She waited an hour. Two hours. The sun moved across the yard. The bread did not come.

So June took her shoes. She walked the two blocks. And she knocked on the baker's door.

Mr. Dale opened it. He looked tired. His hands were wrapped in a bandage, and his eye was a little red.

"I hurt my hand," he said. "I couldn't bake today. I'm sorry."

June looked at him for a moment. Then she reached in her coat pocket and pulled out a small, wrapped square of pie. Apple. She had baked it that morning. She wasn't sure why. She just had.

Here, she said. You haven't had breakfast yet.

And she set the pie on his kitchen counter.

And she walked the two blocks home.

The next morning, the bread was on her doorstep. Warm. Soft. Golden.

And on his counter, a little square of pie.

They never did say much to each other. But every morning, at the two-block walk, at the two doors, something small and warm passed between them.

And it was enough.

# The Long Walk Home

The road was flat and wide, and the sky was big above him.

Miles had been walking since morning. He didn't know why he'd started. He only knew that the house felt too small that morning, and the quiet felt too loud, and his feet had just... gone. So he walked.

The sun moved across the sky. A crow called out from a dead tree by the road. He passed a field of yellow grass. He passed a creek where the water ran thin over pale stones. He drank from it. It was cold and good.

By the time the light started to turn orange, he came to a town. It was small. Maybe ten houses. A church with a broken steeple. And on the corner of the one main street, a bakery.

The smell hit him like a warm hand on his face. Fresh bread. Butter. Something sweet he couldn't name.

He pushed the door open. A bell rang.

A woman stood behind the counter, flour on her apron, a wooden spoon in her hand. She looked at him. He looked at her.

"You look like you've walked a long way," she said.

"I have," he said.

She didn't ask how. She didn't ask where. She just nodded and pulled a round loaf from the shelf. She set it on the counter. Then she made a coffee, the way a person makes coffee for someone who needs it. Steady. No rush.

He sat at a small table by the window. He tore the bread. He ate. It was the best thing he'd tasted in a long time. Maybe ever. He wasn't sure.

When he was done, the woman was wiping down the counter. She caught his eye and smiled.

"You'll turn around out there," she said. It wasn't a question.

He looked outside. The street was dark now, but the bakery window pushed a square of gold onto the pavement. Somewhere back the way he'd come, the road stretched out. Long. Flat. Open.

"Yeah," he said. "I will."

He walked back out into the night. But the walk felt different now. Not endless. Just long. And that was alright.

He walked, and the road carried him home.

# The Day the Rain Stopped

For three weeks, the rain never left.

It fell on the rooftops. It fell on the windows. It fell on the old oak tree in the yard, and the tree just let it.

Every morning, Maren woke to the same sound: a soft, steady tapping on the glass. *Tap, tap, tap.* Like the sky was knocking on the door and asking to come in. She would pull the blanket up to her chin and listen.

Her grandmother, before she passed, used to say, "Rain is just the sky breathing." Maren thought that was the most beautiful thing anyone had ever told her, and she never forgot it.

On the morning of the fourth week, she woke up and the tapping was gone.

Silence. Real, wide, open silence.

Maren sat up. She pulled back the curtain. The sky was a pale, washed-out blue, the color of a kid's drawing of the sky. Not dramatic. Not perfect. Just *there*, quiet and wide.

She threw on her shoes. The soles were old and soft, and she barely felt the ground when she stepped out the back door.

The air smelled like wet stone and green things growing. The grass was dark and heavy. Puddles sat in the yard like little silver mirrors, each one holding a piece of the blue sky above.

Maren walked to the edge of the yard. She didn't step into the puddles. She just looked.

Then she stepped in.

Cold. Right through the thin sole. She laughed out loud, and the sound startled a crow from the oak tree, and it flew off in a wide, black arc.

She walked the whole yard that morning. Heel to toe. Toe to heel. Letting the water creep up past her ankles. The sky stayed blue. The silence stayed quiet. The tree held the sun on its leaves, and for a moment, every single one of them went bright.

Maren stood under it. She closed her eyes.

And she heard it. Faint. Far away. A single drop, falling from a leaf, landing in a puddle.

*Plink.*

The sky, finishing its breath.

Then, quiet again.

She stood there a long while. Then she went inside, made toast, and sat by the window. The sun was warm on her hands. Outside, the world was still wet, and still new, and still entirely, gently, enough.

# The Light and the Cat

Every evening, for thirty-two years, Tom walked the spiral stairs up to the top of the lighthouse. Two hundred and six steps. He never counted them anymore, but his knees still knew each one.

At the top, he wiped the great lens, checked the oil, and turned the key. The light swept out over the dark water, slow and steady, like a lullaby written in gold.

On the night it started to rain, he heard a sound at the bottom of the stairs.

A small, wet sound. A mewing.

He looked down through the round window. A gray cat sat in the doorway, shaking water from its fur like a tiny, sad tornado. Its ribs showed through the wet fur. It looked up at him with one green eye, the other half-closed from the cold.

Tom set his coffee mug on the railing. He walked back down. Two hundred and six steps, and this time, he did count them.

"You're a long way from anywhere, little one," he said, scooping the cat up. It purred. The sound rumbled in his palms like a tiny engine turning over for the first time.

He named her June.

That winter, the lighthouse was no longer just a tower with a light in it. It was a home. June slept in the warm patch on the floor near the oil drum. She chased moths around the lamp room. She batted at the ropes and the nets and the old boots. She sat on the window ledge and watched the rain, and Tom would sit beside her and watch the light turn, and turn, and turn.

People from the village on the hill below would sometimes wave. They'd call up, "Tom! You got a cat now?" and he'd wave back, grinning, and June would meow as if to say, *Yes. I am here. I am the reason he smiles.*

Spring came. The fog lifted. The gulls returned, crying overhead in their rough, laughing voices.

One morning, Tom looked down and saw a boy on the path below, about eight years old, staring up at the lighthouse with his chin in his hands. Waiting.

Tom took the boy up the two hundred and six steps. He showed him the lens. He showed him the light. And he showed him June, who stretched out in a long, lazy yawn and patted the boy's shoe with one soft paw.

The boy stayed. He came back the next day. And the next.

And Tom, who had climbed those stairs alone for thirty-two years, found that they didn't feel so tall anymore.

The light still swept out over the water every night.

But now, someone watched it with him.

And that was enough.

```python
import string

def word_histogram(text):
    # Remove all punctuation characters
    cleaned = text.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    # Convert to lowercase and split into words
    words = cleaned.lower().split()
    # Build the frequency dictionary
    histogram = {}
    for word in words:
        histogram[word] = histogram.get(word, 0) + 1
    return histogram
```

**How it works:**

2. **Normalize case** – `.lower()` converts everything to lowercase so `"Hello"`, `"HELLO"`, and `"hello"` are all treated as the same word.

3. **Split & count** – `.split()` breaks the cleaned string on whitespace into a list of words, and the loop tallies each word's occurrences in a plain dictionary.

```python
def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
    result = []
    for item in lst:
        if not result or result[-1] != item:
            result.append(item)
    return result

class TestRemoveAdjacentDuplicates(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_basic_functionality(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]), [1, 2, 3, 4])

        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7]), [5, 6, 7])
    
    def test_multiple_duplicates(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

**How it works:**

The function iterates through the input list and builds a new `result` list. For each element, it checks two conditions:

1. `not result` — handles the first element (nothing to compare against yet, so it's always added)
2. `result[-1] != item` — only appends the current item if it differs from the last item already in the result

| 3 | `[1, 2, 3]` | `3 != 3` → False | skip |
| 4 | `[1, 2, 3]` | `3 != 4` → True | append → `[1, 2, 3, 4]` |

The time complexity is **O(n)** and space complexity is **O(n)** where n is the length of the input list.

```python
import re

def word_histogram(s):
```

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is that rare novel that operates as a flawless piece of craft while still carrying the emotional weight of a genuine lament. It is the American Dream held up to a dark mirror, and what stares back is beautiful, hollow, and heartbreaking.

## The Story, Briefly

Told by the observant, somewhat self-doubting Nick Carraway, the novel is set in the summer of 1922 on Long Island's East and West Egg. Nick becomes drawn into the orbit of his enigmatic neighbor Jay Gatsby—a self-made millionaire whose glittering parties are legendary, whose love for the gold-digger Daisy Buchanan is all-consuming, and whose past is wrapped in a fog of rumor and self-invention. What begins as a portrait of roaring excess quickly tightens into a tragedy about the impossibility of recapturing the past.

## Why It Works

Fitzgerald's prose is the first thing that hits you, and it keeps hitting. Lines like *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"* don't feel like decoration; they feel like the novel's spine made visible. The writing is lush but never overwrought, lyrical but always in service of meaning. Every metaphor is doing work.

Thematically, the book is deceptively layered. On the surface, it's a romance and a detective story (Who *is* Gatsby? What did he do in the war?). Beneath that, it's a sharp social critique of class, wealth, and the moral emptiness of the upper class. The eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg, the Valley of Ashes, the green light at the end of the dock—these are images that have lodged themselves in the cultural imagination for a century, and they still land with force.

The characters are sharply drawn. Tom and Daisy Buchanan, who *"carelessly broke things and people and then retreated back into their money,"* are among the most damning portraits of moral cowardice in American literature. Gatsby himself is more complicated than the myth he projects, and Fitzgerald is wise enough not to make him either a saint or a pure fraud. Nick, the unreliable narrator who insists on his own decency, is a masterstroke of self-aware irony.

## A Small Caveat

For modern readers expecting a fast pace or a broad ensemble cast, the novel's tight, slightly claustrophobic focus on one summer can feel slow in its middle chapters. The dialogue at the Buchanan dinner party and the long stretches of Gatsby's parties can test patience if you're not in a mood for atmospheric, almost dreamlike storytelling. But that very slowness is the point; Fitzgerald is building the heat before the storm.

## Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is a slim novel—barely 180 pages—but it reads like it contains an entire civilization's worth of meaning. It is a book about illusion and desire, about the gap between who we were and who we pretend to be, and about a country's willingness to mistake glitter for substance. It is as readable on a summer beach as it is in a literature seminar, and it rewards rereading at every age.

It is, in short, the kind of book that earns its place on the "essential" list not by virtue of its reputation, but by the quiet, persistent power of its writing. If you haven't read it, you owe it to yourself. If you have, you owe it to yourself again.

# The First Green

The alarm didn't wake her. The light did.

Mara opened her eyes to a grey, soft morning, the kind that feels like the whole world is still asleep and breathing slow. She pulled on her boots. They were the old ones, the ones with the squishy soles, and she liked the sound they made on the kitchen tile. *Slap, slap, slap.* Small sounds. Good sounds.

She filled the kettle. Outside the window, the garden was a flat stretch of brown and dark. The frost sat on the grass in a thin, tight skin, and the bare branches of the old maple reached up like fingers that had forgotten how to grip.

Nothing moved. Nothing was ready.

She sipped her tea at the counter and watched the frost start to thin at the edges, one slow line at a time. The sky went from grey to a pale, pale blue, and a single bird landed on the fence. It tilted its head. It sang one note, just one, and then it was gone.

Then she saw it.

Right at the base of the tomato plant, where the soil was still dark and cold, a tiny point of green had pushed up. No bigger than a grain of rice. No brighter than a whisper. It had been underground all winter, waiting in the dark, and now, in this quiet, unremarkable morning, it had decided to come up and look at the sky.

Mara set her mug down. She knelt, right there on the cold tile, and she just looked at it.

She didn't pull it closer. She didn't try to make it grow faster. She just looked, and she thought, *Oh. So you're here.*

The frost kept thinning. The sun climbed a little higher, and a warm spot of light fell on the kitchen floor, right next to her boot. The air smelled like wet earth and the last of last night's rain.

She stood up, stretched, and went back to her tea. It had gone lukewarm. She drank it anyway.

Outside, the maple's branches were still bare. The garden was still mostly brown. But the small green point was there, and it was enough. It was all the promise she needed for the day.

She rinsed her mug. She put on her coat. And she stepped out the back door into the quiet, bright, cold morning, ready to see what else had woken up.

# The Orange Cat

Every morning, the baker set out a small plate of bread by the back door. He didn't know why, at first. It was just a habit. A little kindness for the birds.

But the birds never touched the bread.

On a Tuesday in October, a small orange cat sat right down in front of the plate. It looked up at the baker. Its eyes were the color of honey. It didn't meow. It just sat there, very still, and waited.

The baker knelt down. He broke off a piece of the bread. He held it out.

The cat took it.

That was the beginning of it.

Every morning after that, the cat was there. It arrived before the sun came up, walked to the back door, and sat. The baker brought it a bigger piece of bread. Then a little bit of cheese. Then, one rainy Thursday, he brought a small bowl of warm milk.

The cat drank it all.

The baker started to talk to it. He told it about the dough. He told it about the long night before the first loaf. He told it things he hadn't told another person in a very long time. The cat listened. It purred. It tilted its head.

The neighbors began to notice. Mrs. Patel, who lived across the street, left a saucer of cream on her doorstep. The postman stopped by the bakery each morning just to say, "Good morning to the both of you."

The cat never came inside. That was fine. The baker respected that. He would set the door open wide, and the cat would press its nose against the warmth of the oven, then step back into the cool air. In and out. In and out. A small ritual.

Then, one morning in November, the cat didn't come.

The baker set out the bread anyway. He set it out the next morning. And the morning after that.

On the fourth morning, he found the plate full. The bread was gone. And in its place, a single orange feather from a bird, tucked neatly where the cat had been sitting.

The baker picked up the feather. He put it in his pocket, right next to his heart.

He set out the bread the next morning. And the morning after.

Not because the cat would come back. But because some things, once you start, you don't stop. You just keep the door open. You just leave the light on.

And maybe, on a cold night, something small and orange will walk up the path, and sit down, and look at you with eyes like honey.

And you'll say, "Oh. There you are."

And that will be enough.

# The Glass Bottle

Every morning, before the sun crested the hill, old Tom walked down to the shore.

He walked the same path he'd walked for forty years. Past the bakery where Mrs. Chen hung her sign. Past the post office where the bell still chimed, even though it rang for no one. Past the dunes and the dry grass and the row of old pines. Then his boots hit the sand, and he was home.

Tom had fished that water for decades. He'd sold his boat five years ago. His back wouldn't take the rocking anymore. But he still went down. He needed to see the sea the way it looked at dawn, all silver and still, like it was holding its breath.

That Tuesday, the tide had pulled back farther than usual. The sand stretched wide and pale under a grey sky. Tom walked past his usual spot, past the driftwood and the rocks, and there it was.

A glass bottle. Half buried. Filled with something that caught the light.

He dug it out with his fingers. Sand crumbled through his palms. Inside, wrapped in a twist of paper, was a small brass key. And a note.

The handwriting was careful. Slanted. He recognized it.

*For the one who finds it. I left this for my son the year he turned six. He's in the city now. He's a man. I don't think he needs this. So I'm putting it back in the world, where it belongs. To whoever the sea hands it to.*

Tom sat down in the wet sand. He turned the key over in his hand. It was small. Warm from being under the glass so long.

He thought about his own son, working in the city, calling on Sundays. He thought about all the things his father had kept in a drawer, and how he'd only opened the drawer when the drawer was empty.

Tom walked back up the dunes. He went inside. He found the old drawer in the hallway closet. The one he'd stopped opening years ago.

He slid it open.

Inside, there was a photograph. A small wooden boat. A boy in a too-big cap, standing at the stern, grinning up at the camera.

Tom held the photo a long time.

Then he set the brass key on the shelf beside it.

The next morning, he walked down to the shore again. Same path. Same grey sky. The sea held its breath.

He stood there, listening to the waves come in and go.

And for the first time in five years, he didn't feel like he was missing anything.

# The Warm Room

The oven died on a Tuesday.

Not with a bang. Not with smoke. Just a small *click*, and then the warm hum stopped, and the light in the back went dark.

Marcus stood in his kitchen with a wooden spoon in one hand and a smear of flour on his forehead, and he just stared at the little box on the wall. The one that used to tick and glow at four in the morning. The one that had been ticking and glowing for eleven years.

"Okay," he said, to no one. "Okay."

He pried open the bread he was trying to proof and checked the time. He had a market in four hours. Forty loaves. No oven.

He put on his coat. Walked three blocks. Stood in front of a small yellow house with a screen door that stuck.

He knocked.

A woman answered. She was tall, with gray hair pulled back and paint on her apron. She looked at him. He looked at the bread dough still bubbling on his counter, behind him, in his mind.

"I need to borrow an oven," he said.

She blinked. Then she stepped aside.

"My husband's," she said, pointing down a narrow hall. "It's not big. But it's warm."

It was a little old. The kind of oven with a round window and a dial you had to twist with your whole fist. It took twenty minutes to heat up. They stood in the kitchen together, and she made coffee, and he shaped the loaves, and the kitchen filled with the smell of yeast and butter and that low, steady hum.

"You don't have to do this," he said. "I should have called a repairman first."

She poured the second cup. "You would have been calling a repairman at the market. Staring at empty shelves. No. You did the right thing."

The loaves went in. One by one. Twelve at a time. They stood at the window of the oven, watching the crusts turn golden, and neither of them said anything for a long while.

When it was done, she loaded the bread into a big wooden box and set it on his car. He wrote a number on the back of a napkin. Her name, a phone number, and the words *owe you a loaf*.

He drove to the market. Sold every single one.

And on the way home, he stopped at a bakery on the corner, picked up a loaf of her favorite kind, and walked it three blocks back to the yellow house.

He knocked.

The screen door stuck.

"Come in," she said. "The coffee's still good."

And it was.

# The Cat in the Bakery

The rain came down hard that morning. *Tick, tick, tick* it went against the bakery windows. *Slap, slap, slap* it hit the tin roof. And inside, the ovens were warm, and the bread was sweet, and the whole world smelled like butter and sugar.

Tom set a tray of rolls on the shelf. He wiped his hands on his apron. He hummed a small tune. It was a good, quiet kind of Tuesday.

Then he heard it.

A little *mew* from behind the flour sacks. A thin, weak sound, like a thread pulling loose.

Tom knelt down. He moved the sacks aside. And there, in the corner, was a cat. A small one. Wet and gray and shivering, with one ear folded over like a leaf.

"Hey, little guy," Tom said. His voice came out softer than he meant it to. Softer than a man who deals with dough all day should manage.

The cat looked up. Its eyes were yellow and wide. It did not run. It just breathed, and the breath came out in tiny little puffs.

Tom went to the back of the kitchen. He came back with a towel. A bowl. A little saucer of milk, and half a piece of bread, torn small.

He set them down. Then he sat on the floor and waited.

The rain kept tapping. The bread kept baking. The ovens ticked and sighed, filling the air with that thick, golden smell.

The cat ate first. It ate fast, like it hadn't eaten in a while. Then it licked its paws. Then it curled up in the towel and closed its eyes.

Tom sat there for a long time. He didn't go back to work. He just listened to the rain, and the breathing of the cat, and the soft *whoosh* of the oven doors.

When the rain finally stopped, the cat opened its eyes. It looked at Tom. It let out one small, rough *mrrp*, and stretched one paw across his knee.

Tom smiled. He poked it with one finger. The cat purred.

He never did find out where the cat came from. And that was fine. It was gray, and small, and it liked to sleep on the warm floor behind the ovens.

From that Tuesday on, the bakery was never quite so quiet.

# The Red Scarf

Every morning, Mara poured her coffee into the blue mug. Every morning, she stepped onto the back porch with it. Every morning, the fog rolled in from the creek and wrapped the yard in a soft white blanket.

On a Tuesday in November, the fog was a little thicker than usual.

Mara lifted her mug and took a sip. She looked past the fog, toward the edge of the property, where the grass met the old stone wall. And there, sitting very still at the base of the wall, was a small dog.

It was the color of rust and cream, with one ear flopped over and the other standing straight up. It wore a red scarf. A real one, knitted, with long tassels that dragged in the dirt.

"Hey," Mara said.

The dog tilted its head. It did not bark. It did not run. It just looked at her the way a child looks at a stranger who has just walked into a room. *Oh. There you are. I was wondering when you'd come out.*

Mara set her mug on the porch railing. She walked down the steps and across the yard. The grass was cold and wet against her socks. The fog touched her nose like a cold fingertip.

"Hi there," she said again, slower this time.

The dog stood. It stretched one front paw forward, then the other, like it was bowing. Then it trotted the last few steps toward her. The red scarf swayed behind it.

Mara knelt down. The dog pressed its whole body against her knee, warm and solid and shaking just a little. She reached down and put her hand on its head. Its ears were soft. Its eyes were dark and steady and very, very old for a dog that was clearly a puppy.

She didn't know how it got there. She didn't know who had tied the scarf around its neck. She didn't know its name.

But it looked at her with such certainty, like it had been expecting her. Like it had walked a long way to get to this porch, in this fog, on this particular Tuesday.

"You can stay," she said.

The dog's tail gave one single, slow wag.

Mara stood up. Her knees crackled. She carried the dog back up the porch steps, where he set down and immediately curled in the patch of sun that had broken through the fog just for a moment. The red scarf pooled around him like a little puddle of color.

She picked up her blue mug. She took another sip. The coffee was cold now, but she didn't mind.

The fog kept rolling in. The creek kept murmuring. And the small dog slept, one ear straight up, dreaming something warm.

And Mara sat on the porch, and she did not move.

Some things just find their way home. You just have to be the porch they land on.

# Word Histogram Function

Here's a clean solution that handles case-insensitivity and strips punctuation before counting word frequencies:

```python
import string

def word_histogram(s):
    # Convert to lowercase to ignore case
    s = s.lower()
    # Remove all punctuation characters
    s = s.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    # Split into words (handles multiple spaces too)
    words = s.split()
    # Build the frequency dictionary
    histogram = {}
    for word in words:
        histogram[word] = histogram.get(word, 0) + 1
    return histogram
```

## How it works

| Step | Operation | Example (`"Hello, world! Hello."`) |
|------|-----------|-------------------------------------|
| 1 | `.lower()` | `"hello, world! hello."` |
| 2 | `.translate(...)` removes punctuation | `"hello world hello"` |
| 3 | `.split()` → list of words | `["hello", "world", "hello"]` |
| 4 | Loop & count | `{"hello": 2, "world": 1}` |

## Key details

- **`str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation)`** builds a translation table that maps every character in `string.punctuation` (i.e. `!"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~`) to `None`, effectively deleting them.
- **`str.split()`** with no arguments splits on any whitespace and automatically discards empty strings, so extra spaces won't produce empty-key entries.
- **`dict.get(word, 0) + 1`** is a concise way to increment a count, defaulting to `0` for first occurrences.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

## A Gilded Fable That Still Cuts Deep

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that operates on two levels simultaneously: as a taut, almost noir-style mystery and as a sweeping elegy for an era. Set in the summer of 1922 along the Long Island shores of West Egg and East Egg, the story follows narrator Nick Carraway as he becomes drawn into the orbit of his enigmatic neighbor, Jay Gatsby—a self-made millionaire who throws legendary parties and stares across the bay at a single green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock.

## The Story

At its center is a love story, but the kind that has been corroded by time, money, and pride. Gatsby has reinvented himself entirely for one woman, and the novel builds with mounting tension toward the question of whether he can ever recapture the past. The plot moves with the brisk, almost fateful momentum of a Greek tragedy—characters orbit one another, secrets fester, and the consequences of a single reckless afternoon spiral toward a devastating end.

## Style and Craft

Fitzgerald's prose is where the book truly sings. His sentences are lush but controlled, his imagery vivid and often melancholy. The green light, the valley of ashes, the eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg on the billboards—these symbols are woven in so naturally that they feel less like literary devices and more like things you'd actually notice. The novel is remarkably lean for a work of just over 180 pages; nothing is wasted, and the pacing is nearly flawless.

## Themes

Beneath the Jazz Age glamour, Fitzgerald is asking uncomfortable questions. Is the American Dream actually available to those born without privilege, or is it a performance you put on for people who'll never let you in? What do we owe the people we use to construct our identities? How much of "who we are" is just a story we've told ourselves? Gatsby's tragedy is that his dream was never really about Daisy as a person—it was about a symbol of a past that can never be retrieved. The final line captures this with devastating clarity: *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."*

## Weaknesses (and They're Small)

Daisy Buchanan is sometimes less a fully realized character than a function—a thing Gatsby wants and Tom owns. Jordan Baker, while well-drawn, has very little to do. And the novel's social satire, while sharp, occasionally tips into caricature, particularly with Tom and the "old money" crowd. These are minor quibbles in a book that is otherwise remarkably complete.

## Who Should Read It

If you love literary fiction with a plot-driven spine, if you're interested in the architecture of class and desire, or if you simply want a novel you can read in a single sitting and feel haunted by for days afterward—this is it. It's a cornerstone of the American canon, and yes, it earns its place.

## Final Verdict

**4.5 / 5**

*The Great Gatsby* is a masterwork of compression. In barely 200 pages, Fitzgerald builds a world, breaks a heart, and delivers a verdict on a nation that still resonates nearly a century later. It's a book you likely encountered in high school and probably read again as an adult—by which point the green light means something entirely different, and that's exactly how Fitzgerald intended it.

```python
import unittest

def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
    if not lst:
        return []
    result = [lst[0]]
    for i in range(1, len(lst)):
        if lst[i] != result[-1]:
            result.append(lst[i])
    return result

class TestRemoveAdjacentDuplicates(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_basic_functionality(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]), [1, 2, 3, 4])
    
    def test_repeated_elements(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7]), [5, 6, 7])
    
    def test_multiple_duplicates(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

**How it works:**

1. **Edge case:** If the list is empty, return an empty list immediately.
2. **Initialize:** Start the result with the first element of the input list.
3. **Iterate:** For each subsequent element, compare it to the last element in `result`. If it's different, append it; if it's the same (i.e., a consecutive duplicate), skip it.

This gives us an O(n) time complexity solution since we make a single pass through the list, and O(n) space for the new list.

Example trace for `[1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]`:
- Start: `result = [1]`
- `2 != 1` → `result = [1, 2]`
- `2 == 2` → skip
- `3 != 2` → `result = [1, 2, 3]`
- `3 == 3` → skip
- `3 == 3` → skip
- `4 != 3` → `result = [1, 2, 3, 4]`

Margot laughed. It came out too loud, a little ragged, and she stopped. Took a breath.

"Right."

"You okay?"

"I'm fine. I just—" She looked at the counter, at the little ceramic bowl they'd used for keys since 1997, still sitting where it was, still holding nothing. "I just kept thinking last night that she was going to come in and tell me I'd left the stove on. And I was going to yell at her. And then I remembered."

David was quiet for a long time. Long enough that the tick got annoying.

He laughed, quiet and real. "You're right. It's one sugar."

# The Small Bird in the Garden

Marta noticed the bird on a Tuesday.

It was sitting on the edge of her kitchen window, just below the sill. A small brown thing, with a curved beak and one wing that hung a little lower than the other. It did not try to fly. It just watched her with one bright, round eye.

"Well, hello," Marta said. She set down her coffee. She pulled the window open.

The bird hopped in.

That was the start of it. Marta did not know what to do, so she did the only thing she could think of. She lined a small box with an old towel and set it on the table. She put a few crumbs of bread and a little bowl of water beside it. She backed away and let the bird sit in the box for a while.

Over the next three days, the bird stayed.

Marta brought it fresh water every morning. She found a few small worms in the garden and placed them gently on a flat stone. The bird ate. On the second day, it tilted its head up at her. On the third day, it hopped from the box to the windowsill, stretched the lower wing, and gave a single, thin note.

Not a song. Just a small sound. But it was enough.

On the fourth morning, Marta opened the window and stepped outside to water the tomatoes. The air was cool and smelled like damp dirt. She could hear the neighbor's radio through the fence, playing something with a lot of drums.

She looked back up at the windowsill. The box was empty.

She stood there for a moment, feeling a small, quiet pull in her chest. Then she went back inside, swept the last few crumbs from the floor, and washed the bowl.

Later that afternoon, she was out in the garden again, pulling weeds. The sun was warm on her shoulders. And there, on the highest branch of the apple tree, the small brown bird sat with both wings even, both wings strong. It looked down at her. It did not sing. It did not need to. It just looked.

Marta nodded.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is the rare novel that feels simultaneously specific to its moment and timeless in its concerns. Set against the glittering, dissolute backdrop of 1922 Long Island and New York City, it is ostensibly a story about a mysterious millionaire named Jay Gatsby and his obsessive pursuit of Daisy Buchanan. In practice, it is something far more layered: a dissection of class, a critique of the American Dream, and a elegiac meditation on the way the past refuses to stay in the past.

**Style and Structure**

Fitzgerald's prose is, frankly, showstopping. It moves with the rhythm of jazz—syncopated, ornate, occasionally overwrought, but always musical. Descriptions of Gatsby's parties, his "colored silk" shirts spread in a heap before Daisy, the green light at the end of dock, the "valley of ashes" between Manhattan and West Egg—these are images that lodge in the reader's mind and refuse to leave. The novel is narrated by Nick Carraway, a relatively restrained observer, and Fitzgerald wisely uses his perspective as a kind of moral lens. Nick's famous closing line about "beating on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past" works precisely because we've spent the whole book watching him watch.

**Characters**

Gatsby is, of course, the great enigma. Is he a romantic, a deluded fantasist, a criminal, or all three? Fitzgerald lets the reader assemble the man in fragments, and the effect is powerful. Daisy Buchanan is the novel's most debated figure—vulnerable and complicit in equal measure, a beautiful hollow at the center of a web of entitlement. Tom Buchanan is coarse and predatory, and Jordan Baker is coolly amoral. None of them are truly "good," which gives the novel its moral complexity. The tragedy isn't that a good man is destroyed by bad people; it's that everyone, including Gatsby, has participated in a system that was rotten from the start.

**Themes**

The class divide between "old money" East Egg and "new money" West Egg is the novel's structural spine. Fitzgerald argues, with devastating clarity, that wealth in America does not erase social hierarchy; it merely redraws the boundaries. Gatsby can buy the mansion across the bay, but he can never buy a seat at the Buchanan table. The "American Dream" of upward mobility through pure will is exposed as a seductive lie, and the green light across the water becomes a symbol not of hope, but of something perpetually, painfully out of reach.

**What Could Be Critiqued**

For modern readers, the novel's treatment of women is uneven. Daisy and Jordan are largely objects to be gazed at and judged by the men around them, and their interiority is thin by comparison to Gatsby's mythologized longing. Some readers also find the final chapters—particularly the car crash and its aftermath—rushed, as if Fitzgerald is in a hurry to deliver his thesis. And the 1920s setting, while vividly rendered, occasionally tips into a kind of period postcard.

**Final Verdict**

These are minor quibbles against a novel of extraordinary density and beauty. *The Great Gatsby* is under 100 pages of story, yet it operates on so many levels—romantic, social, economic, spiritual—that it rewards rereading decades apart. It is a book that asks whether the life we construct to win the people we love is worth the person we have to become in the process.

Ninety-nine years on, it remains as urgent and as aching as the day it was published. A masterpiece, full stop.

# The Light in the Fog

Every night, the keeper climbed the stairs. One hundred and twelve of them. He counted every single one, the way he had counted them for twenty-three years.

One. Two. Three. Four.

His shoes made a soft, steady rhythm on the stone. *Tap. Tap. Tap. Tap.* Up, up, up, and then the big brass lamp at the top would spin, and the dark sea would catch the light, and the boats would be safe.

It was a good life. A quiet life.

But one night, when he turned the lamp on just after sunset, the fog rolled in. Thick as wool. Heavy as a held breath. The light went out the moment it was born, swallowed whole by the gray.

The keeper wiped the lens. He oiled the gears. He turned the wheel by hand, and the beam cut a small, thin slice through the mist. Not far. Just a few yards. Just enough to see the water.

And there, rocking gently in the fog, was a boat. Small. Wooden. Just the right size for two.

He did not see two. He saw one. A little girl, maybe eight, with a yellow coat and bare feet, sitting very still in the center of the boat. Her eyes were wide. She was not crying. She was not calling out. She was just looking up at the lighthouse, as if she had been waiting a very long time to be seen.

The keeper set down his lamp oil. He went back down the stairs. One hundred and twelve. He counted every single one.

He opened the heavy iron door. The fog rushed in like a cold hand over his face. He waded out to the small boat, splashing, steadying his feet on the rocks.

He knelt down. The girl looked up at him.

"Are you lost?" he asked.

She shook her head. Then she nodded. Then she said, very softly, "I lost my way. I lost it a long time ago."

The keeper smiled. He pulled off his wool coat and wrapped it around her shoulders. Then he took her small, bare hand in his rough, warm one, and he walked her back up the shore.

He did not ask where she was from. He did not ask how she had gotten to the water. Some questions are too big for the fog.

He just brought her inside, and he made her tea, and he put a fire in the hearth. And when the fog finally lifted, the next morning, the sea was empty.

There was no boat. There was no girl.

Just the yellow coat, folded neatly on the chair by the fire, and a single small footprint in the ash.

The keeper looked at it for a long time. Then he smiled, and he swept the ash clean, and he went back up the stairs.

One hundred and twelve.

He counted every single one.
