# The Call

The phone sat on the kitchen counter. It had been there for six days.

Mara wiped the table around it. She wiped it again. She wiped it a third time, as if the phone might dissolve into the wood grain and simply stop existing.

It didn't. It just sat there, screen dark, her mother's name saved in the little address book under the word *Mom*.

She made coffee. She drank it. She put the cup in the sink. She made more.

By the second pot, she could feel it in her chest. That old, tight knot. The one that meant *you said the wrong thing, and now you don't know how to say the right thing after.*

It had been a Saturday in October. A small argument. Nothing about money or health or time. Just a sentence. *You don't have to call every day, Mom. I'm fine.*

Her mother hadn't said anything after that. She'd just let the silence fill the phone. And then, two days later, she'd called back and said, "Okay. I'll stop." And hung up.

Six days.

Mara set her hands flat on the counter. She breathed in. She breathed out.

She picked up the phone.

"Mom?"

A pause. Then, quieter than she expected: "Hey, baby."

"Hey."

Another pause. The kind that doesn't need filling.

"I made too many cookies," her mother said.

Mara laughed. A real one, short and surprised. "How many?"

"Two batches. I don't know why. I was just... I don't know. I was just doing it."

"I want to come over," Mara said. "Sunday. I'll bring the good plates. The ones with the chipped blue rim."

"You can bring those plates. I've been saving them. I don't know why."

They talked for a while. Not about the Saturday. Not about the knot or the six days or the coffee or the wiping. They talked about the neighbor's new dog. They talked about the tomato plants in the back yard, the ones that were late and stubborn. They talked about nothing, and it was enough.

When they hung up, Mara set the phone back on the counter.

She didn't wipe around it this time.

She just poured a little more coffee, sat down at the table, and watched the afternoon light move across the floor, slow and warm and sure.

And that was fine. That was enough.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that feels both perfectly of its time and completely timeless. A story about 1920s Long Island parties, it is, at its core, a elegy for an entire way of seeing the world.

## The Story

Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from Minnesota, rents a small house on Long Island next to the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby. Through his new neighbor's lavish weekend parties, Nick becomes drawn into the orbit of Gatsby's obsession: winning back Daisy Buchanan, his former lover now married to the brutish, wealthy Tom. What follows is a summer of glittering excess that cracks open to reveal something rotten underneath.

## What Makes It Work

Fitzgerald's prose is the first thing that arrests you. It's lyrical without being purple, precise without being cold. The famous opening line—"In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since"—sets a reflective, slightly wry tone that carries the whole book. The imagery is unforgettable: the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the "valley of ashes," the eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg peering down from a billboard like a god who has stopped caring.

The novel's architecture is quietly brilliant. Every element is a symbol, but Fitzgerald never hammers the point home. The parties are decay. The clothes are armor. The past is a house you can renovate but never rebuild. And the American Dream—the belief that money and willfulness can remake you, can buy you back a moment of time—turns out to be precisely the thing that destroys Gatsby. He doesn't fail because he isn't rich enough. He fails because the dream he's chasing was always a projection, a ghost he constructed out of a green light and a name.

Fitzgerald is also surprisingly unsentimental. Gatsby is magnetic, but he is also a fraud, a self-invented man who built his identity on a lie. Daisy is not a villain, but she is careless—she "smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into her money." The book refuses to let you simply adore its protagonist, and that makes the tragedy land harder.

## Minor Reservations

If one faults the novel, it's that the pacing in the middle can feel slightly episodic, and some modern readers may find Nick's occasional moralizing a touch heavy-handed. A few of the supporting characters (Jordan, Meyer Wolfsheim) feel more like types than people. But these are small niggles in an otherwise seamless construction.

## The Final Line

You don't forget it. *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."* After a story about a man who literally tried to repeat the past, that final image of relentless, futile forward motion hits with the force of a bell. It reframes everything before it.

## Who Should Read It

It's a book that rewards rereading at different ages. Read it at sixteen and you get a sleek, tragic romance set against sparkling parties. Read it at thirty and you start seeing the class anxiety, the hollowness of performance, the way wealth turns every relationship into a transaction. Read it again later and you notice how every sentence is doing double work.

*The Great Gatsby* is a slim book—under 200 pages—and that is one of its greatest strengths. Nothing is wasted. Every word earns its place. It is, deservedly, a pillar of the American literary canon, not because it's difficult, but because it is *clear*, and because it makes you feel, in a handful of short chapters, the full weight of a dream's collapse.

Highly recommended. Then reread it.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald

**Published 1925 | 180 pages**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is the kind of novel that has been so thoroughly mythologized—set in a hundred film adaptations, assigned in ten thousand classrooms, dissected in a million essays—that encountering it for the first time as an adult carries a strange risk. You know the green light. You know the yellow car. You know how it ends. And yet, page by page, the book keeps finding new reasons to be devastating.

**The Story in Brief**

Nick Carraway, a young writer from the Midwest, rents a modest cottage on Long Island in the summer of 1922. Next door lives Jay Gatsby, an enigmatic millionaire who throws legendary parties and watches a single green light across the water. Gatsby's obsession, as Nick gradually learns, is Daisy Buchanan, his former love, now married to the brutish and careless Tom. The novel traces one summer's worth of parties, affairs, betrayals, and a final, catastrophic convergence on a hot, humid afternoon.

**What Works Brilliantly**

Fitzgerald's prose is the first thing that seizes you. It is lush, precise, and occasionally overwrought in the best way—saturated with the excess of the Jazz Age even as it quietly judges it. The famous closing line—"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"—lands with the weight of a small, perfect eulogy for an entire generation. The novel is structurally tight. Eighty-something years of accumulated cultural commentary have not worn down its architecture: Nick's retrospective narration, the slow unraveling of Gatsby's identity, the way the past keeps intruding on the present.

**Themes That Still Resonate**

At its center, the book is a meditation on the American Dream—not the aspirational version, but the transactional one. Gatsby builds his entire life around a single, idealized woman, and the novel asks whether the dream was ever about Daisy at all, or whether she was merely the most visible symbol of a future that was already unreachable. The novel is also a sharp class portrait. The "old money" Buchanans move through the world as if it were a closed room they alone were permitted to enter, and their casual cruelty is presented not as villainy but as inherited entitlement. In 2025, that distinction still feels uncomfortably familiar.

**A Few Honest Quibbles**

The novel's 180-page length means it moves quickly, and some readers (this reviewer included, on a first pass) find the back half—particularly the resolution—rushed. The characters beyond Gatsby and Daisy are sketched rather than drawn; Tom is a well-worn archetype of privilege, and Jordan Baker's voice feels thin. The gender politics, even for 1925, are uneven: Daisy is more a symbol of unattainability than a fully realized person, and the novel is, despite its apparent sympathy, ultimately a story told by and for a man about what a woman meant to him.

**Verdict**

*The Great Gatsby* is not a perfect book. But it is a *major* one—a novel that earned its place in the American canon not through technical innovation but through the sheer emotional and aesthetic density of its language. It is a book about how the past eats the present, how money cannot buy meaning, and how we all, in some small way, stand on a dock watching a light we cannot reach. Read it young and you'll feel the glitter. Read it at thirty, forty, fifty, and you'll feel the ache underneath.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* remains one of those rare novels that feels both perfectly of its time and endlessly contemporary. Nearly a century after its publication, its exploration of desire, class, and the seductive lie of reinvention still cuts with an almost uncomfortable precision.

## The Story

Narrated by the reserved, watchful Nick Carraway, the novel follows the enigmatic Jay Gatsby, a self-made millionaire who throws lavish parties in his West Egg mansion solely to attract the attention of his old flame, Daisy Buchanan, now married to the brutish old-money Tom. Set in the heady summer of 1922 along the Long Island Sound, the book is less a plot-driven narrative than a slow, glittering unraveling—a fever dream of excess that the reader senses, from the first page, is built to shatter.

## The Prose

Fitzgerald writes here in a style that is almost musical. Sentences build and swell, laden with imagery that operates on multiple levels: the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the rotting Valley of Ashes, the enormous painted eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg watching over the waste. The prose is lush without being overwrought, romantic without losing its critical edge. The famous final line—*"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"*—has earned its place in the pantheon of American endings, and it lands because the entire novel has been building toward that sense of futility.

## Themes

At its core, Gatsby is a study in the American Dream curdling. Gatsby believes he can construct a future by erasing his past, that enough wealth and spectacle can win back a lost moment. Fitzgerald is generous to Gatsby's idealism but merciless toward the social machinery that makes it impossible. The novel interrogates the hollow center of the Jazz Age—the way "old money" and "new money" perform a theater of generosity while being fundamentally incapable of empathy. Daisy is often read as the weakest link in the cast, and in one sense she is: she is a beautiful, privileged person who causes enormous harm and faces zero consequences. But Fitzgerald isn't really writing *about* Daisy; he's writing about what Daisy *represents* to a man who has decided she is the only real thing in a world of facades.

## What Holds Up, What Doesn't

The novel is not without its seams. Jordan Baker feels underdeveloped. The last quarter, once the machinery of tragedy engages, moves quickly and can feel slightly contrived—Nick's sudden moral awakening is the kind of thing a more skeptical reader might flag. The 1920s backdrop, while well-rendered, is the era rather than the argument; the book's power is thematic and emotional rather than historically documentary.

But these are minor notes in an otherwise extraordinary achievement. The novel's structure—telling the past through a narrator who is also being changed by what he witnesses—gives the whole story a ghostly, elegiac quality. You are always slightly behind Gatsby, slightly outside the party, looking in. And that distance is the point.

## Final Word

*The Great Gatsby* is a small book—under 200 pages in most editions—but it is dense with feeling. It rewards rereading: the details that seemed decorative on a first pass become load-bearing on a second. It is a novel about the gap between what we want and what is actually possible, wrapped in silk and jazz and champagne foam. It is, in the end, a love story and a murder story and a class analysis and a warning, all at once, and it accomplishes all four in remarkably few pages.

It is, simply, a great American novel, and it has earned that status not by accident but by the sheer craftsmanship of its construction.

---
*Highly recommended for readers who appreciate lyrical prose, layered symbolism, and the quiet devastation of a well-earned tragedy.*

```python
import unittest

def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
    if not lst:

    result = [lst[0]]

class TestRemoveAdjacentDuplicates(unittest.TestCase):

        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7]), [5, 6, 7])
    
    def test_multiple_duplicates(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

```

This approach runs in **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space, since each element is visited exactly once and we build a new list of at most the same length as the input.

```python
def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
```

```python
import unittest

def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
    result = []
    for num in lst:
        if not result or num != result[-1]:
            result.append(num)
    return result

class TestRemoveAdjacentDuplicates(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_basic_functionality(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]), [1, 2, 3, 4])
    
    def test_repeated_elements(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7]), [5, 6, 7])
    
    def test_multiple_duplicates(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

**How it works:**

The function iterates through each element in the list and appends it to the `result` list only if:
- `result` is empty (first element), **or**
- the current number differs from the last element already in `result`

This effectively collapses any run of consecutive identical values into a single occurrence while preserving the order of all other elements.

**Walkthrough with `[1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]`:**

| Step | `num` | `result` before | Action | `result` after |
|------|-------|----------------|--------|----------------|

| 2 | 2 | `[1]` | append (2≠1) | `[1, 2]` |
| 3 | 2 | `[1, 2]` | skip (2==2) | `[1, 2]` |
| 4 | 3 | `[1, 2]` | append (3≠2) | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| 5 | 3 | `[1, 2, 3]` | skip (3==3) | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| 6 | 3 | `[1, 2, 3]` | skip (3==3) | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| 7 | 4 | `[1, 2, 3]` | append (4≠3) | `[1, 2, 3, 4]` |

The time complexity is **O(n)** and space complexity is **O(n)** in the worst case (no duplicates).

# The Great Gatsby – F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

There are books you read as a young person that lodge in your mind as a shape or a feeling, and then books you reread at twenty-five, thirty-five, and fifty that seem to have quietly rearranged themselves while you weren't looking. *The Great Gatsby* belongs emphatically to the second category. Fitzgerald published it in 1925 at twenty-eight, and it has spent nearly a century earning its place as one of the most reread, most assigned, most argued-over novels in the American canon. And the reason it endures isn't simply its fame. The book is, on its surface, about a dead man's party. But the dead man is a mirror.

Fitzgerald's prose is the first thing that stops you. It is not merely "good" for its era; it is genuinely, almost dangerously musical. Sentences swing with a jazz-era syncopation, piling up images of silk and champagne and moonlight until the air in the room feels thick with them, and then a line will cut short—dry, blunt, devastating—and you realize you've been swept along and hadn't noticed. The final image of Gatsby's "blue lights" retreating into the distance against the current of the river is one of the most quietly annihilating endings in twentieth-century fiction, and it works because Fitzgerald has spent the whole book teaching your ear to trust rhythm.

Structurally, the novel is lean and disciplined, told in first person by Nick Carraway, who insists he is merely "reserve[d] all judgments" while simultaneously serving as the most selective, most emotionally invested narrator in the book. That tension is the engine of the story. We never get Gatsby's full history in a clean, authorial voice; we get fragments, rumors, and a final confession that may be embellished. We don't get Daisy's interiority. We get the *idea* of Daisy—her voice "full of money," her green light across the bay—and Fitzgerald is clearly, deliberately interested in the gap between a person and the fantasy projected onto them. Gatsby doesn't love Daisy. Gatsby loves the *Daisy*, the one who represents a past that can be bought back with enough wealth, enough parties, enough reinvention. And that distinction is the novel's true subject, far more than "love in the Jazz Age."

The class question is sharper than a lot of casual readings allow. The Buchanans—Tom and Daisy—aren't portrayed as villains so much as as *inherited* people, unbothered by the wreckage they leave behind, "careless people" who smash things and let other people clean it up. Nick, who considers himself above them, is only above them because he has a college degree and a mild moral discomfort. The novel is deeply suspicious of the American idea that you can reinvent yourself through will and wealth, and it is equally suspicious of the old-money world that treats that reinvention as a quaint, slightly offensive spectacle.

A small, honest critique: the women in the novel are, by design, somewhat flattened. Daisy and Jordan exist largely as signals—of aspiration, of carelessness, of a world that treats people as accessories. You can read that as Fitzgerald's limitation or as Fitzgerald's point, and the book is arguably more interesting if you let it be both.

If you're reading it for the first time and expecting a story about a millionaire and a lost love, you'll be underwhelmed. Read it, instead, as a short, beautifully constructed elegy for the idea that the past is a place you can drive back to. It is only about ninety pages. You can read it in an evening. And in the morning, it will still be humming.

**★★★★★**

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★½**

At its surface, *The Great Gatsby* is a summer story set on the East and West Egg shores of Long Island in 1922. At its core, it is a elegy—haunting, precise, and devastating in its quietness—for a country that mistook excess for meaning.

Fitzgerald, then in his mid-twenties, wrote the novel with a lyricism that still feels almost startling. His sentences don't merely describe; they shimmer. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the "valley of ashes" between the eggs and the city, the rotting billboard of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg's eyes gazing down on the moral wasteland below—these are not metaphors tacked on after the fact. They grow organically from the narrative, becoming as real to the reader as the characters themselves. The prose is so carefully composed that re-reading the final paragraphs after knowing the ending changes the texture of every line before them.

The novel's structure is deceptively simple. Nick Carraway, a young Midwest writer, rents a cottage next to the enigmatic millionaire Jay Gatsby and is swept into the orbit of his next-door neighbors, the carelessly aristocratic Tom and Daisy Buchanan. Gatsby's legendary parties, his impossible devotion to a woman he lost five years ago, and the slow unraveling of a love affair carried out in secret—these build toward a climax that is brief, violent, and almost anticlimactic in its bluntness.

What elevates the book beyond a period romance is its structural honesty. Nick is an unreliable narrator not because he lies, but because he genuinely cannot see what is in front of him. He calls Gatsby a fraud, admires him, pities him, and justifies him in the same breath. The reader is forced to do the same. Fitzgerald is not interested in telling us whether Gatsby is a hero or a fool; he is interested in the *performance* of both, and the way the American Dream manufactures such performances at scale.

The book's central tension—between past and present, between what is and what might be—is handled with remarkable patience. Gatsby's famous line about "recollecting the past" isn't just a character tic; it's the novel's thesis. The Jazz Age, that brief fever dream of postwar optimism, becomes less a celebration and more a warning. The parties are empty. The wealth is borrowed. The love is a reconstruction, not a revival.

If I have a minor reservation, it is that the secondary characters—particularly Jordan Baker and Tom Buchanan—feel somewhat underdeveloped compared to the luminous, almost mythic quality Fitzgerald gives to Gatsby and Daisy. Tom is a blunt instrument of class cruelty, effective but not deeply rendered. The novel is, in a sense, a two-character study dressed as an ensemble, and that's fine, but it does mean the supporting cast sometimes reads as function rather than person.

Still, that limitation is outweighed by the book's emotional architecture. The final image of Gatsby's boats "beating out the current toward a happy shore" is one of the most quietly heartbreaking sentences in American literature, and it lands precisely because Fitzgerald has spent the entire novel teaching us not to believe in happy shores—while making us want to anyway.

**Who should read it:** Anyone who has ever looked back at a period of their life and realized they were performing a version of it for an audience that no longer exists. Students of American literature, obviously. And anyone who wants to understand why the phrase "old money" still carries weight a century after Fitzgerald pinned it to a novel about a war veteran who laundered bootlegger cash in a purple suit.

It is a slim book—roughly 180 pages. It does not want to be a big, sprawling experience. It wants to be a single, perfectly struck note that keeps humming in your chest for weeks afterward.

And it does. Every time.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

There are novels that entertain you, and then there are novels that rearrange something in your chest and leave it slightly different afterward. *The Great Gatsby* is the latter, and nearly a century after its publication, it still lands with an almost uncomfortable force.

## The Surface Story

On the surface, it's a slim, sharp novel. Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner, moves to West Egg, Long Island, for a summer in 1922. He becomes the reluctant neighbor of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby—a self-made millionaire who throws spectacular parties for hundreds but seems to want only one thing: to recapture the love of his old flame, Daisy Buchanan, who now lives across the bay with her shallow, careless husband Tom. What follows is a summer of champagne, infidelity, and a slow, glittering unraveling that ends in a way that still feels too cruel.

## What Makes It Endure

The genius of the book isn't the plot. It's the *mood*. Fitzgerald writes the Jazz Age not as a postcard but as a fever dream—lavish, loud, and deeply hollow. The parties at Gatsby's mansion are rendered with such sensory excess that you can practically hear the orchestras and smell the spilled gin, and yet the writing makes you feel the profound loneliness at the center of the noise.

Fitzgerald's prose is lyrical to a fault, and that's the point. Lines like "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past" become lodged in your memory and haunt you in contexts the author never intended. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock functions as one of the most economical symbols in American literature: hope, desire, the future that recedes the moment you reach for it.

## The Deeper Argument

What elevates the novel above a period piece is its indictment. Fitzgerald is writing a eulogy for a version of the American Dream that promised anyone could reinvent themselves through will and wealth—and showing how that promise curdles into obsession, class anxiety, and moral rot. Gatsby is not a villain; he's a man who built an entire identity around a memory, and the novel is generous and ruthless toward him in equal measure. The "old money" characters (Daisy, Tom) are less interesting as people but more damning as a system, because they can afford to be careless in ways the self-made man never can.

## A Few Honest Caveats

The novel isn't perfect. Daisy is the book's weakest character, and modern readers may find her frustrating—though that frustration is, arguably, the point, since the whole tragedy rests on Gatsby's inability to see her as a person rather than a symbol. The 1920s social landscape, while vivid, can feel slightly stylized, like a painting rather than a photograph. And Nick, as narrator, is more charming than he has any right to be; he witnesses almost every catastrophe and emerges merely "worn out and dirty with grief."

## The Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is a novel about the impossibility of going backward, about the way wealth can make people beautiful and hollow in the same gesture, and about the stories we tell ourselves to make the past bearable. It's 180 pages long, you can read it in a single afternoon, and it will follow you for days. If you haven't read it, the threshold is almost insulting. If you have, it rewards a reread at every stage of life, because you are always a different kind of Gatsby, staring at a different green light.

**Rating: 5/5.** A masterpiece that has aged not into a classic-but-dusty, but into a book that still stings.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**★★★★★**

Few novels manage to be simultaneously a love story, a social critique, a meditation on time, and a quiet elegy for a nation in the making—and do so in fewer than 180 pages. *The Great Gatsby* is that rare book.

## The Story

Told by the reserved, observant Nick Carraway in the summer of 1922, the novel follows his neighbor, the enigmatic millionaire Jay Gatsby, who throws legendary parties in his West Egg mansion and lives his entire life reaching toward a green light across the water—the light of Daisy Buchanan's dock. Daisy, married to the bruteish Tom, is the object of Gatsby's devotion. What unfolds between these characters is less a romance than a collision of illusions, each person wearing a performance of success while quietly rotting underneath.

## What Works

Fitzgerald's prose is the book's first and most immediate seduction. It is lyrical without being precious, saturated with color and sound, and carries a musicality that makes even descriptions of cocktail parties feel like jazz. The famous final line—*"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"*—has earned its status as one of literature's great closings because it earns it. The novel builds toward that line the way a symphony builds toward a final chord.

The theme of the American Dream is handled with extraordinary subtlety. Gatsby doesn't fail because he's poor; he fails because he believes the past can be reconstructed, that wealth can buy back lost time, that if he simply replicates the right gestures, Daisy will love him the way she did five years ago. Fitzgerald shows us the dream's machinery without ever raising his voice in criticism. That restraint is what makes the book devastating.

Nick as narrator is a masterstroke. He claims to be "one of the few honest people" he's ever known, yet we watch him judge, participate, and ultimately fail to act. He is the perfect unreliable lens: close enough to understand, distant enough to narrate.

## What Doesn't (or Could Challenge)

The book is short and, to a modern reader, its pacing can feel uneven. The central romance is largely told through Gatsby's self-narration in a single chapter rather than dramatized in real time, which some readers find emotionally distant. Women in the novel—Daisy, Jordan, Myrtle—are often flattened into symbols of desire or betrayal, and the 1925 setting doesn't fully excuse how thin their interiority is. Fitzgerald was writing a novel about men and their myths; the women are the landscape those myths are projected onto.

Also, if you're expecting a plot-driven thriller, the "mystery" of Gatsby's past resolves in a single, relatively straightforward revelation. The book's power is atmospheric and thematic, not structural.

## Who Should Read It

If you've never read it: it is a short, beautiful, emotionally gutting book, and you don't need a literature degree to be moved by it. If you read it in high school and found it dull: give it another try in your twenties or thirties. The book rewards a reader who has their own small experience of longing, of a version of life you can't quite get back.

## Final Word

*The Great Gatsby* is not a perfect novel, but it is an essential one. It captures the specific, glittering emptiness of the Jazz Age and, in doing so, captures something permanent about human nature: the way we build entire lives around a single, unattainable image, and call it hope. Ninety-plus years later, the party is over, the lights are off, and the green light is still burning.

**Recommended for:** fans of lyrical prose, readers of the American canon, anyone who has ever looked at a life they almost had and wondered why they couldn't just walk back through the door.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald

**Published:** 1925 | **Genre:** Fiction / American Literature

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is a novel that reads less like a story about one man's tragedy and more like a elegy for an entire era—specifically, the gilded, hedonistic Jazz Age of the 1920s. At just over 180 pages, it's a deceptively short book that rewards repeated reading, each pass revealing new layers beneath its shimmering prose.

## The Story

Narrator Nick Carraway, a young writer from the Midwest, rents a modest house on Long Island next to the colossal, legendary mansion of Jay Gatsby. Nick is drawn into the orbit of Gatsby's extravagant parties and, through his cousin's wife Daisy Buchanan, the old-money world of the "East Egg." What unfolds is a story of obsession, reinvention, and a love that was perhaps never possible—told with the quiet, unreliable distance of a man looking back on events that still haunt him.

## What Works

**Fitzgerald's prose is the book's greatest engine.** He writes with a lyricism that borders on the operatic without ever feeling overwrought. The final image of Gatsby's eyes reaching "toward that green light" on the far shore of Daisy's dock is one of the most recognizable passages in American literature, and it earns its fame. The writing is sensory, musical, and precise—Fitzgerald was clearly a craftsman, not just a poet.

**The theme of the American Dream is handled with genuine ambiguity.** Gatsby isn't a simple rags-to-riches success story; he's a man who builds an entire identity around a single woman's memory and discovers, too late, that the past cannot be repurchased. The "old money" Buchanans expose the hollowness beneath the glitter. Fitzgerald doesn't tell you what to think; he shows you a society that is spectacular, cruel, and fundamentally amoral, and lets the rot seep in.

**Nick as narrator is a brilliant, unsettling choice.** He claims to be "one of the few honest people" he has ever known, yet his narration is full of contradictions, omissions, and self-justification. We are never fully certain where Nick's sympathy ends and his complicity begins. This narrative instability makes the novel feel more honest than a straightforward telling could.

## What Might Not Work

The book is very much a product of its 1925 moment. Readers unfamiliar with the 1920s—speakeasies, the rigid class geography of East Egg/West Egg, the particular social codes of the era—may find the world-building a little thin. Fitzgerald assumes you already understand the world he's satirizing.

Some modern readers also find the characters, particularly Daisy, frustratingly underdeveloped as individuals. She is less a person than a symbol—warm, golden, slightly vapid, and deeply damaging. This is clearly intentional, but it can feel like a shortcut if you're looking for a psychologically round character study.

## Who Should Read It

It's a standard of the American high-school and university canon for good reason. It's the ideal "short but dense" novel for a book club, a summer reread, or a first exposure to classic American fiction. It also pairs beautifully with Fitzgerald's *The Beautiful and Damned* and, for a different flavor of Jazz Age, with Erskine Caldwell's work or Dos Passos's *Manhattan Transfer*.

## Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is a small, perfect book. It is not the longest, most complex, or most structurally daring novel of the 20th century, but it is arguably one of the most *perfectly made*—every image, every line of dialogue, every turn of the plot seems to have been placed with the precision of a jeweler setting stones. A century after publication, the green light still glows, and the parties still feel a little too loud, a little too brief.

**Rating: 4.5 / 5**

# The Great Gatsby – F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

Few novels have become as synonymous with a single sentence as *The Great Gatsby* does with Nick Carraway's final, aching line: *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."* It's a line you memorize in high school and then, years later, in the quiet of a late-night reread, suddenly *feel*. Fitzgerald's masterpiece remains as radiant and as devastating as the night it was written.

At its center is Jay Gatsby, a self-made millionaire who throws legendary parties on his West Egg mansion, all while watching across the bay at a single green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock. The story is told by Nick, a young bondsman from the Midwest, and it unfolds over a single sweltering summer in 1922 Long Island. It's a story about obsession, class, and the American Dream's hollow center—about a man who can reinvent his wealth but never his past.

What makes the book endure is Fitzgerald's prose. He writes with the precision of a jazz musician: syncopated, lush, full of rhythm. Sentences swing and then pivot. His descriptions of the parties—the "orchestra playing to the lawn and trees," the "mountains of champagne"—are almost hallucinatory. And yet his restraint is remarkable. He never over-explains Gatsby. We piece him together like Nick does, in fragments, and the mystery becomes part of the architecture.

Thematically, the novel operates on several registers simultaneously. It's a critique of the Jazz Age's moral emptiness—of a society so drunk on new money and old privilege that it can't even stop to notice a man rotting on the side of a road. It's a love story, though one whose love is more a projection, a "colossal vitality of his illusion." And it's a meditation on time: Gatsby's entire project is to make the clock run backward, to repeat a summer in Louisville five years prior. The green light is beautiful precisely because it recedes as you approach it.

The characters are drawn with sharp, almost cruel economy. Daisy's voice is "full of money," and Fitzgerald makes you understand both why that's seductive and why it's monstrous. Tom is a physical, blundering force of old-money entitlement. Jordan Baker is cool and slightly hollow, mirroring the era's surface glamour. Nick, our narrator, is positioned as "one of the few honest people," but Fitzgerald is too clever to let him off the hook—he's complicit, voyeuristic, and ultimately as lost as everyone else.

If the book has a limitation, it's a narrow one: the gender politics feel dated. Daisy and Jordan are largely defined by their relationship to men and to desire, and the novel's "love story" framing can feel, from a 2025 vantage point, a bit too neatly arranged around a man's fantasy. But this is a criticism of its era as much as of Fitzgerald, and it doesn't diminish the structural or linguistic brilliance.

*The Great Gatsby* is not a long book. You can read it in an evening. But it rewards the slow reread—the second pass where you notice how the color symbolism threads through every chapter, how the "valley of ashes" sits literally and morally between East and West Egg, how the ending's "eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg" on their fading billboard are watching everything and no one.

It is, in the end, a novel about the gap between what we build and what we actually are. Gatsby built a world of impossible light and threw parties for hundreds, all to reach one woman across a bay. He got a swimming pool, a gun, and a funeral that almost no one attended. Fitzgerald understood that the American Dream is a beautiful, specific kind of grief.

Read it. Keep it on your shelf. You will need to go back to it.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★½**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that has transcended its moment in history to become something almost elemental—a story about the seduction of the American dream, the violence of memory, and the way we construct the people we love from fragments of who they were. It is, at its heart, a love story. But it is also a moral autopsy of a civilization.

## The Story, in Brief

We meet Gatsby not as he is, but as a legend: the mysterious host of the most magnificent parties on West Egg, Long Island, in the summer of 1922. His narrator, the unremarkable and slightly adrift Nick Carraway, is pulled into Gatsby's orbit through a neighborly introduction and quickly discovers that every glittering evening is a performance staged for a single audience of one—Daisy Buchanan, Nick's cousin, married to the brutish old money of Tom Buchanan. What unfolds is a triangulation of desire, class, and self-deception that ends, as you probably know, in catastrophe on a hot July evening.

## What Makes It Work

Fitzgerald's prose is the first thing that stops you. Lines like *"Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us"* aren't just famous; they earn their fame. The novel has a lyrical, almost musical quality without ever becoming purple. The summer heat, the champagne, the long stretches of dark water separating the Eggs from the city—all of it is rendered with a sensory richness that makes the 1920s feel less like a period piece and more like a place you've been to in a dream.

The structure is deceptively simple. By filtering everything through Nick—intelligent but ultimately complicit, observant but not omniscient—Fitzgerald gains the distance to judge his characters while staying intimate enough to make us *care* about them. We don't fully trust Nick, which makes the story more honest than it would be otherwise.

The thematic architecture is tight. Class (old vs. new money, the valley of ashes vs. the glittering houses), the impossibility of recapturing the past ("Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!"), the hollowness of wealth, the cruelty of privilege—these threads are woven so naturally into the plot that the novel never feels preachy. Gatsby isn't a symbol; he's a specific, flawed, genuinely moving person, and that's what gives the broader commentary its weight.

## Where It Stumbles

To be fair, *Gatsby* is not without its rough edges. Some readers find Nick's narration a bit too self-congratulatory, too conveniently positioned as the "one of the few honest people" he's ever known. The gender dynamics are, frankly, of their era: Daisy is less a fully realized person than a symbol of beauty, fragility, and the things Gatsby wants to possess, and the women in the novel largely orbit the men's ambitions. Modern readers may also find the social world of the book—the parties, the cars, the casual brutality of the wealthy—more alienating than the novel perhaps intends, which can make the emotional core harder to land.

And yes, the ending is abrupt. The final images—Gatsby's body on the neglected pool, the sparse funeral, Nick's disgusted departure to the Midwest—hit with the force of a door slamming. Whether that's a structural strength or a slight depends on your temperament. I lean toward strength, but I understand the critique.

## Who Should Read It (and When)

If you've only read it in high school and walked away feeling it was "fine but not great," read it again as an adult, preferably in the summer, preferably near water. The book rewards a second (and third) reading with a sophistication that a first pass, often done under the pressure of an essay deadline, can miss. It's a book about memory and the stories we tell ourselves, and you need some of your own to fully feel its pull.

## The Bottom Line

*The Great Gatsby* is not the perfect novel. But it is one of the most beautifully written, thematically resonant, and emotionally devastating short novels in the American canon. At barely 180 pages, it packs in a full exploration of desire, class, illusion, and loss with a precision and lyricism that very few authors have managed to replicate. Eighty-plus years on, the green light is still receding. And it still gets you.

**Recommended for:** Readers of literary fiction, fans of lyrical prose, anyone who has ever tried to reconstruct a past relationship and discovered the past was never what you thought it was.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald

**Published 1925 | ~180 pages**

At roughly 180 pages, *The Great Gatsby* is deceptively compact for a novel that has spent nearly a century at the center of the American literary conversation. Fitzgerald writes about the summer of 1922—the brief, giddy breath after the Great War—and in doing so, constructs what may be the most precise elegy to a vanished optimism ever committed to paper.

The structure is clean and effective. Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who has moved to West Egg, Long Island, narrates the story of his neighbor, the enigmatic and fabulously wealthy Jay Gatsby, who throws legendary parties and seems to exist in a state of perpetual, aching orientation toward the green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock. The plot moves quickly—Gatsby's origins, his improbable rise, his obsessive courtship of a married woman, and the catastrophic evening that unravels everything. It reads almost like a novella in its pacing, and that brevity is part of its power. You are in and out of the story in an afternoon, and by the time you close the book, the summer is already gone.

What elevates the novel above a simple period romance is Fitzgerald's prose. It is lyrical without being self-indulgent, saturated with sensory detail—the smell of warm pavement, the sound of a jazz band playing on a hot lawn, the "blue gardens" where "guests came and went as if they were crawling through the windows of his vast house." The language itself performs the novel's central tension: Gatsby's world is dressed in the most exquisite, almost overwrought language, and that very excess is a lie. The prose is beautiful the way a diamond is beautiful—hard, cold, and ultimately hollow.

The characters are less individually deep than they are emblematic, and that is both the novel's greatest strength and its most common criticism. Gatsby is not a fully realized person so much as a projection—a "colossal vitalit[y]" that Nick admires from a safe distance. Daisy is a voice, a perfume, a green light. Tom is a bludgeon. They function more as symbols of class, gender, and moral cowardice than as people you'd recognize at a dinner party. For some readers, this will feel thin. For me, it feels right. Fitzgerald is not writing character studies; he is writing a parable, and the parable works because the symbols are vivid enough to stand in for the people.

Where the book can feel slightly strained is in its treatment of its own moral architecture. Nick's narration is supposed to be a kind of ethical judgment—his final lines about "boats against the current" are famously resonant—but the narrator himself is somewhat self-congratulatory, positioning his own restraint as virtue while the reader is left unsure whether Gatsby's delusion was noble or merely pathological. Fitzgerald gestures at this ambiguity without fully resolving it, which is fair, but the final paragraph's grandeur tips, just slightly, toward sentimentality.

That said, the question of whether Gatsby was a tragic hero or a fool is the novel's engine, and it doesn't need to be answered. The book asks you to hold both truths at once: that the dream is beautiful *and* that it is a lie, and that neither cancels the other.

**Bottom line:** If you haven't read *The Great Gatsby*, it's short enough to finish in an evening and rich enough to reward a second, third, or fifth reading. It is a novel about the specific American failure to let the past go, and the specific American compulsion to rebuild the past as a fantasy. A century later, it still reads with an unsettling freshness, because the particular delusion it describes—money as a spell that can transmute history—has never really gone out of style.

**Rating: 9/10.** A near-perfect American novel, minor dings for its symbolic flatness and its overwrought finale. Essential, and not merely for the syllabus.


**How it works:**

| 4 | 7 | `[5, 6, 7]` | 7 ≠ 6 → append |
| 5 | 7 | `[5, 6, 7]` | 7 == 7 → skip |

# Word Histogram Function

Here's a clean solution that strips punctuation, normalizes case, and counts word frequencies:

```python
import string

def word_histogram(s):
    # Remove all punctuation characters
    s = s.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    # Convert to lowercase and split into words
    words = s.lower().split()
    # Build the frequency dictionary
    freq = {}
    for word in words:
        freq[word] = freq.get(word, 0) + 1
    return freq
```

## How it works

1. **`str.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))`** — creates a translation table that maps every punctuation character to `None`, effectively deleting them. This handles commas, periods, exclamation marks, etc.

2. **`.lower().split()`** — normalizes case so "Hello", "hello", and "HELLO" are all treated the same, then splits on whitespace to get individual words.

3. **The counting loop** — uses `dict.get(word, 0)` to safely increment each word's count without needing a separate "does this key exist?" check.

## Verification against the tests

```python
assert word_histogram("Hello, world! Hello.") == {"hello": 2, "world": 1}
assert word_histogram("Python is great. Python is fun!") == {"python": 2, "is": 2, "great": 1, "fun": 1}
assert word_histogram("Test, test, TEST.") == {"test": 3}
```

All three pass. The function correctly:
- Treats `"Hello"`, `"hello"`, and `"Hello"` as the same word (case-insensitive)
- Ignores trailing/leading punctuation like `,` `!` `.`
- Accumulates counts across multiple occurrences

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

## A Glimmering, Tragic Elegy for a Promised Land That Never Was

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that feels both intimately personal and mythically vast. At just under 200 pages, it is deceptively compact—a shimmering surface of parties, champagne, and silk dresses that conceals one of the most devastating critiques of American ambition ever committed to paper.

**The Story, in Brief**

Narrator Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, in the summer of 1922. Next door lives the enigmatic Jay Gatsby, who throws legendary parties but whose past is shrouded in rumor. Nick becomes entangled with Gatsby and his obsession: rekindling a romance with Nick's neighbor, the beautiful and carelessly cruel Daisy Buchanan. What unfolds is a love story, a crime story, and a national parable, all braided together with surgical precision.

**Why It Endures**

Fitzgerald's prose is perhaps the novel's most extraordinary quality. Sentences like "He smiled understandingly—much more than understandingly. It was one of those rare smiles with a quality of eternal reassurance in it" read like incantations. The language is lyrical without ever becoming ornate, formal without ever feeling cold. Every image—Gatsby's green light at the dock, the valley of ashes, the yellow car—lingers in the mind long after the final page.

The novel operates on multiple levels simultaneously. It is a romance, a tragedy, a detective story, a class study, and a meditation on the impossibility of recapturing the past. That final image of boats "beat against the current" toward "a dream that eludes us" transforms a single love affair into something almost Biblical in its scope.

**Characters**

Fitzgerald creates a cast of small, precise, and deeply human figures. Gatsby is not a hero—he is a man who built an entire identity from a single, idealized memory, and the gap between that fantasy and reality is where the tragedy lives. Daisy is far more complex than the "shallow" label often applied to her; she is a woman trapped in a system that demands she be decorative, and her choices are tragic precisely because they are *human*. Nick, the "one of the few honest people" we know, is a narrator of remarkable self-awareness, and his unreliability is itself a theme.

**Criticisms (the honest kind)**

Some readers find the novel thin in its emotional depth, more interested in *describing* feeling than *inhabiting* it. The secondary characters—Tom, Jordan, the party guests—can feel like types rather than people. And the novel's 1925 vantage point occasionally reads as slightly smug in its judgment of the Jazz Age, even as it mourns it. It is a story told by a man looking back, and that distance, while elegant, can create a certain emotional coolness.

**Who Should Read It**

High school students who endured the mandated reading and hated it should give it a second chance as adults. The novel rewards rereading—each pass reveals new ironies and deeper layers of meaning. It is also an ideal entry point for readers drawn to American literature, modernist fiction, or stories about the cost of wanting something you can no longer have.

**Final Thought**

*The Great Gatsby* is not a long book, but it is not a simple one. It asks, with quiet, devastating grace, whether the future is a place we can actually reach, or whether we are always just driving toward a green light on the opposite shore. Eighty-plus years after publication, the question still stings.

**Rating: 5/5** — A modern classic, fully earned.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★★**

There's a particular kind of novel that doesn't just describe a world—it makes you feel the humidity of it, hear the crackle of a radio in a distant room, taste the cheap champagne and the expensive wine at the same time. *The Great Gatsby* is one of those novels. Nearly a century after publication, it remains as luminous and as devastating as its first edition.

## The Surface

On its simplest level, the story is a love triangle with a body count. Narrator Nick Carraway rents a modest cottage on Long Island, New York, in the summer of 1922, next door to the fabulously wealthy Jay Gatsby. Gatsby throws spectacular parties attended by hundreds of strangers, all seemingly to rekindle a romance with his old flame, Daisy Buchanan—married, it turns out, to the brutish and arrogant Tom. What follows is a slow, glittering unraveling that moves from jazz-age excess to a violent, shattering conclusion.

But to call it "a love story" is like calling the ocean "wet."

## The Depth

Fitzgerald's genius lies in what the novel is *actually* about. It is a dissection of the American Dream—not as an inspiring aspiration, but as a beautiful, self-consuming lie. Gatsby reinvents himself from a poverty-stricken officer into a myth, and his entire architecture of wealth exists to buy back a past that cannot be purchased. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock, which the novel closes upon, is one of the most perfect images in American literature: always visible, always receding, never quite graspable.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that exists simultaneously as a tightly wound modernist art object and as an accessible, almost gossipy story about a party you wish you'd been invited to. It is short—barely over a hundred and fifty pages—and yet it carries the emotional and thematic weight of an epic. After more than a century, it remains the single most recommended American novel, and for good reason.

**The Story, Briefly**

In the summer of 1922, Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest, rents a modest cottage on Long Island near two neighbors: the old-money aristocrat Tom Buchanan and his beautiful, restless wife Daisy, and across the water, the enigmatic millionaire Jay Gatsby, who throws legendary parties into which no one quite seems to be invited. What unfolds is a love triangle, a scheme, a car accident, and a funeral no one attends.

**Why It Works**

Fitzgerald's prose is his greatest instrument. The novel is almost lyrically overwrought in places—the famous green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the "ash heap" of the Valley of Ashes, Gatsby's hands reaching toward the light in the final scene—and yet the ornamentation always serves emotional truth rather than mere decoration. Fitzgerald was, above all, a writer of mood, and he captures the specific giddiness and hollowness of the Jazz Age with an ear no other novelist of the period quite matched.

The narrative choice—telling the story through Nick, who insists he is "one of the few honest people" he has ever known—is both the book's greatest strength and its most debated weakness. Nick's narration gives the novel its elegiac, retrospective quality. Gatsby is never quite solid; he is always filtered through Nick's memory, his judgment, his romantic sympathy. Some readers find this distance frustrating; others feel it is essential. The ambiguity of who Gatsby really is—James Gatz, the bootlegger, the officer, the dreamer—depends entirely on how much you trust the man telling the story.

**Themes**

The novel is, at its core, a meditation on the impossibility of recapturing the past. Gatsby's entire fortune, his entire performance, is an engineering project aimed at rewinding time. "Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!" he snaps. Fitzgerald understands, with brutal clarity, that this is the defining delusion not just of one man but of an entire culture. The American Dream in the novel is not about wealth; it is about the belief that the future can be authored, that you can write yourself into a story already in progress. And the novel's devastating conclusion is that the past is already finished, and the river keeps moving.

Class is the novel's other great engine. The Buchanans are old money, comfortable in their cruelty. Gatsby is new money, and for all his millions, he is perpetually a guest in his own world. The social hierarchy of 1920s New York is rendered with the casual, cutting precision of a gossip column.

**Limitations**

The novel is not without its gaps. Daisy is, by design or by the constraints of her era, a largely passive and somewhat opaque figure. Jordan Baker is sketched in almost purely decorative strokes. The Black characters, notably Gatsby's butler, exist mostly as set-dressing. These are the costs of a 1925 sensibility, and they are worth naming. The prose, while beautiful, can feel slightly over-polished, like Fitzgerald showing off his vocabulary at the very party he's describing.

**Final Verdict**

*The Great Gatsby* is a masterpiece of compression. In 150 pages, Fitzgerald delivers a complete portrait of a nation at the moment of its brief, brilliant, self-destructive peak. It is a novel about longing, about the gap between the person you were and the person you performed yourself into being. It rewards rereading at every stage of life, because the green light means something different at twenty than at forty.

**Rating: ★★★★★**

A book to keep on your shelf and return to. Not because it will change how you think, but because it will remind you, every time, of how you feel.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**Rating: ★★★★½**

There are books that change the shape of American literature, and then there are books that change the shape of *how we talk* about literature. *The Great Gatsby* belongs firmly to the second, rarer category. In fewer than 180 pages, F. Scott Fitzgerald constructed a novel so densely layered, so perfectly calibrated in its prose, that it has functioned less as a story and more as a lens through which every subsequent generation has examined wealth, desire, and the American myth.

## The Story

On the surface, the plot is almost disappointingly simple. Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest, moves to Long Island in the summer of 1922 and becomes neighbors with the mysterious, fabulously wealthy Jay Gatsby. Through his old college friend Tom Buchanan and Tom's adulterous wife Daisy, Nick is drawn into Gatsby's orbit—a man who throws spectacular parties for hundreds of strangers, all while fixated on rekindling a romance from five years prior. The triangle of Gatsby, Daisy, and Tom unravels with the inevitability of a clock winding down, and the final chapters detonate with a violence that feels almost accidental after the novel's languorous, sun-drenched openings.

## Why It Still Works

What makes *Gatsby* endure is not the plot—it's the **music**. Fitzgerald's prose is arguably the most imitated and most difficult to replicate in 20th-century American fiction. Lines like *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"* aren't just quotable; they function as philosophical statements compressed into a single rhythmic breath. The novel's structure—told in retrospect by the unreliable, self-questioning Nick—creates a haunting double exposure. We see the events both in their gilded, immediate splendor and filtered through Nick's wiser, sadder distance. That gap is where the tragedy actually lives.

The themes are vast but never overstuffed: the hollowness beneath the glitter of old money (Buchanans) versus new money (Gatsby); the way the past is not recoverable, only *performed*; the American Dream as a specific, seductive, and ultimately corrosive lie. Fitzgerald never moralizes. He simply holds up the crystal and lets it catch the light.

## Characters

Gatsby is the engine, but the novel's truest insights often come from its supporting cast. Nick Carraway is a more complex narrator than he first appears—judgmental, complicit, and more drawn to Gatsby's performance of self than he'd like to admit. Daisy is frequently read as a one-dimensional symbol, and that's a fair criticism; she is *written* to be a symbol, a "golden girl" whose voice is "full of money." But Fitzgerald is making a point, not a slip. Tom is a thuggish, physically dominant presence who embodies the casual cruelty of inherited privilege. Jordan Baker drifts in and out with a coolness that mirrors the emotional weather of the book.

## Minor Quibbles

For a modern reader, the novel can feel slightly stagy—Fitzgerald was writing under the influence of Impressionist painting and modernist theater, and the characters sometimes announce their symbolism a beat too early. The second-person asides and Nick's occasional over-philosophizing can interrupt the momentum. And some contemporary readers may find the gender dynamics of the central relationships genuinely uncomfortable, even when read as Fitzgerald's *critique* of those dynamics rather than an endorsement.

## The Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is not a novel about the 1920s. The 1920s are merely the set. It is a novel about **wanting**—the specific, American, almost spiritual form of wanting that says *if I can just build the right house, throw the right party, buy the right dress, I can reach back across time and repair the one moment that mattered.* It fails, and the novel knows it fails, and the knowing is what makes it devastating.

It is the rare book that is both a masterclass in craft and a genuine emotional experience. It is short, and it should be read in one or two sittings, the way Fitzgerald intended, as a single sustained wave.

**For:** Fans of lyrical prose, literary fiction with thematic heft, anyone who has ever stood at a party where they don't belong.
**Against:** Readers who prefer plot-driven narratives or find symbolic, impressionist writing too allusive for their taste.

*The Great Gatsby* is 100 years old. It does not feel 100 years old. It feels like it was written last summer, for this summer, for a party you weren't invited to.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* – F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**A Luminous, Devastating Elegy for an America That Never Quite Existed**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's *The Great Gatsby* is one of those rare novels that operates on two levels simultaneously: it reads as a taut, almost pulp-like story of wealth, desire, and tragedy, and it functions as a searing anatomical study of a nation in the throes of its own excess. Eight decades after its publication, it remains the American novel most often assigned in high schools and the one most often cited in arguments about whether "classic" is a compliment or a death sentence. The answer, I'd argue, is that it's both—and the tension between those two readings is part of what keeps it alive.

**The Surface Story**

Nick Carraway, a young bondsman from the Midwest, rents a modest cottage on Long Island in the summer of 1922. Next door: the enigmatic, fabulously wealthy Jay Gatsby, whose mansion blazes nightly with parties that seem designed to impress a single woman—Nick's cousin, Daisy Buchanan, married to the brutish Tom Buchanan. What unfolds is a love triangle sharpened by class resentment, old money's contempt for new, and the slow accumulation of small cruelties that no one quite acknowledges until a car, a body, and a pool of chlorinated water settle the argument.

**What Elevates It Beyond a Plot**

The genius of the novel is that its true subject isn't romance. It's the *performance* of identity in a society that equates wealth with virtue. Gatsby reinvents himself so thoroughly that the original Jimmy Gatz from North Dakota is effectively dead, and Fitzgerald treats that erasure as both admirable and horrifying. "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"—that famous closing line captures the novel's central paradox: Gatsby's tragedy is that he's not trying to get ahead. He's trying to go *back*. He wants to repeat a summer, to make a single night of 1917 into a permanent condition. The past is a green light at the end of a dock, and the further you reach for it, the further it recedes.

Fitzgerald's prose is deceptively simple, almost journalistic in places, but he punctuates the narrative with images so precise and recurring they stop feeling like decoration and start feeling like a visual score: the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg on a billboards above the valley of ashes, the white dresses, the yellow car, the rotting garden, the smell of "the old warm world" dissolving. He writes like a painter working in limited palette, letting each color do enormous work.

**Where It Can Stumble**

No review is honest without noting the friction points. The women are largely functional—Daisy is the most frequently cited example—reduced to a symbol of unattainable gentility and the soft, careless cruelty of the privileged. Jordan Baker is wispy. The novel's sympathy for Gatsby is so total that Tom's perspective, the one grounded in a uglier but arguably more *honest* worldview, gets less than two paragraphs of genuine exploration. And the 1920s setting, while historically specific, sometimes reads like a costume: the jazz, the bootlegging, the speakeasies can feel like set dressing rather than lived texture for modern readers who've absorbed the decade through a century of retrospection.

**The Enduring Question**

What strikes me most on rereadings is how *Gatsby* functions as a mirror for whichever era is reading it. Postwar Americans saw the Jazz Age's moral carelessness. The 1990s saw a cautionary tale about "new money" and tabloid celebrity. Today, in an age of influencer economies and the performative self, Gatsby's party—thrown not for joy but for audience, for the one person who might validate the entire fabrication—feels almost prescient. The novel asks whether you can build an identity out of nothing and call it a soul. Fitzgerald's answer is a long, aching *no*, delivered with a grace that makes the answer hurt more.

**Final Verdict**

*The Great Gatsby* is a 180-page masterwork that rewards close, slow reading with an almost musical density of language, but it also works in a single weekend binge if you let the plot pull you forward. It is not a "comfortable" classic. It doesn't end neatly. The last sentence doesn't comfort you; it *haunts* you, the way a minor chord in a song lingers in a room after everyone has gone.

★★★★★ (4.5/5)

*The one star subtracted not for the writing, but for the women. The novel deserves them more than it gave them.*

```python
def word_histogram(s):
    s = s.lower()
    s = s.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
```

```python
import unittest

def remove_adjacent_duplicates(lst):
    if not lst:
        return []
    result = [lst[0]]
    for i in range(1, len(lst)):
        if lst[i] != result[-1]:
            result.append(lst[i])

class TestRemoveAdjacentDuplicates(unittest.TestCase):

        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7]), [5, 6, 7])
    
    def test_multiple_duplicates(self):
        self.assertEqual(remove_adjacent_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5]), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

if __name__ == '__main__':

```

**How it works:**

1. Handle the edge case of an empty list by returning `[]`.
2. Initialize `result` with the first element of the input list.
3. Iterate through the remaining elements. For each element, compare it to the **last element in `result`** (not the previous element in the input). If it's different, append it; otherwise, skip it.

By comparing against `result[-1]` rather than the previous input element, consecutive duplicates are naturally collapsed — no matter how many in a row appear, only the first one makes it into the result.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

**★★★★½ out of 5**

F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel remains one of the most enduring portraits of the American Dream—and its rotting underside. Set in the summer of 1922 on the glittering shores of Long Island, *The Great Gatsby* is at once a taut drama of obsession and betrayal and a quietly devastating elegy for a generation that mistook excess for meaning.

## The Story

Banker Nick Carraway rents a modest cottage next to the enormous, ostentatious estate of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby, a mysterious newly rich man who throws legendary parties every weekend. Nick's sister-in-law, the beautiful and fickle Daisy Buchanan, lives across the bay with her brutish, old-money husband, Tom. As Nick becomes entangled in their orbit, a love triangle ignites—Gatsby has, after all, built his entire extravagant world around the hope of winning Daisy back. The story culminates in a shattering sequence of collisions, both on the road and in the soul.

## What Works

Fitzgerald's prose is the first and most obvious triumph. Lines like *"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"* aren't just quotable; they're structurally perfect—rhythm, image, and thematic weight locked into a single sentence. The novel's imagery (the green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the bleached eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg peering down from the Valley of Ashes) operates on a symbolic level that rewards re-reading decades later.

The book is also genuinely fast. For a novel of roughly 180 pages, it moves with the urgency of a thriller. Fitzgerald keeps the reader in Nick's close, unreliable perspective, so the emotional revelations land with real force. Gatsby, despite being a flawed and somewhat grotesque figure, is rendered with a pathos that makes the tragedy land hard.

## Where It Stumbles

For all its power, the novel has limitations that become more apparent on a second or third reading. Daisy, the emotional engine of the plot, is the thinnest character in the book—less a person than a symbol of unattainable grace and moral vacancy. Jordan Baker is even more of a sketch. The women exist largely as objects around which the men perform their ambitions. This is, of course, a product of its era, and Fitzgerald is at least critiquing that world, but it does limit the novel's emotional range.

The Jazz Age excess, while atmospheric, can feel a bit one-note: parties, champagne, scandal, more parties. The social commentary about the hollowness of old money versus new money is sharp, but it rarely digs much deeper than surface-level class resentment.

## Who Should Read It

If you've only read the summary, or if you're approaching it for the first time as a young adult, the novel will likely feel more immediate than it does on a later reading. The moral clarity—the "Gatsby is a romantic fool, the Buchanans are callous, the rich are inhuman"—is more straightforward than the book becomes once you've absorbed the broader cultural discourse around it. Still, even on a reread, the craftsmanship of the prose and the structural elegance (the way the parties mirror Gatsby's inner life, the way the Valley of Ashes bookends the glitter) keep rewarding the reader.

## Final Thought

*The Great Gatsby* is not a perfect book. It is, however, a *complete* one in the way that matters: every sentence serves the architecture, every image echoes forward, and the final page earns its sorrow. It is a small novel in page count but a large one in ambition, and almost a century later it still does what Fitzgerald intended—it makes you feel, viscerally, what it costs to reach for something you've already lost.

**Recommended.** Best read in a quiet stretch of a summer, perhaps with a cold drink in hand and no particular plans for the evening. You'll feel more alone afterward, and a little more hopeful, in roughly equal measure.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)

## The Setup

In the summer of 1922, New York bank clerk Nick Carraway rents a modest house in West Egg, Long Island, next door to a mansion belonging to a mysterious, fabulously wealthy neighbor named Jay Gatsby. Nick is quickly drawn into Gatsby's orbit—into his wild parties, his elaborate persona, and his quiet, desperate obsession with the woman across the bay: Daisy Buchanan, his lost love from five years prior, now married to the brutish, aristocratic Tom. What follows is a season of excess, a slow unraveling, and a tragedy that lingers long after the final page.

## The Writing

Fitzgerald's prose is the book's most immediate pleasure. It moves with a musicality that mirrors the jazz age it depicts—lyrical, sun-drenched, and sometimes almost too ornate. The famous opening line ("In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since") sets a reflective, elegiac tone that carries the novel. Descriptions like the "valley of ashes" or the green light at the end of Daisy's dock are images that have seeped into the language of American literature itself. That said, the style can feel a touch overwrought in stretches, and some readers may find the narrator's voice a bit too uniformly wistful.

## The Themes

At its core, *Gatsby* is a deconstruction of the American Dream. Gatsby's entire identity is a self-made fiction—money earned through bootlegging, a name invented, a past rewritten—built around a single, idealized memory of a woman. The "green light" is less about Daisy than about the future we construct in our heads and can never actually reach. Fitzgerald extends that critique to an entire class: the old money of East Egg is idle and cruel; the new money of West Egg is loud and desperate; and the "valley of ashes" between them is where the working poor grind themselves to dust while the rich drive their cars through without a glance.

Love, in Fitzgerald's hands, is less a feeling than a projection. Gatsby doesn't love the woman Daisy actually is—he loves a symbol, a moment in 1917 that was never quite as golden as his memory insists. That distinction makes the novel ache in a way that pure romance or pure tragedy cannot.

## The Characters

Gatsby is, of course, the engine of the book, but it's worth noting how much of the novel is filtered through Nick, whose supposed objectivity is constantly under question. Daisy is often read as a shallow gold-digger, and she certainly behaves that way, but Fitzgerald gives her a strange, magnetic vulnerability that makes her harder to dismiss than a simple archetype. Tom is a blunt instrument of privilege—wealth as a birthright that entitles you to destroy others. The supporting cast (Jordan, Myrtle, the party-goers) is leaner than you might want, but Fitzgerald isn't building an ensemble; he's building a single, focused parable.

## The Lasting Impact

Few American novels are assigned as widely in schools, and fewer have shaped how we talk about the country's mythology of self-made success, class stratification, and the gap between who we want to be and who we are. The book has been adapted into films (notably the 1974 version with Robert Redford and the 2013 version with Leonardo DiCaprio), referenced in endless essays, and remains a touchstone for anyone writing about the Jazz Age or the dark side of the American Dream.

## Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is not a long book—around 180 pages—and it doesn't have a sprawling plot or a dense cast. What it has instead is density of meaning. Every image, every line of dialogue, every description of a house or a stretch of water is loaded with thematic weight. It rewards a first, breathless read for its energy and a subsequent, slower read for its architecture. It is, in the end, a small novel that became a very large mirror for a country.

**Rating: ★★★★★**

A book you can read at eighteen and again at forty and find something different in it both times. That's not a small thing.

# Review: *The Great Gatsby* by F. Scott Fitzgerald

**Published 1925 | ~180 pages | Fiction**

There are novels that feel modern the day they're written, and there are novels that seem to age into their meaning. *The Great Gatsby* is the latter. Published in the midst of the Jazz Age it depicts, it was modestly received at first, yet nearly a century later it has become arguably the single most assigned text in American literature—a short, luminous novel that keeps revealing new dimensions with every rereading.

## The Story in Brief

Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner, rents a cottage on Long Island in the summer of 1922 and becomes drawn into the orbit of his mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, a fabulously wealthy man who throws legendary parties and fixates on his old flame, Daisy Buchanan, married across the bay to the brute aristocrat Tom Buchanan. What follows is a brief, ferocious collision of desire, class, memory, and self-deception, ending—inevitably, and the book never quite hides the inevitability—in ruin.

## The Prose

Fitzgerald's language is the novel's first and most persistent enchantment. The opening line—*"In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since"*—is one of the most instantly recognizable in English, and it sets the tone for a book that reads less like narrative than like a slow, melancholy elegy. The prose is musical without being overwrought, precise without being cold. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock, the ash heaps of the Valley of Ashes, the yellow car, the white suits: Fitzgerald builds his world through images that lodge in the reader like splinters.

## Themes and Ambition

At its core, the novel is a dissection of the American Dream, but it resists simple summary. The Dream here is not merely "anyone can make it." It is the dream of *rewriting the past*—Gatsby's entire fortune is an elaborate mechanism for reclaiming a single summer with Daisy, and the novel asks whether identity can be manufactured or whether you are condemned to the life you were born into. The class divide between "old money" Buchanans and "new money" Gatsby is rendered with a precision that still feels urgent. The Buchanans' casual cruelty—Tom's infidelity, Daisy's retreat into her wealth when the consequences arrive—is more damning than any villain's soliloquy.

Fitzgerald also implicates his narrator. Nick presents himself as the one "among the few honest people" he has ever known, yet his complicity, his romanticization of Gatsby, and his selective memory make him deeply unreliable. The famous closing line—"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"—is not Gatsby's philosophy. It is Nick's. That distinction matters.

## Limitations

For all its brilliance, the novel is also, in a sense, a small one. The supporting cast beyond the central quartet is thin. Jordan is sketchy. Myrtle is functional. The "Jazz Age" world of the parties, the speakeasies, the speedboats, is vivid in texture but somewhat impressionistic in social detail; the book is more a mood piece about a specific stratum of wealth than a broad cross-section of 1920s America. Some readers may also find the pacing—three acts compressed into a single summer—feels slightly mechanical, as if the plot is being worked backward from its tragic endpoint. These are minor complaints. They do not dim the novel's power.

## Final Verdict

*The Great Gatsby* is a short, perfect novel about the seductiveness of the past and the impossibility of reaching it. It is a novel about class, yes, but also about the stories we tell to make our lives coherent, and about the gap between the person we construct and the person we are. Its prose is among the finest in 20th-century American literature, and its central image—the green light, always just out of reach—has passed into the language as shorthand for a particular, universal longing.

Whether you encounter it for the first time at seventeen or rediscover it at fifty, it will likely find you a little differently than it did last time. That is the mark of a book that is not merely well-written but genuinely alive.

**★★★★★** — A modern classic in the truest sense of the word.
