Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change word meaning.
Phone: Any distinct speech sound considered as a physical/phonetic unit without regard to its linguistic function.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Syntax: The study of the rules governing the structure of sentences and the arrangement of words.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, particularly at the level of words and sentences.
Pragmatics: The study of how context influences the interpretation of meaning in communication.
Phonetics: The study of the physical properties and production of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of sound systems and the abstract, systematic organization of sounds in a language.
Prosody: The study of rhythm, stress, and intonation in speech.
Morphophonology: The study of the interaction between morphology and phonology.
Morphophonemics: The phonological processes that occur in the context of morphological affixation.
Paradigm: A set of all possible forms of a word (e.g., verb conjugations or noun declensions).
Lexeme: An abstract unit of meaning corresponding to a set of word forms sharing a common stem.
Lexicon: The entire set of words and fixed expressions in a language.
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme (e.g., /s/, /z/, /ɪz/ for English plural).
Morph: The actual phonetic or orthographic realization of a morpheme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (e.g., "dog," "run").
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone and must attach to another morpheme (e.g., -s, un-).
Inflectional morpheme: A bound morpheme that modifies grammatical category without changing word class (e.g., -ed, -s, -ing).
Derivational morpheme: A bound morpheme that creates a new word, often changing grammatical category (e.g., -ness, -ify).
Affix: A morpheme attached to a base or stem to modify or create meaning.
Prefix: An affix attached before the base or stem of a word.
Suffix: An affix attached after the base or stem of a word.
Infix: An affix inserted within the base or stem of a word.
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds a base or stem with two or more parts (e.g., German be-...-en).
Suppletion: The replacement of an expected regular form with an irregular, etymologically unrelated form (e.g., go/went, man/men).
Compounding: A word-formation process combining two or more free morphemes to create a new word.
Conflation (Clipping): Shortening a word while retaining its meaning (e.g., "advertisement" → "ad").
Back-formation: Creating a new word by removing an apparent affix (e.g., "editor" → "edit").
Conversion (Zero derivation): Forming a new word from an existing one without adding an affix (e.g., "to butter" from "butter").
Blending: Combining parts of two words to form a new word (e.g., "brunch" = breakfast + lunch).
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that combines the meaning of two or more morphemes (e.g., "spanglish").
Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that phonetically imitate the sound they represent (e.g., "buzz," "bang").
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a multi-word phrase (e.g., "NASA").
Initialism: A sequence of initial letters pronounced individually (e.g., "FBI").
Abbreviation: A shortened form of a word or phrase.
Reduplication: The repetition of all or part of a word to express grammatical meaning (e.g., "bye-bye," "titi" in some languages for diminutive).
Agglutination: A morphological process where words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each typically carrying a single grammatical meaning.
Fusional (Flectional): A morphological type where a single affix can encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously (e.g., Latin -runt).
Isolating (Analytic): A morphological type where words consist primarily of single morphemes with little or no inflection (e.g., Mandarin Chinese).
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which many morphemes are fused into a single word, sometimes equivalent to an entire sentence (e.g., many Native American languages).
Case: A grammatical category of a noun or pronoun indicating its syntactic role in a sentence (e.g., nominative, accusative, genitive).
Nominative case: The case marking the subject of a clause.
Accusative case: The case marking the direct object of a clause.
Dative case: The case marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive case: The case indicating possession, origin, or other relationships (e.g., "of").
Ablative case: The case indicating separation, source, or agent.
Locative case: The case indicating location or position.
Vocative case: The case used to address or call someone.
Instrumental case: The case indicating the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Allative case: The case indicating direction toward a location.
Translative case: The case indicating change of state or transformation.
Ergativity: A grammatical alignment in which the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently from the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb.
Ergative: The case or form marking the subject of a transitive verb in an ergative language.
Aabsolutive: The case or form marking the object of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb in an ergative language.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A grammatical system in which the subject is marked the same whether the verb is transitive or intransitive, distinct from the object.
Split ergativity: A system in which a language uses ergative alignment for some verb forms (e.g., past tense) and accusative alignment for others (e.g., present tense).
Valency: The number of arguments (participants) a verb requires or can take.
Monotransitive: A verb taking one argument (intransitive).
Bitransitive: A verb taking two arguments (transitive).
Ditransitive: A verb taking three arguments (e.g., "give" with agent, theme, and recipient).
Subcategorization: The specification of the syntactic arguments a lexical item requires or optionally takes.
Complement: A phrase that is a required part of a predicate (e.g., the object of a transitive verb).
Adjunct: An optional modifier that provides additional information (e.g., an adverbial phrase).
Modifier: A word or phrase that describes or qualifies another word or phrase.
Head: The central, most important word in a phrase that determines its grammatical category.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a subordinate clause (e.g., "that," "if," "whether").
Specified Head Argument Construction (SHAC): A construction that requires a pre-specified head, such as "It is raining" or "There is a cat."
Auxiliary (Auxilial) verb: A verb that supports the main verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice (e.g., "will," "have," "be").
Copula: A linking verb that connects a subject to a predicate (e.g., "be," "seem").
Light verb: A verb with minimal lexical meaning that relies on its complement for content (e.g., "have" in "have a look").
Cataphoric: A linguistic element that refers forward to something mentioned later in the text.
Anaphoric: A linguistic element that refers backward to something already mentioned (e.g., a pronoun referring to a prior noun).
Deictic: A word whose reference depends on the context of the utterance (e.g., "here," "now," "this," "I").
Exophoric: Reference to something outside the text, often requiring shared knowledge or physical context.
Endophoric: Reference to something within the text itself.
Coreference: The relationship between two expressions in a text that refer to the same entity.
Hedging: Linguistic strategies used to express uncertainty or soften a claim (e.g., "perhaps," "it seems that").
Presupposition: A background assumption that a speaker takes for granted in an utterance.
Entailment: A logical relationship where the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
Implicature (Conversational): A meaning inferred by the listener based on context and cooperative principles, not explicitly stated.
Illocutionary act: The intended communicative force of an utterance (e.g., requesting, promising, warning).
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the listener (e.g., persuading, alarming).
Performative: An utterance that performs the action it describes (e.g., "I now pronounce you married").
Speech act: An utterance viewed as an action performed by the speaker in a communicative context.
Grice's Maxims: Four principles of cooperative communication: Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner.
Scalar implicature: An inference based on the use of a weaker term when a stronger one was available (e.g., "some" implicating "not all").
Politeness (strategy): Linguistic strategies used to maintain social harmony and manage face (e.g., indirect requests, hedges).
Face (in pragmatics): The public self-image a person claims in interaction; includes positive face (desire to be approved) and negative face (desire for freedom from imposition).
Mitigation: The use of linguistic devices to reduce the force or directness of an utterance.
Directive: A type of speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something.
Commissive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to performing a future action.
Expressive: A type of speech act expressing the speaker's psychological state (e.g., thanking, apologizing).
Declarative (speech act): A type of speech act that changes the world by being uttered (e.g., "I resign").
Representative (Assertive): A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to the truth of a proposition.
Turn-taking: The system by which speakers alternate in conversation.
Repair: The process by which participants identify and correct errors or problems in conversation.
Adjacency pair: A pair of related conversational turns, such as question-answer or greeting-greeting.
Backchanneling: Short utterances or sounds indicating the listener is attending (e.g., "mm-hm," "yeah").
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse or signals the speaker's stance (e.g., "well," "you know," "however").
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that link parts of a text together (e.g., reference, conjunction, lexical repetition).
Coherence: The logical and meaningful connection between ideas in a text, independent of explicit linguistic markers.
Topic chain: A sequence of sentences or clauses in which the topic is maintained or shifted across the discourse.
Information structure: The organization of discourse into given (old) and new (new) information.
Given (old) information: Information already established in the discourse context.
New information: Information not previously established, introduced as novel to the discourse.
Focus: The element in a sentence that is contrasted or highlighted as new or important.
Topic (grammatical): The element about which a sentence or clause makes a statement; often positioned initially.
Rhythm (in discourse): The pattern of information units and their prosodic realization in spoken language.
Intonational phrase: A stretch of speech unified by a single intonation contour.
Prosodic word: A phonological unit corresponding roughly to a lexical word, defined by stress and timing patterns.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable in a word or phrase.
Tone: A distinctive use of pitch at the syllable or word level to differentiate meaning (e.g., in Mandarin).
Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which exactly one mora per word receives a high pitch, distinguishing lexical items.
Intonation: The variation of fundamental frequency over the course of an utterance, contributing to meaning and attitude.
F0 (Fundamental frequency): The primary frequency of vocal fold vibration, perceived as pitch.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during phonation, producing voiced sounds as opposed to voiceless ones.
Aspiration: A puff of air accompanying the release of certain consonants (e.g., /pʰ/ in English "pin").
Gemination: The lengthening or doubling of a consonant or syllable.
Schwa: A mid-central, unstressed vowel sound /ə/, common in English.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which vowels in a word or phrase share a particular feature (e.g., backness, roundedness).
Consonant harmony: The spread of a consonantal feature across adjacent consonants within a word.
Palatalization: A secondary articulation in which the body of the tongue raises toward the hard palate during consonant production.
Velarization: A secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue raises toward the soft palate.
Labialization: A secondary articulation involving rounding of the lips during consonant production.
Rhotacization: A sound change in which /l/ or /r/ becomes /r/, or the influence of /r/ on adjacent sounds.
Umlaut (Umlaut mutation): A historical vowel change triggered by the presence of a back vowel or /u/ in a following syllable (e.g., German "Maus" from "Mūs").
Lenition: A general weakening of consonants, especially in certain morphological or phonological contexts.
Fortition: A strengthening of a sound, often in the opposite direction of lenition.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound to reduce redundancy.
Metathesis: A sound change or process in which the order of two or more segments is reversed (e.g., "ask" ← "aks").
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word to break up a cluster or resolve a phonotactic constraint.
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable, especially in rapid or casual speech.
Coalescence: The merging of two adjacent sounds into a single sound.
Sandhi: The set of phonological changes that occur at the junction of two words or morphemes.
Phonotactics: The rules governing permissible combinations of sounds within a language.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phonological segment and have different meanings (e.g., "pat" vs. "bat").
Contrastive feature: A phonological feature that distinguishes one phoneme from another in a given language.
Autosegment: A phonological representation in which certain features (e.g., tone, stress) are placed on separate tiers from the segmental string.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used to account for syllable structure, typically corresponding to a short vowel or a single consonant.
Syllable: A basic unit of prosodic structure, typically organized around a vowel nucleus.
Nucleus: The most sonorous element of a syllable, usually a vowel.
Coda: The consonant(s) following the nucleus in a syllable.
Onset: The consonant(s) preceding the nucleus in a syllable.
Rime: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and coda.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following consonants, often shared between words.
Prosodic hierarchy: The hierarchical organization of speech into domains: syllable < foot < prosodic word < phonological phrase < intonational phrase.
Stress foot: A prosodic domain containing one stressed syllable (and optionally one or more unstressed syllables).
Trochaic foot: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.
Iambic foot: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
Syllable-timing: A rhythmic type in which syllables tend to be equally spaced in time (e.g., French, Spanish).
Stress-timing: A rhythmic type in which stressed syllables tend to occur at roughly equal intervals (e.g., English, German).
Morae-timing: A rhythmic type in which morae tend to be equally spaced (e.g., Japanese).
VOT (Voice onset time): The interval between the release of a stop consonant and the onset of vocal fold vibration.
Formant: A band of frequencies in the vocal tract that is reinforced during speech production.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of the production of speech sounds by the organs of the vocal tract.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical (acoustic) properties of speech sounds.
Auditory phonetics: The study of the perception of speech sounds.
Spectrogram: A visual display of the frequency content of a speech signal over time.
X-ray: A radiographic technique used to observe the articulatory movements of the vocal tract.
Ultrasound: A technique using high-frequency sound waves to image soft tissues during speech production.
Electroarticulography: A technique using electromagnetic sensors to track the movement of articulators during speech.
Laryngograph: A device that records the vibration pattern of the vocal folds.
Palatograph: A device that records the contact of the tongue with the palate during speech.
Phonological rule: A formal representation of a sound change or alternation in a language.
Underlying representation: The abstract, pre-surface form of a word or phonological structure before rules apply.
Surface representation: The actual phonetic or near-phonetic form of a word as it is pronounced.
Phonological process: A general term for sound changes or alternations governed by phonological rules.
Neutralization: A phonological environment in which two or more contrasts merge (e.g., final /t/ and /d/ in English).
Distinctive feature: A binary property (e.g., [+voice], [+nasal]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological features organized in a hierarchical structure.
Natural class: A set of segments that share one or more distinctive features.
Markedness: A universal tendency for certain phonological categories (marked) to be less common or more complex than others (unmarked).
Correspondence: The regular phonological relationship between related forms or segments across languages or morphemes.
Sound change: A historical shift in the pronunciation of a segment or class of segments over time.
Regular sound change: A sound change that applies uniformly across all contexts in which its structural conditions are met.
Analogical change: A change in form driven by the influence of other related forms in the paradigm.
Reconstruction: The methodological process of hypothesizing the forms and features of a proto-language based on its descendants.
Comparative method: A method of historical linguistics that uses systematic correspondences between related languages to reconstruct proto-forms.
Internal reconstruction: A method of hypothesizing earlier stages of a language using only data from that language.
Cognate: A word in one language that corresponds to a word in another language through common descent from a proto-form.
Borrowing (Loanword): The adoption of a word or element from one language into another.
Code-switching: The alternating use of two or more languages or varieties within a single discourse.
Code-mixing: The blending of linguistic elements from two languages at the phrase or word level within a single utterance.
Diglossia: A sociolinguistic situation in which two distinct varieties of a language (or two languages) coexist with separate functional domains.
Standard language: The variety of a language that is codified, taught in schools, and used in formal domains.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region or social group.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Sociolect: A language variety associated with a particular social group or class.
Ethnolect: A language variety associated with a particular ethnic group.
Register: A variety of language characterized by its use in a particular social context or communicative situation.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular professional or technical group.
Slang: Informal, often ephemeral vocabulary used by a particular social group.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect substitute for a word or expression considered blunt or offensive.
Dysphemism: A harsh or unpleasant term, often the opposite of a euphemism.
Taboo language: Words or expressions considered forbidden, offensive, or socially restricted.
Prestige (linguistic): Social value attached to a particular variety of language, often associated with dominant groups.
Stigma: Negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety or speech pattern.
Linguistic prescriptivism: The view that language should conform to fixed rules and standards.
Linguistic descriptivism: The view that language should be described as it is actually used by its speakers.
Language death: The loss of a language when its last native speaker dies or it ceases to be actively used.
Language revitalization: Efforts to restore or maintain a language that is endangered or already dead.
Language endangerment: The condition of a language whose speaker population is declining, threatening its future use.
Multilingualism: The ability to use two or more languages.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two languages, whether natively or acquired.
Trilingualism: The ability to use three languages.
L1 (First language / Native language): The language acquired first, typically in early childhood.
L2 (Second language): A language acquired after the first language.
Foreign language: A language learned in a context where it is not the dominant local language.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn to use a language, especially in early childhood.
Language learning: The deliberate, formal study of a language, often in contrast to natural acquisition.
Critical period: A hypothesized window in early development during which language acquisition is most facile.
Sensitive period: A developmental window during which a particular skill is especially readily acquired, with a gradual decline afterward.
Universal Grammar (UG): The hypothesized innate, language-specific biological endowment that underlies all human languages.
Language faculty: The cognitive capacity for language, hypothesized as a distinct module of the mind.
Poverty of the stimulus: The argument that children acquire more grammatical knowledge than can be accounted for by the input alone.
Overregularization: The application of a regular rule to irregular forms during language acquisition (e.g., "goed" for "went").
Telegraphic speech: A stage in child language production in which only content words are used, omitting function words.
Holophrase: A single word used by a child to express a complete proposition (e.g., "milk" meaning "I want milk").
Language model: A computational or cognitive model of the probability of sequences of words or phonemes.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic research or computational analysis.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large-scale corpora of natural language data.
Computational linguistics: The application of computer science and AI methods to the analysis and processing of natural language.
Natural language processing (NLP): The field of AI concerned with enabling computers to understand and generate human language.
Token: A single occurrence of a word, morpheme, or other unit in a text or corpus.
Type: A distinct word, morpheme, or unit abstracted from its individual occurrences.
Type-token ratio: The ratio of distinct types to total tokens in a corpus, a measure of lexical diversity.
Zipf's law: The statistical observation that the frequency of a word in a corpus is inversely proportional to its rank.
Hapax legomenon: A word that appears only once in a given corpus or text.
Lemmatization: The process of reducing inflected or derived word forms to their base or dictionary form.
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging: The computational task of assigning a grammatical category (noun, verb, etc.) to each word in a text.
Parsing (Syntactic parsing): The process of determining the grammatical structure of a sentence according to a grammar.
Dependency parsing: A method of syntactic analysis that represents the relationships between words as directed dependencies.
Constituent parsing: A method of syntactic analysis that groups words into hierarchical phrases.
Finite state automaton (FSA): A mathematical model used in phonology and computational linguistics to represent regular patterns of symbols.
Transducer: A computational device that maps an input string to an output string, used in phonological rule application.
Stochastic grammar: A grammar in which productions are assigned probabilities, allowing for probabilistic parsing and generation.
Feature: In formal grammar, a property (often binary or valued) associated with a lexical item or syntactic category.
Government: A syntactic relationship in which a head controls the features or form of a dependent element.
Binding (Principle A/B/C): A set of conditions in binding theory governing the relationship between pronouns, reflexives, and noun phrases.
Control: A syntactic relationship in which an element in one clause determines the reference of an element in another (e.g., "I try to leave").
Raising: A syntactic operation in which a subject of an embedded clause is moved to the subject position of the matrix clause.
Passive: A construction in which the patient (object) of an active clause becomes the subject of the passive clause.
Middle voice: A verbal construction that is intermediate between active and passive, often used for reflexive or inchoative meanings.
Causative: A construction that expresses causing an event, often by adding an agent argument.
Anticausative: A construction that expresses the spontaneous occurrence of an event, often by removing the agent argument.
Applicative: A construction that adds an argument (typically a beneficiary or recipient) to a verb.
Voice: A set of related verbal constructions (e.g., active, passive, middle) that alter the mapping between semantic roles and syntactic positions.
Agent: The semantic role of the initiator or doer of an action.
Patient (Theme): The semantic role of the entity affected or acted upon.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes or is affected by a state or experience.
Goal: The semantic role of the endpoint or destination of a motion or transfer.
Source: The semantic role of the starting point of a motion or transfer.
Instrument: The semantic role of the means by which an action is performed.
Locative: The semantic role of the location at which an event occurs.
Beneficiary: The semantic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Role and Reference Grammar (RRG): A theoretical framework for syntax and semantics that distinguishes grammatical relations from semantic roles.
Lexical-Functional Grammar (LFG): A syntactic theory that distinguishes between a phrase-structure representation (c-structure) and a functional representation (f-structure).
Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG): A constraint-based syntactic and semantic framework using attribute-value matrices.
Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar (GPSG): A rule-based framework for natural language grammar using phrase-structure rules and lexical specifications.
Tree-adjoining grammar (TAG): A formal grammar formalism that uses elementary trees and auxiliary trees for substitution and adjunction.
Categorial grammar: A formal grammar framework in which words are assigned syntactic types and combine via function application.
Minimalism: A syntactic theory proposed by Chomsky that posits a highly reduced set of operations (Merge, Move) and minimal assumptions.
Government and Binding Theory: A syntactic framework from the 1980s incorporating principles, parameters, and X-bar theory.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure positing a three-bar projection level for each phrase category.
Endocentric: A phrase whose grammatical category is the same as that of its head (e.g., "big house" is a noun phrase headed by "house").
Exocentric: A phrase whose grammatical category is different from that of its head (e.g., "the man in the hat" is a noun phrase, but the head "in the hat" is not).
Complement (syntactic): A phrase that completes the meaning of a head and is required by subcategorization.
Specifier: The phrase occupying the position immediately to the left of a head in a phrase-structure tree.
Trace: A silent element left in situ when a constituent has been moved to another position.
Gap: An unoccupied position in a syntactic structure, as in a wh-moved or passivized element.
Wh-movement: The syntactic operation by which a wh-word (who, what, where, etc.) moves to the beginning of a clause.
Expletive (dummy subject): A syntactically required but semantically empty subject (e.g., "it" in "It is raining").
Pro-drop (Null subject): The omission of a pronoun when the verb inflection or context makes the referent clear.
Pro (null anaphor): A silent variable in syntactic theory that represents an omitted pronoun.
Wh-phrase: A phrase headed by a wh-word (e.g., "what book," "which city").
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun or complementizer.
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand alone and is embedded within another clause.
Coordinate clause: A clause joined to another clause by a coordinating conjunction (e.g., "and," "but," "or").
Conjunction (coordinating): A word that joins two elements of equal grammatical status (e.g., "and," "but," "or").
Subordinator (subordinating conjunction): A word that introduces a subordinate clause (e.g., "because," "although," "while").
Complement clause: A clause that functions as a complement to a verb or adjective (e.g., "I think (that she left)").
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverbial modifier (e.g., "after she left").
Fronting: The movement of a constituent to the beginning of a clause for emphasis or topicalization.
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the sentence-initial position to mark it as the topic.
Focus fronting: The movement of a constituent to sentence-initial position to mark it as focus.
Cleft sentence: A construction that places a particular constituent in focus using a "cleft" structure (e.g., "It was John who called").
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction in which the focused element is in a wh-clause (e.g., "What I need is a coffee").
Heavy NP shift: The postposition of a long or complex noun phrase to the end of a sentence for processing ease.
Topicalization (discourse): The process of establishing or shifting the topic of discourse.
Information flow: The organization of information into given and new elements as discourse progresses.
Thematic progression: The pattern of how topics are maintained, shifted, or expanded across a discourse.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression (usually a pronoun) that refers back to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later.
Exophora: Reference to an entity not mentioned in the text but identifiable from the physical or social context.
Bound anaphora: An anaphoric element (typically a reflexive) that is bound to an antecedent within its local domain.
Free anaphora: An anaphoric element (typically a pronoun) that is not syntactically bound to its antecedent.
Antecedent: The expression to which an anaphoric or cataphoric element refers.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it denotes in the discourse or world.
Definiteness: The grammatical marking of an entity as uniquely identifiable to the hearer (e.g., via the definite article "the").
Specificity: A semantic property of a definite or indefinite noun phrase indicating whether the speaker has a particular entity in mind.
Indefiniteness: The grammatical marking of an entity as not uniquely identifiable (e.g., via "a/an," zero article).
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies the quantity or extent of the entities a noun phrase refers to (e.g., "all," "some," "every").
Numeral: A word or symbol expressing a number.
Cardinal numeral: A numeral expressing a quantity (e.g., "three," "seven").
Ordinal numeral: A numeral expressing position in a sequence (e.g., "third," "seventh").
Distributive: A semantic property of a quantifier or operator that applies to each individual member of a set (e.g., "each," "every").
Collective: A semantic property that applies to a set as a whole (e.g., "together," "as a group").
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier, operator, or modifier applies.
Quantifier scope: The range of meaning over which a quantifier's force extends, which can vary with syntactic position.
Presupposition trigger: A word or construction that gives rise to a presupposition (e.g., "again," "stop," "the").
Existential presupposition: A presupposition that an entity exists (e.g., "The king of France is bald" presupposes a king of France exists).
Factive verb: A verb that presupposes the truth of its complement clause (e.g., "know," "realize," "regret").
Non-factive verb: A verb that does not presuppose the truth of its complement (e.g., "think," "believe," "claim").
Scalarity: The property of words or expressions being arranged in a semantic scale (e.g., "some < most < all").
Horn scale: A natural scale of expressions arranged by logical strength (e.g., "all > most > some > none").
Grading scale: A scale of expressions arranged by a gradable property (e.g., "cold < cool < warm < hot").
Implicature (explicature): The explicitly stated propositional content of an utterance, as opposed to implicature.
Entailment (conversational): A meaning that follows from the literal content plus general background knowledge.
Speaker's meaning: The propositional content the speaker intends to convey.
Hearer's meaning: The propositional content the hearer attributes to the speaker's utterance.
Context: The totality of factors (linguistic, situational, cultural, cognitive) that influence the interpretation of an utterance.
Situational context: The immediate physical and social circumstances of the communicative act.
Linguistic context: The surrounding linguistic material (preceding and following text) that constrains interpretation.
Cultural context: The shared knowledge, norms, and practices of a community that influence language use and interpretation.
Register (sociolinguistic): A variety of language characterized by its use in a particular social setting, domain, or mode of communication.
Field: The subject matter or topic area of a communicative context.
Tenor: The social relationship between the participants in a communicative interaction.
Mode: The channel or medium of communication (e.g., spoken, written, signed) and its degree of plannedness.
Genre: A conventionalized form of text with a recognizable structure and purpose (e.g., recipe, news report, academic paper).
Text type: A category of text defined by its communicative purpose and structural features.
Rhetorical structure: The hierarchical organization of a text into spans and relations (as in Rhetorical Structure Theory).
Macro-structure: The global, overall organization of a text's meaning.
Micro-structure: The local, sentence-to-sentence connections and relations in a text.
Cohesive device: A linguistic element that creates a connection between parts of a text (e.g., conjunctions, pronouns, lexical ties).
Lexical cohesion: Cohesion achieved through lexical means such as repetition, synonymy, and collocation.
Grammatical cohesion: Cohesion achieved through grammatical means such as reference, substitution, and ellipsis.
Ellipsis (grammatical): The omission of a word or phrase that is recoverable from the context.
Substitution: The replacement of a word or phrase by a general term (e.g., "one," "do so," "there").
Reference (grammatical): The use of pronouns, demonstratives, or other expressions to point to entities in the text.
Exophoric reference: Reference to an entity outside the text, in the physical or social context.
Endophoric reference: Reference to an entity within the text.
Interlinear reference: Reference to an element in the same clause or sentence.
Interclausal reference: Reference to an element in a different clause or sentence.
Anaphoric reference: Reference to a previously mentioned entity (backward-looking).
Cataphoric reference: Reference to a subsequently mentioned entity (forward-looking).
Nominalization: The process of converting a verb or adjective into a noun (e.g., "decide" → "decision").
Nominal group: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, including its modifiers and determiners.
Verbal group: A phrase headed by a verb, including its auxiliaries and complements.
Adjectival group: A phrase headed by an adjective, including its modifiers.
Adverbial group: A phrase headed by an adverb, including its modifiers.
Prepositional phrase (PP): A phrase headed by a preposition, including its complement (e.g., "on the table").
Preposition: A word that typically precedes a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or spatial relationship.
Postposition: A word that typically follows a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or spatial relationship.
Circumposition: A two-part prepositional or adpositional element that surrounds a noun phrase (e.g., "between...and").
Adposition: A general term for prepositions and postpositions.
Complement (prepositional): The noun phrase or clause that follows a preposition and is governed by it.
Adjunct (prepositional): A prepositional phrase that modifies but is not required by the head verb or noun.
Conjunction (phrase-level): A word or phrase that joins two or more elements of the same grammatical category.
Correlative: A pair of conjunctions or words used together to join two elements (e.g., "both...and," "either...or").
Copula (predicative): The verb that links a subject to a predicate complement (e.g., "is," "seems").
Predicative complement: A noun, adjective, or other phrase that follows a copula and describes or identifies the subject.
Subject complement: A complement that refers back to the subject (e.g., "She is a doctor").
Object complement: A complement that refers back to the object (e.g., "They elected her president").
Predicate nominative: A noun in the complement position of a copular clause that refers to the subject.
Appositive: A noun or noun phrase that renames or identifies another noun adjacent to it (e.g., "My sister, a doctor, lives in Boston").
Vocative: A noun or noun phrase used to address or call the listener (e.g., "John, come here").
Exclamative: An utterance expressing strong emotion, often marked by intonation or interjection (e.g., "Wow!").
Interjection: A word or phrase expressing a sudden emotion or reaction, often outside sentence structure (e.g., "Oh!" "Ouch!").
Discourse particle: A word that does not contribute propositional content but signals the speaker's attitude or manages discourse (e.g., "well," "so," "hmm").
Discourse tag: A clause or phrase attached to the end of an utterance for emphasis or confirmation (e.g., "right?" "don't you think?").
Modal: A word or expression expressing the speaker's attitude toward the truth or desirability of a proposition (e.g., "must," "should," "might").
Modal verb: A verb expressing modality (e.g., "can," "will," "may," "must").
Epistemic modality: Modality expressing the speaker's judgment of certainty or likelihood (e.g., "must be," "might be").
Deontic modality: Modality expressing obligation, permission, or prohibition (e.g., "must go," "may leave").
Dynamic modality: Modality expressing the subject's ability or willingness (e.g., "can swim," "will try").
Aspect (grammatical): The grammatical representation of the temporal structure of an event (e.g., perfective, imperfective, progressive, perfect).
Perfective: An aspect marking an event as a complete, bounded whole.
Imperfective: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, incomplete, or habitual.
Progressive: An aspect marking an event as in progress at a particular time (e.g., "is running").
Perfect: An aspect marking an event as completed prior to a reference point, with present relevance (e.g., "has run").
Pluperfect: The perfect aspect relative to a past reference point (e.g., "had run").
Future perfect: The perfect aspect relative to a future reference point (e.g., "will have run").
Habitual: An aspect or tense marking an event as repeatedly occurring (e.g., used to, would + verb).
Inchoative: An aspect or voice marking the beginning or onset of a state or event.
Iterative: An aspect marking the repeated occurrence of an event.
Frequentative: An aspect marking the frequent (but not necessarily repeated in a single context) occurrence of an event.
Semedi (semelfactive): An aspect marking a single, punctual occurrence of an event.
Telic: An event or state that has a natural endpoint or goal (e.g., "build a house").
Atelic: An event or state that has no inherent endpoint (e.g., "run," "walk").
Accomplishment: A telic, durative event type (e.g., "build a house," "walk to the store").
Achievement: A telic, punctual event type (e.g., "reach the top," "win the race").
Activity: An atelic, durative event type (e.g., "run," "swim").
State: An atelic, non-durative (stative) event type (e.g., "know," "believe," "be tall").
Semelfactive: A punctual, telic event type involving a single occurrence (e.g., "knock," "blink").
Aspectual class: A classification of verbs based on their temporal structure (telic/atelic, punctual/durative).
Durativity: The property of an event or state extending over a period of time.
Punctuality: The property of an event occurring at a single point in time.
Iterativity: The property of an event occurring multiple times.
Reversibility: The property of an event or state that can be undone (e.g., "open" / "close").
Transitivity (semantic): The property of a verb that takes a patient or theme argument.
Intransitivity (semantic): The property of a verb that takes no patient or theme argument.
Ditransitivity: The property of a verb that takes both a theme and a recipient argument (e.g., "give," "show").
Unaccusative: An intransitive verb whose subject is semantically a patient or theme rather than an agent (e.g., "arrive," "fall").
Unaccusative hypothesis: The syntactic theory that unaccusative verbs originate with their subject in an object-like position.
Unergative: An intransitive verb whose subject is an agent or experiencer (e.g., "run," "sleep," "laugh").
Transitivizing: A process or construction that adds a patient/theme argument to a verb.
Ditransitivizing: A process or construction that adds a recipient or goal argument to a verb.
Causativization: A process that adds an agent/cause argument to an intransitive or unaccusative verb.
Dedervation: A process that removes arguments from a verb (e.g., making a transitive verb intransitive).
Middle (construction): A construction in which the subject is a patient and the verb expresses an inherent property (e.g., "This book sells well").
Passivization: The syntactic operation that promotes the patient to subject and demotes or deletes the agent.
Deponent verb: A verb that has passive morphology but active meaning (e.g., Latin "sequor" "I follow").
Stative verb: A verb that describes a state rather than an event (e.g., "know," "have," "be").
Dynamic verb: A verb that describes an event or process involving change (e.g., "run," "build," "think").
Aspectual verb: A verb that inherently encodes aspectual information (e.g., "start," "finish," "continue").
Tense (grammatical): The grammatical marking of the temporal location of an event relative to the time of speech or another reference point.
Present tense: The tense marking the event as simultaneous with the time of speech.
Past tense (Preterite): The tense marking the event as prior to the time of speech.
Future tense: The tense marking the event as subsequent to the time of speech.
Present perfect: A tense/aspect combination marking a past event with present relevance.
Pluperfect (Past perfect): A tense/aspect combination marking an event prior to another past reference point.
Future perfect: A tense/aspect combination marking an event prior to a future reference point.
Relative tense: A tense that locates an event relative to another event rather than the time of speech.
Absolute tense: A tense that locates an event relative to the time of speech.
Reference time (RT): The time relative to which a tense or aspect is evaluated.
Situation time (ST): The time at which the event or state denoted by a verb occurs.
Speech time (TT): The time of the utterance, or the "now" of the conversation.
Temporal deictic: A word that locates an event in time relative to the speech time (e.g., "now," "then," "yesterday").
Spatial deictic: A word that locates an entity in space relative to a reference point (e.g., "here," "there," "this," "that").
Personal deictic: A word that references participants in the conversation (e.g., "I," "you," "he," "she").
Person (grammatical): A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker (1st), the addressee (2nd), and a third party (3rd).
Number (grammatical): A grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, and plural reference.
Gender (grammatical): A grammatical category that classifies nouns (and associated forms) into groups, often with no correspondence to biological sex.
Masculine gender: A grammatical gender category, often associated with male referents in some languages but not always.
Feminine gender: A grammatical gender category, often associated with female referents in some languages but not always.
Neuter gender: A grammatical gender category, often associated with inanimate or non-human referents.
Class (noun class): A system of noun categorization in Bantu and other languages, involving agreement markers across the grammar.
Augmentation: A noun class prefix in Bantu languages.
Agreement: The morphological matching of features (e.g., gender, number, case) between a head and its dependents.
Concord: The use of agreeing markers in a language, especially on verbs or adjectives.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent (e.g., English "gonna" → /gənə/, or clitic pronouns in Romance languages).
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the right of its host.
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the left of its host.
Reduction: A phonological process in which a segment or syllable is weakened or deleted in unstressed or rapid speech.
Flapping: A phonological process in which /t/ or /d/ is realized as a flap [ɾ] between vowels (e.g., "water" → [wɑɾɚ] in American English).
Linking: A phonological process in which a consonant is linked to the onset of a following word (e.g., "next train" → [nɛkstreɪn]).
Intrusion: The insertion of a consonant to facilitate the transition between sounds (e.g., /w/ in "two" → /tuːw/).
Devoicing: A process in which a voiced sound becomes voiceless, often at the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant.
Vowel reduction: The weakening of a vowel to schwa or near-schwa in unstressed syllables.
Stress shift: A change in the position of primary stress within a word or phrase.
Intonational boundary: A prosodic boundary marked by a pitch reset or pause, often corresponding to a phrase or clause boundary.
Boundary tone: A prosodic feature realized at the end of an intonational phrase, often marking statement, question, or other illocutionary force.
Phrase accent: A prosodic feature realized at the end of a prosodic word or phrase, often a slight rise or fall.
Nuclear stress (sentence stress): The primary pitch accent in an intonational phrase, typically on the last content word.
Declarative intonation: The falling pitch contour typical of statements in English.
Interrogative intonation: The rising pitch contour typical of yes/no questions in English.
Wh-question intonation: The falling (or falling-rising) pitch contour typical of wh-questions in English.
List intonation: The series of rising tones with a final fall, typical of enumerating items.
Echo question: A question formed by repeating a portion or all of a preceding utterance with rising intonation.
Tag question: A short question appended to a declarative or negative statement to seek confirmation (e.g., "It's cold, isn't it?").
Continuer: A conversational device (e.g., "mm," "uh-huh") that signals the speaker's continued participation.
Overlap (conversational): The simultaneous production of speech by two or more participants in conversation.
Interruption: The interruption of another speaker's turn in conversation.
Completion: The signal by which a speaker indicates the end of their turn (e.g., falling intonation, pause).
Turn constructional unit (TCU): The smallest unit that can constitute a complete turn in conversation.
Transition relevance place (TRP): A point in a speaker's turn where a turn transition is expected (e.g., the end of a syntactic clause).
Preferred / Dispreferred: Categories of second-pair parts in adjacency pairs; "preferred" responses (e.g., agreement) are produced more quickly and with less mitigation than "dispreferred" ones (e.g., disagreement).
Delaying strategy: A pragmatic device used before producing a dispreferred response (e.g., "Well...," "I mean...," pauses).
Mitigation (pragmatic): Strategies to reduce the social impact of a face-threatening act (e.g., hedging, indirectness).
Face-threatening act (FTA): An action that threatens the positive or negative face of a participant.
Politeness theory: A pragmatic framework (Goffman, Brown & Levinson) analyzing how speakers manage face in interaction.
Positive politeness: Strategies that express solidarity and show the hearer's needs are considered (e.g., compliments, in-group language).
Negative politeness: Strategies that minimize imposition and respect the hearer's autonomy (e.g., apologies, hedges, indirect requests).
Off-record strategy: A politeness strategy in which the speaker's illocutionary force is deniable (e.g., hinting rather than requesting directly).
Bald on-record strategy: A direct, unmitigated speech act with no politeness devices.
On-record positive politeness: Direct strategies that show positive regard for the hearer.
On-record negative politeness: Direct strategies that acknowledge imposition and minimize face threat.
Conversational implicature: An inferred meaning not explicitly stated, derived from Grice's maxims and cooperative principles.
Conventional implicature: A meaning attached to a word or construction that is not part of its truth-conditional content (e.g., "but" implies contrast).
Scalar implicature (again): A specific type of conversational implicature based on the use of a weaker member of a scale.
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose literal form differs from its intended illocutionary force (e.g., "Can you pass the salt?" as a request).
Directive (indirect): A request or command expressed in interrogative or declarative form.
Rhetorical question: A question asked for effect rather than to elicit an answer.
Metaphor: A figurative expression in which one domain of experience is described in terms of another (e.g., "time is money").
Simile: A comparison between two unlike things using "like" or "as."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which one entity is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it (e.g., "The White House announced...").
Irony: A figure of speech in which the intended meaning is the opposite of the literal meaning, often with a sense of humor or criticism.
Sarcasm: A sharp or cutting form of irony, often directed at a specific person.
Litotes: An understatement using a double negative to affirm (e.g., "not bad" meaning "good").
Hyperbole: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect (e.g., "I've told you a million times").
Euphemism (rhetorical): A mild or indirect expression substituted for one that is blunt or offensive.
Oxymoron: A combination of contradictory terms (e.g., "deafening silence," "bittersweet").
Pun: A play on words exploiting multiple meanings or similar sounds for humorous or rhetorical effect.

Morphological terminative: The case that marks the endpoint of a motion or process.
Morphological transit: A case marking movement across or through something.
Morphological lative: The case marking movement toward a point.
Morphological privative: A derivational suffix that indicates the absence of a quality, as in English "-less."
Morphological augmentative: A derivational suffix indicating a larger size or amount, as in Spanish "-ón."
Morphological diminutive: A derivational suffix indicating a smaller size or endearment, as in Spanish "-ito" or Russian "-ka."
Morphological augmentative: A suffix indicating increased size, importance, or intensity.
Morphological pejorative: A suffix indicating contempt or a negative evaluation of the referent.
Morphological factitive: A derivational process that creates a verb meaning "to make X" from an adjective or noun.
Morphological factive: A derivational process that creates a verb meaning "to make into X."
Morphological deverbative: A derivational process that creates an adjective or noun from a verb.
Morphological denominal: A derivational process that creates a verb from a noun, such as "butter" → "to butter."
Morphological de-adjectival: A derivational process that creates a noun from an adjective, such as "happy" → "happiness."
Morphological reciprocal: A derivational process that adds a reciprocal meaning to a verb, such as "see" → "meet."
Morphological reflexive: A derivational process that adds a reflexive meaning, indicating the agent acts upon itself.
Morphological passive: A voice that demotes the agent and promotes the patient to subject position.
Morphological active: The default voice in which the subject is the agent of the action.
Morphological antipassive: A voice that demotes the object of a transitive verb, often to an oblique position.
Morphological middle voice: A voice that indicates the subject is both agent and patient, or that the action is performed on or for the subject.
Morphological causative: A voice or derivational process that adds an external causer to a verb.
Morphological applicative: A voice or derivational process that adds an oblique argument to a verb's core arguments.

Morphological split-ergativity: A system in which ergative-absolutive alignment applies in one domain (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative in another (e.g., present tense).
Morphological polypersonal agreement: Agreement in which a verb is marked for more than one core argument, common in polysynthetic languages.
Morphological portmanteau: A single morpheme that fuses multiple grammatical functions, as in Latin "-mus" marking first person plural in some verb forms.
Morphological boundness: The property of a morpheme that must be attached to another morpheme and cannot appear independently.
Morphological free-standing: The property of a morpheme that can appear as an independent word.
Morphological open-class: A word class that readily accepts new members, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
Morphological closed-class: A word class that is resistant to new members, such as prepositions, conjunctions, articles, and pronouns.
Morphological open category: A grammatical category that is not restricted to a fixed set of forms.
Morphological closed category: A grammatical category with a fixed, limited set of members.
Morphological category: A grammatical property expressed by morphological marking, such as tense, aspect, mood, or number.
Morphological feature: A property of a morpheme or word that can be represented as a formal value in a grammatical description.
Morphological specification: The assignment of particular values to morphological features in a grammatical description.
Morphological underspecification: The absence of explicit values for certain morphological features, to be filled in by context or defaults.
Morphological overgeneration: A situation in which a generative grammar produces forms that are not attested in the language.
Morphological overproductivity: The application of a morphological rule to bases where it is not actually productive.
Morphological productivity: The extent to which a morphological process is available for creating new words.
Morphological neutrality: A form that is not marked for a particular morphological category, serving as the default.
Morphological markedness: A form that is overtly marked for a particular morphological category, as opposed to the unmarked default.
Morphological unmarked: The default or neutral form in a paradigm, such as the singular in English nouns.
Morphological marked: The form that overtly indicates a grammatical category, such as the plural "-s" in English nouns.
Morphological zero: A morpheme that is phonologically empty but semantically or grammatically present, such as the English plural of "sheep."
Morphological identity: The condition in which a morpheme has the same form in all its allomorphs.
Morphological variation: The existence of multiple allomorphs for a single morpheme.
Morphological conditioning: The dependence of a morpheme's form on its phonological or morphological environment.
Morphological environment: The surrounding morphological context that influences the form of a morpheme.
Morphological context: The broader grammatical or semantic context in which a morphological form appears.
Morphological domain: The structural domain within which a morphological rule or process operates.
Morphological scope: The range of material over which a morphological process or feature applies.
Morphological interaction: The effect of one morphological process on another, such as the interaction of compounding and inflection.
Morphological competition: The rivalry between multiple morphological strategies for expressing the same grammatical function.
Morphological convergence: The tendency of a language's morphological system to become more regular and predictable over time.
Morphological divergence: The tendency of a language's morphological system to develop new irregularities or distinctions.

Morphological elaboration: The historical increase in a language's morphological complexity.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages by their dominant morphological type.

Morphological theory: The theoretical framework used to explain and predict the structure and behavior of words.
Morphological grammar: The component of a grammar that describes the structure and formation of words.
Morphological syntax: The interface between morphological structure and syntactic structure.
Morphological semantics: The relationship between morphological form and lexical meaning.
Morphological phonology: The interaction between morphological structure and phonological rules.
Morphological morphology: The study of morphology as a distinct subfield of linguistics.
Morphological typology: The comparative study of morphological systems across languages.
Morphological typology: The classification and comparison of morphological types in the world's languages.

Constituent: A syntactic unit that functions as a single element within a larger structure, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, or prepositional phrase.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular part of speech, consisting of that head plus its dependents, such as "the big red ball."
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate (verb phrase), which may be independent or subordinate.
Sentence: The largest unit of syntax, consisting of one or more clauses that form a complete, grammatically well-formed utterance.
Word: The basic free-standing unit of language that can typically appear alone, consisting of one or more morphemes.
Deep structure: In early generative grammar, the underlying syntactic representation from which surface structure is derived through transformations.
Surface structure: The final, pronounced form of a sentence after all syntactic transformations have been applied.
Phrase structure rule: A rule that specifies how phrases are formed from their components, such as NP → Det N.
Transformational rule: A rule that maps a deep structure to a surface structure by rearranging, inserting, or deleting elements.
X-bar theory: A generative syntactic theory that posits a uniform phrase structure in which every phrase has a specifier, a head, and a complement.
Bar: The notation used in X-bar theory to represent the intermediate projection level between a head and its phrase.
Head: The central element of a phrase that determines its grammatical category, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: A constituent that completes the subcategorization frame of a head, such as the object of a transitive verb.
Adjunct: A constituent that modifies a phrase but is not required by the head, such as a prepositional phrase of location.
Specifier: A constituent that appears at the beginning of a phrase, typically modifying or restricting the reference of the head, such as the determiner in a noun phrase.
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply within the output of its own application, allowing for infinite sentence complexity.
Subordination: The syntactic relationship in which one clause is embedded within another as a dependent element.
Coordination: The syntactic relationship in which two or more elements of equal grammatical status are joined by a conjunction.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, such as a relative or complement clause.
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun, such as "the book that I read."
Complement clause: A clause that serves as the complement of a verb, such as "I think [that she is right]."
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that modifies the main clause, expressing time, reason, condition, or manner.
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, typically including determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its arguments and modifiers.
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, including its modifiers and complements.
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb, including its modifiers and complements.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, consisting of the preposition plus its complement, such as "in the house."
Determiner: A word class that includes articles, demonstratives, and other words that specify the reference of a noun phrase.
Article: A type of determiner that indicates definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" and "a" in English.
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to a specific entity in the discourse or physical context, such as "this" or "that."
Indefinite: A determiner that does not specify a particular referent, such as "a," "some," or "any."
Definite: A determiner that specifies a particular, identifiable referent, such as "the" in English.
Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," "or," "because."
Coordination conjunction: A conjunction that joins elements of equal syntactic status, such as "and," "or," "but."
Subordinating conjunction: A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because," "although," "if."
Preposition: A word that typically precedes a noun phrase to express a spatial, temporal, or abstract relationship, such as "in," "on," "at."
Postposition: A word that typically follows a noun phrase to express a relationship, as in many Asian and Native American languages.
Adposition: A term covering both prepositions and postpositions.
Preposition: A word placed before its complement to form a prepositional phrase.
Postposition: A word placed after its complement to form a postpositional phrase.
Case: A grammatical category that expresses the syntactic or semantic relationship of a noun or pronoun to other elements in a sentence.
Nominative: The case that marks the subject of a finite verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative: The case that marks the direct object of a transitive verb.

Instrumental: The case that marks the means or instrument of an action.
Ablative: The case that marks separation or source.
Allative: The case that marks direction toward a goal.
Vocative: The case used to address a person or entity directly.
Ergative: The case that marks the agent of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Absolutive: The case that marks the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Subject: The grammatical element that typically agrees with the verb and is the primary topic or agent of the clause.
Object: The grammatical element that receives the action of the verb, typically the direct or indirect object.
Direct object: The primary object of a transitive verb, typically marked by the accusative case.
Indirect object: The secondary object of a verb, typically marking the recipient or beneficiary of the action.
Agent: The semantic role of the entity that performs or causes an action.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity that is affected by an action.
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that is moved or experienced.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that perceives or feels something.
Goal: The semantic role of the endpoint toward which something is directed.
Source: The semantic role of the starting point from which something moves.
Path: The semantic role of the route or trajectory of movement.
Location: The semantic role of the place where an event occurs.
Instrument: The semantic role of the tool or means by which an action is performed.
Manner: The semantic role of the way in which an action is performed.
Time: The semantic role of the temporal frame in which an event occurs.
Reason: The semantic role of the cause or motivation for an action.
Condition: The semantic role of a prerequisite or hypothetical circumstance.
Concession: The semantic role of an admitted counterfact
