response.text:
Phoneme: A distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English "pin" and "spin."
Phone: A generic term for any distinct speech sound, whether or not it is contrastive in a particular language.
Segmental: Relating to the individual discrete units of speech (vowels and consonants) as opposed to prosodic or suprasegmental features.
Suprasegmental: Prosodic features that extend over multiple segments, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Prosody: The rhythmic, stress, and intonational patterns of speech beyond the level of individual segments.
Intonation: The variation in pitch across a phrase or sentence, used to convey grammatical structure, attitude, or emphasis.
Tone: The use of pitch contrast on syllables to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Stress: The relative prominence given to certain syllables within a word or phrase, often involving increases in pitch, loudness, or duration.
Syllable: A unit of organization in speech consisting of a peak of sonority (nucleus) optionally surrounded by less sonorous segments (onset and coda).
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster preceding the syllable nucleus.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel or syllabic consonant.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster following the syllable nucleus within a syllable.
Mora: A sub-syllabic unit of timing or weight used in phonological analysis to account for patterns of vowel and consonant length.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permitted in a language's syllable structure.
Minimal pair: A pair of words differing in only one segment in the same phonetic environment, used to demonstrate that two sounds are distinct phonemes.
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two or more variants of a phoneme never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more phonetic variants may occur in the same environment without altering meaning.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, such as nasalization before a nasal consonant.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which sounds that are identical or similar become less alike, often across syllable boundaries.
Lenition: A diachronic or contact-induced weakening of a consonant, such as fortis stops becoming fricatives.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant over time or in certain contexts, the reverse of lenition.
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable in connected speech, such as the /t/ in "water" becoming "wadder" in some dialects.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a segment into a word, often to break up an illicit consonant cluster, such as the /n/ in "hundred" from "hundre."
Metathesis: The transposition of two or more adjacent segments, such as the historical shift from "ask" to "aks" in some dialects.
Voicing: A phonological feature in which the vocal folds vibrate during the production of a sound.
Aspiration: A strong puff of air accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in English [pʰ] in "pat."
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic airstream, in which the glottis is closed and the larynx is raised, creating an outward burst of air.
Implosive: A consonant produced with an ingressive (inward) glottalic airstream, in which the larynx is lowered during the closure.
Plosive (Stop): A consonant produced by completely blocking the oral airflow and then releasing it, as in /p/, /t/, /k/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow, as in /s/, /f/, /ʃ/.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation, as in /tʃ/ as in "church."
Nasal: A consonant produced with the oral tract closed and airflow directed through the nasal cavity, as in /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Approximant: A consonant produced with a narrow constriction that does not create turbulent airflow, including glides and liquids.
Lateral: A consonant in which airflow is directed around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant associated with the /r/ sound, which may be a trill, tap, or approximant depending on the language.
Trill: A consonant produced by rapid vibration of a consonantal articulator, such as the alveolar trill /r/ in Spanish "perro."
Tap (Flap): A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of an articulator, as in the /ɾ/ in American English "butter."
Sibilant: A fricative or affricate produced with a high-frequency, forward-directed jet of air, such as /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/.
Glottal stop: A plosive produced at the glottis by closing the vocal folds, represented as /ʔ/ in languages like Arabic and Hawaiian.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant constriction is made, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is modified to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Bilabial: A sound produced with both lips, such as /p/, /b/, /m/, /w/.
Labiodental: A sound produced with the lower lip and upper teeth, such as /f/, /v/.
Dental: A sound produced with the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth, such as /θ/, /ð/ in English "think" and "this."
Alveolar: A sound produced with the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge, such as /t/, /d/, /n/, /s/, /z/, /l/, /r/.
Post-alveolar: A sound produced with the tongue blade just behind the alveolar ridge, such as /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/.
Retroflex: A sound produced with the tongue tip curled back toward the hard palate, as in the /ʈ/, /ɖ/, /ʂ/ of Hindi.
Palatal: A sound produced with the tongue blade or body raised toward the hard palate, such as /j/, /c/, /ɟ/.
Velar: A sound produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate, such as /k/, /g/, /ŋ/, /x/.
Uvular: A sound produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula, such as /q/, /ʁ/, /χ/.
Pharyngeal: A sound produced with the tongue root or uvula constricting the pharynx, as in /ʁ/ (pharyngealized) or /ħ/, /ʕ/ in Arabic.
Epiglottal: A sound produced with the epiglottis raised toward the pharyngeal wall, as in /ʢ/ in some Semitic and African languages.
Glottal: A sound produced at the level of the glottis (vocal folds), such as /h/ or the glottal stop /ʔ/.
Airstream mechanism: The source of pulmonic (lung) or non-pulmonic (glottalic, velaric) airflow used to produce speech sounds.
Pulmonic: The most common airstream mechanism in which air is expelled from the lungs through the vocal tract.
Glottalic: An airstream mechanism using laryngeal movement (ejectives and implosives) rather than lung air.
Velaric: An airstream mechanism using velar closure to create click consonants.
Categorical perception: The tendency of listeners to perceive speech sounds in discrete categories, grouping phonetic variants into the same phoneme.
Phonemic contrast: A pair of sounds in a language that can distinguish word meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in English.
Phonemic neutralization: A context in which a phonemic contrast is eliminated, such as final /t/ and /d/ becoming [ɾ] in some dialects.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction, typically serving as the syllable nucleus.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
Diphthong: A vowel sequence in which the tongue moves from one position to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "time."
Glide (Semivowel): A sound that has features of both vowels and consonants, functioning as a marginal vowel or approximant consonant, such as /j/ and /w/.
Schwa: The most neutral, central, and often reduced vowel sound, transcribed /ə/, common in unstressed syllables.
Vowel reduction: The weakening of a vowel in unstressed positions, typically toward a schwa or a shorter, more centralized quality.
Tense vowel: A vowel produced with greater muscular tension and a more extreme tongue position, contrasted with a lax vowel.
Lax vowel: A vowel produced with less muscular tension and a more neutral tongue position, as in English /ɪ/ versus /iː/.
Front vowel: A vowel produced with the front of the tongue raised, as in /i/, /e/, /æ/.
Back vowel: A vowel produced with the back of the tongue raised, as in /u/, /o/, /ɑ/.
Central vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue in a mid, neutral position, neither notably front nor back.
Rounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips rounded, as in /u/, /o/.
Unrounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral, as in /i/, /e/.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy at specific frequency bands in a vowel's sound spectrum, used to distinguish vowel qualities.
F0 (Fundamental frequency): The lowest and primary frequency of the vocal fold vibration, corresponding to perceived pitch.
Spectrogram: A visual display of the frequency content of a speech signal over time, showing formant structure and energy distribution.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the physical movements of the speech organs.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds, including frequency, amplitude, and duration.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived by the human auditory system.
Voice onset time (VOT): The interval between the release of a stop closure and the onset of voicing, used to distinguish aspiration and voicing contrasts.
Broad transcription: A phonemic notation using slashes / / that records only contrastive sounds, ignoring allophonic detail.
Narrow transcription: A precise phonetic notation using brackets [ ] that records fine-grained allophonic detail.
International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA): The standardized system of symbols for transcribing the sounds of all human languages.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological features organized in a hierarchical structure, with binary or multi-valued features at different tiers.
Natural class: A set of segments sharing one or more phonological features and thus susceptible to the same sound change or rule.
Autosegmental phonology: A framework in which certain features (e.g., tone, stress) are represented on separate tiers linked to the segmental skeleton.
Metrical phonology: A framework for representing stress and rhythmic patterns using metrical trees and grids of feet, iambs, and trochees.
Optimality Theory (OT): A phonological framework in which well-formedness is determined by a ranked set of violable constraints rather than ordered rules.
Constraint: A condition that outputs in Optimality Theory may violate, with more serious violations penalized according to the constraint ranking.
Phonological rule: A transformational operation that maps underlying phonemic representations to surface phonetic forms.
Phonological process: Any systematic operation affecting sound forms, including assimilation, deletion, insertion, and metathesis.
Vowel harmony: A phonological constraint requiring vowels within a word or phrase to share a specific feature, such as backness or rounding.
Tone sandhi: Contextual changes in tone that occur when tones are adjacent, common in tone languages.
Register (phonological): A laryngeal setting that shifts the entire pitch range, distinct from melodic pitch contours.
Pitch accent: A system in which a single high pitch on a specific syllable distinguishes words, as in Japanese, as opposed to a full tone system.
Contour tone: A tone whose pitch changes over the duration of the syllable, such as a rising or falling tone.
Level tone: A tone whose pitch remains constant over the syllable duration.
Intonational phrase: A prosodic unit delimited by pauses or intonational boundaries, often corresponding to a sentence or clause.
Prosodic word: A prosodic unit corresponding roughly to a lexical word, serving as a domain for stress assignment.
Stress timing: A rhythmic property of languages in which stressed syllables tend to occur at regular time intervals, as in English.
Syllable timing: A rhythmic property of languages in which all syllables tend to have roughly equal duration, as in Spanish or French.
Gemination: The lengthening or doubling of a consonant, producing a geminate.
Geminate: A long consonant that occupies the timing of two segments, as in Italian "palla" versus "pala."
Long vowel: A vowel of greater duration than its short counterpart, often contrastive in the language.
Short vowel: A vowel of lesser duration, contrasted with a long vowel in many languages.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of a language, such as the prefix un- in "unhappy."
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Morpheme (free): A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat" or "run."
Morpheme (bound): A morpheme that cannot stand alone and must attach to another morpheme, such as the prefix "un-."
Root: The core morpheme of a word carrying the primary lexical meaning, such as "act" in "action."
Stem: A root to which inflectional morphemes may be attached, forming the basis of word formation.
Affix: A morpheme attached to a stem, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix attached before the stem, as in "un-" in "undo."
Suffix: An affix attached after the stem, as in "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix inserted within the stem, as in the Indonesian -in- in "me-ng-in-ang-kan."
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds the stem, consisting of two parts, as in German ge-...-t in "ge-macht."
Allomorph: One of two or more phonological forms of the same morpheme, such as /p/, /b/, /f/ as allomorphs of English plural.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon of a single morpheme having multiple phonological realizations.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, such as the conjugated forms of a verb.
Inflectional paradigm: The set of grammatically inflected forms a word can take, such as the case endings of a noun.
Derivation: A word-formation process that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category, as in "teach" to "teacher."
Inflection: A morphological process that marks grammatical categories (tense, number, case) without changing the core lexical category.
Agglutination: A morphological type in which morphemes are strung together with clear, one-to-one correspondences between form and meaning, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional (synthetic): A morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical features, as in Latin or Russian verb endings.
Isolating: A morphological type in which each morpheme typically corresponds to one word with little or no affixation, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which a single word can encode the meaning of an entire clause, as in many Native American languages.
Compounding: A word-formation process that combines two or more free morphemes (or roots) into a single word, as in "blackboard."
Reduplication: A word-formation or inflectional process in which all or part of a stem is repeated, as in Indonesian "jalan" to "berjalan."
Zero morpheme: An implicit morpheme with no phonological content, as in the plural of "sheep" where no overt affix appears.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent, such as English "-'s" or clitic pronouns.
Lexical morpheme: A morpheme that carries core lexical (content) meaning, typically corresponding to a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Grammatical morpheme: A morpheme that carries functional (grammatical) meaning, such as case, tense, number, or agreement markers.
Lexeme: The abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of inflected forms of a word, such as the lexeme RUN encompassing run, runs, ran, running.
Derivational morpheme: An affix that creates a new lexeme, often changing the grammatical category, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Inflectional morpheme: An affix that marks grammatical features within the same lexeme, such as "-s" in "cats."
Bound root: A root that cannot appear as a standalone word in a particular language, requiring affixation.
Free root: A root that can function as an independent word.
Derivational affix: An affix that creates a new word or changes the word's grammatical category.
Inflectional affix: An affix that marks grammatical agreement, case, tense, or number without creating a new lexeme.
Morphological alternation: A change in the form of a stem when different morphemes are attached, as in "man/men" or "go/went."
Suppletion: The use of entirely different, unrelated stems for different forms of a word, as in English "go/went/gone" or "is/were."
Morpheme order: The linear sequence of morphemes within a word, which can vary cross-linguistically (e.g., prefix vs. suffix for plural).
Morpheme boundary: The juncture between adjacent morphemes within a word.
Morphological template: An abstract pattern or slot-and-frame structure that constrains the arrangement of consonants and vowels in a word, common in Semitic languages.
Non-concatenative morphology: A type of morphology in which morphemes are not simply strung together linearly but involve interleaving, as in Semitic root-and-pattern systems.
Concatenative morphology: A type of morphology in which morphemes are attached linearly to a stem.
Productive morphology: A morphological process that is actively used by speakers to form new words.
Unproductive (fossilized) morphology: A morphological pattern that is no longer used to create new forms but persists in established vocabulary.
Allomorphic alternation: The predictable or unpredictable alternation between different allomorphs of a morpheme.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morpheme boundaries affect sound patterns.
Syntax: The study of the rules and principles that govern the structure of sentences.
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a unit within a larger structure, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular category (noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition), such as "the big dog."
Noun phrase (NP): A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, potentially including determiners, adjectives, and modifiers.
Verb phrase (VP): A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements and modifiers.
Adjective phrase (AP): A phrase headed by an adjective, including its modifiers.
Adverb phrase (AdvP): A phrase headed by an adverb.
Prepositional phrase (PP): A phrase headed by a preposition, consisting of the preposition and its noun phrase complement.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a finite verb and its arguments, which may be a full sentence or embedded.
Sentence: The maximal syntactic unit, typically consisting of a subject and predicate, expressing a complete thought.
Predicate: The part of a clause that says something about the subject, typically headed by a verb.
Argument: A participant in a predicate relation, typically realized as a noun phrase (subject, object).
Subject: The primary argument of a clause, often (but not always) the agent or topic.
Object: The argument that receives the action of the verb, including direct and indirect objects.
Complement: An argument required by a particular verb or other head, as in "depend on" requiring a complement.
Adjunct: An optional modifier that adds supplementary information but is not required by the head, such as a temporal or locative phrase.
Specifier: The element preceding the head within a phrase in X-bar theory, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Head: The central element of a phrase that determines the phrase's category and subcategorization, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Head complement: The obligatory argument selected by a head, such as the object of a transitive verb.
Head modifier (adjunct): An optional element modifying the head, such as an adjective in a noun phrase.
X-bar schema: A theoretical model of phrase structure proposing a uniform hierarchical structure with specifier, head, and complement positions.
Phrase structure rule: A generative rule specifying how a phrase can be broken down into its immediate constituents.
Tree diagram: A hierarchical diagram representing the syntactic structure of a sentence as nested branching nodes.
Bracketing: The notation of syntactic structure using nested parentheses to show constituent boundaries.
Constituency test: A diagnostic used to identify constituents, including movement, clefting, substitution, and coordination tests.
Coordination: The syntactic process of joining two or more elements of the same category with a coordinating conjunction (and, or, but).
Subordination: The syntactic process of embedding one clause within another, typically with a subordinating conjunction or complementizer.
Conjunction: A function word or morpheme used to join constituents, classified as coordinating or subordinating.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a complement clause, such as "that" in "I think that she left" or "whether" in "I wonder whether she left."
Determiner: A word that specifies the reference of a noun, including articles (the, a), demonstratives (this, that), and quantifiers (every, some).
Article: A determiner that marks definiteness (the) or indefiniteness (a, an).
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun pointing to a specific referent in context, such as "this," "that," "these," "those."
Quantifier: A word expressing quantity, such as "every," "some," "few," "many."
Recursion: The syntactic property that allows phrases to be embedded within phrases of the same category indefinitely, generating infinitely complex sentences.
Embedding: The inclusion of one clause or phrase within another, as in "I know that she thinks that he left."
Matrix clause: The main (outermost) clause in an embedded structure.
Embedded clause: A clause contained within another clause, such as a complement or relative clause.
Relative clause: A clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or marker, as in "the book that I read."
Noun clause: A clause that functions syntactically as a noun, as in "What she said surprised me."
Adverbial clause: A clause that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb, typically indicating time, place, reason, or condition.
Adjective clause: A clause that modifies a noun, functioning as an attributive modifier.
Subordinate clause: A clause that is syntactically dependent on another clause and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
Coordinate clause: A clause that is joined to another of equal syntactic status by a coordinating conjunction.
Main clause: The independent clause in a sentence that can stand alone.
Displacement (movement): A syntactic operation in which a constituent is moved from its base-generated position to a different position in the structure.
Trace: An empty category left behind in the base position when a constituent undergoes movement.
Ex-situ: A strategy in which a moved element (e.g., a wh-word) appears in a position different from its semantic role.
In-situ: A strategy in which an element (e.g., a wh-word) remains in its base-generated position.
A-movement: Movement of an argument (NP) to a position where it receives a theta role, such as passivization.
A-bar movement: Movement of a non-argument or to a position that does not assign a theta role, such as wh-movement or topicalization.
Theta role (thematic role): The semantic relation a verb assigns to its arguments, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, Goal.
Theta grid: The abstract structure listing the theta roles a predicate assigns to its arguments.
Agent: The theta role of a voluntary, typically animate doer of the action.
Patient: The theta role of the entity most directly affected by the action.
Theme: The theta role of the entity that undergoes a change of location or state.
Goal: The theta role of the destination of a motion.
Source: The theta role of the origin of a motion.
Location: The theta role of a static position or place.
Experiencer: The theta role of an entity that feels, perceives, or undergoes a mental or physical state.
Stimulus: The theta role of the cause of an experience, as in "The movie bored me."
Recipient: The theta role of an entity that receives something.
Beneficiary: The theta role of an entity that benefits from the action.
Possessor: The theta role of an entity that owns or has something.
Instrument: The theta role of an entity used to carry out the action.
Valency (valence): The number of arguments a predicate requires or selects, as in monovalent, bivalent, or trivalent verbs.
Transitive: A verb that takes two arguments (subject and object), as in "The dog chased the cat."
Intransitive: A verb that takes one argument (subject only), as in "The dog slept."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes three arguments, typically a subject, a direct object, and an indirect object, as in "She gave him a book."
Bivalent: A predicate requiring exactly two arguments.
Monovalent: A predicate requiring exactly one argument.
Trivalent: A predicate requiring exactly three arguments.
Copula: A linking verb that connects a subject to a predicative complement, such as "be" in English.
Copular construction: A clause structure in which a copula links a subject to a predicate nominal or adjectival.
Equative sentence: A sentence asserting identity between two noun phrases, as in "The president is that man."
Existential sentence: A sentence asserting the existence or presence of an entity, as in "There is a cat on the mat."
Expletive: A syntactic element with no semantic content, used to satisfy grammatical requirements, such as "there" in "there are problems."
Dummy subject: A pronoun or expression serving as a syntactic subject without referring to an entity, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Extraposition: A syntactic movement in which a heavy constituent (often a clause) is moved to a position later in the sentence.
Topicalization: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is moved to the beginning of a clause for discourse prominence.
Cleft sentence: A construction that places focus on a specific constituent, as in "It was John who called" or "What I need is a break."
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction with an open relative clause, as in "What I need is a break."
Focus: The element in an utterance that carries new or contrastive information, highlighted by intonation, word order, or morphology.
Contrastive focus: Focus that implies a contrast with an alternative, as in "I want the RED apple" (not the green one).
Informational focus: Focus marking new information without necessarily implying a specific alternative.
Deixis: The use of linguistic elements (demonstratives, pronouns, tense, spatial adverbs) that require contextual anchoring for full interpretation.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned antecedent, such as a pronoun referring to a noun.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to a subsequent antecedent.
Antecedent: The expression to which an anaphoric or cataphoric element refers.
Coreference: The relation between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Binding theory: The set of principles governing the interpretation of pronouns, anaphors, and variables in syntax, including Principles A, B, and C.
Principle A: The binding principle requiring an anaphor (e.g., "himself") to be bound by an antecedent within its local domain.
Principle B: The binding principle requiring a pronoun to be free in its local domain.
Principle C: The binding principle requiring an R-expression (e.g., a proper name) to be free everywhere.
Local domain (governing category): The syntactic domain within which binding relations are evaluated.
Case (morphological): The set of inflectional forms a noun or pronoun takes to signal its grammatical function, such as nominative, accusative, or genitive.
Nominative: The case typically marking the subject of a transitive verb.
Accusative: The case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Dative: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive: The case typically marking possession or association.
Instrumental: The case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Locative: The case marking the location of an action or entity.
Ablative: The case marking separation or movement away from a location.
Vocative: The case used for direct address.
Ergative: A case marking the agent of a transitive verb, as in ergative-absolutive languages.
Absolutive: A case marking the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb, as in ergative-absolutive languages.
Ergative-absolutive alignment: A case-marking system in which intransitive subjects are aligned with transitive objects (absolutive), and transitive subjects receive a distinct ergative case.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A case-marking system in which intransitive subjects are aligned with transitive subjects (nominative), and transitive objects receive a distinct accusative case.
Split ergativity: A system in which a language uses ergative-absolutive alignment in some grammatical contexts and nominative-accusative in others.
Absolutive: (see above)
Word order: The typical linear arrangement of major constituents (subject, object, verb) in a language.
SVO: Subject-Verb-Object word order, as in English "The cat chased the mouse."
SOV: Subject-Object-Verb word order, as in Japanese and Turkish.
VSO: Verb-Subject-Object word order, as in Classical Arabic and Irish.
V2 (verb-second): A syntactic property in which the finite verb occupies the second position in main clauses, as in German and Dutch.
Topic: The discourse referent about which a sentence or clause makes a new assertion.
Comment (rheme): The new information asserted about the topic.
Information structure: The organization of discourse into old (given) and new (focus) information.
Given-new (old-new): A discourse principle organizing information flow from previously mentioned to newly introduced content.
Theme: The initial, typically given information in a clause (similar to topic).
Rheme: The final, typically new information in a clause (similar to comment).
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including the meaning of words, sentences, and their relations.
Lexical semantics: The study of word meaning, including sense relations, polysemy, and lexical structure.
Compositional semantics: The study of how sentence meaning is built from the meanings of its parts according to syntactic structure.
Proposition: The truth-evaluable content expressed by a declarative sentence, abstracted from its surface form.
Truth conditions: The circumstances under which a sentence or proposition is true, central to truth-conditional semantics.
Predicate logic: A formal logical system used in semantics to represent the logical structure of natural language sentences.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as in "John is a bachelor" entails "John is male."
Presupposition: Background meaning assumed to be true by both speaker and hearer, as in "John stopped smoking" presupposes that John used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning inferred from context rather than directly encoded in the linguistic form, following Gricean principles.
Gricean maxims: Four conversational maxims (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner) proposed by H.P. Grice that guide cooperative communication.
Cooperative principle: Grice's general max

The user wants a glossary of linguistics terms. The key constraints are:
1. Each term should be on a new line
2. Format: Term: Definition
3. The glossary is evaluated based on total number of terms included
4. So I should maximize the number of terms I can include

Let me write as many linguistics terms as I can, each on its own line with the format "Term: Definition". I'll try to cover all major areas of linguistics: phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, historical linguistics, computational linguistics, etc.

Let me go through systematically and write as many as I can:

Phonetics:
1. Phonetics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds, including their production, transmission, and perception.
2. Articulation: The process by which speech sounds are produced by the movement of the vocal organs.
3. Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound.
4. Consonant: A speech sound produced with a complete or partial closure in the vocal tract.
5. Vowel: A speech sound produced without significant constriction of the vocal tract.
6. Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
7. Manner of articulation: The way in which airflow is modified to produce a consonant sound.
8. Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking airflow and then releasing it in a burst.
9. Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow channel that causes turbulent airflow.
10. Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases as a fricative.
11. Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to pass through the nasal cavity.
12. Liquid: A class of consonants including laterals and rhotics, characterized by free airflow around the constriction.
13. Glide: A consonant that functions as a transitional sound between vowels, produced with a narrow constriction.
14. Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip touching the alveolar ridge, allowing air to flow around the sides.
15. Rhotic: A consonant sound characterized by a raised tongue body, such as [r] or [ɾ].
16. Alveolar: A place of articulation where the tongue tip contacts the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth.
17. Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips.
18. Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth.
19. Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip and the upper teeth.
20. Palatal: A place of articulation involving the front of the tongue and the hard palate.
21. Velar: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the soft palate (velum).
22. Uvular: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the uvula.
23. Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the tongue root and the pharyngeal wall.
24. Glottal: A place of articulation at the glottis (vocal folds).
25. Aspiration: A burst of breath that accompanies the release of certain consonants.
26. Suprasegmental: Features of speech that extend over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
27. Prosody: The pattern of stress, rhythm, and intonation in spoken language.
28. Intonation: The rise and fall of pitch across a phrase or sentence.
29. Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable in a word or utterance.
30. Rhythm: The pattern of alternating stressed and unstressed syllables in speech.
31. Tone: A contrastive use of pitch to distinguish meaning, as in tonal languages.
32. Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy that characterizes the quality of a vowel sound.
33. F0 (Fundamental Frequency): The primary pitch of a voiced sound, determined by the rate of vocal fold vibration.
34. Harmonic: A multiple of the fundamental frequency in a complex periodic waveform.
35. Acoustic phonetics: The branch of phonetics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds as sound waves.
36. Articulatory phonetics: The branch of phonetics that studies how speech sounds are produced by the vocal tract.
37. Auditory phonetics: The branch of phonetics that studies how speech sounds are perceived by the listener.
38. Spectrogram: A visual display of the frequency content of a speech signal over time.
39. Vowel height: The vertical position of the tongue body (high, mid, low) in vowel production.
40. Vowel backness: The horizontal position of the tongue body (front, central, back) in vowel production.
41. Rounding: The protrusion of the lips during the production of a vowel.
42. Tense vowel: A vowel produced with a constricted pharynx and typically higher frequency formants.
43. Lax vowel: A vowel produced with a relaxed pharynx and typically lower frequency formants.
44. Trapping: The shortening of a vowel before a voiceless consonant in some dialects.
45. Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one point of articulation and glides to another within the same syllable.
46. Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel sound [ə], the most common vowel in English.
47. Vowel reduction: The process by which vowels in unstressed syllables are weakened or centralized.
48. Coarticulation: The influence of neighboring sounds on the articulation of a given sound.
49. Liaison: The linking of words in connected speech, often involving the addition or modification of a sound.
50. Assimilation: The process by which a sound changes to become more like a neighboring sound.
51. Dissimilation: The process by which similar sounds in close proximity become less alike.
52. Metathesis: The reversal of the order of two sounds within a word or between words.
53. Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word.
54. Elision: The omission of a sound from a word in connected speech.
55. Lenition: The weakening of a consonant over time or in specific phonological environments.
56. Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant over time or in specific phonological environments.
57. Palatalization: The process by which a consonant is articulated closer to the palate.
58. Velarization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with a secondary articulation at the velum.
59. Labialization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with rounded lips.
60. Devoicing: The process by which a voiced sound becomes voiceless.
61. Voicing assimilation: The process by which a sound's voicing matches that of a neighboring sound.
62. Nasalization: The process by which an oral sound gains a nasal resonance.
63. Velarization of /l/: The pronunciation of /l/ with a secondary velar articulation, as in [ɫ].
64. Fricativization: The process by which a stop consonant becomes a fricative.
65. Deaffrication: The process by which the plosive portion of an affricate is lost, leaving only the fricative.

Phonology:
66. Phonology: The branch of linguistics that studies the systematic organization of sounds in a language.
67. Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound that can distinguish meaning in a language.
68. Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word.
69. Phonemic contrast: A minimal pair demonstrating that two sounds belong to different phonemes.
70. Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one sound in the same position and have different meanings.
71. Complementary distribution: A relationship between two sounds that never occur in the same phonological environment.
72. Free variation: A situation where two or more sounds can be used interchangeably without changing meaning.
73. Phonotactics: The rules governing the permissible combinations of phonemes in a language.
74. Syllable: The basic unit of phonological organization, typically consisting of an onset, nucleus, and coda.
75. Onset: The consonant(s) preceding the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
76. Nucleus: The core vowel or syllabic consonant of a syllable.
77. Coda: The consonant(s) following the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
78. Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and coda.
79. Peak: The most sonorous point in a syllable, typically the vowel nucleus.
80. Syllabification: The process of dividing a string of sounds into syllables.
81. Maximal onset principle: The rule that consonants between vowels are assigned to the onset of the following syllable whenever possible.
82. Phonological rule: A rule that describes a regular change or constraint in the sound system of a language.
83. Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation that organizes distinctive features in a hierarchical structure.
84. Distinctive feature: A binary property (such as [+voice], [+nasal]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
85. Natural class: A group of sounds that share one or more distinctive features and can be targeted by a phonological rule.
86. Archiphoneme: An abstract phoneme that represents a class of sounds sharing common features.
87. Underlying form: The abstract phonological representation of a word before phonological rules are applied.
88. Surface form: The actual phonetic realization of a word after all phonological rules have been applied.
89. Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language.
90. Root: The core morpheme that carries the primary lexical meaning.
91. Affix: A morpheme attached to a root or stem.
92. Prefix: An affix attached before the root.
93. Suffix: An affix attached after the root.
94. Infix: An affix inserted within a root.
95. Circumfix: A pair of affixes attached on both sides of a root.
96. Clitic: A morpheme that is morphologically independent but phonologically dependent on an adjacent word.
97. Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme.
98. Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a morpheme depending on its phonological or morphological environment.
99. Reduplication: A morphological process in which part or all of a morpheme is repeated to create a new form.
100. Suppletion: The use of an entirely different root to express a morphological relationship.

Let me continue with more terms across various subfields:

Morphology:
101. Morphology: The branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
102. Inflection: A morphological process that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or gender.
103. Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech.
104. Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created in a language.
105. Compounding: The process of combining two or more independent words to form a new word.
106. Blending: The process of combining parts of two words to create a new word (e.g., "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch").
107. Clipping: The process of shortening a word without changing its meaning or part of speech (e.g., "ad" from "advertisement").
108. Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase.
109. Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix from an existing word (e.g., "edit" from "editor").
110. Conversion: The process of forming a new word by changing the part of speech without adding an affix (e.g., "to email" from "email").
111. Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that imitate natural sounds (e.g., "buzz," "sizzle").
112. Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
113. Agglutinative: A morphological type in which morphemes are combined with clear boundaries and minimal allomorphy.
114. Fusional: A morphological type in which multiple grammatical categories are fused into a single affix.
115. Isolating: A morphological type in which words consist of a single morpheme and grammatical relations are expressed by word order.
116. Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which many morphemes are combined into a single word to express what would be a full clause.
117. Morpheme boundary: The boundary between morphemes within a word.
118. Stem: The part of a word to which affixes are attached.
119. Base: The form to which a morpheme is attached, which may itself be complex.
120. Parasitic morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must attach to another word.
121. Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot occur independently as a word.
122. Free morpheme: A morpheme that can occur independently as a word.

Syntax:
123. Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles by which sentences are constructed.
124. Sentence: A grammatical unit consisting of one or more clauses.
125. Clause: A grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate.
126. Phrase: A group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger structure.
127. Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun, including its determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
128. Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its objects and adjuncts.
129. Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, typically including an object.
130. Adjunct: A syntactic element that modifies a clause or phrase but is not required for grammaticality.
131. Complement: A syntactic element that is required to complete the meaning of a predicate or head.
132. Subject: The grammatical argument that typically agrees with the verb and is the topic of the clause.
133. Object: The grammatical argument that is acted upon by the verb.
134. Agent: The entity that performs the action expressed by the verb.
135. Patient: The entity that undergoes the action expressed by the verb.
136. Theme: The entity that is moved or located by the action.
137. Experiencer: The entity that experiences a state or event.
138. Goal: The entity or location toward which something moves.
139. Source: The entity or location from which something moves.
140. Path: The trajectory along which something moves.
141. Instrument: The entity used to perform an action.
142. Recipient: The entity that receives something.
143. Possessor: The entity that owns or has a relationship to a possessed entity.
144. Possessum: The entity that is possessed.
145. Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence before surface transformations are applied.
146. Surface structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied.
147. Transformational grammar: A framework for syntax that uses transformational rules to derive surface structures from deep structures.
148. Phrase structure grammar: A framework for syntax that uses rewrite rules to generate hierarchical structures.
149. X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure that proposes a universal hierarchical structure for all phrases.
150. Specifier: The element in a phrase that occupies the specifier position, typically preceding the head.
151. Complement: The element in a phrase that is selected by the head and follows it.
152. Adjunct: An optional element in a phrase that modifies the projection.
153. Head: The central element of a phrase that determines the category of the phrase.
154. Projection: The syntactic structure built around a head.
155. Merge: The basic operation in Minimalist syntax that combines two syntactic objects into a new set.
156. Move: The operation in syntax that displaces an element from one position to another.
157. Trace: The empty element left behind when a constituent is moved.
158. Theta role: The semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate.
159. Theta criterion: The principle that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
160. Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase.
161. Nominative case: The case typically marking the subject of a clause.
162. Accusative case: The case typically marking the direct object of a clause.
163. Dative case: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
164. Genitive case: The case typically marking possession or other genitive relationships.
165. Ergative: A case marking system in which the subject of an intransitive verb is marked the same as the object of a transitive verb.
166. Absolutive: The case in an ergative system that marks the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb.
167. A-grammar: A syntactic framework that classifies arguments into A (agent-like) and B (patient-like) categories.
168. Word order: The linear arrangement of grammatical units in a sentence.
169. SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object.
170. SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb.
171. VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object.
172. VOS: A word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject.
173. OVS: A word order in which the object precedes the verb, which precedes the subject.
174. OSV: A word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb.
175. Free word order: A syntactic system in which word order is not fixed and does not encode grammatical relations.
176. Pro-drop: The omission of a pronoun when its reference is clear from context.
177. Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the front of a sentence to mark it as the topic.
178. Cleft: A syntactic construction that highlights a particular element, often using "it is... that" structures.
179. Passivization: A syntactic process that promotes the object to subject position and demotes the agent.
180. Nominalization: The process of converting a verb or clause into a noun or noun phrase.
181. Subordination: The process of embedding one clause within another as a dependent clause.
182. Coordination: The process of joining two or more clauses or phrases of equal status.
183. Embedding: The inclusion of one clause within another clause.
184. Recursion: The syntactic property that allows structures to be embedded within structures of the same type indefinitely.
185. Island constraint: A syntactic constraint that prevents extraction from certain subordinate structures.
186. Binding theory: A component of syntax that governs the interpretation of anaphoric expressions such as pronouns and reflexives.
187. A-binding: The binding of reflexives and anaphors within a local domain.
188. A-bar binding: The binding of moved or base-generated A-bar positions.
189. C-command: A structural relationship in which a node dominates a sister that contains another node.
190. Government: A structural relationship in which a head directly selects a complement.
191. Theta grid: The assignment of theta roles to arguments in a clause.
192. Argument: A syntactic element that is required by a predicate to be well-formed.
193. Subcategorization: The specification of the arguments that a predicate requires.
194. Valency: The number of arguments a verb requires.
195. Unaccusative: An intransitive verb whose sole argument is semantically a patient or theme rather than an agent.
196. Unergative: An intransitive verb whose sole argument is semantically an agent.
197. Light verb: A verb that contributes little semantic content and relies on its complement for meaning.
198. Auxiliary: A verb that accompanies a main verb to express grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, or mood.
199. Modal verb: A type of auxiliary that expresses necessity, possibility, permission, or obligation.
200. Copula: A verb (such as "be") that links the subject to a predicate nominal or adjective.

Semantics and Pragmatics:
201. Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language.
202. Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to meaning.
203. Lexical semantics: The study of meaning at the word level.
204. Compositional semantics: The study of how the meaning of complex expressions is derived from the meanings of their parts.
205. Truth-conditional semantics: A semantic framework that defines the meaning of a sentence in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
206. Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it denotes in the world.
207. Sense: The linguistic meaning of a word or expression, abstracted from any particular context.
208. Denotation: The class of entities to which a term applies.
209. Connotation: The associative or emotional meaning of a word beyond its literal sense.
210. Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word having multiple related meanings.
211. Homonymy: The phenomenon of distinct words sharing the same form but having unrelated meanings.
212. Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or very similar meanings.
213. Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings.
214. Hyponym: A word whose meaning is a subset of the meaning of a more general word.
215. Hypernym: A word whose meaning encompasses the meanings of more specific words.
216. Meronym: A word that denotes a part of a whole.
217. Holonym: A word that denotes a whole composed of parts.
218. Prototype theory: A semantic theory that posits that category membership is graded based on similarity to a central example.
219. Frame semantics: A semantic approach that organizes word meanings in terms of structured scenes or situations.
220. Cognitive semantics: A semantic approach that grounds meaning in embodied experience and conceptual structure.
221. Conceptual metaphor: A systematic mapping from a source domain to a target domain that structures thought and language.
222. Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another.
223. Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by the name of something associated with it.
224. Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or other operator has effect in a sentence.
225. Ambiguity: The property of a linguistic expression that allows it to be interpreted in more than one way.
226. Syntactic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible syntactic structures.
227. Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple senses.
228. Vagueness: The property of a term that has a gradual boundary of applicability rather than a sharp one.
229. Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for an utterance to be meaningful.
230. Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
231. Implicature: A meaning that is communicated but not explicitly encoded in the linguistic form.
232. Gricean maxims: A set of principles (Quality, Quantity, Relation, Manner) that govern cooperative communication.
233. Conversational implicature: An inferred meaning that arises from the assumption that the speaker is following the maxims of conversation.
234. Scalar implicature: An implicature based on the assumption that the speaker has chosen the strongest relevant term on a scale.
235. Deixis: The linguistic expression of relationships to the surrounding context, such as person, place, and time.
236. Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity.
237. Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse.
238. Coreference: The relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
239. Discourse: Language use in extended communication, beyond the single sentence.
240. Discourse marker: A word or expression that organizes discourse, such as "however," "meanwhile," or "by the way."
241. Topic: The entity or subject about which a discourse or clause is concerned.
242. Focus: The element in an utterance that is presented as new or contrastive information.
243. Given information: Information that is already established in the discourse.
244. New information: Information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
245. Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given and new information.
246. Speech act: A linguistic action performed by uttering a sentence, such as promising, ordering, or asserting.
247. Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance.
248. Illocutionary act: The intended function of an utterance, such as requesting, warning, or declaring.
249. Perlocutionary act: The effect of an utterance on the listener.
250. Indirect speech act: An utterance whose illocutionary force differs from its literal propositional content.
251. Performative: A speech act that brings about the very action it describes by being uttered (e.g., "I hereby declare you married").
252. Politeness strategy: A linguistic device used to mitigate face-threatening acts.
253. Face: The public self-image that a person claims in social interaction.
254. Positive face: The desire to be approved of, liked, and admired by others.
255. Negative face: The desire to be unimpeded and free from imposition.
256. Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation.
257. Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular communicative situation.
258. Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its components.
259. Phraseology: The study of fixed and semi-fixed expressions in a language.
260. Collocation: A typical or habitual co-occurrence of words (e.g., "make a decision" rather than "do a decision").

Sociolinguistics and Dialectology:
261. Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the relationship between language and society.
262. Dialect: A variety of language associated with a particular region, social group, or community.
263. Accent: The phonetic and phonological characteristics of a speaker's variety.
264. Sociolect: A dialect associated with a particular social group.
265. Ethnolect: A dialect associated with a particular ethnic or cultural group.
266. Areal linguistics: The study of linguistic features shared by languages in a geographic area.
267. Sprachbund: A group of languages that share features due to prolonged contact rather than common ancestry.
268. Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages that leads to mutual influence.
269. Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language.
270. Creole: A fully developed language that evolves from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
271. Bilingualism: The ability to use two or more languages.
272. Multilingualism: The ability to use more than two languages.
273. Language dominance: The tendency of one language to be preferred over another in a multilingual context.
274. Language interference: The influence of one language on another in the speech of a bilingual or multilingual speaker.
275. Code-mixing: The alternation between two languages within a single clause or sentence.
276. Borrowing: The adoption of a word or morpheme from one language into another.
277. Loanword: A word adopted from another language.
278. Calque: A loan translation in which the components of a word in one language are translated into another.
279. Interlingua: A constructed language designed to facilitate international communication.
280. Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
281. Language prestige: The social value attributed to a particular language or variety.
282. Standard language: The variety of a language that is codified and used in formal contexts.
283. Vernacular: The native or everyday language of a community.
284. Dialect leveling: The process by which distinctive dialect features are reduced or eliminated.
285. Dialectal differentiation: The process by which a uniform variety develops regional differences.
286. Isogloss: A geographic boundary that separates areas where a particular linguistic feature is or is not used.
287. Linguistic landscape: The visible language use in a physical environment, such as signs, advertisements, and public notices.
288. Language policy: The set of decisions and regulations that govern the use of language in a society.
289. Language planning: The deliberate effort to influence the development or use of a language.
290. Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker.
291. Language revitalization: Efforts to reverse the decline of a language and reestablish its use in a community.
292. Endangerment: The state of a language that is at risk of being lost due to a decline in its speaker community.
293. Language attitude: The beliefs, feelings, and opinions that people hold about languages and their speakers.
294. Linguistic imperialism: The dominance of one language over others through political, economic, or cultural power.
295. Diglossia: A situation in which two varieties of a language or two different languages are used in distinct social domains.
296. Vernacular: The everyday language used in informal settings.
297. High variety: The prestigious variety of language used in formal education and official contexts.
298. Low variety: The informal, everyday variety of language used in casual settings.
299. Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular linguistic variety or feature.
300. Stigmatized feature: A linguistic feature that is negatively judged by the speech community.

Historical Linguistics:
301. Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the origins and changes in languages over time.
302. Comparative method: A methodology for reconstructing proto-languages by comparing related languages.
303. Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of languages is derived.
304. Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestor.
305. Cognate: A word in one language that has a common etymological origin with a word in another language.
306. Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.
307. Sound change: A systematic change in the pronunciation of a language over time.
308. Regular sound change: A sound change that applies uniformly across a language, as opposed to irregular changes.
309. Grimm's Law: The systematic consonant shift that distinguishes Germanic languages from other Indo-European languages.
310. Verner's Law: A phonological rule that explains exceptions to Grimm's Law based on stress patterns.
311. Internal reconstruction: A method of reconstructing an earlier stage of a language using only data from that language itself.
312. Reconstruction: The process of hypothesizing the features of a proto-language based on comparative evidence.
313. Language drift: The gradual, cumulative change in a language over generations.
314. Language shift: The process by which a community of speakers abandons its native language in favor of another.
315. Language isolation: The state of a language that has no demonstrated genetic relationship with any other language.
316. Language stock: A proposed grouping of language families that may share a deeper common ancestor.
317. Macrofamily: A proposed grouping of language families at a higher level than the established family.
318. Phylogenetic tree: A branching diagram showing the proposed evolutionary relationships among languages.
319. Genetic relationship: The relationship between languages that share a common ancestor.
320. Diachronic linguistics: The study of language change over time, as opposed to synchronic study.
321. Synchronic linguistics: The study of a language at a single point in time, without reference to its history.
322. Palaeography: The study of ancient and medieval writing systems and manuscripts.
323. Philology: The study of language in written historical sources, including textual criticism and literary history.
324. Morphological typology: The classification of languages based on their morphological structure.
325. Syntactic typology: The classification of languages based on their syntactic properties.
326. Phonological typology: The classification of languages based on their sound systems.
327. Typological universals: Generalizations about the possible and typical structures across the world's languages.
328. Markedness: The relative complexity or unusualness of a linguistic feature compared to unmarked alternatives.
329. Unmarked form: The default or least marked form in a grammatical paradigm.
330. Marked form: A form that is more complex or less frequent than the unmarked alternative.

Psycholinguistics and Language Processing:
331. Psycholinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the cognitive processes involved in language acquisition, production, and comprehension.
332. Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn language, particularly in childhood.
333. Critical period: A hypothesized period during which language acquisition is most efficient.
334. Language instinct: The innate capacity for language acquisition, as proposed in generative grammar.
335. Universal Grammar: The hypothesized innate knowledge of language principles that all humans possess.
336. Language faculty: The cognitive system specialized for language processing.
337. Lexical access: The process of retrieving word information from the mental lexicon during language processing.
338. Lexical decision: A psycholinguistic task in which participants determine whether a string of letters is a word.
339. Reading span: The amount of text that can be held in memory during reading comprehension.
340. Working memory: The cognitive system that temporarily holds and manipulates information during language processing.
341. Phonological loop: A component of working memory responsible for processing verbal and auditory information.
342. Chunking: The process of grouping individual elements into larger, more manageable units.
343. Sentence processing: The cognitive process of parsing and interpreting the meaning of a sentence.
344. Garden-path sentence: A sentence that leads the reader or listener into an initially incorrect interpretation.
345. Parsing: The process of assigning a syntactic structure to a string of words.
346. Incremental processing: The process of building up a representation of language input as it is received, word by word.
347. Reanalysis: The process of revising a partially built syntactic or semantic representation.
348. Tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: The experience of being unable to retrieve a known word despite partial knowledge of it.
349. Lexical retrieval: The process of accessing a word's phonological form from its semantic and syntactic information.
350. Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage that impairs language production, comprehension, or both.
351. Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech production.
352. Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech and impaired comprehension.
353. Specific language impairment: A developmental condition in which a child has difficulty acquiring language without an identifiable cause.
354. Stuttering: A fluency disorder characterized by repetitions, prolongations, or blocks in speech production.
355. Language lateralization: The tendency for language processing to be concentrated in one hemisphere of the brain, typically the left.
356. Broca's area: A region in the left frontal lobe associated with speech production and syntactic processing.
357. Wernicke's area: A region in the left temporal lobe associated with language comprehension.
358. Angular gyrus: A brain region involved in the integration of visual, auditory, and language information.
359. Arcuate fasciculus: A bundle of nerve fibers connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas.
360. Neural network model: A computational model of language processing inspired by the structure of the brain.

Computational and Theoretical Linguistics:
361. Computational linguistics: The application of computer science methods to the study and processing of language.
362. Natural language processing: The field of computer science concerned with enabling machines to understand and generate human language.
363. Token: An individual instance of a word in a text.
364. Type: A unique word form in a text, regardless of frequency.
365. Type-token ratio: The ratio of unique words to total words in a text, used as a measure of lexical diversity.
366. Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic analysis.
367. Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large collections of text data.
368. Frequency analysis: The statistical analysis of how often words or linguistic features occur in a corpus.
369. Collocation: A pair or group of words that co-occur with higher frequency than expected by chance.
370. N-gram: A sequence of n consecutive words in a text.
371. Language model: A statistical model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words.
372. Part-of-speech tagging: The process of assigning grammatical categories to words in a text.
373. Named entity recognition: The process of identifying and classifying proper nouns and other named entities in text.
374. Dependency parsing: A method of syntactic analysis that identifies the dependencies between words in a sentence.
375. Constituency parsing: A method of syntactic analysis that identifies the hierarchical phrase structure of a sentence.
376. Machine translation: The automated translation of text from one language to another.
377. Speech recognition: The process of converting spoken language into text using computational methods.
378. Text-to-speech: The process of converting written text into spoken language using computational methods.
379. Computational phonology: The application of computational methods to the study of sound systems.
380. Computational semantics: The application of computational methods to the study of meaning in language.
381. Semantic role labeling: The task of identifying the semantic roles of arguments in a sentence.
382. Word sense disambiguation: The process of determining the correct sense of a word in a given context.
383. Ontology: A formal representation of knowledge in a domain, used in computational semantics.
384. Knowledge representation: The method of encoding information in a form that can be used by a computer system.
385. Statistical natural language processing: The use of statistical methods for language processing tasks.
386. Neural language model: A language model based on neural network architectures.
387. Transformer model: A neural network architecture that uses self-attention mechanisms for sequence processing.
388. Tokenization: The process of breaking a text stream into individual tokens.
389. Lemmatization: The process of reducing a word to its base or dictionary form.
390. Stemming: The process of reducing a word to its stem by removing affixes.

Theoretical and Structural:
391. Generative grammar: A framework for linguistics that seeks to describe the set of grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules.
392. Noam Chomsky: The linguist who founded modern generative grammar and the theory of Universal Grammar.
393. Deep structure: The underlying representation of a sentence in early generative grammar.
394. Surface structure: The observed form of a sentence after transformations are applied.
395. Transformational rule: A rule in generative grammar that converts one representation into another.
396. X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure positing a universal pattern of projection for all categories.
397. Government and Binding theory: A framework within generative grammar that organizes syntactic theory around principles and parameters.
398. Minimalist Program: The most recent iteration of generative grammar, seeking to reduce syntactic operations to a minimal set.
399. Feature: A property that distinguishes one linguistic element from another.
400. Merge: The operation in Minimalist syntax that combines two syntactic objects.
401. Phase: A domain of computation in Minimalist syntax.
402. Phase head: The element that defines the boundaries of a phase.
403. Phase edge: The outermost position within a phase to which material can be moved.
404. vP: The projection of a light verb, containing the verb and its internal arguments.
405. VP: The projection of a main verb, containing the verb and its arguments.
406. IP: The projection of inflection, containing the subject and the verb phrase.
407. CP: The projection of complementizer, the highest phrase in a clause.
408. DP: The projection of determiner, proposed to be the head of the noun phrase.
409. NP: The projection of noun, containing the noun and its modifiers.
410. AP: The projection of adjective.
411. PP: The projection of preposition.
412. AdvP: The projection of adverb.
413. NumP: The projection of numeral.
414. DegP: The projection of degree.
415. FocP: The projection of focus.
416. TopP: The projection of topic.
417. ForceP: The projection of illocutionary force.
418. MoodP: The projection of modal mood.
419. Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the speech time.
420. Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure of an event.
421. Perfective aspect: An aspect that presents an event as a whole, without internal structure.
422. Imperfective aspect: An aspect that presents an event as ongoing or in progress.
423. Progressive aspect: An aspect that marks an event as ongoing at a particular time.
424. Perfect aspect: An aspect that marks an event as completed with present relevance.
425. Pluperfect aspect: An aspect that marks an event as completed before another past event.
426. Habitual aspect: An aspect that marks an event as recurrent or customary.
427. Inchoative aspect: An aspect that marks the beginning of an event or state.
428. Punctual aspect: An aspect that presents an event as a single point in time.
429. Durative aspect: An aspect that presents an event as having duration.
430. Aorist aspect: An aspect that presents an event without specifying its internal temporal structure.
431. Voice: A grammatical category that indicates the relationship between the arguments of a verb.
432. Active voice: A voice in which the subject is the agent of the action.
433. Passive voice: A voice in which the subject is the patient of the action.
434. Middle voice: A voice that expresses the subject as acting upon itself or with a special involvement in the action.
435. Reflexive: A construction in which the subject and object are the same entity.
436. Reciprocal: A construction expressing a mutual relationship between two or more entities.
437. Causative: A morphological or syntactic process that adds an agent to a verb, making a non-causative verb into a causative one.
438. Applicative: A morphological process that adds an oblique argument to a verb, promoting it to a core argument.
439. Antipassive: A construction that demotes the object of a transitive verb, making the clause intransitive.
440. Intransitivization: A process that reduces the valency of a verb by one.
441. Transitivization: A process that increases the valency of a verb by one.
442. Valency: The number of arguments a verb can take.
443. Obligatoriness: The degree to which an argument is required by a verb.
444. Semantic role: The role an argument plays in the event or state described by a predicate.
445. Agentivity: The degree to which an argument is a voluntary, controlling participant in an event.
446. Patienthood: The degree to which an argument is affected by the event.
447. Role and Reference Grammar: A theoretical framework that distinguishes semantic roles from grammatical relations.
448. Construction grammar: A framework that treats pairings of form and meaning as the basic units of linguistic analysis.
449. Construction: A pairing of form, meaning, and use in construction grammar.
450. Schema: An abstract construction that captures the common properties of a class of specific constructions.
451. Image schema: A basic conceptual structure derived from bodily experience, such as container, path, or force.
452. Frame semantics: A theory of meaning that organizes lexical knowledge into structured frames.
453. Prototype: The most central or typical member of a category.
454. Graded category: A category with no sharp boundary, where membership is a matter of degree.
455. Family resemblance: The phenomenon where members of a category share overlapping but non-universal features.
456. Radical construction: The most basic construction from which other constructions are derived.
457. Transitive construction: A construction expressing a two-place relation.
458. Intransitive construction: A construction expressing a one-place relation.
459. ditransitive construction: A construction expressing a three-place relation, typically involving a giver, a thing given, and a recipient.
460. Resultative construction: A construction expressing a change of state resulting from an action.

More terms:
461. Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morphemes affect each other's pronunciation.
462. Morphophonemic: Relating to the interaction between morphological and phonological processes.
463. Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached.
464. Stem: The core part of a word that carries the primary meaning.
465. Morphoallomorph: A morpheme that has allomorphic variation in its surface form.
466. Suppletive: A morpheme whose form is not phonologically related to other forms in the paradigm.
467. Paradigm: A set of related word forms that exhibit a particular grammatical pattern.
468. Morphological paradigm: The set of all inflected forms of a word.
469. Lexeme: A unit of lexical meaning that includes all its inflected forms.
470. Word form: The specific phonological or orthographic realization of a word.
471. Inflectional class: A set of words that share the same pattern of inflectional morphology.
472. Irregular verb: A verb that does not follow the regular pattern of inflection in a language.
473. Regular verb: A verb that follows the standard pattern of inflection in a language.
474. Strong verb: A verb that forms its past tense by changing the vowel (ablaut) rather than adding an affix.
475. Weak verb: A verb that forms its past tense by adding a dental suffix.
476. Ablaut: A systematic vowel alternation in a word paradigm, as in English "sing-sang-sung."
477. Umlaut: A vowel change caused by a following back vowel or consonant, often preserved as a grammatical marker.
478. Aumlaut: The raising of a vowel caused by a following /u/ or /w/.
479. I-umlaut: The raising of a vowel caused by a following /i/ or /j/.

483. Mute: A voiceless stop consonant.
484. Sonant: A voiced consonant, particularly a nasal, liquid, or glide.
485. Sonority: The relative loudness or perceptual prominence of a speech sound.
486. Sonority scale: The ordering of speech sounds from least to most sonorous.

496. Mora: A unit of syllable weight, used to account for syllable structure in metrical and phonological analysis.
497. Heavy syllable: A syllable that contains a long vowel or a short vowel followed by a consonant.
