response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A contextual variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated [pʰ] and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phonetics: The study of the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of the abstract, systematic organization of sounds within a particular language or across languages.
Phone: Any distinct speech sound considered as a physical event, without regard to whether it is phonemically distinctive.
Segmental: Pertaining to the individual consonants and vowels that make up speech, as opposed to suprasegmental features like stress or tone.
Suprasegmental: Phonetic and prosodic features that extend over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Manner of articulation: The description of how airflow is obstructed or modified in the vocal tract, including stops, fricatives, nasals, approximants, and liquids.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, velar, or glottal.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound; voiced sounds include [b, d, g], while voiceless include [p, t, k].
Aspiration: A burst of breath accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in the [pʰ] of English "pat" compared to the [p] of "spat."
Nasalization: The lowering of the velum during articulation, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity, as in [n] or nasalized vowels.
Palatalization: The modification of a consonant so that the tongue body raises toward the hard palate, often producing a [j]-like quality.
Labialization: The rounding of the lips during the articulation of a sound, as in the French vowel [ø] or the consonant [w].
Velarization: The retraction of the tongue body toward the soft palate during articulation, as in the Scottish [l̪] or the "dark" [ɫ] of English "ball."
Consonant: A speech sound in which the airflow is significantly obstructed or constricted in the vocal tract.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction, allowing relatively free airflow.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one position of articulation and glides to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "price."
Triphthong: A vowel sequence gliding through three distinct positions of articulation within a single syllable, as in /aɪə/ in "fire."
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic organization in speech, typically consisting of an onset, a nucleus (usually a vowel), and an optional coda.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the vowel nucleus within a syllable.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the vowel nucleus within a syllable.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel, around which the syllable is organized.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable comprising the vowel nucleus and any following consonant coda, as in the "-at" of "cat" and "hat."
Phonotactics: The set of rules and constraints governing which sequences of sounds are permissible in a given language.
Glottal: Pertaining to the glottis, the space between the vocal folds; includes sounds like the glottal stop [ʔ] and the fricative [h].
Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow channel that forces air to pass through, generating turbulent noise, as in [s] or [f].
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking the airflow and then releasing it in a burst, also called a stop, as in [p], [t], [k].
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation, as in [tʃ] in "church."
Lateral: A consonant produced with a constriction in the center of the tongue while allowing airflow around the sides, as in [l].
Liquid: A category of consonants including laterals and rhotics, characterized by relatively free airflow, such as [l] and [r].
Approximant: A consonant produced with a constriction in the vocal tract that is not tight enough to create turbulence, including glides and semivowels.
Semivowel: A vowel-like sound that functions as a consonant in the onset or coda of a syllable, such as [w] and [j].
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to escape through the nose, including [m], [n], and [ŋ].
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, often considered the most neutral and common vowel sound in many languages.
Prosody: The study of the rhythmic and intonational aspects of speech, including stress, pitch, timing, and phrasing.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation across a phrase or utterance, used to convey grammatical, pragmatic, or emotional meaning.
Stress: The relative prominence given to a syllable or word, realized through increased loudness, pitch, or duration.
Tone: The use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in the four tones of Mandarin Chinese.
Pitch: The perceptual correlate of fundamental frequency, perceived as how high or low a sound is.
Duration: The length of time a sound, syllable, or segment lasts, which can serve as a distinctive feature in some languages.
Fundamental frequency: The lowest frequency of a periodic sound wave, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration, perceived as pitch.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum of a speech sound, determined by the resonant properties of the vocal tract.
Spectrogram: A visual display showing the distribution of sound energy across frequencies over time, used in acoustic phonetics.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are produced by the movements and configurations of the speech organs.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds as they travel through the air, including frequency, amplitude, and duration.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the listener's auditory system.
Coarticulation: The overlapping and mutual influence of adjacent sounds during speech production, causing each sound to be affected by its neighbors.
Gemination: The lengthening of a consonant, as in Italian "pizza" [pitsːa], distinguishing it from a single short consonant.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in English "input" → [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which adjacent or nearby sounds become less alike, as in the development of Latin "caper" to English "kid."
Elision: The deletion or omission of a sound or syllable in natural speech, as in "going to" becoming "gonna."
Metathesis: The transposition or swapping of two or more sounds within a word, as in historical English "ask" from Old English "æscian."
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, often to break up a disallowed consonant cluster, as in "comfortable" pronounced with an extra /ə/.
Sandhi: A set of phonological changes that occur at the boundaries of words or morphemes in continuous speech.
Neutralization: A phonological context in which a contrast between two or more phonemes is lost, as in the final position of English where /t/ and /d/ may both be unreleased.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phonological unit representing a set of phonemes whose contrast has been neutralized in a particular context.
Allophonic: Describing the relationship between a phoneme and its variant allophones, indicating they are not in contrastive distribution.
Complementary distribution: A relationship between two or more phones where each occurs in a different phonetic environment and they never appear in the same context.
Contrastive distribution: A relationship between two or more phones where they can appear in the same environment and distinguish different words, indicating separate phonemes.
Free variation: The interchangeable use of two or more allophones in the same phonetic environment without any change in meaning.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the sounds are contrastive, such as "pat" and "bat."
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized in a hierarchical, tiered structure.
Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property of a speech sound, such as [+nasal], [−voice], or [±anterior], used to characterize phonemes.
Phonemic inventory: The complete set of phonemes that a language uses to distinguish words.
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word in a generative phonological system.
Surface form: The actual phonetic output of a word after all phonological rules have been applied.
Prosodic word: The unit of prosodic hierarchy that corresponds roughly to a word, governing stress and accent assignment.
Intonational phrase: A stretch of speech with a single intonational contour, corresponding roughly to a clause or a pause-delimited unit.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used in metrical and phonological analysis, typically corresponding to a short vowel or a coda consonant.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (˘ /).
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (/ ˘).
Morpheme: The smallest meaning-bearing unit of a language, such as the prefix "un-" or the suffix "-s" in English.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Morph: The concrete, phonological realization of a morpheme in a particular context.
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that occurs in different phonological or morphological environments, such as /ɪ/ and /ə/ in the English indefinite article.
Root: The core, unanalyzable morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify or create meaning, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix attached to the beginning of a root or stem, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix attached to the end of a root or stem, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix inserted within the root or stem of a word, as in Cebuano "uma-" or English "abso-lutely."
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds a root with two parts, one at the beginning and one at the end, as in German "be-...-en."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-ness" or "un-."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat" or "run."
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-tion" in "information."
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or aspect without changing the part of speech, such as "-ed" or "-s."
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, such as the conjugation of a verb or the declension of a noun.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each typically expressing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix may encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes and grammatical relations are expressed through word order and function words, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which words can incorporate multiple morphemes, including arguments, into a single complex word, as in many Native American languages.
Compounding: The process of combining two or more free morphemes to form a new word, such as "blackboard" or "toothpaste."
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories without creating a new lexical item.
Derivation: The process of creating a new word from an existing one by adding derivational morphemes, often changing the meaning or part of speech.
Conjugation: The systematic paradigm of verb forms expressing person, number, tense, mood, and aspect.
Declension: The systematic paradigm of noun, adjective, or pronoun forms expressing case, number, and gender.
Zero morpheme: An abstract morpheme that is present in the paradigm but has no overt phonological form, as in the English singular noun where no suffix is added.
Portmanteau: A single morpheme or word that fuses the meaning of two or more morphemes, as in the English ending "-ing" combining progressive aspect and nominalization.
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a word is shortened, as in "gym" from "gymnasium" or "phone" from "telephone."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words into a new word, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical meaning, as in "bye-bye" or "tik-tik."
Suppletion: The use of an unrelated, non-derivable form to express a grammatical distinction, as in the English "go / went / gone."
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morphological structure affects phonological processes and vice versa.
Productive: A morphological or grammatical pattern that is actively used and can be extended to new items by speakers.
Unproductive: A morphological or grammatical pattern that is still recognized but is no longer actively extended to new items.
Non-concatenative morphology: Morphological processes in which meaning is added without simply adding segments, such as internal vowel change (ablaut), reduplication, or tone change.
Template morphology: A model of non-concatenative morphology in which consonants are mapped onto a fixed vowel pattern, common in Semitic languages.
Incorporation: A morphological process in which a noun is incorporated into a verb, common in polysynthetic languages.
Nominalization: A derivational process that converts a verb or clause into a noun, as in "decide" → "decision."
Verbalization: A derivational process that converts a noun or adjective into a verb, as in "modern" → "modernize."
Causativization: A morphological or syntactic process that adds an external agent to a predicate, as in "die" → "kill."
Passivization: A syntactic or morphological process that promotes the object of a transitive verb to subject and demotes or deletes the agent.
Reciprocal: A grammatical category expressing a mutual action between participants, as in "meet" or "fight" when both parties perform the action on each other.
Reflexive: A grammatical category in which the subject and object of a verb are the same entity, as in "she hurt herself."
Antipassive: A valency-reducing operation that demotes the object of a transitive verb to an oblique, common in ergative languages.
Intransitivization: A process that reduces the valency of a transitive verb to make it intransitive, often by removing or obliquing the object.
Syntax: The study of the structure of sentences and the rules governing how words combine to form phrases and clauses.
Constituency: The property of a group of words forming a syntactic unit that behaves as a single element in the structure of a sentence.
Phrase structure rule: A rule in grammar that specifies how a phrase is built from its constituent elements, such as NP → Det N.
Binary branching: The property of a syntactic structure in which each node branches into exactly two daughters.
Deep structure: In transformational grammar, the abstract syntactic representation of a sentence before it is transformed into its surface form.
Surface structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied, closely corresponding to the spoken or written form.
Transformational grammar: A theoretical framework in which surface structures are derived from underlying structures through a set of transformational rules.
Head: The central, obligatory element of a phrase that determines its category, such as the noun in a noun phrase or the verb in a verb phrase.
Complement: A constituent that follows the head of a phrase and is required to complete its meaning, such as the noun phrase following a transitive verb.
Specifier: A constituent that precedes the head of a phrase, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Adjunct: An optional, non-essential constituent that can be added to a phrase or clause without changing its core structure.
Subcategorization: The specification of the types and number of complements that a particular verb or other head requires.
Valency: The number and type of arguments a verb or predicate requires or permits.
Transitive: A verb or predicate that takes a subject and a direct object, such as "eat" in "She eats an apple."
Intransitive: A verb or predicate that takes only a subject and no direct object, such as "sleep" in "She sleeps."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct object and an indirect object, such as "give" in "She gave him a book."
Ergative: A grammatical case that marks the subject of a transitive verb, in contrast to the absolutive case which marks objects and intransitive subjects.
Absolutive: A grammatical case that marks the object of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb, typical of ergative languages.
Nominative: A grammatical case that typically marks the subject of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative: A grammatical case that typically marks the direct object of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Genitive: A grammatical case expressing possession, origin, or other relations, as in "the book's cover."
Dative: A grammatical case typically marking the indirect object of a verb or the recipient of an action.
Instrumental: A grammatical case marking the means or tool by which an action is performed, as in Latin "gladio" in "gladio interficit."
Locative: A grammatical case marking location or position, as in "in the house."
Vocative: A grammatical case used to address or call someone directly, as in "O God!"
Oblique: A grammatical case that is neither nominative nor accusative, often used for indirect objects, locations, or other non-core arguments.
Agreement: The morphological process by which a word changes form to match the grammatical features of another word, such as subject-verb agreement.
Binding: A principle in syntactic theory governing the distribution of pronouns, anaphors, and variables relative to their antecedents.
Control: A syntactic relation in which the subject of a non-finite clause is determined by an element in the matrix clause, as in "She tried [to leave]."
Raising: A syntactic process in which an argument is moved from an embedded clause to a higher clause, as in "Seems [to be a problem]."
Anaphora: A linguistic element whose interpretation depends on a co-occurring element in the same discourse, such as a pronoun referring to a noun.
Cataphora: A type of anaphora in which the antecedent follows the anaphoric expression, as in "He said, 'I will leave,' and John packed his bag."
Coreference: The relation between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Deixis: The linguistic expression of relations to the context of utterance, including person (I, you), space (here, there), and time (now, then).
Topic: The discourse element about which a clause or sentence is predicated, often the starting point of a new piece of information.
Focus: The discourse element that carries the main new or contrastive information in an utterance.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) information and new information, often realized through topic and focus.
Word order: The conventional sequence of syntactic constituents in a language, such as Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) or Subject-Object-Verb (SOV).
Subordinate clause: A clause that depends on a main clause and cannot stand alone, often introduced by a subordinating conjunction.
Coordinate clause: A clause joined to another clause of equal rank by a coordinating conjunction such as "and," "but," or "or."
Finite clause: A clause containing a verb that is inflected for tense, person, and number, as opposed to a non-finite clause.
Non-finite clause: A clause containing a verb that is not inflected for tense, such as infinitival or participial clauses.
Constituent: A syntactic element, such as a phrase or word, that functions as a single unit within a larger structure.
Complementizer: A functional word that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "that," "if," or "whether" in English.
Complementizer phrase: A syntactic projection headed by a complementizer, often serving as the root of a clause.
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, including articles (a, the), demonstratives (this, that), and quantifiers.
Classifier: A word used in some languages, particularly in Chinese and Japanese, to categorize nouns in certain syntactic contexts, such as the "piece" classifier for objects.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of related word forms, such as the lexeme RUN encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word, such as "run" for the forms "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Lexicon: The inventory of words and morphemes in a language, or the mental dictionary a speaker possesses.
Morpho-syntactic: Pertaining to the interaction between morphological structure and syntactic structure.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Lexical semantics: The study of meaning as stored in the lexicon, including sense relations such as synonymy, antonymy, and hyponymy.
Compositional semantics: The study of how the meaning of a complex expression is built up from the meanings of its parts according to syntactic structure.
Pragmatics: The study of how context and speaker intention contribute to the interpretation of meaning beyond the literal semantic content.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying a proposition, such as promising, ordering, or thanking.
Locutionary act: The act of literally producing a meaningful utterance, as opposed to the illocutionary or perlocutionary acts.
Illocutionary act: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as asserting, questioning, commanding, or promising.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the listener, such as persuading, frightening, or entertaining.
Implicature: An inference a listener draws about a speaker's intended meaning that is not explicitly stated, as in Grice's theory of conversational implicature.
Gricean maxims: A set of four principles of cooperative communication—Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner—proposed by H. P. Grice.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as in "She is a bachelor" entails "She is male."
Presupposition: A background assumption that must hold for an utterance to be meaningful, such as "The king of France is bald" presupposing that there is a king of France.
Synonymy: A semantic relation between words or expressions that have the same or nearly the same meaning.
Antonymy: A semantic relation between words that have opposite or contrasting meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one term is included within the meaning of another, as "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Meronymy: A semantic relation between a part and the whole, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word having multiple related senses, as in "head" meaning the body part, the top of something, or a leader.
Homonymy: The phenomenon of two or more distinct words having the same form but different meanings, as in "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river edge).
Ambiguity: A property of an expression that allows it to be interpreted in more than one way, whether lexical or structural.
Prototype: A central, typical exemplar of a category that other members are compared to, as in the concept of "bird" prototypically including a sparrow rather than a penguin.
Frame semantics: A semantic theory in which meaning is understood in terms of structured situations or frames that organize related concepts, as in the "buying" frame.
Cognitive linguistics: A theoretical approach to linguistics that emphasizes the role of general cognitive processes, such as perception, categorization, and imagery, in language.
Conceptual metaphor: A cross-domain mapping in which one conceptual domain is understood in terms of another, as in "ARGUMENT IS WAR" or "TIME IS MONEY."
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework developed by Ronald Langacker that integrates grammar and meaning, treating linguistic forms as symbolic units linking phonological and conceptual structure.
Construction grammar: A theoretical framework in which the basic units of grammar are pairings of form and meaning called constructions, ranging from full sentences to single words.
Grammaticalization: The diachronic process by which lexical items or phrases develop into grammatical markers, such as the English "shall" developing from a full verb to a future tense marker.
Reanalysis: A process in language change in which the structural boundaries or category membership of a linguistic element are reassessed by speakers.
Creole: A stable natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a new generation of speakers.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language, typically without native speakers.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, which can lead to borrowing, interference, pidginization, or creolization.
Borrowing: The adoption of words, morphemes, or phonological features from one language into another, as in English "sushi" from Japanese.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or even sentence.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral language, such as the Indo-European family.
Comparative method: A historical linguistic method for reconstructing proto-languages by comparing related daughter languages to identify systematic sound correspondences.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed through the comparative method, such as Proto-Indo-European.
Sound change: A regular, systematic shift in the pronunciation of a language over time, as in the Great Vowel Shift in English.
Grimm's Law: A set of sound correspondences between Proto-Indo-European and Germanic languages describing regular shifts of stops, identified by Jacob Grimm.
Neogrammarian: A school of historical linguistics in the late 19th century that held that sound change is regular, exceptionless, and mechanical.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including dialect, social variation, and language attitudes.
Dialect: A variety of a language spoken by a particular group, differing from other varieties in pronunciation, vocabulary, or grammar.
Register: A variety of language associated with a particular social context or communicative purpose, such as formal, informal, legal, or technical.
Prestige dialect: A dialect or variety that is socially valued and associated with higher social status or education.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular dialect or linguistic variety.
Linguistic variation: The existence of multiple forms for expressing the same meaning within a language, varying by region, social group, or context.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language based on large collections of authentic text or speech data, called corpora.
Corpus: A systematically assembled collection of texts or transcriptions used for linguistic analysis.
Computational linguistics: The interdisciplinary field applying computer science and statistical methods to the analysis and modeling of natural language.
Natural language processing: A subfield of computer science focused on enabling machines to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological processes that underlie language acquisition, comprehension, and production.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans, especially children, learn a language, whether as a first (L1) or second (L2) language.
Critical period: A hypothesized window in early development during which language acquisition occurs most easily and naturally.
Universal Grammar: A theoretical framework proposed by Noam Chomsky positing innate, language-specific structural principles shared by all human languages.
Government and Binding: A syntactic framework within the generative program that explains syntactic relations through principles such as government, binding, and case assignment.
Principles and Parameters: A theoretical framework in generative linguistics that accounts for cross-linguistic variation through a limited set of binary or multi-valued parameters.
Minimalist Program: The current stage of the generative grammar framework, seeking to explain linguistic structure in terms of the most economical computational and interface requirements.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure in which every phrase has the same internal organization consisting of a specifier, a head, and a complement, represented as XP → Spec X′, X′ → X CP.
Government: A syntactic relation in which a head governs the elements in its local domain, determining which phrases can be its complements.
Case assignment: The process by which a functional head assigns grammatical case to a noun phrase, such as a verb assigning accusative case to its object.
Theta role: The semantic role assigned by a predicate to its arguments, including Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Goal, and Theme.
theta criterion: A principle in syntactic theory stating that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
Filter: A principle in Government and Binding theory that constrains the possible positions of certain elements, such as the NP Movement Constraint.
Trace: An abstract syntactic element left behind when a constituent moves to a higher position in the tree structure.
Move: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is copied in a higher position, leaving a trace in the original position.
Merge: The fundamental operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects into a larger structure.
Phase: A domain of computation in the Minimalist Program, typically the verb phrase and the complementizer phrase, within which certain operations apply.
Phase Impenetrability Condition: A principle stating that once a phase is complete, its internal domain is no longer accessible to operations outside the phase.
Economy principle: A general principle in the Minimalist Program that linguistic computation should be as economical as possible, preferring simpler operations and fewer steps.
Interface: The connection between the syntactic system and external systems such as the phonological system (PF) and the semantic/conceptual system (LF).
Phonological Form: The output level of syntax in the generative model, where the sound structure of the sentence is determined.
Logical Form: The output level of syntax in the generative model, where the semantic and pragmatic interpretation of the sentence is determined.
Morphological Form: The representation of a word's morphological structure, mediating between syntax and phonology.
Orthography: The system of writing a language, including the set of letters or symbols and the rules for their use.
Alphabet: A writing system in which individual letters represent phonemic units, such as the Latin or Greek alphabets.
Syllabary: A writing system in which each symbol represents a syllable, as in Japanese hiragana and katakana.
Logogram: A writing system in which each symbol represents a word or morpheme, as in Chinese characters.
Morpheme-based orthography: A writing system in which the basic unit of the script is the morpheme rather than the phoneme.
Abjad: A writing system that primarily represents consonants, with vowels indicated optionally or not at all, as in Arabic and Hebrew scripts.
Abugida: A writing system in which each consonant symbol inherently represents a syllable with a default vowel, which can be modified with diacritics, as in Devanagari.
Diacritic: A mark added to a letter to modify its pronunciation or distinguish between different letters, such as accents or umlauts.
Morphosyntax: The study of the interface between morphology and syntax, examining how morphological structure interacts with syntactic structure.
Morphosyntactic alignment: The systematic correspondence between syntactic relations (subject, object) and morphological case marking.
Nominative-accusative alignment: An alignment in which subjects of both transitive and intransitive verbs are treated alike (nominative), and objects of transitive verbs are marked distinctly (accusative).
Ergative-absolutive alignment: An alignment in which objects of transitive verbs and subjects of intransitive verbs are treated alike (absolutive), and subjects of transitive verbs are marked distinctly (ergative).
Split ergativity: A system in which ergative-absolutive alignment appears in some grammatical contexts (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative in others (e.g., present tense).
Noun class: A grammatical category in which nouns are grouped into classes, often requiring agreement on other words, as in Bantu languages.
Gender: A grammatical category in which nouns are classified into sets (masculine, feminine, neuter, etc.), often requiring agreement in other parts of the sentence.
Animacy: A grammatical or semantic distinction in which nouns are classified as animate or inanimate, often affecting case marking or agreement.
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular, plural, dual, trial, and other quantities of participants.
Dual number: A grammatical category marking exactly two participants, found in languages such as Hindi, Slovenian, and several Australian languages.
Trial number: A grammatical category marking exactly three participants, found in some Oceanic languages.
Aspect: A grammatical category expressing the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, progressive, or habitual.
Perfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as a complete, bounded whole, without reference to its internal temporal structure.
Imperfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded, with attention to its internal temporal structure.
Progressive aspect: An aspect marking an event as in progress or ongoing at a reference time, as in "I am eating."
Perfect aspect: An aspect linking a past event to the present, often expressing relevance or continuing effect, as in "I have eaten."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates the time of an event relative to the time of speaking, typically past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the propositional content, such as indicative, subjunctive, imperative, or conditional.
Subjunctive: A mood used to express hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations, common in Romance and Germanic languages.
Imperative: A mood used to issue commands or requests, as in "Close the door!"
Conditional: A mood or construction expressing a situation that is dependent on a condition, as in "If I were you, I would go."
Evidentiality: A grammatical category encoding the source of a speaker's information, such as direct experience, hearsay, or inference.
Aspectual class: A lexical semantic classification of verbs based on their inherent temporal structure, such as states, activities, achievements, and accomplishments (Vendler's categories).
State: An aspectual class of verb denoting a condition or situation without inherent change or endpoint, such as "know" or "belong."
Activity: An aspectual class of verb denoting an ongoing process without a natural endpoint, such as "run" or "swim."
Achievement: An aspectual class of verb denoting a instantaneous change of state, such as "recognize" or "arrive."
Accomplishment: An aspectual class of verb denoting a bounded process with a natural endpoint, such as "build a house" or "write a letter."
Telicity: The property of a verb phrase denoting an event with a natural endpoint, as opposed to atelic events that lack a defined boundary.
Aspectual shift: A change in the aspectual interpretation of a verb due to syntactic or morphological context.
Lexical aspect: The inherent aspectual properties of a verb or verb phrase as determined by its lexical content, also called lexical aspect or event structure.
Event structure: The abstract representation of the temporal and causal structure of an event, including its boundaries, internal composition, and participants.
Morpho-phonological: Pertaining to the interaction between morphological and phonological processes, such as how affixation triggers sound changes.
Morpheme boundary: The edge between two morphemes within a word, often relevant to phonological processes like stress or assimilation.
Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created, including compounding, derivation, blending, clipping, and borrowing.
Productivity: A measure of how freely a word-formation pattern can be applied to new or existing stems to create new words.
Lexical entry: The complete set of information associated with a word in the mental lexicon or a dictionary, including its phonological form, morphological properties, syntactic behavior, and semantic content.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected or derived forms of a word, as in the full conjugation of a verb.
Lexical gap: A situation in which a language lacks a specific lexical item for a concept that is expressed in other languages.
Compound: A word formed by combining two or more free morphemes, such as "toothbrush" or "hotdog."
Compound noun: A compound word that functions as a noun, such as "sunflower" or "basketball."
Compound verb: A compound word that functions as a verb, such as "understand" (Old English under-stān) or "set up."
Derivative: A word formed from a base by adding one or more derivational affixes, such as "unhappiness" from "happy."
Base: The central morpheme to which affixes are attached in word formation.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may include derivational morphemes.
Root: The most basic, unanalyzable morpheme in a word that carries the core lexical meaning.
Derivational suffix: A suffix that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-ness" or "-tion."
Inflectional suffix: A suffix that marks grammatical information without changing the part of speech, such as "-s" (plural) or "-ed" (past tense).
Zero derivation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created without adding any overt affix, as in "the green of the grass" (adjective to noun).
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its part of speech without any change in form, as in the noun "butterfly" becoming the verb "to butterfly."
Neologism: A newly coined or newly attested word or expression entering a language.
Archaism: A word or expression that is no longer in common use, preserved in formal, literary, or historical contexts.
Coinage: A word-formation process in which a new word is invented with no etymological connection to existing words, such as "laser" or "robot."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a series of words and pronounced as a single word, such as "NASA" or "UNESCO."
Initialism: A sequence of initial letters from a series of words that is pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "CIA."
Onomatopoeia: A word that phonetically imitates or suggests the sound it describes, such as "buzz," "sizzle," or "bang."
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression substituted for one considered harsh, blunt, or offensive, such as "passed away" for "died."
Dysphemism: An unpleasant or disparaging word or expression used instead of a neutral one, the opposite of a euphemism.
Taboo: A socially or culturally prohibited topic, often leading to the avoidance of certain words or the use of euphemisms.
Manner of speech: A sociolinguistic concept referring to the way a speaker articulates sounds, including rate, loudness, and quality.
Accent: The particular way in which sounds are pronounced by a speaker, often associated with a regional or social group.
Dialectology: The study of the geographic and social distribution of linguistic variation and dialects.
Geolinguistics: The study of the spatial distribution of language features, dialects, and language boundaries.
Lingua franca: A language adopted as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Lingua ignota: A hypothetical or constructed language that is not widely understood, sometimes used in the context of ciphers or secret codes.
Lingua mortua: A language that no longer has any native speakers, such as Latin in its classical form.
Lingua viva: A language that is currently spoken by a community of native speakers.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be a living means of communication.
Language revitalization: Efforts to restore a endangered or dormant language to active use by a community of speakers.
Language endangerment: The condition of a language that is at risk of losing its last native speakers due to social, economic, or political pressures.
Language policy: The set of decisions and actions taken by governments, institutions, or communities regarding the status and use of languages.
Language planning: The deliberate efforts to influence the structure, function, or status of a language, including standardization, codification, and promotion.
Standard language: A codified variety of a language that serves as the model for education, media, and official communication.
Hypercorrection: An overapplication of standard language norms, often resulting in an error, as in pronouncing "comfortable" as "com-ter-ta-bul."
Hypernym: A word with a broad, general meaning that encompasses the meaning of more specific words, as "animal" is a hypernym of "dog."
Hyponym: A word with a specific meaning that is included within the broader meaning of a hypernym, as "dog" is a hyponym of "animal."
Meronym: A word denoting a part, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Holonym: A word denoting a whole, as in "car" is a holonym of "wheel."
Tautology: The use of more words than necessary to express an idea, often with redundant meaning, as in "ATM machine."
Synecdoche: A figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole or vice versa, as in "all hands on deck."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another, implying a similarity without using "like" or "as."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it, as in "the White House announced."
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual words, as in "kick the bucket."
Formulaic language: Pre-constructed, stored sequences of words that are used as single units, including phrases, idioms, and collocations.
Collocation: A habitual or conventional pairing of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Phrase: A group of words that functions as a single syntactic unit, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: A unit of syntax containing a subject and a predicate, which may be a complete sentence or a subordinate element.
Sentence: The highest level of syntactic structure, typically containing at least one finite clause and expressing a complete thought.
Discourse: Language as it is used in extended, connected communication beyond the individual sentence level.
Text: A stretch of written or spoken language that forms a coherent, unified whole.
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that create surface-level connections between elements in a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical ties.
Coherence: The overall logical and semantic connectedness of a text, going beyond surface-level linguistic markers.
Register: A variety of language associated with a particular social setting, purpose, or field, characterized by specific vocabulary and grammatical features.
Genre: A conventional type of discourse or text with recognized features and purposes, such as a recipe, a legal contract, or a news report.
Rhetoric: The art of persuasive or effective communication, involving strategies of argument, style, and audience engagement.
Argumentation: The process of constructing and evaluating logical arguments, central to fields like linguistics, philosophy, and law.
Enunciation: The articulation of speech, or a short, formal statement of an idea or belief.
Prosody: The system of rhythmic and intonational patterns in a language, governing stress, tone, and phrasing at levels above the individual segment.
Scansion: The analysis of the metrical pattern of a verse or poem, identifying stressed and unstressed syllables.
Meter: The patterned arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables in poetry, such as iambic pentameter.
Foot: A basic unit of poetic meter, consisting of a fixed combination of stressed and unstressed syllables.
Line: A single sequence of words in a poem, typically broken by a line break.
Stanza: A group of lines in a poem, forming a roughly regular unit, analogous to a paragraph in prose.
Couplet: Two consecutive lines of verse that rhyme and are of equal length, often forming a complete thought.
Quatrain: A stanza of four lines of verse.
Couplet rhyme: A rhyme scheme in which pairs of lines rhyme (AABB).
Assonance: The repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words, as in "The mellow horn is a bellowing balm."
Alliteration: The repetition of initial consonant sounds in closely connected words, as in "Peter Piper picked."
Consonance: The repetition of consonant sounds within or at the end of nearby words, as in "The big bug buzzed."
Onomatopoeia: Words that phonetically imitate the sound they represent, such as "crash," "hiss," or "splash."
Phonemic: Relating to or characterized by phonemes as the basic units of sound.
Phonemicization: The process of identifying and organizing the phonemic system of a language.
Phonological: Relating to the abstract, rule-governed organization of sounds in a language.
Phonotactic constraint: A rule that specifies which sequences of sounds are allowed or forbidden in a language.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a word or string of sounds into syllables.
Moraic: Pertaining to the mora, a unit of phonological weight; a moraic segment is one that contributes to syllable weight.
Weight: The phonological property of a syllable determined by the number of moras it contains, distinguishing light and heavy syllables.
Light syllable: A syllable with a single short vowel and no coda, containing one mora.
Heavy syllable: A syllable with a long vowel, a diphthong, or a coda consonant, containing two or more moras.
Syllable weight: The phonological property distinguishing syllables based on their duration and internal structure, relevant to stress assignment and metrical structure.
Coda constraint: A phonological restriction on the types of consonants or consonant clusters that may appear in the syllable coda.
Onset constraint: A phonological restriction on the types of consonants or consonant clusters that may appear in the syllable onset.
Syllable template: An abstract representation of the internal structure of a syllable, specifying the positions for onset, nucleus, and coda.
Autosegmental phonology: A framework in which certain phonological features, such as tone and vowel length, are represented on separate tiers from the segmental tier.
Tone: In autosegmental phonology, a feature represented on a separate tier and linked to segments or mora
