response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated [pʰ] and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phonology: The study of the systematic organization of sounds in a particular language or across languages.
Phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds, including their production, transmission, and reception.
Prosody: The study of suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable within a word or phrase, often marked by greater loudness, longer duration, or higher pitch.
Intonation: The variation in pitch across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical or pragmatic meaning.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch at the syllable level to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Syllable: A unit of speech organized around a vowel nucleus, serving as a basic building block of phonological structure.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Nucleus: The vowel or syllabic consonant at the center of a syllable, around which the syllable is organized.
Rime: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda.
Mora: A unit of syllable weight or timing used in phonological analysis, typically corresponding to a short vowel or a long vowel component.
Segment: A discrete sound unit (consonant or vowel) in phonetic or phonological analysis.
Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that extends over multiple segments, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Phonotactics: The set of rules in a language governing permissible combinations of phonemes within syllables or words.
Assimilation: A sound change in which a segment becomes more like a neighboring segment, as in "input" realized as [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: A sound change in which neighboring similar segments become less alike, as in Latin "perper" to "peper."
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable in connected speech, as in "gonna" for "going to."
Metathesis: The reversal or transposition of two adjacent sounds, as in the historical change from "ask" to "aks" in some dialects.
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, often to break up a consonant cluster, as in "chocolate" from "choclate."
Coarticulation: The influence of one articulatory gesture on the production of an adjacent sound during speech.
Manner of articulation: The way in which airflow is obstructed in the vocal tract to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound; a key contrastive feature in many languages.
Consonant: A speech sound produced by a significant obstruction or narrowing of the vocal tract.
Vowel: A speech sound produced without significant constriction of the vocal tract, characterized by formant patterns.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one position in the mouth and glides to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "my."
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound that maintains a single steady position throughout its duration, such as /iː/ in "fleece."
Nasal: A consonant or vowel produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity.
Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow channel that causes turbulent airflow, such as /s/ or /f/.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air, such as /p/, /t/, /k/.
Affricate: A consonant produced as a stop followed immediately by a fricative at the same place of articulation, such as /tʃ/ in "church."
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip creating a closure while air flows around the sides of the tongue, such as /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant in the /r/ class, which varies significantly across languages as trill, tap, fricative, or approximant.
Glottal: An articulation or sound produced at the level of the glottis, such as the glottal stop /ʔ/.
Palatal: A consonant or vowel articulated with the body of the tongue raised toward the hard palate.
Velar: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate (velum).
Labial: An articulation involving the lips, including bilabial, labiodental, and labiovelar manners.
Alveolar: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip or blade against or near the alveolar ridge.
Dental: A consonant articulated with the tongue against the upper teeth, as in the English /θ/ and /ð/.
Uvular: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula, as in the French /ʁ/.
Pharyngeal: A consonant articulated with the tongue root retracted toward the pharyngeal wall, as in Arabic /ʕ/.
Epiglottal: A consonant articulated with the root of the tongue or epiglottis raised, as in some Semitic languages.
Labiodental: A consonant articulated with the lower lip against the upper teeth, as in /f/ and /v/.
Labiovelar: A consonant with simultaneous lip rounding and velar closure, as in /kw/ or /gw/.
Bilabial: A consonant articulated with both lips pressed together, as in /p/, /b/, and /m/.
Retroflex: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip curled back toward the middle of the palate, common in Dravidian and Indo-Aryan languages.
Apical: An articulation involving the tip of the tongue, as opposed to laminal articulation with the blade.
Laminal: An articulation involving the blade of the tongue rather than the tip.
Coronal: An articulation involving the front part of the tongue (tip or blade), encompassing alveolar, dental, retroflex, and palatal sounds.
Dorsal: An articulation involving the body of the tongue, encompassing palatal, velar, uvular, and pharyngeal sounds.
Aspiration: A burst of extra pulmonic airflow released after the closure of a plosive, as in English "pin" vs. "spin."
Breathy voice: A creaky or murmured voice quality characterized by partial adduction of the vocal folds, used contrastively in some languages.
Creaky voice: A laryngeal state in which the vocal folds vibrate in a low-frequency, irregular pattern, producing a rough or creaky sound.
Nasalization: The coloring of a vowel or consonant with nasal airflow due to velum lowering.
Velarization: Secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue is raised toward the velum, as in the "hard" /k/ of Russian.
Palatalization: Secondary articulation in which the tongue body is raised toward the palate, as in the "soft" /k/ of Russian.
Lenition: A historical or dialectal process of sound weakening, such as /p/ to /f/ to /β/ to /ɸ/ to zero.
Fortition: A sound change involving strengthening or hardening of a consonant, such as /f/ to /p/.
Neutralization: A situation in which a phonological contrast is lost in a particular phonological environment, such as final obstruent devoicing in German.
Complementary distribution: A relationship between two sounds that never occur in the same phonological environment, often indicating they are allophones of one phoneme.
Minimal pair: Two words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, used to prove the phonemic status of a sound.
Distinctive feature: A binary or privative property of a sound used to characterize and contrast phonemes, such as [+voice] or [−nasal].
Feature geometry: A theoretical model organizing distinctive features in a hierarchical structure, allowing for natural class description.
Autosegment: A phonological element (such as tone or register) that occupies its own tier in a multi-tiered representation, linking to multiple segments.
Floating segment: A phonological element that is not linked to any segment in its current environment but may resurface later.
Prosodic word: A unit of prosodic structure, typically corresponding to a word or phrase, that governs stress assignment and intonation.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of one stressed syllable and its associated unstressed syllables, such as an iamb or trochee.
Syllable weight: A measure of syllable complexity based on the number of morae, distinguishing light from heavy syllables.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (× ˈ).
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (ˈ ×).
Moraic theory: A framework in which syllables are built from morae, accounting for vowel length, coda consonants, and stress patterns.
Open syllable principle: A constraint stating that two onsetless syllables (CV.V) are dispreferred or banned in certain languages.
Markedness: A concept in which one member of a contrast is considered more complex, less common, or more "marked" than its counterpart.
Natural class: A set of sounds that can be described by a single feature specification or a small set of shared features.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phoneme that represents a set of allophones in a particular environment where no specific phoneme applies.
Allophonic rule: A rule specifying the conditions under which a particular allophone of a phoneme is realized.
Sound change: A historical process in which the phonetic realization of a phoneme shifts over time, such as the Great Vowel Shift.
Sound law: A regular and systematic pattern of sound change, such as Grimm's Law or Verner's Law.
Neogrammarianism: A 19th-century school of historical linguistics emphasizing that sound changes are regular, exceptionless, and conditioned.
Chain shift: A set of interlocking sound changes in which the shift of one segment creates room for the next, as in the English Great Vowel Shift.
Sound correspondence: A systematic relationship between sounds in two related languages, used in comparative reconstruction.
Phonetic transcription: The representation of speech sounds using a symbol system such as the International Phonetic Alphabet.
Narrow transcription: A phonetic transcription that records fine-grained articulatory or acoustic detail, enclosed in square brackets with slashes or extra symbols.
Broad transcription: A phonemic transcription that records only the distinctive sounds of a language, ignoring allophonic variation.
International Phonetic Alphabet: A standardized system of symbols for representing the sounds of all human languages, maintained by the IPA.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of speech sounds through their physical acoustic properties, such as frequency, amplitude, and formant structure.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are produced by the movements of the vocal organs.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the listener's auditory system.
Voice onset time: The interval between the release of a stop consonant and the onset of vocal fold vibration, distinguishing voicing categories.
Formant: A band of enhanced acoustic energy in a speech sound, produced by resonances of the vocal tract.
Fundamental frequency: The lowest and primary frequency of the vocal fold vibration, perceived as pitch.
Pitch: The perceptual correlate of fundamental frequency, perceived as how high or low a sound is.
Amplitude: The magnitude of pressure variation in a sound wave, perceptually corresponding to loudness.
Spectrogram: A visual display of the frequency content of a signal over time, used extensively in acoustic phonetics.
Hertz: The unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second, used to measure pitch and formant values.
Decibel: A logarithmic unit used to measure the intensity or amplitude of sound.
Tone sandhi: A systematic change in the realization of tones depending on their phonological or tonal context.
Contour tone: A tone whose pitch changes in a specific pattern across the syllable, such as rising, falling, or dipping.
Level tone: A tone that maintains a relatively constant pitch throughout the syllable, such as a high or low tone.
Register: A suprasegmental contrast involving a change in the phonation type (e.g., modal vs. breathy voice) rather than pitch.
Downstep: A lowering of the overall pitch range of a phrase or intonational unit.
Upstep: A raising of the overall pitch range of a phrase or intonational unit.
Boundary tone: A pitch accent or intonational contour associated with the edge of a prosodic domain, marking phrase or utterance boundaries.
Phrase accent: A prosodic marker associated with the edge of a phrase, distinct from word-level accent.
Nuclear stress: The primary stress or pitch accent in an intonational phrase, typically falling on the most salient syllable.
Secondary stress: A stress mark of lesser prominence assigned to non-nuclear stressed syllables.
Stress shift: A change in the position of stress within a word or phrase, often triggered by morphological or syntactic context.
Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which a single pitch accent marks the head of a phrase or word, as in Japanese.
Stress accent: A prosodic system in which the primary word stress is fixed or predictable, as in English.
Syllable timing: A temporal pattern of speech in which each syllable tends to occupy roughly equal time, characteristic of languages like Spanish.
Stress timing: A temporal pattern of speech in which stressed syllables occur at roughly equal intervals, characteristic of English.
Mora timing: A temporal pattern in which each mora occupies roughly equal time, characteristic of languages like Japanese.
Isochrony: The tendency for certain rhythmic units to be produced at equal time intervals in a given language.
Prosodic word: A prosodic constituent at the word level, governing internal stress patterns and interacting with phonological rules.
Phonological word: A unit of phonological structure corresponding roughly to a word, serving as the domain for stress and other rules.
Maximal onset principle: A principle stating that syllabification should assign the maximum possible number of consonants to the onset.
Syllable structure: The abstract template describing the permissible arrangement of onset, nucleus, and coda in a language.
Empty onset: A theoretical empty consonantal slot in a syllable's onset, used in some models of syllable structure.
Empty nucleus: A theoretical empty vocalic slot in a syllable's nucleus, used to account for syllabic consonants.
Mu: A theoretical sub-syllabic unit or node in autosegmental phonology, sometimes used to anchor tones or stress.
Skeletal slot: An abstract timing position in a syllable or word to which segments are linked in autosegmental phonology.
Tier: A parallel level of representation in autosegmental phonology, such as a segmental tier, tonal tier, or stress tier.
Association line: A line linking an autosegment to its skeletal slot or segment in a multi-tiered phonological representation.
Linking: The association of an autosegment (such as a tone) to a segment or timing position on a lower tier.
Delinking: The removal of an association between an autosegment and its target, often triggered by segment deletion.
Spreading: The process by which a feature or autosegment extends to additional segments or positions.
Dissociation: The splitting of a single autosegment's association into two separate positions.
Tone bearing unit: A segment (usually a vowel or mora) that serves as the host or carrier of a tone.
Autosegmental phonology: A theoretical framework in which certain features and elements are represented on separate tiers and linked to segments.
Metrical phonology: A branch of phonology that uses metrical trees or grids to represent and derive stress and rhythm patterns.
Metrical tree: A hierarchical binary branching structure used to represent stress patterns and rhythmic feet.
Metrical grid: A two-dimensional representation of stress in which stressed syllables are marked with columns of X's.
Stress window: A constraint on stress assignment that limits the range of syllables from which stress can be assigned.
Stress assignment: The process or rule system by which a language determines which syllable(s) receive stress.
Prosodic hierarchy: A hierarchy of prosodic constituents from small to large, including mora, syllable, foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase, and intonational phrase.
Phonological phrase: A prosodic domain between the prosodic word and the intonational phrase, governing certain intonational and phonological processes.
Intonational phrase: The largest prosodic domain, typically corresponding to a clausal or sentence-level unit with a single intonational contour.
Utterance: The largest domain of prosodic and phonological organization, encompassing one or more intonational phrases.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent word but syntactically independent, such as English "-s" or French "en."
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the end of a host word.
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the beginning of a host word.
Infix: A morpheme inserted within the stem of a word, as in Tagalog -um- or English "ab-so-lutely."
Prefix: A morpheme attached to the beginning of a word or stem.
Suffix: A morpheme attached to the end of a word or stem.
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds a stem, with one part prefixed and one part suffixed, as in German "be-...-en."
Suprafix: A morpheme that alters the suprasegmental properties (such as tone or stress) of a stem without adding segments.
Subfix: A morpheme that attaches below the base of a word, affecting its suprasegmental features.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further divided into smaller meaningful parts.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules by which they are formed.
Morph: The smallest phonological form that carries a grammatical function, which may correspond to one or more allomorphs.
Allomorph: A phonological variant of a morph, such as the English plural morph /s/ in "cats," /z/ in "dogs," and /ɪz/ in "boxes."
Stem: The core part of a word to which affixes are attached.
Root: The most basic morpheme of a word, carrying the core lexical meaning, from which derived forms are built.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a stem or root, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that modifies a word for grammatical purposes without changing its core meaning or category, such as "-s" for plural.
Derivation: The process of forming a new word from an existing one by adding a derivational morpheme.
Inflection: The process of modifying a word's form to express grammatical categories such as number, tense, case, or agreement.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed by the absence of any overt phonological material, such as the English plural of "sheep."
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that expresses more than one grammatical meaning simultaneously, as in the Latin ending "-runt."
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical features simultaneously, as in many Romance languages.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which each grammatical feature is expressed by a separate, typically one-to-one affix, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which a single word can encode what would be a full clause in analytic languages, as in many Native American languages.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words are typically single morphemes with little or no affixation, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Inflectional class: A set of words that share the same inflectional patterns, such as strong and weak verbs in English.
Suppletion: The irregular use of an entirely different word form to express a grammatical contrast, as in English "go" and "went."
Analogy: A linguistic change in which a word form is regularized on the model of other, more productive forms, such as "children" influencing "oxen" to "oxes."
Reanalysis: A change in the perceived structural boundaries within a word or phrase, such as "a napron" being reanalyzed as "napron."
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Morpheme template: The abstract schematic representation of a word's morphological structure, specifying the slots for roots, affixes, and their order.
Order of affixation: The sequence in which affixes are added to a stem during word formation.
Morphological alternation: A predictable phonological change in a root or stem when different affixes are attached, as in "speak" / "spoke" / "spoken."
Morphological conditioning: The restriction of a phonological or morphological process to specific morphological contexts.
Morphophonology: The study of the interaction between morphological and phonological rules, explaining alternations between morphs.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatically meaningful unit in a language, such as "un-" in "unhappy" or "-ed" in "walked."
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word or word class, such as the conjugation of a verb.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of vocabulary representing a set of related word forms sharing a common meaning, such as the lexeme "run" encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," "running."
Lemma: The base or citation form of a word under which its various inflected forms are grouped in a dictionary.
Word: A free morpheme or a complex of morphemes that can function as a syntactic unit, often defined by its ability to stand alone.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent host but syntactically independent, straddling the word-morpheme boundary.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their dominant morphological strategies: isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Productive: A morphological process or pattern that is actively used by speakers to form new words.
Fossilized: A morphological pattern that is no longer actively productive and is limited to a fixed set of items.
Dead morpheme: A morpheme that is no longer understood or productive in a language but remains as a historical remnant.
Live morpheme: A morpheme that is actively productive and semantically transparent to current speakers.
Morpho: A bound morpheme that is not a full morpheme but a part of one, used in the analysis of complex morphs.
Morpheme: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function.
Derivational: Pertaining to the formation of new lexemes through the addition of affixes or other word-formation processes.
Categorial: Pertaining to the assignment or change of grammatical category (noun, verb, adjective) through word formation.
Non-categorial: Pertaining to word-formation processes that do not change the grammatical category of the base.
Compounding: The formation of a new word by combining two or more free morphemes, as in "blackboard" or "toothpaste."
Blending: A type of compounding in which parts of two words are combined, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Clipping: The shortening of a word without a change in meaning, as in "phone" from "telephone" or "lab" from "laboratory."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a multi-word expression, pronounced as a word, such as "laser" or "radar."
Initialism: An abbreviation formed from initial letters that is pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "NASA."
Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix, as in "edit" from "editor" or "burgle" from "burglar."
Conversion: The formation of a new word by changing the grammatical category of a base without any overt affixation, such as "to google" from "Google."
Reduplication: The repetition of all or part of a morpheme to express grammatical or semantic meaning, common in Southeast Asian and other languages.
Total reduplication: The complete repetition of a morpheme, as in Indonesian "kita-kita" for "we."
Partial reduplication: The repetition of only part of a morpheme, as in Indonesian "minum-minum" for "drink a little."
Ablaut: A historical or synchronic vowel alternation within a paradigm, as in the English "sing-sang-sung."
Umlaut: A fronting or raising of a back or low vowel as a historical grammatical marker, as in German "Maus" to "Mäuse."
Suppletion: The use of an entirely unrelated form to express a grammatical contrast, as in English "man-men" or "go-went."
Morphological case: A grammatical category expressed by inflection that indicates the syntactic role of a noun phrase.
Nominative: The grammatical case marking the subject of a transitive clause, common in ergative-absolutive and nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative: The grammatical case marking the direct object of a transitive clause.
Dative: The grammatical case marking the indirect object or recipient of an action.
Genitive: The grammatical case marking possession, origin, or various other relationships, as in "the book's cover."
Instrumental: The grammatical case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Locative: The grammatical case marking location or position.
Ablative: The grammatical case marking separation, source, or origin.
Allative: The grammatical case marking direction or goal toward which movement occurs.
Vocative: The grammatical case used in direct address, as in "O God" or "Maria!"
Ergative: The grammatical case marking the subject of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Absolutive: The grammatical case marking the object of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A case-marking pattern in which the intransitive subject (S) is marked like the transitive subject (A).
Ergative-absolutive alignment: A case-marking pattern in which the intransitive subject (S) is marked like the transitive object (P).
Split ergativity: A system in which a language uses ergative-absolutive alignment in some contexts and nominative-accusative in others, often conditioned by tense or aspect.
Morphosyntax: The study of the interface between morphological and syntactic structure.
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, mood, number, or case without creating a new lexical item.
Agreement: A grammatical process in which a word's form changes to match a feature (such as person, number, or gender) of another word in the clause.
Concord: A synonym for agreement, referring to the matching of grammatical features between syntactically related words.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to a reference point: past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, progressive, or habitual.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, imperative, or optative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category encoding the source or type of evidence for a proposition, such as direct, reported, or inferred.
Valency: The number of arguments (participants) a predicate requires or can take.
Transitive: A verb or clause that takes a subject and a direct object.
Intransitive: A verb or clause that takes only a subject.
Ditransitive: A verb that takes a subject, a direct object, and an indirect object, as in "give" or "show."
Antipassive: A voice operation that demotes or deletes the direct object of a transitive verb, making the clause intransitive.
Passive: A voice construction in which the object of an active clause becomes the subject and the agent is demoted or omitted.
Causative: A voice or derivation operation that adds an agent argument to a verb, causing the original subject to become the object.
Applicative: A morphological operation that adds an argument (often a beneficiary or location) to a verb's argument structure.
Reciprocal: A construction expressing a mutual action between participants, as in "They met each other."
Reflexive: A construction in which the subject and object of a clause are the same entity, as in "She saw herself."

Adverbialization: The process of converting a word or phrase into an adverbial modifier.

Heavy verb: A verb that carries substantial lexical meaning and does not require a complement for its core semantics.
Copula: A linking verb such as "be" that connects a subject to a predicate nominal or adjective.
Existential: A verb or construction expressing the existence or presence of an entity, as in "there is" or "there were."
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, modality, or voice.

Modal verb: A verb expressing necessity, possibility, permission, or ability, such as "can," "must," or "should."
Semi-modal: A verb with modal-like semantics but full verbal inflection, such as "need" or "dare."
Phrasal auxiliary: A multi-word auxiliary such as "used to" or "ought to."
Periphrastic: A multi-word construction that expresses a grammatical category, as in "will go" for future or "have gone" for perfect.
Synthetic: A single-word form that expresses a grammatical category through inflection, as in "went" or "gone."
Morphosyntactic alignment: The mapping between grammatical relations (subject, object) and case marking or agreement patterns in a language.
A-structure: The initial, underlying argument structure of a clause before any movement or voice operations.
A'-structure: The derived argument structure after movement operations such as passive or relativization.
θ-role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a verb, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Theme.

Goal: The θ-role of the destination of a motion event.

Recipient: The θ-role of the entity that receives something.
Undergoer: The θ-role of the entity that is affected by a state change or action.
Experiencer: The θ-role of the entity that perceives or experiences a mental or emotional state.

Role and Reference Grammar: A theoretical framework that analyzes verbal argument structure in terms of semantic roles and syntactic functions.
Lexical Semantics: The study of the meaning of words and the relationships between them.
Semantic field: A set of words related by a common concept or domain of meaning, such as color words or kinship terms.
Prototype: A central or typical member of a category that serves as a reference point for categorization.
Prototype theory: A cognitive model of categorization in which categories are organized around typical or central members rather than strict boundaries.
Family resemblance: A Wittgensteinian concept in which category membership is based on overlapping similarities rather than a single defining feature.
Sense: A distinct meaning of a word or expression, such as the multiple senses of "bank" (financial, river edge).
Lemma sense: A sense associated with a particular lemma in a lexical database.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or expression has multiple related senses.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two unrelated words share the same form, such as "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Monosemy: The property of a word or expression having only a single sense.
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is included within the meaning of a more general word, as in "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernym: A word with a broader meaning that includes the meanings of more specific words, as in "bird" is a hypernym of "sparrow."
Synonym: Two or more words with the same or very similar meaning, such as "big" and "large."
Antonym: Two words with opposite or contrasting meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Gradable antonym: A pair of antonyms that admit intermediate values, such as "long" and "short."
Complementary antonym: A pair of antonyms with no intermediate values, such as "dead" and "alive."
Contradictory: A logical relationship in which two propositions cannot both be true or both be false.
Contrary: A logical relationship in which two propositions cannot both be true but can both be false.
Subcontrary: A logical relationship in which two propositions cannot both be false but can both be true.
Subordinate: A logical relationship in which the truth of one proposition implies the truth of another.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as in "She is a bachelor" entails "She is male."
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for a statement to be meaningful, such as "The king of France is bald" presupposing a king of France.
Implicature: An inferred meaning that is not part of the literal semantic content of an utterance, derived from pragmatic context.
Conventional implicature: A type of implicature associated with specific lexical or grammatical items, independent of context, such as "but" implying contrast.
Particularized implicature: A context-dependent implicature derived from the specific conversational situation.
Scalar implicature: An implicature arising from the use of a weaker term on a semantic scale, as in "Some students passed" implying "Not all students passed."
 Horn clause: A logical formula in which at most one literal is positive, named after Alfred Tarski's work on logic.
Gricean maxims: A set of four conversational principles (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner) proposed by H.P. Grice to explain implicature.
Conversational maxim: A general principle of cooperation in conversation, of which the Gricean maxims are specific instances.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred by the listener based on the assumption that the speaker is following conversational principles.
Neutrality: The semantic property of a form that does not commit the speaker to a particular truth value, as in "or" being neutral.
Inclusiveness: The semantic property of a disjunctive operator that allows both disjuncts to be true.
Exclusiveness: The semantic property of a disjunctive operator that requires exactly one disjunct to be true.
Scalar: Pertaining to an ordered set of semantic items, such as "some, many, most, all."
Hedge: A linguistic device that softens or qualifies a statement, reducing its commitment to truth.
Vagueness: The property of a term that lacks precise boundaries, such as "tall," "bald," or "young."
Ambiguity: The property of an expression that can be interpreted in two or more distinct ways.
Syntactic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible syntactic structures, as in "The old man the boats."
Semantic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible meanings of a word or phrase, as in "I saw the man with the telescope."
Pragmatic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible pragmatic interpretations or implicatures.
Distributivity: The property of a predicate that applies individually to each member of a set, as in "Each student passed."
Collectivity: The property of a predicate that applies to a set as a whole rather than to individual members, as in "The students formed a circle."
Plurality: The semantic property of an expression denoting a plurality or set of entities.
Mass noun: A noun that refers to an uncountable substance or concept, not divided into discrete units, as in "water" or "furniture."
Count noun: A noun that refers to discrete, countable entities, as in "chair" or "book."
Uncountable noun: A synonym for mass noun.
Individual noun: A noun that refers to a single, individuated entity.
Generic noun: A noun used to refer to a kind or class rather than a specific instance, as in "Dogs are loyal."
Proper noun: A noun that refers to a unique, named entity, such as "Paris" or "Shakespeare."
Common noun: A noun that refers to a member of a class rather than a unique entity, such as "city" or "author."
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "she," "it," "they," "this," "who."
Anaphoric: Referring backward to a previously mentioned entity, as in "John said he was tired."
Cataphoric: Referring forward to an entity mentioned later, as in "He was tired, John."
Exophoric: Referring to an entity outside the immediate discourse, such as "that building" pointing to a visible structure.
Bound anaphora: An anaphoric expression whose reference is determined by the antecedent in a specific structural relationship, as in "Every student his own."
Free anaphora: An anaphoric expression whose reference is not structurally bound, as in "John thinks Mary is smart" where "she" is free.
Coreference: A relationship in which two expressions in a discourse refer to the same entity.
Discourse referent: An entity tracked in a discourse through a chain of referring expressions.
File: A discourse representation associated with a referent, containing information about its properties and relations.
Discourse Representation Theory: A framework for modeling discourse meaning using structured representations called DRSes with discourse referents and conditions.
File change score: A metric in Discourse Representation Theory that scores how a new sentence changes the discourse model.
Accessibility: A property of a discourse representation determining which referents can be anaphorically accessed.
Salience: The degree to which a discourse referent is prominent or accessible in the current discourse context.
Given: A discourse entity that is already established in the common ground of the conversation.
New: A discourse entity that has not yet been introduced into the common ground.
Given-new contrast: A pragmatic principle stating that sentence structure tends to present given information first and new information last.
Topic: The discourse entity about which a sentence or clause is predicated.
Comment: The information asserted about the topic in a sentence or clause.
Rheme: The new or informative part of a sentence, typically corresponding to the focus.
Focus: The constituent of a sentence that carries the primary information or contrastive emphasis.
Narrow focus: Focus restricted to a single constituent within a larger phrase.
Wide focus: Focus encompassing an entire clause or sentence.
Contrastive focus: Focus that highlights a contrast with an alternative, as in "I want the RED book, not the blue one."
Inferential focus: Focus that marks information that can be inferred from context.
Accusative focus: Focus on the object of a transitive clause.
Agent focus: Focus on the subject or agent of a clause.
Focus accent: A prosodic mark (stress, pitch, or length) that signals the focused constituent.
Information structure: The organization of discourse into topics, foci, and their hierarchical relationships.
Given: An entity already known to the hearer in the common ground.
New: An entity being introduced to the hearer for the first time.
Shared: An entity known to both speaker and hearer.
Private: An entity known to only one participant in the conversation.
Common ground: The set of propositions and assumptions that both speaker and hearer take to be mutually known.
Mutual knowledge: A level of common ground in which both participants know that they both know a fact.
Presupposition trigger: A linguistic item or construction that introduces a presupposition, such as "again," "still," "even," or factive verbs.
Accommodation: The process by which a hearer adds a presupposed proposition to the common ground to make an utterance interpretable.
Projection: The behavior of presuppositions under logical operators, determining whether they survive in negation, questions, or conditionals.
Cancelability: The property of an implicature that can be explicitly contradicted by the speaker without producing a contradiction.
Relevance: A central concept in relevance theory, stating that communication aims to maximize the ratio of cognitive effects to processing effort.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic framework developed by Sperber and Wilson that explains communication in terms of mutual relevance.
Cognitive effect: A change in the hearer's beliefs or knowledge resulting from processing an utterance.
Processing effort: The mental cost of processing an utterance, including parsing, integrating, and computing inferences.
Optimal relevance: The expectation that an utterance will yield sufficient cognitive effects for the processing effort invested.
Satisfaction: The fulfillment of a presupposition in the discourse context.
Violation: The failure of a presupposition to be met, leading to a pragmatic anomaly.
Failure: The inability of a presupposition to be either satisfied or violated, as in "The king of France is bald" if there is no king of France.
Syntax: The study of the rules and principles that govern the structure of sentences and phrases.
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a unit within a larger syntactic structure.
Phrase: A syntactic constituent headed by a word of a particular category, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be finite or non-finite.
Sentence: A maximal syntactic projection, typically a clause with its own intonation, capable of standing as an independent utterance.
Tree: A hierarchical diagram representing the syntactic structure of a sentence, showing constituent relationships.
Binary branching: The property of a syntactic structure in which each node has exactly two daughters.
Non-binary branching: A syntactic structure in which a node has more than two daughters.
Constituency test: A diagnostic used to determine whether a group of words forms a constituent, such as substitution, fronting, or clefting.
Substitution: A constituency test in which a potential constituent is replaced by a pronoun or pro-form.
Fronting: A constituency test in which a potential constituent is moved to the beginning of the sentence, as in topicalization.
Clefting: A constituency test in which a potential constituent is embedded in a cleft construction, as in "It is the cat that sat on the mat."
Coordination: A syntactic operation that joins two or more elements of the same category, as in "the cat and the dog."
Subordination: A syntactic operation in which one clause is embedded within another, as in "I know that she left."
Embedding: The inclusion of one clause or phrase within another, creating a hierarchical structure.
Recursion: The ability to embed structures within structures of the same type indefinitely, a key property of human language.
X-bar theory: A syntactic framework that represents phrase structure in terms of X, X', and X'' projections.
Complement: The argument of a head that completes its valency, such as the object of a transitive verb.
Specifier: The constituent that occupies the position immediately above the head in an XP, typically providing additional information.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase or clause, such as an adverbial or relative clause.
Head: The central or determining word of a phrase, as in the noun in a noun phrase or the verb in a verb phrase.
Head noun: The central noun in a noun phrase that determines its grammatical properties.
Head verb: The central verb in a verb phrase that determines the valency of the clause.
Head adjective: The central adjective in an adjective phrase.
Head preposition: The central preposition in a prepositional phrase.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, taking a complement, as in "in the house."
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun, determiner, or pronoun, as in "the tall building."
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, as in "saw the movie."
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, as in "very tall."
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb, as in "quickly and quietly."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, such as "the," "a," "this," "my."
Article: A specific type of determiner, including definite ("the") and indefinite ("a," "an") articles.
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to a specific entity, such as "this," "that," "these," "those."
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies the quantity of a noun phrase's referent, such as "every," "some," "many," "few."
Numeral: A word expressing a number, such as "one," "two," "three."
Pronoun: A word that stands in for a noun phrase, such as "he," "she," "it," "they," "I."
Personal pronoun: A pronoun that refers to a person, including subject, object, and possessive forms.
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to the subject, such as "himself," "herself," "itself."
Reciprocal pronoun: A pronoun expressing a mutual relationship, such as "each other" or "one another."
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used in questions, such as "who," "what," "which."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause, such as "who," "which," "that," "whose."
Indefinite pronoun: A pronoun that refers to a non-specific entity, such as "someone," "anything," "none."
Pronominalization: The process of replacing a noun phrase with a pronoun to avoid repetition.
Anaphora: A linguistic relationship in which one expression (the anaphor) refers to an entity established by a prior expression (the antecedent).
Antecedent: The expression that a pronoun or other anaphoric element refers back to.
Binding: A syntactic or semantic relationship in which a pronoun's reference is determined by a specific antecedent.
Binding Theory: A component of generative syntax that governs the distribution of anaphoric expressions (reflexives, pronouns, names).
Principle A: The binding principle stating that reflexives must be bound within their governing category.
Principle B: The binding principle stating that pronouns must be free in their governing category.
Principle C: The binding principle stating that names (R-expressions) must be free everywhere.
Governing category: The smallest syntactic domain containing a node and its governor, used in Binding Theory.
Local domain: A small syntactic domain such as a clause or NP, within which binding principles operate.
Long-distance anaphora: An anaphoric relationship in which the antecedent and anaphor are in different clauses or domains.
Short-distance anaphora: An anaphoric relationship within a local domain.
Co-indexation: The marking of two expressions as coreferential by assigning them the same index in a notation.
Trace: An empty category left behind by syntactic movement, indicating the original position of a moved constituent.
Operator: A syntactic element (such as a wh-word or quantifier) that binds a trace or variable through movement.
Wh-movement: The syntactic operation by which a wh-word moves to the specifier of CP, as in "What did you buy?"
Wh-word: An interrogative or relative word such as "what," "who," "where," "when," "why," "which."
Wh-island: A syntactic domain from which wh-movement is blocked, such as a complex NP or a wh-clause.
Island: A syntactic domain that constrains or blocks movement operations.
Subjacency: A condition on movement stating that a constituent cannot move across more than one bounding node at a time.
Subjunctive: A mood marker used in certain embedded clauses, as in "I demand that he be present."
Indicative: The mood used for statements of fact or certainty.
Imperative: A mood used for commands or requests, as in "Close the door."
Optative: A mood expressing a wish or hope, as in "God save the queen."

Counterfactual: A construction expressing a proposition contrary to fact, as in "If I had known, I would have come."
Conditional: A construction expressing a condition and its consequence, as in "If it rains, we will stay inside."
Hypothetical: A construction expressing a supposition or assumption, often using subjunctive or irrealis markers.

Realis: A grammatical category marking situations that are factual or actual.
Evidential: A grammatical category marking the source of the speaker's knowledge, such as visual, hearsay, or inferential.

Reported evidential: A marker indicating the information was obtained through hearsay or report.
Inferential evidential: A marker indicating the information was inferred from evidence.
Apparent evidential: A marker indicating the information is based on assumption or conjecture.
Cleft: A construction that highlights a particular constituent, as in "It was John who did it" or "What I need is a coffee."

Extraposition: The movement of a constituent to a position after the main clause, as in "It is likely that he will come."
Expletive: A syntactically required but semantically empty element, such as "it" in "It is raining" or "there" in "There are three cats."

There-existential: A construction using "there" to introduce a new entity, as in "There is a problem."

Topic: The discourse entity that a sentence is about, often occupying a preverbal position.
Topicalization: The syntactic operation of moving a constituent to the sentence-initial position to mark it as the topic.

Right dislocation: A construction in which an additional element is placed after the clause, as in "He's great, John."

Scrambling: A syntactic process in which arguments of a clause can appear in various orders, common in Japanese and other languages.
Word order: The sequence in which constituents appear in a sentence, such as SVO, SOV, VSO, VOS, OVS, or OSV.

OSV: A word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb.

Postverbal object: An object that appears after the verb, as in most SVO and VOS languages.
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice.
Copula: A linking verb such as "be" that connects a subject to a predicate.
Light verb: A verb with minimal lexical meaning that relies on a complement for its semantic content.

Verb: A word that expresses an action, state, or occurrence and serves as the predicate of a clause.

Adverb: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb, often indicating manner, time, or degree.

Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "or," "but."
Coordinate conjunction: A conjunction that joins elements of equal syntactic status, such as "and" or "or."
Subordinating conjunction: A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because," "although," "if."
Interjection: A word or expression used to express emotion or reaction, such as "oh," "wow," "ouch."
Exclamation: A sentence or expression used to express strong emotion, typically ending with an exclamation mark.
Question: A sentence or clause used to elicit information, typically marked by intonation or interrogative words.
Declarative: A sentence type used to state a fact or assertion.
Interrogative: A sentence type used to ask a question.
Imperative: A sentence type used to issue a command or request.
Exclamative: A sentence type used to express strong emotion or surprise.
Rhetorical question: A question asked not to elicit an answer but to make a point.
Tag question: A short question appended to a statement to seek confirmation, as in "It's cold, isn't it?"
Yes-no question: A question that can be answered with "yes" or "no."
Wh-question: A question introduced by a wh-word, such as "What did you do?"
Multiple wh-question: A question containing more than one wh-word, as in "Who saw what?"
Embedded question: A question embedded within a larger clause, as in "I know where he lives."
Indirect question: A question expressed in the form of a statement, as in "Can you tell me where the bank is?"
Direct question: A question expressed in its standard interrogative form, as in "Where is the bank?"
Polarity: The property of a proposition or utterance being affirmative or negative.
Negation: The grammatical operation that reverses the polarity of a proposition, as in "He did not come."
Sentence negation: Negation that applies to the entire proposition of a clause.
Constituent negation: Negation that applies to a specific constituent, as in "He saw no one" vs. "He did not see no one."
Negative polarity item: An expression that is grammatical only in the scope of negation or another licensing element, such as "any" or "ever."
Positive polarity item: An expression that is grammatical only in affirmative contexts, such as "some" or "at all."
Negative concord: A syntactic pattern in which multiple negative elements co-occur to express a single negation, as in "I didn't see nothing."
Double negation: The co-occurrence of two negative elements, which in Standard English cancels to a positive but in other dialects or languages expresses a single negation.
Minimality: A semantic property in which a negative expression asserts the existence of at least one negative instance.
Negative scope: The domain within which a negative element exerts its logical effect.
C-command: A structural relationship in which one node dominates another node without dominating its mother.
Dominance: A structural relationship in which one node is an ancestor of another in a tree.

Sisterhood: A structural relationship in which two nodes share the same immediate mother.
