response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A contextually conditioned variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English "pin" and "spin."
Phone: Any distinct speech sound regardless of whether it is phonemically contrastive in a particular language.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sound sequences are permissible in a given language, such as English allowing "str" but not "tsr" at the beginning of words.
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic organization in speech, typically consisting of an optional onset, a vowel nucleus, and an optional coda.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, usually a vowel, around which the rest of the syllable is organized.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the syllable nucleus.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the syllable nucleus within a syllable.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound, distinguishing voiced sounds like [b] from voiceless sounds like [p].
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed or modified in the production of a consonant, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Aspirate: A consonant pronounced with a strong burst of following breath, as in the [pʰ] of English "pin."
Ejective: A consonant produced by closing the glottis and raising the larynx to build up pressure, released as a pop of air, common in African and Caucasian languages.
Implosive: A plosive consonant produced by lowering the larynx during the closure, causing the airstream to move inward, as in the [ɓ] of Hausa.
Nasal: A consonant produced by closing the oral cavity while opening the nasal passage, allowing airflow through the nose, as in [m], [n], and [ŋ].
Oral: A sound produced with the nasal passage closed and the velum raised, directing airflow through the mouth.
Labial: A consonant or vowel articulated with the lips as the primary point of contact.
Dental: A consonant produced with the tongue tip against the upper teeth, such as the English [θ] and [ð].
Alveolar: A consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge, such as English [t], [d], [s], and [z].
Postalveolar: A consonant produced just behind the alveolar ridge, such as English [ʃ], [ʒ], and [tʃ].
Retroflex: A consonant produced by curling the tongue tip back toward the hard palate, as in Hindi [ɖ] and [ʈ].
Palatal: A consonant or vowel produced with the body of the tongue raised toward the hard palate.
Velar: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate (velum), such as English [k], [g], and [ŋ].
Uvular: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue or the uvula, such as French [ʁ] and [q].
Pharyngeal: A consonant produced with the pharyngeal wall, such as Arabic [ʔ] and [ħ].
Glottal: A sound produced at the glottis, including the glottal stop [ʔ] and the glottal fricative [h].
Vowel: A sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction, characterized by tongue height, backness, and rounding.
Consonant: A sound produced with a significant constriction or closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
Diphthong: A vowel glide in which the sound transitions from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable, such as [aɪ] in English "eye."
Monophthong: A single vowel sound produced with a relatively stable tongue position, such as [i] in "see" or [a] in "father."
Schwa: The mid-central vowel [ə], the most common vowel sound in English, typically occurring in unstressed syllables.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a particular syllable within a word or phrase, affecting pitch, duration, and loudness.
Prosody: The rhythmic and intonational features of speech that go beyond individual segments, including stress, pitch, and duration.
Intonation: The variation in pitch across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical and pragmatic information, such as questions versus statements.
Tone: A distinctive use of pitch on a syllable that distinguishes word meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese where "ma" can mean "mother," "horse," "hemp," or "scold" depending on pitch contour.
Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Segmental: Pertaining to individual discrete sounds (phonemes) as opposed to prosodic or suprasegmental features.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phoneme in the same context, demonstrating the phonemic status of that sound, such as "bat" and "cat."
Complementary distribution: A relationship between two sounds that never occur in the same phonological environment, suggesting they are allophones of the same phoneme.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more allophones can occur in the same environment without changing meaning, such as [w] and [v] for some English speakers in "vase."
Phonological rule: A rule that describes how underlying phonological representations are transformed into surface forms, such as a rule of nasal place assimilation.
Underlying form: The abstract phonological representation of a word or morpheme before phonological rules are applied.
Surface form: The actual phonetic or phonemic representation of a word after all phonological rules have been applied.
Distinctive feature: A binary or gradational property used to characterize and distinguish phonemes, such as [+voiced], [+nasal], or [-anterior].
Neutralization: A context in which a phonemic contrast is suspended, so that two or more phonemes are realized by the same allophone, as in final-obstruent devoicing in German.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which one sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in the [n] before [p] in "input" becoming [m].
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound to avoid excess repetition, as in the change from *haram to "harim" in some Arabic dialects.
Metathesis: The transposition of two adjacent segments within a word, as in the shift from "ask" to "aks" or "brick" to "brik."
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable in speech, such as the loss of /t/ in "water" → [wɔːr].
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra segment into a word, often to break up a prohibited consonant cluster, as in the /ə/ in some pronunciations of "athlete" [ˈæθəliːt].
Apocope: The loss of a final syllable or sound in a word, as in "comfortable" → "comfortable" [ˈkʌmfərtəbəl] or "Monday" → "Mandy."
Apheresis: The loss of an initial syllable or sound in a word, as in "every" → "e'" or "university" → "niversity."
Sandhi: Any phonological process that occurs at the boundary between two words or morphemes, including assimilation, elision, and coalescence.
Vowel harmony: A phonological rule requiring all vowels in a word to share a particular feature, such as frontness or backness, as in Turkish and Finnish.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used in syllable structure theory; a short vowel counts as one mora, a long vowel or diphthong as two, and a syllabic consonant as one.
Syllabic: Describing a consonant that can serve as the nucleus of a syllable, such as the [l] in English "bottle" [ˈbɒtl̩].
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of a stressed syllable plus one or more adjacent unstressed syllables, used in metrical theory.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable, as in "aMERICAN."
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable, as in "GIRLfriend."
Anapest: A metrical foot consisting of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable, as in "in the MOONlight."
Dactyl: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables, as in "MERriest."
Homonym: A word that has the same form but two or more distinct meanings, such as "bank" (financial institution) and "bank" (river edge).
Homophone: Words that sound the same but have different meanings and often different spellings, such as "flower" and "flour."
Homograph: Words that are spelled the same but have different pronunciations and meanings, such as the noun "tear" [tɪr] and the verb "tear" [tɛr].
Heteronym: A word that is spelled the same but pronounced differently and has different meanings, as in "read" (present) vs. "read" (past).
Allomorph: A phonological variant of a morpheme, such as the [-s], [z], and [ɪz] allomorphs of the English plural morpheme.
Morpheme: The smallest meaning-bearing unit of a language, such as "un-" in "undo" or "-ed" in "walked."
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning and to which affixes may be attached, such as "act" in "action."
Stem: The base form of a word to which inflectional morphemes are attached, which may include a root plus derivational affixes.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a stem or root, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix attached before the stem of a word, such as "un-" in "undo" or "pre-" in "preview."
Suffix: An affix attached after the stem of a word, such as "-ness" in "happiness" or "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: A morpheme inserted within the root of a word, as in the English colloquial "abso-lutely" or the tagalog infix "-in-" in "sulat" → "sulatin."
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that consists of two parts, one prefixed and one suffixed, surrounding a stem, as in German "be-...-en" in "begreifen."
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent word but syntactically independent, such as English contractions "don't" or "I'm."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "un-" or "-ing."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat," "walk," or "happy."
Derivational morpheme: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-ness" turning "happy" into "happiness."
Inflectional morpheme: An affix that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without creating a new lexical item, such as "-s" for third person singular.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by concatenating morphemes with relatively little overlap or allomorphy, as in Turkish and Japanese.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical features simultaneously, as in the Latin ending "-am" marking both singular and accusative.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes and grammatical relationships are expressed by word order and separate particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which words can be extremely long and incorporate multiple stems and affixes, as in many Native American languages like Mohawk.
Morphological alternation: A change in the form of a morpheme or root that depends on the morphological context, such as the voicing alternation in English plural "cat/cats" vs. "dog/dogs."
Productive: A morphological or syntactic process that is actively used to create new forms in a language, as opposed to a frozen or unproductive one.
Backformation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor" or "scapegoat" from "to scapegoat."
Blending: The formation of a new word by combining parts of two words, such as "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "motel" (motor + hotel).
Clipping: The shortening of a longer word without changing its meaning, such as "phone" from "telephone" or "gym" from "gymnasium."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as a word, such as "NASA" or "laser."
Compound: A word formed by combining two or more free morphemes, such as "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Sentence: A minimal grammatical unit that expresses a complete thought and typically contains a subject and a predicate.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular word that may contain other words but does not contain a full clause, such as "the old man" (noun phrase).
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate (verb phrase), which may be independent or subordinate.
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence and functions as a constituent within a larger clause, such as "after she left" in "I left after she left."
Main clause: An independent clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence and may contain one or more subordinate clauses.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, such as the complement clause in "I think (that) she is here."
Noun phrase: A phrase whose head is a noun or pronoun, such as "the tall woman in the red coat."
Verb phrase: A phrase whose head is a verb, including any auxiliaries, objects, and complements, such as "has been running quickly."
Adjective phrase: A phrase whose head is an adjective, including any modifiers, such as "very large."
Adverb phrase: A phrase whose head is an adverb, such as "extremely quickly."
Prepositional phrase: A phrase consisting of a preposition and its object, such as "in the garden" or "from New York."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies reference, including articles, demonstratives, and quantifiers, such as "the," "a," "this," and "some."
Article: A determiner that marks definiteness or indefiniteness of a noun, such as English "the" (definite) and "a/an" (indefinite).
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for or refers back to a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "they," or "it."
Noun: A word that refers to an entity, concept, or class, and typically functions as the subject or object of a sentence.
Verb: A word that expresses an action, state, or occurrence and serves as the predicate of a clause, such as "run," "be," or "think."
Adjective: A word that modifies a noun by attributing a property or quality, such as "red," "tall," or "happy."
Adverb: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb, often indicating manner, time, frequency, or degree, such as "quickly," "very," or "yesterday."
Preposition: A word that precedes a noun phrase to express a spatial, temporal, or abstract relationship, such as "in," "on," "at," or "by."
Postposition: A word that follows a noun phrase to express a grammatical relationship, as in Japanese "ni" or Korean "e."
Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," "or," and "although."
Complement: A word or phrase required or selected by a particular verb, adjective, or preposition to complete its meaning, such as the direct object in "She read the book."
Complementizer: A word that introduces a complement clause, such as English "that" in "I think that she left" or "whether" in "I wonder whether she left."
Subject: The noun phrase that typically agrees with the verb and performs or undergoes the action in an active clause.
Object: The noun phrase that is acted upon or affected by the verb, as in "She ate the apple."
Indirect object: The noun phrase that denotes the recipient or beneficiary of an action, as in "She gave him a book."
Direct object: The noun phrase that directly receives the action of the verb, as in "She kicked the ball."
Dative: A grammatical case marking the recipient or beneficiary of an action, or an object noun phrase in ditransitive constructions.
Genitive: A grammatical case marking possession, association, or a part-whole relationship, as in "the man's hat."
Accusative: A grammatical case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Nominative: A grammatical case typically marking the subject of a finite clause.
Vocative: A grammatical case used to address someone, as in "O Mary, hear my plea" or Greek vocative forms.
Instrumental: A grammatical case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed, as in Sanskrit or Russian.
Locative: A grammatical case marking location, as in "in the house" or the Hindi locative suffix "-mẽ."
Ablative: A grammatical case marking the source or origin from which something moves, as in "from the city."
Allative: A grammatical case marking the goal or destination of motion, as in "toward the city."
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object, such as "eat" in "She ate an apple."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, such as "sleep" in "She slept."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes two objects, as in "give" in "She gave him a book."
Valency: The number of arguments a predicate (usually a verb) requires, such as monovalent (one argument), bivalent (two arguments), or trivalent (three arguments).
Argument: A syntactic constituent that is semantically required or optionally selected by a predicate, such as the subject and object of a transitive verb.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned by a predicate to its arguments, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Theme.
Agent: The theta role of the entity that deliberately performs an action, typically the subject of an active transitive verb.
Patient: The theta role of the entity that undergoes the action or is affected by the event, typically the direct object of a transitive verb.
Experiencer: The theta role of the entity that undergoes a mental or emotional state, such as the subject in "She feared the dark."
Theme: The theta role of the entity that is moved, created, or represented, such as "a letter" in "She wrote a letter."
Recipient: The theta role of the entity that receives something, such as "him" in "She gave him a book."
Source: The theta role of the origin or starting point of a motion or transfer.
Goal: The theta role of the destination or endpoint of a motion or transfer.
Location: The theta role of the place where an event occurs or an entity is situated.
Instrument: The theta role of the means or tool used to carry out an action, such as "a hammer" in "He built the house with a hammer."
Cause: The theta role of the entity that causes an event without directly performing the action.
Result: The theta role of the entity or state that results from an event.
Beneficiary: The theta role of the entity that benefits from an action, such as "for her" in "He cooked dinner for her."
Possessor: The theta role of the entity that owns, contains, or is associated with another entity, as in "the man's dog."
Possessive: A grammatical construction or case that expresses ownership or association, marked in English by the clitic "-s" or "of."
Causative: A syntactic or morphological process that adds an agent causing an event, as in "She broke the vase" → "She made him break the vase."
Passive: A voice construction in which the patient or theme of an event becomes the subject, and the agent is omitted or demoted, as in "The ball was kicked."
Active voice: The default voice in which the agent of an action is the subject of the sentence, as in "The cat chased the mouse."
Middle voice: A voice construction intermediate between active and passive, often expressing an action performed on oneself or a reflexive-like event, common in Greek and some Romance languages.
Antipassive: A voice construction that demotes the object of a transitive verb to an oblique or non-core position, reducing the valency of the verb, common in ergative languages.
Ergative: A grammatical case marking the agent of a transitive verb, contrasting with the absolutive case that marks the intransitive subject and the object of a transitive verb.
Absolutive: A grammatical case marking both the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive systems.
Split ergativity: A system in which a language uses ergative-absolutive marking in some contexts (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative in others (e.g., present tense), as in Hindi-Urdu.
Nominative-accusative: An alignment system in which the intransitive subject and the transitive agent share one case (nominative), while the transitive patient receives another (accusative).
Active-stative: An alignment system in which intransitive subjects are marked differently depending on their semantic role (agent-like vs. patient-like), as in many Australian and Mayan languages.
Word order: The conventional arrangement of constituents (subject, verb, object) in a sentence, which can be SVO, SOV, VSO, etc.
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English "She eats apples."
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese and Korean.
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in classical Arabic and Irish.
VOS: A word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject, as in some Malagasy constructions.
OVS: A word order in which the object precedes the verb, which precedes the subject, rare cross-linguistically but attested in some Hixkaryana and Warao sentences.
OSV: A word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb, found in some Manam and Tariana clauses.
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice, such as "will," "have," or "be" in English.
Modal verb: An auxiliary verb that expresses modality such as obligation, possibility, or permission, such as "must," "can," "should," and "may" in English.
Copula: A verb that links a subject to a predicate nominative or adjective, such as "be" in "She is a teacher" or "is" in "He is tall."
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event, such as whether it is completed, ongoing, or habitual, independent of tense.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of utterance, such as past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, imperative, or optative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of information, such as whether a statement is based on direct observation, hearsay, or inference, as in Turkish or Quechua.
Irrealis: A grammatical category marking events that are not actual, such as hypothetical, desired, or future events.
Realis: A grammatical category marking events that are actual, real, or certain.
Perfective: An aspect marking an event as a complete, bounded whole, without internal structure.
Imperfective: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, internal, or unbounded, including progressive and habitual readings.
Progressive: An aspect marking an event as ongoing or in progress at a reference time, as in "She is running."
Habitual: An aspect marking an event as repeated or customary over a period of time, as in "She runs every morning."
Stative: An aspect or verb class describing a persistent state or condition rather than a dynamic event, such as "know" or "be tall."
Inchoative: An aspect marking the beginning or onset of a state or event, as in "The door began to open."
Iterative: An aspect marking the repeated occurrence of an event, as in "He knocked and knocked."
Semelfactive: An aspect marking a single, punctual occurrence of an event, as in "He knocked once."
Durative: An aspect or verb class describing an event or state that has measurable duration.
Punctual: An aspect or verb class describing an event that has no internal duration, occurring at a single point in time.
Telic: An event or verb that has a natural endpoint or goal, such as "build a house" or "drink a glass of water."
Atelic: An event or verb that has no inherent endpoint, such as "run," "think," or "be a teacher."
Inceptive: An aspect marking the beginning of a state, as in "She became angry."
Ingressive: An aspect marking the transition into a state, as in "He fell asleep."
Egressive: An aspect marking the transition out of a state, as in "He woke up."
Cessative: An aspect marking the ending or ceasing of an event, as in "He stopped running."
Nantative: An aspect or morphological category marking an event that did not occur or a state that did not hold.
Negative: A grammatical element that reverses the truth value of a proposition, such as "not" in English or "ne" in French.
Interrogative: A sentence form or grammatical construction used to ask a question, marked in English by word order change, "wh-" words, or intonation.
Imperative: A mood or sentence type used to give a command or request, as in "Close the door!"
Optative: A mood expressing a wish or desire, as in "God save the queen" or Greek "εἴη" (may it be).
Jussive: A mood expressing a command, wish, or recommendation, often used in subordinate clauses, as in "I insist that he leave."
Conditional: A mood or clause type expressing a hypothetical or contingent situation, often paired with a main clause, as in "If it rains, we will stay home."
Subjunctive: A verb mood expressing doubt, desire, possibility, or hypothetical situations, as in "I suggest that she go" or French "que elle aille."
Indicative: The verb mood used for statements of fact or certainty, as in "She goes to school every day."
Declarative: A sentence type that asserts or states a proposition, as in "The sky is blue."
Exclamative: A sentence type expressing strong emotion or emphasis, often with inverted word order or exclamatory intonation, as in "How beautiful she is!"
Topic: The aboutness of an utterance; the entity or subject that the discourse is revolving around, often marked by word order or special particles.
Focus: The element of an utterance that is being highlighted, contrasted, or presented as new information, often marked by clefting or intonation.
Theme: The starting point of a sentence or utterance; the given or known information from which the message proceeds.
Rheme: The new or informative part of a sentence that adds to the theme, carrying the primary communicative payload.
Given: Information assumed to be already known or accessible in the discourse context, often realized as the topic.
New: Information that is not yet established in the discourse, typically realized as the focus or rheme.
Presupposition: Background information that is taken for granted or assumed true by a speaker, regardless of whether the sentence is affirmed or negated, such as the existence of "the king" in "The king of France is bald."
Implicature: Information that is not explicitly stated but is communicated through the speaker's intent and can be canceled without contradiction, as in "Some of the students passed" implicating "not all."
Entailment: A logical relationship between two propositions where the truth of one guarantees the truth of the other, as in "She won the race" entails "She participated in the race."
Contradiction: A logical relationship in which two propositions cannot both be true, as in "She is in" and "She is not in."
Paraphrase: A restatement of a sentence in different words that preserves the same truth conditions.
Synonymy: A relationship between words or expressions that have the same or nearly the same meaning in a given context.
Antonymy: A semantic relationship between words that have opposite meanings, such as "hot/cold" or "alive/dead."
Hyponymy: A relationship of specific-to-general meaning, as in "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Meronymy: A part-to-whole semantic relationship, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which one entity is referred to by something closely associated with it, as in "The White House announced a policy."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one entity is described in terms of another based on a perceived resemblance, as in "Time is money."
Polysemy: A phenomenon in which a single word has multiple related meanings, such as "head" (body part, leader, head of a pin).
Homonymy: A phenomenon in which the same word form has two or more unrelated meanings, such as "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Ambiguity: A property of an expression that allows two or more distinct interpretations, such as "I saw the man with the telescope."
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or construction becomes a fixed lexical entry in a language, such as "butterfly" from Old English "butterflyinge."
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules used to combine them.
Generative grammar: The theoretical framework introduced by Noam Chomsky that aims to describe the infinite set of sentences a language can generate from a finite set of rules.
Transformational grammar: A model of grammar in which deep structures are transformed into surface structures by a set of rules, central to Chomsky's early theories.
Universal Grammar: The hypothesis that all human languages share an underlying system of grammatical principles and parameters, innate to the human cognitive endowment.
X-bar theory: A component of phrase structure theory that generalizes the internal structure of phrases, proposing that every phrase has a head, a specifier, and a complement in a uniform schematic.
Government and binding: A framework within generative grammar that explains syntactic relations through a small set of general principles and parameters, including binding, case, and control.
Minimalist Program: The most recent theoretical framework in generative grammar, seeking to reduce the generative machinery to a minimal set of operations, primarily Merge and Move, motivated by computational efficiency.
Case grammar: A framework developed by Zellig Harris and later Noam Chomsky that analyzes verbs in terms of the semantic roles (deep cases) they assign to their arguments.
Role and reference grammar: A functional-syntactic theory developed by Ronald Langacker that distinguishes between semantic roles and syntactic reference, emphasizing the speaker's perspective.
Cognitive grammar: A theory developed by Ronald Langacker that treats language as a form of conceptual structure, with meaning and form paired as symbolic units.
Construction grammar: A theoretical framework that treats constructions (pairings of form and meaning, from words to complex patterns) as the basic units of linguistic knowledge.
Functional grammar: A family of theories that prioritize the functional and communicative motivations for linguistic form, as opposed to formal or structuralist approaches.
Typology: The comparative study of language structures across the world's languages, identifying patterns of universals, tendencies, and parametric variation.
Parameter: A small set of language-particular options within a universal system, such as the Null Subject Parameter or the Head Direction Parameter.
Syntactic tree: A hierarchical diagram representing the structural organization of a sentence into phrases and their constituents.
Dominance: A structural relation in which one node in a tree is higher than another, such that it c-commands or governs it.
C-command: A structural relation in which a node X c-commands a node Y if the first branching node above X also dominates Y, and X does not dominate Y.
Theta criterion: A syntactic principle stating that each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument, and each argument receives exactly one theta role.
Binding theory: A component of generative grammar that governs the interpretation of anaphoric expressions (reflexives, reciprocals) and pronominals relative to their antecedents.
Anaphor: A reflexive or reciprocal expression that must be bound by an antecedent within a local domain, such as "himself" or "each other."
Antecedent: The noun phrase that a pronoun, reflexive, or reciprocal refers back to, such as "John" in "John hit himself."
Reciprocal: A word expressing a mutual or reciprocal relationship, such as "each other" or "one another."
Bound variable: A variable in formal semantics that is linked to a quantifier or operator, such as the variable in "Every student x read a book x."
Free variable: A variable in a logical or semantic representation that is not bound by any quantifier, representing an open or unassigned entity.
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or operator is interpreted, as in the ambiguity of "Every student read every book."
Quantifier: An expression that specifies the quantity or amount of entities in a domain, such as "every," "some," "no," or "most."
Operator: A syntactic or semantic element that binds a variable or has a scope, such as a quantifier, negation, or focus.
Merge: The operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects to form a new constituent, the fundamental operation of syntax.
Phase: A unit of derivation in the Minimalist Program (vP and CP) that determines the locality of operations and the points at which material is sent to the interfaces.
Interface: The point of connection between a linguistic component (such as syntax) and an external system (such as the conceptual-intentional or phonetic systems).
Theta role assignment: The process by which a predicate assigns semantic roles to its arguments, typically occurring in the base structure.
Case assignment: The syntactic process by which grammatical case (nominative, accusative, dative, etc.) is assigned to noun phrases.
Case filter: A syntactic requirement that every overt noun phrase must be assigned grammatical case.
Empty Category Principle: A principle of Government and Binding stating that certain empty positions (like traces of NP-movement) must be governed.
Extended Projection Principle: A principle requiring that every clause must have a subject, whether overt or an empty category like "pro" or "prole."
Trace: An empty element left in the original position of a moved constituent, representing its origin.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from one position to another, leaving a trace or copy behind, such as subject raising or question formation.
Raising: A syntactic process in which an element from a lower clause is moved to a subject or object position in a higher clause, as in "John seems to be happy."
Control: A syntactic relationship in which an overt element (controller) determines the reference of an empty category (controlled) in an infinitival or non-finite clause, as in "John promised to leave."
Exceptional Case Marking: A process in which a matrix verb assigns case to the subject of an embedded infinitival clause, as in "I consider him to be smart."
Rogue: A term sometimes used for syntactic elements that do not fit neatly into the standard theoretical categories.
Island: A syntactic domain from which extraction (movement) is blocked, such as relative clauses, complex NP, and coordinate structures.
Complex NP Constraint: An island constraint that blocks extraction from within a noun phrase containing a relative clause or another embedded clause.
Subject island: An island constraint that blocks extraction of an element from a subject position of an embedded clause.
Coordinate structure constraint: An island constraint that blocks extraction of an element from within a conjunct of a coordination.
Wh-movement: The movement of an interrogative or relative word (a "wh-" word) to the specifier of CP, as in "What did you buy?"
Expletive: A word that fills a syntactic position but contributes little or no semantic content, such as "it" in "It is raining" or "there" in "There are many books."
Prole: An empty expletive subject in an infinitival clause, as in "John wants to leave."
Pro: An empty pronoun with phonetic content in languages that allow null subjects, such as Italian "Mangia" ("He/She is eating").
Null subject: A subject position that is syntactically present but phonologically unpronounced, as in Italian "Parlo" ("I speak").
Subject-verb agreement: The requirement that the subject and the verb in a clause match in person, number, and sometimes gender.
Cliticization: The process by which a clitic attaches phonologically to an adjacent word, often a verb, as in French "je le vois" or English "I'm."
Incorporation: A morphological or syntactic process in which a noun or another word is fused with a verb to form a single complex word, as in Inuit or Mohawk.
Predication: The syntactic and semantic relation by which a property or event is attributed to an entity, as in "She is happy."
Predicative: A use of an adjective that appears in the predicate position, often after a copula, as in "The house is large."
Attributive: A use of an adjective that modifies a noun directly within a noun phrase, as in "a large house."
Genitive construction: A syntactic structure expressing possession or association, such as "the man's hat" or "a hat of the man."
Extraposition: The movement of a constituent, typically a clause, to a position later in the sentence, as in "It is likely that she will come" (from "That she will come is likely").
Fronting: The movement of a constituent to the beginning of a clause for emphasis or discourse reasons, as in "That book, I really enjoyed."
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the front of a clause to mark it as the topic, often with a pause or intonational break.
Cleft sentence: A construction that splits a sentence into two parts to create emphasis or focus, such as the it-cleft "It was John who broke the vase" or the wh-cleft "What I need is a cup of coffee."
Pseudo-cleft: A cleft construction with a wh-clause as the focus and a noun phrase as the theme, as in "What she wants is a new car."
It-cleft: A cleft construction using "it" as the topic and a relative clause as the focus, as in "It is the book that I read."
A-split: A cleft construction found in many non-European languages, particularly in Australian and Papuan languages, used to mark focus.
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or a relative marker, as in "the woman who lives next door."
Noun clause: A clause that functions as a noun in a larger sentence, as in "What she said was surprising."
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverb, modifying the main clause, as in "After she finished, she left."
Adjective clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adjective, modifying a noun, essentially a relative clause.
Appositive: A noun or noun phrase that renames or identifies the noun it follows, as in "Paris, the capital of France, is beautiful."
Partitive: A construction expressing a part of a whole, as in "some of the students" or "a piece of the cake."
Genitive: A construction or case marking a relationship of possession, origin, or association between two nouns.
Copular: A verb or construction that equates or identifies the subject with a predicate, as in "She is a doctor."
Equative: A sentence type that equates two nominal expressions, as in "A bachelor is an unmarried man."
Predicative adjective: An adjective appearing in the predicate, typically after a copula, as in "The sky is blue."
Nominal: A word or phrase functioning as a noun, including nouns, pronouns, and nominalized phrases.
Adnominal: Modifying a noun, as in "red" in "a red car."
Preverbal: Positioned before a verb in a syntactic structure.
Postverbal: Positioned after a verb in a syntactic structure.
Clausal: Pertaining to or constituting a clause.
Non-clausal: Not forming a complete clause, as in a bare noun phrase or an infinitival complement without a subject.
Finite: A verb form that is marked for tense, person, and number, as in "she goes" (as opposed to "to go" or "going").
Non-finite: A verb form that is not marked for tense, person, or number, such as infinitives, gerunds, and participles.
Infinitive: A non-finite verb form, often marked by "to" in English, as in "to eat" or German "essen."
Gerund: A verb form ending in "-ing" that functions as a noun, as in "Swimming is fun."
Participle: A non-finite verb form used to form passive or progressive constructions, such as "broken" or "running."
Present participle: The "-ing" form of a verb used in progressive aspects and as an adjective, as in "a running stream."
Past participle: A verb form used in perfect and passive constructions, as in "written," "broken," or "eaten."
Periphrastic: A construction that uses multiple words or morphemes to express a grammatical category that could in principle be expressed with a single form, as in "will go" vs. a synthetic future.
Synthetic: A grammatical form that expresses a category with a single affix or fused form, as in the Latin "amabo" for future first person singular.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word across all grammatical categories, such as all conjugations of a verb.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Morpheme string: The sequence of morphemes that make up a word or phrase.
Morphophonemic: Pertaining to the interaction between morphology and phonology, such as how phonological changes are conditioned by morphological structure.
Morpho-phonological: Relating to the interface of morphological and phonological processes.
Morphosyntactic: Pertaining to the interface between morphology and syntax, such as how case is assigned and marked.
Morphosemantic: Pertaining to the relationship between morphological structure and semantic content.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their predominant morphological strategies (isolating, agglutinative, fusional, polysynthetic).
Morphological markedness: The degree to which a morphological form is more complex or less basic than an unmarked form, such as plural being marked vs. singular being unmarked.
Morphological alternation: A change in the phonological form of a morpheme or root that depends on the morphological context, such as "man/men" or "go/went."
Irregular morphology: Morphological forms that do not follow the regular productive patterns of a language, such as "went" for "go" or "mice" for "mouse."
Suppletion: The use of an entirely different root form to express a grammatical or lexical distinction, as in "go/went" or "good/better/best."
Zero morpheme: The absence of a morphological marker where a grammatical feature is expressed by the lack of an overt form, as in the absence of "-s" marking singular in English.
Morpheme order: The linear arrangement of morphemes within a word, such as the order of tense, aspect, and mood markers.
Morpheme ordering: The rules governing the linear sequence of morphemes in a word or phrase.
Morpheme slot: A designated position within a word for a particular type of morpheme.
Morpheme template: A schematic representation of the slots available for morphemes in a word, as in Semitic root-and-pattern morphology.
Root-and-pattern morphology: A morphological system in which consonantal roots are combined with fixed vowel patterns to create words, as in Arabic and Hebrew.
Non-concatenative morphology: Morphological processes that do not simply attach affixes, including reduplication, tonal change, and internal vowel alternation.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which a part or all of a word is repeated to express a grammatical or semantic distinction, such as "bi-bi" for "very beautiful" in Indonesian.
Tonal morphology: The use of tone as a morphological marker, as in some Bantu and West African languages where tone changes mark aspect or number.
Morphological allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has multiple phonological forms, such as the English plural [-s], [z], [ɪz].
Morphological complexity: The degree to which a language or a particular word involves multiple morphemes, alternations, or irregular forms.
Morphological productivity: The extent to which a morphological pattern is actively used to form new words in a language.
Morphological opacity: A situation in which the morphological structure of a word is not transparent due to historical changes, irregularities, or phonological processes.
Morphological economy: A tendency in language for morphological systems to minimize redundancy and complexity.
Morphological richness: The number of grammatical categories and distinctions a language encodes morphologically.
Morphological depth: The number of derivational and inflectional steps that separate a word form from its root.
Morphological derivation: The process of creating new words by adding derivational affixes, as in "happy" → "happiness."
Morphological inflection: The process of modifying a word form to mark grammatical categories, as in "walk" → "walks," "walked," "walking."
Morphological paradigm: The set of all related forms of a word that are generated by a set of morphological rules.
Morphological class: A category of words or morphemes that share a particular morphological behavior, such as strong and weak verbs in German.
Morphological default: An unmarked or default form used in the absence of a specific marking, such as the singular being the default number in English.
Morphological overgeneration: The production of forms that are morphologically possible but semantically odd or unacceptable, such as "ungraspable" (which is actually acceptable) or some unattested combinations.
Morphological undergeneration: The failure of a morphological system to produce all formally possible combinations.
Morphological blocking: The suppression of a regular morphological form by an existing alternative, as in "worse" blocking "***worser."
Morphological exception: A form that deviates from the regular morphological patterns of a language.
Morphological product: The output or result of a morphological process, such as the word form "unhappiness."
Morphological input: The base or input to a morphological process, such as the root "happy" before adding "-ness."
Morphological output: The surface form of a word after all morphological processes have been applied.
Morphological input-output pair: The mapping from an underlying morphological structure to a surface form in morphological theory.
Morphological rule: A rule in a morphological system that specifies how morphemes combine or alternate.
Morphological representation: The abstract structural representation of a word in morphological theory.
Morphological parsing: The process of decomposing a word into its constituent morphemes.
Morphological analysis: The study and description of the structure and processes of morphology.
Morphological description: The detailed account of a language's morphological system.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages by their morphological characteristics.
Morphological typological survey: A comprehensive examination of morphological patterns across languages.
Morphological universals: Generalizations about morphological patterns that hold across languages.
Morphological markedness: The relative complexity or "extra-ness" of one morphological form compared to another.
Morphological naturalness: The degree to which a morphological form or pattern conforms to typologically common or cognitively motivated patterns.
Morphological iconicity: The correspondence between morphological form and meaning, such as the linear order of affixes reflecting the order of meanings.
Morphological transparency: The ease with which the morphological structure of a word can be identified and parsed.
Morphological regularity: The degree to which morphological forms follow consistent, predictable patterns.
Morphological irregularity: Deviation from the regular morphological patterns of a language.
Morphological innovation: The emergence of a new morphological pattern or process in a language.
Morphological change: The diachronic evolution of a language's morphological system.
Morphological leveling: The process by which irregular forms are replaced by regular ones over time.
Morphological fossilization: The preservation of an older morphological form in a frozen or restricted context.
Morphological archaism: A morphological form or pattern that is retained from an earlier stage of the language but no longer productive.
Morphological neologism: A newly coined morphological form or word.
Morphological calque: The borrowing of a morphological structure from one language into another, such as the English "undo" modeled on Romance "des-faire."
Morphological borrowing: The transfer of a morpheme or morphological pattern from one language to another.
Morphological interference: The influence of a speaker's first language morphology on their use of a second language.
Morphological transfer: The application of L1 morphological patterns in L2 production.
Morphological acquisition: The process by which children or adults learn the morphological system of a language.
Morphological processing: The cognitive processes involved in parsing and producing morphologically complex words.
Morphological awareness: A metalinguistic skill involving the ability to manipulate and reflect on morphological structure.
Morphological competence: A speaker's knowledge of the morphological system of a language.
Morphological performance: The actual use of morphological forms in speech or writing.
Morphological error: A mistake in the application of morphological rules, such as "goed" for "went" in early L2 acquisition.
Morphological overregularization: The application of a regular morphological pattern to an irregular form, as in "goed" or "mouses."
Morphological underspecification: A situation in which a morphological form does not fully specify all relevant grammatical features.
Morphological overspecification: A situation in which a morphological form specifies more features than are contextually required.
Morphological ambiguity: A situation in which a word form can be parsed into morphemes in more than one way.
Morphological productivity ranking: A ranking of morphological patterns by their frequency and willingness to be extended to new items.
Morphological frequency: The number of times a particular morphological pattern or form occurs in a corpus.
Morphological complexity index: A quantitative measure of the morphological complexity of a language or text.
Morphological richness measure: A metric quantifying the number of distinct morphological forms a language possesses.
Morphological depth measure: A metric quantifying the maximum number of morphemes in a word or the number of derivational steps.
Morphological typological parameter: A variable dimension along which languages differ in their morphological organization.
Morphological universality: A generalization about morphological systems that holds across all or nearly all of the world's languages.
Morphological tendency: A probabilistic generalization about morphological patterns that holds for a majority of languages.
Morphological exception to a universal: A language or pattern that deviates from a stated morphological universal.
Morphological typological correlation: A statistical or functional relationship between two or more morphological features across languages.
Morphological map: A graphical or schematic representation of the morphological structure of a language or word.
Morphological grid: A tabular representation of the paradigmatic and syntagmatic relations among morphemes.
Morphological box model: A framework for representing the multidimensional space of morphological forms.
Morphological component: A subsystem of grammar responsible for the formation of words from morphemes.
Morphological theory: The theoretical framework or model used to describe and explain the morphology of a language.
Morphological modeling: The construction of formal models of morphological systems for theoretical or computational purposes.
Morphological algorithm: A step-by-step procedure for generating or parsing morphological forms.
Morphological parser: A computational tool that decomposes a word into its morphemes.
Morphological generator: A computational tool that produces well-formed words from morphemes according to a language's rules.
Morphological lexicon: The inventory of morphemes and their properties in a language.
Morphological rule ordering: The specification of the sequence in which morphological rules are applied.
Morphological rule interaction: The way in which one morphological rule affects the application or output of another.
Morphological rule cancellation: The suppression or neutralization of one morphological rule by the application of another.
Morphological rule blocking: The prevention of one morphological rule from applying due to the presence of another form or rule.
Morphological rule competition: A situation in which multiple morphological rules could apply to the same input, requiring a selection mechanism.
Morphological rule generalization: The extension of a morphological rule to new items or contexts.
Morphological rule restriction: The limitation of a morphological rule to a subset of its potential applicability.
Morphological rule exception: A specific item or context in which a general morphological rule does not apply.
Morphological rule productivity: The degree to which a morphological rule is extended to new forms.
Morphological rule opacity: The degree to which the application of a morphological rule is not transparent to the speaker.
Morphological rule regularity: The degree to which a morphological rule applies consistently across all relevant contexts.
Morphological rule irregularity: The degree to which a morphological rule has exceptions or gaps.
Morphological rule markedness: The degree to which a morphological rule is associated with marked or less basic forms.
Morphological rule naturalness: The degree to which a morphological rule aligns with cross-linguistically natural patterns.
Morphological rule economy: The tendency for morphological rules to be as simple and general as possible.
Morphological rule redundancy: The presence of overlapping or unnecessary morphological rules.
Morphological rule convergence: The tendency for separate morphological rules to merge or simplify over time.
Morphological rule divergence: The tendency for a single morphological rule to split into multiple distinct rules over time.
Morphological rule innovation: The emergence of a new morphological rule in a language.
Morphological rule loss: The disappearance of a morphological rule from a language over time.
Morphological rule change: The diachronic modification of a morphological rule.
Morphological rule stability: The degree to which a morphological rule resists change over time.
Morphological rule variation: The coexistence of alternative morphological rules in a language or dialect.
Morphological rule variation gradient: A cline of usage between two or more competing morphological rules.
Morphological rule standardization: The process by which one of several competing morphological rules becomes the norm.
Morphological rule fossilization: The freezing of a morphological rule in a restricted or archaic form.
Morphological rule reanalysis: A shift in the perceived morphological structure of a word or pattern.
Morphological rule remotivation: The reassignment of a morphological form to a different rule or pattern.
Morphological rule analogy: The extension of a morphological pattern from one set of items to another by analogy.
Morphological rule generalization from analogy: The process by which an analogical morphological pattern becomes productive.
Morphological rule exception listing: A list of forms that are exceptions to a general morphological rule.
Morphological rule paradigm: The set of all forms that a morphological rule generates for a particular lexical item.
Morphological rule distribution: The phonological, morphological, and syntactic environments in which a morphological rule applies.
Morphological rule conditioning: The factors (phonological, morphological, syntactic, semantic) that determine when a morphological rule applies.
Morphological rule interaction effect: The combined effect of multiple morphological rules on a single form.
Morphological rule ordering problem: The challenge of determining the correct sequence of rule application in a morphological system.
Morphological rule cyclicity: The phenomenon in which morphological rules are applied multiple times in a cycle, as in derivational morphology.
Morphological rule recursion: The repeated application of a morphological rule to its own output.
Morphological rule base: The underlying morphological structure to which rules are applied.
Morphological rule output: The surface form resulting from the application of morphological rules.
Morphological rule well-formedness: The condition that the output of a morphological rule must conform to the phonotactic and morphotactic constraints of the language.

The user wants a story that's easy to read aloud, and it will be evaluated based on the total number of words that alliterate with adjacent words. So I need to maximize the number of instances where two consecutive words start with the same letter/sound.

Let me think about what "alliterate with adjacent words" means.
