Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, as in the contrast between /p/ and /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A phonetic variant of a phoneme that occurs in a predictable context without changing word meaning, such as the aspirated [pʰ] in "pin" versus the unaspirated [p] in "spin."
Phonetics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of the abstract, systematic organization of sounds in a language, including how sounds pattern and contrast.
Consonant: A speech sound produced by a complete or partial obstruction of the airstream in the vocal tract, as opposed to a vowel.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction, serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely closing the vocal tract, building up air pressure, and then releasing it abruptly, such as /p/, /t/, /k/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow without complete closure, such as /s/, /f/, /ʃ/.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, as in /tʃ/ in "church" or /dʒ/ in "judge."
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip touching the alveolar ridge while air flows around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Trill: A consonant produced by rapid, repeated vibrations of a part of the vocal tract, such as the Spanish rolled /r/.
Tap: A single, brief contact of the tongue with the alveolar ridge, as in the "tt" sound in American English "butter."
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable, as in /aɪ/ in "time."
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound whose articulation remains stable throughout its duration, as in /iː/ in "see."
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal folds at the glottis, as in the /ʔ/ in "uh-oh" or in many Polynesian languages.
Aspiration: The burst of breath that accompanies the release of certain voiceless stops, as in the [pʰ] in English "pin."
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during speech production; voiced sounds (like /b/) involve vocal fold vibration, while voiceless sounds (like /p/) do not.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where the primary constriction occurs for a consonant, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The method by which airflow is obstructed or modified in the vocal tract to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Suprasegmental: A prosodic feature that extends over more than one phoneme, including stress, tone, and intonation.
Prosody: The study of rhythmic, stress, and intonation patterns in spoken language.
Intonation: The variation of pitch across an utterance to convey grammatical or pragmatic information, such as rising intonation for yes/no questions.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable or word, typically marked by greater loudness, longer duration, or higher pitch.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch on syllables or words to distinguish meaning, as in the four tones of Mandarin Chinese.
Pitch: The perceptual correlate of fundamental frequency, perceived as the "highness" or "lowness" of a sound.
Duration: The length of time a sound, syllable, or utterance is produced, a parameter relevant to both segmental and suprasegmental phonology.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the speech signal, produced by resonances of the vocal tract, critical for distinguishing vowels.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of speech sounds as physical sound waves, including their frequency, amplitude, and waveform properties.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the movements and configurations of the articulators in the vocal tract.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the human auditory system.
IPA: The International Phonetic Alphabet, a standardized system of symbols for representing the sounds of all human languages.
Transcription: The process of writing down speech using phonetic symbols to represent the sounds actually produced.
Broad transcription: A phonemic transcription using a limited set of symbols to represent the underlying phonemic structure of an utterance.
Narrow transcription: A detailed phonetic transcription that captures all allophonic and articulatory details of an utterance.
Minimal pair: Two words that differ in only one phoneme in the same context, demonstrating that the phoneme is contrastive, as in "pat" and "bat."
Phonemic contrast: A contrast between two sounds that distinguishes meaning in a particular language, confirming that they are separate phonemes.
Complementary distribution: A relationship between two sounds where each occurs in mutually exclusive environments, suggesting they may be allophones of one phoneme.
Free variation: A situation where two or more sounds may be used interchangeably in the same environment without changing meaning.
Neutralization: A process in which a phonemic contrast is lost in a particular phonological environment, as in the final consonant devoicing in German.
Aperture: The degree of opening of the mouth during the production of a vowel, ranging from close to open.
Labial: A manner or place of articulation involving the lips, such as bilabial consonants /p/, /b/, /m/.
Dental: A consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth, such as the English /θ/ and /ð/.
Alveolar: A consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade at the alveolar ridge, such as /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/.
Palatal: A consonant produced with the body of the tongue raised toward the hard palate, such as /j/ in "yes" or the palatal nasal /ɲ/.
Velar: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate (velum), such as /k/, /ɡ/, /ŋ/.
Uvular: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula, such as the French /ʁ/.
Pharyngeal: A consonant produced with the tongue root retracted toward the pharyngeal wall, as in Arabic /ħ/ and /ʕ/.
Glottal: A consonant or vowel feature produced at the level of the vocal folds in the larynx, such as the glottal stop /ʔ/ or the glottal fricative /h/.
Laryngeal: Relating to the larynx as a site of articulation; in some languages, laryngeal consonants (pharyngeals and epiglottals) are contrastive.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing permissible sequences of sounds in a language, such as which consonant clusters are allowed at the beginning of a word.
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic organization in speech, typically consisting of an onset, nucleus (vowel), and optional coda.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
Nucleus: The vowel (or syllabic consonant) that forms the core of a syllable.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable from the onset onward, consisting of the nucleus and coda; in poetry, the matching of these elements.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a string of sounds into syllables according to a language's phonological rules.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or grammatical function, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Morphology: The branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules governing word formation.
Root: The core, morphologically unanalyzable part of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning, such as "play" in "playing" or "playful."
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix attached before the root of a word, such as "un-" in "undo" or "pre-" in "preview."
Suffix: An affix attached after the root of a word, such as "-ed" in "walked" or "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix inserted within a root, as in the English expletive infix "-f-" in "abso-freaking-lutely."
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds a stem on both sides, such as the German "be-…-en" in "bedanken" (to thank).
Derivational morpheme: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-ness" in "happiness" or "un-" in "unhappy."
Inflectional morpheme: An affix that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without changing the word's basic meaning or part of speech, such as "-s" in "cats."
Allomorph: A phonological variant of a morpheme that appears in different phonological environments, such as the three allomorphs of English plural: /s/ in "cats," /z/ in "dogs," /ɪz/ in "boxes."
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonological content but is inferred from the morphological contrast, as in the singular form "cat" versus the plural "cats."
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical meanings, such as the French past tense ending "-ait" encoding third person, singular, and imperfect.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more independent roots or stems are combined to create a new word, as in "blackboard" or "fireplace."
Agglutination: A morphological process in which morphemes are concatenated to a root with clear boundaries, each morpheme typically carrying a single grammatical meaning, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional morphology: A morphological system in which a single affix simultaneously encodes multiple grammatical features, as in Latin "amavi" (I loved), where the ending encodes person, number, tense, and aspect.
Isolating morphology: A morphological type in which words are typically monomorphemic, and grammatical relations are expressed by separate function words, as in Mandarin Chinese or Vietnamese.
Polysynthetic morphology: A morphological type in which a single word can incorporate numerous morphemes, often equivalent to an entire clause, as in many Native American languages like Mohawk or Inuktitut.
Morphophonology: The study of the interaction between morphology and phonology, particularly how morphological processes trigger phonological alternations.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of related word forms, such as the lexeme "run" encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word, used as the headword, such as "go" for the paradigm including "goes," "went," and "gone."
Inflection: The modification of a word to express grammatical categories like tense, number, case, or comparison, without changing its fundamental lexical meaning.
Derivation: A word-formation process that creates a new lexeme from an existing root or stem, often by adding derivational affixes, such as "care" to "careful."
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word showing its morphological alternations across grammatical categories, such as the full conjugation of a verb.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and the next begins within a word, often marked in linguistic analysis by a hyphen, as in "un-happy-ness."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-un" or "re-."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat," "run," or "the."
Clipping: A word-formation process that shortens a longer word, as in "phone" from "telephone" or "lab" from "laboratory."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words into a new word, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor" or "babysit" from "babysitter."
Converse formation: A word-formation process that creates a new verb from an existing noun, as in "email" (noun) to "to email" (verb).
Neologism: A newly coined or recently introduced word or expression that has not yet been fully established in the lexicon.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which part or all of a word is repeated to create a new form, as in "bi-bi" (Indonesian for "walk") or "mama" for "mother."
Suppletion: The use of an etymologically unrelated form to express an inflectional alternation, as in "go" → "went" or "man" → "men" in English.
Conjugation: The systematic pattern of inflectional changes a verb undergoes to express person, number, tense, aspect, mood, and voice.
Declension: The systematic pattern of inflectional changes a noun, adjective, or pronoun undergoes to express case, number, and gender.
Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created in a language, including compounding, derivation, blending, clipping, and borrowing.
Base: The morpheme to which an affix is attached in a word-formation process; in multi-affix words, the base may itself contain affixes.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may include both a root and derivational affixes, as in "happi-" in "happier."
Morph: A theoretical linguistic sign consisting of a paired form and meaning; the abstract counterpart of a morpheme before its phonological realization.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has multiple phonological realizations, such as the English past tense morpheme realized as /t/, /d/, /ɪd/.
Morphological productivity: The degree to which a particular word-formation pattern is actively used to create new words in a language.
Morpheme family: A set of related words that share a common root or derivational base, such as "act," "action," "active," "activate," and "react."
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the structure of phrases and sentences.
Phrase: A group of words headed by a single category (noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition) that functions as a constituent within a sentence.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate (verb phrase), which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: A maximal syntactic unit that expresses a complete thought, typically consisting of at least one clause.
Tree diagram: A graphical representation of the hierarchical constituency structure of a sentence, showing how phrases are nested.
Constituency: The property of a string of words forming a grammatical unit that can be tested for through movement, substitution, or clefting.
Constituent: A part of a sentence that functions as a unit within the syntactic structure, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Phrase structure grammar: A model of syntax that uses rewrite rules to generate the hierarchical structure of sentences from terminal symbols.
Immediate constituent analysis: A method of syntactic analysis that recursively divides a sentence into its largest parts until each part is a single word.
Deep structure: In generative grammar, the underlying syntactic representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface structure: In generative grammar, the final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied, corresponding to the actual word order.
Transformation: A rule in transformational grammar that maps a deep structure to a surface structure, such as moving an element to a different position.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure that posits a three-barbracket structure (XP, X̄P, X) for all phrases, with a head, specifier, and complement.
Head: The central, category-determining element of a phrase, such as the noun in a noun phrase or the verb in a verb phrase.
Complement: The constituent that is directly selected by a head and follows it within a phrase, such as the object following a transitive verb.
Specifier: The constituent that precedes the head within a phrase, such as the determiner in a determiner phrase.
Adjunct: An optional, peripheral constituent that modifies a phrase without being selected by its head, such as a manner adverb or a relative clause.
Trace: An unpronounced copy of a moved element left behind at the original position, as in "What did you buy ___?"
Movement: A syntactic operation in which an element is displaced from one position to another, as in question formation or passive constructions.
Binding: The set of principles governing the relationship between a pronoun, a reflexive, or an anaphor and its antecedent within a syntactic domain.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Theme, Goal, or Source.
Case: A morphological or syntactic category marking the grammatical function of a noun phrase, such as nominative, accusative, dative, or genitive.
Agreement: The requirement that certain grammatical features (number, gender, person) match between a head and its dependent, as in subject-verb agreement.
Binding theory: A component of generative grammar that specifies the conditions under which anaphoric expressions (reflexives, reciprocals, pronouns) can be bound by an antecedent.
Government and Binding: A major framework in generative syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s, comprising Principles and Parameters, Case theory, and the Empty Category Principle.
Universal Grammar: The theory that all human languages share a common underlying set of structural principles and parameters, innate to the human mind.
Generative grammar: A model of linguistics, developed by Noam Chomsky, that aims to describe the infinite set of grammatical sentences a language can generate from a finite set of rules.
Phrase marker: A labeled tree diagram in generative grammar showing the syntactic structure of a constituent at a particular stage of derivation.
Lexical insertion: The process in generative grammar by which lexical items (words) are associated with terminal nodes in a phrase structure tree.
Recursion: The syntactic property that allows phrases to contain phrases of the same category, enabling the generation of sentences of arbitrary length, as in "the book that the man that the dog chased wrote."
Subcategorization: The property of a lexical item that specifies the number and types of arguments (complements) it requires, as in "give" requiring both a direct and an indirect object.
Government: A structural relationship in syntax in which a head selects and licenses certain arguments within a local domain, crucial in Case assignment.
Empty Category Principle: A syntactic principle requiring that a trace or pro must be properly governed, constraining the positions from which elements can be moved.
Subjacency: A syntactic constraint limiting the distance an element can move in a single step, preventing extraction across certain barriers.
Island constraints: A set of syntactic restrictions that prevent extraction (movement) from certain domains such as relative clauses, complex noun phrases, and wh-islands.
Scrambling: A syntactic process in which the canonical word order of arguments is rearranged, as in Japanese or Hindi-Urdu, without altering the thematic roles.
Word order: The linear arrangement of grammatical elements (subject, object, verb) in a sentence, which varies across languages.
SVO: Subject-Verb-Object word order, the most common order in the world's languages, found in English, Mandarin, and French.
SOV: Subject-Object-Verb word order, found in Japanese, Korean, Turkish, and Latin.
VSO: Verb-Subject-Object word order, found in Classical Arabic, Irish, and Welsh.
VOS: Verb-Object-Subject word order, found in some Bantu languages and certain dialects of Malagasy.
OVS: Object-Verb-Subject word order, found in a small number of languages such as Hixkaryana.
OSV: Object-Subject-Verb word order, found in a very small number of languages such as Ay Maranui.
Coordination: A syntactic process in which two or more elements of the same category are joined by a coordinating conjunction, as in "bread and butter."
Subordination: A syntactic process in which one clause is embedded within or dependent on another, typically introduced by a subordinating conjunction, as in "because it rained."
Embedding: The syntactic process by which one clause is placed within the internal structure of another clause.
Relative clause: A clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or relative marker, as in "the book that I read."
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, optionally preceded by determiners and adjectives, and followed by post-modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its auxiliaries, objects, and complements.
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, optionally preceded by degree adverbs and followed by complements.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, followed by its complement, as in "in the garden."
Determiner phrase: A phrase headed by a determiner (article, demonstrative, quantifier), as in "the book" or "some water."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event or state in time relative to the moment of utterance (past, present, future).
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event, such as perfective (completed) or imperfective (ongoing).
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Voice: A grammatical category that expresses the relationship between the participants in an event and the syntactic roles they occupy, primarily active and passive.
Active voice: The default voice in which the agent of an action is the grammatical subject, as in "The cat chased the mouse."
Passive voice: A voice construction in which the patient or theme of an action becomes the grammatical subject, as in "The mouse was chased by the cat."
Reflexive: A pronoun or morpheme that refers back to the subject of the clause, as in "She saw herself."
Reciprocal: An expression indicating a mutual relationship between participants, as in "They met each other."
Causative: A morphological or syntactic construction that adds an agent who causes an event, as in "break" (intransitive) to "break" (transitive: "She broke the window").
Anticausative: A construction in which a transitive verb is used intransitively without an overt agent, as in "The vase broke."
Ergativity: A transitivity pattern in which the subject of an intransitive verb (absolutive) is treated grammatically like the object of a transitive verb (absolutive), while the agent of a transitive verb (ergative) is marked differently.
Split ergativity: An ergativity pattern in which a language uses ergative alignment in some grammatical contexts (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative alignment in others (e.g., present tense).
Absolutive: The unmarked case in an ergative language, used for the object of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb.
Nominative: The case typically marking the subject of a clause in nominative-accusative languages, as in English "She" (subject) vs. "her" (object).
Accusative: The case marking the direct object of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages, as in English "him," "her," "them."
Dative: The case marking the indirect object or recipient of an action, as in Latin "libro" (to the boy) or German "dem Mann."
Genitive: The case expressing possession, origin, or other relational meanings, as in English "John's book" or Latin "libri."
Instrumental: The case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed, as in Sanskrit or Russian.
Locative: The case marking the location or position of an entity, as in "in the house" or the Latin locative "urbe."
Ablative: The case marking separation, source, or origin, as in "from the city" or Latin "ex urbe."
Allative: The case marking motion toward or arrival at a location, as in Finnish "talon" (to the house).
Vocative: The case used for direct address, as in "O Zeus!" or Latin "Roma!"
Semantics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the study of meaning in language, including word meaning, sentence meaning, and the relationship between language and the world.
Meaning: The interpretive content of a linguistic expression, encompassing both its truth-conditional properties and its pragmatic implications.
Sense: A distinct meaning of a word or expression, as in the multiple senses of "bank" (financial institution vs. river edge).
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it picks out in the world.
Denotation: The set of all entities in the world to which a word or phrase applies, as opposed to connotation.
Connotation: The associated, implied, or emotional meanings of a word beyond its literal denotative content.
Lexical semantics: The study of meaning at the level of individual words and their relationships in the lexicon.
Compositional semantics: The principle and study that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Predicate: A logical or linguistic expression that describes a property of or relation between one or more arguments, as in "is red" or "loves."
Argument: An entity to which a predicate is applied, typically corresponding to a noun phrase in the sentence.
Selectional restriction: A semantic constraint on the arguments of a predicate, as in "*The rock sang" violating the agent restriction on "sing."
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word has multiple related meanings, as in "head" (body part, leader, head of a department).
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form but have different meanings, as in "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or nearly the same meaning in some context, as in "buy" and "purchase."
Antonymy: A semantic relationship between words with opposite meanings, including gradable (hot/cold), complementary (dead/alive), and relational (buy/sell) antonyms.
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one term (hyponym) is included in the meaning of another (hypernym), as in "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernymy: The reverse of hyponymy; the more general or inclusive term in a semantic hierarchy, as in "animal" for "dog."
Meryonymy: A part-whole semantic relationship, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Metonymy: A figurative relationship in which one entity stands for another based on contiguity or association, as in "the White House announced" for "the President announced."
Metaphor: A figurative mapping between two domains based on perceived similarity, as in "Time is money."
Trope: A general category of figurative language, including metaphor, metonymy, and synecdoche.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another, as in "She is a bachelor" entails "She is a man."
Presupposition: Background information that is assumed to be true for a statement to be meaningful, as in "John stopped smoking" presupposes that John used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning that is conveyed by an utterance but is not part of its literal, encoded content, inferred by the hearer from context.
Scalar implicature: An implicature derived from a scale of alternatives, as in "Some of the students passed" implicating "Not all of the students passed."
Contradiction: A semantic relationship in which two statements cannot both be true, as in "It is raining" and "It is not raining."
Paradox: A logically self-contradictory or seemingly impossible statement, such as "This sentence is false."
Ambiguity: The property of an expression having more than one possible interpretation, whether lexical ("bank") or structural ("I saw the man with the telescope").
Vagueness: The property of a term whose boundaries of application are not sharply defined, as in "tall," "bald," or "young."
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or operator exercises its logical force, as in the difference between "Every student read every book" (each book read by all) and the reverse scope.
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies quantity, such as "every," "some," "no," "most," or "three."
Scope ambiguity: An ambiguity arising from the different logical scopes that a quantifier can take, as in "Every boy loves a girl" (each boy loves some girl vs. there is one girl all boys love).
Logical form: The formal, abstract representation of the semantic content of a sentence used in formal semantics.
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines the meaning of linguistic expressions in terms of the conditions under which they are true.
Montague semantics: A formal framework developed by Richard Montague that translates natural language into a formal logical language to analyze meaning compositionally.
Lambda calculus: A formal system of mathematical logic used in formal semantics to represent and manipulate functions of meanings.
Intension: The set of possible worlds in which a term is true or has a referent, as opposed to its extension in the actual world.
Extension: The set of actual entities in the world to which a term applies, as opposed to its intension across possible worlds.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to meaning in communication, including speech acts, implicature, and deixis.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to (or instead of) conveying a proposition, such as promising, ordering, or declaring.
Locution: The actual words uttered and their literal propositional content in the analysis of a speech act.
Illocution: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as a request, a warning, or a declaration, in speech act theory.
Perlocution: The actual effect an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, alarming, or enlightening.
Illocutionary force: The communicative intention behind an utterance, distinguishing, for example, a question from a statement with the same words.
Perlocutionary effect: The consequence or impact an utterance produces in the audience, which may be unintended.
Performative: A speech act that brings about the very state of affairs it describes, as in "I now pronounce you husband and wife."
Constative: A statement that describes a state of affairs and can be evaluated as true or false, as opposed to a performative.
Cooperative principle: Paul Grice's postulate that participants in conversation generally cooperate with one another, adhering to certain maxims.
Maxim of quantity: Grice's maxim that one should make one's contribution as informative as required, and no more informative than required.
Maxim of quality: Grice's maxim that one should not say what one believes to be false or for which one lacks adequate evidence.
Maxim of relation: Grice's maxim that one should be relevant to the ongoing conversation.
Maxim of manner: Grice's maxim that one should be clear, brief, orderly, and avoid ambiguity and obscurity.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred by the hearer from the assumption that the speaker is adhering to Grice's maxims, without it being part of the literal meaning.
Indirect speech act: A speech act whose illocutionary force differs from its locutionary form, such as "Can you pass the salt?" being a request rather than a question.
Deixis: The linguistic expression of reference relative to the context of utterance, including person, place, and time deictics like "I," "here," and "now."
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity, as in "John saw Mary, and she waved."
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse, as in "When the storm hit, it destroyed the farm" (where "it" refers to "the storm").
Discourse: Language use beyond the sentence level, including the organization of meaning across multiple sentences, turns, or texts.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse, signals speaker attitudes, or manages conversation flow, such as "well," "actually," or "by the way."
Topic: The entity or proposition about which a clause or discourse segment is directed, representing the starting point of information flow.
Focus: The part of an utterance that is presented as new or contrastive information, typically marked by stress or intonation.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) and new information, guiding the hearer's attention.
Given-new contrast: The principle that discourse typically proceeds from previously established (given) information to newly introduced information.
Relevance theory: A cognitive-pragmatic framework by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson that explains communication in terms of the optimization of relevance between cognitive effort and contextual effects.
Politeness theory: A framework by Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson analyzing face-threatening acts and the strategies speakers use to mitigate social imposition.
Face: In politeness theory, the public self-image a person claims; positive face is the desire to be approved of, negative face is the desire for freedom from imposition.
Face-threatening act: An utterance that jeopardizes the positive or negative face of the speaker or hearer, such as a request, criticism, or refusal.
Mitigation: A linguistic strategy used to soften the force of a face-threatening act, such as using hedges, modals, or indirect forms.
Repair: A conversational strategy by which a speaker corrects or revises a problematic utterance, either self-initiated or other-initiated.
Turn-taking: The system by which participants in a conversation alternate speaking roles, governed by overlap, pause, and transition-relevance points.
Adjacency pair: A two-part conversational sequence in which the second part is a conventional response to the first, such as question-answer, greeting-greeting, or request-compliance.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The use of lexical items or phrases from one language within the grammatical structure of another, often at the word or phrase level.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social context, defined by field, tenor, and mode of discourse.
Field: The subject matter or topic domain of a discourse, as in medical, legal, or academic register.
Tenor: The social relationship and roles of the participants in a discourse, influencing choices of formality and vocabulary.
Mode: The channel and function of the discourse, such as spoken or written, or whether it is interactive or monologic.
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that link elements within a text, including reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical items.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a text, ensuring that ideas flow in a comprehensible and purposeful manner.
Textual connectivity: The overall structural organization of a text that makes it readable and interpretable as a unified whole.
Ellipsis: The omission of words that are recoverable from context, as in "Who did you see?" / "I saw John, and she ___" (omitting "saw John").
Substitution: The replacement of a word or phrase with a pro-form, such as "do," "one," "it," or "so," to avoid repetition.
Conjunction: The use of logical connectives and discourse markers to express relationships between propositions, such as "however," "therefore," or "meanwhile."
Lexical cohesion: The use of lexical relationships (repetition, synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy) to create semantic links between parts of a text.
Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and social identity.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular geographic region or social group, differing from other varieties in vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as age, class, occupation, or education level.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker, incorporating personal quirks in vocabulary, pronunciation, and syntax.
Standard language: The variety of a language that has been codified in grammar and dictionaries and is used in formal education, media, and government.
Prestige: The positive social value attached to a particular language variety, often associated with education, power, or social mobility.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety, often associated with lower social status or out-group identity.
Language variation: The diversity of linguistic forms within and between speech communities, including dialectal, social, and stylistic differences.
Language change: The systematic and gradual transformation of a language's phonological, morphological, syntactic, and lexical systems over time.
Dialect contact: The interaction between speakers of different dialects or languages, which can lead to borrowing, convergence, or the formation of new varieties.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speakers and is no longer used in everyday communication.
Language extinction: The final stage of language death in which no living person can speak the language.
Endangered language: A language at risk of falling out of use, typically with few native speakers, most of whom are elderly.
Language revitalization: Efforts to revive or strengthen a language that has lost many or all of its native speakers, through education, media, and community programs.
Language policy: The set of official or institutional decisions and actions that influence the status and use of languages in a society.
Language planning: The deliberate, organized efforts to influence the development, structure, or functions of a language or language community.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages, whether simultaneously or sequentially acquired.
Multilingualism: The use of three or more languages by an individual or community.
Language dominance: The tendency of one language in a bilingual speaker's repertoire to be more proficient or preferred over another.
Language attitude: The beliefs, feelings, and evaluations that speakers hold about their own and others' language varieties.
Ethnolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and culture, including how language reflects and shapes cultural identity.
Creole: A stable, natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community, with full grammatical complexity.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops for basic communication between groups with no common language, typically without native speakers.
Patois: A colloquial term for a non-standard dialect or a creole/pidgin variety, used in various contexts across the English-speaking world.
Koine: A simplified, common form of a language that arises from the leveling of dialectal differences, as in Koine Greek.
Linguistic landscape: The visible language features in public spaces, such as signs, advertisements, and government documents, reflecting the multilingual character of a community.
Language and gender: The study of how language use and perception are shaped by and contribute to social gender categories and identities.
Language and identity: The study of how language is used to construct, express, and negotiate social, ethnic, and personal identities.
Dialectology: The branch of linguistics that studies the geographic and social distribution of dialectal variation.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a dialect map separating areas that use different linguistic forms for a particular feature.
Dialect continuum: A chain of mutually intelligible dialects spread across a geographic area, where neighboring dialects are mutually intelligible but distant ones may not be.
Intelligibility: The degree to which a language variety can be understood by a listener, whether native or non-native.
Mutual intelligibility: The ability of speakers of two varieties to understand each other without prior study, a common criterion for distinguishing languages from dialects.
Lingua franca: A language adopted as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages, such as English in international business.
Psycholinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the psychological and neurological processes underlying language acquisition, comprehension, and production.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn a language, whether their first language (L1) in childhood or a second language (L2) later in life.
First language acquisition: The process by which infants and young children acquire their native language, typically from birth to about age five.
Second language acquisition: The process by which an individual learns a language other than their first language, through formal instruction or immersion.
Critical period hypothesis: The proposal that there is a biologically determined window in childhood during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and completely.
Language faculty: The hypothesized innate cognitive capacity in the human brain that enables language learning and use, central to Chomskyan theory.
Phonological development: The process by which infants and young children acquire the sound system of their native language, progressing from babbling to adult-like phonology.
Morphological development: The process by which children acquire and use morphological structures, from simple plural marking to complex derivations.
Syntactic development: The process by which children acquire the syntactic rules of their language, progressing from single words to complex sentences.
Semantic development: The process by which children expand and refine their understanding of word meanings and the relationships between words.
Pragmatic development: The process by which children learn the social and contextual rules of language use, including turn-taking, requests, and indirect speech.
Baby talk: Informal, simplified language used by adults when speaking to infants, characterized by high pitch, exaggerated intonation, and short sentences.
Parentese: The distinctive speech style adults use with infants, featuring higher pitch, slower tempo, shorter utterances, and exaggerated prosody.
Cooing: The production of vowel-like vocalizations by infants, typically around two to three months of age.
Babbling: The stage of infant vocal development, around six to twelve months, characterized by repetitive consonant-vowel combinations like "ba-ba-ba."
Holophrase: A single word used by a toddler to express a complete sentence's meaning, as in "Milk!" meaning "I want milk."
Telegraphic speech: The stage of child language development in which children produce short, grammatically incomplete sentences using only content words, as in "Doggy run park."
Overgeneralization: A developmental error in which a child applies a regular grammatical pattern to an irregular form, as in "goed" for "went" or "footies" for "feet."
Underregularization: A developmental error in which a child fails to apply a regular grammatical pattern where it should, often due to relying on an irregular memorized form.
Language processing: The cognitive mechanisms by which individuals parse, interpret, and produce language in real time.
Parsing: The real-time process by which a listener or reader assigns a syntactic structure to an incoming string of words.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word's meaning and properties from the mental lexicon during comprehension or production.
Working memory: The cognitive system that temporarily holds and manipulates information, critical for holding sentences in mind while parsing them.
Reading comprehension: The cognitive process of understanding and interpreting written text, involving decoding, parsing, inference, and background knowledge.
Comprehension: The process of understanding spoken or written language, integrating phonological, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic information.
Production: The process of formulating and articulating or writing an utterance, involving conceptualization, grammatical encoding, and phonological/articulatory encoding.
Fluency: The smooth, uninterrupted flow of speech, characterized by appropriate rate, rhythm, and minimal disfluencies.
Slips of the tongue: Unintentional errors in speech production, such as word substitutions, blends, or omissions, that reveal the structure of the language production system.
Malapropism: The unintentional use of a word in place of a similar-sounding word, resulting in a humorous or absurd effect, as in "an orphan of ideas" for "an orphan of words."
Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage, affecting the ability to produce and/or comprehend language.
Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia resulting from damage to Broca's area (left frontal cortex), characterized by non-fluent, agrammatical speech.
Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia resulting from damage to Wernicke's area (left posterior temporal cortex), characterized by fluent but meaningless or jargon-like speech.
Agrammatism: A syntactic impairment in which the patient omits or misuses grammatical morphemes and function words, as in "Man walk park" for "The man is walking in the park."
Anomia: A language disorder in which the patient has difficulty retrieving or producing specific words, particularly nouns, while other language abilities remain relatively intact.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural basis of language, investigating how brain structures and processes support language abilities.
Language lateralization: The tendency for language functions to be predominantly localized in the left cerebral hemisphere in most right-handed individuals.
Mirror neuron: A type of neuron that fires both when an individual performs an action and when the individual observes the same action performed by another, implicated in action understanding.
Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the development, reconstruction, and classification of languages over time.
Comparative method: A systematic procedure in historical linguistics for establishing genetic relationships between languages by identifying regular correspondences in sound and meaning.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of related languages is reconstructed, such as Proto-Indo-European.
Reconstructed form: A hypothetical word or sound in a proto-language, typically marked with an asterisk (e.g., *bʰer-), based on comparative evidence.
Sound change: A systematic shift in the pronunciation of one or more sounds across a language's vocabulary, such as the English Great Vowel Shift.
Regular sound change: A sound change that applies uniformly to all applicable words in the lexicon, as opposed to analogy or borrowing.
Irregular change: A sound or grammatical change that does not apply uniformly across all relevant words, often due to lexical exception or analogy.
Analogy: A language change process in which the form of a word is altered to make it more regular or to match a pattern found in other words, as in "oxen" being replaced by "oxes" in some dialects.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or linguistic feature from one language into another, as in English borrowing "ballet" from French.
Loanword: A word adopted from one language and integrated into the vocabulary of another, often with phonological adaptation, as in English "kitchen" from Old French "cuisine."
Loan translation: A word or phrase in which each morpheme is translated into the target language while preserving the structure of the source, as in "bookworm" translating German "Buchwurm."
Calque: A loan translation in which the target-language word is formed by translating the components of a foreign word, as in "superman" translating German "Übermensch."
Substrate: The language of the original inhabitants of a region that influences the vocabulary, grammar, or phonology of a later-dominant language.
Superstrate: The language of a conquering or dominant group that contributes lexical or structural features to the substrate language of the region.
Adstrate: A language in contact with another that is neither the substrate nor the superstrate but exerts ongoing influence through lateral contact.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral proto-language, such as the Indo-European or Sino-Tibetan family.
Language branch: A major subdivision within a language family, such as the Germanic branch of Indo-European or the Slavic branch.
Language stock: A grouping of languages or families that share a common ancestor but for which the genetic relationship is less certain than within a family.
Cognate: Words in different languages that share a common etymological origin in a proto-language, such as English "father" and Latin "pater."
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words, including their form, meaning, and the process of their change over time.
Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that phonetically imitate or suggest the sound they represent, such as "buzz," "crash," or "meow."
Ablaut: A type of vowel gradation in which the vowel within a root alternates to mark grammatical distinctions, as in English "sing/sang/sung" or German "schreiben/schrieb/geschrieben."
Umlaut: A process of vowel mutation triggered by a following back vowel or semivowel in an earlier stage, as in the English plural "foot/feet" or "mouse/mice."
Grimm's Law: A systematic set of consonant shifts from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic, such as *p → f, *t → θ, *k → h, and *b → p.
Verner's Law: A follow-up to Grimm's Law explaining why some Proto-Indo-European voiced stops became voiceless fricatives in Proto-Germanic when not preceded by stress.
Lexicon: The mental vocabulary of a language or speaker, comprising all the words and multi-word expressions a language has.
Lexicography: The practice and study of compiling, editing, and writing dictionaries.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts, either written or transcribed spoken language, used for linguistic research and analysis.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large electronic corpora to identify patterns, collocations, and usage frequencies.
Computational linguistics: The application of computational methods and techniques to the analysis and processing of natural language.
Natural language processing: The field of computer science and linguistics concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Machine translation: The use of software to automatically translate text or speech from one language to another.
Speech recognition: The technology that converts spoken language into written or digital text, using acoustic and language models.
Text linguistics: The study of the structure and organization of texts, including coherence, cohesion, genre, and discourse.
Stylistics: The study of style and variation in language use, often at the intersection of linguistics and literary analysis.
Rhetoric: The art of effective persuasion and argumentation through the strategic use of language, encompassing ethos, pathos, and logos.
Discourse analysis: The study of language in extended use beyond the sentence, examining how meaning is constructed across utterances and social contexts.
Conversation analysis: The detailed study of the structure of spoken conversation, focusing on turn-taking, repair, adjacency pairs, and sequential organization.
Narrative: A discourse genre that organizes events in temporal sequence, typically involving characters, a setting, and a plot.
Genre: A category of textual form defined by conventional features of structure, style, and purpose, such as the legal contract, the academic paper, or the fairy tale.
Cohesion: The network of explicit linguistic links (reference, conjunction, lexical items) that hold a text together at the surface level.
Coherence: The underlying logical and thematic connectedness of a text that makes it interpretable as a unified communicative act.
Phonemic: Pertaining to phonemes or the system of phonemic contrasts in a language.
Morphophonological alternation: A predictable change in the form of a morpheme depending on its phonological environment, as in the English plural [s]/[z]/[ɪz] alternations.
Morphological blocking: The prevention of an expected word-formation process due to the existence of a competing form, as in "sheep" blocking the expected plural "sheeps."
Morphological allomorphy: The phenomenon of a single morpheme having different phonological forms in different morphological contexts, such as English plural -s/-es/-/-(e)s.
Morpheme ordering: The linear sequence in which morphemes appear within a word, constrained by morphological rules, as in English where derivational prefixes precede the root and inflectional suffixes follow.
Morphological opacity: The degree to which the internal structure of a word is not transparently accessible, as in "swim/swam/swum" where the connection is not obvious.
Morphological transparency: The property of a word whose morphological structure is clearly decomposable into identifiable morphemes, as in "un-happi-ness."
Morphological productivity: The degree to which a particular affix or word-formation pattern is actively used to create new, understood words in a language.
Morphological exception: A word that does not follow a regular morphological pattern, such as "went" instead of the expected "goed."
Morphological regularization: A language change process in which irregular forms are replaced by regular ones, as in the gradual replacement of "knew" with regular forms in some dialects.
Morphological productivity gradient: The ranking of word-formation patterns by the extent to which they are used to create new words, from highly productive to obsolete.
Morphological ambiguity: The property of a word that can be decomposed into morphemes in more than one way, as in "old men's" (old men's vs. old men's).
Morphological complexity: The degree to which a language's word structure involves multiple morphemes, complex affixation, or intricate internal changes.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their dominant morphological strategies, such as isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Morphological economy: The principle that languages tend to minimize the number of distinct forms needed to express grammatical distinctions.
Morphological markedness: The property of a form or category that deviates from the unmarked or default pattern, often requiring extra morphological material.
Morphological default: The unmarked or most frequent form in a paradigm, often the one that spreads to override marked forms, such as the regular plural in English.
Morphological hierarchy: The layered structure of a word, from root to stem to inflected form, reflecting the order of morphological operations.
Morphological rule: A rule of grammar that describes how morphemes combine to form words, including the order of affixes and any phonological adjustments.
Morphological derivation: The process of creating a new word or lexeme by adding derivational morphology to a base, changing its meaning or part of speech.
Morphological inflection: The process of modifying a word to express grammatical relationships without creating a new lexeme, such as marking tense or number.
Morphological compounding: The process of forming a new word by combining two or more free morphemes or stems into a single compound.
Morphological blending: The process of creating a new word by overlapping parts of two source words, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Morphological clipping: The process of shortening a word by deleting one or more segments, as in "ad" from "advertisement" or "flu" from "influenza."
Morphological back-formation: The process of creating a new word by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "escalate" from "escalator."
Morphological conversion: The process of changing a word's part of speech without adding an affix, as in the noun "water" becoming the verb "to water."
Morphological suppletion: The use of an etymologically unrelated stem to express a grammatical distinction, as in "good/better/best" or "is/are/was/were."
Morphological reduplication: The process of repeating all or part of a morpheme to express grammatical meaning, as in "pipi" (Indonesian) or "titi" (Hokkien).
Morphological infixation: The process of inserting a morpheme within the stem of a word, as in the Indonesian "ke-…-kan" or English "-f-" in expletives.
Morphological circumfixation: The process of adding a morpheme pair that surrounds the stem, as in German "be-…-en" or Germanic "ge-…-en."
Morphological derivation vs. inflection: The fundamental distinction between processes that create new lexemes (derivation) and those that mark grammatical relationships within a paradigm (inflection).

1. Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word.

4. Phonology: The study of the sound systems and patterns of a language.
5. Segment: A discrete unit of sound, typically a consonant or vowel.
6. Suprasegmental: Features of speech that extend across multiple segments, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
7. Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction.
8. Consonant: A speech sound produced with a constriction or complete closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
9. Voiced: A sound produced with vibration of the vocal folds.
10. Voiceless: A sound produced without vibration of the vocal folds.
11. Aspiration: A burst of air accompanying the release of a stop consonant.
12. Bilabial: A sound produced with both lips, such as /p/ or /m/.
13. Labiodental: A sound produced with the lower lip against the upper teeth, such as /f/ or /v/.
14. Dental: A sound produced with the tongue against the upper teeth, such as /θ/ or /ð/.
15. Alveolar: A sound produced with the tongue against the alveolar ridge, such as /t/, /d/, /n/, /l/, /s/, /z/.
16. Postalveolar: A sound produced just behind the alveolar ridge, such as /ʃ/ or /ʒ/.
17. Retroflex: A sound produced with the tongue tip curled back toward the hard palate, such as /ʈ/ or /ɖ/.
18. Palatal: A sound produced with the body of the tongue against the hard palate, such as /ɲ/ or /j/.
19. Velar: A sound produced with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, such as /k/, /g/, /ŋ/.
20. Uvular: A sound produced with the back of the tongue against the uvula, such as /q/ or /ʁ/.
21. Pharyngeal: A sound produced with constriction in the pharynx, such as /ʕ/ or /ħ/.
22. Glottal: A sound produced at the glottis, such as the glottal stop /ʔ/.
23. Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release of air, also called a stop.
24. Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel creating turbulence, such as /s/ or /f/.
25. Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, such as /tʃ/ or /dʒ/.
26. Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
27. Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue sides allowing air to flow around the sides, such as /l/.
28. Approximant: A consonant produced with a narrowing of the vocal tract that is not sufficient to create turbulent airflow, such as /w/, /j/, /ɹ/.
29. Glide: A transitional sound between a vowel and a consonant, such as /w/ or /j/.
30. Trill: A consonant produced by rapid vibration of an articulator, such as the alveolar trill /r/.
31. Flap: A consonant produced by a single rapid tap of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, as in the American English /t/ in "butter."
32. Tap: A consonant produced by a brief, single contact of an articulator, essentially the same as a flap.
33. Broad transcription: A phonemic level of transcription that captures only the phonemically relevant distinctions.
34. Narrow transcription: A phonetic level of transcription that captures all phonetic detail, including allophonic variation.
35. IPA: The International Phonetic Alphabet, a standardized system for representing the sounds of spoken language.
36. Stress: The relative prominence of one syllable over others in a word or phrase, involving loudness, duration, or pitch.
37. Tone: A contrast in pitch used to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Chinese or Vietnamese.
38. Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical or pragmatic meaning.
39. Prosody: The study of suprasegmental features including stress, rhythm, tone, and intonation.
