# Glossary of Linguistics Terms

Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word (e.g., /p/ and /b/ in "pat" vs. "bat").
Allophone: A phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word (e.g., the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English "pin" and "spin").
Phonology: The study of the sound systems of languages, including how sounds function, contrast, and pattern within a particular language.
Phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds, including their articulation, acoustic characteristics, and perceptual processing.
Seguement: A discrete unit of sound in speech, typically a vowel or consonant, as opposed to a suprasegmental feature.
Suprasegmental: A linguistic feature that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase, often marked by greater loudness, pitch, or duration.
Tone: A contrast in pitch used to distinguish lexical items or grammatical features, as in Mandarin Chinese or Yoruba.
Intonation: The rise and fall of pitch across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical or pragmatic meaning, such as question or statement.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, allowing air to flow freely without significant constriction.
Consonant: A speech sound produced by a constriction or complete blockage of the airflow in the vocal tract.
Stop: A consonant produced by completely blocking the airflow and then releasing it, also called a plosive (e.g., /p, t, k/).
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel to create turbulent noise (e.g., /f, s, ʃ/).
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a stop and releases as a fricative (e.g., /tʃ/ as in "church").
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity (e.g., /m, n, ŋ/).
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue body raised but allowing air to flow around the sides of the tongue (e.g., /l/).
Rhotic: A consonant associated with the English letter "r," including trills, taps, and approximants (e.g., /r, ɾ/).
Plosive: Another term for a stop consonant, produced by a complete closure followed by a release of air.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a speech sound; sounds can be voiced (e.g., /b/) or voiceless (e.g., /p/).
Place of Articulation: The location in the vocal tract where the primary constriction occurs for a consonant (e.g., bilabial, alveolar, velar).
Manner of Articulation: The manner in which airflow is modified to produce a consonant (e.g., stop, fricative, nasal, approximant).
Aspiration: A burst of breath accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in English "pin" [pʰɪn].
Palatalization: A secondary articulation in which the body of the tongue approaches the hard palate during the production of a consonant.
Velarization: A secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue approaches the soft palate during the production of a consonant.
Uvular: Relating to the uvula; a place of articulation for consonants such as /q/ and /ʁ/.
Alveolar: Relating to the alveolar ridge; a common place of articulation for consonants such as /t, d, s, z, n, l, ɾ/.
Bilabial: A place of articulation in which both lips are involved in producing a sound, as in /p, b, m/.
Labiodental: A place of articulation in which the lower lip contacts the upper teeth, as in /f, v/.
Dental: A place of articulation in which the tongue contacts the upper teeth, as in the English "th" sounds /θ, ð/.
Front Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the front of the mouth (e.g., /i, e/).
Back Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the back of the mouth (e.g., /u, ɑ/).
Central Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in a neutral, mid position, as in the schwa /ə/.
High Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised close to the roof of the mouth (e.g., /i, u/).
Low Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in a lowered position (e.g., /a, ɑ/).
Mid Vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body at an intermediate height between high and low (e.g., /e, o, ə/).
Tense Vowel: A vowel produced with relatively high muscle tension and a more extreme articulatory position, as in English "beat" /iː/.
Lax Vowel: A vowel produced with relatively low muscle tension and a less extreme articulatory position, as in English "bit" /ɪ/.
Rounded Vowel: A vowel produced with the lips rounded into a circular shape, as in /u, o/.
Unrounded Vowel: A vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral, as in /i, e/.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one quality to another within a single syllable, as in /aɪ/ in "eye."
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound that does not change quality during its articulation, as in /iː/ in "fleece."
Schwa: The mid-central vowel /ə/, the most common vowel in English, often found in unstressed syllables (e.g., the "a" in "about").
Minimal Pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phonemic segment and have different meanings, such as "pat" and "bat."
Complementary Distribution: A relationship between two sounds that never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of the same phoneme.
Free Variation: A relationship between two sounds that can occur in the same phonetic environment without changing the meaning of a word.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound (e.g., "input" pronounced as [ɪmpʊt]).
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound changes to become less like a neighboring sound (e.g., Latin "piscina" to English "basin").
Metathesis: A phonological process in which two adjacent sounds swap their order, as in "ask" from Old English "æcsian."
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable, as in "gotten" becoming "got" in some dialects.
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, often to break up difficult consonant clusters (e.g., "in't" for "in it").
Deletion: The removal of a sound from a word or phrase, as in "comfortable" becoming "comftable."
Coarticulation: The overlapping of articulatory gestures for adjacent sounds, so that the articulation of one sound is influenced by neighboring sounds.
Syllable: The basic unit of organization in the sound structure of a word, typically containing a vowel nucleus (e.g., the word "cat" has one syllable).
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, preceding the vowel nucleus.
Nucleus: The core or center of a syllable, typically a vowel sound that provides the syllabic peak.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, following the vowel nucleus.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda (e.g., "-at" in "cat").
Peak: The highest point of sonority in a syllable, typically the vowel nucleus.
Margin: The consonantal portions of a syllable, including the onset and coda, as opposed to the vocalic peak.
Open Syllable: A syllable that ends in a vowel, with no coda consonant (e.g., "go" /goʊ/).
Closed Syllable: A syllable that ends in a consonant, with a coda present (e.g., "cat" /kæt/).
Syllabification: The process of dividing a string of sounds into syllables according to a language's phonotactic rules.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used to measure syllable structure; a light syllable has one mora, a heavy syllable has two.
Foot: A unit of metrical structure consisting of one or two syllables, with one or more stressed syllables, used to describe the rhythmic pattern of a language.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (e.g., "be-LOVE").
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (e.g., "MA-ter").
Spondee: A metrical foot consisting of two stressed syllables (e.g., "STAND FIRM").
Anapest: A metrical foot consisting of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable (e.g., "in the SPITE").
Dactyl: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables (e.g., "MER-ri-ly").
Prosody: The study of rhythmic and tonal aspects of speech, including stress, intonation, and rhythm.
Prosodic: Relating to the suprasegmental features of speech, such as stress, tone, and intonation, rather than individual segments.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to the frequency of vocal fold vibration.
Amplitude: The magnitude of pressure variation in a sound wave, perceived as loudness.
Duration: The length of time a speech sound or unit lasts.
Juncture: The pause or boundary between words or phrases in speech, signaling prosodic groupings.
Morphology: The study of the structure and formation of words, including the smallest meaningful units (morphemes) and the rules governing their combination.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatically meaningful unit in a language, such as "un-" in "unhappy" or the plural "-s" in "cats."
Allomorph: A phonological variant of a morpheme, such as the different pronunciations of the English plural morpheme in "cats" /s/, "dogs" /z/, and "geese" /ɪz/.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning and cannot be further decomposed (e.g., "act" in "action").
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached; it may consist of a root plus derivational affixes (e.g., "action" in "actions").
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a stem or root to form a new word or modify meaning, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before the root or stem of a word (e.g., "un-" in "unhappy").
Suffix: An affix that is attached after the root or stem of a word (e.g., "-ness" in "happiness").
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root or stem of a word, as in some Austronesian languages.
Circumfix: An affix that consists of two parts, one before and one after the stem, as in German "ge-…-t" in "gesagt" (said).
Interfix: A morpheme inserted between two other morphemes in a compound word, as in "o" in "tomato" (from "tom" + "ato").
Bound Morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "un-" or "-ness."
Free Morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat" or "run."
Lexical Morpheme: A morpheme that carries lexical or content meaning, typically a root (e.g., "dog," "happy").
Functional Morpheme: A morpheme that carries grammatical or relational meaning rather than core lexical content, such as articles, prepositions, and inflectional affixes.
Inflectional Morpheme: A morpheme that modifies a word for grammatical purposes without changing its lexical category (e.g., plural "-s," past tense "-ed," third person "-s").
Derivational Morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the lexical category (e.g., "-ness" turning "happy" into "happiness").
Agglutinative: A morphological typology in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each with a single grammatical function, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional: A morphological typology in which a single morpheme can express multiple grammatical features simultaneously, as in Latin or Spanish.
Isolating: A morphological typology in which each word typically corresponds to a single morpheme, with little or no affixation, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological typology in which words can incorporate many morphemes, including arguments and predicates, as in Mohawk or Inuktitut.
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical or lexical meanings, as in Latin "amavi" (I loved), which encodes person, number, and tense.
Zero Morpheme: A morpheme with no phonological content, indicated by the absence of an overt form, such as the plural in English "sheep" (one sheep, many sheep).
Suppletion: An irregular morphological alternation in which the allomorphs of a morpheme are unrelated in form, as in English "go" / "went."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical or semantic meaning, as in "by-and-by" or "chit-chat."
Compounding: A morphological process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to form a new word, as in "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Back-Formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor."
Clipping: The shortening of a longer word without changing its meaning, as in "phone" from "telephone" or "flu" from "influenza."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words to create a new word, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a series of words, pronounced as a single word, such as "NASA" or "laser."
Derivation: The process of creating new words by adding derivational affixes to existing roots or stems, often resulting in a change of lexical category.
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without changing the word's lexical category.
Paradigm: A set of related word forms that are conjugated or declined together, such as the paradigm of a verb across all tenses and persons.
Productive: A morphological or phonological pattern that can be freely applied to new or novel items, as opposed to an unproductive or frozen pattern.
Unproductive: A morphological or syntactic pattern that is no longer used to form new words but remains in the existing vocabulary, as in English "-eth" for third person singular.
Morpheme Boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word, often marked by phonological alternations or prosodic features.
Affixation: The process of attaching an affix (prefix, suffix, infix, or circumfix) to a root or stem to form a new word or word form.
Syntax: The study of the rules and principles by which words are combined to form phrases, clauses, and sentences.
Syntactic: Relating to the structure of sentences and phrases as governed by the rules of syntax.
Phrase: A constituent of a sentence that functions as a unit within a larger structure, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be independent (main clause) or dependent (subordinate clause).
Sentence: A complete grammatical unit expressing a proposition, typically consisting of at least one clause with a subject and a predicate.
Constituent: A part of a sentence that functions as a unit, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, or prepositional phrase.
Head: The central or most important element of a phrase, determining the category and many properties of the phrase (e.g., the noun in a noun phrase).
Complement: A constituent that completes the meaning of a head, such as the object in a transitive verb phrase or the complement of an adjective.
Specifier: A constituent that appears before the head in a phrase, often adding limiting or quantifying information, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Modifier: A constituent that provides additional descriptive information about a head or another constituent, such as an adjective in a noun phrase or an adverb in a verb phrase.
Determiner: A word that precedes a noun and specifies its reference, such as articles ("the," "a") or demonstratives ("this," "those").
Noun Phrase: A phrase whose head is a noun, including any determiners, modifiers, and complements (e.g., "the big red dog").
Verb Phrase: A phrase whose head is a verb, including any auxiliaries, objects, and complements (e.g., "ate a big apple").
Adjective Phrase: A phrase whose head is an adjective, including any modifiers and complements (e.g., "very happy about the result").
Adverb Phrase: A phrase whose head is an adverb, modifying a verb, adjective, or other adverb (e.g., "surprisingly quickly").
Prepositional Phrase: A phrase consisting of a preposition and its complement (usually a noun phrase), functioning as a modifier or complement (e.g., "in the house").
Embedded Clause: A clause that functions as a constituent within another clause, such as the object of a verb or the complement of an adjective.
Main Clause: An independent clause that can stand as a complete sentence and is not embedded within another clause.
Subordinate Clause: A dependent clause that cannot stand as a complete sentence and functions as a constituent within a main clause.
Matrix Clause: The main or outermost clause in a sentence that contains one or more embedded (embedded) clauses.
Finite Clause: A clause whose verb is inflected for tense, person, and number, such as "she left."
Non-finite Clause: A clause whose verb is not inflected for tense, person, or number, such as an infinitival ("to leave") or participial ("leaving") clause.
Relative Clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun or relative marker (e.g., "the book that I read").
Noun Clause: A subordinate clause that functions as a noun in the sentence, such as the subject or object (e.g., "What he said surprised me").
Adverbial Clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverb, modifying the main clause (e.g., "After she left, I went home").
Subject: The noun phrase or pronoun that performs the action or is described by the predicate in a clause.
Object: The noun phrase or pronoun that receives the action of the verb or is affected by it.
Predicate: The part of a sentence that contains the verb and provides information about the subject, typically including complements and modifiers.
Agent: The entity that performs or causes an action, typically encoded as the subject in active sentences (e.g., "the boy" in "the boy kicked the ball").
Theme: The entity that is acted upon or moves in a process, also called the patient or object (e.g., "the ball" in "the boy kicked the ball").
Experiencer: The entity that undergoes or feels an event or state, such as the subject in "John is happy" or "John likes pizza."
Recipient: The entity that receives something in a ditransitive construction (e.g., "Mary" in "John gave Mary a book").
Goal: The endpoint or destination of a motion event or the target of a directed action (e.g., "the door" in "He pushed the door").
Source: The starting point or origin of a motion event (e.g., "the house" in "She left the house").
Patient: The entity that undergoes a change of state or is acted upon, similar to the theme in some frameworks.
Instrument: The entity used to carry out an action, often expressed with a preposition (e.g., "with a hammer" in "He hit the nail with a hammer").
Locative: A spatial argument indicating the location of an event or entity (e.g., "in the park" in "They sat in the park").
Transitive: A verb that requires a direct object to complete its meaning (e.g., "eat" in "She ate the apple").
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object (e.g., "sleep" in "She slept").
Ditransitive: A verb that takes two objects, a direct object and an indirect object (e.g., "give" in "She gave him a book").
Valency: The number of arguments (participants) that a predicate requires or can license, such as the valency of a transitive verb being two.
Theta Role: The semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Theme, Experiencer, Recipient, Goal, or Source.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic and semantic role of a noun phrase, often through inflection (e.g., nominative, accusative, dative).
Nominative Case: A grammatical case that typically marks the subject of a transitive or intransitive verb.
Accusative Case: A grammatical case that typically marks the direct object of a transitive verb.
Genitive Case: A grammatical case that typically marks possession or other relations, such as "of" relationships.
Dative Case: A grammatical case that typically marks the indirect object or recipient of an action.
Instrumental Case: A grammatical case that marks the instrument or means by which an action is performed.
Ablative Case: A grammatical case that marks the source or starting point of a motion or the agent of a passive verb.
Vocative Case: A grammatical case used to address or call someone directly (e.g., "O John!").
Ergative: A grammatical relation or case that marks the subject of a transitive verb, contrasting with the absolutive, which marks the subject of intransitive verbs and the object of transitive verbs.
Absolutive: A grammatical relation or case that marks the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in ergative languages.
Word Order: The standard sequence in which the major constituents (subject, verb, object) appear in a sentence.
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English ("The cat ate the mouse").
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese and Turkish.
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in classical Arabic and Irish.
VOS: A word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject, as in some constructions in Malagasy.
Topic: The entity about which a sentence or clause is predicated, often placed in a prominent position such as the sentence-initial position.
Focus: The new or emphasized information in an utterance, contrasted with given or presupposed information.
Rheme: The new or informative part of a sentence, as opposed to the theme or given information.
Cleft: A syntactic construction that divides a sentence into two parts to place focus on a particular element (e.g., "It was John who broke the window").
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction in which a wh-clause occupies the pre-cleft position (e.g., "What I want is a drink").
Extraposition: A syntactic process that moves a heavy constituent (such as a clause) to the end of the sentence, replacing it with a light element (e.g., "It is said that he left").
Raising: A syntactic process in which a subject of an embedded clause appears as the subject of the matrix verb (e.g., "He seems to be happy").
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject of a non-finite clause is interpreted as co-referential with an argument of the matrix verb (e.g., "John tried to leave").
Binding: A syntactic relationship that governs the distribution of pronouns, anaphors, and reflexive elements relative to their antecedents.
Anaphor: A linguistic expression that must be bound by an antecedent within a specific syntactic domain, such as a reflexive pronoun ("himself") or a relative pronoun.
Reflexive: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause (e.g., "Himself broke his own leg" → "He broke himself a drink" → more naturally: "He broke his own arm" / "She saw herself in the mirror").
Reciprocal: A pronoun or expression indicating a mutual relationship between two or more participants (e.g., "They looked at each other").
Pronominal: Relating to or involving a pronoun, as opposed to a full noun phrase.
Antecedent: The expression to which a pronoun, anaphor, or other referring expression points or refers.
C-command: A structural relationship in which a node governs a sister node and all of its descendants, used in binding theory to determine the domains of anaphors and pronouns.
Binding Domain: The smallest clause containing the element and a governing verb, within which a reflexive must find its antecedent (Principle A) and a pronoun must be free (Principle B).
A-movement: A type of syntactic movement that preserves the argumental (theta role) status of the moved element, such as passive or raising constructions.
A-bar Movement: A type of syntactic movement that does not preserve the theta role, such as wh-movement, topicalization, or focus movement.
Wh-movement: The syntactic process of moving a wh-word (who, what, where, when, why, how) to the beginning of a clause in forming a question.
Topicalization: A syntactic process that moves a constituent to the beginning of the sentence to give it topic status (e.g., "This book, I really enjoyed").
Passive: A voice in which the object of an active clause becomes the subject (e.g., "The ball was kicked by the boy").
Active: A voice in which the subject of a clause is the agent of the action (e.g., "The boy kicked the ball").
Voice: A grammatical category that affects the syntactic structure of a clause, primarily distinguishing between active and passive constructions.
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, mood, or voice (e.g., "will," "have," "be").
Modal: A type of auxiliary verb that expresses modality, such as ability, permission, obligation, or possibility (e.g., "can," "must," "should").
Copula: A linking verb that connects the subject to a predicate complement, such as "be" in "She is a teacher."
Negation: A grammatical element that reverses the truth value of a proposition, typically expressed by a negative word such as "not" or "never."
Conjunction: A word or construction that links words, phrases, or clauses of equal syntactic status (e.g., "and," "but," "or").
Coordination: The syntactic process of joining two or more elements of the same category with a conjunction (e.g., "bread and butter").
Subordination: The syntactic process of joining a dependent clause to a main clause with a subordinating conjunction or relative marker.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a complement clause, such as "that" in "I think that she left" or the wh-words in "I know where she went."
Relative Pronoun: A word that introduces a relative clause and serves as a constituent within that clause (e.g., "who," "which," "that" in "the man who called").
Interrogative: A sentence or clause that asks a question, marked by wh-words, intonation, or auxiliary inversion.
Declarative: A sentence or clause that states a fact or proposition (e.g., "The cat is on the mat").
Imperative: A sentence or clause that expresses a command or request (e.g., "Close the door!").
Exclamatory: A sentence or clause that expresses strong emotion or surprise, often marked by exclamation (e.g., "What a beautiful day!").
Constituent Test: A set of syntactic operations (such as substitution, movement, or clefting) used to determine the boundaries of phrase constituents in a sentence.
Phrase Structure Rule: A rule in generative grammar that specifies how a phrase is composed of smaller constituents (e.g., NP → Det N).
Tree Diagram: A graphical representation of the hierarchical structure of a sentence, showing how constituents are embedded within one another.
Bracketing: A notation using brackets [ ] to indicate the hierarchical grouping of constituents in a sentence (e.g., [[The cat] [ate [the mouse]]]).
Ambiguity: A property of a sentence that allows it to have more than one interpretation, whether structural or lexical.
Structural Ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from more than one possible syntactic structure for the same string of words (e.g., "I saw the man with the telescope").
Lexical Ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having more than one meaning (e.g., "bank" as a financial institution or a river edge).
Recursion: The ability to embed clauses or phrases within clauses or phrases of the same type, allowing for sentences of potentially infinite length.
Embeddedness: The degree to which a clause or phrase is nested within other clauses or phrases in a sentence.
Generative Grammar: A theory of language, associated with Noam Chomsky, that aims to describe the set of all grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules.
Transformational Grammar: An earlier model of generative grammar in which surface structures are derived from deep structures through a series of transformational rules.
Deep Structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence, prior to the application of transformations, encoding the basic argument structure.
Surface Structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied, corresponding to the observable word order.
Merge: An operation in Minimalist syntax that combines two syntactic objects to form a larger structure, replacing recursive application of phrase structure rules.
Feature: A property of a syntactic or morphological element used in grammar, such as [+Noun], [-Past], [+Definite], or [+Animate].
Agreement: A grammatical relationship in which one element (typically a verb) shares features such as number, person, or gender with another element (typically its subject).
Concord: Another term for agreement, referring to the matching of grammatical features between related elements in a sentence.
Government: A syntactic relationship in which a head (such as a preposition or verb) determines the category or case of its complement.
Subcategorization: The specification of the types and number of complements or modifiers that a lexical item requires or allows.
Selection: The syntactic requirement imposed by a verb on the category of its complement (e.g., "believe" selects a clausal complement).
Licensing: A grammatical condition that must be satisfied for a particular structure, element, or interpretation to be well-formed.
Empty Category Principle: A principle in government and binding theory stating that empty categories (such as traces or PRO) must be licensed by a governor.
Trace: An empty syntactic element left behind when a constituent moves, marking the original position of the moved element.
PRO: An empty category that appears as the subject of an infinitival clause and is not controlled by an overt argument in the matrix clause (e.g., "It's hard for PRO to please everyone").
Empty Category: A syntactic position that is filled by an element with no phonological content, such as a trace, PRO, or zero pronoun.
Head-Complement Order: The linear order of a head and its complement in a phrase, which varies across languages (e.g., VO vs. OV).
Head-Initial: A typological parameter indicating that the head of a phrase precedes its complement (e.g., English "eat apples").
Head-Final: A typological parameter indicating that the head of a phrase follows its complement (e.g., Japanese "ringo o taberu").
Specifier-Head Order: The linear relationship between the specifier and the head of a phrase, which can vary across languages.
Complementizer Phrase: The highest projection of a clause, headed by a complementizer such as "that" or a wh-word.
Inflectional Phrase: A projection headed by an inflectional element, encoding tense, agreement, and other inflectional features.
Verb Phrase (VP): The projection headed by a verb, containing its complement and modifying adverbs.
Noun Phrase (NP): The projection headed by a noun, containing its determiner, modifiers, and complements.
Determiner Phrase: A revised phrase structure in which the determiner, not the noun, is the head of the nominal phrase.
Extended Projection Principle: A principle in syntax requiring that every clause have a subject (a spec-VP position or equivalent).
Case Filter: A principle in syntax requiring that every overt noun phrase receive structural case or be in a position that licenses it.
Theta Criterion: A principle requiring that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
Extended Projection Principle (EPP): A principle requiring that the subject position of every clause be filled by a (possibly expletive) element.
Expletive: A phonologically realized element that occupies a syntactic position without contributing semantic content, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Dummy: Another term for expletive, referring to elements like "there" in "There is a problem."
Existential: A construction that asserts the existence of an entity, typically using "there" or "it" as a dummy subject.
Split: A construction in which a single semantic argument is expressed by two separate syntactic elements (e.g., "the fact that he left").
Gapping: A form of ellipsis in which a repeated verb or auxiliary is omitted in the second conjunct of a coordination (e.g., "John ate apples and Mary ate [∅] pears").
Sluicing: A form of ellipsis in which everything in a clause except a wh-phrase is omitted (e.g., "John left, but I don't know when").
VP Ellipsis: The omission of a verb phrase that is recoverable from context (e.g., "John can swim, and Mary can [∅] too").
Right Node Raising: A construction in which a shared constituent appears at the right edge of a coordination (e.g., "John will go to the store, and Mary will [∅] too").
Stripping: A form of ellipsis that leaves only a negative or affirmative tag (e.g., "John left, and Mary didn't").
Fragment: A syntactically incomplete utterance that lacks a full clause structure but is interpretable (e.g., "A book!" in response to "What did you buy?").
Ungrammatical: A sentence or string that violates the grammatical rules of a language and is therefore not well-formed.
Well-Formed: A sentence or structure that satisfies all the grammatical rules and constraints of a language.
Derivation: In syntax, the process of building a sentence from the lexicon through successive applications of Merge and Move operations.
Derive: To construct or generate a sentence through the step-by-step application of grammatical rules.
Converge: In syntactic theory, the process by which a derivation meets the interface conditions of the phonological and semantic components.
Convergent: Relating to a derivation that successfully satisfies all interface conditions and yields an interpretable representation.
Divergent: A derivation that fails to satisfy interface conditions and therefore crashes or is ruled out.
Crash: The failure of a syntactic derivation because it cannot be interpreted at the phonological or semantic interface.
Converge and Emerge: The process in Minimalist syntax where the derivation must converge on representations that are interpretable at both interfaces (PF and LF).
Semantic Component: The interface between syntax and meaning, responsible for the interpretation of syntactic representations.
Phonological Component: The interface between syntax and sound, responsible for the pronunciation of syntactic representations.
Logical Form: The level of representation at which semantic and pragmatic interpretation takes place, including quantifier scope and binding.
Phonetic Form: The level of representation at which pronunciation and intonation are determined.
Interpretation: The process of assigning meaning to a syntactic or phonological representation.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Compositional Semantics: A framework for defining the meaning of complex expressions in terms of the meanings of their components.
Truth-Conditional Semantics: A semantic framework that defines the meaning of a sentence in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
Proposition: A unit of meaning that can be true or false, corresponding to the semantic content of a declarative sentence.
Truth Value: The evaluation of a proposition as true or false in a given state of affairs.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs in the world it picks out or denotes.
Referent: The entity in the world that a linguistic expression refers to.
Denotation: The semantic value or set of entities to which a linguistic expression refers (e.g., the denotation of "dog" is the set of all dogs).
Connotation: The associative, emotional, or cultural meaning of a word beyond its literal or dictionary definition.
Polysemy: The relationship between a single word or expression that has multiple related meanings (e.g., "head" as body part, leader, or top).
Homonymy: The relationship between two words that are identical in form but have unrelated meanings (e.g., "bank" as financial institution and river bank).
Homophone: Two or more words that are pronounced the same but have different spellings and meanings (e.g., "flower" and "flour").
Homograph: Two or more words that are spelled the same but have different pronunciations and meanings (e.g., "lead" /liːd/ and "lead" /lɛd/).
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or very similar meanings (e.g., "begin" and "commence").
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings (e.g., "hot" and "cold").
Hyponymy: A semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word is included in the meaning of another (e.g., "rose" is a hyponym of "flower").
Hypernymy: The reverse of hyponymy; the relationship in which a more general term includes more specific terms (e.g., "flower" is a hypernym of "rose").
Meronymy: A part-whole relationship in which one term refers to a part of another (e.g., "wheel" is a meronym of "car").
Holonymy: The whole-part relationship, the reverse of meronymy (e.g., "car" is a holonym of "wheel").
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition necessarily implies the truth of another (e.g., "John is a bachelor" entails "John is male").
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for an utterance to be meaningful, independent of its truth value (e.g., "John stopped smoking" presupposes John used to smoke).
Implicature: A meaning that is conveyed by an utterance but is not part of its literal semantic content, inferred by the hearer (e.g., Gricean conversational implicature).
Metaphor: A figurative expression in which one domain is described in terms of another based on perceived similarity (e.g., "time is money").
Metonymy: A figurative expression in which one entity is referred to by another entity that is spatially or conceptually related (e.g., "The White House announced..." for the U.S. administration).
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsher or more blunt one (e.g., "passed away" for "died").
Dysphemism: An expression that is deliberately harsh, offensive, or blunt, the opposite of a euphemism.
Litotes: A form of understatement that affirms something by negating its opposite (e.g., "not bad" meaning "good").
Tautology: The use of redundant words or phrases that express the same idea (e.g., "free gift" or "advance warning").
Oxymoron: A figure of speech in which two contradictory terms are juxtaposed (e.g., "deafening silence" or "bittersweet").
Collocation: A habitual or conventional combination of words that frequently co-occur (e.g., "make a decision" rather than "do a decision").
Selectional Restriction: A semantic constraint on the types of arguments that a predicate can take (e.g., "drink" typically selects a liquid as its object).
Quantifier: A word or expression that indicates quantity or amount, such as "every," "some," "no," "most," or "three."
Quantifier Scope: The domain over which a quantifier's force extends in a sentence, affecting the truth conditions of the proposition.
Atelic: An event or state that does not have an inherent endpoint (e.g., "run" in "She ran for an hour").
Telic: An event that has an inherent endpoint or goal (e.g., "build a house" implies the house is completed).
Inchoative: A verbal construction that describes the beginning of a state or change of state without an external causer (e.g., "The door opened").
Change of State: A semantic event type in which an entity transitions from one state to another (e.g., "The ice melted").
Causative: A construction in which an agent causes an event or state change in a theme (e.g., "The wind broke the window" vs. "The window broke").
Stative: A verb or predicate that describes a state or condition rather than an action or process (e.g., "know," "believe," "be tall").
Dynamic: A verb or predicate that describes an action or process involving change (e.g., "run," "break," "build").
Durative: An event or state that extends over a period of time (e.g., "sleep," "wait").
Punctual: An event that occurs at a single point in time with no duration (e.g., "knock," "die" in its instantaneous sense).
Semelfactive: An event type that occurs once and is completed, a single bounded action (e.g., "knock," "blink").
Iterative: An event type that occurs repeatedly or habitually (e.g., "She knocks every morning").
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure of an event, such as progressive, perfective, or imperfective.
Progressive: An aspect that presents an event as ongoing or in progress (e.g., "She is running").
Perfective: An aspect that presents an event as a completed whole (e.g., "She ran").
Imperfective: An aspect that presents an event as ongoing, habitual, or internally unbounded (e.g., "She was running," "She used to run").
Perfect: An aspect that relates a past event to the present, often expressed with "have" + past participle in English (e.g., "She has left").
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking, typically past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the attitude of the speaker toward the propositional content, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Indicative: The mood used to state facts or express opinions (e.g., "She is happy").
Subjunctive: A mood used to express hypothetical, wished-for, or non-real situations (e.g., "If I were you, I would leave").
Imperative Mood: The mood used for commands and requests (e.g., "Leave now!").
Aspectual: Relating to the grammatical aspect of a verb, describing the internal temporal structure of an event.
Verbal: Relating to or involving a verb or verbal element.
Nominal: Relating to or involving a noun or nominal element.
Adjectival: Relating to or involving an adjective or adjectival element.
Adverbial: Relating to or involving an adverb or adverbial element.
Prepositional: Relating to or involving a preposition or prepositional element.
Conjunctive: Relating to or involving a conjunction.
Interrogative Word: A word used to form questions, such as "who," "what," "where," "when," "why," or "how."
Exclamatory: A sentence or expression that conveys strong emotion or surprise.
Declarative Sentence: A sentence that states a proposition or fact.
Interrogative Sentence: A sentence that asks a question.
Imperative Sentence: A sentence that issues a command or request.
Yes-No Question: A question that can be answered with "yes" or "no" (e.g., "Are you coming?").
Wh-Question: A question introduced by a wh-word that seeks specific information (e.g., "Where are you going?").
Echo Question: A question that repeats part or all of a previous utterance to express surprise or seek confirmation (e.g., "You did WHAT?").
Tag Question: A short question appended to a declarative sentence to seek confirmation (e.g., "It's cold, isn't it?").
Rhetorical Question: A question asked for effect rather than to obtain an answer (e.g., "Who wouldn't want that?").
Indirect Question: A question embedded within a larger sentence, not requiring inversion (e.g., "I wonder where she went").
Direct Question: A question that stands as an independent sentence with interrogative word order.
Embedded Question: A question clause that functions as a constituent within another clause (e.g., "I know that she left" vs. "I know where she went").
Pragmatics: The study of how context contributes to meaning, including how speakers use and interpret language in social situations.
Pragmatic: Relating to the use of language in context, as opposed to its formal structure.
Speech Act: An action performed by saying something, such as promising, ordering, or declaring.
Illocutionary Act: The intended function or force of an utterance, such as the act of warning, promising, or requesting.
Perlocutionary Act: The effect of an utterance on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Locutionary Act: The basic act of producing a meaningful utterance with a particular semantic content.
Performative: A word or expression that is used to carry out the action it describes (e.g., "I hereby pronounce you married").
Directive: A type of speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something (e.g., commands, requests).
Commissive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to performing a future action (e.g., promises, offers).
Expressive: A type of speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state (e.g., thanking, apologizing, congratulating).
Declaration: A type of speech act that brings about a change in the institutional state of affairs by being uttered (e.g., "I now declare this meeting open").
Representational: A type of speech act that describes or states a state of affairs (e.g., asserting, stating, reporting).
Indirect Speech Act: A speech act in which the illocutionary force is not directly encoded in the semantic content of the utterance (e.g., "Can you pass the salt?" as a request).
Gricean Maxims: A set of conversational principles proposed by H.P. Grice, including the maxims of quality, quantity, relation, and manner.
Maxim of Quality: The principle that one should not say what one believes to be false or lack evidence for.
Maxim of Quantity: The principle that one should provide as much information as needed, and no more than needed.
Maxim of Relation: The principle that one should be relevant to the ongoing conversation.
Maxim of Manner: The principle that one should be clear, orderly, and brief, avoiding ambiguity and obscurity.
Cooperative Principle: Grice's overarching principle that participants in a conversation should generally cooperate with one another's communicative goals.
Conversational Implicature: An implicature generated by the assumptions of the Cooperative Principle and its maxims, rather than by the semantic content of the utterance.
Scalar Implicature: An implicature generated by the use of a weaker member of a scale, implicating that a stronger member is not the case (e.g., "Some students passed" implicates "Not all students passed").
Free-Choice Implicature: An implicature generated by the use of "any" or "or," suggesting that the choice is free or unconstrained.
Horn's Scale: A semantic scale used in the theory of scalar implicature, such as <all, most, some, few, none>.
Relevance Theory: A pragmatic framework developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson that explains communication in terms of the search for optimal relevance.
Politeness: The social strategies speakers use to minimize face-threatening acts and maintain social harmony.
Face: A person's public self-image or social identity, which can be threatened by certain speech acts.
Positive Face: The desire to be approved of, liked, or admired by others.
Negative Face: The desire to have one's freedom of action and choices unimposed upon by others.
Face-Threatening Act: A speech act that poses a threat to the positive or negative face of the speaker or hearer.

Phonetics & Phonology:
1. Phoneme: A minimal unit of sound that distinguishes meaning in a language.
2. Allophone: A variant pronunciation of a phoneme in a specific phonetic context.
3. Articulatory phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the physical movements of the articulators.
4. Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds.
5. Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived by the listener.
6. Consonant: A speech sound produced with a complete or partial closure of the vocal tract.
7. Vowel: A speech sound produced without a significant constriction of the vocal tract.
8. Stop: A consonant produced by completely blocking and then releasing airflow (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/).
9. Fricative: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow (e.g., /s/, /f/).
10. Affricate: A consonant that begins as a stop and releases into a fricative (e.g., /tʃ/).
11. Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity (e.g., /m/, /n/).
12. Approximant: A consonant produced by narrowing but not closing the vocal tract (e.g., /l/, /r/, /w/).
13. Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue body raised while allowing airflow along the sides (e.g., /l/).
14. Rhotic: A consonant associated with the letter 'r', such as trills, taps, or approximants.
15. Glottal: A sound produced at the glottis, involving the vocal folds (e.g., /h/, /ʔ/).
16. Voiced: A sound produced with the vocal folds vibrating.
17. Voiceless: A sound produced without vocal fold vibration.
18. Aspirated: A consonant produced with a strong burst of breath after release.
19. Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
20. Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is modified to produce a consonant.
21. Phonotactic: Pertaining to the rules governing permissible sound sequences in a language.
22. Syllable: A basic unit of rhythmic organization in a word, typically consisting of a peak of sonority.
23. Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster preceding the syllable nucleus.
24. Nucleus: The most sonorous element of a syllable, typically a vowel.
25. Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster following the syllable nucleus.
26. Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word to break up an impermissible cluster.
27. Assimilation: A sound process in which a sound changes to become more like a neighboring sound.
28. Dissimilation: A sound process in which similar sounds in proximity become less similar.
29. Metathesis: The transposition of two or more adjacent sounds within a word.
30. Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound in a word or word sequence.
31. Lenition: The weakening of a consonant over time or in certain positions.
32. Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant over time or in certain positions.
33. Prosody: The study of stress, rhythm, intonation, and other suprasegmental features.
34. Intonation: The variation in pitch over the course of an utterance.
35. Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase.
36. Tone: A phonologically distinctive pitch pattern on a syllable that distinguishes lexical meaning.
37. Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that extends over more than one segment, such as stress or tone.
38. Segmental: Pertaining to individual speech sounds (phonemes) as discrete units.
39. Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating phonemic contrast.
40. Complementary distribution: The situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment.
41. Free variation: The interchangeable use of two or more phonetic forms in the same environment.
42. Phonological rule: A formal description of how underlying representations map to surface forms.
43. Underlying form: The abstract mental representation of a word before phonological rules apply.
44. Surface form: The actual phonetic realization of a word after phonological rules have applied.
45. Feature: A binary or multi-valued property used to characterize phonological segments (e.g., [±voice]).
46. Feature geometry: A model organizing distinctive features into hierarchical tiers.
