Phonetics: the branch of linguistics concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds, including their production, transmission, and perception.
Phone: any distinct speech sound, regardless of whether it is a phoneme or not; the concrete physical realization of a sound.
Transcription: the representation of speech sounds using a written system, typically the International Phonetic Alphabet.
Broad transcription: a phonemic transcription that records only the distinctive phonemic units of a language, enclosed in slashes.
Narrow transcription: a phonetic transcription that records the precise articulatory and acoustic details of speech, enclosed in square brackets.
International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA): a standardized system of symbols for representing the sounds of all human languages.
Articulatory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are produced by the movement of the articulators, such as the tongue, lips, and vocal folds.
Acoustic phonetics: the study of the physical properties of speech sounds as they travel through the air, including frequency, amplitude, and duration.
Auditory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are perceived by the human ear and brain.
Formant: a band of frequencies of sound energy that is relatively amplified in the vocal tract, characteristic of vowel qualities.
Fundamental frequency (F0): the lowest frequency in the harmonic series of a voice, perceived as pitch.
Harmonic: one of the integer multiples of the fundamental frequency in the acoustic signal of a voice.
Hertz: the unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second, used to measure pitch and formant values.
Vowel: a speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, without significant constriction, and typically with pulmonic voiced airflow.
Consonant: a speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
Plosive: a consonant produced by a complete closure in the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air, such as /p/, /t/, /k/.
Fricative: a consonant produced by a narrow constriction that causes turbulent airflow, such as /s/, /f/, /ʃ/.
Affricate: a consonant that begins as a plosive and releases as a fricative, such as /tʃ/ or /dʒ/.
Nasal: a consonant produced with the oral cavity closed and airflow directed through the nasal cavity, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Lateral: a consonant produced with the tongue blade creating a central closure while allowing airflow around the sides of the tongue, such as /l/.
Approximant: a consonant produced with a narrow constriction that does not create turbulent airflow, such as /w/, /j/, /ɹ/.
Trill: a consonant produced by rapid vibration of a single articulator, such as the alveolar trill /r/.
Tap: a consonant produced by a single rapid contact of an articulator, such as the English flap /ɾ/ in "butter."
Glide: a vowel-like consonant, such as /w/ or /j/, that typically functions as a syllable onset.
Glottal stop: a consonant produced by the complete closure of the vocal folds, represented as /ʔ/.
Voicing: the vibration of the vocal folds during speech, distinguishing voiced consonants like /b/ from voiceless ones like /p/.
Aspiration: a burst of turbulent airflow following the release of a plosive, as in the /p/ of "pin" versus "spin."
Place of articulation: the location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: the manner in which a consonant is produced, such as plosive, fricative, or nasal.
Bilabial: a place of articulation produced with both lips, such as /p/, /b/, /m/.
Labiodental: a place of articulation produced with the lower lip against the upper teeth, such as /f/, /v/.
Dental: a place of articulation produced with the tongue against the upper teeth, such as the English /θ/ and /ð/.
Alveolar: a place of articulation produced with the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge, such as /t/, /d/, /n/, /s/, /z/.
Postalveolar: a place of articulation produced with the tongue blade behind the alveolar ridge, such as /ʃ/ and /ʒ/.
Retroflex: a place of articulation produced with the tongue tip curled back toward the palate, such as /ʈ/ and /ɖ/.
Palatal: a place of articulation produced with the tongue body against the hard palate, such as /j/.
Velar: a place of articulation produced with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, such as /k/, /g/, /ŋ/.
Uvular: a place of articulation produced with the back of the tongue against the uvula, such as /q/ and /ʁ/.
Pharyngeal: a place of articulation produced with the tongue body or epiglottis against the pharyngeal wall.
Epiglottal: a place of articulation produced at or near the epiglottis, such as the Arabic /ʔ/ and /ħ/.
Glottal: a place of articulation at the vocal folds, such as the glottal stop /ʔ/.
Front vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the front of the mouth, such as /i/ or /ɛ/.
Back vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the back of the mouth, such as /u/ or /ɔ/.
Central vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body in a neutral, central position, such as /ə/.
High vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the palate, such as /i/ or /u/.
Mid vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body in an intermediate vertical position, such as /e/ or /o/.
Low vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue body lowered toward the floor of the mouth, such as /a/.
Close vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue raised as high as possible, synonymous with "high vowel."
Open vowel: a vowel produced with the tongue lowered as far as possible, synonymous with "low vowel."
Rounded vowel: a vowel produced with the lips rounded, such as /u/, /o/, /ø/.
Unrounded vowel: a vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral, such as /i/, /e/, /a/.
Diphthong: a vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "price."
Monophthong: a single, steady vowel sound with a fixed tongue position, such as /iː/ in "fleece."
Triphthong: a complex vowel sound that passes through three different vowel qualities, such as /aɪə/ in "fire" in some dialects.
Vowel length: the duration of a vowel sound, which may be phonemically contrastive, as in German /i/ versus /iː/.
Creaky voice: a laryngeal voice quality characterized by irregular vibration of the vocal folds, producing a rough, creaky sound.
Whispered voice: a voice quality in which the vocal folds are spread, producing breathy, unvoiced speech.
Pharyngealization: a secondary articulation in which the pharyngeal constrictor is raised, adding a "guttural" quality to a sound.
Ejective: a consonant produced by the closure and release of the glottis, ejecting air from the lungs, common in languages like Georgian.
Implosive: a consonant produced by lowering the larynx, creating a negative pressure that draws air into the mouth, such as /ɓ/ or /ɗ/.
Click: a consonant produced by a sharp release of negative pressure in the mouth, found primarily in Bantu and Khoisan languages.
Labial click: a click consonant produced with the lips, such as /ʘ/.
Dental click: a click consonant produced with the tongue tip against the teeth, such as /ʅ/.
Alveolar click: a click consonant produced with the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge, such as /ɢ/.
Palatal click: a click consonant produced with the tongue blade against the palate, such as /ɺ/.
Velar click: a click consonant produced with the back of the tongue against the velum, such as /ʄ/.
Voiceless: a consonant produced without vocal fold vibration, such as /p/, /s/, /k/.
Voiced: a consonant produced with vocal fold vibration, such as /b/, /z/, /g/.
Sonorant: a class of consonants that include nasals, liquids, and glides, which are perceived as resonant and continuous.
Obstruent: a class of consonants that include plosives, fricatives, and affricates, produced with a significant constriction.
Frication: the turbulent airflow produced by a narrow constriction in the vocal tract during the production of fricatives.
Turbidity: the quality of a consonant produced with the vocal folds in a partially adducted state, between fully voiced and fully voiceless.
Breathiness: a voice quality in which the vocal folds are spread but not fully open, allowing air to leak past them.
Phonology: the branch of linguistics that studies the sound systems of languages, including the patterns, rules, and functions of phonemes.
Phoneme: the smallest unit of sound that can distinguish meaning in a particular language, such as /p/ versus /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: a variant realization of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word, such as the aspirated and unaspirated /p/ in English.
Minimal pair: a pair of words that differ in only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the two sounds are distinct phonemes, as in "pat" and "bat."
Complementary distribution: the condition in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of a single phoneme.
Free variation: the condition in which two or more allophones can be used interchangeably in the same phonetic environment without changing meaning.
Distinctive feature: a property of a speech sound that serves to distinguish one phoneme from another, such as [±voiced] or [±nasal].
Feature geometry: a model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized hierarchically into nodes and tiers.
Autosegment: a phonological element, such as tone or stress, that is represented on a separate tier from the segmental consonant-vowel tier and associates to segments.
Syllable: the basic unit of prosodic organization, typically consisting of an optional onset, a mandatory nucleus (usually a vowel), and an optional coda.
Onset: the consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the nucleus of a syllable, such as the /str/ in "strength."
Rhyme: the portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda, such as the /aɪn/ in "rain."
Nucleus: the core of a syllable, typically a vowel, to which other syllabic elements attach.
Coda: the consonant or consonant cluster that follows the nucleus of a syllable, such as the /kt/ in "act."
Cleft: the division of a syllable into the onset and the rhyme, or further into onset, nucleus, and coda.
Syllabification: the process of assigning segments to syllables, determining which consonant belongs to the onset or coda of a given syllable.
Epenthesis: the insertion of a sound, usually a vowel, into a word to break up a disallowed consonant cluster, as in "comfortable" for "comfort-able."
Elision: the deletion of a sound or syllable in connected speech, such as the /t/ in "not" in "don't" (from "do not").
Metathesis: the transposition of two adjacent sounds within a word, such as the historical change from "ask" to "aks."
Assimilation: the process by which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound in some feature, such as the nasal /n/ becoming /m/ before /p/.
Dissimilation: the process by which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound, such as the Greek change from "akko" to "aggo."
Lenition: the weakening of a consonant over time or in a particular phonological environment, such as the change from /p/ to /f/ in Latin to Greek.
Fortition: the strengthening of a consonant over time or in a particular phonological environment, the opposite of lenition.
Sound change: a systematic alteration in the pronunciation of a language's sounds over time, such as the English Great Vowel Shift.
Neutralization: the loss of a phonemic contrast in a particular phonological environment, such as the neutralization of voiced-voiceless in English word-final clusters.
Archiphoneme: an abstract phoneme that represents a neutralized set of phonemes in a particular environment.
Phonological rule: a statement that describes a systematic process affecting the sounds of a language, such as "voicing assimilation" in English.
Underlying form: the abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word or morpheme before phonological rules are applied.
Surface form: the actual, realized phonetic output of a word after all phonological rules have been applied.
Tone: the use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese or Yoruba.
Tone sandhi: the alteration of a tone's realization due to the influence of neighboring tones in a phrase or word.
Vowel harmony: a phonological process in which vowels in a word or phrase must share a particular feature, such as frontness or roundedness.
Umlaut: a type of vowel harmony in which a back vowel is fronted to match a front vowel in a suffix, as in German "Mann" to "Männer."
Ablaut: the systematic alternation of vowel quality in a word as part of its morphological paradigm, as in English "sing," "sang," "sung."
Sandhi: a general term for any phonological process that occurs at the boundary between words or morphemes.
Stress: the relative prominence of one syllable over others in a word or phrase, typically marked by greater pitch, duration, or intensity.
Prosody: the study of suprasegmental features such as stress, intonation, rhythm, and tone that overlay the segmental level of speech.
Intonation: the melodic contour of pitch across a phrase or sentence, used to mark question, statement, emotion, and other discourse functions.
Suprasegmental: a phonological feature that spans more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation, as opposed to segmental features.
Pitch accent: a prosodic system in which pitch is used to mark a single syllable (the accent) rather than a specific pitch value per syllable, as in Japanese.
Stress accent: a prosodic system in which a syllable is marked as prominent through a combination of features, typically increased loudness, duration, and pitch.
Tone language: a language in which pitch is used to distinguish the meaning of words, as in Mandarin Chinese, Yoruba, or Thai.
Phonotactics: the study of the permissible combinations of sounds within a language, such as which consonant clusters are allowed at the beginning or end of words.
Syllable structure: the set of constraints governing what segments can appear in the onset, nucleus, and coda of a syllable in a given language.
Maximal onset: a principle of syllabification that assigns shared consonants to the onset of the following syllable whenever possible.
Syllable weight: a measure of a syllable's phonological "heaviness" based on its segmental content, such as light (CV) versus heavy (CVC or CVV).
Iamb: a metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable following an unstressed one (weak-strong), as in "a-BOVE."
Trochee: a metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable following a stressed one (strong-weak), as in "HA-mo."
Foot: the basic unit of metrical structure, a group of syllables organized around a pattern of stress, such as an iamb or trochee.
Meter: the rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in poetry or verse.
Mora: a unit of prosodic timing used in phonological and metrical analysis, typically corresponding to a short vowel or a single consonant in a coda.
Prominence: the degree to which a syllable or sound is perceptually salient, often marked by stress, pitch, or duration.
Contour: the shape of a pitch or prosodic pattern across a stretch of speech, such as rising or falling intonation.
Register: a level of pitch or a particular set of laryngeal settings used in a language, such as the high and low registers in some tonal languages.
Pitch: the perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to the frequency of the sound wave.
Duration: the length of time a sound, syllable, or prosodic unit is held.
Intensity: the loudness of a sound, corresponding to the amplitude of the sound wave.
Phonological word: a prosodic unit consisting of a content word plus its associated affixes and clitics.
Prosodic word: a unit of prosodic structure corresponding roughly to a lexical word plus its clitics, serving as the domain for certain phonological processes.
Phonological phrase: a prosodic unit larger than a word, typically corresponding to a clitic group or a short phrase.
Phonological clause: a prosodic unit corresponding to a full clause, serving as the domain for intonational phenomena.
Boundary: a prosodic or phonological point at which a change in intonation, duration, or segmental realization occurs, marking the edge of a prosodic unit.
Pause: a period of silence or reduced articulation in speech, marking a prosodic or syntactic boundary.
Juncture: the phonetic and prosodic cues that signal the boundary between words or phrases in connected speech.
Linking: the process by which sounds are connected across word boundaries in connected speech, such as liaison in French or linking in English.
Coarticulation: the simultaneous or anticipatory influence of neighboring sounds on the articulation of a given segment.
Hyperarticulation: an exaggerated or careful mode of speech production, as in slow, deliberate speech or singing.
Hypoarticulation: a reduced or lax mode of speech production, as in casual or rapid speech.
Phonetic reduction: the weakening of a segment in unstressed or rapid speech, such as the reduction of /æ/ to /ə/ in English "about."
Schwa: the mid-central vowel /ə/, often the most reduced vowel sound in a language, as in the first syllable of "about."
Degemination: the process by which a geminate (long) consonant becomes a singleton (short) consonant.
Gemination: the lengthening or doubling of a consonant, which may be phonemically contrastive in languages like Italian or Japanese.
Deletion: the removal of a segment from a word or phrase, either historically or in specific phonological environments.
Insertion: the addition of a segment to a word or phrase, such as epenthetic vowels.
Substitution: the replacement of one segment by another, as in a sound change or a phonological process.
Fusion: the merging of two segments into a single segment, as in the historical change from Latin /kt/ to /k/ in English "night."
Fission: the splitting of one segment into two, as in the development of a glide plus vowel from a single vowel.
Spirantization: the change of a plosive into a fricative, such as the change from /p/ to /f/ in certain dialects.
Palatalization: the process by which a consonant acquires a palatal quality, often due to influence from a following front vowel, such as /k/ becoming /tʃ/.
Velarization: the process by which a consonant acquires a velar quality, often due to influence from a following back vowel.
Rhotacization: the change of a consonant into a rhotic sound, such as the Latin change from /s/ to /r/ (e.g., "lapis" to "lapid-" in compounds).
Labialization: the process by which a consonant acquires a rounded-lip quality, such as the change from /s/ to /ʃ/ before /w/.
Fronting: the movement of a vowel or consonant toward a more front position in the vowel space.
Backing: the movement of a vowel or consonant toward a more back position in the vowel space.
Raising: the movement of a vowel to a higher position in the vowel space, such as /a/ to /æ/.
Lowering: the movement of a vowel to a lower position in the vowel space, such as /i/ to /e/.
Tensing: the movement of a vowel toward a more tense (longer, higher) quality, as in the historical English /u/ to /uː/.
Laxing: the movement of a vowel toward a more lax (shorter, lower) quality, the opposite of tensing.
Morphology: the branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules by which they are formed.
Morpheme: the smallest meaningful unit of language, such as the -s in "cats" or the root "cat."
Allomorph: a variant form of a morpheme, such as the allomorphs /s/, /z/, /ɪz/ of the English plural morpheme.
Root: the core, meaning-bearing part of a word to which affixes may be attached, such as "act" in "action" or "actor."
Stem: the part of a word to which inflectional affixes are added, which may include the root plus derivational affixes.
Affix: a morpheme that is attached to a stem to form a word, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: an affix attached before the root or stem of a word, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: an affix attached after the root or stem of a word, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: an affix inserted within the root or stem of a word, such as the Tagalog "-in-" in "gumuhit."
Circumfix: an affix that surrounds a stem with two or more parts, such as the German "be-...-en" in "begreifen."
Clitic: a morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a neighboring word but syntactically independent, such as the English "-'s" in "John's" or the French "le" in "je le vois."
Bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-un-" or "-ness."
Free morpheme: a morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat," "run," or "green."
Derivational morpheme: an affix that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-ness" in "happiness" or "un-" in "unhappy."
Inflectional morpheme: an affix that modifies a word for grammatical purposes without changing its basic part of speech, such as "-s" in "cats" or "-ed" in "walked."
Agglutinative: a morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each carrying a single grammatical meaning, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional: a morphological type in which a single affix may encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: a morphological type in which morphemes are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by word order and function words, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: a morphological type in which a single word can express what is a full sentence in other languages, by incorporating multiple roots and affixes, as in many Native American languages.
Inflection: the modification of a word's form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person.
Derivation: the process of forming a new word from an existing root or stem by adding derivational affixes or other word-formation processes.
Compounding: the formation of a new word by combining two or more free morphemes, such as "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Reduplication: a morphological process in which part or all of a word is repeated to express grammatical or semantic meaning, such as "bye-bye" or "kita-kita."
Zero morpheme: a morpheme that has no phonetic content but is posited to explain a morphological alternation, such as the plural of "sheep" or the past tense of "put."
Morphological alternation: a change in the form of a root or stem depending on the affixes attached, such as "sugar" to "sugars" or "knife" to "knives."
Paradigm: the complete set of inflected forms of a word or a class of words, such as the noun, verb, or adjective paradigms in a language.
Lexical entry: the representation of a word in the mental lexicon, including its phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic properties.
Morphological productivity: the extent to which a particular word-formation pattern is actively used to create new words in a language.
Back-formation: a word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, such as "edit" from "editor."
Blend: a type of compound in which parts of two words are merged into a single word, such as "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Portmanteau: a word that combines the form and meaning of two or more words, such as "motel" (motor + hotel) or "chortle" (chuckle + snort).
Acronym: a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as a word, such as "laser" or "NASA."
Initialism: a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "DNA."
Conversion: a word-formation process in which a word changes its part of speech without any affixation, such as the noun "email" becoming the verb "to email."
Suppletion: a morphological process in which the allomorphs of a single morpheme are derived from entirely different roots, such as "go" and "went" or "man" and "men."
Allomorphy: the phenomenon in which a single morpheme has two or more phonological realizations, such as the English plural /s/, /z/, /ɪz/.
Morphophonemics: the study of the relationship between the underlying form of a morpheme and its phonological alternations.
Morphotactics: the rules governing the order and combination of affixes in a word, such as the hierarchy of suffixes in English.
Base: the word or morpheme to which an affix is attached in a derivation process.
Theme: a morpheme that is not a root or an affix but serves as a connecting element in derivation, such as the "-er" in "worker."
Morpheme boundary: a notional division within a word that marks the junction between morphemes, often relevant for phonological processes.
Lexical: pertaining to or stored in the lexicon, as opposed to being generated by productive grammatical rules.
Paradigmatic: relating to the set of choices available at a given position in a linguistic structure, as opposed to the linear, syntagmatic relation.
Syntagmatic: relating to the linear, positional relations between elements in a linguistic structure, as opposed to the paradigmatic, substitutive relation.
Morphological: pertaining to the structure and formation of words.
Derivational: pertaining to the creation of new words or parts of speech through affixation or other processes.
Inflectional: pertaining to the modification of word forms for grammatical agreement or other inflectional purposes.
Syntax: the branch of linguistics that studies the structure and rules of sentence formation, including the arrangement of words and phrases.
Phrase structure: the hierarchical organization of words into phrases and clauses in a sentence, typically represented by tree diagrams.
Tree diagram: a visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence, with nodes indicating constituents and branches indicating dominance.
Dominance: a structural relation in which one node (the parent) is higher in the tree than another node (the child), indicating that the parent contains the child.
Immediate dominance: a dominance relation in which one node is the direct parent of another, with no intervening nodes.
C-command: a structural relation in which a node governs all nodes that are dominated by the closest common ancestor that also dominates the c-commanding node.
S-structure: the surface syntactic structure of a sentence after all transformations have been applied, in the Government and Binding framework.
D-structure: the deep syntactic structure of a sentence before movement operations, in the Government and Binding framework.
Deep structure: the underlying hierarchical representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface structure: the actual hierarchical representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied.
Transformational grammar: a theory of syntax in which the deep structure of a sentence is converted to its surface structure through a series of transformational rules.
Movement: a syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from one position to another, such as wh-movement or passive movement.
Trace: an empty category left in the original position of a moved constituent, indicating where the element originated.
Theta role: a semantic role (such as Agent, Patient, Goal, Experiencer) assigned to an argument by a predicate, as defined in theta theory.
Theta theory: a component of syntactic theory that accounts for the assignment of semantic roles to arguments and the constraints on their expression.
Case: a grammatical category that marks the syntactic role of a noun phrase in a sentence, such as nominative, accusative, or genitive.
Nominative case: the case typically marking the subject of a clause, as in "The cat" in "The cat sat."
Accusative case: the case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb, as in "I saw the cat."
Genitive case: the case typically marking possession or association, as in "the cat's tail" or "a box of cats."
Dative case: the case typically marking the indirect object or recipient, as in "I gave the book to the cat."
Instrumental case: the case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed, as in "with a hammer."
Locative case: the case marking the location of an event, as in "in the room."
Ablative case: the case marking the source or origin of movement, as in "from the room."
Vocative case: the case used for direct address, as in "Oh, Mary!"
Ergative case: the case marking the agent of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment system.
Absolutive case: the case marking both the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment system.
Government: a syntactic relation in which a head element (typically a verb or preposition) licenses and determines the properties of a dependent element.
Binding: a set of principles governing the relationship between a pronoun or anaphor and its antecedent in a sentence.
Anaphor: a linguistic element, such as a reflexive pronoun or reciprocal, that must have an antecedent within a certain domain, such as "himself" in "John saw himself."
Reflexive: a pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "myself," "yourself," "himself."
Reciprocal: a pronoun expressing a mutual relationship, such as "each other" or "one another."
Antecedent: the noun phrase or expression that a pronoun or anaphor refers back to, such as "John" in "John saw himself."
Empty category: a syntactic position that is not filled by an overt word but is required by the grammar, such as a trace or PRO.
PRO: an empty category that functions as the subject of a non-finite clause, as in "John tried to PRO leave."
Null subject: a sentence in which the subject position is not filled by an overt noun phrase, as in Spanish "Llego" (I arrive) or Italian "Parlo" (I speak).
Wh-movement: the movement of an interrogative or relative pronoun to the front of a clause, as in "What did you buy?" from "You bought what."
Topicalization: the movement of a constituent to the beginning of a clause to establish it as the topic, as in "The book, I finished it yesterday."
Clefting: a construction in which a clause is restructured to highlight a particular constituent, such as "It was John who called" or "What I want is coffee."
Extraposition: the movement of a constituent, typically a clause, to a position after the verb, replacing it with a placeholder like "it" or "there," as in "It seems that he is here."
Raising: a syntactic process in which the subject of an embedded clause is moved to the subject position of the matrix clause, as in "John seems to be happy" from "John seems that he is happy."
Control: a syntactic relation in which the subject of a non-finite clause is not overtly expressed but is determined by an element in the matrix clause, as in "John tried [to PRO leave]."
Binding Theory: a component of syntactic theory, developed in the Government and Binding framework, that accounts for the distribution of pronouns, anaphors, and reflexives.
Principle A: the binding condition that an anaphor must be bound within its local domain (governing category).
Principle B: the binding condition that a pronoun must be free within its local domain.
Principle C: the binding condition that an R-expression (referring expression) must be free everywhere in the sentence.
Island constraint: a restriction that prevents movement of a constituent out of certain syntactic structures, such as complex NPs, subject islands, and wh-islands.
Subject condition: the restriction that a subject cannot be moved out of its clause, as in the ungrammaticality of "*What seems to be happy?" (with a subject reading).
Complex NP constraint: the restriction that a constituent cannot be extracted from within a complex noun phrase.
Adjacency constraint: the requirement that certain syntactic elements must be adjacent to each other in the surface structure.
Case filter: a constraint requiring that every phonetically realized noun phrase must receive Case from a head.
Extended Projection Principle (EPP): a principle requiring that every finite clause must have a subject position filled, either by an overt or null pronoun.
Theta criterion: a constraint stating that each argument must receive exactly one theta role, and each theta role must be assigned to exactly one argument.
Extended theta criterion: a version of the theta criterion that allows for additional constraints on argument structure, such as the requirement that not every theta role be assigned.
Subcategorization: the specification of the syntactic and semantic properties of the complements that a head (such as a verb or preposition) requires.
Government and Binding (GB): a major theoretical framework in syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s, organizing syntax into modules like theta theory, case theory, and binding theory.
Minimalist Program: the current generative syntax framework, introduced by Chomsky in 1995, which seeks to reduce syntactic operations to a minimal set of mechanisms like Merge, Move, and Agree.
Merge: the fundamental operation in the Minimalist Program by which two syntactic objects are combined to form a new constituent.
Move: the operation in the Minimalist Program by which a constituent is copied from one position to another, leaving a trace.
Phase: a unit of derivational computation in the Minimalist Program, typically a vP or CP, whose internal structure is made inaccessible to further operations once the phase is complete.
Phase Impenetrability Condition (PIC): the condition that the complement of a phase head is inaccessible to operations outside the phase, except at the edge of the phase.
Probe: a syntactic head with uninterpretable features that searches its c-command domain for a matching goal in the Minimalist Program.
Goal: a syntactic element with interpretable features that satisfies the requirements of a probe in the Minimalist Program.
Agree: the operation in the Minimalist Program by which a probe and a goal enter into a feature-matching relationship, often resulting in feature valuation.
Label: the identity of a constituent in the Minimalist Program, determined by the features of its head or by a specific labeling algorithm.
Feature checking: the process by which uninterpretable features on syntactic heads are valued or deleted through agreement with interpretable features on goals.
Copy theory: the approach to movement in which the moved element is copied in the new position while the original remains, as opposed to the trace theory approach.
Chain: a set of positions occupied by a moved element, linked together in a derivational sequence.
Coreference: the relation between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity, such as "John" and "he" in "John arrived. He was tired."
Binding domain: the minimal clause containing a subject that governs a particular element, within which binding conditions are evaluated.
Specifier: the constituent that precedes a head and its complement in a phrase, occupying the left-branch position in a binary-branching structure.
Head: the central, meaning-determining element of a phrase, to which other elements are related, such as the verb in a verb phrase or the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: the constituent that follows a head and is selected by it, such as the object noun phrase in a verb phrase.
Phrase: a constituent headed by a lexical category (noun, verb, adjective, preposition) together with its modifiers and complements.
Clause: a syntactic unit containing a verb and its arguments, which may be finite or non-finite, main or embedded.
Sentence: a maximal syntactic unit, typically a finite clause or a set of clauses, that expresses a complete thought.
Noun phrase (NP): a constituent headed by a noun or determiner, such as "the tall woman" or "every student."
Verb phrase (VP): a constituent headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts, such as "ate a sandwich."
Adjective phrase (AdjP): a constituent headed by an adjective, such as "very happy" or "quite old."
Prepositional phrase (PP): a constituent headed by a preposition, such as "in the garden" or "with a knife."
Determiner phrase (DP): a constituent headed by a determiner, proposed as the head of noun phrases in the DP hypothesis, such as "the book" or "some ideas."
Inflectional phrase (IP): a constituent headed by an inflectional element (such as tense or agreement), which in later terminology is often called a Tense phrase (TP).
Tense phrase (TP): a constituent headed by a tense head (T), which encodes temporal features and hosts the finite verb.
Complementizer phrase (CP): a constituent headed by a complementizer, such as "that," "if," or a wh-word, often the highest projection in a clause.
Transitive verb: a verb that takes a direct object, such as "eat" in "She eats apples."
Intransitive verb: a verb that does not take a direct object, such as "sleep" in "She sleeps."
Ditransitive verb: a verb that takes two objects, such as "give" in "She gave him a book."
Causative verb: a verb that expresses causing an action or state, such as "break" in "She broke the window" versus "The window broke."
Light verb: a verb that contributes little lexical meaning and relies on its complement for content, such as "have" in "have a chat" or "take" in "take a walk."
Copula: a verb that links the subject to a predicate complement, such as "be" in "She is a teacher."
Auxiliary verb: a verb that helps form a grammatical construction, such as "will," "have," or "be" in "She will go" or "They are singing."
Modal verb: a type of auxiliary expressing modality, such as "can," "must," "should," or "might."
Main verb: the lexical verb in a clause, as opposed to an auxiliary or modal, such as "eat" in "She is eating."
Subject: the noun phrase that agrees with the verb and typically fills the highest argument position in a clause.
Object: a noun phrase that serves as a complement to a verb, such as the direct object or indirect object.
Direct object: the noun phrase that receives the action of a transitive verb, such as "the ball" in "She kicked the ball."
Indirect object: the noun phrase that denotes the recipient or beneficiary in a ditransitive construction, such as "him" in "She gave him a book."
Predicate: the part of a sentence that provides information about the subject, typically including the verb and its complements.
Complement: a phrase required by a head to complete its meaning, such as the object of a transitive verb.
Adjunct: an optional, non-essential modifier in a phrase or clause, such as an adverbial or prepositional phrase, which can often be omitted.
Constituent: a word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger syntactic structure.
Constituent test: a set of syntactic tests, such as clefting, fronting, and substitution, used to identify the boundaries of constituents.
Cleft: a construction that divides a sentence into two parts to highlight a constituent, such as "It is [the book] that I want."
Fronting: the movement of a constituent to the beginning of a clause for emphasis or topicalization.
Substitution test: a syntactic test in which a constituent is replaced by a pro-form, such as "it" or "do so," to verify constituency.
Conjunction: a word that connects two or more syntactic elements of the same type, such as "and," "but," or "or."
Co-argument: a pair of arguments that are introduced together by the same predicate, as in the two objects of a ditransitive verb.
Argument: a noun phrase that is a required complement of a verb, as opposed to an optional adjunct.
Oblique: an argument or adjunct that is marked by a preposition or case, as opposed to a core argument marked by nominative or accusative.
Expletive: a syntactic element that occupies a position required by the grammar but carries no semantic content, such as "it" in "It is raining" or "there" in "There are books."
Dummy subject: a non-referential subject, such as "it" or "there," used in constructions like "It is raining" or "There are problems."
Raising-to-object: a process in which the subject of an embedded non-finite clause is promoted to the object position of the matrix verb, as in "She expected [him to leave]."
Passive: a voice construction in which the object of an active clause becomes the subject, and the agent is demoted or omitted, as in "The ball was kicked by John."
Active: the default voice in which the agent of an action is expressed as the subject, as in "John kicked the ball."
Middle voice: a voice construction in which a transitive verb is used intransitively with an intermediate meaning, as in "This book reads well."
Antipassive: a voice construction in which a transitive verb is used intransitively by demoting the object, common in ergative languages.
Applicative: a construction that adds an extra argument to a predicate, often an indirect object, such as in Bantu "I gave the child the book" with an applicative suffix.
Incorporation: a morphological process in which a noun or other word is incorporated into a verb to form a complex verb, as in many polysynthetic languages.
Noun incorporation: the incorporation of a noun stem into a verb, as in "bird-hunt" in "She bird-hunts."
Verb incorporation: the incorporation of a verb into another verb or a noun, forming a complex predicate.
Serial verb construction: a construction in which two or more verbs appear in a single clause without overt subordination, as in "He run go market" (He ran to the market) in some African and Southeast Asian languages.
Predicate cleft: a cleft construction that focuses on the predicate, such as "What John did was leave early."
Noun cleft: a cleft construction that focuses on a noun phrase, such as "It is John who left."
Pseudo-cleft: a construction with a wh-clause as the subject and a focused constituent as the predicate, such as "What I want is coffee."
Wh-island: a syntactic island in which extraction of a constituent from within a wh-question or relative clause is blocked.
Superiority: a constraint on multiple wh-questions that the higher-ranked wh-phrase (typically the subject) must be the one that moves to the clause-initial position.
Multiple wh-question: a question with two or more wh-words, as in "What did who buy?"
Embedded question: an interrogative clause that is embedded within a larger clause, as in "I wonder what he did."
Echo question: a question formed by repeating a previously stated utterance with rising intonation, expressing surprise or seeking clarification.
Tag question: a short interrogative tag added to a declarative statement, as in "You're coming, aren't you?"
Yes-no question: a question that can be answered with "yes" or "no," typically formed with subject-auxiliary inversion, as in "Are you coming?"
Wh-question: a question introduced by a wh-word such as "what," "who," "where," "when," "why," or "how."
Subject-auxiliary inversion: the syntactic process of reversing the order of the subject and auxiliary verb in questions and certain other constructions.
Nominative-accusative alignment: a case-marking pattern in which the subjects of both transitive and intransitive verbs are marked the same (nominative) and objects are marked differently (accusative).
Ergative-absolutive alignment: a case-marking pattern in which the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently (ergative) from the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb (absolutive).
Split-S alignment: a case-marking pattern in which the subject of an intransitive verb is marked like the object of a transitive verb (absolutive) when it is animate or agentive, and like the subject of a transitive verb (ergative) when it is inanimate or non-agentive.
Nominative: the case form typically used for the subject of a clause in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative: the case form typically used for the direct object in nominative-accusative languages.
Semi-ergative: a case-marking pattern that shows ergative alignment in some grammatical contexts and nominative-accusative in others.
Semantic: relating to meaning in language, as studied in the field of semantics.
Semantics: the branch of linguistics that studies the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Lexical semantics: the study of meaning as stored in the dictionary, including the meanings of individual words.
Compositional semantics: the study of how the meaning of a complex expression is built from the meanings of its parts and the rules of combination.
Sense: a particular meaning or interpretation of a word, such as the "bank" (river edge) versus "bank" (financial institution) senses of "bank."
Denotation: the set of entities in the world to which a word or expression refers, such as the denotation of "dog" being the set of all dogs.
Reference: the relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it picks out in a particular context, such as the name "Paris" referring to the city.
Connotation: the additional, often emotional or cultural, associations that a word carries beyond its literal denotation.
Connotation: the additional associative or emotional meaning that a word carries beyond its core denotative meaning.
Polysemy: the phenomenon in which a single word has multiple related senses, such as "head" (body part, leader, top).
Homonymy: the phenomenon in which a single word form has multiple unrelated meanings, such as "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Antonymy: a semantic relation between words that have opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "buy" and "sell."
Hyponymy: a semantic relation in which the meaning of one term is included within the meaning of another, such as "rose" being a hyponym of "flower."
Hypernym: a more general term in a hyponymy relation, such as "flower" in the relation "rose" (hyponym) to "flower" (hypernym).
Meronymy: a semantic relation between a part and a whole, such as "wheel" to "car" or "page" to "book."
Troponymy: a hyponymy relation based on the manner or type of an action, such as "crawl," "jog," and "stroll" as troponyms of "walk."
Synonymy: a semantic relation between words that have the same or very similar meanings, such as "big" and "large."
Collocation: a habitual or conventional combination of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "*do a decision" or "strong coffee" rather than "*powerful coffee."
Selectional restriction: a constraint on the semantic properties of the arguments that a predicate can take, such as "drink" requiring a liquid.
Frame: a structured set of roles, relations, and properties that organize the meaning of a predicate and its arguments, as in frame semantics.
Proto-role: an idealized, prototypical instance of a semantic role, such as a prototypical Agent being a volitional, animate, conscious entity.
Prototype: a central, most typical member of a category, used in prototype theory to explain the graded membership of category members.
Cognitive semantics: an approach to meaning that emphasizes the role of cognition, experience, and conceptual structure in shaping linguistic meaning.
Conceptual metaphor: a cross-domain mapping that structures understanding of one domain in terms of another, such as "ARGUMENT IS WAR" (as in "He attacked my points").
Image schema: a basic, abstract structure derived from bodily experience, such as the CONTAINER, PATH, or SOURCE-PATH-GOAL schemas, that underlies metaphorical and figurative meaning.
Metaphor: a figurative linguistic device in which one domain is described in terms of another, such as "time is money" or "she is a ray of sunshine."
Metonymy: a figurative linguistic device in which one entity is referred to by another with which it is closely associated, such as "The White House announced..." for the President.
Synecdoche: a type of metonymy in which a part represents the whole or vice versa, such as "All hands on deck" for "all sailors."
Litotes: an understatement formed by negating the opposite of what is meant, such as "He's not bad" to mean "He's good."
Euphemism: a mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsher or more direct one, such as "passed away" for "died."
Dysphemism: an unpleasant or offensive word or expression, the opposite of a euphemism.
Pleonasm: the use of more words than necessary, such as "absolutely essential" or "ATM machine."
Tautology: a statement that is true by necessity or definition, or a redundant repetition of meaning, such as "free gift."
Connotation: the set of emotional, cultural, or associative meanings attached to a word beyond its literal denotation.
Extension: the range of application or the set of entities to which a word applies, as opposed to its intension.
Intension: the set of properties or the definition that determines the meaning of a word, as opposed to its extension.
Truth value: the value (true or false) of a proposition in a given state of the world.
Entailment: a semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as in "He is a bachelor" entails "He is a man."
Presupposition: a background assumption that must be true for a sentence to be meaningful, as in "John stopped smoking" presupposes that John used to smoke.
Conversational implicature: an implied meaning that is not part of the literal meaning of an utterance but is inferred from the context and conversational principles.
Scalar implicature: a type of implicature based on a scale of meaning, such as "Some of the students passed" implicating "Not all of them passed."
Pragmatics: the branch of linguistics that studies how context and speaker intention affect the interpretation of meaning in communication.
Speech act: a unit of communication that performs an action, such as a request, promise, or declaration, in addition to conveying information.
Locution: the actual words spoken in a speech act, as opposed to the illocutionary or perlocutionary force.
Illocution: the intended force or function of a speech act, such as requesting, warning, or promising.
Perlocution: the effect of a speech act on the listener, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Searle's taxonomy: the classification of speech acts into five categories: representative, directive, commissive, expressive, and declarative.
Performative: a sentence that explicitly names the speech act being performed, such as "I hereby declare this meeting open."
Felicity conditions: the conditions that must be met for a speech act to be successful, such as the authority of the speaker for a declaration.
Deixis: the linguistic phenomenon in which the meaning of an expression depends on the context of utterance, such as "here," "now," "I," "this."
Person deixis: the use of personal pronouns (I, you, we) that shift reference depending on who is speaking.
Spatial deixis: the use of deictic expressions that refer to location relative to the speaker, such as "here," "there," "this," "that."
Temporal deixis: the use of deictic expressions that refer to time relative to the moment of utterance, such as "now," "then," "yesterday."
Anaphora: a linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity, such as "he" referring to "John" in "John came. He was tired."
Cataphora: a linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later, such as "He" in "He is tall, but John is taller."
Exophora: a deictic reference to something outside the immediate linguistic context, such as pointing to an object and saying "that."
Endophora: a reference to something within the linguistic context, either previously mentioned (anaphora) or about to be mentioned (cataphora).
Discourse: the study of language as it is used in extended, connected text or conversation, beyond the level of the individual sentence.
Coherence: the logical and semantic connectedness of a discourse, in which ideas flow in a meaningful and organized way.
Cohesion: the linguistic devices that create surface-level connections between sentences, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical repetition.
Topic: the entity or subject about which a discourse or a particular stretch of discourse is centered.
Comment: the information or statement made about the topic in a discourse.
Information structure: the organization of information in a discourse into given (old) and new elements.
Given: information in a discourse that has been previously established or is assumed to be known to the listener.
New: information in a discourse that has not been previously established and is being introduced to the listener.
Focus: the part of a sentence or discourse that contains the new or contrastive information.
Topic structure: the organization of a discourse around a central topic that is maintained across sentences.
Rhetorical structure: the hierarchical organization of a text into units with specific rhetorical relations, such as contrast, elaboration, or consequence.
Text linguistics: the study of the properties that distinguish a coherent text from a mere sequence of sentences.
Register: a variety of language used in a particular social setting or for a particular purpose, such as formal, informal, or technical.
Style: the distinctive features of a writer's or speaker's language use, or a particular variety of language associated with a social group.
Jargon: specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or subculture.
Slang: informal, often creative or playful vocabulary used by a particular social group, often in contrast to standard language.
Dialect: a variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group, differing from other varieties in grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation.
Creole: a natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Pidgin: a simplified language that develops for communication between groups with different native languages, typically not anyone's native language.
Language contact: the interaction between speakers of different languages, leading to borrowing, interference, or the development of pidgins and creoles.
Borrowing: the adoption of words, phrases, or grammatical structures from one language into another.
Code-switching: the practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties in a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: the interweaving of elements from two or more languages within a single sentence or discourse.
Language death: the process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be spoken.
Language revitalization: efforts to revive a language that is endangered or has lost its native speaker community.
Endangered language: a language that is at risk of falling out of use because fewer people are learning it as a native language.
Language family: a group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral language, such as the Indo-European family.
Proto-language: the hypothetical ancestral language from which a group of related languages is believed to have descended, such as Proto-Indo-European.
Comparative method: a method of historical linguistics that uses systematic sound correspondences to reconstruct proto-languages and establish genetic relationships between languages.
Sound correspondence: a regular pattern of similarity between sounds in related languages, evidence of a common ancestor.
Grimm's Law: the first major sound shift in the development of the Germanic languages from Proto-Indo-European, such as Proto-IE */p/ to Germanic */f/.
Verner's Law: a phonological rule that accounts for the exceptions to Grimm's Law, based on the position of the accent in Proto-Indo-European.
The Great Vowel Shift: a major series of changes in the pronunciation of English long vowels that occurred roughly between the 15th and 18th centuries.
Noun class: a grammatical category in which nouns are grouped into classes that determine the forms of associated words, as in Bantu languages.
Gender: a grammatical category that divides nouns into classes, such as masculine, feminine, and neuter in many European languages.
Person: a grammatical category that distinguishes the speaker (first person), the addressee (second person), and others (third person).
Number: a grammatical category that distinguishes singular, plural, and sometimes dual or other forms.
Dual: a grammatical number category referring to exactly two entities, found in languages like Arabic and many Pacific Island languages.
Trials: a grammatical number category referring to exactly three entities, found in some Native American and Slavic languages.
Case marking: the grammatical marking of the syntactic role of a noun phrase through changes in form, such as adding endings or using particles.
Ergativity: a grammatical alignment in which the subject of an intransitive verb is marked the same as the object of a transitive verb, and the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently.
Noun phrase: a syntactic constituent consisting of a noun and its modifiers, determiners, and complements.
Word order: the linear arrangement of words or phrases in a sentence, such as SVO, SOV, or VSO.
SVO: a word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English "She eats apples."
SOV: a word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese "She apples eats."
VSO: a word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in Classical Arabic or Welsh.
Head-marking: a strategy in which the grammatical relationships between words are marked on the head of a phrase rather than on the dependent, as in many agglutinative languages.
Dependent-marking: a strategy in which the grammatical relationships between words are marked on the dependent element rather than the head, as in English with prepositions and articles.
Agglutination: a morphological process in which words are formed by adding a series of morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical or semantic feature.
Isolating morphology: a morphological type in which words are typically single morphemes and grammatical relations are expressed by separate function words and word order.
Morphological typology: the classification of languages according to their morphological structure, such as isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Typology: the study of the properties and classifications of languages across the world, focusing on patterns of similarity and difference.
Universal grammar: the hypothesis, central to generative linguistics, that there are innate, language-specific constraints on the possible structures of human language.
Language universal: a property or pattern that is found in all or nearly all human languages, such as the existence of nouns and verbs.
Greenberg's universals: a set of 45 typological generalizations proposed by Joseph Greenberg in 1963 based on a sample of languages.
Typological correlation: a statistical tendency for two or more linguistic features to co-occur across languages, such as the correlation between SOV word order and postpositions.
