Mora: a unit of syllable weight or timing, used to account for syllable weight, stress assignment, and prosodic constraints.
Moraic: relating to or consisting of morae; describing a segment that contributes to syllable weight.
Open syllable: a syllable that ends in a vowel (no coda consonant), as in "ma" in "mama."
Closed syllable: a syllable that ends in a consonant, as in "cat."
Heavy syllable: a syllable that is metrically long, typically containing a long vowel or a vowel plus a coda consonant.
Light syllable: a syllable that is metrically short, typically containing a short vowel and no coda consonant.
Branching: having two or more segments in a position, such as a branching onset or coda.
Non-branching: having a single segment in a position, such as a single-consonant onset or coda.
Sonority: the relative loudness or voicing of a sound; vowels are more sonorous than approximants, which are more sonorous than fricatives, which are more sonorous than stops.
Sonority hierarchy: an ordering of consonant and vowel types from most sonorous to least, such as vowels > glides > liquids > nasals > fricatives > stops.
Syllabification: the process of dividing a string of segments into syllables according to a language's phonotactic rules.
Prosodic tree: a hierarchical representation of the prosodic structure of an utterance, including levels such as syllable, foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase, and intonational phrase.
Prosodic word: a prosodic unit roughly corresponding to a phonological word, typically a stressed syllable plus associated unstressed syllables.
Phonological phrase: a prosodic unit larger than a prosodic word, often corresponding to a phrase in syntactic structure.
Intonational phrase: the largest prosodic unit, corresponding to a complete intonational unit or sentence.
Utterance: a single spoken or written unit of communication, typically a sentence or clause.
Deletion: a phonological process in which a segment or feature is removed from the underlying representation.
Insertion: a phonological process in which a segment is added to the underlying form, such as epenthetic vowels.
Permutation: a phonological process in which segments are rearranged, as in metathesis.
Reduplication: a morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to create a new form, often for plural, distributive, or intensifying meanings.
Tone sandhi: a rule-governed change in the tone of a syllable due to its interaction with adjacent syllables.
Register: a variety of language associated with a particular social context, domain, or purpose, such as formal, informal, or technical register.
Pitch accent: a prosodic system in which a single pitch contrast (high vs. low) is assigned to a specific mora within a word to distinguish lexical items, as in Japanese.
Glottal: relating to the glottis, the space between the vocal folds; a place of articulation.
Glottal stop: a consonant produced by closing the vocal folds, as in the /ʔ/ in "uh-oh" or "button."
Devoicing: a phonological process in which a voiced sound becomes voiceless, such as /b/ → [p] in final position in some languages.
Voicing assimilation: a process in which a consonant adopts the voicing value of an adjacent consonant.
Deaffrication: the process by which an affricate loses its stop portion and becomes a fricative.
Fortition: a process in which a weaker consonant becomes a stronger one.
Lenition: a process in which a stronger consonant becomes a weaker one.
Palatalization: a phonological or historical process in which a consonant becomes fronted or palatal due to the influence of a neighboring front vowel or palatal glide.
Velarization: a secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue is raised toward the velum during the production of a consonant.
Pharyngealization: a secondary articulation in which the pharyngeal constrictor is raised, narrowing the pharyngeal cavity.
Labialization: a secondary articulation in which the lips are rounded during the production of a consonant.
Uvular: a place of articulation involving the uvula, as in /q/ or the French /ʁ/.
Pharyngeal: a place of articulation involving the pharyngeal wall, as in the Arabic /ħ/ or /ʕ/.
Alveolar: a place of articulation involving the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge, as in English /t/, /d/, /n/, /s/, /z/.
Dental: a place of articulation involving the tongue tip against the upper teeth, as in English /θ/ and /ð/.
Retroflex: a consonant produced with the tongue tip curled back toward the postalveolar region, common in Dravidian and Indo-Aryan languages.
Postalveolar: a place of articulation just behind the alveolar ridge, as in /ʃ/ and /ʒ/.
Palatal: a place of articulation involving the tongue body against the hard palate, as in /j/ or the palatalized stops.
Alveolar flap: a consonant produced by a single, quick tap of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge, as in the /ɾ/ in American English "butter."
Trill: a consonant produced by the rapid vibration of the tongue tip or uvula, such as Spanish /r/.
Tap: a consonant produced by a single, brief contact of the tongue tip with the alveolar ridge, similar to a very short trill.
Flap: a consonant produced by a single, quick contact, as in the American English /ɾ/ in "butter."
Nasal consonant: a consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing nasal airflow, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Approximant: a consonant produced with a narrowing but no turbulent airflow, including glides, liquids, and some rhotics.
Semi-vowel: a glide consonant that functions similarly to a vowel in some contexts, such as /w/ and /j/.
Tap/flap: a consonant produced by a single, quick contact of the articulator.
Trill: a consonant produced by the rapid, repeated vibration of the articulator.
Laminal: describing an articulation made with the blade or body of the tongue, as opposed to apical (tip) or coronal.
Apical: describing an articulation made with the tip of the tongue.
Coronal: a place-of-articulation category for sounds made with the front of the tongue (tip or blade) toward the alveolar or postalveolar region.
Dorsal: a place-of-articulation category for sounds made with the back of the tongue toward the palate or velum.
Morpheme: the smallest meaning-bearing unit of language, such as the "un-" in "unhappy" or the root "happy."
Morphology: the branch of linguistics that studies the structure and formation of words.
Allomorph: a variant form of a morpheme, such as the three phonetic forms of the English plural: /s/ (cats), /z/ (dogs), /ɪz/ (boxes).
Free morpheme: a morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "book" or "run."
Bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand alone and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-s," "un-," or "-ing."
Root: the core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning, to which affixes may be added.
Affix: a bound morpheme that attaches to a root or stem to form a new word or word form.
Prefix: an affix that is added before the root or stem, as in "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: an affix that is added after the root or stem, as in "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: a morpheme inserted within the root or stem, as in the Tagalog "-in-" or the English interjection "abso-bloody-lutely."
Circumfix: a morpheme consisting of two parts (prefix and suffix) that attach around a root simultaneously, as in German "ge-...-t" in "gemacht."
Interfix: a linking element used to join two roots in a compound, as in the "o" in "gasoline."
Derivational: relating to morphological processes that create new words or change the syntactic category of a stem, as in "act" (verb) → "action" (noun).
Inflectional: relating to morphological processes that mark grammatical categories without changing the word's core lexical meaning, as in "walk" → "walks."
Compounding: a word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to create a new word, as in "toothbrush."
Inflection: the process of modifying a word to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person.
Derivation: the process of creating a new lexeme by adding derivational affixes to a base, as in "care" → "careful."
Paradigm: the complete set of inflected forms of a word in a grammatical category, such as the full conjugation of a verb.
Isomorph: a morpheme that has only one phonological form, with no allomorphs.
Agglutinative: a morphological type in which words are built by concatenating morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical function, as in Turkish or Turkish.
Fusional: a morphological type in which a single affix can express multiple grammatical features simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: a morphological type in which words are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: a morphological type in which a single word can encode information that in other languages would require an entire sentence, as in many Native American languages.
Suppletion: a morphological process in which a form is derived from an entirely unrelated root, as in "go" → "went."
Productive: a morphological process or pattern that is actively used to form new words by speakers of the language.
Unproductive: a morphological process or pattern that is no longer actively used but is retained in existing vocabulary.
Zero morpheme: an implicit or null form of a morpheme, such as the absence of a suffix for the English singular noun or the present tense.
Portmanteau: a morphological or lexical form in which a single unit encodes multiple grammatical or semantic features, as in the Latin "amant-" (they love).
Back-formation: a word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix, as in "edit" from "editor" or "abridge" from "abridgment."
Blend: a word-formation process in which parts of two or more words are merged, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Clipping: a word-formation process that shortens a word while retaining its core meaning, as in "phone" from "telephone" or "lab" from "laboratory."
Neologism: a newly coined word or expression entering the lexicon.
Allomorphy: the existence of two or more phonological variants (allomorphs) of a single morpheme.
Morphophonemic: relating to the interaction between morphology and phonology, especially the selection of allomorphs by phonological environment.
Word: a free linguistic unit that can function independently, typically a sequence of morphemes with a particular phonological structure.
Word form: a specific inflected realization of a lexeme, such as "walked" as a word form of the lexeme "walk."
Word class: a syntactic category such as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb, defined by distributional and morphological properties.
Lexeme: the abstract unit of the lexicon grouping all inflected forms of a word, such as the lexeme WALK encompassing "walk," "walks," "walked," "walking."
Stem: the part of a word to which inflectional affixes are added; may or may not be identical to the root.
Base: the underlying form to which derivational or inflectional morphemes are added.
Morph: a theoretical unit of morphology that may or may not correspond to a phonologically independent segment.
Syntax: the branch of linguistics that studies the structure and rules governing the arrangement of words and phrases into sentences.
Sentence: a maximal projection of a clause, typically containing a verb and expressing a complete thought.
Clause: a grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate (typically a verb phrase), which may be independent or dependent.
Phrase: a syntactic unit headed by a word of a particular category, such as a noun phrase (NP) or verb phrase (VP).
Constituent: a word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger syntactic structure.
Constituency: the property of being a constituent; the testable status of a string of words as a syntactic unit.
Tree diagram: a graphical representation of syntactic structure showing hierarchical branching from a root to terminal nodes.
Immediate constituent: a direct component of a phrase in a binary branching tree analysis.
Immediate dominance: a structural relation in which one node is the direct parent of another in a tree.
Terminal: a leaf node in a tree diagram, representing a word or morpheme.
Non-terminal: an internal node in a tree diagram, representing a phrase or projection.
Branch: a node in a tree diagram that dominates two or more daughter nodes.
Subtree: a portion of a tree diagram consisting of a node and all its descendants.
Dominance: a structural relation in which one node in a tree is higher than another.
C-command: a structural relation in which a node A c-commands node B if the first branching node above A also dominates B, and A does not dominate B.
X-bar theory: a model of phrase structure proposing that each category X has three projections: XP, X', and X.
Head: the central word in a phrase that determines the phrase's grammatical category, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: a constituent that is required by a head to complete its valency, such as the object of a transitive verb.
Specifier: a constituent that occupies the leftmost position in a phrase (in head-initial languages), often a determiner or subject.
Adjunct: an optional modifier that adds information but is not required by the head, such as a manner adverbial.
Projection: a syntactic node that represents a phrase or word in a tree structure.
Maximal projection: the highest projection of a head in a phrase, traditionally labeled as NP, VP, etc.
Intermediate projection: the middle projection in X-bar theory (X'), typically containing the head and its complements.
Minimal projection: the lowest projection, corresponding to the bare head (X⁰).
Case: a grammatical category marking the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase, expressed by inflection, position, or particles.
Nominative: a case typically marking the subject of a clause.
Accusative: a case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Genitive: a case expressing possession, origin, or association.
Dative: a case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
Instrumental: a case expressing the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Ablative: a case expressing motion away from a source or location.
Locative: a case expressing location or position.
Vocative: a case used for direct address, as in "John, come here!"
Ergative: a case marking the agent of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment.
Absolutive: a case marking both the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment.
Split ergativity: a system in which ergative-absolutive alignment is used in some contexts (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative in others (e.g., present tense).
Nominative-accusative: a case-marking pattern in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs receives one case (nominative) and the object of transitive verbs receives another (accusative).
Tripartite alignment: a case-marking pattern in which the subject of transitive verbs, the subject of intransitive verbs, and the object of transitive verbs all receive distinct cases.
Active-stative alignment: a case-marking pattern in which the alignment depends on the semantic role (agent vs. non-agent) rather than transitivity.
Split S: a system in which the subject of an intransitive verb is split into two classes based on semantic properties such as animacy or agency.
Theta role: a semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, or Goal.
Theta criterion: a syntactic principle requiring that each argument receive exactly one theta role and each theta role be assigned to exactly one argument.
Theta theory: a component of GB and related frameworks that accounts for the assignment and interpretation of semantic roles.
Government: a syntactic relation in which a head assigns case or controls the form of a complement.
Binding: a set of principles governing the distribution of anaphoric expressions such as reflexives, pronouns, and names.
Anaphor: an expression that must be bound by a local antecedent, such as a reflexive pronoun ("himself") or a reciprocal ("each other").
Reflexive: a pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "myself" or "himself."
Reciprocal: a pronoun expressing a mutual relation, such as "each other" or "one another."
Pronoun: a word that stands in for a noun phrase, such as "he," "she," "it," "they."
R-expression: a referring expression that cannot be bound by a pronoun, such as a proper name or definite description.
Binding Theory: a component of GB syntax comprising Principles A, B, and C governing anaphoric expressions.
Principle A: a binding principle requiring that an anaphor be bound in its governing category, such as "John_i saw himself_i."
Principle B: a binding principle requiring that a pronoun be free in its governing category, such as "John_i said he_i left" (not "John_i said him_i left").
Principle C: a binding principle requiring that an R-expression be free everywhere, such as "*Him_i saw John_i."
Case filter: a syntactic principle requiring that every overt noun phrase receive structural case.
EPP: the Extended Projection Principle, a syntactic requirement that every clause must have a subject.
Deep structure: in early transformational grammar, the initial syntactic representation before transformations apply.
Surface structure: the final syntactic representation after all transformations have been applied.
S-structure: the syntactic representation in GB theory at which phonological interpretation takes place.
D-structure: the syntactic representation in GB theory at which theta roles are assigned.
Transformational grammar: a framework of syntax in which surface structures are derived from deep structures via transformations.
Wh-movement: the syntactic movement of a wh-word (who, what, where, etc.) to the specifier of CP to form a question.
Passivization: a syntactic transformation in which the object of a transitive verb becomes the subject, as in "The dog chased the cat" → "The cat was chased by the dog."
Raising: a syntactic process in which the subject of an embedded clause moves to the subject position of the matrix clause, as in "John seems to be tired."
Control: a syntactic-semantic relation in which the implicit subject (PRO) of a non-finite clause is determined by an element in the matrix clause, as in "John tried to leave."
Equi: short for equi-deletion; a process in which the subject of an embedded infinitive is identified with and deleted from the matrix subject, as in "John tried to leave."
PRO: an unpronounced pronoun that serves as the subject of a non-finite clause in control and other constructions.
Empty category: a syntactic node with no phonetic content, such as PRO, pro, or a trace.
Null subject: a subject position that is syntactically present but phonologically silent, common in pro-drop languages.
Null object: an object position that is syntactically present but phonologically silent.
Pro-drop: the grammatical omission of a subject pronoun when it is recoverable from context, common in Spanish, Italian, Japanese, and other languages.
Word order: the linear arrangement of constituents in a sentence, typically described in terms of the relative positions of S, V, and O.
SVO: a word order in which the subject precedes the verb and the object follows, as in English.
SOV: a word order in which the subject precedes the verb and the object precedes the verb, as in Japanese and Turkish.
VSO: a word order in which the verb precedes the subject and the object follows, as in Classical Arabic and Irish.
VOS: a word order in which the verb precedes the object and the subject follows, found in a small number of languages.
OVS: a word order in which the object precedes the verb and the subject follows, found in a small number of languages.
OSV: a word order in which the object precedes the subject and the verb follows, found in a small number of languages.
Embedding: the syntactic process of placing one clause within another, as in "I think [that John left]."
Recursion: the property of a grammar that allows structures to be embedded within structures of the same type to an unbounded depth.
Coordination: the syntactic process of joining two or more constituents of the same type with a coordinating conjunction, as in "bread and butter."
Subordination: the syntactic process of embedding a clause as a modifier or complement of another clause, typically with a subordinating conjunction.
Conjunction: a word that links words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "or," "but."
Subordinator: a word or particle that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because," "although," or "if."
Head final: a structural parameter in which the head of a phrase follows its dependents, as in Japanese "gakkō e ita" (school to went).
Head initial: a structural parameter in which the head of a phrase precedes its dependents, as in English "the big red ball."
Scrambling: a syntactic process in which constituents are freely reordered within a clause, as in Japanese and German.
Inversion: a syntactic process in which the normal order of subject and verb or other constituents is reversed, as in questions or topicalization.
Fronting: the movement of a constituent to a position earlier than its canonical position, often for topicalization or focus.
Topicalization: the movement of a constituent to the left periphery of a clause to mark it as the topic of the utterance.
Focus fronting: the movement of a focused constituent to a position before the verb or to the left periphery.
Left dislocation: a construction in which a constituent is placed at the beginning of a sentence and coreferenced by a pronoun in the main clause, as in "John, he left."
Right dislocation: a construction in which a constituent is placed at the end of a sentence, typically preceded by a pause or comma, as in "He left, John."
Extraposition: the movement of a constituent, typically a clause, to the end of a sentence, as in "It is surprising that John left."
Cleft: a construction that divides a clause into a focused constituent and a relative or pseudorelative clause, as in "It was John who left."
Pseudocleft: a cleft construction in which the focused element is a wh-clause, as in "What John did was leave."
