Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words, such as /p/ and /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A variant pronunciation of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phonetics: The branch of linguistics that studies the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Phonology: The branch of linguistics that studies the sound systems of languages, including how sounds pattern and combine.
Segment: A discrete sound unit in speech, typically a vowel or consonant, that can be analyzed as a component of a syllable.
Suprasegmental: A phonological property that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Consonant: A speech sound produced by a partial or complete closure of the vocal tract, typically involving obstruction of airflow.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, without significant constriction of airflow.
Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips, as in the sounds /p/, /b/, and /m/.
Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip against the upper teeth, as in /f/ and /v/.
Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue against the upper teeth, as in the English /th/ sounds.
Alveolar: A place of articulation involving the tongue against the alveolar ridge, as in /t/, /d/, /s/, and /z/.
Postalveolar: A place of articulation just behind the alveolar ridge, as in /ʃ/ (sh) and /tʃ/ (ch).
Rhotic: A consonant that involves some form of tongue retraction or trilling, as in the various realizations of /r/.
Palatal: A place of articulation involving the tongue against the hard palate, as in /j/ (the "y" sound).
Velar: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue against the soft palate, as in /k/, /g/, and /ŋ/.
Uvular: A place of articulation involving the uvula, as in the French /ʁ/ and Arabic /q/.
Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the pharyngeal wall, as in the Arabic /ʁ/ and /ħ/ sounds.
Glottal: A place of articulation at the glottis, as in the voiceless glottal stop /ʔ/ found in many languages.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release of air, as in /p/, /t/, and /k/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that creates turbulent airflow, as in /f/, /s/, and /ʃ/.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity, as in /m/, /n/, and /ŋ/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with airflow directed around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple vibrations of a speech organ, such as the alveolar trill [r] in Spanish.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact, as in the English /ɾ/ in the "tt" of "butter" in many accents.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that transitions between two positions in the mouth during a single syllable, as in /aɪ/ in "my."
Monophthong: A single, steady vowel sound without a transition, as in /iː/ in "see."
Schwa: The mid-central, unreduced vowel /ə/, which is the most common vowel in many languages, especially in unstressed syllables.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum of a vowel, corresponding to the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract.
F0: The fundamental frequency of a sound, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration and perceived as pitch.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, primarily determined by the fundamental frequency.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Chinese and Vietnamese.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation across a phrase or utterance that conveys grammatical structure, emotion, or information focus.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase, typically marked by increased loudness, length, or pitch.
Syllable: The basic unit of prosodic structure, typically consisting of a vowel or syllabic consonant optionally preceded and/or followed by consonants.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel, around which the syllable is organized.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Syllabic: Pertaining to a sound that functions as the nucleus of a syllable, such as syllabic [n] in "button."
Mora: A unit of syllable weight used to measure the timing of syllables in prosodic and metrical systems.
Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property of a phoneme used to distinguish it from other phonemes in a system, such as [+voice] or [±nasal].
Minimal pair: Two words that differ in only one phoneme at the same position, demonstrating a phonemic contrast, as in "pat" and "bat."
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of the same phoneme.
Assimilation: A sound change in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in "input" [ɪmpʊt] for "input" [ɪnpʊt].
Dissimilation: A sound change in which similar sounds become less alike, often to reduce perceptual difficulty.
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound in a particular context, as in "going to" becoming "gonna."
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word, often to break up consonant clusters, as in the "u" in "quartz."
Metathesis: The reversal of the order of two sounds within a word, as in the historical change from "ask" to "aks" in some dialects.
Lenition: A weakening of a consonant over time, such as the shift from /p/ to /f/ or /t/ to /θ/.
Fortition: A strengthening of a consonant, the opposite of lenition, as in the shift from a fricative to a stop.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound; voiced sounds include /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, and /v/.
Place of articulation: The specific location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The type of airflow obstruction used to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Vowel height: The vertical position of the tongue body during vowel production, categorized as high, mid, or low.
Vowel backness: The horizontal position of the tongue body, categorized as front, central, or back.
Vowel rounding: The degree to which the lips are rounded during vowel production.
ATR: Advanced Tongue Root, a feature in vowel systems distinguishing vowels with a more retracted tongue root (typically higher) from those without.
Aspiration: A burst of breath accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in the [pʰ] in English "pat."
Pharyngealization: A secondary articulation in which the pharyngeal constrictor muscles are tensed, as in Arabic pharyngealized consonants.
Labialization: A secondary articulation in which the lips are rounded, as in the French /k̞ʷ/ or the rounded /o/ vowel.
Neutralization: A context in which a phonemic contrast is lost, as in the final consonant devoicing in Russian.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permissible in a language, such as English not allowing /ŋ/ in onset position.
Coarticulation: The simultaneous or overlapping articulation of adjacent sounds, causing each to be influenced by the other.
Prosody: The suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, tone, intonation, and rhythm, that organize speech beyond the segmental level.
Prosodic structure: The hierarchical organization of speech into larger units such as syllables, feet, prosodic words, phrases, and intonational phrases.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit in a language, such as the prefix "un-" or the suffix "-ed."
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme, such as the different pronunciations of the English past-tense suffix: /t/ in "walked," /d/ in "played," and /ɪd/ in "wanted."
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning, to which affixes may be added.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to create a new word or modify meaning, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before the root of a word, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix that is attached after the root of a word, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root of a word, as in the English "ab-so-lutely" or in many Austronesian languages.
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds a root, consisting of two parts, such as the German "ge-…-t" in "gekauft."
Derivational: A type of morphological process that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category, as in "happiness" from "happy."
Inflectional: A type of morphological process that creates grammatical variants of a word without changing its core meaning, as in "walks," "walked," and "walking."
Compounding: A morphological process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to form a new word, such as "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical categories, as in many polysynthetic and fusional languages.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonetic form but carries grammatical meaning, such as the plural in English "sheep."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-un" in "unhappy."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can function as an independent word, such as "cat" or "run."
Agglutinative: A language type in which morphemes are added in a regular, one-to-one fashion, with each morpheme representing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional: A language type in which a single affix can encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Spanish.
Isolating: A language type that relies primarily on separate words and word order rather than affixation, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A language type in which single words can encode what would require a full sentence in other languages, as in many Native American languages.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may itself contain a root and derivational affixes.
Base: The morpheme to which an affix is attached in a particular derivational or inflectional operation.
Radical: A root morpheme, especially in Semitic languages, where the same set of consonants can appear in different patterns.
Productivity: The degree to which a morphological process is still actively used to create new words in a language.
Morphological paradigm: The set of all inflected forms of a particular word, showing how it changes across grammatical categories.
Suppletion: The replacement of one morpheme entirely by a different, unrelated form, as in "go" / "went" or "man" / "men."
Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparently affixal element from an existing word, as in "burglar" from "burglary."
Clipping: The shortening of a word without changing its meaning or grammatical category, as in "phone" from "telephone."
Blend: A word formed by combining parts of two or more words, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "motel" (motor + hotel).
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced as a word, such as "NASA" or "laser."
Initialism: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "UNESCO."
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their predominant morphological processes, such as isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the structure of sentences and the combination of words into phrases and clauses.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular word category, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase, that functions as a constituent in a larger structure.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing at least a subject and a predicate, which may be independent or embedded within another clause.
Sentence: A complete syntactic unit that expresses a proposition and typically contains a subject and a predicate.
Constituent: A syntactic unit that functions as a single element within a larger structure, testable through movement, substitution, or coordination.
Constituency: The property of being a constituent in a syntactic structure.
Head: The central or governing element of a phrase that determines the category of the phrase, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: An obligatory dependent of a head that completes its meaning, such as the object in a transitive verb phrase.
Specifier: An optional element at the beginning of a phrase that modifies or determines the head, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Adjunct: An optional, non-obligatory modifier that adds extra information to a phrase, such as an adverbial phrase.
Modifier: A syntactic element that adds descriptive or restrictive information to another element without being its complement.
Argument: A semantic role associated with a predicate, typically realized by a noun phrase, such as the agent or patient.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Theme.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase, such as nominative, accusative, or dative.
Nominative: The grammatical case typically marking the subject of a clause in accusative-case languages.
Accusative: The grammatical case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb in accusative-case languages.
Dative: The grammatical case typically marking indirect objects or recipients, as in "I gave the book to her."
Genitive: The grammatical case typically marking possession or origin, as in "the book of the author" or "the author's book."
Locative: The grammatical case marking location or position, as in "in the house" or "on the table."
Instrumental: The grammatical case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed, as in "with a hammer."
Ergative: A grammatical case marking the agent of a transitive verb, as in ergative-absolutive languages like Basque or Guaraní.
Absolute: A grammatical case marking the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive systems.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object, as in "She broke the window."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, as in "She left."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object, as in "She gave him the book."
Voice: A grammatical category that relates the subject of a clause to the participants in the event, as in active and passive voice.
Active voice: A voice in which the subject is the agent of the action, as in "The cat chased the mouse."
Passive voice: A voice in which the subject is the patient or recipient of the action, as in "The mouse was chased by the cat."
Middle voice: A voice that indicates the subject is both the agent and the patient of the action, as in "The book sold quickly."
Agent: The entity that performs or causes an action, typically the subject in active sentences.
Patient: The entity that undergoes or is affected by an action, typically the direct object in active sentences.
Experiencer: The entity that undergoes a mental or emotional state, as in "She felt happy."
Theme: The entity that is moved or positioned, as in "She placed the book on the shelf."
Goal: The endpoint or destination of a directed action or motion, as in "She walked to the store."
Source: The starting point of a directed action or motion, as in "She walked from the store."
Recipient: The entity that receives something, as in "She gave him the book."
Beneficiary: The entity for whom an action is performed, as in "She made a cake for her child."
Instrument: The means or tool used to perform an action, as in "She cut the bread with a knife."
Word order: The arrangement of syntactic elements (subject, verb, object, etc.) in a sentence, which varies across languages.
SVO: Subject-Verb-Object, a basic word order found in languages like English and Mandarin Chinese.
SOV: Subject-Object-Verb, a basic word order found in languages like Japanese, Turkish, and Korean.
VSO: Verb-Subject-Object, a basic word order found in languages like Irish, Welsh, and Classical Arabic.
V2: The verb-second constraint, found in languages like German and Dutch, where the finite verb occupies the second position in a main clause.
Free word order: A word order pattern in which constituents can appear in multiple positions, as in many case-marking languages like Polish or Latin.
Fixed word order: A word order pattern in which the order of constituents is rigidly determined, as in English.
Coordination: A syntactic process in which two or more elements of the same category are joined by a conjunction, as in "bread and butter."
Subordination: A syntactic process in which one clause is embedded within and dependent on another, as in "I left because it was raining."
Embedding: The inclusion of one syntactic structure within another, as in "I think that she knows the answer."
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply repeatedly, allowing the embedding of structures within the same type of structure, as in "I know that she knows that he left."
Movement: A syntactic operation in which an element is displaced from its base position to a higher position in the structure, as in wh-movement or topicalization.
Deletion: A syntactic operation in which an element is omitted from the surface structure, often due to ellipsis or pro-drop.
Ellipsis: The omission of one or more words from a sentence where they can be understood from context, as in "I like apples, and she likes ___ (them) too."
Trace: A theoretical empty element left behind in the original position of a moved constituent in generative syntax.
Empty category: A theoretical element in syntax that has no phonetic realization but plays a structural role, such as a trace, variable, or pro.
Binding: The set of principles governing the relationship between anaphoric elements (like pronouns and reflexives) and their antecedents.
Anaphora: A linguistic element that refers back to a previously mentioned entity, as in the "her" in "Mary left because she was tired."
Cataphora: A linguistic element that refers forward to an entity mentioned later, as in "The fact that she left surprised everyone."
Deixis: The use of linguistic elements that depend on the context of utterance for interpretation, such as "I," "here," "now," and "this."
Referent: The entity in the world that a linguistic expression points to or denotes.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it denotes or points to in the world.
Antecedent: The earlier-occurring expression to which a pronoun or other anaphoric element refers.
Co-reference: The relationship between two or more expressions that refer to the same entity, such as "John" and "he" in "John said that he was tired."
Binding Theory: A framework in generative syntax that governs the distribution of anaphors, pronouns, and variables relative to their antecedents.
Government: A syntactic relationship in which a head element governs or determines the properties of a complement.
Selection: A semantic or syntactic constraint in which a head determines the category or features of its complement, as a verb selecting a particular type of object.
Government and Binding: A theoretical framework in generative syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s, consisting of modules like Phrase Structure, Binding, Case, and Theta Theory.
X-bar theory: A theory of phrase structure that proposes a uniform schema for all phrases, with a specifier, a head, and a complement at each level.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of words and phrases within a sentence, often represented as a tree diagram.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence, showing constituent relationships.
Dominance: A structural relationship in a tree diagram in which one node is higher than and governs another node.
Immediate dominance: A structural relationship in which one node is directly above another with no intervening nodes.
C-command: A structural relationship in which a node dominates all nodes of a particular category but is not itself dominated by them.
Category: A grammatical class to which a word belongs, such as noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, or determiner.
Phrase level: A syntactic level of analysis dealing with the structure of phrases as units.
Word level: A syntactic level of analysis dealing with the internal structure of individual words.
Clause level: A syntactic level of analysis dealing with the structure of clauses and their relationships.
Sentence level: A syntactic level of analysis dealing with the structure of complete sentences.
Discourse level: A level of analysis dealing with the organization of language beyond the sentence, including paragraphs and extended texts.
Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context influences the interpretation of meaning in communication.
Sememe: The smallest unit of meaning in a language, analogous to the phoneme at the sound level.
Sign: A linguistic entity that pairs a form (signifier) with a meaning (signified), as defined in semiotics.
Signifier: The physical form of a linguistic sign, such as a sound pattern, written string, or gesture.
Signified: The concept or meaning associated with a linguistic sign.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-defined meaning of a word or expression.
Connotation: The associated, implied, or emotional meanings of a word beyond its literal definition.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a linguistic expression, as in the multiple senses of "bank."
Proposition: The truth-conditional content of a sentence, independent of its particular linguistic expression.
Truth value: The status of a proposition as true or false in a given context or state of the world.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as "She is a bachelor" entails "She is male."
Presupposition: Background information that is assumed to be true for a sentence to be meaningful, such as the presupposition in "She stopped smoking" that she used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning that is communicated by a speaker but is not part of the literal meaning of the sentence, often derived through conversational principles.
Gricean maxims: Four conversational principles (Quality, Quantity, Relation, and Manner) proposed by H.P. Grice that govern cooperative communication.
Cooperative principle: Grice's general assumption that participants in a conversation aim to make their contributions relevant and informative.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action beyond merely describing a state of affairs, such as promising, ordering, or declaring.
Illocutionary act: The intended function of an utterance, such as warning, requesting, or promising.
Perlocutionary act: The actual effect of an utterance on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or inspiring.
Performative: A verb that names the speech act being performed, as in "I promise," "I apologize," or "I pronounce you married."
Locutionary act: The basic act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific semantic content.
Context: The surrounding circumstances, including linguistic and extralinguistic factors, that influence the interpretation of an utterance.
Synonymy: The relationship between words or expressions that have the same or very similar meanings, as in "begin" and "commence."
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings, as in "hot" and "cold" or "big" and "small."
Hyponymy: A semantic relationship in which one term's meaning is included within another's, as in "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernymy: The reverse of hyponymy; the relationship in which a general term's meaning includes more specific terms, as in "bird" is a hypernym of "sparrow."
Monymy: The relationship between a part and the whole, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Holonymy: The reverse of meronymy; the relationship between a whole and its parts, as in "car" is a holonym of "wheel."
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word or expression having multiple related meanings, as in "head" (body part, leader, top).
Homonymy: The phenomenon of two or more distinct words having the same form but unrelated meanings, as in "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river edge).
Ambiguity: A situation in which a linguistic expression has more than one possible interpretation, as in "I saw the man with the telescope."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which a term is applied to something it is not literally, based on perceived similarity, as in "time is money."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which one entity is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it, as in "the White House announced."
Synecdoche: A figure of speech in which a part is used to refer to the whole or vice versa, as in "all hands on deck."
Irony: A figure of speech in which the intended meaning is opposite to the literal meaning, often for humorous or emphatic effect.
Sarcasm: A form of irony in which a person says something contrary to what they mean, typically to mock or convey contempt.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh, blunt, or unpleasant one, as in "passed away" for "died."
Dysphemism: A deliberately harsh, offensive, or unpleasant expression used in place of a neutral or mild one.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual words, as in "kick the bucket."
Collocation: A habitual or conventional combination of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Semantic field: A set of words related by a common concept or domain, such as the field of "kitchen utensils."
Prototype: A central or most typical example of a category, around which other, less typical members are organized, as in a robin being a prototype bird.
Frame: A structured set of concepts and relationships that organizes a domain of knowledge, such as the "purchase" frame involving a buyer, seller, item, and price.
Script: A structured representation of a sequence of events or actions in a familiar situation, such as the "restaurant" script involving entering, ordering, eating, paying, and leaving.
Frame semantics: A theory of meaning that organizes word meanings in terms of structured frames of knowledge and experience.
Semantic role: The function an entity plays in an event, such as agent, patient, instrument, or recipient, as represented in thematic grammar.
Event: A semantic unit representing an action, change, or occurrence, as opposed to a state or property.
State: A semantic unit representing a condition or property that persists over time, as in "She is tall" or "The door is closed."
Process: A semantic unit representing an ongoing action or change, as in "The water is boiling."
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, progressive, or habitual.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of utterance, typically past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the content of a proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of information for a proposition, such as direct perception, hearsay, or inference.
Epistemic modality: A type of modality that expresses the speaker's assessment of the likelihood or certainty of a proposition, as in "It might be true."
Deontic modality: A type of modality that expresses obligation, permission, or prohibition, as in "You must leave" or "You may stay."
Dynamic modality: A type of modality that expresses the ability or disposition of an entity, as in "She can swim" or "The door will not open."
Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and social context.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community, differing in pronunciation, vocabulary, or grammar.
Accent: The distinctive pronunciation or prosodic features of a speaker, often associated with a particular region or social group.
Idiolect: The unique linguistic variety of an individual speaker, encompassing their particular vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as a class, profession, or age group.
Register: A variety of language associated with a particular communicative situation, purpose, or domain, such as formal, informal, technical, or legal.
Style: The set of linguistic choices a speaker or writer makes to suit a particular audience, purpose, or context.
Code: A particular linguistic variety or set of linguistic resources used by a speaker in a given context.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The blending of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance, more closely integrated than code-switching.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language (or two languages) are used in complementary social domains, such as a "high" and a "low" variety.
Bilingualism: The ability or practice of using two languages, either by an individual or a community.
Multilingualism: The ability or practice of using more than two languages, either by an individual or a community.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be actively used.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons its native language in favor of another.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, which can lead to borrowing, convergence, or the creation of new varieties.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or linguistic feature from one language into another, such as "sushi" from Japanese into English.
Loanword: A word adopted from one language into another, often with some phonological or morphological adaptation.
Calque: A word or phrase formed by translating a foreign expression word for word into the structure of the target language, as in "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Language family: A group of languages that share a common ancestor, such as the Indo-European or Sino-Tibetan family.
Language isolate: A language with no known genetic relationship to any other language, such as Basque or Korean.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language, typically without native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that evolves from a pidgin, with native speakers and a complex grammar of its own.
Lingua franca: A language widely used as a common means of communication among speakers of different native languages, such as English or Arabic in certain regions.
Superstrate: A language of a dominant group that influences a substrate language, often contributing vocabulary and prestige features.
Substrate: A language of a subordinate or conquered group that influences the superstrate language, often contributing phonological or structural features.
Adstrate: A language that influences another through prolonged contact between communities of roughly equal status.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects in which adjacent dialects are mutually intelligible, but the extremes of the chain may not be.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line marking the extent of a particular linguistic feature in a dialect survey.
Toponym: A name of a place, often reflecting historical or linguistic information about the area.
Ethnonym: A name used by or for an ethnic group, which may carry connotations of identity, power, or derogation.
Language prestige: The social value or status associated with a particular variety of language, often influenced by the social power of its speakers.
Stigmatization: The negative social evaluation attached to certain linguistic varieties or features, often associated with lower social status.
Language planning: The deliberate efforts to influence the development, use, or status of a language or its varieties.
Language policy: A set of government or institutional decisions regarding the use, promotion, or regulation of particular languages.
Language ideology: The beliefs, attitudes, and assumptions that communities hold about language, its varieties, and its speakers.
Linguistic landscape: The visible linguistic features of a physical environment, such as signs, advertisements, and public notices.
Dialectometry: A quantitative method of dialect classification based on the measurement of linguistic differences across a geographic grid.
Sociolinguistic variable: A linguistic feature that varies systematically according to social factors such as class, age, gender, or ethnicity.
Stylistic variation: The range of linguistic forms a speaker can use across different registers and contexts.
Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the origins, development, and change of languages over time.
Comparative method: A systematic technique for reconstructing proto-languages and establishing genetic relationships among languages by comparing cognate forms.
Reconstruction: The process of proposing a hypothetical proto-language or proto-form based on systematic correspondences in descendant languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed from its descendant languages, such as Proto-Indo-European or Proto-Norse.
Cognate: Words in different languages that are descended from a common ancestral form, such as English "mother," German "Mutter," and Latin "māter."
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words, including their form, meaning, and usage over time.
Sound change: A systematic phonological shift that affects a class of sounds in a language over time, such as the Great Vowel Shift in English.
Sound law: A regular, rule-governed pattern of sound change, such as Grimm's Law in the Germanic languages.
Grimm's Law: The systematic consonant shift that distinguishes Proto-Germanic from other Indo-European branches, such as /p/ → /f/ and /t/ → /θ/.
Verner's Law: A sound change that explains apparent exceptions to Grimm's Law, whereby voiceless fricatives become voiced in certain accentual environments.
Internal reconstruction: A method of historical linguistics that infers earlier sound systems from alternations within a single language.
External reconstruction: A method of historical linguistics that uses comparative data from related languages to reconstruct earlier forms.
Diachronic: Pertaining to the study of language change over time, as opposed to the study of a language at a single point in time.
Synchronic: Pertaining to the study of a language at a particular point in time, without reference to its history.
Typology: The branch of linguistics that classifies and compares languages according to structural features, identifying patterns and universals across the world's languages.
Universal: A linguistic feature or constraint that holds across all or a significant majority of the world's languages.
Sprachbund: A group of languages that share structural features due to prolonged contact rather than common descent, such as the Balkan Sprachbund.
Glottolog: A comprehensive online catalog of the world's languages, their genetic relationships, and their geographic distribution.
Swadesh list: A list of 100 or 200 basic vocabulary items used in lexicostatistics and computational phylogenetics to compare languages.
Grammaticalization: The process by which lexical words or phrases evolve into grammatical morphemes or constructions, such as "going to" becoming "gonna."
Reanalysis: A change in the structural parsing of a linguistic form without a change in its surface form, as when a compound is reinterpreted as a phrase.
Analogical change: A linguistic change in which a form is altered to align with a more regular or dominant pattern, as in "oxen" vs. "mice."
Leveling: The reduction of irregular variation in a set of related forms, as when "bound" replaces an older irregular past participle.
Archaism: A word, form, or construction that has fallen out of general use but persists in specialized or literary contexts.
Neologism: A newly coined word, expression, or usage, such as "selfie" or "deepfake."
Obsolescence: The gradual disappearance of a word, form, or construction from active use in a language.
Language drift: The gradual, cumulative change in a language's structure and vocabulary over time.
Divergence: The process by which related languages or dialects become increasingly different over time.
Convergence: The process by which unrelated or distant languages or dialects become structurally more similar, often through contact.
Substratum: The influence of a previously spoken language on a later, dominant language in the same region.
Superstratum: The influence of a later, dominant language on a previously spoken language in the same region.
Adstratum: The influence of a coexisting language of roughly equal status on another through contact.
Language isolation: The condition of a language having no known genetic relatives, making it a language isolate.
Genetic relationship: A demonstrable historical connection between languages that share a common ancestor.
Areal: Pertaining to the geographic distribution of linguistic features, as opposed to genetic relationships.
Phylum: A hypothetical grouping of language families that may share a very distant common ancestor, such as the proposed Nostratic or Bantu-Cushitic phyla.
Language branch: A subdivision within a language family, such as the Germanic branch of Indo-European.
Language group: A subdivision within a language branch, such as the West Germanic group within the Germanic branch.
Language stock: An intermediate grouping between a language family and a branch, used in some taxonomic systems.
Discourse: Language as it is used in extended communication beyond the sentence level, including conversation, narrative, and argumentation.
Text: A stretch of language that forms a unified, coherent whole, whether spoken or written.
Cohesion: The set of grammatical and lexical devices that link elements within a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical cohesion.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a text, in which ideas are organized in a meaningful and interpretable way.
Topic: The entity or subject about which a clause or discourse segment is made.
Theme: The given or starting-point information in a sentence, typically the first element.
Rheme: The new or end-point information in a sentence, typically following the theme.
Given: Information that is already known or established in the discourse, often realized as the theme.
New: Information that is not yet established in the discourse, often realized as the rheme.
Information structure: The organization of a sentence or discourse in terms of what is given and what is new, and how focus and topic are marked.
Focus: The element in a sentence that carries new or contrastive information, often marked by stress or word order.
Contrastive focus: A type of focus that highlights a difference or alternative, as in "I didn't go to the STORE, I went to the MARKET."
Informational focus: A type of focus that introduces entirely new information, as opposed to contrasting with alternatives.
Topic structure: The organization of discourse around a central topic, with subtopics and related ideas.
Paragraph: A unit of written discourse consisting of one or more sentences that develop a single idea or theme.
Co-text: The linguistic context provided by the surrounding text, as opposed to the extralinguistic context.
Intertextuality: The relationship between a text and other texts, through allusion, quotation, parody, or other means of reference.
Metadiscourse: Language that comments on or organizes the discourse itself, such as "as I mentioned earlier" or "in conclusion."
Metalanguage: Language used to describe or analyze language, as in linguistic terminology or grammatical rules.
Metalinguistic: Pertaining to the ability to reflect on and manipulate language as an object of thought.
Meta-communicative: Pertaining to communication about communication, such as clarifying how a message should be interpreted.
Pragmatic inference: The process of deriving implied meanings beyond the literal content of an utterance, based on context and conversational principles.
Hearer: The recipient of a communicative act, who interprets the speaker's intended meaning.
Speaker: The producer of a communicative act, who selects linguistic forms to convey meaning.
Communicative competence: A speaker's ability to use language appropriately and effectively in social contexts, beyond mere grammatical knowledge.
Linguistic competence: A speaker's underlying knowledge of the grammatical, lexical, and phonological rules of a language.
Performance: The actual use of language in real communicative situations, which may deviate from competence due to memory, attention, or social factors.
Universal Grammar: The hypothetical innate, language-specific knowledge that all human speakers possess, providing the constraints and parameters for possible language structures.
Parameter: A binary or multi-valued setting in Universal Grammar that can take different values across languages, such as the head-parameter (head-initial vs. head-final).
Feature geometry: A model of phonological features that organizes distinctive features in a hierarchical structure, such as the laryngeal or place-of-articulation hierarchy.
Optimality Theory: A framework in phonology and syntax that ranks constraints and selects the optimal output from a set of candidates.
Construction grammar: A theoretical framework that treats the basic units of grammar as form-meaning pairings, or constructions, rather than separate components.
Cognitive grammar: A framework that integrates form, meaning, and use in a single system, emphasizing embodied cognition and image schemas.
Lexical-functional grammar: A theoretical framework that separates syntactic structure from functional and lexical information, using a lexicon and functional equations.
Head-driven phrase structure grammar: A framework that uses attribute-value matrices and unification to represent grammatical information and constituency.
Distributed morphology: A theoretical framework that treats the relationship between phonology and morphology as a post-syntactic process, separating lexical roots from their phonological form.
Generative grammar: The theoretical tradition, initiated by Noam Chomsky, that aims to describe the set of grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules or principles.
Transformational grammar: The first model of generative grammar (1957) that used transformational rules to derive surface structures from deep structures.
Minimalism: The most recent version of generative grammar, which seeks to reduce the machinery of the grammar to the minimal set of necessary operations and principles.
Merge: The core operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects to form a new one, building the structure of a sentence.
Feature checking: The process in generative syntax by which uninterpretable features on a syntactic element are matched and valued against interpretable features on another element.
Agree: A syntactic operation in which a head probes its domain and matches its features with those of a goal, as in subject-verb agreement.
Move: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is copied from one position and the copy is deleted, leaving a trace or copy in the original position.
Phase: A structural unit in the Minimalist Program (typically vP and CP) at which the computational system interfaces with other modules, limiting the search space for operations.
Derivational: Pertaining to processes that create new lexical items or change the grammatical category of a word.
Inflectional: Pertaining to processes that create grammatical variants of a word without changing its core lexical meaning or category.
Compounding: The process of combining two or more free morphemes to form a new word, as in "notebook" or "firefighter."
Inflection: The morphological marking of grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person on a word.
Derivation: The morphological process of creating a new word from an existing one, often changing its category or core meaning.
Internal change: A morphological process in which a word's internal vowel or consonant changes to indicate a grammatical or lexical distinction, as in English "sing/sang/sung" or Arabic root patterns.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morphological processes interact with phonological rules.
Morphosyntax: The interface between morphology and syntax, studying how morphological structure interacts with syntactic structure.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and their meanings in a language, as opposed to the grammatical rules that combine them.
Lexical item: A basic entry in the lexicon, including a word or multi-word expression and its semantic, syntactic, and phonological properties.
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word, as in "run" being the lemma for "runs," "running," and "ran."
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word, sometimes marked orthographically with a hyphen or underscore.
Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a morpheme depending on its phonological or morphological environment, such as "cat/cats" vs. "bus/buses."
Morphological productivity: The degree to which a particular morphological process is actively and freely used to create new forms in a language.
Morphological family: The set of all words derived from a common root, such as the English family including "act," "action," "actor," "react," and "interactive."
Paradigm: The full set of inflected forms of a word, arranged to show the pattern of changes across grammatical categories.
Paradigmatic relation: A relationship between linguistic elements that can occupy the same structural position, as in the alternatives "cat," "dog," and "bird" in "The ___ barked."
Syntagmatic relation: A relationship between linguistic elements that occur in sequence within a structure, as in the linear relationship between "The," "cat," and "slept."
Paradigm: The set of grammatical forms of a word or class of words, such as the case forms of a noun or the conjugation of a verb.
Paradigmatic: Relating to the selection of alternatives at a given position in a structure, as opposed to the combination of elements in sequence.
Syntagmatic: Relating to the linear combination of elements in a structure, as opposed to the selection of alternatives at a single position.
Syntactic category: The grammatical class assigned to a word or phrase, such as N, V, Adj, Adv, P, D, C.
Phrasal category: A syntactic category that heads a phrase, such as NP, VP, AP, PP.
Lexical category: A syntactic category that corresponds to a word class, such as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Functional category: A syntactic category that corresponds to a grammatical or functional word, such as determiner, complementizer, or auxiliary.
Open class: A word class that is open to the addition of new members, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
Closed class: A word class that is closed to the addition of new members, such as prepositions, conjunctions, and determiners.
Content word: A word that carries lexical or referential meaning, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and most adverbs.
Function word: A word that serves a grammatical or structural role, such as articles, prepositions, conjunctions, and auxiliary verbs.
Determiner: A word that precedes a noun to specify its reference, such as "the," "a," "this," or "every."
Complementizer: A word that introduces a complement clause, such as "that" in "I think that she left" or "whether" in "I wonder whether she left."
Auxiliary: A verb that supports the main verb to express tense, aspect, modality, or voice, such as "will," "have," or "be."
Copula: A verb that links a subject to a predicate complement, as in "is" in "She is a teacher" or "The sky is blue."
Modal verb: An auxiliary verb that expresses modality, such as "can," "must," "should," or "might."
Light verb: A verb that contributes little semantic content and relies on a complement for its meaning, such as "take" in "take a walk" or "have" in "have a look."
Causative: A construction or morphological process that expresses the causing of an action or state, as in "She broke the window" vs. "She had the window broken."
Applicative: A construction or morphological process that adds an argument to a verb, typically promoting a peripheral argument to direct object status.
Antipassive: A construction that reduces the transitivity of a verb, often demoting the direct object to an oblique or adverbial argument.
Absolutive: The unmarked case in ergative-absolutive languages, marking the subject of intransitive verbs and the object of transitive verbs.
Ergative: The marked case in ergative-absolutive languages, marking the agent of transitive verbs.
Split ergativity: A system in which the ergative-absolutive pattern applies in some contexts and the accusative pattern in others, often conditioned by tense, aspect, or animacy.
Nominative-accusative: A case-marking pattern in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is marked nominative, and the object of transitive verbs is marked accusative.
Ergative-absolutive: A case-marking pattern in which the subject of intransitive verbs and the object of transitive verbs are marked absolutive, and the subject of transitive verbs is marked ergative.
Animacy hierarchy: A ranking of noun phrases by animacy, from human to inanimate, which influences case marking, word order, and agreement in many languages.
Inclusive: A first-person plural pronoun or form that includes the addressee, as in "we" meaning "you and I."
Exclusive: A first-person plural pronoun or form that excludes the addressee, as in "we" meaning "I and someone else."
Inclusivity: A grammatical distinction between first-person plural forms that include or exclude the listener.
Deictic: Pertaining to linguistic elements whose interpretation depends on the situational context of the utterance, such as person, place, and time expressions.
Phoric: A broader term than deictic, referring to elements whose interpretation depends on any context, including the linguistic context (anaphora) or the situational context (deixis).
Indexical: A word or expression whose reference is determined by the context of use, such as "I," "here," or "now."
Demonstrative: A word that points to a specific referent, often based on spatial or discourse distance, such as "this," "that," "these," and "those."
Personal pronoun: A word that refers to participants in the discourse, such as "I," "you," "he," "she," "we," and "they."
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "myself," "himself," or "themselves."
Reciprocal pronoun: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship between two or more participants, such as "each other" or "one another."
Indefinite pronoun: A pronoun that refers to a non-specific entity, such as "someone," "anything," or "no one."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to an antecedent, such as "who," "which," or "that" in "the woman who called."
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used to ask questions, such as "who," "what," "which," or "whose."
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, serving as a referent without directly naming the entity.
Determiner phrase: A phrase headed by a determiner, as in "the cat" or "this book," which may or may not include a noun.
Nominal: A word or phrase that functions as a noun or noun phrase, including nouns, pronouns, and nominalized adjectives.
Nominalization: The process of converting a verb, adjective, or clause into a noun or noun phrase, as in "decide" → "decision" or "to be kind" → "kindness."
Verbalization: The process of converting a noun or adjective into a verb, as in "friend" → "befriend" or "angry" → "anger" (less common).
Adjectivalization: The process of converting a noun or verb into an adjective, as in "gold" → "golden" or "break" → "broken."
Adverbialization: The process of converting an adjective, prepositional phrase, or other element into an adverb, as in "quick" → "quickly" or "on purpose" → "purposefully."
Nominal head: A noun or nominal element that heads a noun phrase, determining its category and core meaning.
Verbal head: A verb that heads a verb phrase, determining its syntactic and semantic properties.
Adjectival head: An adjective that heads an adjective phrase, determining its syntactic properties.
Prepositional head: A preposition that heads a prepositional phrase, determining the grammatical function of its complement.
Complementizer head: A complementizer that heads a complement clause, determining the type of clause introduced.
Auxiliary head: An auxiliary verb that heads an auxiliary phrase or T (tense) phrase, determining tense, aspect, or modality.
Determiner head: A determiner that heads a determiner phrase or DP, determining reference and specificity.
Head movement: A syntactic operation in which a head element moves to a higher functional head, as in verb movement to T or C in many languages.
Head adjacency: The linear contiguity of a head and its complement or specifier in a phrase.
Head government: The structural relationship in which a head selects and governs its complement.
Specified head: A head that has a specifier, as in a determiner phrase where the determiner specifies the noun.
Bare head: A head that appears without a specifier or complement, as in a bare noun.
Functional head: A head that is associated with a functional category rather than a lexical category, such as T, C, D, or Agr.
Lexical head: A head that is associated with a lexical category, such as N, V, or A.
Extended projection principle: A principle in generative syntax requiring that every clause have a subject, which may be overt or a null element like "there" or "pro."
Theta criterion: A principle requiring that each argument receive exactly one theta role and each theta role be assigned to exactly one argument.
Case filter: A principle requiring that every overt nominal receive structural or inherent case.
Proper binding: A condition on anaphoric elements requiring them to be bound within a certain structural domain.
Principle A: A binding principle requiring anaphors (reflexives, reciprocals) to be bound in their governing category.
Principle B: A binding principle requiring pronouns to be free in their governing category.
Principle C: A binding principle requiring R-expressions (names, definite descriptions) to be free in their entire discourse.
Empty Category Principle: A principle requiring empty categories (traces, variables) to be in subject position or in a position governed by an active verb.
Subjacency: A condition on movement requiring that no more than one bounding node (typically NP and TP) is crossed in a single movement step.
ECP (Empty Category Principle): A condition on the distribution of empty categories, requiring them to be properly governed.
A-chain: A chain linking an anaphor to its antecedent, governed by Principle A.
A'-chain: A chain linking a moved element to its trace or copy, as in wh-movement or topicalization.
Wh-movement: The syntactic process of moving a wh-phrase (what, who, where, etc.) from its base position to the specifier of CP.
Topicalization: The syntactic process of moving a constituent to the front of a sentence for discourse or information-structural purposes.
Extraposition: The movement of a heavy constituent to a position after the main clause, as in "I found it strange that he left" → "I found it that he left strange" (less natural in English but common in other languages).
Passivization: The syntactic process of converting an active clause into a passive one, typically demoting the agent and promoting the patient to subject.
Raising: A syntactic process in which an argument of an embedded clause is promoted to a position in the matrix clause, as in "John seems to be leaving."
Control: A syntactic process in which the subject of an embedded non-finite clause is controlled by an argument in the matrix clause, as in "John wants to leave" (John controls the subject of "to leave").
Exceptional case marking: A process in which a matrix verb assigns case to the subject of an embedded clause, as in "I consider him to be smart."
Dative shift: An alternation between a prepositional dative and a bare noun phrase indirect object, as in "I gave the book to her" vs. "I gave her the book."
Locative alternation: An alternation between a transitive and an intransitive use of a verb, as in "She smeared the wall with paint" vs. "She smeared paint on the wall."
Causative alternation: An alternation between a transitive and intransitive use of a verb, as in "She broke the window" vs. "The window broke."
Unaccusative: A verb that takes only a subject which is semantically a patient or theme, as in "The bottle broke" or "She arrived."
Unergative: A verb that takes only a subject which is semantically an agent, as in "She laughed" or "He worked."
Copular: A verb that serves as a copula, linking a subject to a predicate adjective, noun, or clause, as in "be," "become," "seem," or "appear."
Predicative: An adjective that appears in predicate position, as in "She is tall," as opposed to attributive position.
Attributive: An adjective that appears in pre-nominal or modifier position, as in "a tall woman."
Pre-nominal: An adjective that appears before the noun it modifies, as in "a tall woman."
Post-nominal: An adjective that appears after the noun it modifies, as in "the woman tall enough to reach the shelf" (in English, typically in relative clauses).
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, as in "very tall" or "quite old."
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb, as in "very quickly" or "almost never."
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, as in "in the house" or "on the table."
Complement clause: A clause that functions as a complement of a verb, adjective, or noun, as in "I think (that) she is right."
Relative clause: A clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or relative operator, as in "the book that I read."
Adverbial clause: A clause that functions as an adverbial modifier, expressing time, condition, reason, or concession, as in "when she arrived" or "because it rained."
Noun clause: A clause that functions as a noun phrase, as in "What she said was true" or "That he left is a fact."
Predicate: The part of a clause that provides information about the subject, typically consisting of a verb and its arguments and modifiers.
Subject: The argument that controls the grammatical properties of the clause, typically the entity about which something is predicated.
Object: The argument that is affected by or receives the action of the verb, typically the direct or indirect object.
Indirect object: The argument that is the recipient or beneficiary of an action, as in "She gave him the book."
Direct object: The argument that is directly affected by the action of the verb, as in "She broke the window."
Obligatory argument: An argument that must be present for the grammaticality of a clause, as in the direct object of a transitive verb.
Optional argument: An argument that may or may not be present, as in the indirect object of a dative verb.
Saturate: To fill all the argument slots of a predicate, resulting in a complete clause.
Valency: The number of arguments a predicate requires, such as zero for intransitive verbs like "sleep," one for transitive verbs like "eat," and two for ditransitive verbs like "give."
Subcategorization: The specification of the syntactic and semantic properties of the arguments and complements that a lexical item requires.
Selectional restriction: A semantic constraint on the types of arguments a predicate can take, as in "bachelor" requiring a male adult.
Collocational restriction: A constraint on which words can co-occur with which other words, as in "make a mistake" but not *"do a mistake."
Frame semantics: A theory of lexical meaning that organizes word meanings in terms of structured frames of situations, roles, and relationships.
Role: A participant in a frame or event, such as buyer, seller, item, and price in a purchase frame.
Thematic role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Theme, Goal, Source, Instrument, or Recipient.
Event structure: The semantic decomposition of a verb's meaning into basic temporal and causal components, such as [cause [state [agent [become [state [theme]]]]]].
Manner of action: The way in which an action is performed, as in "She walked quickly" or "He ran fast."
Aspectual class: The classification of verbs by their internal temporal structure, such as stative, activity, achievement, and accomplishment (Vendler's categories).
Stative: A verb that describes a state or condition that persists over time, as in "know," "believe," or "be."
Activity: A verb that describes an ongoing action with no inherent endpoint, as in "run," "walk," or "swim."
Achievement: A verb that describes an instantaneous change of state with no duration, as in "arrive," "recognize," or "win."
Accomplishment: A verb that describes a bounded action with a duration and an inherent endpoint, as in "build a house" or "read a book."
Inchoative: A verb form or construction that expresses the beginning of a state or action, as in "The door began to open."
Cessative: A verb form or construction that expresses the end of a state or action, as in "The rain stopped."
Iterative: A grammatical category or verb form that expresses repeated or habitual action, as in "He kept knocking."
Frequentative: A grammatical category that expresses frequent or repeated occurrence, similar to but distinct from the iterative.
Distributive: A grammatical category that expresses the distribution of an action or state over multiple participants or events.
Cumulative: A semantic property in which combining events of the same type results in a single larger event, as in "drinking a liter of water" vs. "drinking two liters."
Semi-lexical: A word or expression that is stored in the lexicon but whose meaning is partially compositional, such as fixed collocations or idiomatic expressions.
Lexical gap: A situation in which a language lacks a word or expression for a concept that is expressed in other languages.
Semantic bleaching: The process by which a word or expression loses its original specific meaning and becomes more generic or grammatical.
Semantic expansion: The broadening of a word's meaning over time, as in "bird" expanding from "young bird" to any bird.
Semantic narrowing: The restriction of a word's meaning over time, as in "meat" shifting from "food" to "animal flesh."
Semantic shift: The change in the meaning of a word over time, encompassing broadening, narrowing, metaphorical extension, and metonymic extension.
Metaphorical extension: The extension of a word's meaning based on perceived similarity, as in "head" extending from "body part" to "leader" to "top."
Metonymic extension: The extension of a word's meaning based on contiguity or association, as in "the crown" referring to the monarchy.
Pejoration: The degradation of a word's meaning over time, as in "villain" shifting from "farm servant" to "criminal."
Amelioration: The improvement of a word's meaning over time, as in "nice" shifting from "ignorant" to "pleasant."
Taboo: A social prohibition against the use of certain words, often related to death, disease, sexuality, or bodily functions, leading to the creation of euphemisms.
Euphemistic cycle: The pattern in which euphemisms are coined, become conventional, lose their euphemistic force, and are eventually replaced by new euphemisms.
Sememe: The smallest unit of meaning, analogous to the phoneme in phonology, as in the meaning components of "bachelor" as [+human, +male, +adult, +unmarried].
Componential analysis: A method of semantic analysis that decomposes word meanings into a set of binary or multi-valued features.
Tautology: The use of two or more words with the same meaning, as in "free gift" or "ATM machine."
Oxymoron: A combination of two contradictory or opposing terms, as in "deafening silence" or "bittersweet."
Hyperbole: A figure of speech involving deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect, as in "I've told you a million times."
Litotes: A figure of speech that uses understatement, often through double negation, as in "not bad" meaning "good."
Chiasmus: A rhetorical structure in which the second half parallels the first in reverse order, as in "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country."
Antithesis: A rhetorical device that juxtaposes contrasting ideas in balanced phrases, as in "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."
Parallelism: The use of the same grammatical structure for two or more parts of a sentence or passage.
Rhetorical question: A question asked for effect rather than to obtain an answer, as in "Who wouldn't want to go?"
Rhetoric: The art of persuasive or effective use of language, including the study and practice of figures of speech and argumentation.
Rhetorical strategy: A deliberate choice of linguistic or discursive means to achieve a persuasive or communicative goal.
Argumentation: The process of constructing, presenting, and evaluating arguments, including premises, conclusions, and evidence.
Premise: A statement or proposition that serves as a basis for a conclusion in an argument.
Conclusion: The statement or proposition that is derived from or supported by the premises in an argument.
Inference: The process of deriving a conclusion from premises or evidence, whether logical, inductive, or abductive.
Deductive inference: A logical process in which the conclusion necessarily follows from the premises, as in "All humans are mortal; Socrates is a human; therefore, Socrates is mortal."
Inductive inference: A reasoning process in which the conclusion is probable but not guaranteed by the premises, as in generalizing from specific observations.

Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, as in /tʃ/ or /dʒ/.

Lateral: A consonant produced with a central blockage by the tongue blade while air flows around the sides, as in /l/.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid vibrations of a speech organ against another, as in the Spanish /r/.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of the tongue against a surface, as in the /ɾ/ of American English "butter."
Approximant: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract without creating turbulence, as in /w/, /j/, /ɹ/.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal folds in the glottis, transcribed as /ʔ/.
Aspiration: A burst of air accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in the puff of air in /p/ in English "pin."
Formant: A frequency band of amplified sound energy in a vowel, produced by resonances of the vocal tract.
Glottis: The space between the vocal folds in the larynx through which air passes.
Larynx: The cartilaginous structure in the throat containing the vocal folds, essential for phonation.
Palate: The roof of the mouth, divided into the hard palate (anterior) and the soft palate or velum (posterior).
Alveolar: A place of articulation at the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth.
Velar: A place of articulation at the soft palate, as in /k/, /ɡ/, /ŋ/.
Uvular: A place of articulation at or near the uvula, as in /ʁ/ or /q/.
Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips, as in /p/, /b/, /m/.
Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip and the upper teeth, as in /f/ and /v/.
Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth, as in /θ/ and /ð/.
Interdental: A place of articulation with the tongue tip positioned between the upper and lower teeth.
Labial: A place of articulation involving the lips in the production of a sound.
Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the constrictions of the pharyngeal wall, as in /ʕ/ or /ħ/.
Epiglottal: A place of articulation at or near the epiglottis, as in certain Arabic stops.
Constriction: The narrowing of the vocal tract at a particular point during the production of a speech sound.
Anterior: Describing a place of articulation or vowel quality toward the front of the oral cavity.
Posterior: Describing a place of articulation or vowel quality toward the back of the oral cavity.
Central: Describing a vowel produced with the tongue positioned between the front and back extremes.
Front: Describing a vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the hard palate.
Back: Describing a vowel produced with the tongue body retracted toward the pharynx.

Low: Describing a vowel produced with the tongue body lowered in the mouth, as in /a/.
