Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A specific phonetic realization of a phoneme in a particular phonetic context, such as the aspirated [pʰ] in "pin" versus the unaspirated [p] in "spin."
Phone: Any individual sound of speech, considered as a physical event, without regard to its phonemic status.
Phonology: The study of the sound systems of languages and the patterns and rules governing the arrangement and combination of phonemes.
Phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds, including their production, transmission, and perception.
Articulatory phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the physiological mechanisms of speech production, such as the movement of the tongue, lips, and vocal folds.
Acoustic phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the physical and measurable properties of speech sounds as they travel through the air.
Auditory phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the human ear and auditory system.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, without significant constriction, typically serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a complete or partial obstruction of the airflow in the vocal tract.
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel, creating turbulent noise, as in /s/, /f/, or /ʃ/.
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking the airflow and then releasing it in a burst, as in /p/, /t/, or /k/.
Nasal: A consonant produced by lowering the velum to direct airflow through the nasal cavity, as in /m/, /n/, or /ŋ/.
Approximant: A consonant produced by bringing articulators close together without creating turbulent airflow, including glides, lateral approximants, and trills.
Lateral: A consonant in which the airstream is directed around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant that functions as a variant of /r/ in a language, including trills, taps, and approximants.
Voiced: A sound produced with periodic vibration of the vocal folds.
Voiceless: A sound produced without vibration of the vocal folds.
Aspiration: The release of a puff of air following a consonant closure, as in the [pʰ] of English "pin."
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where the primary constriction occurs during the production of a consonant, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The type of airflow obstruction used to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Suprasegmental: A feature of speech that extends over more than one phonemic segment, such as stress, tone, intonation, or rhythm.
Segment: A discrete unit of sound in speech, typically a vowel or consonant phoneme.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a word consisting of a vowel (nucleus) optionally preceded by an onset and optionally followed by a coda.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, preceding the vowel nucleus.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, following the vowel nucleus.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel, around which the syllable is structured.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda, also called the rime.
Creaky voice: A phonation type characterized by irregular, low-frequency vibration of the vocal folds, producing a rough or creaky sound.
Frication: Turbulent airflow noise produced when air passes through a narrow constriction in the vocal tract.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, as in /tʃ/ (English "church") or /dʒ/ (English "judge").
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, often to break up a difficult consonant cluster, such as the /r/ in "water" from "wat-er."
Deletion: The loss or omission of a sound that is expected to be present in a word, as in the dropping of /r/ in some dialects of English.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which one sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in the nasalization of a vowel before a nasal consonant.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which sounds that are too similar become less similar, as in the alternation between /s/ and /z/ in some languages.
Metathesis: A phonological process in which two sounds swap positions within a word, as in the historical change from "askew" to "askew" or "calfs" to "cliffs."
Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable in rapid or connected speech, such as the loss of /t/ in "next day" pronounced as "nex day."
Coarticulation: The simultaneous or overlapping articulation of adjacent speech sounds, in which the articulatory gestures for one sound influence the production of a neighboring sound.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the spectrum of a vowel, determined by the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract.
Frequency: The number of complete cycles of a sound wave per second, measured in Hertz (Hz), corresponding to the perceived pitch of a sound.
Amplitude: The magnitude of a sound wave, corresponding to the perceived loudness or intensity of a sound.
Duration: The length of time a sound or syllable lasts, measured in milliseconds or seconds.
F0: The fundamental frequency of a sound, corresponding to the rate of vibration of the vocal folds and perceived as pitch.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to its frequency.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch to distinguish word meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese, where "ma" can mean "mother," "horse," " hemp," or "to scold" depending on tone.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable in a word or phrase, typically involving greater loudness, longer duration, and higher pitch.
Intonation: The melodic contour of a phrase or sentence, involving the rise and fall of pitch over time, used to convey attitude, sentence type, or emphasis.
Prosody: The suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, rhythm, tone, and intonation, that convey meaning beyond the segmental level.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used to measure syllable structure, with different syllables containing different numbers of morae.
Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property used to characterize phonemes, such as [±voice], [±nasal], or [±anterior], that distinguishes one sound from another.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized into hierarchical levels, such as root, place, and manner nodes.
Contrast: A phonological opposition in which two sounds have different meanings, such as /p/ and /b/ distinguishing "pat" from "bat" in English.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by exactly one phoneme in the same phonological position and have different meanings, such as "pat" and "bat."
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds (allophones) never occur in the same phonetic environment and thus can be treated as variants of the same phoneme.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more allophones can occur in the same phonetic environment without changing the meaning of a word.
Phonological rule: A formal statement describing a systematic change to a phonological representation, such as a rule of assimilation or deletion.
Optimality Theory: A theoretical framework in phonology that evaluates candidate outputs against a set of ranked constraints, selecting the optimal (least violating) output.
Constraint: A universal condition or requirement in Optimality Theory that candidate outputs are evaluated against, such as MAX, DEP, IDENT, or NOCODA.
Autosegmental phonology: A model of phonological representation in which certain features, such as tone or stress, are assigned to a separate tier and linked to segments.
Metrical phonology: The study of rhythmic patterns and stress assignment in language, often analyzed using metrical trees or grids.
OCP (Obligatory Contour Principle): A phonological constraint that prohibits identical or redundant elements on the same prosodic tier, favoring contour or spread representations.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further broken down into smaller meaningful units, such as the /-s/ in "cats."
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that occurs in different phonological environments, such as /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/ as allomorphs of the English plural morpheme.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning, such as "play" in "playing," "player," or "playful."
Stem: A morpheme to which affixes can be attached, which may consist of a root or a root plus one or more morphemes.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix that is attached to the beginning of a root or stem, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix that is attached to the end of a root or stem, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within a root or stem, as in the Tagalog reduplicative infix "-in-" as in "gutom" (hungry) becoming "gumutom" (to be hungry).
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that is split into two parts surrounding a stem, such as the German past-tense circumfix "ge-...-t" in "gekauft" (bought).
Inflectional morphology: The system of morphological processes that mark grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, gender, and person without changing the word class.
Derivational morphology: The system of morphological processes that create new words or change word classes, such as adding "-ness" to "happy" to form "happiness."
Agglutination: A morphological process in which a word is formed by concatenating multiple morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusion: A morphological process in which a single morpheme expresses multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in the Latin suffix "-avi" expressing past tense, first person, and singular.
Isolation: A morphological type in which words are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relationships are expressed through word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthesis: A morphological type in which words can contain numerous morphemes, often encoding what would be a full sentence in analytical languages, as in many Native American languages.
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical functions, such as the Latin ending "-runt" encoding third person, plural, and perfect tense.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a free word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as the English prefix "un-" or the suffix "-ness."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can function as a standalone word, such as "cat," "run," or "blue."
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of related word forms, such as the lexeme "run" encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Paradigm: A set of related word forms that are conjugated or declined together, such as the verb paradigm of "be" in English (am, is, are, was, were, been).
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express a grammatical category, such as adding "-s" for third person singular or "-ed" for past tense.
Conjugation: The system of verb inflection expressing categories such as tense, mood, person, and number.
Declension: The system of noun, adjective, or pronoun inflection expressing categories such as case, number, and gender.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more independent roots or words are combined to create a new word, such as "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a word is shortened, such as "phone" from "telephone" or "ad" from "advertisement."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an affix from an existing word, such as "editor" from "edit" or "babysit" from "babysitter."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its grammatical class without any change in form, such as the noun "butter" becoming the verb "to butter."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical or lexical meaning, such as plural, aspect, or intensity.
Suppletion: A morphological process in which an irregular alternation between two entirely different word forms marks a grammatical distinction, such as "go" and "went" in English.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed by the absence of any overt form, such as the past tense of "cut" or the plural of "sheep."
Word: A free morpheme or a combination of bound and free morphemes that can function as an independent unit in a sentence.
Derivational affix: An affix that creates a new word or changes the grammatical class of a word, such as "-er" in "teacher" or "un-" in "unhappy."
Inflectional affix: An affix that marks a grammatical category without changing the word's core meaning or class, such as "-s" for plural or "-ed" for past tense.
Syntax: The branch of linguistics concerned with the structure and rules governing the arrangement of words into phrases, clauses, and sentences.
Phrase: A grammatical unit consisting of one or more words, one of which functions as the head, such as "the big red dog" (NP) or "quickly ran" (VP).
Clause: A grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may function as an independent sentence or as part of a larger structure.
Sentence: The highest-level unit of syntactic structure, typically consisting of a clause that can stand alone and express a complete thought.
Constituent: A grammatically well-formed unit within a sentence that functions as a single element, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, or prepositional phrase.
Head: The central word of a phrase that determines its grammatical category and core meaning, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: A mandatory constituent that completes the meaning of a head word or phrase, such as the direct object of a transitive verb.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase or clause, adding information about time, manner, place, or reason, such as adverbial phrases.
Specifier: The constituent that precedes the head of a phrase within its immediate phrasal projection, such as a determiner in a DP or a subject in a TP.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of constituents within a sentence, typically represented as a tree diagram.
X-bar theory: A framework in generative syntax that proposes a uniform set of structural principles for all phrases, including X, X', and XP levels.
Tree diagram: A hierarchical visual representation of syntactic structure, showing the branching relationships between constituents.
Binary branching: A structural principle in generative syntax in which each node in a tree branches into exactly two daughters.
Immediate constituent: The smallest constituents that combine to form a larger constituent in a phrase-structure analysis.
Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence, generated before movement operations, reflecting thematic relations.
Surface structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all movement operations have been applied, corresponding to word order.
Transformational grammar: A model of grammar in which surface structures are derived from deep structures through a series of transformational rules.
Universal Grammar: The innate, language-specific faculty of the human mind that provides the structural principles and parameters underlying all human languages.
Phrase structure rule: A rule in generative grammar that specifies how constituents combine to form larger constituents, such as S → NP VP.
Subcategorization: A lexical property of a verb, noun, or adjective that specifies the types of complements it requires or permits.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Goal.
Case: A grammatical category marking the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase, such as nominative, accusative, dative, or genitive.
Agreement: A grammatical process in which one element changes its form to match properties such as person, number, or gender of another element.
Concord: The grammatical agreement of a verb with its subject in person and number, or of a determiner with a noun in gender and number.
Subject: The noun phrase that serves as the grammatical subject of a clause, typically the entity performing or experiencing the action.
Object: The noun phrase that receives the action of the verb, functioning as a direct or indirect object in a clause.
Indirect object: The noun phrase that denotes the recipient or beneficiary of the action in a ditransitive construction, such as "her" in "gave her a book."
Transitive: A verb that requires a direct object to complete its meaning, such as "eat" in "eat an apple."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, such as "sleep" in "sleep soundly."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct object and an indirect object, such as "give" in "gave her a book."
Copula: A linking verb such as "be" that connects a subject to a predicate nominal or adjective, as in "She is a teacher."
Predicate: The part of a clause that contains the verb and its complements, expressing what is said about the subject.
Argument: A syntactic constituent that is required by the meaning of a predicate, such as the subject and object of a transitive verb.
A-movement: A type of syntactic movement of an argument, such as subject raising, passivization, or wh-movement of an object.
A-bar movement: A type of syntactic movement that is not subject to binding theory conditions, such as topicalization, focus fronting, or wh-movement.
Trace: A silent, phonetically null element left behind by a moved constituent, serving as a placeholder in the syntactic structure.
Binding theory: A set of principles in generative grammar that govern the distribution of anaphors, pronouns, and referential expressions relative to their antecedents.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned or understood antecedent, such as a reflexive pronoun or a definite description.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to a later-mentioned antecedent, such as "this" in "This is what I mean: I disagree."
Reflexive: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "himself" in "He hurt himself."
Intensive: A reflexive pronoun that emphasizes the subject rather than serving as a separate argument, such as "himself" in "He himself did it."
Passive: A voice in which the subject of the clause is the patient or theme rather than the agent, often with the agent demoted or omitted, as in "The ball was kicked."
Active voice: The default voice in which the subject of the clause is the agent performing the action, as in "The boy kicked the ball."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun phrase, typically introduced by a relative pronoun such as "who," "which," or "that."
Subordinate clause: A clause that is embedded within another clause and cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
Coordinate clause: Two or more clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as "and," "but," or "or," each of which can stand alone.
Complement clause: A subordinate clause that functions as the complement of a verb, adjective, or noun, such as "that she left" in "I know that she left."
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, including any determiners, adjectives, and modifiers, such as "the tall woman in the red dress."
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts, such as "quickly ate a sandwich."
Prepositional phrase: A phrase consisting of a preposition and its complement, such as "in the house" or "on the table."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, including articles, demonstratives, quantifiers, and possessives.
Article: A determiner that specifies the definiteness or indefiniteness of a noun phrase, such as "the" (definite) and "a/an" (indefinite).
Quantifier: A word or phrase that expresses quantity or scope, such as "every," "some," "many," "few," or "all."
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "she," "it," "they," or "this."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speech, such as past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the temporal structure or internal profile of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, or progressive.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the event, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Voice: A grammatical category that relates the subject of a clause to the participants in the event, distinguishing active, passive, middle, and other constructions.
Word order: The sequence in which the major constituents of a sentence appear, such as Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) or Verb-Subject-Object (VSO).
Scrambling: A syntactic process in which the order of constituents is freely permuted, as in Japanese or Turkish, without altering the basic meaning.
Topic: The entity or theme about which a clause or sentence is predicated, often marked by special word order or particles.
Focus: The element in a sentence that carries the primary new information or contrastive emphasis.
Clefting: A syntactic construction that divides a sentence into two parts for emphasis, such as "It was John who broke the window."
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction in which the focus is in an initial wh-clause, such as "What I need is a cup of coffee."
Wh-movement: The syntactic process in which a wh-word (such as "who," "what," or "where") moves to the front of a clause to form a question.
Do-support: The insertion of the auxiliary "do" in English interrogative and negative sentences where no other auxiliary is present, as in "Do you like it?"
Negation: The grammatical process of expressing the opposite or denial of a proposition, typically using a negator such as "not" or "no."
Negative polarity item: A word or expression that is only grammatical in the scope of negation or certain downward-entailing contexts, such as "any" in "I don't have any."
Island constraint: A set of syntactic restrictions that prevent extraction (movement) from certain types of embedded structures, such as complex NPs, subjects, or adjuncts.
Subjacency: A principle in Government and Binding theory that limits movement to crossing at most one barrier per step.
Minimal Link Condition: A principle in the Minimalist Program that requires the closest eligible element to be moved in a given derivation.
Case Filter: A principle requiring that all noun phrases bearing theta roles receive Case from a Case-assigning element.
Theta Criterion: A principle requiring that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
C-command: A structural relation in which a node dominates all siblings of a node and is higher than it in the tree, serving as the structural basis for binding and government.
Government: A structural relation in which a head governs its complement, playing a central role in Case assignment and binding in GB theory.
Merge: The fundamental operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects to form a new constituent.
Phase: A domain of syntactic derivation in the Minimalist Program, typically CP or vP, after which certain material becomes inaccessible to further computation.
VP-ellipsis: The deletion of an entire verb phrase when it is identical to a previously mentioned one, as in "He left and she did [VP leave] too."
NP-ellipsis: The deletion of a noun phrase, as in "John likes his dog and Bill [NP his dog]."
Sluicing: The deletion of everything in a clause except a wh-word, as in "I don't know who left."
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the front of a sentence for topic-establishing purposes, as in "This book, I really enjoyed."
Extraposition: The movement of a constituent, typically a heavy phrase, to a post-verbal position, as in "What I'm interested in is [the long list of problems]."
Left-dislocation: The placement of a constituent at the beginning of a sentence, followed by a resumptive pronoun, as in "John, I think he's great."
Right-dislocation: The placement of a constituent at the end of a sentence, typically with a preceding pronoun, as in "I think he's great, John."
Heavy NP shift: The rightward movement of a long or complex noun phrase across a shorter object, as in "He gave [the long list] to [her] rather than [her] to [the long list]."
Semantics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary definition of a word or expression, referring to the set of entities to which it applies.
Connotation: The associated, emotional, or cultural meanings of a word that go beyond its literal denotation.
Sense: A particular meaning of a word or expression, one of possibly multiple meanings, as in the different senses of "bank" (financial institution vs. river edge).
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or set of entities in the world it picks out.
Referent: The actual entity or object in the world to which a linguistic expression refers.
Synonymy: A semantic relation between two words or expressions that have the same or very similar meanings, such as "big" and "large."
Antonymy: A semantic relation between two words or expressions that have opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "give" and "take."
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one word (the hyponym) is a subset of the meaning of another (the hypernym), as in "rose" is a hyponym of "flower."
Hypernymy: The inverse of hyponymy, in which the meaning of one word is a superset of another, as in "flower" is a hypernym of "rose."
Meronimy: A semantic relation expressing a part-whole relationship, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Holonymy: The inverse of meronymy, in which the whole is expressed, as in "car" is a holonym of "wheel."
Homonymy: A semantic relation in which two distinct words have the same form but unrelated meanings, such as "bank" (river) and "bank" (financial).
Polysemy: A semantic relation in which a single word has multiple related meanings, such as "head" (body part, leader, top).
Metonymy: A semantic or pragmatic process in which one entity is referred to by the name of another entity with which it is associated, such as "The White House announced..."
Metaphor: A semantic or cognitive process in which one concept is understood and expressed in terms of another, typically from a more concrete to a more abstract domain.
Scalar implicature: A pragmatic inference based on the use of a word on a scale, such as inferring "not all" from "some."
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics in which the meaning of a sentence is identified with the conditions under which it is true.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules used to combine them.
Logical form: The level of semantic representation in generative grammar that encodes the logical structure of a sentence for interpretation.
Montague semantics: A formal approach to natural language semantics that uses mathematical logic and lambda calculus to derive compositional meanings.
Intension: The set of possible worlds in which a proposition is true, or the function from possible worlds to extensions.
Extension: The set of actual entities in the world to which a term refers, or the truth value of a proposition in the actual world.
Ambiguity: A property of a linguistic expression that allows more than one interpretation, such as syntactic or lexical ambiguity.
Lexical entry: The complete specification of a word in the mental lexicon, including its phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic properties.
Prototype theory: A cognitive approach to categorization in which categories are organized around central, typical members rather than by necessary and sufficient features.
Frame semantics: An approach to lexical meaning that defines words in terms of structured scenes or frames of knowledge, as developed by Charles Fillmore.
Cognitive semantics: A theoretical approach to semantics that grounds meaning in embodied experience, usage, and conceptual structure rather than formal logic.
Semantic field: A group of words that are semantically related and belong to the same area of meaning, such as a field of color terms or kinship terms.
Collocation: A statistically or habitually frequent co-occurrence of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision" in English.
Semantic role: The relationship between an argument and the predicate it participates in, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Instrument, or Goal.
Agent: The semantic role of the entity that performs or causes an action, typically mapped to the subject in active transitive sentences.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes an action or is affected by it, typically mapped to the direct object.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes a mental or emotional experience, such as "fear" or "love."
Goal: The semantic role of the intended endpoint or destination of an action or motion.
Source: The semantic role of the point of origin or departure of a motion or transfer.
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that is moved, transferred, or described.
Instrument: The semantic role of the tool or means by which an action is performed.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics concerned with how context contributes to meaning, including speech acts, implicature, and discourse.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action, such as promising, requesting, warning, or declaring, in addition to (or instead of) conveying information.
Illocutionary force: The intended communicative function of an utterance, such as asserting, questioning, requesting, or commanding.
Perlocutionary effect: The effect that an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, alarming, or entertaining.
Locutionary act: The literal meaning of an utterance, considered as a sequence of words with a propositional content.
Direct speech act: An utterance in which the illocutionary force matches the grammatical form, such as a question that asks a question.
Indirect speech act: An utterance in which the illocutionary force differs from the grammatical form, such as "Can you pass the salt?" functioning as a request.
Performative: A sentence that performs the action it describes, such as "I promise to come" or "I hereby pronounce you husband and wife."
Presupposition: A background assumption that is taken for granted in an utterance and is not part of its explicit propositional content, such as the existence of the referent in "The king of France is bald."
Implicature: A pragmatic inference that is not part of the literal meaning of an utterance but is derived from context and conversational principles.
Cooperative principle: Grice's assumption that participants in a conversation generally aim to be cooperative and contribute to the shared goal of communication.
Maxim of quantity: A conversational principle that one should make one's contribution as informative as required, but not more informative than required.
Maxim of quality: A conversational principle that one should not say what one believes to be false or for which one lacks adequate evidence.
Maxim of relation: A conversational principle that one should be relevant to the current topic of conversation.
Maxim of manner: A conversational principle that one should be clear, orderly, brief, and avoid ambiguity.
Flouting: A deliberate and recognizable violation of a conversational maxim to generate an implicature, such as using understatement for sarcasm.
Context: The total set of circumstances surrounding an utterance, including linguistic, physical, social, and cognitive factors that influence interpretation.
Deixis: The use of linguistic expressions whose interpretation depends on the context of the utterance, such as "here," "now," "this," or "I."
Demonstrative: A word such as "this," "that," "these," or "those" that points to an entity in the context of the utterance.
Temporal deixis: The use of time expressions such as "now," "then," "yesterday," or "next week" that are anchored to the time of utterance.
Spatial deixis: The use of spatial expressions such as "here," "there," "this," or "that" that are anchored to the location of the speaker or hearer.
Personal deixis: The use of person expressions such as "I," "you," "we," or "they" that are anchored to the participants in the conversation.
Discourse: Language as it is used in extended communication beyond the sentence level, including conversation, narrative, and text.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes or signals relationships between utterances, such as "well," "anyway," "meanwhile," or "however."
Turn-taking: The system by which participants in a conversation alternately produce and receive utterances, governed by social and linguistic rules.
Adjacency pair: A two-part exchange in conversation in which the second part is typically conditioned by the first, such as question-answer, greeting-greeting, or request-response.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The integration of elements from one language into the grammatical structure of another, as opposed to switching between whole phrases.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social setting or communicative context, such as formal, informal, academic, or colloquial.
Jargon: The specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or community, often unfamiliar to outsiders.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be predicted from the literal meanings of its individual words, such as "kick the bucket" or "spill the beans."
Formulaic language: Pre-fabricated, multi-word expressions that are stored and retrieved as single units, such as "by and large" or "once upon a time."
Information structure: The organization of a discourse into given (old) and new information, influencing word order, focus, and topic marking.
Given-new structure: A principle of discourse organization in which given information typically precedes new information in a sentence or clause.
Salience: The degree to which a referent is accessible, prominent, or cognitively available to the hearer at a given point in discourse.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic framework by Sperber and Wilson that explains communication in terms of the search for optimal relevance between cognitive effort and cognitive effects.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, such as "John is married" entailing "John has a spouse."
Face: The public self-image or social identity that a person claims and expects others to recognize, as theorized by Goffman and Brown and Levinson.
Face-threatening act: An utterance or action that undermines the positive or negative face of the hearer, requiring politeness strategies.
Politeness: The set of linguistic and social strategies used to maintain or redress face in communication, including hedges, indirectness, and deference.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a direct or blunt one, often to avoid offense, such as "passed away" for "died."
Hedges: Linguistic devices that reduce the strength, certainty, or commitment of a statement, such as "sort of," "kind of," or "I think."
Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and identity.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group, differing in vocabulary, grammar, or pronunciation from other varieties.
Accent: The pronunciation of a language variety that distinguishes it from other varieties, without necessarily differing in grammar or vocabulary.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as a class, occupation, or community.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language, typically with no native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that evolved from a pidgin, serving as the native language of a speech community.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication among speakers of different native languages, such as English in international business.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two or more languages, either in a single speaker or in a speech community.
Multilingualism: The use or knowledge of more than two languages by an individual or a speech community.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be actively used.
Language revitalization: Efforts to reverse language decline and restore a language as a living, community language.
Language contact: The influence and interaction between two or more languages in a speech community, leading to borrowing, convergence, or new language varieties.
Borrowing: The adoption of words, morphemes, or structural elements from one language into another.
Loanword: A word that has been adopted from one language into another, such as "safari" from Swahili into English.
Calque: A word or phrase that is a loan translation, in which the meaning of a foreign expression is translated word-for-word, such as "skyscraper" from English into Spanish as "rascacielos."
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually adopts a different language and abandons its original one.
Diglossia: A stable sociolinguistic situation in which two language varieties (or languages) coexist in a community, each serving distinct social functions.
Style: A variety of language that a speaker selects for a particular communicative context, ranging from formal to informal.
Style-shifting: The alternation between different language varieties or registers by the same speaker in response to social or communicative demands.
Language attitude: The beliefs, feelings, and evaluations that individuals or groups hold about a language, dialect, or speech variety.
Prestige: The positive social value or status associated with a particular language variety, often the standard or dominant variety.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation or judgment associated with a particular language variety, often a non-standard dialect.
Language ideology: The beliefs and assumptions that speakers and communities hold about language and its relationship to society, identity, and power.
Language planning: The deliberate and systematic efforts to influence the structure, acquisition, or use of a language, such as standardization or policy decisions.
Language policy: The official rules, regulations, and decisions made by governments or institutions regarding the use of languages in public life.
Standardization: The process by which a particular variety of a language is selected, codified, and promoted as the standard form.
Orthography: The conventional system of writing a language, including its alphabet, spelling rules, and punctuation.
Alphabet: A writing system in which individual letters represent phonemes or a small set of phonemes, such as the Latin or Greek alphabets.
Writing system: A system of graphic symbols used to represent language, including alphabets, syllabaries, logosyllabaries, and logographies.
Script: The set of graphic symbols used in a particular writing system, such as the Arabic script, Devanagari script, or Cyrillic script.
Phonemic orthography: A writing system in which letters correspond to phonemes, as in many modern European languages.
Morphemic orthography: A writing system in which letters or character combinations correspond to morphemes rather than phonemes, as in English "kn-" or "-tion."
Logography: A writing system in which characters represent whole words or morphemes, as in Chinese characters.
Syllabary: A writing system in which characters represent syllables, as in Japanese hiragana and katakana.
Abjad: A writing system in which characters represent consonants, with vowels typically marked optionally, as in Arabic or Hebrew.
Abugida: A writing system in which each character represents a consonant-vowel combination, with diacritics or modifications to indicate different vowels, as in Devanagari.
Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the study of language change and the reconstruction of proto-languages.
Comparative method: A method in historical linguistics for identifying genetic relationships between languages by systematically comparing regular sound correspondences.
Reconstruction: The process of hypothesizing the features of an unattested proto-language based on the comparative evidence from its descendant languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a set of related languages are descended, such as Proto-Indo-European or Proto-Germanic.
Cognate: A word in two or more related languages that derives from a common ancestral word in the proto-language, such as English "father" and German "Vater."
Sound change: A systematic change in the phonological system of a language over time, such as the voicing of Latin initial consonants.
Sound law: A regular, exceptionless correspondence between sounds in related languages or between stages of a language, such as Grimm's Law.
Analogical change: A linguistic change driven by analogy, in which a form is changed to resemble other related forms, as in "oxen" influencing "mice" from "mice."
Leveling: A linguistic process in which irregular alternations are reduced or eliminated, such as the simplification of verb conjugation patterns.
Simplification: A general tendency in language change toward reducing complexity, such as the loss of case endings in English.
Diffusion: The spread of linguistic features, such as sounds or grammatical patterns, from one language or dialect to another through contact.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line separating areas where a particular linguistic feature is present from areas where it is absent.
Dialect chain: A chain of neighboring dialects in which each differs slightly from its neighbors, but the end members may be mutually unintelligible.
Sprachbund: A group of geographically neighboring languages that share features due to prolonged contact, regardless of genetic relationship.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common proto-language, such as the Indo-European or Sino-Tibetan families.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language, such as Basque or Japanese.
Language stock: A hypothesized grouping of language families that share a common ancestor beyond the reach of reliable reconstruction.
Substrate: A language that is replaced by a new language, leaving traces in the vocabulary, phonology, or grammar of the new language.
Superstrate: A language imposed on a community by a dominant group, influencing the vocabulary and structure of the substrate language.
Adstrate: A neighboring language that influences another through contact, without replacing it.
Semantic change: The process by which the meaning of a word shifts over time, such as broadening, narrowing, or pejoration.
Narrowing: A type of semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more specific, such as "meat" shifting from "food" to "animal flesh."
Broadening: A type of semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more general, such as "bird" from "young bird" to "any bird."
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more negative connotation over time, such as "silly" from "blessed" to "foolish."
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive connotation over time, such as "nice" from "foolish" to "pleasant."
Taboo: A social prohibition on the use of certain words, often related to death, sex, or bodily functions, leading to euphemistic replacement.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words, including their forms, meanings, and semantic changes.
Grimm's Law: A systematic sound change in Proto-Germanic that shifted Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops to voiceless fricatives and voiced stops to voiceless stops.
Verner's Law: A sound change in Proto-Germanic that voiced certain consonants derived by Grimm's Law when the preceding syllable was unstressed.
Great Vowel Shift: The systematic change in the pronunciation of long vowels in English between the 15th and 18th centuries.
Psycholinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the psychological and neurobiological processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition.
Language acquisition: The process by which children or adults learn and internalize a language, from first utterances to full grammatical competence.
Critical period: A hypothesized time window in life, typically before puberty, during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and completely.
Poverty of the stimulus: The observation that the linguistic input available to children is insufficient to account for the full grammatical knowledge they acquire, suggesting an innate endowment.
Babbling: The stage of early language development in which infants produce repeated syllables and consonant-vowel combinations, such as "ba-ba-ba" or "da-da-da."
One-word stage: A stage in child language development, typically around 12–18 months, in which children use single words to express complete meanings.
Two-word stage: A stage in child language development, typically around 18–24 months, in which children combine two words to form simple utterances, such as "want milk."
Telegraphic speech: The stage of child language development in which children produce short, content-word-only utterances, omitting function words, such as "Daddy go store."
Overgeneralization: A stage in child language development in which children apply a grammatical rule too broadly, such as saying "goed" instead of "went."
Overregularization: The application of a regular grammatical pattern to irregular forms, such as "mouses" for "mice" or "runned" for "ran."
Language attrition: The loss or weakening of language knowledge and ability, typically occurring in bilingual or multilingual individuals who use one language less frequently.
Language processing: The set of cognitive operations involved in understanding or producing language, including parsing, lexical access, and integration.
Word recognition: The process of identifying and accessing the meaning of a written or spoken word in the mental lexicon.
Sentence processing: The cognitive process of parsing and interpreting the structure and meaning of a sentence as it is heard or read.
Garden path: A sentence structure that initially leads the parser down an incorrect interpretation, requiring reanalysis, such as "The horse raced past the barn fell."
Parsing: The process of assigning a syntactic structure to a sentence, determining how words are grouped into phrases and clauses.
Lexical access: The retrieval of a word's representation from the mental lexicon, including its phonological, morphological, and semantic information.
Priming: A phenomenon in which exposure to a stimulus (a word or concept) facilitates the processing of a related stimulus, such as "doctor" priming "nurse."
Mental lexicon: The hypothesized mental store of words and their associated information, including form, meaning, and grammatical properties.
Lexical-semantic network: A theoretical model of the mental lexicon in which words are represented as nodes connected by various semantic relations such as synonymy, hyponymy, and co-occurrence.
Phonological loop: A component of working memory that holds and rehearses auditory and verbal information, as proposed in Baddeley's model of working memory.
Working memory: A cognitive system for temporarily holding and manipulating information, essential for language comprehension and production.
Speech production: The process of planning, formulating, and executing the articulatory gestures needed to produce spoken language.
Speech perception: The process of receiving, analyzing, and interpreting the acoustic signal of spoken language to recover phonological, lexical, and prosodic information.
Phonological awareness: The ability to consciously perceive, analyze, and manipulate the sound structure of spoken language, a key predictor of reading ability.
Dyslexia: A learning disability characterized by difficulty in reading and decoding written language, often associated with phonological processing deficits.
Agrammatism: A language impairment, typically associated with damage to Broca's area, characterized by the omission or error of grammatical function words and difficulty producing complex structures.
Wernicke's aphasia: A language impairment associated with damage to Wernicke's area, characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech and impaired comprehension.
Broca's aphasia: A language impairment associated with damage to Broca's area, characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
Anomia: A language impairment characterized by difficulty in word retrieval or naming, often seen in various types of aphasia and dementia.
Conduction aphasia: A language impairment characterized by impaired repetition and phonological errors in speech production, with relatively preserved comprehension.
Global aphasia: A severe language impairment affecting both production and comprehension, typically resulting from extensive damage to the left hemisphere.
Transcortical aphasia: A language impairment in which repetition is relatively preserved but production and/or comprehension is impaired, depending on the subtype.
Apraxia: A motor planning disorder that can affect speech, characterized by difficulty in sequencing the articulatory movements needed to produce sounds.
Language dominance: The tendency for one language to be preferred or more accessible than another in a bilingual individual, influenced by frequency of use, context, and individual factors.
Lateralization: The specialization of one cerebral hemisphere for particular functions, with language typically dominant in the left hemisphere for most right-handed individuals.
Cognitive linguistics: A theoretical framework that emphasizes the role of general cognitive processes, embodied experience, and usage in shaping linguistic structure and meaning.
Conceptual metaphor: A mapping from a more concrete source domain to a more abstract target domain that structures thought and language, such as "time is money."
Image schema: A basic, recurring pattern of spatial or experiential experience, such as container, path, force, or balance, that structures abstract reasoning and language.
Force dynamics: A cognitive framework describing the relationships between agents and patients in terms of forces, resistance, and causation, as analyzed in cognitive semantics.
Container schema: A basic image schema in which entities are conceptualized as being inside or outside bounded regions, underpinning prepositions like "in," "out," and "through."
Source-path-goal: A basic image schema describing motion events in terms of a starting point, a path of movement, and an endpoint, underlying spatial language.
Categorization: The cognitive process of grouping entities into categories based on shared properties, relevant to the organization of lexical and semantic knowledge.
Basic level: The level of categorization at which most concrete nouns are most informative and cognitively salient, such as "dog" rather than "animal" or "poodle."
Superordinate: A higher-level category in a hierarchical classification, such as "animal" above "dog."
Subordinate: A lower-level category in a hierarchical classification, such as "poodle" below "dog."
Family resemblance: A Wittgensteinian concept in which category membership is determined by overlapping networks of shared features rather than a single set of necessary and sufficient conditions.
Graded category: A category whose membership is not all-or-nothing but varies along a continuum, with central (prototypical) members and peripheral members.
Embodied cognition: The hypothesis that cognitive processes, including language, are fundamentally shaped by the body's interactions with the physical environment.
Relevance: The balance between cognitive effects and processing effort that, according to Relevance Theory, guides human communication and inference.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, structured collections of written or spoken texts (corpora) to identify patterns, frequencies, and collocations.
Corpus: A large, organized collection of texts (written or transcribed spoken) used as a data source for linguistic analysis.
Frequency: The number of times a particular word, form, or pattern occurs in a corpus or text.
N-gram: A sequence of n consecutive words, syllables, or characters in a text, used in corpus and computational linguistics, such as a bigram (2-word) or trigram (3-word).
KWIC: Key Word In Context, a method of displaying corpus search results in which the target word is centered in a line of surrounding context.
Balanced corpus: A corpus designed to represent the major genres, registers, and text types of a language in proportionally representative amounts.
Representative corpus: A corpus that aims to be a fair and accurate representation of the language it purports to describe, with careful sampling procedures.
Collocate: A word that frequently occurs in the context of a particular target word, reflecting habitual or expected co-occurrence.
Lexicography: The practice of compiling dictionaries, including the selection, arrangement, and definition of lexical entries.
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word to which all its inflected forms are referred, such as "run" being the lemma for "runs," "ran," and "running."
Headword: The main word or phrase that serves as the entry point for a definition in a dictionary.
Morphosyntax: The interface between morphology and syntax, studying how morphological structure constrains syntactic processes and vice versa.
Morphological case: The case marking expressed by affixes or other morphological means on a noun phrase, as opposed to syntactic case assigned by structural position.
Syntactic case: Case that is assigned by the syntactic structure of the clause rather than by morphological marking, such as structural accusative or dative.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their predominant morphological strategies, such as isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Isolating language: A language in which words are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed through word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Agglutinative language: A language in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish or Finnish.
Fusional language: A language in which a single morpheme can express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin, Arabic, or Russian.
Polysynthetic language: A language in which a single word can encode what would be an entire sentence in an analytical language, as in many Indigenous languages of the Americas.
Minimalist Program: The current theoretical framework in generative syntax, initiated by Noam Chomsky in 1995, which seeks to characterize the most economical computational system for human language.
Government and Binding: A framework in generative syntax (1981) that replaced earlier transformational grammar, organizing syntactic theory around principles and parameters.
Feature checking: The process in the Minimalist Program in which a head checks its uninterpretable features against the interpretable features of a goal, triggering movement or deletion.
Label: The category assigned to a merged set in the Minimalist Program, which is necessary for the construction to be interpretable at the interfaces.
V-to-I movement: The movement of a finite verb from the verb position to the inflectional position, observed in languages like French or Italian.

Topic-comment structure: A discourse structure in which the topic (what the utterance is about) precedes the comment (what is said about the topic), common in many languages.
Discourse particle: A small word or morpheme that does not contribute propositional content but signals discourse functions such as emphasis, hesitation, or topic shift, such as "well," "hmm," or "yeah."
Mitigation: A politeness strategy that softens the force of a face-threatening act, such as using "perhaps" instead of "you must" or "a bit" instead of "very."
Softener: A linguistic device that reduces the directness or intensity of an utterance, such as "just," "only," or "sort of."
World language: A language that is spoken as a first or second language by communities across many countries, such as English, Spanish, or Mandarin.
Global language: A language that is used as a lingua franca in international communication, trade, and diplomacy, regardless of the number of native speakers.
Linguistic imperialism: The dominance of one language (often English) over others in global communication, education, and media, marginalizing local languages.

Phonemic principle: The principle in writing system design that each phoneme is represented by a unique and consistent grapheme or grapheme sequence.
Morphology: The branch of linguistics concerned with the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.

Generative linguistics: A theoretical tradition, initiated by Chomsky, that seeks to capture the infinite set of grammatical sentences a speaker can produce using a finite set of rules or principles.
Descriptive linguistics: The objective, data-driven description of how a language is actually used by its speakers, as opposed to prescriptive rules about how it "should" be used.
Prescriptive linguistics: The normative approach to language that prescribes rules about correct usage, often associated with grammar books and style guides.
Theoretical linguistics: The branch of linguistics concerned with developing formal models and theories of the structure and function of human language.
Applied linguistics: The use of linguistic theory and findings to address practical problems in education, translation, language policy, forensic science, and technology.
