Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning; for example, /p/ and /b/ in English distinguish "pat" from "bat."
Allophone: A context-dependent variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phone: Any distinct speech sound regardless of whether it carries meaning in a particular language.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit that carries meaning, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Morph: The physical or realizable form of a morpheme, such as the sound or spelling sequence that appears in a word.
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme, such as the plural morpheme appearing as /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/ in English.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permissible in a given language.
Syllable: A unit of oral organization consisting of a single peak of articulatory effort, typically built around a vowel.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster at the beginning of a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable from the vowel nucleus through any following coda consonants.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, usually a vowel.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster at the end of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Aspiration: A burst of air accompanying the release of a stop consonant, as in the [pʰ] of English "pat."
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound, distinguishing pairs like /s/ and /z/.
Place of articulation: The anatomical location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed or modified, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that spans more than one segment, including stress, tone, and intonation.
Tone: The use of pitch to distinguish lexical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese, where "ma" in different tones means different words.
Stress: The relative prominence given to a syllable within a word or phrase, often marked by greater loudness, pitch, or duration.
Intonation: The rise and fall of pitch across a phrase or sentence, conveying grammatical and pragmatic information.
Prosody: The aspects of speech beyond individual segments, including rhythm, stress, tone, and intonation.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant narrowing of airflow.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a constriction or closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to escape through the nose, as in /m/, /n/, and /ŋ/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow channel that causes turbulent airflow, as in /s/, /f/, or /ʃ/.
Stop: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a release of air, as in /p/, /t/, and /k/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with air flowing around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant associated with the English letter "r," such as the alveolar trill or tap found in various languages.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal folds at the glottis, as in the "uh-oh" of English or the /ʔ/ in many Pacific languages.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word that was not present in the original form, as in "quarto" for "four."
Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable, as in "gonna" for "going to" or "hotel" from French "hôtel."
Assimilation: A sound change in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in "input" becoming [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: A sound change in which sounds become less like neighboring sounds to avoid repetition.
Metathesis: The transposition of two adjacent sounds, as in "ask" from Old English "æcsian."
Metaphony: A change in one vowel triggered by the presence of another vowel elsewhere in the word.
Phonemic: Relating to the system of phonemes in a language; a distinction is phonemic if it can distinguish meaning.
Distinctive feature: A binary property of a phoneme that can distinguish it from other phonemes, such as [+nasal] or [-voiced].
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the sounds are distinct phonemes.
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two phonetic variants occur in mutually exclusive environments and are allophones of the same phoneme.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more sounds can be substituted for each other in the same environment without changing meaning.
Neutralization: A phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is lost in a particular environment.
Archiphoneme: A theoretical abstract unit used when two or more phonemes are neutralized in a given environment.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to form a new word, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix that is attached to the beginning of a word, such as "un-" in "undo."
Suffix: An affix that is attached to the end of a word, such as "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within a root, as in the Malagasy prefix-infix "i-...aka" (e.g., "manaka" from "haka").
Circumfix: An affix consisting of two parts that surround a stem, such as German "ge-...-t" in "gelaufen."
Root: The core, unanalyzable morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may include derivational morphology.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of words related by inflection, such as the lexeme RUN encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, such as the present-tense conjugation of a verb.
Agglutination: A morphological process in which each morpheme carries a single grammatical meaning and is clearly segmented, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Inflectional morphology: The process of modifying a word to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, or case without changing its core meaning.
Derivational morphology: The process of creating new words by adding affixes or altering a base, often changing the word's part of speech or meaning.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more independent morphemes are combined to create a new word, such as "blackboard."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes grammatical category without adding an affix, such as "to email" from "email."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened, such as "phone" from "telephone" or "gym" from "gymnasium."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words to create a new word, such as "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Portmanteau: A word formed by merging two words that overlap in sound or meaning, such as "smog" from "smoke" and "fog."
Suppletion: Irregular alternation between morphologically related forms that share no phonological resemblance, such as "go" and "went."
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonological content, such as the English plural in "sheep" or the past tense in "cut."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a free word and must be attached to other morphemes, such as "-un" in "unhappy."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word, such as "happy" or "run."
Bound root: A root morpheme that cannot occur as a free word, such as "-mit" in "admit" or "submit."
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically behaves like a separate word, such as the English possessive "'s."
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the beginning of a host word, such as the English "to" in "I'm going to."
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the end of a host word, such as the English possessive "'s" or the clitic "n't" in "don't."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical meaning, as in "tic-tac" or Indonesian "kita-kita."
Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix, such as "burgle" formed from "burglary."
Phrase: A grammatical unit consisting of one or more words headed by a particular part of speech, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: A grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: The largest grammatical unit that can stand alone as a complete expression, typically containing at least one clause.
Constituency: The property of a group of words forming a grammatical unit that functions as a single element within a larger structure.
Head: The central word of a phrase that determines its grammatical category, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: A phrase or word required by a head to complete its grammatical function, such as the noun phrase complement of a preposition.
Adjunct: An optional phrase that modifies a head or clause, adding descriptive or circumstantial information.
Specifier: A phrase or word that appears at the beginning of a phrase, modifying or specifying its content, such as the determiner in a noun phrase.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure proposing that all phrases have a uniform hierarchical structure with a head, a complement, and an optional specifier.
C-command: A syntactic relationship in which a node dominates a sister node that in turn dominates another node, relevant to binding theory.
Binding: The syntactic and semantic relationship between a pronoun, anaphor, or variable and its antecedent.
Antecedent: The noun phrase that a pronoun or anaphor refers to.
Anaphor: A linguistic element that must be bound to an antecedent, such as a reflexive pronoun like "himself."
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Theme.
Argument: A noun phrase that is required by a verb to complete its meaning, typically the subject or object.
Predicate: The part of a clause that provides information about the subject, typically the verb phrase.
Transitive: A verb that requires a direct object, such as "eat" in "She eats an apple."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, such as "sleep" in "She sleeps."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object, such as "give" in "She gave him a book."
Ergative: A grammatical case marking the subject of an intransitive verb, part of an ergative-absolutive alignment system.
Absolutive: A grammatical case marking the object of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb in an ergative-absolutive system.
Nominative: A grammatical case typically marking the subject of a transitive verb in a nominative-accusative alignment system.
Accusative: A grammatical case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Genitive: A grammatical case indicating possession, origin, or association, as in "the man's book."
Dative: A grammatical case marking the indirect object or the goal of an action, as in "I gave it to her."
Instrumental: A grammatical case indicating the means or tool by which an action is performed, as in "with a hammer."
Vocative: A grammatical case used when directly addressing someone, as in "O Mary, please come."
Locative: A grammatical case indicating the location where an event takes place.
Ablative: A grammatical case indicating separation, source, or origin, such as "from" in "from the table."
Allative: A grammatical case indicating the goal or destination toward which an action is directed.
Topic: The entity about which a sentence or discourse is making an assertion; the "aboutness" of the utterance.
Focus: The element of a sentence or discourse that is being highlighted or contrasted with alternatives.
Cleft sentence: A construction that uses a clause to emphasize a particular constituent, such as "It was John who did it."
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction in which a wh-clause functions as the subject, such as "What I want is a new car."
Extraposition: A syntactic movement in which a constituent is moved to a position later than its canonical position, such as "It is likely that she will come."
Wh-movement: The syntactic operation in which a wh-word moves to the front of a clause to form a question or relative clause.
Topicalization: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is moved to the front of a sentence to establish it as the topic.
Raising: A syntactic process in which the subject of an embedded clause is promoted to become the subject of the matrix clause, as in "John seems to be tired."
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject or object of a non-finite clause is determined by an element in the main clause, as in "John tried to leave."
Passivization: A syntactic transformation in which the object of an active sentence becomes the subject of a passive sentence.
Nominalization: A word-formation process in which a verb or clause is converted into a noun, such as "decision" from "decide."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun, as in "the book that I read."
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on a main clause for its meaning.
Main clause: An independent clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence and may contain subordinate clauses.
Recursion: The property of syntax allowing a constituent to be embedded within another constituent of the same type, enabling infinite sentence complexity.
Coordinate structure: A construction in which two or more syntactically parallel elements are joined by a coordinator such as "and" or "but."
Trace: The theoretical residue left behind when a constituent moves to a new position in a syntactic derivation.
Ellipsis: The omission of a word or phrase that is understood from context, such as in "She likes coffee, and I like ___ too."
Pro-drop: A grammatical property of a language in which subject pronouns can be omitted when recoverable from context, as in Spanish or Italian.
Subject: The noun phrase that typically agrees with the verb and performs or experiences the action of the predicate.
Object: The noun phrase that receives the action of the verb, either as a direct or indirect object.
Oblique: A noun phrase marked by a preposition or case marking other than nominative or accusative, as in "with the dog."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, such as "the," "a," or "this."
Article: A type of determiner that marks definiteness ("the") or indefiniteness ("a," "an") in a noun phrase.
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies the quantity or extent of reference, such as "every," "some," or "three."
Negation: A grammatical element that reverses the truth value of a proposition, such as "not" in English.
Auxiliary verb: A verb that supports a main verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice, such as "will" or "have."
Copula: A verb that links the subject to a predicate complement, such as "is" in "She is a teacher."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking, such as past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, or progressive.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Voice: A grammatical category that reflects the relationship between the verb's arguments, such as active, passive, or middle.
Agreement: The grammatical requirement that certain elements in a sentence match in features such as number, gender, or person.
Concord: The grammatical agreement between a verb and its subject or between other elements in a sentence.
Case: A grammatical category marking the syntactic role of a noun phrase in a clause, such as nominative, accusative, or dative.
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular from plural (and sometimes dual, trial, or augmentative) forms.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing first, second, and third person, sometimes further divided into singular, dual, and plural.
Gender: A grammatical classification of nouns into categories such as masculine, feminine, and neuter, or animate and inanimate.
Animacy: A semantic scale or grammatical category distinguishing living or sentient beings from non-living things, often affecting case marking or agreement.
Definiteness: A property of noun phrases indicating whether the referent is unique or identifiable to the listener.
Specificity: A property of noun phrases indicating whether the speaker has a particular referent in mind, regardless of definiteness.
Sememe: The smallest unit of meaning in a language, analogous to a phoneme in the phonological system.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a lexical item.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it denotes in the world.
Denotation: The set of entities to which a word or phrase truly applies in a given context.
Connotation: The associative or emotional meaning attached to a word beyond its literal denotation.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or expression has multiple related senses.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more distinct words have identical forms but unrelated meanings, as in "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Homograph: A word that is spelled identically to another word but has a different pronunciation or meaning, such as "lead" (verb) and "lead" (metal).
Homophone: A word that sounds identical to another word but has a different spelling and meaning, such as "flower" and "flour."
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or very similar meanings, such as "begin" and "commence."
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is a more specific instance of a broader term, such as "sparrow" as a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernym: A word whose meaning encompasses the meanings of more specific terms, such as "bird" as a hypernym of "sparrow."
Meronym: A word that denotes a part of a whole, such as "wheel" as a meronym of "car."
Holonym: A word that denotes a whole of which other words are parts, such as "car" as a holonym of "wheel."
Prototype: The most central or typical member of a lexical category, around which other members are organized by degree of similarity.
Frame semantics: An approach to lexical semantics in which word meanings are understood in terms of structured situations or frames that organize related concepts.
Compositional semantics: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules used to combine them.
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines the meaning of a sentence in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
Model-theoretic semantics: A formal approach to semantics that interprets linguistic expressions relative to mathematical structures called models.
Intension: The set of possible worlds or circumstances in which an expression is true or applies, as opposed to its extension.
Extension: The set of actual entities in the world to which a word or phrase refers.
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be taken for granted for an utterance to be meaningful, such as the assumption that a unique king of France exists in "The king of France is bald."
Implicature: A meaning that is not explicitly stated but is inferred by the listener based on the context and conversational principles.
Entailment: A logical relationship in which the truth of one sentence guarantees the truth of another, as in "She is a widow" entails "She was married."
Scope: The range of application of an operator such as a quantifier or negation within a sentence.
Coreference: The relationship between two or more expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Coindexation: The formal marking in a derivation of two elements that refer to the same entity, often indicated by identical indices.
Anaphora: A linguistic element that refers back to a previously mentioned entity, such as a pronoun referring to a prior noun phrase.
Cataphora: A linguistic element that refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse, such as "He" at the beginning of a sentence referring to the subject.
Deixis: The use of linguistic expressions that depend on the context of utterance for their interpretation, such as "here," "now," "I," and "this."
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose referent is determined by the context of utterance, such as "I," "here," or "now."
Demonstrative: A word that points to a specific entity in the discourse or physical context, such as "this," "that," "these," or "those."
Pragmatics: The study of how context, speaker intention, and shared knowledge contribute to the interpretation of linguistic expressions.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action beyond merely conveying information, such as promising, commanding, or apologizing.
Locution: The literal, propositional content of an utterance, independent of its illocutionary force.
Illocution: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as requesting, warning, or declaring.
Perlocution: The effect an utterance has on the listener, such as persuading, frightening, or amusing.
Performative: An utterance that performs the action it describes by being uttered, such as "I now pronounce you husband and wife."
Directive: A type of speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something, such as a command, request, or suggestion.
Commissive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to a future action, such as a promise or offer.
Expressive: A type of speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state, such as thanking, apologizing, or congratulating.
Declarative: A type of speech act that changes the state of the world by virtue of being uttered, such as "I resign" or "I name this ship."
Assertive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to the truth of a proposition, such as stating, claiming, or reporting.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred by the listener through the assumption that the speaker is following Grice's maxims of cooperative communication.
Conventional implicature: A meaning that is directly encoded in the lexical or grammatical form of an expression, independent of context.
Scalar implicature: An implicature arising from the assumption that the speaker would have used a stronger term on a semantic scale if it were true, as in "Some of the students passed" implying "Not all passed."
Horn implicature: A conventional implicature associated with a specific word or construction, such as "even" in "Even John passed" implying that John is the least likely candidate.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic framework, developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson, proposing that communication is guided by the principle of maximizing relevance.
Cooperative principle: Grice's generalization that participants in a conversation assume each other is contributing relevantly and cooperatively to the exchange.
Maxim of quality: Grice's maxim that one should not say what one believes to be false or lack evidence for.
Maxim of quantity: Grice's maxim that one should provide as much information as is needed and no more.
Maxim of relation: Grice's maxim that one should be relevant and keep contributions pertinent to the topic.
Maxim of manner: Grice's maxim that one should be clear, orderly, brief, and avoid ambiguity.
Indirect speech act: An utterance that performs a speech act other than the one directly expressed, such as "Can you pass the salt?" functioning as a request rather than a question.
Politeness theory: A framework, developed by Brown and Levinson, that explains linguistic behavior in terms of the management of face in social interactions.
Face: The positive social self-image that a person claims and that others are expected to acknowledge in social interaction.
Face-threatening act: A speech act that poses a threat to the listener's or speaker's face, requiring mitigation or redress.
Positive face: The desire to be approved of, liked, and included by others, as part of Brown and Levinson's politeness theory.
Negative face: The desire to have one's actions unimpeded and freedom from imposition, as part of Brown and Levinson's politeness theory.
Mitigation: The use of linguistic strategies to soften the impact of a face-threatening act, such as hedging or using indirect forms.
Hedging: The use of linguistic expressions that reduce the strength or commitment of an assertion, such as "perhaps," "it seems," or "I think."
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including how social factors influence language use and variation.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular geographic region or social group, differing in pronunciation, vocabulary, or grammar.
Language variety: Any identifiable form of a language distinguished by features such as pronunciation, vocabulary, or grammar.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language, typically with no native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that emerges from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Mixed language: A language that draws substantial structural elements from two or more parent languages, such as Media Lengua (Quechua-Spanish).
Jargon: A specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession or group, such as legal or medical jargon.
Slang: Informal, often trendy vocabulary used within a particular social group, frequently marked by a sense of in-group identity.
Argot: A specialized set of words and expressions used by a particular group to conceal meaning from outsiders, such as the argot of criminals.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker, encompassing their particular pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammatical preferences.
Standard language: The variety of a language that is codified in dictionaries, grammar books, and used in formal education and media.
Lingua franca: A language adopted as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages, either to varying degrees of proficiency or simultaneously.
Multilingualism: The use of three or more languages by an individual or within a community.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The mixing of elements from two or more languages within a single sentence or clause.
Language contact: The phenomenon of interaction between speakers of different languages, leading to mutual influence and borrowing.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word, morpheme, or grammatical structure from one language into another.
Interference: The influence of one language on another in the speech of a bilingual or multilingual speaker, often resulting in errors.
Substratum: The influence of a previously spoken or minority language on a dominant language, often visible in phonology or vocabulary.
Superstratum: The influence of a politically or socially dominant language on a subordinate language, as in French influence on English after 1066.
Adstratum: The influence between two languages of roughly equal prestige or power.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be a living, evolving system.
Language extinction: The final state in which a language has no remaining native speakers and is no longer used in any community.
Language endangerment: The condition of a language that is at risk of losing its native speakers, often due to social, economic, or political pressures.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers of a language and to restore its use in education, media, and daily life.
Language planning: The deliberate efforts by individuals, groups, or governments to influence the development, spread, or status of a language.
Language policy: The set of regulations, decisions, and practices by which a language is managed in a political or institutional context.
Language ideology: The beliefs and attitudes that speakers hold about language varieties, their legitimacy, and their social value.
Linguistic landscape: The visibility and prominence of language elements in the physical environment, such as signs, banners, and public displays.
Diglossia: A stable sociolinguistic situation in which two distinct varieties of a language are used for different social functions, such as high and low registers.
Sociolect: A language variety associated with a particular social group, distinguished by features reflecting social class, profession, or subculture.
Dialectology: The study of the geographic and social distribution of linguistic variation within a language.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary along which a particular linguistic feature changes, mapping a dialectal division.
Dialect continuum: A range of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but the most distant varieties are not.
Language drift: The gradual, incremental change in a language variety over time within a community, as opposed to sudden contact-driven change.
Shift: A sociolinguistic process in which a community abandons one language or variety in favor of another.
Maintenance: The sociolinguistic process in which a community continues to use and transmit a language or variety to future generations.
Language attrition: The gradual loss of language proficiency in an individual who no longer uses the language regularly.
Heritage language: A language spoken in a domestic setting by individuals whose first language is the dominant language of the surrounding society.
Mother tongue: The first language acquired by a speaker in early childhood, also called a native language.
First language: The language a person acquires first, typically in early childhood, used as a primary means of communication.
Second language: A language acquired after the first language, either naturally or through formal instruction.
Accent: The particular way a speaker pronounces sounds, often reflecting regional origin or social background.
Stigmatization: The social devaluation of a particular language variety, accent, or speech pattern, often associated with marginalized groups.
Prestige: The social value or desirability associated with a particular language variety or accent.
Dominant language: The language that holds the greatest social, economic, and political power in a given context.
Minority language: A language spoken by a smaller group within a larger community where a dominant language prevails.
Endonym: The name that the speakers of a language use for their own language, such as "English" for English.
Exonym: The name that an outside group uses for a language, such as "English" as used by non-speakers to refer to the language.
Historical linguistics: The study of how languages change over time and the relationships among related languages.
Comparative method: A systematic approach to reconstructing proto-languages by comparing regular sound correspondences across related languages.
Sound law: A regular, systematic change in a sound system, such as a shift in consonant place or manner of articulation.
Grimm's Law: A sound law describing the shift of Proto-Indo-European stops to Germanic consonants, such as /p/ to /f/.
Verner's Law: A sound law that explains exceptions to Grimm's Law, where voiceless fricatives become voiced in certain phonological environments.
Chain shift: A series of interlocking sound changes in which each sound shifts to the position vacated by the previous one, as in the Great Vowel Shift.
Great Vowel Shift: The major change in English long vowel pronunciation during the 15th to 18th centuries that altered the spelling-pronunciation relationship.
Sound change: Any systematic or idiosyncratic alteration in the phonetic or phonological realization of a language over time.
Regular sound change: A phonological change that applies uniformly across the lexicon in a given environment, as opposed to an irregular or analogical change.
Analogical change: A grammatical or phonological change in which a form is altered to match a more common or predictable pattern, such as "oxen" influencing "ox."
Morphological leveling: A process in which irregular forms are replaced by regular forms to reduce paradigmatic complexity, such as "goed" replacing "went" in some dialects.
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word or expression over time, such as "mouse" originally meaning a small animal and later a computer device.
Broadening: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more general, as in "holiday" shifting from a religious feast day to any day off.
Narrowing: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific, as in "meat" shifting from "food" to "animal flesh."
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive connotation, as in "nice" shifting from "foolish" to "pleasant."
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more negative connotation, as in "silly" shifting from "happy" to "foolish."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase is replaced by another with which it is closely associated, such as "the White House said" for "the President said."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another based on a perceived similarity, such as "time is money."
Synecdoche: A figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole or vice versa, such as "all hands on deck."
Reanalysis: A change in the grammatical parsing or interpretation of a linguistic form, such as the reanalysis of "a stone bridge" leading to the indefinite article "a."
Grammaticalization: The diachronic process by which lexical items or phrases develop into grammatical markers, such as "going to" becoming "gonna."
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or construction becomes a fixed lexical item, such as "by and large" becoming a set expression.
Functionalization: The process by which a word acquires a new grammatical or discourse function, such as "well" becoming a discourse marker.
Relexification: The replacement of the lexical content of a language with words from another language while retaining the grammatical structure.
Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestral proto-language, such as the Indo-European family.
Proto-language: A hypothetical reconstructed ancestor language from which a family of related languages is believed to have descended.
Reconstructed form: A hypothesized word form from a proto-language, typically marked with an asterisk, such as *bʰérs- for 'bear, carry.'
Cognate: A word in one language that is descended from the same ancestral word as a word in another language, such as English "father" and Latin "pater."
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words, including their form and meaning over time.
Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that phonetically imitate or suggest the sound they represent, such as "buzz," "crash," or "hiss."
Loan translation: The translation of a foreign word or phrase into the native language's own morphemes, such as "superman" from Latin "super" and "man."
Calque: A loan translation in which the structure of a foreign expression is replicated using native words, such as "skyscraper" from French "gratte-ciel."
Doublet: Two words in the same language that derive from the same source but through different routes, such as "court" and "cohort" from Latin "cohors."
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression that has recently entered the lexicon.
Obsolescence: The gradual process by which a word or expression falls out of common use and becomes archaic.
Archaism: A word or expression that was once common but is now out of ordinary use, understood only in historical or literary contexts.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological factors that enable humans to acquire, use, and understand language.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn to understand and produce a language, whether as a first or second language.
Critical period: The hypothesized window of time in early development during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and easily.
Sensitive period: A period of heightened plasticity during which a particular skill, such as language acquisition, is most readily developed.
Universal Grammar: The theoretical innate linguistic knowledge proposed by Chomsky that underlies all human languages and guides first language acquisition.
Nativism: The theoretical position that language acquisition is guided by innate, language-specific biological endowments.
Connectionism: A computational and cognitive model of language that emphasizes learning through statistical patterns and neural activation rather than explicit rules.
Usage-based approach: A theoretical framework in which linguistic knowledge is derived from the learner's experience with specific language instances and their entrenchment.
Competence: The underlying linguistic knowledge that a speaker possesses, as distinguished from actual language use.
Performance: The actual production and comprehension of language in real-time, which may deviate from underlying competence.
Interlanguage: The evolving linguistic system that a second language learner develops between their first and second language.
Fossilization: The stabilization of incorrect linguistic forms in a second language learner's interlanguage, resisting further correction.
Transfer: The influence of a learner's first language on their acquisition of a second language, either facilitating or interfering.
Positive transfer: The beneficial influence of a first language on second language acquisition when the two languages share features.
Negative transfer: The detrimental influence of a first language on second language acquisition when the two languages differ.
Phonological awareness: The metalinguistic ability to perceive, identify, and manipulate the sound structure of spoken language.
Morphological awareness: The metalinguistic ability to recognize and manipulate the morphemic structure of words.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word from the mental lexicon for comprehension or production.
Word recognition: The process of identifying a word in written or spoken form and accessing its meaning.
Fluency: The smooth, effortless, and automatic production or comprehension of language, reflecting well-practiced processing.
Working memory: The cognitive system that temporarily holds and manipulates information during language processing tasks.
Automaticity: The ability to perform a language task with minimal conscious effort, indicating well-practiced and efficient processing.
Chunking: The process of grouping individual linguistic elements into larger, pre-compiled units to reduce processing load.
Priming: A cognitive phenomenon in which exposure to one stimulus facilitates the processing of a related stimulus, such as a related word.
Lexical decision: A psycholinguistic task in which participants determine whether a string of letters is a real word or a nonword.
Slip: An unintentional error in speech production in which a planned element is substituted, omitted, or displaced.
Block: A momentary inability to retrieve a specific word during speech production, often accompanied by a pause or filler.
False start: An initial beginning of an utterance that is abandoned and corrected before continuing.
Disfluency: A break or interruption in the smooth flow of speech, including pauses, fillers, repetitions, and false starts.
Pause: A break in the flow of speech, which may be filled with silence, a filler, or a hesitation marker.
Filler: A word or sound used to hold a turn in conversation while the speaker plans the next utterance, such as "um" or "uh."
Discourse: Language use that extends beyond the sentence level, encompassing the organization of meaning across utterances, texts, or conversations.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse, signals shifts in topic, or manages conversational flow, such as "well," "anyway," or "you know."
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that link elements within a text, such as reference, substitution, conjunction, and lexical ties.
Coherence: The logical and semantic unity of a discourse, in which ideas are connected in a way that makes the text understandable as a whole.
Anaphoric cohesion: A cohesive device in which a later element refers back to an earlier one, such as a pronoun referring to a prior noun phrase.
Exophoric cohesion: A cohesive device in which a linguistic element refers to something outside the text, such as a demonstrative pointing to a physical object.
Substitution: A cohesive device in which a word is replaced by a pronoun, adverb, or other substitute to avoid repetition.
Thematic progression: The pattern by which the theme of one sentence becomes the rheme of the next, or how topics are developed across a discourse.
Rheme: The part of a sentence that provides new information about the theme, as opposed to the topic.
Given information: Information that is already established in the discourse or shared between speaker and listener.
New information: Information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse and is unknown to the listener.
Information structure: The organization of a sentence or discourse into given and new information, typically reflected in word order, stress, and topic-focus structure.
Conversation analysis: A sociolinguistic approach to the study of naturally occurring spoken interaction, focusing on the structure and organization of turns, sequences, and repairs.
Turn-taking: The system by which speakers in a conversation manage the allocation of speaking rights, organizing who speaks next.
Repair: The process by which speakers identify and correct errors, misunderstandings, or problems in the course of a conversation.
Adjacency pair: A two-part sequence of turns in conversation in which the first part sets up an expectation for a specific type of second part, such as question-answer or greeting-greeting.
Transition relevance: The point in a turn where the current speaker can yield the floor to another participant, creating an opportunity for turn transition.
Interruption: An overlap in which one speaker begins speaking before the current speaker has completed their turn, potentially disrupting the flow.
Overlap: A period in which two speakers are simultaneously producing speech, which can be cooperative or competitive.
Backchannel: A brief vocal or non-vocal response that signals the listener's continued attention and encouragement, such as "mm-hmm" or "I see."
Genre: A category of discourse defined by its conventional purpose, structure, and linguistic features, such as a news report, recipe, or legal contract.
Register: A variety of language characterized by its use in a particular communicative situation or social context, distinguished by vocabulary, syntax, and formality.
Register theory: The study of how language varies systematically across different communicative situations and their associated parameters.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, structured collections of real-world text and speech data, known as corpora.
Corpus: A large, organized collection of texts or recordings used for linguistic research, often searchable with specialized software.
Collocation: The statistically significant co-occurrence of words in a language, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Collocate: A word that habitually occurs in the vicinity of another word, forming a characteristic association.
N-gram: A sequence of n adjacent words or tokens in a corpus, used for frequency analysis and pattern recognition.
Frequency: The number of times a particular linguistic form or pattern occurs within a given corpus or dataset.
Concordance: A display of all occurrences of a particular word or pattern in a corpus, showing the surrounding context for each instance.
Collocational range: The variety of different contexts or linguistic environments in which a particular word can appear.
Frame: A structured unit of knowledge that organizes the participants, properties, and actions relevant to a particular situation or concept.
Prototype theory: A cognitive linguistic framework proposing that categories are organized around central, typical examples rather than strict necessary and sufficient conditions.
Radial category: A lexical category organized as a network of interconnected subtypes radiating from a central prototype, rather than a flat set of members.
Image schema: A basic, abstract pattern of spatial or experiential organization, such as container, path, or source-goal, that structures meaning.
Conceptual metaphor: A cross-domain mapping in which concepts from one domain are understood in terms of another, as in "ARGUMENT IS WAR" or "TIME IS MONEY."
Cognitive linguistics: A school of linguistic theory emphasizing the role of general cognitive processes, embodiment, and experience in the structure and use of language.
Embodiment: The principle in cognitive linguistics that language and thought are grounded in bodily experience and sensorimotor interaction with the world.
Grammatical metaphor: The process by which semantic or pragmatic relationships are recast into grammatical form, as in "It is important that..." replacing "We should..."
Construction grammar: A theoretical framework in which the basic units of grammar are form-meaning pairings called constructions, ranging from words to full sentence patterns.
Construction: A conventionalized form-meaning pairing in construction grammar, such as the ditransitive construction "X gave Y Z."
Schematization: The cognitive process of abstracting a general pattern from specific instances, forming the basis of constructions and categories.
Entrenchment: The degree to which a specific linguistic instance is deeply familiar and stored in the mental grammar, resisting generalization.
Productive: A linguistic process or pattern that can be freely extended to new forms, such as regular past tense formation in English.
Unproductive: A linguistic process or pattern that is no longer extended to new forms but survives in existing vocabulary, such as the "-ed" past tense of "bet" as "bed."
Transitivity: A grammatical property of verbs indicating the number and type of arguments they require, from intransitive to ditransitive.
Valency: The number of arguments that a verb or predicate requires, such as zero for "happen" and two for "give."
Diathesis: A grammatical pattern that relates a set of syntactic forms expressing the same underlying event, such as the active and passive.
Ditransitive construction: A syntactic pattern in which a verb takes a subject, a direct object, and an indirect object, as in "She gave him a book."
Dative construction: A syntactic pattern that assigns a dative role to a participant, realized variously as an indirect object or prepositional phrase.
Causative: A grammatical construction that adds an agent to an event, changing an intransitive verb to a transitive one, as in "break" to "break something."
Applicative: A grammatical process that adds an argument to a verb, typically promoting an oblique to a core object, common in Bantu and other languages.
Anticausative: A grammatical process that removes an agent argument from a transitive verb, turning it into an intransitive, as in "The door opened."
Ergativity: A grammatical alignment in which the subject of an intransitive verb is treated like the object of a transitive verb, and the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A grammatical alignment in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is marked the same way (nominative), and the object is marked differently (accusative).
Split ergativity: A grammatical alignment in which ergative and accusative patterns are used in different grammatical contexts, such as for different tenses or aspectual distinctions.
Absolutive: The unmarked case in an ergative-absolutive system, marking the subject of intransitive verbs and the object of transitive verbs.
Ergative: The marked case in an ergative-absolutive system, marking the subject of transitive verbs.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "that" in "I think that she is right" or "if" in "I wonder if he will come."
Conjunction: A word or morpheme that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," or "or."
Coordination: The syntactic process of joining two or more syntactically parallel elements with a conjunction.
Subordination: The syntactic process of embedding one clause within another, making one dependent on the other.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, as in "I know [that she is here]."
Matrix clause: The main or outer clause in a complex sentence that contains one or more embedded clauses.
Finite clause: A clause whose verb is marked for tense, person, and number, as in "She walks."
Non-finite clause: A clause whose verb is in an infinitival, participial, or gerundial form, as in "to walk" or "walking quickly."
Infinitival clause: A non-finite clause headed by the infinitive form of a verb, such as "to leave" in "She wants to leave."
Participial clause: A non-finite clause headed by a participle, such as "having finished" in "Having finished the work, she left."
Gerundive clause: A non-finite clause in which the verb appears in a gerundial form, functioning as a noun, such as "swimming" in "Swimming is fun."
Control clause: A non-finite clause in which the subject is not overtly expressed but is controlled by an argument in the matrix clause.
Raising clause: A clause in which the subject is semantically associated with the embedded verb but syntactically positioned as the subject of the matrix verb.
Expletive: A syntactic element that has no semantic content but occupies a structural position, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Dummy subject: A syntactic subject with no referential content, used to satisfy grammatical requirements, as in "It is raining."
Expletive object: A syntactic object with no referential content, as in "I find it difficult to explain."
Expletive subject: A subject position filled by a form with no semantic content, as in "There is a problem."
There-insertion: A syntactic construction in which "there" introduces the existence of an entity, as in "There are three cats on the mat."
Existential construction: A sentence structure asserting the existence or location of an entity, as in "There is a book on the table."
Pronoun: A word that refers to or substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "she," "it," or "they."
Personal pronoun: A pronoun that refers to the speaker, addressee, or a third party, such as "I," "you," "he," "she," "we," "they."
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "himself," "herself," or "themselves."
Reciprocal pronoun: A pronoun expressing a mutual relationship between participants, such as "each other" or "one another."
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used to ask a question, such as "who," "what," "which," or "whose."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers to an antecedent noun, such as "who," "which," or "that."
Indefinite pronoun: A pronoun that refers to a non-specific entity, such as "someone," "anything," or "nobody."
Demonstrative pronoun: A pronoun that points to a specific entity, such as "this," "that," "these," or "those."
Possessive pronoun: A pronoun that indicates ownership or association, such as "mine," "yours," "his," "hers," or "theirs."
Pronominalization: The syntactic process of replacing a noun phrase with a pronoun to avoid redundancy.
Anaphoric pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to a previously mentioned noun phrase, as in "John said that he was tired."
Cataphoric pronoun: A pronoun that refers forward to a noun phrase that appears later in the discourse.
Empty pronoun: A theoretical syntactic element with no phonological content, used to represent an unexpressed argument, such as in pro-drop languages.
Pro: The theoretical empty pronoun used in generative grammar to represent a null subject in pro-drop languages.
Proleptic: A syntactic element that anticipates or refers forward to a clause or proposition that has not yet been introduced.
Anticipatory: A construction in which a pronoun or placeholder is used before the clause it refers to, as in "There is no doubt that she will succeed."
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, such as "in the house" or "with great care."
Adpositional: Pertaining to a word class that includes prepositions, postpositions, and circumpositions.
Postposition: A word that follows its noun phrase complement, as in Japanese "no" (of) or "ni" (to, in).
Circumposition: A pair of particles that surround a noun phrase, as in German "von ... aus" (from) or "zwischen ... und" (between).
Preposition: A word that typically precedes a noun phrase and indicates a semantic relationship, such as location, direction, or time.
Locative preposition: A preposition that expresses spatial location, such as "in," "on," "at," or "under."
Temporal preposition: A preposition that expresses time relationships, such as "before," "after," "during," or "until."
Directional preposition: A preposition that expresses movement toward or away from a location, such as "to," "from," "into," or "out of."
Instrumental preposition: A preposition that expresses the means or instrument of an action, such as "with," "by," or "using."
Agentive preposition: A preposition that introduces the agent in a passive construction, such as "by" in "The book was written by her."
Allative preposition: A preposition that expresses the goal or destination of a motion, such as "to" or "toward."
Ablative preposition: A preposition that expresses the source or starting point of a motion, such as "from" or "out of."
Comitative preposition: A preposition that expresses accompaniment, such as "with" in "I went with her."
Pariative preposition: A preposition that expresses comparison, such as "than" or "as" in "taller than him."
