Phoneme: the smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Allophone: a variant form of a phoneme that does not change word meaning.
Phonotactics: the set of rules governing which sequences of phonemes are permissible in a language.
Morpheme: the smallest grammatical unit of a language that carries meaning or grammatical function.
Allomorph: a variant phonological form of a single morpheme.
Phonology: the study of the systematic organization of sounds in a language.
Phonetics: the study of the physical properties of speech sounds, including their production, transmission, and reception.
Articulatory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are produced by the organs of the vocal tract.
Acoustic phonetics: the study of the physical and measurable properties of speech sounds in the sound wave.
Auditory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the human auditory system.
Consonant: a speech sound produced with a constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
Vowel: a speech sound produced without significant constriction in the vocal tract, allowing free airflow.
Diphthong: a vowel sound that glides from one position to another within a single syllable.
Triphthong: a vowel sequence composed of three distinct vowel elements within a single syllable.
Glottal stop: a consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal folds at the glottis.
Aspiration: the burst of air accompanying the release of a voiceless plosive or the onset of a vowel.
Voicing: the vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a speech sound.
Place of articulation: the location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
Manner of articulation: the type and degree of constriction involved in producing a consonant.
Nasal: a consonant produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity.
Plosive: a consonant produced with complete closure followed by a sudden release of air.
Fricative: a consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow.
Affricate: a consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation.
Lateral: a consonant produced with air flowing around the sides of the tongue.
Rhotic: a consonant or feature associated with the tongue tip or blade, such as trills, taps, or approximants.
Trill: a consonant produced by several rapid vibrations of a speech organ, typically the tongue tip.
Tap: a consonant produced by a single rapid contact of a speech organ with another.
Approximant: a consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract without creating turbulent airflow.
Semivowel: a sound that is phonetically a vowel but functions syllabically as a consonant, such as /w/ or /j/.
Syllable: the basic unit of prosodic structure, typically containing a vowel nucleus.
Onset: the consonant or consonant cluster preceding the nucleus of a syllable.
Nucleus: the core vowel or syllabic sonorant of a syllable.
Coda: the consonant or consonant cluster following the nucleus of a syllable.
Rime: the portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and coda.
Rhyme: the portion of a syllable from the nucleus onward, often used in poetic meter.
Stress: the relative prominence of one syllable over others in a word or phrase.
Suprasegmental: a phonological feature that spans more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Tone: the use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning in a language.
Intonation: the melodic contour of a phrase or sentence, often conveying mood, attitude, or grammatical function.
Pitch: the perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to the frequency of the fundamental.
Length: the duration of a segment or prosodic unit, which may be phonemically distinctive.
Prosody: the pattern of stress, rhythm, intonation, and related features in speech.
Mora: a unit of metrical weight in phonology, roughly equivalent to the duration of a short vowel.
Distinctive feature: a binary or multi-valued property used in phonology to characterize and distinguish phonemes.
Minimal pair: a pair of words that differ in only one phonological element at the same position, demonstrating contrast.
Complementary distribution: a relationship in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, making them allophones.
Free variation: a situation in which two or more phonetic realizations can occur in the same environment without changing meaning.
Neutralization: the loss of a phonological contrast in a particular environment, such as final obstruent devoicing in German.
Contrast: a relationship between two or more phonological elements that distinguish meaning in a given position.
Feature geometry: a model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized hierarchically.
Autosegment: a phonological representation in which certain features, such as tone or stress, are placed on separate tiers.
Metathesis: a sound change or process in which two adjacent segments exchange their order.
Elision: the omission or deletion of a sound or syllable, especially in casual or rapid speech.
Assimilation: a phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound in some feature.
Dissimilation: a phonological process in which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound.
Epenthesis: the insertion of a segment into a word, often to break up consonant clusters or repair syllable structure.
Lenition: a phonological process or sound change in which a consonant becomes weaker or less obstructive.
Fortition: a phonological process or sound change in which a consonant becomes stronger or more obstructive.
Sandhi: a set of phonological rules governing how sounds change at morpheme or word boundaries.
Coarticulation: the simultaneous influence of neighboring sounds on the articulation of a given segment.
Formant: a concentration of acoustic energy in the speech signal resulting from resonances of the vocal tract.
Fundamental frequency: the lowest frequency in the harmonic series of a voiced sound, corresponding to vocal fold vibration rate.
Spectrogram: a visual display of the frequency content of a speech signal over time.
Vowel space: the two-dimensional plot of the first and second formant frequencies used to classify vowels.
IPA: the International Phonetic Alphabet, a standardized system for transcribing the sounds of all human languages.
Electropalatography: a technique for measuring tongue-palate contact during speech using an array of electrodes.
Ultrasound imaging: a diagnostic technique using high-frequency sound waves to visualize vocal tract articulators in real time.
Morphology: the study of the structure of words and the rules by which they are formed.
Root: the core morpheme that carries the primary lexical meaning of a word and cannot be further reduced.
Stem: the part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached.
Affix: a bound morpheme that is added to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: an affix that is attached before the root or stem of a word.
Suffix: an affix that is attached after the root or stem of a word.
Infix: an affix that is inserted within the root of a word.
Circumfix: an affix composed of two parts that surround a stem, such as the German ge- -t.
Bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free morpheme: a morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word.
Lexeme: an abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of inflected or derived word forms.
Lemma: the canonical or dictionary form of a word, from which other forms are derived.
Inflection: a morphological process that modifies a word for grammatical purposes without changing its core lexical meaning.
Derivation: a morphological process that creates a new word or lexeme from an existing one.
Agglutinative: a morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes with clear boundaries.
Fusional: a morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical features simultaneously.
Isolating: a morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes with little or no affixation.
Polysynthetic: a morphological type in which many morphemes are fused into a single word to express what other languages render as full sentences.
Portmanteau: a single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical categories.
Zero morpheme: a morpheme that is realized with no overt phonological or orthographic content.
Suppletion: the irregular alternation between unrelated forms for different paradigms of the same lexeme.
Reduplication: a morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to modify its meaning.
Compound: a word formed by combining two or more free morphemes or roots.
Clipping: the shortening of a word to a shorter form, such as "phone" from "telephone."
Blending: the creation of a new word by combining parts of two or more existing words, such as "brunch."
Acronym: a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, often pronounced as a word, such as "NATO."
Back-formation: the creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, such as "edit" from "editor."
Syntax: the study of the rules and principles governing the structure of sentences.
Phrase: a syntactic unit headed by a single lexical or functional word, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: a syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: a complete grammatical unit that can express a proposition and typically contains a finite verb.
Constituent: a word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger syntactic structure.
Head: the central or most important word in a phrase that determines its category and core meaning.
Complement: a required argument or adjunct of a head that completes its subcategorization frame.
Specifier: the constituent that precedes the head within a phrase, often marking features such as definiteness.
Projection: the syntactic category formed by a head and its associated material, such as a noun projecting to a noun phrase.
Phrase structure: the hierarchical arrangement of phrases and constituents within a sentence.
Tree diagram: a graphical representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence.
Dominance: a relationship in which one node in a tree structure is higher than another, encompassing it.
Immediate dominance: a relationship in which one node is directly above another in a syntactic tree, with no intervening nodes.
C-command: a structural relationship in which a node is the first branching node above another node and c-commands it.
Binding: the syntactic relationship between an anaphor or pronoun and its antecedent governed by structural conditions.
Subject: the argument of a clause that typically agrees with the finite verb and is in the nominative case.
Object: the argument of a clause that is typically in the accusative or oblique case and does not agree with the verb.
Agent: the semantic role of the entity that performs or initiates an action.
Patient: the semantic role of the entity that is affected or undergoes an action.
Theme: the semantic role of the entity that is moved, created, or is the focus of perception.
Experiencer: the semantic role of the entity that has a mental or emotional state.
Dative: the grammatical case or argument slot associated with the indirect object, typically a recipient or goal.
Voice: a grammatical category that relates the participants of a predication to the structure of the clause.
Active voice: a clause in which the subject is the agent of the action.
Passive voice: a clause in which the subject is the patient and the agent is demoted or omitted.
Nominalization: the process of deriving a noun from a verb or adjective, such as "decision" from "decide."
Subjunctive: a verb mood used to express wishes, hypotheticals, or non-factual situations.
Optative: a verb mood expressing a wish or desire, sometimes distinct from the subjunctive.
Mood: a grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the content of the utterance.
Tense: a grammatical category that locates the time of an event relative to the moment of speech.
Aspect: a grammatical category that describes the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective or progressive.
Evidentiality: a grammatical category that encodes the source of the speaker's information, such as witnessed or reported.
Serial verb construction: a construction in which two or more verbs appear in sequence within a single clause without overt subordination.
Relative clause: a subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun or particle.
Noun clause: a subordinate clause that functions as a noun within a larger sentence.
Adverbial clause: a subordinate clause that modifies the main clause by indicating time, place, reason, or condition.
Coordination: a syntactic process that links two or more elements of equal rank using a conjunction.
Subordination: a syntactic process in which one clause is made dependent on another through a subordinating element.
Embedding: the inclusion of one clause within another, creating a hierarchical structure.
Recursion: the syntactic property that allows constituents of a given type to contain further constituents of the same type without limit.
Island constraint: a restriction in syntax that prevents certain kinds of movement or extraction from specific structural positions.
Movement: a syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from its base position to a new position.
Trace: a silent copy left in the original position of a moved constituent.
Theta role: a semantic role assigned by a verb or predicate to its arguments, such as agent, patient, or goal.
Government and Binding: a theory of syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s, organized around principles and parameters.
Generative grammar: a theoretical framework that aims to describe the full set of grammatical sentences a language permits.
Chomsky hierarchy: a classification of formal grammars into types based on their generative power, from regular to unrestricted.
Context-free grammar: a formal grammar in which no production rule has a context, meaning the left-hand side is a single nonterminal.
Context-sensitive grammar: a formal grammar in which the applicability of a production rule depends on the surrounding symbols.
Phrase structure grammar: a grammar that uses rules to build sentences from phrases and constituents.
Deep structure: the underlying syntactic representation from which surface structure is derived through transformations.
Surface structure: the final syntactic representation that corresponds to the spoken or written form of a sentence.
X-bar theory: a generalization in phrase structure grammar stating that all phrases share a common hierarchical schema.
Minimalist Program: Chomsky's most recent syntactic framework, seeking to reduce syntax to the fewest possible operations.
Merge: the basic operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects into a larger one.
Move: the operation in the Minimalist Program that copies a syntactic object to a higher position.
Feature checking: the process by which uninterpretable features are matched with interpretable features on a functional head.
Phase: a domain of computation in the Minimalist Program, typically a verb phrase or complementizer phrase, within which movement is c-commanded.
Phase Impenetrability Condition: a principle stating that material within a phase is inaccessible to operations outside that phase.
Universal Grammar: the innate, language-specific cognitive endowment that constrains the possible forms all human languages can take.
Language acquisition device: a hypothetical innate mechanism that enables children to acquire language.
Critical period: the hypothesized developmental window during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and completely.
Poverty of the stimulus: the argument that children acquire grammatical knowledge that is not fully present in the input they receive.
Generativity: the property of a language that permits the production of an infinite number of novel sentences.
Finite verb: a verb form that is marked for person and number and can serve as the predicate of an independent clause.
Semantics: the study of meaning in language, including the meanings of words, phrases, and sentences.
Lexical semantics: the study of the meanings of individual words and the relations between them.
Compositional semantics: the study of how the meanings of complex expressions are built from the meanings of their parts.
Predicate logic: a formal system used in formal semantics to represent the logical structure of sentences.
Truth conditions: the state of affairs in the world under which a sentence would be true.
Sense: the cognitive or conceptual content of a word or expression as understood by speakers.
Reference: the relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity in the world it denotes.
Denotation: the set of entities in the world to which a linguistic expression applies.
Connotation: the subjective or associative meanings attached to a word beyond its literal definition.
Polysemy: the phenomenon in which a single word has multiple related senses.
Homonymy: the phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form.
Hyponymy: a semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word is included within the meaning of another.
Hypernymy: a semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word encompasses the meanings of several others.
Meronimy: a semantic relationship expressing a part-to-whole relation between two words.
Antonymy: a semantic relationship between words with opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Synonymy: a semantic relationship between words with the same or nearly the same meaning.
Metonymy: a figure of speech in which one entity is referred to by something closely associated with it.
Metaphor: a figure of speech that describes one thing in terms of another based on perceived similarity.
Presupposition: a background assumption that must be true for a sentence to be interpretable.
Entailment: a semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
Implicature: a meaning conveyed by an utterance that is not part of its literal semantic content but is inferred by the listener.
Scalar implicature: a type of implicature derived from the use of weaker terms on a scale, such as "some" implicating "not all."
Gricean maxims: four conversational principles proposed by Paul Grice: quantity, quality, relation, and manner.
Cooperative principle: Grice's general maxim that speakers contribute to conversation in the way their conversational purpose requires.
Pragmatics: the study of how context contributes to the interpretation of meaning in language.
Speech act: an utterance that performs an action, such as promising, ordering, or requesting, in addition to conveying information.
Illocutionary force: the intended function or purpose of a speech act, such as asserting, commanding, or questioning.
Perlocutionary effect: the actual effect an utterance has on the listener, such as persuading or frightening.
Performative: a word or expression that names the action being performed by its utterance, such as "I hereby declare."
Indirect speech act: an utterance that performs a speech act different from its literal illocutionary force, such as "Can you pass the salt?" as a request.
Deixis: the use of linguistic expressions whose interpretation depends on the context of utterance, such as "here," "now," or "I."
Anaphora: a linguistic element that refers back to an antecedent previously mentioned in the discourse.
Cataphora: a linguistic element that refers forward to an antecedent that will be introduced later in the discourse.
Discourse coherence: the logical and semantic connectedness of a text or conversation across its parts.
Topic: the entity or subject about which a discourse or clause is developing information.
Focus: the element of a sentence that carries new or contrastive information.
Information structure: the organization of discourse into given and new information.
Salience: the degree to which an entity is prominent or active in a discourse context.
Discourse marker: a word or phrase that signals a discourse function, such as "however," "meanwhile," or "well."
Sociolinguistics: the study of the relationship between language and society, including variation and change.
Dialect: a variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group.
Accent: the distinctive pronunciation of a language associated with a particular region or social group.
Register: a variety of language associated with a particular social setting or function.
Code-switching: the alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single discourse.
Code-mixing: the interleaving of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance.
Language contact: the interaction between speakers of different languages that may lead to mutual influence.
Pidgin: a simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language.
Creole: a fully developed natural language that evolves from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
Lethy: a creole language that has been significantly restructured by a new influx of L2 learners.
Bilingualism: the ability to use two or more languages, either in one individual or in a speech community.
Multilingualism: the use of more than two languages by an individual or within a speech community.
Diglossia: a stable situation in which two varieties of a language coexist, each with a distinct social function.
Language death: the final death of the last native speaker of a language, after which it is no longer actively spoken.
Language revitalization: the effort to restore a declining or dormant language to active use.
Language endangerment: the condition of a language whose number of speakers is declining or whose transmission to children is interrupted.
Ethnolinguistics: the study of the relationship between language and ethnic identity and culture.
Sociolinguistic variation: the systematic patterns of linguistic variation associated with social factors such as class, age, or gender.
Vernacular: the informal, everyday variety of a language used in casual communication.
Prestige: the social value and admiration accorded to a particular language variety or speaker.
Stigma: the negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety or speaker.
Linguistic prejudice: a negative attitude or stereotype directed at speakers based on their language variety or accent.
Linguistic discrimination: the unfair treatment of individuals based on their language or accent.
Language policy: the set of decisions and regulations made by a government or institution regarding the use of languages.
Language planning: the deliberate effort to influence the development, status, or use of a language or its varieties.
Standard language: the variety of a language that has been codified and promoted as the norm for formal use.
Lingua franca: a language adopted as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Endonym: the name a language or place is called by its own speakers.
Exonym: the name a language or place is called by speakers of other languages.
Isogloss: a geographic boundary line separating areas where a particular linguistic feature is present from areas where it is not.
Dialect continuum: a chain of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but the extreme ends may not be.
Patodialect: a dialect variety that is the result of the amalgamation of two or more previously distinct dialects.
Dialectometry: a quantitative method for measuring the degree of linguistic distance between varieties using word-list comparisons.
Sociophonetics: the study of the relationship between social factors and phonetic variation in speech.
Variationist sociolinguistics: the subfield of sociolinguistics that studies systematic patterns of linguistic variation using quantitative methods.
Historical linguistics: the study of how languages change over time and the reconstruction of earlier stages of languages.
Comparative method: the primary technique for reconstructing proto-languages by comparing regular correspondences across related languages.
Proto-language: a hypothetical ancestor language reconstructed from the comparison of its descendant languages.
Reconstruction: the process of hypothesizing the form of an unattested ancestral language based on systematic sound correspondences.
Sound change: a systematic shift in the pronunciation of a phoneme or set of phonemes over time.
Regular sound change: a sound change that applies uniformly across all words in the appropriate environment, with no exceptions.
Irregular sound change: a sound change that does not apply uniformly, often affecting only a subset of words.
Grimm's Law: the set of consonant shifts that distinguish the Germanic languages from other Indo-European languages.
Verner's Law: a rule describing the voicing of certain consonants that had become voiceless under Grimm's Law, depending on the accent.
Chain shift: a sequence of sound changes in which the result of one change triggers the next, as in the Great Vowel Shift.
Great Vowel Shift: the major series of vowel lengthening and raising changes in English between the 15th and 18th centuries.
Palatalization: a sound change in which a consonant becomes palatal or palatalized, often before front vowels.
Uvularization: a sound change in which a consonant's place of articulation shifts toward the uvula.
Apocope: the loss of a final sound or syllable in a word, as in "music" from earlier "musicke."
Syncope: the loss of a sound or syllable from the middle of a word, as in "comfort" from "com-fo-t."
Apheresis: the loss of a sound or syllable from the beginning of a word, as in "unction" from "unction."
Prothesis: the addition of a sound or syllable at the beginning of a word, as in "island" from Old English "iland."
Anaptaxis: the insertion of a vowel between two consonants to break up a sequence, as in "advantage" from Latin "advantagium."
Drift: the slow, gradual, and often unpredictable direction of linguistic change over long periods.
Divergence: the process by which related languages become increasingly different over time.
Convergence: the process by which unrelated or distantly related languages become more similar through prolonged contact.
Substratum: the influence of a previously spoken language on a later, dominant language in the same region.
Superstratum: the influence of a socially dominant or invading language on the languages it displaces.
Adstratum: the mutual influence between languages of roughly equal social status in contact.
Loanword: a word borrowed from one language and integrated into the vocabulary of another.
Borrowing: the process by which a language adopts words, morphemes, or other elements from another language.
Calque: a loan translation in which the meaning of a word or phrase is rendered element by element in the target language.
Semantic shift: a change in the meaning of a word or expression over time.
Semantic bleaching: the gradual loss of specific semantic content in a grammaticalized word, as in "go" in "I'm going to leave."
Semantic narrowing: a change in which the meaning of a word becomes more restricted, as in "meat" from "food."
Semantic broadening: a change in which the meaning of a word becomes more general, as in "mouse" from "rodent" to any similar creature.
Pejoration: a semantic change in which a word acquires a negative or derogatory connotation.
Amelioration: a semantic change in which a word acquires a positive or elevated connotation.
Metonymic extension: a semantic change in which a word's meaning shifts through an associative or contiguity-based link.
Etymology: the study of the origin and historical development of words and their meanings.
Cognate: a word in two or more related languages that has a common origin in a proto-language.
Swadesh list: a standardized list of about 200 basic vocabulary items used in lexicostatistics and comparative linguistics.
Glottochronology: a method of estimating the time depth of language divergence based on assumed rates of vocabulary replacement.
Phylogenetics: the method of representing language relationships as a branching tree, analogous to biological phylogenetics.
Language family: a group of languages that are descended from a common proto-language.
Language isolate: a language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language.
Language area: a geographic region in which unrelated languages share common features due to prolonged contact.
Sprachbund: a group of languages in a geographic area that share structural features through areal diffusion rather than common ancestry.
Areal linguistics: the study of linguistic features shared by languages in a geographic area due to contact rather than descent.
Typology: the study of the structural diversity and commonalities across the world's languages.
Word order: the typical arrangement of major clause constituents such as subject, object, and verb.
Ergative: a grammatical case marking the agent of a transitive verb.
Absolutive: a grammatical case that marks the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb.
Nominative: a grammatical case that typically marks the subject of an intransitive verb and the agent of a transitive verb.
Accusative: a grammatical case that typically marks the direct object of a transitive verb.
Split ergativity: a system in which ergative-absolutive case marking applies to some grammatical contexts and nominative-accusative to others.
Case marking: the morphological or syntactic means by which a language indicates the grammatical role of a noun phrase.
Agreement: the morphological matching of features such as number, person, or gender between a verb and its subject or object.
Concord: a broader term for the requirement that certain elements in a sentence share grammatical features.
Typological parameter: a binary or multi-valued setting that characterizes a structural choice a language makes.
Absolute universal: a structural property claimed to hold in all known human languages without exception.
Statistical universal: a structural tendency that holds in the vast majority of languages but admits of exceptions.
Greenberg's universals: a set of 175 typological statements about correlations among grammatical features, proposed by Joseph Greenberg in 1963.
Word order typology: the classification of languages according to their dominant order of subject, object, and verb.
Typological markedness: the tendency for certain structural properties to be less frequent or more complex across languages than others.
Markedness hierarchy: an ordered ranking of linguistic categories in which lower-ranked elements are less common or more restricted.
Morphosyntax: the study of the interaction between morphological structure and syntactic structure.
Number: a grammatical category that distinguishes one, two, or more than two entities, as in singular, dual, or plural.
Person: a grammatical category that distinguishes the speaker, addressee, and third party, as in first, second, and third person.
Gender: a grammatical category that classifies nouns into groups such as masculine, feminine, or neuter.
Class: a grammatical categorization of nouns, often called noun class in African languages, that governs agreement and morphology.
Polarity: the grammatical distinction between affirmative and negative forms.
Animacy: a semantic or grammatical distinction between living and non-living entities that may affect case marking or agreement.
Definiteness: a grammatical feature distinguishing unique or identifiable referents from non-unique ones, often marked by articles.
Specificity: a semantic property indicating that the referent of a noun phrase is identifiable to the speaker, though not necessarily to the listener.
Plurality: the grammatical marking of a quantity greater than one.
Dual: a grammatical number category specifically referring to exactly two entities.
Paucal: a grammatical number category referring to a small number greater than two.
Augmentative: a derivational morpheme that increases the size, intensity, or importance of a referent.
Diminutive: a derivational morpheme that decreases the size, intensity, or importance of a referent, or adds affection.
Superlative: the grammatical form expressing the highest degree of a quality, as in "tallest."
Comparative: the grammatical form expressing a higher degree of a quality relative to another, as in "taller."
Typological markedness hierarchy: an ordering of linguistic categories from least to most marked based on cross-linguistic frequency.
Complementizer: a word or particle that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "that" in English.
Copula: a verb that links a subject to a predicate, as in "is" in "She is a teacher."
Auxiliary: a verb that supports a main verb to express tense, aspect, modality, or voice.
Modal verb: a verb expressing modality, such as ability, obligation, or possibility, as in "can," "must," "should."
Copular construction: a clause in which a copula links the subject to a predicative complement.
Predicate: the part of a clause that says something about the subject, typically containing the verb.
Subject-verb agreement: the requirement that the verb's morphological form match the subject's person and number.
Dative shift: a syntactic change in which a verb that originally took an oblique object comes to take a direct object.
Nominal case: a grammatical category assigned to nouns and noun phrases to indicate their syntactic role.
Instrumental case: a grammatical case marking the means or tool by which an action is performed.
Locative case: a grammatical case marking location or position.
Ablative case: a grammatical case marking separation, source, or origin.
Allative case: a grammatical case marking direction toward a location.
Vocative case: a grammatical case used to address a person or entity directly.
Genitive case: a grammatical case expressing possession, origin, or association.
Partitive case: a grammatical case expressing a part of a whole.
Instrument: the semantic role of the means or tool used to carry out an action.
Recipient: the semantic role of the entity that receives something.
Goal: the semantic role of the entity or location toward which something moves.
Source: the semantic role of the entity or location from which something moves.
Beneficiary: the semantic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Psych-verb: a verb that expresses a mental or emotional state and often triggers special syntactic patterns.
Causative: a morphological or syntactic construction that adds an agent who causes an event.
Anticausative: a morphological process that removes the external agent from a transitive clause.
Applicative: a morphological process that promotes an oblique argument to the status of a direct object.
Light verb: a verb that carries little lexical meaning and relies on its complement for content, such as "give" in "give a shout."
Resultative: a predicate or complement expressing the result or state resulting from an event.
Resultative clause: a clause describing the end state brought about by the event in the main clause.
Resultative adjective: an adjective describing the resultant state of a patient, as in "The window broke."
Resultative particle: a grammatical element, common in East Asian languages, that marks the result of an action.
Evidential marker: a grammatical element that encodes the source or type of evidence for a statement.
Hortative: a verb mood expressing a suggestion or urging to perform an action.
Imperative: a verb mood used for giving commands or requests.
Jussive: a verb mood expressing a wish, command, or permission, often distinct from the imperative.
Subjunctive mood: a verb mood used to express hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations.
Indicative mood: the verb mood used to state facts or express certainty.
Interrogative: a question form, often marked by a special particle, intonation pattern, or word order.
Negative polarity item: a word or expression that is grammatical only in the scope of negation or other downward-entailing contexts.
Polarity: the grammatical or semantic property of being positive or negative.
Negation: the grammatical expression of the absence or denial of a proposition.
Double negation: the use of two or more negators in a single clause, which may cancel out or intensify negation depending on the language.
Emphatic: a grammatical or prosodic device that adds emphasis or force to an utterance.
Cleft sentence: a construction that divides a clause into two parts to place emphasis on one constituent, as in "It was John who left."
Pseudo-cleft: a cleft construction introduced by a wh-phrase, as in "What I want is coffee."
Focus-fronting: a syntactic operation in which a focused constituent is moved to a position at the beginning of the clause.
Topic-fronting: a syntactic operation in which the topic of a sentence is placed at the beginning for discourse coherence.
V2 order: a word order pattern in which the finite verb occupies the second position in a main clause, as in German or Dutch.
Free word order: a typological property in which the linear order of major clause constituents is largely unconstrained.
Scrambling: the syntactic process by which arguments of a verb are reordered, common in languages like Japanese and Korean.
Word formation: the set of processes by which new words are created, including compounding, derivation, and blending.
Productive morpheme: a morpheme that can be applied to new or novel bases to create new words.
Unproductive morpheme: a morpheme that no longer generates new words but persists in existing vocabulary.
Derivational morphology: the study of processes that create new words or change the grammatical category of a word.
Inflectional morphology: the study of processes that modify a word for grammatical categories without changing its core meaning.
Suppletion: the use of an entirely different root to express a grammatical distinction, as in "go" and "went."
Paradigm: the complete set of inflected forms of a lexeme across all grammatical categories.
Morphological paradigm: the set of all possible inflected forms a word can take in a language.
Paradigmatic relation: the relationship between linguistic elements that can occupy the same slot in a structure.
Syntagmatic relation: the relationship between linguistic elements that co-occur in a linear sequence.
Paradigm: the set of all possible inflected or derived forms of a word in a language.
Morpho-phonemic rule: a rule that describes how phonological processes interact with morphological boundaries.
Morpho-phonemic alternation: the predictable variation in the phonological form of a morpheme depending on its phonological environment.
Prosodic word: a unit of prosodic structure that corresponds roughly to an orthographic word or compound.
Prosodic phrase: a unit of prosodic structure larger than a prosodic word, corresponding roughly to an intonational group.
Intonational phrase: a prosodic unit that corresponds to a single intonational contour, typically a clause or short sentence.
Utterance: the largest unit of spoken discourse, bounded by pauses and marked by a complete intonational contour.
Discourse: language use extended beyond the sentence level, involving the organization of meaning across multiple utterances.
Narrative: a discourse structure in which events are presented in a sequence, often with a beginning, middle, and end.
Dialogue: a discourse structure consisting of alternating turns between two or more speakers.
Turn-taking: the system by which speakers in conversation alternate in producing utterances.
Repair: a discourse mechanism by which a speaker identifies and corrects a problem in a preceding utterance.
Topic shift: the transition in a conversation from one subject to another.
Coherence: the property of a discourse in which its parts are logically and thematically connected.
Cohesion: the use of explicit linguistic devices, such as reference and conjunction, to link parts of a discourse.
Anaphoric chain: a sequence of expressions in a discourse that all refer to the same entity.
Exophoric reference: a reference to an entity that is not mentioned in the discourse but is present in the physical or situational context.
Endophoric reference: a reference to an entity that has been mentioned elsewhere in the discourse.
Cataphoric reference: a reference to an entity that is introduced later in the discourse than the referring expression.
Antecedent: the expression that is referred to by an anaphoric or pronominal expression.
Coreference: the relationship between two or more expressions that refer to the same entity.
Exhaustive: a presupposition that the set of entities described by a phrase is complete.
Exhaustive presupposition: a presupposition triggered by clefts or focus that the highlighted element is the only one satisfying the predicate.
Focus particle: a word or morpheme that marks or strengthens the focus of a sentence, such as "only" or "even."
Information focus: the element of a sentence that conveys new information to the listener.
Contrastive focus: a focus that contrasts the highlighted element with one or more alternatives.
Given information: information that is already established or accessible in the discourse context.
New information: information that has not yet been established in the discourse and is being introduced for the first time.
Given-new chain: the progression of a discourse in which the given information of one clause becomes the new information of the next.
Thematic progression: the pattern by which topics are introduced, sustained, and shifted across a discourse.
Rheme: the part of a clause that introduces new information about the topic.
Thema: the part of a clause that establishes the topic to which the rheme relates.
Deictic expression: a linguistic expression whose interpretation depends on the spatiotemporal context of the utterance.
Person deixis: the use of pronouns to refer to the speaker, addressee, or a third party.
Spatial deixis: the use of words like "here," "there," or directional terms to refer to locations relative to the speaker.
Temporal deixis: the use of words like "now," "then," "today," or "tomorrow" to refer to times relative to the utterance.
Anaphoric pronoun: a pronoun that refers back to a previously mentioned noun phrase.
Demonstrative: a word that points to or identifies a particular entity, such as "this" or "that."
Definite article: a word that marks a noun phrase as referring to a specific, identifiable entity, such as "the" in English.
Indefinite article: a word that marks a noun phrase as referring to a non-specific or non-identifiable entity, such as "a" in English.
Zero article: the absence of an article where one might be expected, as in "I went to school."
Noun phrase: a phrase headed by a noun, which may include determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: a phrase headed by a verb, which may include objects, complements, and adverbials.
Adjective phrase: a phrase headed by an adjective that modifies a noun.
Adverb phrase: a phrase headed by an adverb that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb.
Prepositional phrase: a phrase headed by a preposition that typically takes a noun phrase complement.
Complement phrase: a phrase that serves as a complement to a verb, adjective, or noun.
Modifier: a word or phrase that adds descriptive or limiting information to a head word.
Adjunct: a syntactically optional constituent that adds non-essential information to a clause.
Appositive: a noun or noun phrase that renames or identifies another noun adjacent to it.
Parenthetical: a word or phrase inserted into a sentence that can be omitted without affecting its grammatical structure.
Interjection: a word or expression used to express emotion or reaction, such as "oh," "well," or "ouch."
Discourse marker: a word or phrase, such as "well," "you know," or "by the way," that organizes discourse or signals the speaker's stance.
Hedging: the use of linguistic expressions that soften or qualify a statement to reduce its commitment or assertiveness.
Mitigation: the use of linguistic strategies to reduce the perceived force or directness of an utterance.
Politeness strategy: a linguistic approach, such as indirectness or hedging, used to maintain social harmony and face.
Face: the positive or negative public self-image that a person maintains in social interaction.
Positive face: the desire to be approved of, admired, or liked by others.
Negative face: the desire to be unimpeded and not imposed upon by others.
Face-threatening act: an utterance that risks damaging the listener's or speaker's positive or negative face.
Mitigated request: a request expressed in an indirect or softened form to reduce face threat.
Imperative form: the verb form used to issue direct commands or instructions.
Interrogative form: the syntactic structure used to pose questions, often involving inversion or a question particle.
Declarative form: the syntactic structure used to state facts or make assertions.
Exclamative form: the syntactic structure used to express strong emotion or surprise.
Tag question: a short question appended to a declarative statement to seek confirmation, such as "It's cold, isn't it?"
Rhetorical question: a question asked not to elicit an answer but to make a point or emphasize a statement.
Echo question: a question formed by repeating part or all of a preceding utterance to express surprise or seek clarification.
Backchannel: a brief non-verbal or verbal signal, such as "mm-hmm" or "I see," that indicates the listener is following the conversation.
Repair initiation: the first step in a conversational repair sequence where a problem in the preceding talk is identified.
Self-repair: a correction made by the speaker who produced the problematic utterance.
Other-repair: a correction made by the listener of a problematic utterance.
Turn constructional unit: a segment of speech that is understood by the listener as a complete contribution to the conversation.
Completion: the point at which a speaker's turn is understood to be finished and the other speaker may take the floor.
Transition relevance place: a point in a turn at which a change of speaker is expected or possible.
Overlap: the simultaneous production of speech by two or more speakers in conversation.
Interruption: the act of one speaker breaking in on another speaker's turn before its completion.
Floor: the right or opportunity to speak at a given moment in a conversation.
Floor-giving: a speaker's indication that they are ready to yield the right to speak to another.
Floor-take: the act of a speaker beginning to talk, either in response to a floor-give or by taking the floor.
Conversational maxims: the informal norms governing the flow and content of spoken interaction.
Adjacency pair: a pair of related conversational turns, such as a question and answer or a greeting and response.
First pair part: the initial element of an adjacency pair, such as a question, offer, or greeting.
Second pair part: the expected response to a first pair part, such as an answer, acceptance, or return greeting.
Preferred response: the response that is culturally expected and relatively unmarked in an adjacency pair.
Dispreferred response: the response that is culturally marked, often delayed, hedged, or accompanied by mitigations.
Narrative structure: the organization of a narrative into a pre-narrative, orienting, complicating, evaluating, and concluding segments.
Evaluation: the part of a narrative in which the narrator expresses their stance or the significance of the events.
Complicating action: the core events of a narrative that create a problem or conflict.
Resolution: the part of a narrative in which the problem or conflict is addressed or concluded.
Recount: a narrative form that presents a sequence of events without a clear evaluative or moral focus.
Experience tale: a narrative form in which the narrator recounts a personal experience, often with an evaluative frame.
Narrative evaluation: the speaker's explicit or implicit commentary on the significance of the narrative events.
Conversational implicature: a meaning inferred from an utterance based on the Gricean maxims and the context of the conversation.
Scalar hierarchy: an ordered scale of meanings, such as "none < some < many < all," that underlies scalar implicature.
Horn scale: a scale of linguistic expressions ordered by strength, such as "impossible < unlikely < possible < likely < certain."
Langacker scale: a scale of linguistic expressions ordered by the degree of commitment to the truth of a proposition.
Presupposition projection: the process by which the presuppositions of an embedded clause are projected to the level of the whole sentence.
Accommodated presupposition: a presupposition that a listener accepts as part of the shared background despite its not being explicitly stated.
Inferential meaning: meaning that is not encoded in the linguistic form but is derived through reasoning and context.
Pragmatic inference: the process by which a listener derives the intended meaning of an utterance beyond its literal semantic content.
Speech act theory: the framework, developed by Austin and Searle, that analyzes utterances as actions performed in language.
Perlocutionary act: the effect of an utterance on the beliefs, emotions, or actions of the listener.
Illocutionary act: the conventional force of an utterance, such as asserting, questioning, or commanding.
Propositional content: the underlying proposition or state of affairs expressed by an utterance, independent of its form.
Performative verb: a verb that names the speech act performed by its utterance, such as "promise," "warn," or "apologize."
Conventional indirectness: the use of a formulaic expression whose conventional meaning differs from its literal meaning, such as "How do you do?"
Non-conventional indirectness: the use of an expression in a non-formulaic context where its indirect meaning is inferred contextually.
Discourse representation: a formal model that represents the information state of a discourse, including entities, relations, and presuppositions.
Discourse Representation Structure: a specific formalism in dynamic semantics that represents the evolving information state of a discourse.
Dynamic semantics: an approach to semantics in which the meaning of a sentence is a function that updates an information state rather than a truth value.
File change score: the change in the listener's information state produced by an utterance, as modeled in dynamic semantics.
Update semantics: an approach that treats the meaning of a sentence as a transformation on a set of possible worlds or information states.
Possible world: a complete and consistent way the world might be, used in modal semantics to evaluate the truth of propositions.
Intensional semantics: an approach to semantics that treats the meaning of expressions as functions from possible worlds to extensions.
Extension: the set of entities in the actual world to which an expression applies.
Intension: the function from possible worlds to extensions that represents the meaning of an expression.
Modal verb: a verb that expresses modality, such as necessity, possibility, or permission.
Epistemic modality: the expression of the speaker's degree of certainty or knowledge about a proposition.
Deontic modality: the expression of obligation, permission, or prohibition.
Bouletic modality: the expression of desire or volition.
Dynamic modality: the expression of an agent's ability, willingness, or physical necessity.
Root modality: modality that affects the truth of the proposition itself, such as ability or permission.
Modal operator: a logical operator, such as "necessarily" or "possibly," that modifies the scope of a proposition.
Quantifier: a word or expression that indicates the number or amount of entities to which a predicate applies, such as "every" or "some."
Universal quantifier: a quantifier that applies to all members of a domain, such as "every" or "all."
Existential quantifier: a quantifier that asserts the existence of at least one member of a domain, such as "some" or "there is."
Indefinite pronoun: a pronoun that refers to an unspecified member of a set, such as "someone" or "anything."
Definite description: a noun phrase that refers to a unique entity, typically marked by a definite article, such as "the king of France."
Russellian semantics: an approach to definite descriptions that analyzes them as quantificational expressions rather than as referring terms.
Donkey sentence: a sentence involving a quantifier and an anaphoric pronoun that resists straightforward logical analysis, such as "Every farmer who owns a donkey beats it."
Bound variable: a variable in a formal semantic representation that is bound by a quantifier and ranges over a domain.
Free variable: a variable in a formal semantic representation that is not bound by a quantifier.
Variable binding: the process in formal semantics in which a quantifier takes scope over a variable and assigns it a range.
Scope ambiguity: the ambiguity that arises when a quantifier can take scope over different portions of a sentence.
Wide scope: the interpretation in which a quantifier takes scope over a larger domain than another element.
Narrow scope: the interpretation in which a quantifier takes scope over a smaller domain than another element.
Scope: the domain over which a quantifier or modal operator applies in a semantic interpretation.
Quantifier scope: the range of propositions or entities over which a quantifier ranges in a sentence.
Modal scope: the range of propositions over which a modal operator applies in a sentence.
Scope taking: the process by which a quantifier or operator is assigned a particular scope in a semantic interpretation.
Logical form: the abstract, language-independent semantic representation of a sentence.

Argument: a required participant in a predication, typically expressed as a noun phrase.
Adjunct: an optional participant in a predication that adds additional information.

Optional argument: a core participant that is permitted but not required by a predicate's argument structure.
Argument structure alternation: a change in the number or type of arguments a verb permits, as in the dative alternation.
Dative alternation: the alternation between a double-object construction and a prepositional dative construction.

Semantic field: a group of words that are semantically related and form a conceptual domain.

Semantic prime: a basic, irreducible concept proposed in Natural Semantic Metalanguage as a component of cross-linguistic meaning.
Conceptual metaphor: a mapping from a concrete source domain to an abstract target domain, as in "ARGUMENT IS WAR."
Conceptual metonymy: a mapping within the same domain based on contiguity, as in "THE WHITE HOUSE" for the U.S. presidency.
Image schema: a basic, pre-linguistic pattern of experience, such as container, path, or force, that structures abstract meaning.
Cognitive semantics: a theoretical framework that grounds meaning in embodied experience, usage, and conceptual structure rather than formal logic.
Usage-based linguistics: a theoretical framework that grounds linguistic structure in patterns of language use and frequency rather than innate rules.
Construction grammar: a framework that treats pairings of form and meaning, called constructions, as the basic units of linguistic knowledge.
Construction: a pairing of a linguistic form with a meaning, grammatical function, or pragmatic interpretation.
Argument structure construction: a construction that specifies the number and type of arguments a predicate takes.
Slot and frame: a model of lexical semantics in which words are organized around central slots (concepts) with associated frames (contexts).
Frame semantics: an approach to semantics that organizes word meanings around situations or scenes called frames.
Frame evocation: the activation of a structured set of expectations or concepts by a word or phrase.
Lexical entry: the complete set of information about a word stored in a lexicon, including its forms, meanings, and grammatical properties.
Lexicon: the inventory of words and their associated information in a language.
Mental lexicon: the hypothetical repository of word knowledge in a speaker's mind.
Lexicalization: the process by which a phrase or expression becomes a single word or fixed unit in the lexicon.
Idiom: a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be predicted from the meanings of its individual components.
Phraseological unit: a fixed or semi-fixed multi-word expression, such as a compound, idiom, or collocation.
Collocation: a statistically frequent co-occurrence of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Colloquialism: a word or expression characteristic of informal or spoken language.
Neologism: a newly coined or recently introduced word or expression.

Extinct language: a language that has no remaining speakers at all.
Sleeping language: a language with no living native speakers that is being revived or studied.
Revitalized language: a language that has been restored to active use after a period of dormancy.
Language documentation: the systematic recording and description of a language's structure, use, and speakers.
Field linguistics: the on-site study and description of languages, often in underserved or endangered communities.
Corpus linguistics: the study of language using large collections of authentic text or speech data.
Corpus: a large, structured collection of text or speech data used for linguistic analysis.
Frequency analysis: the examination of how often words, forms, or constructions occur in a corpus.

Collocational analysis: the study of which words tend to co-occur with a given target word in a corpus.

Token: an individual occurrence of a word or symbol in a text.
Type: a unique word form in a text, regardless of how many times it occurs.

Tip of the tongue: the phenomenon in which a speaker cannot immediately retrieve a known word from memory.

Diphthong: A vowel that glides from one quality to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/.
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable in natural speech, as in "gonna" for "going to."
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word, often to break up difficult consonant clusters.

Front: A vowel quality category in which the tongue body is advanced toward the front of the mouth.
Glottal: Pertaining to the glottis as a place of articulation, as in /h/ or the glottal stop.
Glottalization: The partial or complete closure of the vocal folds during speech production.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of one unstressed syllable followed by one stressed syllable.
Insertion: The addition of a phonological segment not present in the underlying representation.
Isochrony: The tendency in a language to produce syllables or stressed syllables at roughly equal time intervals.
Labial: Pertaining to the lips as a place of articulation.
Labialization: The rounding of the lips during the production of a non-labial consonant, as in /kʷ/.
Labiovelar: A consonant articulated simultaneously with lip rounding and velar closure, such as /kw/.
Lateral: A consonant that allows airflow along the sides of the tongue, such as /l/.
Liquid: A consonant that is either a lateral or a rhotic.
Long: A vowel or consonant of greater duration than its short counterpart in a given language.
Manner of articulation: The classification of a consonant by how the airflow is obstructed (stop, fricative, nasal, etc.).
Merger: The historical loss of a phonemic distinction so that two formerly separate sounds become one.
Metathesis: The transposition of two adjacent segments, as in "ask" from older "aks."
Mid: A vowel height category intermediate between high and low.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by exactly one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating phonemic contrast.
Moraic: Relating to moras, the timing units that determine syllable weight.
Nasality: The quality of a sound produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the oral tract closed and the velum lowered, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Nucleus: The central vowel or syllabic consonant of a syllable.
Obstruent: Any consonant produced with a complete or partial obstruction of the airflow, including stops, fricatives, and affricates.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster preceding the syllable nucleus.
Palatal: A consonant articulated with the body of the tongue against the hard palate, such as /ʃ/ or /j/.

Pharyngeal: Pertaining to the pharynx as a place of articulation, as in Arabic /ħ/ or /ʕ/.
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, such as /p/ vs. /b/ in "pat" vs. "bat."
Phonemic: Relating to or consisting of phonemes.
Phonological: Relating to the abstract, rule-governed sound system of a language.
Phonotactics: The system of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permitted in a language.
Place of articulation: The precise location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release, also called a stop.
Postvocalic: Following a vowel, as in the /t/ in "cat."
Prosody: The suprasegmental properties of speech, including stress, tone, and intonation.
Prosodic: Relating to the suprasegmental structure of speech.
Register: A distinct configuration of the vocal folds producing a different voice quality, such as falsetto or fry.

Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic and phonological organization in speech.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a continuous string of segments into syllables.
Syllable weight: The classification of a syllable as light or heavy based on the moraic structure of its rhyme.
Tone: The use of pitch contour to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable.
Unrounded: A vowel produced with spread or neutral lips, as in /i/ or /e/.
Unvoiced: Produced without vibration of the vocal folds, as in /s/ or /f/.
Voiced: Produced with vibration of the vocal folds, as in /z/ or /v/.
Voicing: The phonological feature distinguishing sounds by the presence or absence of vocal fold vibration.

Velarization: The retraction of the tongue body toward the velum during consonant production, as in /ɰ/.
Vowel: A sound produced without significant narrowing of the vocal tract, serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Consonant: A sound produced with a significant narrowing or closure in the vocal tract.
Suprasegmental: A property of speech that extends over multiple segments, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation across a phrase or sentence that conveys attitude or grammatical structure.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase, often correlated with greater loudness, length, or pitch.
Contour: The shape of a pitch pattern over the course of an utterance.
Plateau: A flat, level segment of a pitch contour.
Melody: The overall pitch pattern of an utterance or phrase.
Feature geometry: A model organizing phonological features into a hierarchical, geometric structure.
Distinctive feature: A binary or gradational property used to distinguish one phoneme from another in a phonological system.
Complementary distribution: The condition in which two sound variants never occur in the same phonetic environment.
Phonological rule: A generalization describing a systematic alternation or change in the sound system.
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word.
Surface form: The phonetic output of a word after all phonological rules have applied.
Optimality Theory: A framework in which phonological outputs are selected by ranking violable constraints.
Markedness: The property of a linguistic form or feature being less natural, less common, or more structurally complex.
Faithfulness: A type of constraint in Optimality Theory requiring the output to remain identical to the input.
Constraint: A violable, universal rule in Optimality Theory that is evaluated and ranked.
Constraint ranking: The linear ordering of constraints that determines which candidate output is optimal.
Lenition: The diachronic or synchronic weakening of a consonant, such as /p/ becoming /f/.
Fortition: The diachronic or synchronic strengthening of a consonant, such as /f/ becoming /p/.
Mutation: A systematic change to the initial consonant of a word conditioned by the preceding morpheme, as in Celtic languages.
Umlaut: A fronting or raising vowel change triggered by a following front or high vowel.
Ablaut: A system of internal vowel alternation indicating morphological or grammatical distinctions, as in English "sing/sang/sung."
Gradation: A system of vowel or consonant alternation across related word forms.
Assimilation: The process by which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound in place, manner, or voicing.
Dissimilation: The process by which two similar sounds in a word become less alike.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phonemic category that subsumes several distinct phonemes.
Phonotactic: Relating to the permissible sound sequences of a language.
Syllabic: Capable of serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Syllabic consonant: A consonant, typically /l/ or /n/, that functions as the syllable nucleus, as in the second syllable of "bottle."
Schwa: The mid-central vowel /ə/, typically the default vowel in unstressed syllables in many languages.
Hiatus: The juxtaposition of two vowels across a morpheme or syllable boundary without an intervening consonant.
Glide: A consonantal sound, typically /w/ or /j/, whose articulation resembles a vowel.
Semivowel: A sound that is intermediate in articulation and phonological behavior between a vowel and a consonant.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single, brief contact of the tongue with the alveolar ridge, as in American English "butter."
Flap: A consonant produced by a single, rapid, light contact of the articulator against the target.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid contacts of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, as in Spanish /r/.

Stop: Another term for a plosive consonant.

Ingressive: An airstream direction in which air flows into the oral cavity.
Egressive: An airstream direction in which air flows out of the oral cavity.
Phonation: The state of the vocal folds during speech, including modal, breathy, creaky, and voiceless types.
Modal: Normal phonation in which the vocal folds vibrate in a regular, periodic manner.

Phonetic: Relating to the physical, measurable production and perception of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of the abstract, rule-governed sound systems and patterns of languages.
Broad transcription: A phonemic-level notation that captures only contrastive sound distinctions.
Narrow transcription: A detailed phonetic notation capturing all relevant articulatory details.
Diacritic: A mark added to a basic character to indicate a modification in pronunciation.
IPA: The International Phonetic Alphabet, a standardized system for transcribing the sounds of all languages.
Transcription: The process of representing spoken language using a writing system or the IPA.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning, such as "un-" or "-s."
Morph: The observable phonological form of a morpheme.
Allomorph: A variant phonological form of a single morpheme, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "happy" and "happy."
Allomorphy: The existence of multiple phonological forms for a single morpheme.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries its primary lexical meaning and to which affixes attach.
Stem: The base form of a word to which inflectional morphemes are attached, which may include derivational affixes.
Affix: A morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: An affix attached before the root or stem of a word.
Suffix: An affix attached after the root or stem of a word.
Infix: An affix inserted within the root or stem of a word, as in Indonesian "se-…-ang."
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds the root or stem, consisting of two or more parts, as in German "be-…-en."
Interfix: A morpheme that links two roots in a compound, as in "foot-stone" (German "Stein").
Derivational morpheme: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category, such as "-ness" or "un-."
Inflectional morpheme: An affix that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, or case without creating a new lexical item.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "cat" or "run."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-un" or "pre-."
Bound root: A root morpheme that is not a free word and must be attached to an affix, as in Latin "script-" in "inscription."
Bound affix: An affix that is phonologically bound to a stem but may carry independent meaning.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to create a new word.
Derivation: A word-formation process that adds derivational affixes to a root to create a new word.
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, gender, or case.
Conjugation: The paradigm of a verb's inflected forms, typically varying by person, number, tense, and mood.
Declension: The paradigm of a noun, adjective, or pronoun's inflected forms, typically varying by case and number.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word or word class.
Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a morpheme depending on its phonological or morphological context.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme with no phonetic content, indicating a grammatical category by its absence, such as the absence of a plural suffix for "sheep."
Portmanteau: A single morpheme or word that fuses the meaning of two or more morphemes, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch).
Suppletion: The use of an entirely different root to express a grammatical contrast, as in "go" and "went."
Suppletive: An irregular, non-derived form that replaces the expected regular form, as in "man/men" or "good/better."
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical category.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes and grammatical relations are expressed by word order or particles.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which single words can encode information equivalent to entire clauses, as in many Native American languages.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing word formation.
Word: The basic unit of free use in a language, typically defined by prosodic and syntactic criteria.
Word formation: The processes by which new words are created, including derivation, compounding, and conversion.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphological structure and phonological rules, accounting for alternations.
Morphotaxonomy: The study of how morphological structure affects or is affected by syntactic arrangement.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent, such as the English "-'s" in "John's."
Particle: A small, often monomorphemic word that modifies a verb or phrase, such as "up" in "give up."
Affixoid: A morpheme that exhibits properties of both a clitic and an affix.
Syntax: The study of the structure of sentences and the rules governing how words are combined.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a word of a particular category, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate (verb), which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: A syntactically complete unit expressing a proposition, typically consisting of at least one clause.
Constituent: A sub-part of a sentence that functions as a single unit and can be moved or replaced as a block.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of phrases and their immediate dominance relationships.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence.
Deep structure: The abstract syntactic representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface structure: The final, pronounceable syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations.
Transformational grammar: A framework in which sentences are generated by applying transformational rules to deep structures.
Generative grammar: A theory of syntax that aims to characterize the set of all well-formed sentences of a language.
Government and Binding: A syntactic framework organized around principles and parameters, including Binding, Case, and the theta criterion.

X-bar theory: A generalization stating that all phrasal categories (NP, VP, etc.) share a common structural template.
Specifier: The element occupying the position immediately above the head within a phrase, such as the determiner in an NP.
Head: The word that determines the category of a phrase and governs its complements, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: The phrase or word that follows a head and is required or selected by it, such as the object after a transitive verb.
Adjunct: An optional modifier that adds information to a phrase or clause, such as a prepositional phrase of time or place.
Argument: A participant in a predication that is required by the verb's semantic structure, such as the subject and object of "give."
Theta role: The semantic role assigned to an argument by the verb, such as Agent, Patient, or Experiencer.
Theta criterion: The requirement that each argument receive exactly one theta role and each theta role be assigned to exactly one argument.
Binding theory: A component of syntax governing the distribution of pronouns, reflexives, and names within a sentence.

Government: A syntactic relationship in which a head c-commands and licenses a complement.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase, such as nominative or accusative.
