Transitive: A verb that takes two core arguments, typically a subject and an object.
Intransitive: A verb that takes a single core argument, typically a subject.
Diathesis: The structural pattern of a clause in terms of the roles of its arguments, such as active or passive.
Voice: A grammatical category that alters the mapping between semantic roles and syntactic positions, such as active vs. passive.
Active voice: The voice in which the agent is the grammatical subject.
Passive voice: The voice in which the patient is promoted to subject and the agent is demoted or omitted.
Middle voice: A voice in which the subject is both the agent and the patient, as in "the book reads well."
Causative: A voice or construction in which an additional agent argument is added to a verb.
Applicative: A morphological process that promotes an oblique argument to a core object position.
Reciprocal: A construction or verb meaning that the participants in an action affect each other mutually.
Reflexive: A construction in which the subject and object of a verb refer to the same entity.
Copula: A verb such as "be" that links a subject to a predicate adjective, noun, or complement.
Copular: Relating to or functioning as a copula.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "that" or "if."
Subordinate clause: A clause that depends on a main clause and cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
Coordinate clause: A clause joined to another of equal rank by a coordinating conjunction such as "and" or "but."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun such as "who" or "which."
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverb, modifying the main clause, typically introduced by "because," "although," etc.
Nominal clause: A clause that functions as a noun phrase, such as "What you said is true."
Subcategorization: The specification of the type and number of arguments or complements a lexical item requires.
Subcategorization frame: The set of syntactic frames in which a lexical item can appear, e.g., "give" allows [NP V NP PP] and [NP V NP NP].
Valency: The number of arguments a verb requires.
Valence: The total number of arguments a predicate can take, including optional ones.
Argument structure: The mapping between semantic roles and syntactic positions.
External argument: The argument of a clause that is not selected by the verb's complement, typically the subject.
Internal argument: The argument of a clause that is selected by the verb as a complement, typically the object.
Agent: The theta role of the volitional initiator of an action.
Patient: The theta role of the entity affected by an action.
Theme: The theta role of the entity that is moved, perceived, or described.
Goal: The theta role of the destination of a movement or transfer.
Experiencer: The theta role of the entity that perceives, feels, or is aware of a state or event.
Instrument: The theta role of the means by which an action is performed.
Location: The theta role of the place where an event occurs.
Source: The theta role of the origin of a movement or transfer.
Path: The theta role of the trajectory along which an entity moves.
Cause: The theta role of the entity or force responsible for bringing about an event.
Beneficiary: The theta role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Possessor: The theta role of the entity that owns or is associated with something.
Conjunction: A word that joins two words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "or," "but."
Coordinator: A conjunction used to join elements of equal syntactic rank.
Subordinating conjunction: A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because" or "although."
Correlative: A pair of words that work together to join two clauses or elements, such as "either...or" or "both...and."
Expletive: A phonologically realized element with no semantic content, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Dummy subject: An expletive that occupies the subject position, as in "It is raining" or "There are three cats."
PRO: An unpronounced, covert subject in non-finite clauses, as in "John wants [PRO to leave]."
pro: A phonologically null pronoun used in pro-drop languages, such as Spanish or Italian.
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject of a non-finite clause is co-indexed with a matrix argument.
Raising: A syntactic process in which an argument is moved from a lower clause to a higher clause, as in "John seems [to be happy]."
Raising to subject: A raising construction in which the subject of an embedded clause moves to the subject position of the matrix clause.
Raising to object: A raising construction in which the subject of an embedded clause moves to the object position of the matrix clause.
Object control: A control relationship in which the matrix object determines the identity of the embedded PRO.
Subject control: A control relationship in which the matrix subject determines the identity of the embedded PRO.
Equi: A term for subject control in which the matrix subject and the embedded PRO are co-referent.
A-structure: The position of an argument that receives a theta role (subject or object position).
A'-position: A position reached by movement, such as a trace or the landing site of wh-movement.
C-command: A structural relationship in which one node dominates another without being dominated by it.
Dominance: The hierarchical relationship in a tree in which one node is an ancestor of another.
Govern: A structural relationship in which a head c-commands and is the closest potential governor of a complement.
Theta grid: The representation of the assignment of theta roles to arguments in a clause.
Selectional restriction: A semantic constraint on the type of argument a verb can take, e.g., "devour" requires an edible object.
Subcategorization: The specification of the complements a head requires or permits.
Empty category: A position in a syntactic structure that is phonetically unrealized, such as a trace or PRO.
Trace: The phonologically null residue left by a moved constituent in its original position.
Movement: A syntactic operation that displaces a constituent from one position to another.
Wh-movement: The movement of a wh-word (who, what, where, etc.) to the specifier of CP in interrogatives.
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the beginning of a clause for discourse or focus purposes.
Focus: The element in a sentence that conveys new or contrastive information.
Topic: The element in a sentence about which the assertion is made.
Information structure: The organization of a sentence into topic, focus, and background components.
Scrambling: The free reordering of arguments in a clause, as in Japanese or Hindi.
Word order: The canonical arrangement of syntactic constituents in a clause, such as SVO or SOV.
SVO: Subject-Verb-Object, a basic word order type found in English, French, and Mandarin.
SOV: Subject-Object-Verb, a basic word order type found in Japanese, Turkish, and Hindi.
VSO: Verb-Subject-Object, a basic word order type found in Arabic, Irish, and Welsh.
V2: The syntactic constraint requiring the finite verb to occupy the second position in a main clause, as in German and Scandinavian languages.
Constituent: A syntactically well-formed sub-part of a sentence.
Immediate dominance: The direct parent-child relationship in a syntactic tree.
Categorial grammar: A framework for analyzing syntax using phrase-structure rules and type assignment.
Dependency grammar: A framework in which syntactic structure is represented by binary relations between heads and dependents.
Head-driven phrase structure grammar (HPSG): A constraint-based, unification-based framework for modeling syntax and semantics.
LFG: Lexical Functional Grammar, a framework linking syntactic structure (c-structure) to functional structure (f-structure).
Case grammar: A framework by Chomsky that represents argument structure using semantic cases rather than grammatical case.
Semantic role: The role an argument plays in the event described by a verb, such as Agent or Patient.
Semantic compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and their mode of composition.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including lexical, compositional, and discourse-level meaning.
Lexical semantics: The study of word meaning and the relationships between word meanings.
Compositional semantics: The study of how the meanings of complex expressions are built from the meanings of their parts.
Denotation: The set of entities in the world to which a term or expression refers.
Sense: A distinct meaning or interpretation of a word or expression.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it points to.
Reference: The entity or state of affairs a linguistic expression points to in context.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression whose interpretation depends on a preceding antecedent, such as a pronoun.
Antecedent: The expression to which an anaphor refers.
Co-reference: The relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
Coreferential: Referring to the same entity.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression whose interpretation depends on a following expression.
Antonymy: The semantic relationship between words with opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Synonymy: The semantic relationship between words with the same or very similar meanings.
Hyponymy: The semantic relationship in which one term's meaning is included within another's, such as "rose" under "flower."
Hypernymy: The reverse of hyponymy; the more general term in a hyponymy relation.
Meronymy: The semantic relationship between a part and a whole, such as "wheel" and "car."
Tautology: A statement that is true by virtue of its logical form alone.
Contradiction: A statement that is false by virtue of its logical form alone.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: Background information assumed to be true for an utterance to be interpretable.
Implicature: A meaning that is not literally encoded in the utterance but is inferred by the listener.
Conversational implicature: An implicature generated by the violation of Grice's conversational maxims.
Scalar implicature: An implicature based on the violation of the maxim of quantity, such as "some" implying "not all."
Gricean maxims: The four principles (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner) governing cooperative communication.
Pragmatics: The study of how context contributes to the interpretation of utterances.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action, such as a promise, request, or declaration.
Locution: The actual words spoken in a speech act.
Illocution: The intended function or force of a speech act, such as requesting or asserting.
Perlocution: The effect a speech act has on the listener, such as persuading or alarming.
Performative: An utterance that brings about the action it describes, such as "I now pronounce you married."
Deixis: The linguistic expression of relation between a speaker, a time, and a place, as in "this," "here," and "now."
Indexical: A word whose referent depends on the context of utterance, such as "I," "now," or "here."
Demonstrative: A word that points to an entity in the context, such as "this," "that," "these," "those."
Discourse: Language use beyond the sentence level, including coherence, cohesion, and information flow.
Discourse analysis: The study of language in extended contexts, focusing on how meaning is constructed across utterances.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse, such as "well," "however," or "meanwhile."
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a discourse.
Cohesion: The use of linguistic devices (reference, conjunction, ellipsis) to link parts of a discourse.
Ellipsis: The omission of words that are recoverable from context, such as "I'll go tomorrow, and she will [go tomorrow] too."
Anaphoric: Referring back to a previously mentioned element in discourse.
Cataphoric: Referring forward to a subsequently mentioned element in discourse.
Topic continuation: The discourse strategy of maintaining focus on the same topic across utterances.
Topic shift: The discourse strategy of moving to a new topic.
Information flow: The movement of given and new information across a discourse.
Given: Information that is already established in the discourse.
New: Information that is not yet established in the discourse.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group.
Dialectology: The study of dialects and their geographical and social distribution.
Dialectal: Pertaining to or characteristic of a particular dialect.
Diatopic: Relating to the geographic variation of language.
Diastratic: Relating to the social variation of language.
Diaphasic: Relating to the variation of language across different situations or registers.
Diglossia: A situation in which two varieties of a language coexist, each with distinct functional domains.
Creole: A stable, natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language, without native speakers.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, leading to borrowing, interference, or mixed languages.
Borrowing: The adoption of words or structures from one language into another.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single discourse.
Code-mixing: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single clause or sentence.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be actively used.
Language revival: Efforts to restore a dormant or endangered language to active use.
Endangered language: A language at risk of losing its last native speakers.
Endogamy: The practice of marrying within a particular language community, relevant to language maintenance.
Exogamy: The practice of marrying outside a particular language community.
Linguistic relativity: The hypothesis that the structure of a language influences or determines the cognition and perception of its speakers.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: A specific formulation of linguistic relativity, ranging from the strong (linguistic determinism) to the weak (linguistic influence) version.
Linguistic determinism: The strong version of linguistic relativity claiming that language determines thought.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social context or purpose.
Style: The set of linguistic features characteristic of a particular author, period, or social context.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used within a particular profession or group.
Slang: Informal, often ephemeral vocabulary used within a particular social group.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a blunt or offensive one.
Taboo: A word or concept that is avoided or replaced by a euphemism due to social or cultural sensitivity.
Politeness strategy: A linguistic device used to minimize face-threatening acts in interaction.
Face: The public self-image a person claims in social interaction, as described by Brown and Levinson.
Face-threatening act: An action or utterance that may damage the positive or negative face of a participant.
Negative face: The desire to be free from imposition or restriction.
Positive face: The desire to be approved of and appreciated by others.
Honorific: A linguistic form used to show respect or deference to a listener or referent.
Address form: The form used to directly address another person, varying by social relationship.
Prestige: The positive social value attached to a particular variety or form of language.
Stigma: The negative social value attached to a particular variety or form of language.
Stereotype: A widely held, often oversimplified belief about a social group's language.
Attitude: The evaluations and beliefs speakers hold about languages, dialects, and speakers.
Language ideology: The set of beliefs and assumptions a community holds about language.
Linguistic anthropology: The study of language in its social and cultural context.
Ethnography: The method of studying language through participant observation in natural settings.
Corpus: A large, systematically collected body of text used for linguistic analysis.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large electronic collections of texts.
Frequency: The number of times a linguistic item occurs in a corpus or sample.
Collocation: A habitual or statistically predictable combination of words, such as "strong tea" or "make a decision."
N-gram: A sequence of N consecutive words in a corpus.
Collocational: Relating to the typical or habitual combinations of words.
Noun class: A system in which nouns are grouped into classes, often marked by prefixes or agreement, as in Bantu languages.
Gender: A grammatical classification of nouns, often but not always correlated with biological sex.
Number: A grammatical category marking the quantity of entities, such as singular, plural, or dual.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker (first), the addressee (second), and others (third).
Tense: A grammatical category locating an event in time relative to the utterance, such as past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category describing the internal temporal structure of an event, such as perfective or imperfective.
Perfective: An aspect marking an event as a complete, bounded whole.
Imperfective: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded.
Progressive: An aspect marking an event as ongoing at a particular time.
Perfect: An aspect marking an event as completed with relevance to the present.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Indicative: The mood used for statements of fact or reality.
Subjunctive: The mood used for hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations.
Imperative: The mood used for commands or requests.
Conditional: A mood or clause type expressing a hypothetical situation and its consequence.
Hypothetical: Relating to a situation that is not asserted as fact.
Subjunctive: (already listed)
Evidentiality: A grammatical category indicating the source of the speaker's information, such as direct observation or hearsay.
Evidential: A morphological or syntactic marker indicating the source or reliability of information.
Factivity: The presupposition that the content of a complement clause is true.
Factive verb: A verb that presupposes the truth of its complement, such as "know" or "realize."
Non-factive verb: A verb that does not presuppose the truth of its complement, such as "think" or "believe."
Presupposition: Background information taken for granted in an utterance.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement logically guarantees the truth of another.
Contradiction: A semantic relationship in which two statements cannot both be true.
Tautology: A statement that is true by virtue of its logical form alone.
Modal verb: A verb expressing necessity, possibility, permission, or obligation, such as "must," "can," or "should."
Modal: Relating to modality, the expression of possibility, necessity, or obligation.
Deontic modality: The expression of obligation, permission, or prohibition.
Epistemic modality: The expression of the speaker's degree of certainty or knowledge.
Dynamic modality: The expression of ability, willingness, or permission inherent in the subject.
Aspectual: Relating to grammatical aspect.
Aspectual class: The classification of verbs into categories such as stative, activity, accomplishment, and achievement.
Stative: An aspectual class for verbs describing states rather than events, such as "know" or "love."
Activity: An aspectual class for verbs describing unbounded events, such as "run" or "swim."
Accomplishment: An aspectual class for verbs describing bounded events with a durative process, such as "build a house."
Achievement: An aspectual class for verbs describing instantaneous, punctual events, such as "arrive" or "recognize."
Atelic: Describing an event or predicate that does not have an inherent endpoint.
Telic: Describing an event or predicate that has an inherent endpoint.
Inchoative: A verb or construction that introduces the beginning of a state or process.
Inchoative: (already listed)
Causative: (already listed)
Anticausative: A construction in which a caused event is expressed without an external agent, as in "The door opened."
Reciprocal: (already listed)
Reflexive: (already listed)
Middle: A verb form or construction in which the subject is affected by the action but no explicit agent is expressed.
Delexical verb: A verb with little lexical content that contributes mainly to the event structure, such as "have" in "have a look."
Light verb: A verb that contributes little meaning and relies on a nominal complement for content, such as "give" in "give a shout."
Resultative: A construction expressing the result state of an event, such as "He hammered the metal flat."
Resultative: (already listed)
Result state: The state of affairs that exists after an event is completed.
Event structure: The decomposition of a verb's meaning into sub-events, such as a causing event and a result state.
Vendlerian classification: The classification of verbs into states, activities, accomplishments, and achievements.
Halle and Keyser: The classic framework for classifying verb aspectual properties.
Lexicalized: A form or meaning that is stored in the mental lexicon as a fixed unit.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning is not predictable from the meanings of its individual words.
Idiomatic: Having a meaning that is not predictable from the literal meanings of the components.
Colloquial: Informal, everyday language usage.
Archaic: A word or form no longer in current use.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
Morphosemantics: The study of the semantic relationships within and between morphemes.
Semantic decomposition: The analysis of a word's meaning into simpler, more primitive semantic components.
Semantic feature: A basic unit of meaning used to characterize and contrast lexical items.
Prototype theory: The theory that categories are organized around typical exemplars rather than strict necessary and sufficient conditions.
Cognitive linguistics: An approach to linguistics that emphasizes the role of cognition, perception, and embodied experience in language.
Conceptual metaphor: A mapping from a concrete source domain to an abstract target domain, as in "time is money."
Metaphor: A figurative expression in which one domain is described in terms of another.
Metonymy: A figurative expression in which one entity is referred to by the name of a related entity, such as "the White House announced."
Image schema: A basic, pre-linguistic pattern of experience, such as container, path, or force, that structures meaning.
Cognitive grammar: A framework developed by Langacker that treats linguistic structure as conceptual structure.
Radical construction grammar: A usage-based framework in which grammatical knowledge consists of a continuum of constructions.
Construction grammar: A theoretical approach in which the basic unit of linguistic knowledge is a construction pairing form with meaning.
Usage-based: An approach to language that emphasizes the role of frequency, embodiment, and general cognitive mechanisms.
Embodied cognition: The theory that cognition is deeply shaped by the body and its interactions with the environment.
Prototype: The most typical or central member of a category.
Categorical extension: The extension of a word's meaning from a prototype to more peripheral members.
Polysemy: The property of a word or expression having multiple related meanings.
Homonymy: The property of two or more distinct words having the same form but different meanings.
Ambiguity: The property of an expression having two or more possible interpretations.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity at the word level, such as "bank" (financial institution vs. river edge).
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the syntactic structure of a sentence.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and their meanings in a language.
Mental lexicon: The cognitive representation of a speaker's word knowledge.
Lexical entry: The complete representation of a word in the lexicon, including phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic information.
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word.
Lexical item: A word or multi-word expression stored as a unit in the lexicon.
Compounding: (already listed)
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes category without affixation, such as "to google."
Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix, such as "edit" from "editor."
Clipping: The shortening of a word without changing its meaning, such as "phone" from "telephone."
Blend: A word formed by combining parts of two words, such as "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, such as "NASA" or "UNESCO."
Abbreviation: A shortened form of a word or phrase, including initialisms and clippings.
Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that imitate natural sounds, such as "buzz" or "sizzle."
Pejoration: The historical deterioration of a word's meaning.
Amelioration: The historical improvement of a word's meaning.
Semantic bleaching: The loss of specific lexical meaning, often in grammaticalized function words.
Semantic drift: The gradual change in the meaning of a word over time.
Broadening: The extension of a word's meaning to cover a wider range of referents.
Narrowing: The restriction of a word's meaning to a narrower range of referents.
Metonymy: (already listed)
Metaphor: (already listed)
Pragmatic enrichment: The addition of meaning beyond the literal semantic content through pragmatic inference.
Grice: Paul Grice, the philosopher who formulated the theory of conversational implicature.
Maxim of Quantity: The principle of being as informative as required but no more.
Maxim of Quality: The principle of being truthful and not asserting what one lacks evidence for.
Maxim of Relation: The principle of being relevant.
Maxim of Manner: The principle of being clear, orderly, and brief.
Flout: A deliberate, recognizable violation of a maxim to generate an implicature.
Breach: An undeliberate violation of a maxim.
Opt-out: A speaker's explicit disclaimer of the truthfulness of a statement, e.g., "or so they say."
Conversational implicature: (already listed)
Particularized implicature: An implicature that depends on the specific context in which an utterance is made.
Generalized conversational implicature: An implicature that is generated in a wide range of contexts.
Presupposition: (already listed)
Accommodating: The process by which a listener adjusts their background knowledge to make sense of an utterance.
Implicature: (already listed)
Speech act theory: The framework developed by Austin and Searle for analyzing the actions performed by utterances.
Illocutionary act: The act performed by the utterance itself, such as promising, warning, or requesting.
Perlocutionary act: The effect the utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, scaring, or inspiring.
Performative verb: A verb that names the speech act it performs, such as "promise" in "I promise to be there."
Constative: A type of utterance that describes a state of affairs and can be true or false.
Direct speech: The reporting of another's words in quotation marks.
Indirect speech: The reporting of another's words in the reporter's own words and syntax.
Reported speech: The grammaticalized reporting of another's utterance, including tense shift and pronoun change.
Free indirect speech: A narrative technique that blends a character's thoughts with the narrator's voice without quotation marks.
Historical linguistics: The study of how languages change over time.
Diachronic: Relating to the study of language change over time, as opposed to synchronic description.
Synchronic: Relating to the study of a language at a single point in time.
Comparative method: The method of reconstructing proto-languages by comparing related modern languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed through the comparative method.
Reconstruction: The process of inferring the phonological, morphological, and lexical properties of a proto-language.
Sound change: A systematic phonological change that affects all instances of a sound in a language.
Regular sound change: A sound change that applies uniformly without exceptions, as described by Neogrammarian theory.
Neogrammarian: The historical-linguistic school that posited the exceptionlessness of sound change.
Exceptionlessness: The principle that sound changes are regular and do not have individual exceptions.
Analogical change: A change in form driven by pattern-matching and regularization rather than a regular sound law.

Split: The diachronic division of a single phoneme into two or more phonemes.
Neutralization: The loss of a phonemic contrast in a particular environment.
Phonemic split: The historical division of one phoneme into two.
Phonemic merger: (already listed)
Reanalysis: The reinterpretation of the boundaries or structure of a linguistic form.
Morphologization: The process by which a lexical item becomes a grammatical morpheme.
Grammaticalization: The process by which lexical items evolve into grammatical markers over time.
Delexicalization: The loss of specific lexical content during grammaticalization.
Function word: A word that primarily expresses grammatical relationships, such as prepositions, conjunctions, and articles.
Content word: A word that carries lexical meaning, such as nouns, verbs, and adjectives.
Open class: A word class that readily accepts new members, such as nouns and verbs.
Closed class: A word class that does not readily accept new members, such as prepositions and determiners.

Morphosyntax: The interface between morphological and syntactic structure.
Agreement: The morphological marking of a relationship between a head and a dependent, such as subject-verb agreement.
Concord: Another term for agreement, especially in the context of noun-adjective or noun-article agreement.
Government: The relationship in which one element determines the form of another, such as case assignment.
Subordination: The syntactic relationship in which one clause depends on another.
Coordination: The syntactic relationship in which two elements of equal rank are joined.

Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb.
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective.
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition.
Determiner phrase: A phrase headed by a determiner.
Complement clause: A clause that functions as the complement of a verb, adjective, or noun.

Interrogative clause: A clause that expresses a question, such as "whether he came" or "what she said."
Embedded question: A question that is embedded within a larger clause, such as "I don't know where he is."
Tag question: A short question appended to a statement, such as "It's cold, isn't it?"
Vocative: The grammatical case or form used to address someone directly.
Interjection: A word expressing a sudden emotion, such as "oh," "wow," or "ouch."

Preposition: A word placed before a noun or pronoun to express a relationship, such as "in," "on," "at."
Postposition: A word placed after a noun to express a relationship, common in Japanese and Turkish.
Circumposition: A prepositional-like element that surrounds a noun phrase with two parts.
Case marker: A morpheme that marks the grammatical case of a noun phrase.
Case government: The assignment of a particular case to a noun phrase by a governing element.

Nominative-accusative: An alignment system in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is marked the same way.
Ergative-absolutive: An alignment system in which the subject of intransitive verbs is marked the same as the object of transitive verbs.
Split-S: An alignment system in which the subject is marked differently depending on person, number, or animacy.
Split-ergative: A system that alternates between ergative and nominative-accusative alignment depending on tense, aspect, or person.
Alignment: The system by which languages mark the roles of arguments in transitive and intransitive clauses.
A-marked: The form or case marking the subject of an intransitive verb (S) in an ergative system.
A-ergative: The form or case marking the subject of a transitive verb (A) in an ergative system.
O-marked: The form or case marking the object of a transitive verb (O) in an ergative system.
