response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Allophone: A specific phonetic realization of a phoneme that does not contrastively change word meaning.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permitted in a given language.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a speech sound that typically has a peak (nucleus) of sonority and may include an onset and coda.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster at the beginning of a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster at the end of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel or syllabic consonant.
Mora: A unit of syllable weight used in prosodic phonology to account for syllable duration and stress patterns.
VOT: Voice Onset Time, the interval between the release of a stop consonant and the onset of voicing.
Coarticulation: The overlapping of articulatory gestures so that the production of one sound influences adjacent sounds.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less similar to a neighboring sound.
Metathesis: A phonological process in which the order of two or more sounds is reversed.
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable in connected speech.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word, typically to ease pronunciation or resolve a prohibited sequence.
Deletion: The removal of a segment from a phonological representation.
Palatalization: A sound change or feature in which a consonant is articulated with the tongue body raised toward the hard palate.
Velarization: A secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue is raised toward the soft palate.
Labialization: A secondary articulation involving rounding of the lips on a consonant or vowel.
Pharyngealization: A secondary articulation involving constriction of the pharyngeal wall.
Glottalization: The closure or near-closure of the glottis during the articulation of a sound.
Spirantization: A lenition process in which a stop consonant changes into a fricative.
Fortition: A sound change in which a weaker sound becomes a stronger one.
Lenition: A sound change in which a stronger sound becomes a weaker one.
Vowel Harmony: A phonological process in which vowels within a word or phrase agree in some feature such as frontness, backness, or height.
Consonant Harmony: A phonological process in which consonants within a word agree in a particular feature.
Neutralization: A situation in which a phonemic contrast is lost in a particular environment, so that two sounds merge.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phoneme representing a set of phonemes that are in complementary distribution and have no free variation.
Minimal Pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the sounds are contrastive.
Complementary Distribution: A relationship between two sounds that never occur in the same phonetic environment.
Free Variation: A situation in which two or more allophones may occur in the same environment without changing meaning.
Distinctive Feature: A binary property (such as [+voice] or [-nasal]) used to distinguish phonemes from one another.
Feature Geometry: A theoretical model organizing distinctive features into hierarchical tiers to account for their behavior in phonological processes.
Prosody: The suprasegmental aspects of speech, including stress, tone, intonation, rhythm, and length.
Suprasegmental: A phonological property that extends across more than one segment, such as tone, stress, or intonation.
Segment: A single discrete unit of sound (consonant or vowel) in the phonological representation.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch to distinguish lexical meaning or grammatical function, as in tonal languages.
Register: A high or low pitch level used to distinguish word meaning, particularly in some tonal languages.
Intonation: The melody or pitch contour of an utterance that conveys grammatical, pragmatic, or attitudinal information.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable, typically realized through greater duration, louder amplitude, and higher pitch.
Rhythm: The patterning of stressed and unstressed syllables (or mora/timing units) over the course of an utterance.
Creaky Voice: A type of laryngeal phonation in which the vocal folds vibrate irregularly, producing a raspy sound.
Whistle Vowel: A vowel produced with a constriction in the vocal tract that creates a high-frequency whistle-like formant.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, without a significant constriction.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
Plosive: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air.
Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that causes turbulent airflow.
Nasal: A consonant produced with closure in the oral cavity and airflow through the nasal passage.
Lateral: A consonant produced with a closure in the center of the tongue and airflow directed around the sides.
Rhotic: A consonant that is the typical "r" sound in a language, realized as a trill, tap, fricative, or approximant.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid vibrations of a articulator, such as the tongue tip.
Tap: A single, brief contact of an articulator, such as a single tap of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge.
Flap: A consonant similar to a tap, produced by a single rapid movement of the tongue body.
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic airstream mechanism, involving a sharp closure and release of the glottis.
Implosive: A consonant produced with an ingressive glottalic airstream, involving a lowering of the larynx.
Voiced: A consonant or other sound produced with the vocal folds vibrating during articulation.
Voiceless: A consonant or other sound produced with the vocal folds apart and not vibrating.
Aspirated: A consonant, typically a stop, followed by a strong burst of breath.
Unaspirated: A stop consonant released with little or no burst of breath.
Labial: A consonant or vowel articulated with the lips.
Dental: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth.
Alveolar: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge.
Postalveolar: A consonant articulated just behind the alveolar ridge.
Retroflex: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip curled back toward the mid-palate.
Palatal: A consonant articulated with the tongue body raised toward the hard palate.
Velar: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate.
Uvular: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue or the pharyngeal wall near the uvula.
Pharyngeal: A consonant articulated with the tongue root and the pharyngeal wall in close approximation.
Glottal: A consonant or sound produced at the level of the glottis.
Front Vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue body raised toward the front of the mouth.
Back Vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue body raised toward the back of the mouth.
Central Vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue body in a mid, non-front, non-back position.
Open Vowel: A vowel produced with the jaw lowered and the tongue low in the mouth.
Closed Vowel: A vowel produced with the jaw raised and the tongue high in the mouth.
Mid Vowel: A vowel produced with a moderate degree of tongue elevation.
Tense Vowel: A vowel produced with relatively greater muscular tension and longer duration.
Lax Vowel: A vowel produced with relatively less muscular tension and shorter duration.
Rounded Vowel: A vowel articulated with lip rounding.
Unrounded Vowel: A vowel articulated with unrounded, spread, or neutral lips.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum of a vowel, produced by the resonating vocal tract.
F0: The fundamental frequency of a voice, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration.
Acoustic Phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of their physical properties, including frequency, amplitude, and duration.
Articulatory Phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the movements and positions of the articulators.
Auditory Phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of their perception by the human ear and auditory system.
X-ray Phonetics: A method of articulatory phonetics using X-ray imaging to observe the movements of articulators during speech.
Electropalatography: A technique using electrical sensors in a prosthetic palate to measure tongue-palate contact during speech.
Ultrasound: A high-frequency imaging technique used to observe subcutaneous articulatory movements, especially of the tongue and larynx.
Chain Shift: A systematic, ordered series of sound changes in which each segment shifts to the position vacated by another.
Sound Change: A systematic phonological change in a language over time.
Sound Law: A regular, predictable pattern of historical sound change, such as Grimm's Law.
Grimm's Law: The first of the three sounds shifts of Germanic, describing the changes from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic stops.
Verner's Law: A phonological rule explaining the voicing of certain Germanic fricatives in alternation with their voiceless counterparts.
Rhotacism: A sound change in which a lateral or other consonant becomes an r-like sound.
Umlaut: A sound change in which a vowel is fronted or raised due to the influence of a following, typically deleted, vowel.
Apheresis: The loss of a sound or syllable at the beginning of a word.
Apocope: The loss of a sound or syllable at the end of a word.
Syncope: The loss of a sound or syllable from the interior of a word.
Assibilation: A sound change in which a stop or affricate acquires a fricative (sibilant) release.
Debuccalization: A sound change in which a consonant is weakened to a glottal sound or deleted entirely.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or grammatical function.
Morph: The smallest unit of a word that is a manifestation of a morpheme.
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme, such as the English plural morpheme realized as /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem, such as a prefix or suffix.
Prefix: An affix that precedes the root or stem of a word.
Suffix: An affix that follows the root or stem of a word.
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root or stem of a word.
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that surrounds a stem, consisting of a prefix and suffix that function as a unit.
Suprafix: A bound morpheme realized as a suprasegmental feature, such as stress or tone, added to a stem.
Root: The core, unanalyzable morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning.
Stem: The base form of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached.
Bound Morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free Morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word.
Derivational Morpheme: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech or meaning.
Inflectional Morpheme: An affix that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without creating a new word.
Agglutination: A morphological type in which words are formed by concatenating multiple morphemes with relatively little or no phonological alteration.
Fusion: A morphological type in which multiple grammatical categories are expressed by a single affix or portmanteau morpheme.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words typically consist of a single morpheme and grammatical relations are expressed by word order or particles.
Polysynthesis: A morphological type in which words can incorporate multiple morphemes representing what other languages express as entire phrases or clauses.
Suppletion: An irregular morphological alternation in which a morpheme has an entirely unrelated allomorph, as in English "go/went."
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes or stems are combined to create a new word.
Reduplication: A word-formation or grammatical process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express a change in meaning or grammar.
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened without changing its meaning, as in "phone" for "telephone."
Blending: A word-formation process in which parts of two words are combined to create a new word, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "editor" from "edit."
Borrowing: The process by which a language adopts a word from another language.
Onomatopoeia: A word that phonetically imitates or suggests the sound or sensation it refers to, such as "buzz" or "splash."
Interlinguistic Borrowing: The adoption of words or morphemes from one language into another through contact.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.
Cognate: A word in two or more languages that shares a common ancestral form in a proto-language.
Loanword: A word borrowed from another language and integrated into the borrowing language's vocabulary.
Calque: A word or expression translated literally from another language, word by word or morpheme by morpheme.
False Friend: A word pair in two languages that looks or sounds similar but has a different meaning.
Paradigm: The complete set of grammatical forms of a word, such as all the conjugated forms of a verb or the declensions of a noun.
Morphological Type: A classification of languages based on the predominant strategies of word formation and grammatical marking.
Morpheme Boundary: The juncture between morphemes within a word, which may or may not be phonologically marked.
Morphological Process: A rule or operation that generates new forms from existing morphemes, such as affixation or reduplication.
Morphological Productivity: The degree to which a particular word-formation process is actively used to create new words in a language.
Zero Morpheme: The absence of a morphological marker where a grammatical function is still understood from context.
Portmanteau: A single morpheme or affix that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical categories.
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, gender, or case.
Conjugation: The paradigm of a verb, showing all its grammatical forms across person, number, tense, mood, and aspect.
Declension: The paradigm of a noun, adjective, or pronoun, showing its forms across case, number, and gender.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word from an existing root or stem, often with a change in part of speech.
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its grammatical category without any overt morphological change, as in "to walk" (verb) from "walk" (noun).
Zero Derivation: Derivation that involves no overt affixation or phonological change.
Inflectional Class: A set of words that share the same pattern of inflectional endings.
Productive Morphology: Morphological processes that are actively used by speakers to form new words.
Unproductive Morphology: Morphological processes that are no longer actively used but persist in existing vocabulary.
Bound Root: A root morpheme that cannot appear as a free word and must be combined with other morphemes.
Floating Vowel: A vocalic element in a language's phonology that is not syllabified in every context but appears in certain morphological or prosodic environments.
Morphophonemic: Pertaining to the interaction between morphology and phonology, where morpheme realization depends on the surrounding morphemes.
Allomorphy: The existence of multiple phonological forms for a single morpheme.
Morpheme Complexity: The number and arrangement of morphemes within a word or morphological structure.
Agglutinative Morpheme: A morpheme that is added to a stem with minimal or no phonological interaction with the stem or adjacent affixes.
Fusional Morpheme: A single affix that encodes more than one grammatical feature simultaneously.
Supra-segmental Morphology: Morphological processes that involve suprasegmental properties such as stress, tone, or length rather than segmental changes.
Tone Morphology: The use of pitch contrasts to mark grammatical or lexical distinctions.
Stress Morphology: The use of stress placement to distinguish words or grammatical categories.
Length Morphology: The use of segmental or syllabic length to mark grammatical distinctions.
Morphological Alignment: The consistent mapping between grammatical relations and morphological case marking across a language.
Nominative-Accusative Alignment: A case-marking system in which the subject of a transitive verb is grouped with the subject of an intransitive verb (nominative) and the object is in a distinct case (accusative).
Ergative-Absolutive Alignment: A case-marking system in which the subject of an intransitive verb is grouped with the object of a transitive verb (absolutive) and the subject of a transitive verb is in a distinct case (ergative).
Ergativity: The property of a language or construction in which the agent of a transitive verb is marked differently from the subject of an intransitive verb and the object.
Split Ergativity: A system in which a language uses both ergative and nominative-accusative alignment, typically conditioned by tense, aspect, or transitivity.
Tripartite Alignment: A case-marking system in which the subject of transitive verbs, the subject of intransitive verbs, and the object of transitive verbs are all marked with distinct cases.
Absolutive: The case marking the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive system.
Ergative: The case marking the subject of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive system.
Nominative: The case typically marking the subject of a clause in a nominative-accusative system.
Accusative: The case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb in a nominative-accusative system.
Dative: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient in a clause.
Genitive: The case expressing possession, origin, or a relation similar to a possessive.
Instrumental: The case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Locative: The case marking location or position.
Ablative: The case marking separation or movement away from something.
Allative: The case marking movement toward or arrival at a location.
Vocative: The case used in direct address.
Instrumental Case: The case form marking the tool or means used to perform an action.
Case Marking: The use of grammatical case to indicate the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase.
Morphological Case: Case expressed through bound affixes on the noun itself.
Syntactic Case: Case expressed through separate particles, prepositions, or postpositions.
Noun Class: A grammatical category of nouns, often marked by agreement on other words, as in Bantu noun class systems.
Gender: A grammatical categorization of nouns (and associated words) into classes such as masculine, feminine, and neuter.
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, plural, and other quantities.
Dual: The grammatical number form referring to exactly two entities.
Paucal: The grammatical number form referring to a few entities, between dual and plural.
Mass Noun: A noun that refers to a substance or concept not naturally divided into countable units.
Count Noun: A noun that refers to entities that can be counted as discrete units.
Collective Noun: A noun that refers to a group of individuals as a single unit.
Diminutive: A morphological form expressing smallness or endearment.
Augmentative: A morphological form expressing largeness or emphasis.
Pejorative: A morphological form expressing contempt, dislike, or a derogatory quality.
Honorific: A grammatical or morphological form expressing respect or social deference.
Politeness: A set of linguistic and paralinguistic strategies used to manage social relations and face.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker, addressee, and third party, typically marked on verbs and pronouns.
Clitic: A word that depends on a neighboring word for its phonological or syntactic behavior but has some independent morphological status.
Particle: A small function word or morpheme that modifies or adds nuance to a sentence or phrase.
Interjection: A word or expression used to express a sudden emotion or reaction, often outside the syntactic structure of a sentence.
Determiner: A word that introduces and specifies a noun phrase, such as articles or demonstratives.
Classifier: A word or morpheme used with nouns, especially in classifier languages, to categorize them by shape, type, or function.
Nominalizer: A morpheme that converts a verb or clause into a noun phrase.
Gerund: The -ing form of a verb used as a noun, as in "swimming is fun."
Infinitive: The base form of a verb, often marked by a particle, as in "to swim" in English.
Participle: A verb form used as an adjective or in perfect/continuous constructions, as in "broken" or "having gone."
Gerundive: A verbal adjective expressing necessity or obligation, as in Latin "legendus" (to be read).
Periphrasis: The use of a multi-word construction to express a meaning that is otherwise expressed by a single word or morpheme.
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to form a verbal complex, expressing tense, aspect, mood, or voice.
Modal Verb: An auxiliary expressing modality, such as ability, obligation, permission, or likelihood.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speech, such as past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event, such as completeness, duration, or repetition.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of the speaker's information, such as direct observation, hearsay, or inference.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as whether it is asserted, commanded, or desired.
Indicative Mood: The mood used for statements of fact or questions about reality.
Subjunctive Mood: The mood used for hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations.
Imperative Mood: The mood used for commands or requests.
Optative Mood: The mood used to express wishes or hopes.
Jussive Mood: The mood used for commands, often with a second or third person subject.
Conditional Mood: The mood expressing a hypothetical situation and its consequence.
Voice: A grammatical category that relates the arguments of a verb to their roles in the event.
Active Voice: A construction in which the subject of the verb is the agent of the action.
Passive Voice: A construction in which the subject of the verb is the patient or theme of the action, and the agent is demoted or omitted.
Middle Voice: A voice construction in which the subject is both agent and patient, often implying self-directed action.
Reflexive: A construction in which the subject and object of a verb are the same entity.
Reciprocal: A construction expressing a mutual action between two or more participants.
Causative: A voice construction in which an agent causes another participant to perform an action.
Inchoative: A voice construction in which a theme comes to be in a state without an external agent.
Stative: A verb type that describes a state rather than an action or process.
Perfective Aspect: An aspectual category presenting an event as a complete, bounded whole.
Imperfective Aspect: An aspectual category presenting an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded.
Habitual Aspect: An aspectual category expressing repeated or regular occurrence of an event.
Ingressive Aspect: An aspectual category marking the beginning of a state or event.
Egressive Aspect: An aspectual category marking the end of a state or event.
Durative Aspect: An aspectual category emphasizing the duration or ongoing nature of an event.
Punctual Aspect: An aspectual category presenting an event as occurring at a single point in time.
Aorist: An aspectual or temporal category, historically in Greek, presenting an action without reference to its internal temporal structure.
Futurate: A tense or aspect form referring to an event in the future.
Perfect: A grammatical category linking a past event to the present, often implying present relevance.
Pluperfect: A grammatical category expressing an event completed before another past event.
Progressive: An aspect or tense form expressing an ongoing action at a particular time.
Iterative: An aspectual or verbal form expressing repeated or repeated-attempt action.
Frequentative: A verbal form expressing the repeated or frequent occurrence of an action.
Semelfactive: A verbal form expressing a single, brief occurrence of an action.
Cognitivism: A theoretical orientation in linguistics emphasizing the role of general cognitive processes in language.
Cognitive Linguistics: A theoretical framework that analyzes language in terms of general cognitive mechanisms such as categorization, conceptual metaphor, and image schemas.
Conceptual Metaphor: A cross-domain mapping in which one conceptual domain (source) structures understanding of another (target), as in "ARGUMENT IS WAR."
Image Schema: A basic, pre-conceptual structure of experience, such as container, path, or force, that underlies linguistic expression.
Prototype Theory: A theory of categorization in which categories have a central, prototypical member with more typical features, and membership is graded rather than bounded.
Graded Membership: The idea that category membership is a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing property.
Frame Semantics: A theory of lexical meaning in which word meaning is understood in terms of background knowledge structures or frames.
Lexical Conceptual Structure: A model of lexical meaning that includes semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic information.
Radial Category: A word sense structure in which senses are organized around a central prototype with related but distinct extensions.
Mental Lexicon: The cognitive representation of a speaker's knowledge of word forms, meanings, and grammatical properties.
Lexical Access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word from the mental lexicon during comprehension or production.
Semantic Field: A set of words related to a common topic or conceptual domain.
Polysemy: The property of a single word having multiple related meanings.
Homonymy: The property of two or more unrelated words sharing the same form.
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or very similar meaning.
Antonymy: The relationship between words with opposite meanings.
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is included within the meaning of a broader word, such as "sparrow" being a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernym: A word whose meaning encompasses the meanings of more specific words, such as "bird" being a hypernym of "sparrow."
Meronym: A word whose meaning represents a part of the whole denoted by another word, such as "wheel" being a meronym of "car."
Holonym: A word whose meaning represents the whole of which another word is a part, such as "car" being a holonym of "wheel."
Entailment: A logical relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be accepted as true for an utterance to be interpretable.
Implicature: A meaning conveyed by an utterance that is not part of its literal semantic content but is inferred by the hearer.
Conversational Implicature: An implicature derived from the application of Grice's conversational maxims.
Conventional Implicature: An implicature associated with a specific word or expression regardless of context.
Gricean Maxims: Four principles of conversation (quantity, quality, relation, and manner) proposed by H.P. Grice.
Cooperative Principle: Grice's overarching principle that participants in a conversation generally cooperate in making their contributions relevant and informative.
Speech Act: An utterance that performs an action beyond merely describing a state of affairs, such as promising, ordering, or declaring.
Illocutionary Act: The action performed in the course of making an utterance, such as warning, promising, or requesting.
Perlocutionary Act: The effect of an utterance on the hearer's beliefs, emotions, or actions.
Locutionary Act: The basic act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific semantic content.
Direct Speech Act: An utterance in which the form of the sentence directly matches the illocutionary force.
Indirect Speech Act: An utterance in which the illocutionary force differs from what the sentence form would ordinarily convey.
Performative: A speech act that brings about a change in the world by virtue of being uttered, such as "I now pronounce you husband and wife."
Directive: A speech act category in which the speaker attempts to get the hearer to do something.
Commissive: A speech act category in which the speaker commits to performing a future action.
Expressive: A speech act category in which the speaker expresses a psychological state about a state of affairs.
Assertive: A speech act category in which the speaker commits to the truth of a proposition.
Exclamative: A speech act category in which the speaker expresses strong emotion or reaction.
Deixis: The use of words whose reference depends on the context of the utterance, such as "I," "here," and "now."
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to an antecedent mentioned earlier in discourse.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an antecedent mentioned later in discourse.
Coreference: A relation between two expressions in a text that refer to the same entity.
Binding: The syntactic and semantic rules governing the reference of pronouns and other anaphoric expressions.
Binding Theory: A component of syntax that specifies conditions on the interpretation of pronouns, reflexives, and noun phrases.
A-command: A structural relation in which one node is the first sister of a node that dominates the first node.
C-command: A structural relation in which one node dominates all sisters of another node and does not dominate the other node itself.
Theta Role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a verb, such as agent, patient, theme, goal, or source.
Theta Criterion: The principle that each theta role must be assigned to exactly one argument, and each argument must receive exactly one theta role.
Trace: An empty category left behind in a syntactic structure when an element has been moved from its original position.
PRO: An unexpressed, non-pronoun subject, typically found in non-finite clauses.
Pro: A null pronoun that is syntactically and semantically full but not phonologically realized, found in pro-drop languages.
Empty Category: A position in a syntactic structure that is not filled by a pronounced element.
Government and Binding: A syntactic framework developed by Chomsky in the 1980s, comprising modules including theta theory, case theory, binding theory, and trace theory.
Principles and Parameters: A theoretical framework in which universal principles of syntax are combined with language-specific parameters to account for cross-linguistic variation.
Universal Grammar: The innate, language-specific cognitive system that underlies all human languages.
Language Acquisition Device: A hypothetical innate mechanism proposed by Chomsky to explain how children acquire language.
Critical Period: A hypothesized window of developmental time during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and easily.
First Language Acquisition: The process by which infants and children acquire their native language.
Second Language Acquisition: The process by which individuals learn a language after already having acquired one or more other languages.
Input: The linguistic data a language learner is exposed to, including the sentences and structures they hear.
Output: The linguistic production a language learner generates during acquisition.
Overregularization: A developmental error in which a learner applies a regular rule to an irregular form, as in "goed" instead of "went."
Telegraphic Speech: A stage in first language acquisition in which children produce short, content-word-only utterances.
Holophrase: A single word used by a toddler to express a complete thought or sentence.
Morpheme Order Hypothesis: The observation that children acquire morphemes in a relatively consistent order across languages.
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or multi-word expression becomes a single word or fixed lexical item.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be predicted from the literal meanings of its individual components.
Collocation: A statistically frequent and natural co-occurrence of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "*do a decision."
Phrasal Verb: A multi-word verb consisting of a verb and one or more particles or prepositions, such as "give up" or "look after."
Compounded: Formed by the combination of two or more words into a single word.
Portmanteau Word: A single word formed by blending parts of two words, as in "brunch" or "smog."
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression in a language.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or activity.
Slang: Informal, often transient vocabulary used within a particular social group.
Register (Stylistic): A variety of language associated with a particular social context, audience, or purpose.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community.
Idiolect: The unique variety of language used by an individual speaker.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as by class, education, or profession.
Ethnolect: A variety of language associated with an ethnic or cultural group.
Standard Language: A variety of a language that is codified, often in a grammar and dictionary, and used in formal contexts.
Prestige Variety: A dialect or register that is socially valued and associated with higher social status.
Stigmatized Variety: A dialect or register that is socially devalued and associated with lower social status.
Linguistic Prestige: The social value attributed to particular language varieties, accents, or registers.
Linguistic Stereotype: A fixed, often negative, association between a linguistic variety and a social group.
Language Attitude: A person's feelings, beliefs, and evaluations regarding a language or dialect.
Diglossia: A situation in which two varieties of a language are used in complementary social domains, such as a high and a low variety.
Code-Switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-Mixing: The practice of combining elements of two or more languages within a single utterance or sentence.
Bilingualism: The ability or practice of using two languages.
Multilingualism: The ability or practice of using more than two languages.
Trilingualism: The ability or practice of using three languages.
Heritage Language: A non-majority language maintained within a family or community as a second or home language.
Lingua Franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language.
Creole: A natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Lexifier: The language that provides most of the vocabulary of a creole or pidgin.
Substrate: A language that influences a superstrate language in a contact situation, typically contributing phonological or syntactic features.
Superstrate: A language of the socially dominant group that influences a substrate language in a contact situation.
Adstrate: A language of the same social level as another that mutually influences it through contact.
Language Contact: The interaction between two or more languages in a shared speech community, leading to mutual influence.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a map that separates areas with different linguistic features.
Isophone: A boundary line separating areas with different phonological features.
Isograph: A boundary line separating areas with different grammatical features.
Dialect Continuum: A chain of dialects in which adjacent varieties are mutually intelligible but non-adjacent varieties may not be.
Mutual Intelligibility: The degree to which speakers of two language varieties can understand each other without prior study.
Language Family: A group of languages that descend from a common proto-language, established through the comparative method.
Language Isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language.
Proto-Language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed from its descendant languages.
Comparative Method: A systematic method of historical linguistics used to establish genetic relationships between languages through regular sound correspondences.
Reconstruction: The process of inferring the form and features of a proto-language from its attested descendant languages.
Diachronic Linguistics: The study of language change over time.
Synchronic Linguistics: The study of a language at a single point in time, without reference to its history.
Generative Grammar: A framework of syntax, originally developed by Chomsky, that seeks to characterize the set of all grammatical sentences of a language.
Transformational Grammar: An early generative framework in which surface structures are derived from deep structures through transformational rules.
Deep Structure: The abstract syntactic representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface Structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformational rules have been applied, corresponding to the spoken form.
Phrase Structure Rule: A rule that specifies how constituents combine to form larger constituents in a phrase structure.
Constituency: The property of a string of words forming a single grammatical unit that can be treated as a whole in syntactic operations.
Constituent: A grammatical unit within a sentence that functions as a single element, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Constituent Structure: The hierarchical arrangement of constituents within a sentence.
X-bar Theory: A framework in syntax that describes the internal structure of phrases using a generalized schema (X, X-bar, X') common to all phrase types.
Spec (Specifier): The position within a phrase that is external to the complement and X-bar but internal to the maximal projection.
Complement: The constituent that follows a head and completes its meaning.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase, often expressing manner, time, place, or reason.
Head: The central, most semantically prominent element of a phrase that determines its category.
Head Complement: The relationship between a head and the phrase that follows it and is selected by it.
Head Modification: The relationship between a head and a following modifier that is not selected by the head.
Subcategorization: The specification of the arguments and/or adjuncts that a particular predicate requires or allows.
Subcategorization Frame: The set of argument and adjunct requirements associated with a particular verb or predicate.
Selectional Restriction: A semantic constraint on the arguments of a predicate, such as the requirement that "eat" takes a edible theme.
Valency: The number of arguments a predicate requires to form a complete proposition.
Valence: The number and type of arguments a predicate can or must have.
Argument Structure: The set of semantic roles and syntactic positions associated with a predicate.
Theta Grid: The mapping of theta roles to syntactic positions in a clause.
External Argument: The argument of a clause that is not part of the verb phrase, typically the subject.
Internal Argument: The argument(s) of a clause that are part of the verb phrase, typically the object(s).
Unaccusative: A verb whose sole argument is a theme or patient, as in "fall" or "arrive."
Unergative: A verb whose sole argument is an agent, as in "sleep" or "laugh."
Unaccusative Hypothesis: The proposal that unaccusative verbs differ from unergative verbs in the theta role of their single argument.
Causative/Inchoative Alternation: A verb alternation in which a transitive causative form and an intransitive inchoative form share a common root.
Passive Alternation: A verb alternation in which a transitive active form and an intransitive passive form are related.
Anticausative: A construction in which an agent is omitted or not expressed, as in "The door opened" versus "Someone opened the door."
Light Verb: A verb with minimal lexical meaning that combines with a nominal complement, as in "make a decision" or "have a look."
Heavy NP Shift: A syntactic movement in which a long or complex noun phrase is moved to the right, typically after a verb and adverb.
Extraposition: A syntactic process in which a constituent, often a clause, is moved out of its original position to a clause-final or clause-initial position.
Left Dislocation: A construction in which a constituent is fronted and resumed by a pronoun in the main clause.
Right Dislocation: A construction in which a constituent is appended after the main clause and resumed by a pronoun within it.
Topic: The element of a sentence or discourse about which the utterance is made.
Focus: The element of a sentence that conveys new, contrastive, or emphasized information.
Information Structure: The organization of an utterance in terms of given (old) and new (new) information, topic and focus.
Given: Information that is already established or presupposed in the discourse.
New: Information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
Topic-Focus Articulation: The division of a clause into a preverbal topic and a postverbal focus.
Scrambling: A syntactic process, common in languages like Japanese and Turkish, in which the linear order of arguments is freely permutable.
Word Order: The linear arrangement of words and constituents in a sentence.
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object.
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb.
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object.
V2: A property of clause structure in which the finite verb occupies the second position in a main clause, as in German and Dutch.
Head Initial: A phrase structure in which the head precedes its complement.
Head Final: A phrase structure in which the head follows its complement.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a clause, such as "that" in English or "if" in conditionals.
Subordinate Clause: A clause that is embedded within another clause and cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
Main Clause: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence and is not embedded within another clause.
Matrix Clause: The outer clause in an embedding relationship, within which another clause is embedded.
Embedded Clause: A clause that is contained within the structure of another clause.
Relative Clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and contains a relative pronoun or a gap.
Relative Pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause, such as "who," "which," or "that" in English.
Gap: An empty position in a clause where an element has been extracted, such as the missing object in "the book [that I read ___]."
Wh- Movement: A syntactic process in which an interrogative or relative phrase moves to a clause-initial position, as in English.
Wh- In-Situ: A strategy in which a wh-phrase remains in its base-generated position rather than moving, as in Chinese.
Question Word: A word used to form a question, such as "who," "what," "where," "when," "why," or "how."
Ergative: A case or construction marking the agent of a transitive verb distinctly from the intransitive subject and transitive object.
Split-Intransitivity: The phenomenon in which intransitive verbs behave like transitive verbs with respect to certain grammatical categories.
Ergative-Absolutive: A case-marking system that groups the intransitive subject with the transitive object.
Alignment: The systematic relationship between syntactic roles and morphological case marking in a language.
Obligatory: Requiring the presence of a particular grammatical element.
Optional: Not requiring the presence of a particular grammatical element.
Overt: Phonetically or graphically realized; visible in the surface form.
Covert: Not phonetically or graphically realized; abstract or underlying.
Phonologically: Pertaining to the phonological representation of linguistic forms.
Syntactically: Pertaining to the syntactic structure of sentences.
Semantically: Pertaining to the meaning of linguistic forms.
Morphologically: Pertaining to the internal structure of words.
Pragmatically: Pertaining to the use of language in context.
Prosodically: Pertaining to the suprasegmental properties of speech.
Orthographically: Pertaining to the written form of a language.
Grapheme: The smallest unit of a writing system that represents a sound or sequence of sounds.
Alphabet: A writing system in which individual letters represent individual phonemes or phonetic segments.
Syllabary: A writing system in which each character represents a syllable.
Logography: A writing system in which each character represents a word or morpheme.
Abjad: A writing system that primarily represents consonants, with vowels indicated optionally or by context.
Abugida: A writing system in which each character represents a consonant-vowel combination, with diacritics modifying the vowel.
Morphemic Orthography: A writing system in which spelling reflects morphological rather than purely phonological structure.
Phonemic Orthography: A writing system in which spelling directly reflects the phonemic representation of words.
Deep Phonology: An approach to phonology that posits a level of representation underlying the surface forms.
SPE Phonology: The framework of Chomsky and Halle's "The Sound Pattern of English" (1968), influential in generative phonology.
Autosegmental Phonology: A framework in which certain features (such as tone or vowel quality) are represented on separate tiers linked to the segmental tier.
Optimality Theory: A framework in phonology and syntax that selects the optimal output from a set of candidates by applying ranked constraints.
Constraint: A well-formedness condition in Optimality Theory that outputs must satisfy to varying degrees.
Faithfulness Constraint: A class of constraints in Optimality Theory that require the output to remain similar to the input.
Markedness Constraint: A class of constraints in Optimality Theory that require outputs to be structurally simple or unmarked.
Correspondence: A relation between segments of the input and output in Optimality Theory.
Candidate: A potential output form evaluated by constraints in Optimality Theory.
Harmonic: An output that satisfies all or most of the active constraints in Optimality Theory.
Disharmonic: An output that violates one or more active constraints in Optimality Theory.
Strict Dominance: A constraint ranking in which all constraints of a higher-ranked set dominate all constraints of a lower-ranked set.
Lexical Rule: A phonological or morphological rule that applies only to specific lexical items.
Cyclic: A property of rules that apply iteratively to each morpheme within a word, from the innermost outward.
Postcyclic: A property of rules that apply only once to the entire word after all cyclic rules have been applied.
Noncyclic: A property of rules that apply to specific lexical items and not as part of the general derivational process.
Derivation: The step-by-step construction of a word or phrase from its constituent morphemes or substructures.
Derivational Morphology: Morphology that creates new words by adding derivational affixes.
Inflectional Morphology: Morphology that marks grammatical categories on existing words.
Word Internal: Pertaining to processes or properties that operate within the boundaries of a single word.
Word Final: Occurring at the end of a word.
Word Initial: Occurring at the beginning of a word.
Pretonic: Pertaining to the syllables before the stressed syllable in a word.
Posttonic: Pertaining to the syllables after the stressed syllable in a word.
Stress Rule: A phonological rule that determines the placement of stress in a word.
Tone Rule: A phonological rule that determines the assignment or realization of tones.
Metrical Tree: A hierarchical representation of syllable or foot structure used to account for stress and rhythm.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of one or two syllables, typically containing one stressed syllable.
Prosodic Word: The prosodic constituent that corresponds roughly to a phonological word.
Prosodic Phrase: A prosodic constituent larger than a word, corresponding roughly to a phrase or intonational unit.
Intonational Phrase: A prosodic constituent that corresponds to a major pause or intonational contour in speech.
Utterance: A complete spoken or written unit of communication, typically a sentence or a group of sentences.
Discourse: Language use that extends beyond a single sentence to include coherent stretches of text or conversation.
Discourse Marker: A word or phrase that signals a discourse function, such as "well," "meanwhile," or "anyway."
Cohesion: The linguistic connections within a text that link sentences and clauses together.
Coherence: The overall logical and semantic connectedness of a discourse.
Reference: The relation between a linguistic expression and an entity or situation in the world or in discourse.
Antecedent: The expression or entity to which a referring expression points back in discourse.
Discourse Representation: A theoretical representation of the propositional content and discourse structure of an utterance.
Discourse Representation Theory: A semantic framework that models the interpretation of sentences and discourse using structured representations of discourse referents.
Anaphoric: Referring back to a previously mentioned entity or expression.
Cataphoric: Referring forward to an entity or expression that will be mentioned later.
Exophoric: Referring to an entity outside the linguistic context, such as a physical object in the environment.
Endophoric: Referring to an entity within the linguistic context of the discourse.
Presupposition Projection: The process by which presuppositions are inherited from embedded constituents to the whole sentence.
Presupposition Accommodation: The process by which a hearer accepts a presupposition as true to make an utterance interpretable.
Pragmatic Inference: A reasoning process by which a hearer derives meaning beyond the literal semantic content of an utterance.
Scalar Implicature: An implicature based on a scale of meaning, such as "some" implying "not all."
 Horn Scale: A scale of lexical items ordered by strength of meaning, used in the generation of scalar implicatures.
Gambier Scale: A scale of modal verbs ordered by strength of obligation, used in modal implicatures.
Pragmatic Strengthening: The process by which a weaker expression is interpreted as having a stronger meaning in context.
Conversational Repair: The process by which participants in a conversation correct or repair misunderstandings or errors.
Turn-Taking: The system by which speakers in a conversation alternate speaking turns.
Overlap: The simultaneous production of speech by two or more participants in a conversation.
Backchannel: A brief response, such as "mm" or "I see," that signals listening without taking the floor.
Repair: The process of identifying and correcting a problematic utterance in conversation.
Self-Initiated Repair: A repair initiated by the speaker who produced the problematic utterance.
Other-Initiated Repair: A repair initiated by a listener in response to a problematic utterance.
Mishearing: A failure to correctly perceive or interpret a spoken utterance.
Hesitation: A pause or filler, such as "um" or "uh," that signals a speaker is formulating or searching for language.
Filler: A non-lexical sound or word used to hold the floor or indicate a pause in speech.
Trailing Off: The process of ending an utterance without grammatical completion, often signaling a pause or shift.
Interruption: The act of cutting off another speaker's turn in conversation.
Floor: The right or opportunity to speak in a conversation.
Floor-Giving: The act of yielding the speaking turn to another participant.
Floor-Taking: The act of seizing the speaking turn from another participant.
Adjacency Pair: A pair of related utterances, such as a question and answer or a greeting and response.
Second Position Construction: A construction in which an expression appears as the second element in a pair, such as "well" in response to a question.
Discourse Structure: The hierarchical organization of discourse into topics, subtopics, and other units.
Rhetorical Structure: A model of discourse organization in which spans are related by rhetorical relations such as elaboration, contrast, or cause.
Topic Chain: A sequence of discourse elements that share a common topic.
Thematic Progression: The pattern by which topics are introduced, maintained, or shifted in discourse.
Mood Particles: Small words or particles that express the speaker's attitude, such as "maybe" or "indeed," often found in East Asian languages.
Sentence-Final Particle: A particle at the end of a sentence that modifies its pragmatic force, as in many Asian languages.
Question Particle: A particle that marks an utterance as a question, as in "ka" in Japanese.
Imperative Marker: A grammatical element that marks a sentence as a command or request.
Interrogative: Relating to a question or the grammatical marking of questions.
Declarative: Relating to a statement or assertion of fact.
Interrogative Mood: The mood used to form questions.
Negative: A grammatical element that expresses negation, such as "not" or "no."
Negation: The grammatical process of expressing the denial or opposition of a proposition.
Double Negative: A construction in which two negative elements cancel out to produce an affirmative meaning, or reinforce negation.
Negative Polarity Item: A word or expression that is grammatical only in the scope of negation, such as "any" in "I don't have any."
Positive Polarity Item: A word or expression that is grammatical only in affirmative contexts, such as "ever" in "I've ever seen."
Negative Concord: A construction in which multiple negative elements co-occur but express a single negation, as in non-standard English "I don't know nothing."
Scope of Negation: The range of material over which a negation is interpreted.
Scope Ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the different possible scopes of a quantifier or negation.
Quantifier: A word or expression that indicates quantity, such as "all," "some," "many," "few," or "every."
Quantifier Scope: The domain over which a quantifier ranges.
Quantifier Raising: A syntactic process in which a quantifier is moved from its base position to a higher position in the clause.
Bearing: The semantic relation of a word to its referent.
Reference Class: A category of linguistic expressions based on their mode of reference, such as proper names, definite descriptions, or indexicals.
Proper Name: A word or phrase that directly refers to a unique entity without describing it, such as "Socrates" or "Paris."
Definite Description: A noun phrase with a determiner that picks out a unique referent, such as "the current president of France."
Indefinite Description: A noun phrase with an indefinite determiner that does not pick out a unique referent, such as "a book."
Indexical: A word whose reference is determined by the context of utterance, such as "I," "you," "here," or "now."
Demonstrative: A word that points to a specific entity, such as "this" or "that," often with spatial or discourse-based reference.
Anaphoric Expression: A linguistic expression that refers to a previously mentioned entity.
Exophoric Expression: A linguistic expression that refers to an entity in the physical or situational context of the utterance.
Cataphoric Expression: A linguistic expression that refers to an entity mentioned later in the discourse.
Co-reference: The relation between two or more expressions that refer to the same entity.
Co-referential: Describing expressions that refer to the same entity.
Discourse Marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse and signals the speaker's attitude, such as "well," "so," or "anyway."
Pragmatic Function: The communicative purpose of a linguistic expression in a given context.
Speech Act Theory: A framework in pragmatics, developed by Austin and Searle, that analyzes utterances in terms of the actions they perform.
Illocutionary Force: The communicative intention behind an utterance, such as asserting, questioning, or commanding.
Perlocutionary Effect: The actual effect an utterance has on the hearer's beliefs, emotions, or actions.
Conversational Context: The situational, cultural, and interpersonal factors that shape the interpretation of an utterance.
Pragmatic Competence: A speaker's ability to use and interpret language appropriately in context.
Linguistic Competence: A speaker's internalized knowledge of the grammatical rules of their language.
Communicative Competence: A speaker's ability to use language effectively and appropriately in social contexts.
Pragmatic Failure: A breakdown in communication due to a failure to produce or interpret pragmatic meaning.
Face: A person's public self-image that they wish to maintain in social interactions.
Face-Threatening Act: A speech act that threatens the hearer's or speaker's face.
Positive Face: The desire to be approved of, liked, and accepted by others.
Negative Face: The desire to be unimpeded in one's actions and not to be imposed upon.
Politeness Strategy: A linguistic strategy used to mitigate face-threatening acts, such as hedges, indirectness, or honorifics.
Mitigation: The softening of a face-threatening act through linguistic strategies.
Blindness: The failure to recognize the pragmatically appropriate form of an utterance in a given context.
Pragmatic Transfer: The application of L1 pragmatic norms to L2 speech, leading to pragmatic errors.
Pragmatic Development: The acquisition of pragmatic competence in first and second language acquisition.
Discourse Analysis: The study of language in extended use, focusing on how meaning is constructed across sentences and in context.
Conversation Analysis: The study of the organization and structure of naturally occurring conversation.
Ethnography of Communication: The study of language use in its cultural and social context, including the rules and norms governing communication.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society.
Variationist Sociolinguistics: A branch of sociolinguistics that studies systematic variation in language use across social factors.
Apparent Time: A method in sociolinguistics in which differences between age groups are used to infer language change.
Real Time: The direct observation of language change as it occurs across a period of time.
Language and Social Class: The study of how linguistic features correlate with socioeconomic status.
Language and Gender: The study of how language use and attitudes differ by gender.
Language and Power: The study of how language is used to establish, maintain, or challenge social hierarchies.
Linguistic Hegemony: The dominance of one language variety over others in a multilingual society.
Language Ideology: Beliefs and attitudes that people hold about language and its relationship to social structures.
Linguistic Repertoire: The full range of language varieties and registers available to a speaker.
Communicative Practice: A recurring pattern of language use associated with a particular social activity.
Field: The subject matter or topic of a communicative event.
Tenor: The social relationship between the participants in a communicative event.
Mode: The channel and form of communication, such as spoken or written, formal or informal.
Register (Hallidayan): A variety of language defined by field, tenor, and mode in a given communicative situation.
Systemic Functional Linguistics: A theoretical framework developed by Halliday that analyzes language in terms of its social functions.
Transitivity: A grammatical and semantic system in SFL that describes how experiences are represented through clause structure.
Mood (SFL): The system in SFL that encodes the speaker's stance toward the proposition, including indicative and interrogative.
Theme: The point of departure of a clause in SFL, typically the first element.
Rheme: The remainder of the clause after the theme, carrying new information.
Given-Information Structure: The arrangement of a clause to distinguish known from new information.
Halliday: M.A.K. Halliday, the founder of Systemic Functional Linguistics.
Functional Grammar: A theoretical framework that analyzes grammatical structure in terms of communicative functions.
Role and Reference Grammar: A functional grammar developed by Sandra Thompson that uses semantic roles and referential functions.
Cognitive Grammar: A framework developed by Ronald Langacker that integrates syntax, semantics, and pragmatics in a usage-based model.
Construction Grammar: A usage-based framework in which the basic units of grammar are constructions pairing form with meaning.
Usage-Based Model: A theoretical approach that explains linguistic knowledge in terms of frequency-based generalizations over individual language instances.
Frequency Effect: The influence of the frequency of a linguistic form or pattern on its processing, acquisition, or production.
Chunk: A pre-fabricated or semi-pre-fabricated linguistic unit that is stored and retrieved as a whole.
Formulaic Language: A fixed or semi-fixed multi-word expression that is processed as a unit, such as "by and large" or "I beg your pardon."
Collocational Preference: The tendency of particular words to co-occur with certain other words.
Collocational Strength: The degree to which two words are expected to co-occur based on statistical frequency.
N-gram: A sequence of n consecutive words or tokens in a text or corpus.
Corpus Linguistics: A branch of linguistics that uses large collections of real-language data (corpora) to study language.
Corpus: A large, systematically compiled collection of text or speech data used for linguistic analysis.
Concordance: A display of all occurrences of a word or pattern in a corpus, with surrounding context.
Collocation Analysis: The statistical examination of words that tend to co-occur with a target word.
Keyword Analysis: A corpus-based method for identifying words that are statistically significant in a text relative to a reference corpus.
Register Analysis: The corpus-based study of the linguistic features characteristic of a particular register.
Lexical Frequency: The rate at which a word occurs in a text or corpus, often measured as occurrences per million words.
Type Token Ratio: The ratio of the number of unique word types to the total number of word tokens in a text, used as a measure of lexical diversity.
Zipf's Law: The observation that the frequency of a word in a text is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table.
Manning's Law: An observation about the distribution of word frequencies in large corpora.
Herdan's Law: An observation about the relationship between word frequency and vocabulary size.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurological processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition.
Language Production: The cognitive and motor processes involved in generating spoken or written language.
Language Comprehension: The cognitive processes involved in understanding spoken or written language.
Speech Production: The motor and cognitive processes involved in producing articulate speech.
Articulatory Phonetics: The study of the physical movements involved in speech production.
Acoustic Phonetics: The study of the physical properties of speech sounds as they travel through the air.
Auditory Phonetics: The study of the perception of speech sounds.
Perceptual Phonetics: The study of how listeners perceive and categorize speech sounds.
Categorical Perception: The phenomenon in which listeners perceive sounds in discrete categories rather than along a continuous scale.
Perceptual Magnet Effect: The finding that prototype stimuli within a perceptual category are more accurately identified than peripheral stimuli.
Phoneme Discrimination: The ability to distinguish between different phonemes.
Phoneme Detection: The ability to detect the presence of a phoneme in a speech stream.
Speech Perception: The process by which listeners extract linguistic information from the acoustic signal of speech.
Word Recognition: The process by which a listener identifies a spoken word.
Sentence Processing: The cognitive processes involved in understanding the syntactic and semantic structure of a sentence.
Garden-Path Sentence: A sentence that leads the reader or listener to an initial, incorrect parse that must be revised.
Structural Ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible syntactic parses of the same sentence.
Lexical Ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple meanings.
Garden-Path Effect: The phenomenon in which a sentence structure initially leads the parser to an incorrect interpretation.
Syntactic Parsing: The cognitive process of determining the syntactic structure of a sentence.
Incremental Parsing: A model of parsing in which syntactic structure is built up word by word as input arrives.
Garden-Path Theory: A theory of sentence processing in which the parser initially commits to a single interpretation and must revise if it proves incorrect.
Constraint-Based Parsing: A model of parsing in which multiple constraints (syntactic, semantic, pragmatic) are used simultaneously to determine the structure.
Prediction: The use of linguistic expectations to anticipate upcoming elements in a sentence.
Reanalysis: The process of revising an initial syntactic interpretation in light of new information.
Spelling: The conventional way of writing words in a language.
Orthography: The writing system of a language, including the rules for spelling.
Alphabetic Orthography: A writing system in which letters correspond to phonemes.
Morpheme-Based Orthography: A spelling system in which morphemes are spelled consistently regardless of their phonetic realization.
Phonologically Regular: Having a spelling that directly reflects the pronunciation.
Phonologically Irregular: Having a spelling that does not directly reflect the pronunciation.
Etymological Spelling: A spelling that preserves historical or etymological connections to other words.
Irregular Verb: A verb that does not form its past tense or past participle by adding the regular -ed suffix.
Irregular Noun: A noun that does not form its plural by adding the regular -s or -es suffix.
Strong Verb: A verb that forms its past tense through internal vowel change (ablaut), as in "sing/sang/sung."
Weak Verb: A verb that forms its past tense by adding a dental suffix, as in "walk/walked."
Ablaut: A type of vowel alternation in Germanic strong verbs, as in "sing/sang/sung" or "drive/drove/driven."
Suppletive Verb: A verb whose forms are derived from unrelated roots, as in "go/went/gone" or "be/was/been."
Allomorphic: Having multiple allomorphs.
Morphophonemic Process: A rule that determines the form of a morpheme in different phonological environments.
Morphophonemics: The study of the interaction between morphological structure and phonological form.
Lexical Phonology: A framework in which phonological rules apply at different levels of lexical representation, some in the lexicon and some in the post-lexical component.
Two-Level Morphology: A framework in which morphological processes are represented as simultaneous correspondences between strings of symbols.
Transduction: In two-level morphology, a mapping between two parallel strings representing the surface and underlying forms.
Constraint-Based Phonology: A framework in which phonological well-formedness is determined by constraints rather than ordered rules.
Autosegmental: A phonological framework in which certain phonological features are represented on separate tiers.
Tier: A separate level of representation in autosegmental phonology, such as the consonant tier, vowel tier, or tone tier.
Linking: The association of elements on one tier to elements on another tier in autosegmental phonology.
Spreading: The process by which a feature on one tier is extended to dominate additional segments on the segmental tier.
Deplication: The process by which a single segment on the segmental tier is associated with multiple elements on a higher tier.
Tone Tier: A separate level of representation for tonal features in autosegmental phonology.
Vowel Tier: A separate level of representation for vowel quality features in autosegmental phonology.
Consonant Tier: A separate level of representation for consonantal features in autosegmental phonology.
Metrical Phonology: The study of stress and rhythm using metrical trees and grids.
Stress Assignment: The process by which a language determines which syllables receive stress.
Stress Shift: A change in the position of stress, often due to the addition of an affix.
Tone Assignment: The process by which a language assigns tones to syllables or morphemes.
Tone Spreading: A phonological process in which a tone extends over a longer domain.
Tone Sandhi: A systematic change in tone that occurs in a particular phonological environment, common in tonal languages.
Tone Neutralization: A process in which a tonal contrast is lost in a particular environment.
Pitch Accent: A prosodic system in which the pitch contour distinguishes words or morphemes, as in Japanese.
Accentual Phrase: A prosodic unit defined by its stress or accent pattern.
Phrase Accent: The accentual pattern associated with a particular type of phrase.
Intonational Contour: The overall pattern of pitch movement across an utterance or intonational phrase.
Declarative Intonation: The typical falling pitch contour associated with declarative sentences.
Interrogative Intonation: The typical rising pitch contour associated with yes-no questions.
Statement Intonation: The pitch pattern used to mark a statement.
Question Intonation: The pitch pattern used to mark a question.
List Intonation: The pitch pattern used in enumerating items, often with a rising contour on each item and a falling contour on the final item.
Sentence Stress: The pattern of stress on specific syllables within a sentence, often on content words.
Prominence: The degree to which a syllable or word stands out in the prosodic structure of an utterance.
Phonological Phrase: A prosodic constituent that corresponds roughly to a syntactic phrase.
Prosodic Hierarchy: The nested structure of prosodic constituents, from syllable to word to phrase to intonational group to utterance.
Prosodic Structure: The hierarchical organization of an utterance into prosodic units.
Syllable Weight: The degree of heaviness of a syllable, typically determined by the number and type of segments in the rhyme.
Light Syllable: A syllable with a short vowel and no coda consonant, or a short vowel followed by a single consonant.
Heavy Syllable: A syllable with a long vowel, a diphthong, or a vowel followed by two or more consonants.
