PHONETICS & PHONOLOGY:
1. Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
2. Allophone: A variant pronunciation of a phoneme that does not change word meaning.
3. Phone: Any distinct speech sound, regardless of whether it carries meaning in a particular language.
4. Suprasegmental: A phonological feature (such as stress, tone, or intonation) that extends over more than one segment.
5. Prosody: The pattern of stress, intonation, and rhythm in speech.
6. Intonation: The rise and fall of pitch across a phrase or sentence.
7. Tone: The use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in tone languages.
8. Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable within a word or phrase.
9. Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction.
10. Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
11. Plosive (stop): A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a release.
12. Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that creates turbulent airflow.
13. Affricate: A consonant combining a plosive onset with a fricative coda at the same place of articulation.
14. Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity.
15. Lateral: A consonant produced with a central closure and side channels for airflow.
16. Rhotic: A consonant associated with the /r/ sound, varying by language (e.g., trill, tap, or approximant).
17. Glide (semivowel): A sound intermediate between a vowel and a consonant, such as /w/ or /j/.
18. Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
19. Manner of articulation: The way airflow is modified to produce a consonant (e.g., stop, fricative, nasal).
20. Voicing: The vibration of the vocal cords during speech production.
21. Aspiration: A burst of breath accompanying the release of a voiceless plosive.
22. Velarization: Secondary articulation involving the back of the tongue approaching the velum.
23. Palatalization: Secondary articulation involving the body of the tongue approaching the hard palate.
24. Labialization: Secondary articulation involving rounding of the lips.
25. Syllable: The basic unit of organization in the sound structure of a word, typically containing a vowel peak.
26. Onset: The initial consonant(s) of a syllable before the vowel nucleus.
27. Nucleus: The vowel (or syllabic consonant) at the center of a syllable.
28. Coda: The consonant(s) at the end of a syllable following the nucleus.
29. Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and coda.
30. Syllabification: The process of dividing a word or string of sounds into syllables.
31. Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permissible in a language.
32. Minimal pair: Two words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating a phonemic contrast.
33. Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones.
34. Free variation: A situation in which two or more phonetic forms may be used interchangeably without change in meaning.
35. Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable.
36. Monophthong: A single, steady vowel sound without a glide.
37. Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, common in English and many other languages.
38. Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which the vowels in a word are restricted to sharing a particular feature (e.g., frontness or roundness).
39. Tone sandhi: The process by which the tone of one syllable is altered by the tone of an adjacent syllable.
40. Foot: A prosodic unit smaller than a phrase, typically consisting of one stressed syllable and one or more unstressed syllables.
41. Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
42. Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable.
43. Mora: A unit of prosodic weight used to measure syllable length, often considered the lightest unit of metrical structure.
44. Heavy syllable: A syllable with greater moraic weight, typically containing a long vowel or a vowel plus coda consonant.
45. Light syllable: A syllable with lesser moraic weight, typically containing a short vowel with no coda.
46. Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound (vowel or consonant) into a word to make its pronunciation more natural.
47. Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable in casual or rapid speech.
48. Metathesis: The transposition of two or more adjacent sounds within a word.
49. Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound changes to become more like a neighboring sound.
50. Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound changes to become less like a neighboring sound.
51. Lenition: A diachronic sound change in which consonants become weaker or moresonant (e.g., /p/ > /f/ > /h/).
52. Fortition: A diachronic sound change in which consonants become stronger or more occlusive.
53. Sandhi: Any phonological change that occurs at the boundary between words or morphemes.
54. Gemination: The lengthening or doubling of a consonant sound.
55. Devoicing: The phonological process by which a voiced sound becomes voiceless.
56. Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized in a hierarchical structure.
57. Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property of a sound (e.g., [+voice], [−nasal]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
58. Natural class: A set of segments that share a particular distinctive feature value and can be targeted by a single phonological rule.
59. Archiphoneme: A theoretical abstract phoneme representing a set of phonemes that are in free variation in a particular environment.
60. Prosodic word: A prosodic unit corresponding roughly to a morphological word, containing stress patterns.
61. Prosodic phrase: A prosodic unit larger than a word, typically corresponding to a syntactic phrase, with its own intonational contour.
62. Intonational phrase: A prosodic unit corresponding to a clause or intonation group, marked by a boundary tone.
63. Autosegmental phonology: A theoretical framework representing certain features (like tone) on separate tiers that associate with segmental tiers.
64. Optimality Theory: A theoretical framework in phonology that selects the optimal output from a set of candidates ranked by universal constraints.
65. Phonological rule: A formal description of a systematic sound change or alternation within a language.
66. Strict cycle: The principle that phonological rules apply cyclically, first to the innermost morpheme and then outward.
67. Phonemic transcription: A broad transcription using only the phonemic inventory of a language, ignoring allophonic variation.
68. Phonetic transcription: A narrow transcription capturing precise phonetic detail, often using diacritics.
69. Broad transcription: A level of transcription that records phonemic contrasts but not all allophonic details.
70. Narrow transcription: A level of transcription that records fine phonetic details of individual utterances.
71. IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet): A standardized system of symbols for representing the sounds of spoken language.
72. Syllable weight: The prosodic heaviness of a syllable, determined by its internal structure (onset, nucleus, coda).
73. Glottal stop: A plosive produced by complete closure of the vocal cords at the glottis, symbolized as /ʔ/.
74. Uvular: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the uvula.
75. Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the tongue and the pharyngeal wall.
76. Epiglottal: A place of articulation involving the tongue or tip of the tongue and the epiglottis.
77. Alveolar: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip or blade and the alveolar ridge.
78. Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue and the upper front teeth.
79. Retroflex: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip curled back to the postalveolar or palatal region.
80. Palatal: A place of articulation involving the body of the tongue and the hard palate.
81. Velar: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the velum (soft palate).
82. Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip and the upper front teeth.
83. Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips.
84. Labial: A general term for sounds articulated with the lips.
85. Glottal: A place of articulation involving the vocal cords at the glottis.
86. Front vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the front of the mouth.
87. Back vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the back of the mouth.
88. Central vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in a neutral position between front and back.
89. Open vowel: A vowel produced with the jaw widely open and the tongue body low.
90. Close vowel: A vowel produced with the jaw nearly closed and the tongue body high.
91. Mid vowel: A vowel produced with the jaw in an intermediate position.
92. Tense vowel: A vowel associated with a more constricted or raised articulation.
93. Lax vowel: A vowel associated with a less constricted or lower articulation.
94. Register: A phonological distinction in which the laryngeal configuration (e.g., creaky vs. clear voice) contrasts phonemically.
95. Contour tone: A tone in which pitch moves (rises or falls) over the duration of a syllable.
96. Level tone (register tone): A tone in which pitch remains relatively constant over the duration of a syllable.
97. Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which a single pitch accent within a word distinguishes meaning, as in Japanese.
98. Syllable peak: The point of greatest sonority in a syllable, typically a vowel.
99. Sonority: The perceived loudness or strength of a sound; vowels are more sonorous than consonants.
100. Sonority hierarchy: The ranking of sound classes by sonority, from vowels (most sonorous) to stops (least sonorous).

MORPHOLOGY:
101. Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language.
102. Morph: A physical realization of a morpheme in a particular form.
103. Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that appears in different phonological environments.
104. Root: The core morpheme that carries the primary lexical meaning of a word.
105. Stem: A root to which one or more affixes have been added; the base for further derivation or inflection.
106. Affix: A morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
107. Prefix: An affix that is attached before the root or stem.
108. Suffix: An affix that is attached after the root or stem.
109. Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root or stem.
110. Circumfix: A pair of affixes that appear simultaneously at the beginning and end of a root or stem.
111. Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a free word (e.g., prefixes, suffixes, bound roots).
112. Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word.
113. Derivational morpheme: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category.
114. Inflectional morpheme: An affix that marks a grammatical category (e.g., number, tense, case) without changing the word's category.
115. Derivation: The process of forming new words from existing ones by adding derivational affixes or other word-formation processes.
116. Inflection: The modification of a word's form to express a grammatical category.
117. Conjugation: The systematic inflection of a verb for grammatical categories such as person, number, and tense.
118. Declension: The systematic inflection of a noun, adjective, or pronoun for grammatical categories such as case and number.
119. Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word.
120. Suppletion: A morphological process in which unrelated forms are used for different inflected forms of a word (e.g., go/went).
121. Reduplication: A morphological process in which a root or stem is partially or wholly repeated.
122. Agglutination: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together distinct morphemes, each with a single grammatical function.
123. Fusion (fusional morphology): A morphological type in which a single affix encodes multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
124. Polysynthesis: A morphological type in which words can contain a very large number of morphemes, often expressing what would be a full clause in less synthetic languages.
125. Isolating (analytic) morphology: A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes and grammatical relations are expressed by word order or separate particles.
126. Lexeme: An abstract unit representing a set of related word forms sharing the same core meaning (e.g., the lexeme RUN encompasses run, runs, ran, running).
127. Lemma: The dictionary form or canonical form of a word, used as the head entry in a lexicon.
128. Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created (e.g., compounding, derivation, blending, clipping).
129. Compound: A word formed by combining two or more independent morphemes or words.
130. Portmanteau (blend): A word formed by merging parts of two words (e.g., "brunch" from "breakfast" + "lunch").
131. Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened (e.g., "ad" from "advertisement").
132. Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word (e.g., "edit" from "editor").
133. Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as a word (e.g., "NASA").
134. Initialism: An abbreviation formed from initial letters and pronounced letter by letter (e.g., "FBI").
135. Onomatopoeia: A word that phonetically imitates or suggests the sound it refers to (e.g., "buzz," "sizzle").
136. Productive: A morphological process or pattern that is actively used to form new words.
137. Unproductive: A morphological process or pattern that is no longer actively used to form new words but survives in existing vocabulary.
138. Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed by the absence of any overt phonological material (e.g., the zero plural in "sheep").
139. Portmanteau morph: A single morpheme that encodes the meaning of what would otherwise be two or more separate morphemes.
140. Bound root: A root morpheme that cannot stand as an independent word and must occur with other morphemes.
141. Morphological typology: The classification of languages based on their predominant morphological strategies (isolating, agglutinative, fusional, polysynthetic).
142. Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or construction becomes a fixed single word or expression in the lexicon.
143. Lexicon: The inventory of words and fixed expressions in a language.
144. Lexicography: The art and science of compiling dictionaries.
145. Lexicology: The study of the vocabulary of a language, including word formation, meaning, and usage.
146. Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
147. Word family: A set of related words derived from the same root (e.g., act, action, actor, active, react).

SEMANTICS & LEXICAL MEANING:
148. Semantics: The study of meaning in language.
149. Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it points to in the world.
150. Sense: The conceptual meaning of a linguistic expression, independent of its specific referent.
151. Denotation: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word or phrase.
152. Connotation: The set of associated or implied meanings that a word carries beyond its literal denotation.
153. Intension: The set of properties or conditions that define the meaning of a term.
154. Extension: The set of entities in the world to which a term applies.
155. Proposition: The basic unit of meaning expressed by a sentence, a truth-evaluable statement.
156. Propositional attitude: The speaker's stance toward a proposition (e.g., belief, desire, knowledge).
157. Truth value: The property of a proposition being true or false.
158. Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines the meaning of expressions in terms of the conditions under which they are true.
159. Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
160. Frege's Principle: The principle that the meaning of a whole expression is a function of the meanings of its parts (a cornerstone of compositionality).
161. Semantic role (thematic role): The role an entity plays in the event or state described by a verb (e.g., Agent, Patient, Goal).
162. Agent: The semantic role of the doer or causer of an action.
163. Patient (Theme): The semantic role of the entity undergoing an action or change.
164. Goal: The semantic role of the endpoint or destination of a motion or transfer.
165. Source: The semantic role of the starting point or origin of a motion or transfer.
166. Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that experiences a state or mental event.
167. Instrument: The semantic role of the means or tool by which an action is performed.
168. Location: The semantic role of the place where an event occurs.
169. Time: The semantic role indicating when an event occurs.
170. Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or expression has multiple related meanings.
171. Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form (e.g., "bank" as a financial institution and "bank" of a river).
172. Homophone: Words that sound the same but have different meanings (e.g., "flower" and "flour").
173. Homograph: Words that are spelled the same but have different pronunciations or meanings (e.g., "lead" the metal and "lead" to guide).
174. Synonym: Words that have the same or very similar meanings.
175. Antonym: A word with a meaning opposite to that of another word.
176. Contrary: A pair of antonyms that allow for intermediate values (e.g., "hot" and "cold").
177. Contradictory: A pair of antonyms in which one must be true if the other is false, with no intermediate value (e.g., "alive" and "dead").
178. Gradable antonym: An antonym pair where the opposite is not absolute and a scale exists between the two (e.g., "big" and "small").
179. Complementary antonym: An antonym pair where the truth of one implies the falsity of the other with no middle ground.
180. Reciprocal antonym: A pair of antonyms that are relative to each other (e.g., "buy" and "sell").
181. Hyponym: A word whose meaning is a specific instance of a more general word (e.g., "rose" is a hyponym of "flower").
182. Hypernym: A word whose meaning encompasses the meaning of a more specific word (e.g., "flower" is a hypernym of "rose").
183. Meronym: A word denoting a part of something (e.g., "wheel" is a meronym of "car").
184. Holonym: A word denoting a whole composed of parts (e.g., "car" is a holonym of "wheel").
185. Troponym: A word denoting a specific way of performing the action denoted by a more general verb (e.g., "stroll" is a troponym of "walk").
186. Componential analysis: A method of analyzing word meaning by breaking it down into a set of semantic features or components.
187. Prototype theory: A theory of categorization in which category members are organized around a central prototype, with graded membership.
188. Semantic field: A set of words that are semantically related and belong to the same conceptual domain.
189. Conceptual metaphor: A cognitive mechanism in which one conceptual domain is understood in terms of another (e.g., "ARGUMENT IS WAR").
190. Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase is used to refer to something closely associated with its literal meaning (e.g., "The White House announced...").
191. Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described as being another, implying a similarity (e.g., "Time is money").
192. Semantic bleaching: The process by which a word loses some of its specific meaning and becomes more general or grammatical.
193. Semantic narrowing: A diachronic process in which the meaning of a word becomes more specific over time.
194. Semantic broadening: A diachronic process in which the meaning of a word becomes more general over time.
195. Pejoration: A diachronic semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more negative or derogatory.
196. Amelioration: A diachronic semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more positive or elevated.
197. Taboo: A social or cultural prohibition against the use of certain words, often leading to euphemistic replacements.
198. Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one considered harsh, blunt, or offensive.
199. Dysphemism: A word or expression that is deliberately harsh, blunt, or offensive.
200. Ambiguity: The property of a linguistic expression having more than one possible interpretation.
201. Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the way a sentence's constituents can be grouped (e.g., "old men and women").
202. Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having more than one meaning (e.g., "bank").
203. Scope ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the different possible scopes of quantifiers or operators in a sentence.
204. Garden path sentence: A sentence that leads the reader down an incorrect structural interpretation that must be revised.

SYNTAX:
205. Syntax: The study of the rules and principles by which words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
206. Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular lexical category (e.g., noun phrase, verb phrase).
207. Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be a full sentence or a subordinate unit.
208. Sentence: A complete grammatical unit expressing a proposition, typically containing a subject and a predicate.
209. Noun phrase (NP): A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, functioning as an argument in a clause.
210. Verb phrase (VP): A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts.
211. Prepositional phrase (PP): A phrase headed by a preposition, typically consisting of the preposition and its noun phrase complement.
212. Determiner phrase (DP): A phrase headed by a determiner, encompassing the determiner and its noun phrase complement.
213. Head: The central word of a phrase that determines the phrase's category and core meaning.
214. Specifier: The constituent that precedes the head in a phrase, typically adding determinative or quantificational information.
215. Complement: The constituent that follows the head and completes its valency requirements.
216. Adjunct: An optional constituent that adds extra information to a phrase or clause but is not required by the head's valency.
217. Constituency: The property of a string of words forming a single syntactic unit (a constituent).
218. Immediate constituent: A constituent that is directly contained within a larger constituent, with no intervening constituent between them.
219. Phrase structure rule: A rule specifying how a constituent can be broken down into smaller constituents.
220. X-bar theory: A framework in syntactic theory that posits a uniform structure for all phrasal categories (X, X', XP).
221. C-command: A structural relationship in which a node dominates the head of a sister constituent; central to syntactic binding and scope.
222. Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence before movement operations have been applied.
223. Surface structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all movement operations have been applied.
224. Movement (dislocation): A syntactic operation in which a constituent is moved from its base position to a new position.
225. A-movement: A type of movement that preserves theta-role assignment (e.g., passivization, raising).
226. A-bar movement: A type of movement that does not preserve theta-role assignment (e.g., wh-movement, topicalization).
227. Theta role (theta grid): The semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, as specified in the theta grid.
228. Theta Criterion: The principle that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
229. Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic role of a noun phrase (e.g., subject, object).
230. Nominative case: The case typically marking the subject of a clause.
231. Accusative case: The case typically marking the direct object of a transitive clause.
232. Dative case: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
233. Genitive case: The case typically marking possession or a close associate of a noun.
234. Instrumental case: The case marking the means or tool by which an action is performed.
235. Locative case: The case marking the location of an event.
236. Ablative case: The case marking the source or point of departure.
237. Vocative case: The case used in direct address.
238. Ergative case: The case marking the subject of a transitive clause in an ergative-absolutive language.
239. Absolutive case: The case marking the subject of an intransitive clause and the object of a transitive clause in an ergative-absolutive language.
240. Case assignment: The syntactic process by which a functional element (e.g., a verb or preposition) assigns case to its argument.
241. Case government: The rule governing which case a predicate or preposition assigns to its arguments.
242. Case stacking: The phenomenon in which a noun phrase bears multiple case markers simultaneously.
243. Case syncretism: The phenomenon in which the same morphological form is used for two or more different cases.
244. Ergative-absolutive alignment: A case alignment system in which the intransitive subject and transitive object are grouped together (absolutive) and the transitive subject is marked differently (ergative).
245. Nominative-accusative alignment: A case alignment system in which intransitive and transitive subjects are grouped together (nominative) and transitive objects are marked differently (accusative).
246. Active-stative alignment: A case alignment system that distinguishes agents and patients across both transitive and intransitive clauses.
247. Subject: The grammatical argument of a clause that controls agreement and is typically the nominative or ergative-contrastive argument.
248. Object: The grammatical argument of a clause that is the direct recipient or patient of the verb's action.
249. Core argument: A grammatically required argument of a verb (subject, direct object, or oblique object), as opposed to an adjunct.
250. Oblique: A grammatical argument marked by a preposition or non-nominative/accusative case.
251. Valency (valence): The number of arguments a predicate requires.
252. Subcategorization: The specification of the type and number of complements that a lexical item requires.
253. Subcategorization frame: The set of complement structures associated with a particular verb or lexical item.
254. Complementizer: A functional word (e.g., "that," "if," "whether") that introduces a clausal complement.
255. Wh-word (wh-operator): An interrogative or relative word (e.g., "who," "what," "where") that triggers movement in questions or relative clauses.
256. Wh-movement: The syntactic movement of a wh-word from its base position to the clause-initial specifier position.
257. Wh-question: An interrogative sentence containing a wh-word.
258. Yes-no question: An interrogative sentence that can be answered with "yes" or "no," typically involving subject-auxiliary inversion.
259. Negation: The syntactic and semantic operation that inverts the truth value of a proposition.
260. Focus: The element in a sentence that carries new or contrastive information.
261. Topic: The element in a sentence that is the subject of discussion or the point of reference.
262. Information structure: The organization of sentence constituents into given (old) and new (informational) components.
263. Contrastive: A type of focus marked by a specific intonational or syntactic pattern that highlights a contrast with an alternative.
264. Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or operator exercises its effect.
265. Scope ambiguity: Ambiguity in which two quantifiers or operators can take scope in either order, yielding different interpretations.
266. Attachment ambiguity: Ambiguity in which a phrase or clause can be attached to more than one possible syntactic position.
267. Main clause: The independent clause that can stand alone as a sentence.
268. Subordinate clause: A clause that is embedded within another clause and cannot stand alone.
269. Coordinate clause: A clause that is joined to another clause of equal status by a coordinating conjunction.
270. Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or marker.
271. Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverb, modifying the main clause (e.g., temporal, causal, conditional).
272. Noun clause: A subordinate clause that functions as a noun (e.g., subject, object, complement).
273. Adjectival (adjective) clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adjective, modifying a noun.
274. Participial clause: A non-finite clause headed by a participle, often functioning as an adjunct or modifier.
275. Gerund clause: A non-finite clause headed by a gerund (V-ing form), functioning as a noun phrase.
276. Infinitival clause: A non-finite clause headed by an infinitive (e.g., "to go"), functioning as a noun phrase or complement.
277. Finite clause: A clause whose verb is marked for tense, person, and number.
278. Non-finite clause: A clause whose verb is not marked for tense, person, or number (e.g., participial, gerund, infinitival).
279. Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking (e.g., past, present, future).
280. Aspect: A grammatical category that characterizes the temporal internal structure of an event (e.g., perfective, progressive).
281. Perfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as a complete, bounded whole.
282. Imperfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded.
283. Progressive aspect: An aspect marking an event as ongoing or in progress at a particular time.
284. Perfect aspect: An aspect marking an event as completed with relevance to a subsequent time.
285. Habitual aspect: An aspect marking an event as a repeated or customary occurrence.
286. Inchoative aspect: An aspect marking the beginning or onset of a state or event.
287. Ingressive aspect: An aspect marking the entry into a state.
288. Egressive aspect: An aspect marking the exit from a state.
289. Resultative aspect: An aspect marking the resulting state after an event.
290. Stative aspect: An aspect characterizing states or conditions rather than dynamic events.
291. Durative aspect: An aspect characterizing events that extend over a period of time.
292. Punctual aspect: An aspect characterizing events that occur at a point in time with no internal duration.
293. Iterative aspect: An aspect marking the repeated occurrence of an event.
294. Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the action (e.g., indicative, subjunctive, imperative).
295. Indicative mood: The mood used for statements of fact or reality.
296. Subjunctive mood: The mood used for hypothetical, desired, or non-real situations.
297. Imperative mood: The mood used for commands or requests.
298. Optative mood: The mood expressing a wish or hope.
299. Conditional mood: The mood expressing a hypothetical situation dependent on a condition.
300. Jussive mood: The mood expressing a command or suggestion, distinct from the imperative in some languages.
301. Realis: A grammatical category marking events as actual, factual, or certain.
302. Irrealis: A grammatical category marking events as non-actual, hypothetical, or uncertain.
303. Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of information for a statement (e.g., direct observation, hearsay, inference).
304. Evidential: A grammatical marker that indicates the source or type of evidence for a statement.
305. Direct evidence: An evidential marking indicating the speaker personally witnessed or experienced the event.
306. Indirect evidence: An evidential marking indicating the speaker's knowledge comes from a non-primary source (hearsay, inference, etc.).
307. Reported evidence: An evidential marking indicating the information was reported by another source.
308. Inferred evidence: An evidential marking indicating the speaker's knowledge is based on logical inference.

PRAGMATICS:
309. Pragmatics: The study of how context contributes to the interpretation of utterances beyond their literal meaning.
310. Speech act: An act performed by uttering a sentence, such as promising, requesting, or asserting.
311. Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific propositional content.
312. Illocutionary act: The intended communicative force of an utterance (e.g., the act of warning, requesting, or asserting).
313. Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the listener (e.g., persuading, alarming, or convincing).
314. Performative: A sentence that performs the action it describes (e.g., "I hereby pronounce you married").
315. Cooperative Principle: Grice's principle that participants in a conversation generally aim to be cooperative in their communication.
316. Maxim of quantity: A conversational maxim that one should make one's contribution as informative as required but no more.
317. Maxim of quality: A conversational maxim that one should not say what one believes to be false or lack evidence for.
318. Maxim of relation (relevance): A conversational maxim that one's contribution should be relevant to the ongoing topic.
319. Maxim of manner: A conversational maxim that one should be clear, brief, and orderly in one's contribution.
320. Conversational implicature: An inferred meaning that arises from the assumption that speakers are following Grice's maxims.
321. Scalar implicature: An implicature derived from a linguistic scale (e.g., "some" implicating "not all").
322. Horn scale: A default linguistic scale used in scalar implicature (e.g., "all > most > some > few").
323. Reverse Horn scale: A non-default scale used in scalar implicature, often context-dependent (e.g., "and > or").
324. Presupposition: A background assumption that a speaker takes for granted as shared knowledge, which must hold for the utterance to be felicitous.
325. Presupposition trigger: A linguistic expression that gives rise to a presupposition (e.g., "again," "stop," factive verbs like "regret").
326. Presupposition accommodation: The process by which a listener adds a presupposition to the common ground when it is not already assumed.
327. Presupposition projection: The property that presuppositions are inherited by larger linguistic constructions containing the triggering expression.
328. Presupposition failure: The failure of an utterance when its presupposition is not met, leading to a sense of inappropriateness.
329. Deixis: The use of linguistic expressions that require contextual information for full interpretation (e.g., "I," "here," "now").
330. Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity or proposition.
331. Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to a subsequently mentioned entity or proposition.
332. Coreference: The relationship between two or more expressions that refer to the same entity.
333. Discourse: Language use beyond the sentence level, including the organization and coherence of extended communication.
334. Discourse analysis: The study of language as it is used in extended contexts, examining coherence, cohesion, and structure.
335. Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes or signals discourse structure (e.g., "however," "meanwhile," "well").
336. Discourse cohesion: The use of linguistic devices (reference, conjunction, ellipsis, lexical repetition) to create surface-level connectedness in discourse.
337. Discourse coherence: The logical and semantic well-formedness of discourse at a deeper, non-linguistic level.
338. Theme: The given or old information at the beginning of a sentence, setting the point of departure for the discourse.
339. Rheme: The new or informative information at the end of a sentence, carrying the main communicative payload.
340. Topic-comment structure: The discourse structure in which the topic (given information) precedes the comment (new information).
341. Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST): A framework for describing the organization of discourse in terms of relations between text spans.
342. Information structure: The organization of utterances into given (old) and new (informational) components.
343. Given: Information in a discourse that has already been established or is assumed to be known by the participants.
344. New (informational): Information in a discourse that is being introduced for the first time or is the focus of the current utterance.
345. Contrastive focus: A type of focus that highlights a contrast between the focused element and a set of alternatives.

HISTORICAL & COMPARATIVE LINGUISTICS:
346. Historical linguistics (diachronic linguistics): The study of how languages change over time.
347. Comparative method: A systematic approach to identifying genetic relationships between languages by comparing regular sound correspondences.
348. Internal reconstruction: A method of reconstructing earlier stages of a language by analyzing alternations within the language itself.
349. Proto-language (protoform): A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed from its descendant languages.
350. Reconstructed form: A hypothesized form in a proto-language, typically marked with an asterisk (e.g., *bʰer-).
351. Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestral language.
352. Language isolate: A language with no demonstrable genetic relationship to any other known language.
353. Language stock: A major subdivision within a language family, larger than a branch.
354. Language branch: A subdivision of a language family or stock.
355. Language group: A subdivision of a language branch, representing a more recent common ancestor.
356. Sound change: A systematic shift in the pronunciation of a sound or set of sounds in a language over time.
357. Regular sound correspondence: A consistent relationship between sounds in related languages, evidence of a common ancestor.
358. Grimm's Law: The systematic sound changes between Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Germanic consonants.
359. Verner's Law: A sound change that modified the outcomes of Grimm's Law based on the position of the accent in Proto-Germanic.
360. Divergence: The process by which related languages develop different forms from a common ancestor.
361. Convergence: The process by which unrelated or distant languages develop similar features, often through contact.
362. Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, leading to mutual influence.
363. Borrowing (loanword): The adoption of a word or expression from one language into another.
364. Calque (loan translation): The translation of a word or expression from one language into another, word by word.
365. Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
366. Code-mixing: The mixing of linguistic elements (words, morphemes, phrases) from two or more languages within a single utterance.
367. Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages.
368. Multilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use more than two languages.
369. Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language (or two different languages) are used in complementary social domains.
370. Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language.
371. Creole: A natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
372. Mixed language: A language that combines substantial structural elements from two or more distinct source languages.
373. Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker.
374. Language shift: The process by which a community or individual stops using one language and adopts another.
375. Language maintenance: The efforts to preserve a language and its use within a community.
376. Language revitalization: The process of reversing language decline and increasing the number of speakers of a language.
377. Endangered language: A language at risk of losing its last native speakers.
378. Extinct language: A language that no longer has any native speakers.
379. Mother tongue (L1, native language): The first language acquired by a speaker in early childhood.
380. Second language (L2): A language acquired after the first language, through study or immersion.
381. Heritage language: The language of one's family or ethnic background, acquired at home but in a context where another language is dominant.
382. Lingua franca: A language adopted as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
383. Koine: A simplified form of a language that develops as a common means of communication across a wide area.
384. Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular group of speakers, defined by geographical, social, or ethnic factors.
385. Dialectology: The study of the geographical and social distribution of dialects and linguistic variation.
386. Isogloss: A geographical boundary separating areas that differ in a particular linguistic feature.
387. Isophone: An isogloss specifically marking a phonological feature.
388. Isograph: An isogloss specifically marking a grammatical feature.
389. Lexical isogloss: An isogloss marking a difference in vocabulary.
390. Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group or class.
391. Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
392. Register: A variety of language associated with a particular communicative situation or domain (e.g., formal, informal, technical).
393. Style: The overall pattern of language use characteristic of a particular context or speaker.
394. Jargon: The specialized vocabulary of a particular profession, group, or activity.
395. Slang: Informal, often colloquial language associated with particular social groups, often considered non-standard.
396. Standard language: The variety of a language that is codified in dictionaries, grammar books, and used in formal education and media.
397. Autonym: The name that speakers of a language use for their own language.
398. Exonym: The name given to a language by speakers of another language.
399. Toponym: A name for a geographical location.
400. Anthroponym: A personal name.
401. Hydronym: A name for a body of water.
402. Onym (proper name): A name that designates a particular individual entity as opposed to a class.
403. Onomastics: The study of proper names and the principles behind their formation and use.
404. Eponym: A name derived from a person or thing (e.g., "sandwich" from the Earl of Sandwich).

SOCIOLINGUISTICS & PSYCHOLINGUISTICS:
405. Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society.
406. Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological processes that underlie language acquisition, comprehension, and production.
407. Language acquisition: The process by which humans, particularly children, learn to understand and produce language.
408. Language development: The broader study of how language abilities emerge and change over the lifespan.
409. Critical period: The hypothesized window in early life during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and effortlessly.
410. Language universal: A feature or principle that is (hypothesized to be) common to all human languages.
411. Typology (linguistic typology): The classification of languages according to their structural features, independent of genetic relationships.
412. Word order: The typical sequence of major syntactic constituents (subject, object, verb) in a language.
413. SVO language: A language whose basic word order is Subject-Verb-Object.
414. SOV language: A language whose basic word order is Subject-Object-Verb.
415. VSO language: A language whose basic word order is Verb-Subject-Object.
416. Pro-drop (null subject): A language feature in which subject pronouns can be omitted when recoverable from context.
417. Ergativity: A case alignment system in which the subject of an intransitive verb is grouped with the object of a transitive verb.
418. Split ergativity: A system in which ergative alignment is used in some grammatical contexts (e.g., past tense) and nominative-accusative in others (e.g., present tense).
419. Noun class system: A grammatical system in which nouns are assigned to classes that affect agreement with other words (e.g., gender, animacy).
420. Grammatical gender: A system of noun classes based on non-semantic or partially semantic criteria (e.g., masculine, feminine, neuter).
421. Semantic gender: A noun class system based on biological or natural gender distinctions.
422. Gender agreement: The requirement that certain words (e.g., adjectives, articles) agree in gender with the noun they modify.
423. Number: A grammatical category marking the quantity of entities (e.g., singular, plural, dual, trial).
424. Dual: A grammatical number marking exactly two entities.
425. Trial: A grammatical number marking exactly three entities.
426. Plural: A grammatical number marking more than one (or more than two in dual systems) entity.
427. Singular: A grammatical number marking exactly one entity.
428. Augmentative: A grammatical number or size marker indicating a larger-than-normal entity.
429. Diminutive: A grammatical number or size marker indicating a smaller-than-normal entity.
430. Pejorative diminutive: A diminutive form that carries a derogatory or contemptuous connotation.
431. Inanimate animate distinction: A grammatical distinction between nouns referring to animate and inanimate entities.
432. Animacy hierarchy: A ranked ordering of noun types by animacy (human > animate > inanimate) that influences syntactic behavior.
433. Gender (biological): The natural classification of entities as male, female, or neither, as distinct from grammatical gender.
434. Gender identity: An individual's internal sense of their own gender, as distinct from biological sex or grammatical gender.
435. Gendered language: Language that explicitly encodes biological or grammatical gender distinctions.
436. Gender-neutral language: Language that avoids encoding gender distinctions, often through the use of plural forms or alternative terms.
437. Sexism in language: The use of language that perpetuates or reinforces gender stereotypes or inequalities.
438. Gender bias in language: Systematic patterns in language that privilege one gender over another.
439. Sex-based language: Language that explicitly refers to biological sex categories.
440. Gender-specific language: Language that explicitly marks gender distinctions.
441. Gender-inclusive language: Language that is designed to be inclusive of all gender identities.
442. Gender-neutral pronoun: A pronoun that does not encode gender (e.g., "they" in English, or language-specific neopronouns).
443. Epicene gender: A single grammatical gender that applies to both male and female referents.
444. Neuter gender: A grammatical gender category for inanimate or non-gendered referents.
445. Masculine gender: A grammatical gender category, often (but not always) applied to male referents.
446. Feminine gender: A grammatical gender category, often (but not always) applied to female referents.
447. Default gender: The grammatical gender used when no other gender is specified or applicable.
448. Natural gender: The biological sex of a referent, as opposed to grammatical gender.
449. Animate gender: A grammatical gender category for living beings.
450. Inanimate gender: A grammatical gender category for non-living things.
451. Common gender: A grammatical gender that includes both male and female as well as some neuter referents (as in Scandinavian languages).

Aprosodeia: A speech disorder involving the loss of normal prosodic melody.
Archaism: A word, form, or construction that is outdated or restricted to specific formal or literary registers.
Areal feature: A linguistic trait shared by languages in a geographic region due to contact rather than genetic relationship.
Articulation: The production of speech sounds by coordinated movements of the tongue, lips, jaw, velum, and larynx.
Articulatory phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the physical production of speech sounds in the vocal tract.
Aspiration: A strong burst of air accompanying the release of a stop consonant, as in English /p/ in "pin."
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound adopts features of an adjacent sound.
Assimilatory: Describing a sound change driven by influence from a neighboring segment.
Assibilization: A sound change in which a stop or affricate develops into a sibilant fricative.
Autosegmental: A phonological framework in which certain features (tone, nasality, length) are represented on separate tiers from segmental phonemes.
Ablation: (not standard linguistics — skipped)
Backness: A feature of vowel quality indicating the retracted position of the tongue body.
Back-formation: A word-formation process creating a new word by removing an apparent affix, as in "edit" from "editor."
Barytone: A word or syllable with stress on the final syllable, a term from Ancient Greek prosody.
Bilingualism: The use of two languages by an individual or community.
Blend: A lexical item formed by fusing parts of two or more source words, as in "brunch."
Blending: A word-formation process combining portions of two words into one.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand as a free word and must attach to another morpheme.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or structural feature from one language into another.
Boundedness: A semantic property of a noun or verb implying a natural endpoint or limit.
Broca's aphasia: A non-fluent language disorder from damage to Broca's area, marked by agrammatical, effortful speech.
Broca's area: A region in the left inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44–45) critical for speech production and syntax.
C-left: (not standard — skipped)
C-command: A structural relation in which one node dominates another and is not dominated by it, governing binding and movement constraints.
Calque: A word-for-word translation of a foreign expression into the native language, as in "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Cataphora: A referring expression that points forward to an antecedent appearing later in the discourse.
Causative: A verbal form expressing the causing of an event or state, as in "break" versus "have break."
Causativization: A morphological or syntactic process converting a non-causative verb into a causative.
Cleft: A syntactic construction that isolates and highlights a constituent, typically using an "it...that" or "what" frame.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically behaves as a separate word.
Cliticization: The process of attaching a clitic phonologically and prosodically to a host word.
Clipping: A word-formation process that shortens a word, as in "gym" from "gymnasium."
Closed class: A word category (prepositions, conjunctions, determiners) that rarely admits new members.
Coarticulation: The simultaneous or overlapping articulation of adjacent sounds, causing mutual influence.
Code-mixing: The use of elements from two or more languages within a single clause or sentence.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a discourse.
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework by Ronald Langacker that grounds grammar in conceptual structure and usage.
Cognitive linguistics: An approach to language that integrates it with general cognitive science, emphasizing embodiment and usage-based processing.
Cognate: A word in one language historically derived from the same ancestral form as a word in another.
Cohesion: Grammatical and lexical links (reference, conjunction, substitution, ellipsis) that bind a text together.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a discourse or text.
Collocation: A habitual or statistically frequent pairing of words, such as "make a decision."
Colloquial: A register of language that is informal and typical of everyday conversation.
Combinatorics: The set of rules governing which linguistic units can be combined.
Complement: A constituent selected by a head to complete its valency.
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two variants never occur in the same environment, indicating they are variants of one unit.
Complementation: The syntactic selection and licensing of complements by heads.
Complementizer: A functional word introducing a complement clause, such as "that" or "if."
Compound: A lexical unit formed by combining two or more free morphemes.
Compounding: The morphological process of creating compounds.
Concomitant: (not standard — skipped)
Concrete: A semantic property of a word referring to a physically perceivable entity.
Conjunction: A word or class of words joining words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," "or."
Conjunctive adverb: An adverb expressing a logical relation between clauses, such as "therefore" or "however."
Connotation: The associative, emotional, or evaluative meaning of a word beyond its literal sense.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
Consonant cluster: A sequence of two or more consonants without an intervening vowel.
Constraint: A condition that restricts permissible forms or structures in a grammatical theory.
Constraint-based grammar: A syntactic approach in which well-formedness is determined by a set of constraints rather than generative rules.
Context: The linguistic, situational, or discourse environment in which a language form is produced or interpreted.
Context-free grammar: A formal grammar where every production has a single non-terminal on the left-hand side.
Context-sensitive grammar: A formal grammar where the environment surrounding a rewritten non-terminal affects applicable rules.
Contrast: A meaningful opposition between two or more linguistic elements.
Contrastive: Relating to or establishing a distinction between linguistic forms.
Contrastive analysis: A method comparing two languages to predict second-language learning difficulties.
Contrastive stress: The deliberate use of phrasal stress to highlight a specific word for pragmatic emphasis.
Contrastive phonology: The study of how sounds form distinctive, meaning-bearing contrasts within a language.
Contraction: The shortening of a word or phrase by omitting sounds, as in "don't" for "do not."
Convention: A socially established rule governing the form, use, or interpretation of a linguistic sign.
Convergence: The development of similar features in languages through prolonged contact.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred from the application of Grice's maxims to an utterance in context.
Conversational maxim: One of four cooperative principles proposed by Grice: quantity, quality, relation, and manner.
Copula: A verb linking the subject to a predicate nominal or adjectival complement, such as "be."
Correlative: A word or morpheme linking parallel elements, often in pairs such as "both...and."
Corpus: A systematically collected body of text data for linguistic research.
Corpus linguistics: The subfield studying language through the empirical analysis of large text collections.
Creole: A stable natural language that evolved from a pidgin when it became a community's native language.
Creolization: The process by which a pidgin develops into a full creole with native speakers.
Cleft sentence: A construction dividing a clause to emphasize a constituent, as in "It was John who called."
Clause: A grammatical unit with a subject and a finite verb, either independent or embedded.
Clitic: A phonologically bound but syntactically free morpheme.
Cliticization: The prosodic and syntactic attachment of a clitic to a host.
Collective noun: A noun denoting a group, such as "flock," "herd," or "jury."
Comitative: A grammatical case or marker expressing accompaniment, as in "with."
Complementarity: A semantic relation in which two words mutually exclude, as in "alive" and "dead."
Complementary: Relating to a complement or to complementary distribution.
Complex: Consisting of internal structure with multiple constituents.
Complex sentence: A sentence containing at least one main clause and one or more subordinate clauses.
Compounding: The process of forming compounds by combining roots or stems.
Comprehension: The process of deriving meaning from linguistic input.
Computational linguistics: The interdisciplinary application of computer science and linguistics to natural language processing.
Computation: The algorithmic processing of linguistic data.
Concord: Grammatical agreement between elements in a sentence, such as subject-verb agreement.
Concreteness: A scalar property of lexical items ranging from physical to abstract referents.
Conjunction: A word class or element joining syntactic constituents.
Conjunctive: Expressing or relating to the combining of elements.
Connotation: The associative meaning of a word beyond its core sense.
Consonant: A speech sound with a vocal tract constriction.
Consonant cluster: A sequence of consonants without an intervening vowel.
Contour: The melodic or intonational shape of an utterance over time.
Contour tone: A tonal value involving a pitch movement within a syllable.
Contrast: A meaning-distinguishing opposition between linguistic elements.
Contrastive: Relating to a distinction between linguistic forms.
Contrastive stress: Phrasal stress used for pragmatic highlighting.
Contraction: The omission of sounds from a word or phrase.
Convention: A social rule governing linguistic form and use.
Convergence: Shared feature development through contact.
Copula: A linking verb.
Cleft: A focus-construction isolating a constituent.
Clause: A unit with a subject and finite verb.
Clitic: A bound but syntactically free morpheme.
Correlative: A linking element in parallel structures.
Corpus: A collection of language data.
Creole: A natural language descended from a pidgin.
