response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phonology: The branch of linguistics that studies the systematic organization and patterning of sounds in a language.
Phonetics: The study of the physical production, acoustic properties, and perception of speech sounds.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one vowel quality and glides to another within a single syllable, as in "boy."
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound that remains constant in quality throughout its duration, as in the vowel in "bit."
Aspirate: A consonant pronounced with a strong burst of air, as in the [p] in English "pin" versus "spin."
Voiced: A sound produced with vibration of the vocal folds, as in [b], [d], [g], and most vowels.
Voiceless: A sound produced without vibration of the vocal folds, as in [p], [t], [k], and [s].
Consonant: A speech sound in which the airstream is obstructed by the oral or pharyngeal cavity.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, allowing air to flow freely without significant obstruction.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a word consisting of a peak (usually a vowel) optionally surrounded by consonants.
Mora: A unit of rhythmic timing in a syllable, often used to account for the weight or length of vowels and consonants.
Prosody: The suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, tone, intonation, and rhythm.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch on a syllable to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase, often marked by greater loudness, length, or pitch.
Intonation: The melodic contour of a phrase or sentence, used to convey grammatical information or speaker attitude.
Articulation: The manner and place by which the speech organs produce a particular sound.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The type of constriction or airflow pattern involved in producing a consonant, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to escape through the nasal cavity, as in [m], [n], [ŋ].
Plosive: Also called a stop; a consonant produced by completely blocking the airstream and then releasing it, as in [p], [t], [k].
Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow constriction that causes turbulent airflow, as in [s], [f], [ʃ].
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, as in [tʃ] in "church."
Approximant: A consonant produced with a partial constriction that is not tight enough to cause turbulent airflow, as in [l], [r], [w], [j].
Lateral: A consonant in which air flows around the sides of the tongue, as in [l].
Rhotic: A consonant involving the tip or blade of the tongue, such as [r], which varies widely across languages.
Glottal: Pertaining to the glottis; produced at the level of the vocal folds, as in the glottal stop [ʔ].
Velar: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue against the soft palate (velum), as in [k], [g], [ŋ].
Palatal: A consonant produced with the body of the tongue raised toward the hard palate, as in [c], [ɟ], [ʝ].
Alveolar: A consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade at the alveolar ridge, as in [t], [d], [s], [z], [l], [n].
Dental: A consonant produced with the tongue tip against the upper teeth, as in the English "th" in "think."
Labial: A consonant produced with the lips, either bilabial (both lips) or labiodental (lower lip and upper teeth).
Labiodental: A consonant produced with the lower lip against the upper teeth, as in [f], [v].
Alveopalatal: A consonant produced with the tongue blade at the alveolar ridge and the tongue body near the palate, as in [ʃ], [ʒ].
Pharyngeal: A consonant produced with the tongue root or epiglottis against the pharyngeal wall, as in Arabic [ʕ] and [ħ].
Uvular: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue against or near the uvula, as in French [ʁ] or German [x].
Epiglottal: A consonant produced with the tongue root against the epiglottis, as in some Arabian Peninsula languages.
Trill: A consonant produced by vibrating the tongue tip or uvula against an articulatory target, as in Spanish [r].
Flap: A consonant produced by a single, rapid contact of the tongue tip with the alveolar ridge, as in the "tt" in American English "butter."
Tap: A brief, light contact consonant, essentially identical to a flap in most descriptions.
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic airstream mechanism, involving a sharp closure and release of the glottis, common in Caucasian and Native American languages.
Implosive: A consonant produced by lowering the larynx during closure, creating negative pressure in the oral cavity, common in Bantu and Dravidian languages.
Laryngeal: Pertaining to the larynx; sounds produced at or below the level of the vocal folds.
Suprasegmental: Pertaining to phonetic features that extend over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Segmental: Pertaining to individual discrete units of sound, i.e., vowels and consonants, as opposed to suprasegmental features.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the two sounds are contrastive, as in "pat" and "bat."
Contrastive: A relationship between two or more phonemes that distinguish meaning in a language.
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of a single phoneme.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more allophonic variants may occur in the same environment without changing meaning.
Phonotactics: The rules governing which sequences of phonemes are permissible in a language.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a word into syllables according to a language's phonological rules.
Coda: The consonant or consonants that close a syllable, following the nucleus.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that begins a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Nucleus: The core of a syllable, typically a vowel or a syllabic consonant, around which the syllable is organized.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any coda, as opposed to the onset.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word that was not present in the underlying form, as in "autumn" pronounced /ˈɔːtəm/.
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable from a word or phrase, as in "gonna" for "going to."
Metathesis: The transposition of two adjacent sounds or segments within a word, as in "ask" historically pronounced "aks."
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in "input" becoming [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound, as in Latin "perperam" from "praperam."
Lenition: The weakening of a consonant over time or in certain phonological contexts, as in the shift from /p/ to /f/ or /w/.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant, the opposite of lenition, such as a fricative becoming a stop.
Palatalization: A sound change in which a consonant becomes palatal, often due to a following front vowel, as in the development of [t] to [ts] before /i/.
Velarization: A secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue is raised toward the velum during the production of a consonant.
Rounding: A secondary articulation in which the lips are rounded during the production of a vowel or consonant.
Backness: A dimension of vowel classification indicating how far back the tongue is positioned in the mouth, from front to back.
Height: A dimension of vowel classification indicating how close the tongue is to the roof of the mouth, from close to open.
Tenseness: A dimension of vowel or consonant articulation referring to the degree of muscular tension, often correlated with duration.
Neutralization: A phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is eliminated in a particular environment, as in English final consonant devoicing.
Archiphoneme: A hypothetical phoneme that accounts for a neutralized position where multiple phonemes may appear.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of one or more syllables with a particular stress pattern, such as a trochee or iamb.
Prosodic word: A prosodic unit that corresponds roughly to a phonological word and is the domain for certain phonological rules.
Syllabic: Pertaining to a consonant that forms the nucleus of a syllable, such as the [l] in "bottle" or [n] in "button."
Non-syllabic: Pertaining to a consonant that does not serve as a syllable nucleus, occurring in onsets or codas.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language, such as "un-", "play", or "-s" in "unplays."
Morphology: The branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules by which they are formed.
Allomorph: A phonological variant of a morpheme, such as /n/ and /ŋ/ as allomorphs of the English plural morpheme in "ten" and "singing."
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries its primary lexical meaning and to which affixes may be attached.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to form a new word or grammatical form, such as a prefix or suffix.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before a root or stem, as in "un-" in "undo."
Suffix: An affix that is attached after a root or stem, as in "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within a root, as in the Malay infix "-in-" as in "gulung" to "menggulung."
Circumfix: An affix that consists of two parts surrounding a root, such as the German "be-...-en" in "befreien."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word, such as "-ness" or "un-."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word, such as "cat" or "run."
Derivational: A type of morphological process that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, as in "happiness" from "happy."
Inflectional: A type of morphological process that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, or case without creating a new lexical word.
Agglutination: A morphological strategy in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each typically carrying one grammatical meaning, as in Turkish.
Fusional: A morphological strategy in which a single morpheme encodes multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by word order and particles, as in Mandarin.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which a single word can contain multiple morphemes encoding what would be a full clause in less polysynthetic languages, as in Inuktitut.
Morphophonology: The study of the interaction between morphology and phonology, particularly how morphological processes affect phonological form.
Suppletion: A morphological process in which a word form is replaced by an entirely different root, as in "go" and "went."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical meaning, common in Southeast Asian and African languages.
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened, as in "phone" from "telephone" or "lab" from "laboratory."
Blending: A word-formation process combining parts of two words into one, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Portmanteau: A single word that combines the meaning and sound of two or more words, such as "smog" from "smoke" and "fog."
Conflation: A word-formation process that merges two or more words into a hybrid, overlapping the segments of the source words.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme with no phonetic form, used to represent a grammatical category, such as the plural in "sheep."
Parasitic morpheme: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but morphologically independent, sometimes considered a borderline clitic.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent, such as the English "n't" in "don't."
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the end of a host word, as in the French "-en" in "il y en a."
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the beginning of a host word, as in the English "n't" in some analyses or the clitic pronouns in Romance languages.
Inflection: The modification of a word's form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, gender, or case.
Derivation: The process of creating a new word from an existing one by adding affixes or other morphological operations, often resulting in a change of meaning or part of speech.
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase, compound, or grammatical construction becomes a fixed lexical item in a language.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to create a new word, as in "blackboard."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes part of speech without any change in form, as in the noun "water" becoming the verb "to water."
Productivity: The degree to which a particular morphological pattern or word-formation process is actively used and can be extended to new words.
Opaque: A morphological or semantic relationship in which the meaning of a compound or derived word cannot be easily predicted from its parts, as in "butterfly."
Transparent: A morphological or semantic relationship in which the meaning of a word can be directly predicted from its constituent parts, as in "toothbrush."
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the structure and rules governing the formation of phrases and sentences.
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger syntactic structure, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a particular word class, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, or adverb phrase.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be finite or non-finite, main or subordinate.
Sentence: A syntactic unit that is the largest free combination of words expressing a complete thought, typically containing at least one finite clause.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of syntactic structure showing the hierarchical arrangement of constituents within a sentence.
Dominance: A syntactic relationship in which one node in a tree structure is above another, indicating that the higher node governs or includes the lower.
Immediate dominance: A syntactic relationship in which one node is directly above another in a tree, with no intervening nodes.
C-command: A syntactic relationship in which a node dominates all material after its sister node, important for binding and movement theory.
Binding: A syntactic principle governing the relationship between pronouns, reflexives, and their antecedents within a sentence.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to arguments by a verb, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, or Experiencer.
Trace: An empty category left behind in syntactic structure when a constituent moves to a new position.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from its base-generated position to a new position in the structure.
A-movement: Syntactic movement of arguments to positions associated with case assignment and theta roles, such as raising and passive.
A-bar movement: Syntactic movement of non-arguments to positions associated with discourse or focus, such as wh-movement and topicalization.
Wh-movement: The displacement of an interrogative or relative pronoun to the beginning of a clause, as in "What did you buy?"
Passivization: A syntactic transformation in which the object of an active sentence becomes the subject of a passive sentence, as in "The ball was kicked."
Topicalization: A syntactic process in which a constituent is fronted to the beginning of a clause for discourse or focus purposes.
Cleft: A sentence structure that divides a clause into two parts, one containing the focus, as in "It was John who called."
Pseudo-cleft: A cleft construction beginning with "what," as in "What I need is a coffee."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, introduced by a relative pronoun or complementizer, as in "the man who left."
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, often introduced by a complementizer such as "that."
Main clause: The highest-level clause in a sentence that is not embedded within another clause.
Subordinate clause: A clause that functions as a constituent within a larger clause, such as an adverbial or relative clause.
Coordinate clause: A clause joined to another of equal status by a coordinating conjunction such as "and" or "but."
Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, either coordinating (and, but, or) or subordinating (because, although).
Disjunction: A logical or grammatical relationship expressed by "or," indicating an alternative between two or more options.
Negation: The grammatical expression of denial or absence, realized through particles, prefixes, or other morphological means.
Quantifier: A word or expression that indicates the quantity or scope of a noun phrase, such as "every," "some," or "no."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, including articles, demonstratives, and possessives.
Article: A type of determiner that indicates the definiteness of a noun phrase, such as "the" or "a/an" in English.
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to a specific entity in the physical or discourse context, such as "this" or "that."
Possessive: A grammatical form or determiner indicating ownership or association, such as "John's" or "my."
Pronoun: A word that functions in place of a noun or noun phrase, referring back to or forward to an antecedent.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity, such as a pronoun referring to its antecedent.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse.
Exophora: A reference to an entity outside the immediate linguistic context, such as a demonstrative pointing to a physical object.
Antecedent: The noun or noun phrase to which a pronoun or other referring expression points.
Coreference: A relationship between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Government and Binding: A theoretical framework in syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s, organizing syntactic principles into modules.
Minimalist Program: Noam Chomsky's current theoretical framework for syntax, emphasizing economy of derivation and the operations Merge and Move.
X-bar: A generalization in phrase structure theory stating that all phrases have a similar internal structure consisting of a specifier, head, and complement.
Specifier: The constituent that precedes the head in an XP, often providing additional specification, such as the subject in a TP.
Head: The central word in a phrase that determines the category and core meaning of that phrase, such as the noun in an NP.
Complement: The constituent that follows the head in an XP and is required or selected by the head, such as the VP complement of a transitive verb.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase, providing additional information such as time, place, or manner.
Projection: A syntactic node or phrase built around a head, extending that head's properties to the entire phrase.
Phrase structure rule: A rule specifying the internal structure of a phrase in terms of its constituents, such as NP → Det N.
Recursion: The property of a grammar that allows phrases to be embedded within phrases of the same category to an unbounded depth.
Embedding: The syntactic process of placing one clause or phrase within another, creating hierarchical structure.
Isomorphism: A one-to-one correspondence between the elements or structures of two systems, often discussed in relation to syntax and semantics.
Lexicon: The mental dictionary or inventory of words and morphemes that a speaker knows, including their forms and meanings.
Merge: The fundamental operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects into a single set.
Move: The operation in syntactic theory that displaces a constituent from one position to another in the derivation.
Feature: An atomic property assigned to lexical items or syntactic categories, such as [+human], [+past], or [±definite].
Extended Projection Principle: A principle in GB theory stating that every clause must have a subject.
Case: A grammatical category marking the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase, realized through inflection or word order.
Nominative: The case typically marking the subject of a transitive or intransitive clause.
Accusative: The case typically marking the direct object of a transitive clause.
Dative: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient of a transitive clause.
Genitive: The case typically marking possession or association, as in "John's book."
Instrumental: The case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed, common in Slavic and Sanskrit.
Locative: The case marking location or position, as in "in the house."
Ablative: The case marking separation or source, indicating motion away from something.
Vocative: The case used to address someone directly, as in "O John!"
Ergative: The case marking the agent of a transitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment system.
Absolutive: The case marking the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb in ergative-absolutive alignment.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object, as in "She kicked the ball."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, as in "She slept."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object, as in "She gave him a book."
Agent: The entity that performs or initiates the action expressed by a verb.
Patient: The entity that is acted upon or affected by the action of a verb.
Theme: The entity that undergoes a change of state or location, or is the content of a perceptual or cognitive verb.
Goal: The endpoint or destination of a motion or transfer event.
Source: The starting point or origin of a motion or transfer event.
Experiencer: The entity that undergoes a mental or emotional state, as in "She feared the storm."
Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to meaning, including implied meaning and speaker intention.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a word, distinct from other meanings it may have.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it denotes in the real world.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-style meaning of a word or expression, as opposed to its connotative or pragmatic meaning.
Connotation: The set of associations, feelings, or cultural meanings that a word carries beyond its literal definition.
Entailment: A logical relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another, as in "He is a bachelor" entails "He is a man."
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be taken for granted for an utterance to be meaningful, as in "She stopped smoking" presupposes she used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning that is not explicitly stated but is inferred by the hearer based on context and conversational principles.
Conventional implicature: An implicated meaning that is semantically encoded in a lexical item or construction, such as the implication in "but" or "even."
Conversational implicature: An implicated meaning derived from the application of Grice's conversational maxims to a particular context.
Gricean maxims: Four principles of conversation proposed by H.P. Grice—Quality, Quantity, Relation, and Manner—that underlie cooperative communication.
Co-operation principle: Grice's overarching principle that participants in a conversation generally cooperate by making contributions that are appropriate to the purpose of the exchange.
Quality maxim: The maxim that one should make contributions that are true and for which one has adequate evidence.
Quantity maxim: The maxim that one should make contributions as informative as required but not more informative than necessary.
Relation maxim: Also called the maxim of Relation or Relevance; the maxim that one should be relevant to the topic at hand.
Manner maxim: The maxim that one should be clear, brief, and orderly, avoiding ambiguity and obscurity.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying information, such as promising, ordering, or apologizing.
Locutionary act: The act of literally producing an utterance with a particular propositional content.
Illocutionary act: The act performed in saying something, such as requesting, warning, or asserting, beyond the mere utterance of words.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or inspiring.
Performative: A sentence that, when uttered in appropriate circumstances, performs the action it describes, as in "I promise" or "I hereby declare."
Directive: A type of speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something, such as commands, requests, or suggestions.
Commissive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to a future course of action, such as promising, offering, or threatening.
Expressive: A type of speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state toward a state of affairs, such as thanking, apologizing, or congratulating.
Declarative: A type of speech act that brings about a change in the world simply by being uttered, such as "I now pronounce you married."
Assertive: A type of speech act in which the speaker commits to the truth of a proposition, such as stating, claiming, or reporting.
Deixis: The linguistic marking of the spatial, temporal, or person-oriented context in which an utterance is made, as in "here," "now," or "I."
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose reference depends on the context of utterance, such as "I," "here," or "tomorrow."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates the time of an event relative to the time of speaking or another reference point.
Aspect: A grammatical category that characterizes the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, progressive, or habitual.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source or type of evidence for a statement, such as direct perception, inference, or hearsay.
Irrealis: A grammatical category marking situations that are not presented as actual or factual, such as hypothetical, future, or desired events.
Realis: A grammatical category marking situations that are presented as actual or factual.
Scope: The range of elements over which a linguistic expression, such as a quantifier or negation, applies.
Ambiguity: A property of an expression that can be interpreted in two or more distinct ways, whether structural, lexical, or semantic.
Polysemy: A relationship between a single word or expression that has multiple related senses, such as "head" as the body part and the top of something.
Homonymy: A relationship between two or more distinct words that share the same form but have unrelated meanings, as in "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Synonymy: A relationship between two or more words that have the same or very similar meanings, as in "big" and "large."
Antonymy: A relationship between words with opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "buy" and "sell."
Hyponymy: A semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word (hyponym) is included within the meaning of another (hypernym), as in "rose" under "flower."
Hypernymy: A semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word (hypernym) encompasses the meanings of other more specific words (hyponyms).
Meronimy: A semantic relationship in which one term denotes a part of another, as in "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by the name of something associated with it, as in "The White House announced..."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another, implying a similarity, as in "Time is money."
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual words, as in "kick the bucket."
Collocation: A habitual or customary combination of words that co-occur more frequently than expected by chance, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Collocate: A word that frequently co-occurs with another word in a particular grammatical or semantic relationship.
Lexical field: A set of words that are semantically related to a central concept or topic, such as the field of "agriculture."
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social setting, purpose, or audience, distinguished by vocabulary, grammar, and style.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, trade, or interest group.
Slang: Informal, often creative vocabulary used by particular social groups, characterized by rapid change and low formality.
Archaism: A word or expression that was once common but is no longer in general use, retained in formal, literary, or historical contexts.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression that has recently entered the lexicon of a language.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one that is blunt, harsh, or offensive, as in "passed away" for "died."
Dysphemism: An expression that is deliberately harsh, offensive, or negative, the opposite of a euphemism.
Litotes: A form of understatement in which an affirmative is expressed by negating its opposite, as in "not bad" for "good."
Hyperbole: A figure of speech involving deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect, as in "I've told you a million times."
Understatement: A figure of speech that deliberately represents something as less significant or serious than it actually is.
Irony: A figure of speech or situation in which the intended meaning is opposite to the literal meaning, or in which outcomes are contrary to expectations.
Sarcasm: A form of verbal irony that is cutting or mocking, often directed at a specific person.
Relevance theory: A framework in pragmatics developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson, explaining communication in terms of cognitive relevance and optimal explicature.
Salience: A property of a concept that makes it more easily accessible in memory due to frequency, recency, or inherent prominence.
Cognitive effort: The mental resources required to process or interpret an utterance, a key concept in relevance theory.
Communicative effect: The contextual assumptions a hearer gains from an utterance, which together with cognitive effort determine relevance.
Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies the relationship between language and society, including variation, identity, and power.
Dialect: A variety of a language spoken by a particular group or in a particular region, differing in phonology, vocabulary, or grammar.
Dialectology: The study of the geographical distribution and historical development of dialects.
Dialect continuum: A series of neighboring dialects that are mutually intelligible to adjacent speakers but may be unintelligible to speakers at opposite ends.
Isogloss: A boundary line on a map showing the geographical extent of a particular linguistic feature.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker, reflecting personal habits and background.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, class, or community.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language, typically with no native speakers.
Creole: A natural, fully developed language that arises when a pidgin becomes the primary language of a community and is acquired as a first language by children.
Vernacular: The everyday, native language or dialect spoken in a particular community, as opposed to a standard or literary variety.
Standard language: The variety of a language that is codified, used in formal education and media, and often holds prestige.
Prestige: The social value or esteem attached to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature.
Stigma: A negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature.
Language variety: Any identifiable form of a language, whether dialect, sociolect, register, or idiolect.
Variability: The property of linguistic use in which speakers alternate between different forms in similar contexts, central to sociolinguistic study.
Stylistic: Pertaining to the conscious or unconscious choice of linguistic forms to achieve particular effects in discourse.
Covert prestige: The hidden social value attached to a stigmatized or non-standard variety, often associated with in-group solidarity.
Overt prestige: The openly recognized social value attached to a standard or dominant variety, associated with social advancement.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The insertion of words or phrases from one language into the grammatical structure of another within a single utterance.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages, either simultaneously or sequentially.
Multilingualism: The use of more than two languages by an individual or community.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be used as a living language.
Language revitalization: Efforts to reverse language decline and restore the use of an endangered or dormant language in a community.
Language endangerment: The state of a language at risk of losing its native speakers and falling out of use.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language or two different languages are used in complementary social domains.
Multiglossia: A more complex form of diglossia involving more than two language varieties or languages in complementary domains.
Pluriglossia: The presence of multiple language varieties within a speech community, each serving different social functions.
Ethnolinguistics: The interdisciplinary study of the relationship between language, culture, and ethnic identity.
Language ideology: Beliefs and attitudes that speakers hold about language, its varieties, and its users, which influence language use and policy.
Linguistic prejudice: Negative attitudes or discrimination based on a person's way of speaking or the variety of language they use.
Linguistic relativity: The hypothesis that the structure of a language influences or determines the way its speakers perceive and categorize the world.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The linguistic relativity hypothesis named after Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, proposing that language shapes thought.
Strong version: The deterministic form of linguistic relativity claiming that language determines thought and that speakers of different languages perceive the world fundamentally differently.
Weak version: The softer form of linguistic relativity claiming that language influences thought and that speakers of different languages may tend to think differently.
Universal grammar: The hypothetical set of innate linguistic principles and parameters shared by all human languages, proposed in Chomskyan linguistics.
Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestral proto-language, such as Indo-European or Sino-Tibetan.
Language branch: A subdivision of a language family sharing a more recent common ancestor, such as the Germanic branch of Indo-European.
Language group: A smaller subdivision of a language branch, such as the North Germanic group within the Germanic branch.
Language stock: A proposed larger grouping of language families that are hypothesized to share a very remote common ancestor.
Language phylum: A very large grouping of language families, sometimes used synonymously with "stock," such as the proposed Nostratic phylum.
Proto-language: A hypothetical reconstructed ancestral language from which a group of related languages is believed to have descended.
Reconstructed: Pertaining to a proto-language or form that has been inferred through the comparative method but was not directly attested in writing.
Comparative method: A historical linguistics technique that compares related languages to reconstruct features of their common ancestor.
Cognate: A word in one language that corresponds to a word in another language, both derived from a common ancestral form, such as English "father" and Latin "pater."
Loanword: A word borrowed from one language and integrated into another, often with some phonological or morphological adaptation.
Borrowing: The process by which a language adopts words, structures, or sounds from another language, especially through prolonged contact.
Calque: A word or phrase that is a direct translation of a word or phrase from another language, such as "skyscraper" from French "gratte-ciel."
Contact linguistics: The study of how languages influence each other through prolonged contact between speech communities.
Substrate: The language of a previously resident population that influences the superstrate language after a language shift.
Superstrate: A language imposed by a politically dominant group that influences the substrate language of the previously resident population.
Adstrate: A language that influences another through prolonged contact between communities of roughly equal social status.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons its native language in favor of another.
Language maintenance: The efforts and conditions under which a community preserves its native language across generations.
Heritage language: A non-dominant language inherited by immigrant families, often acquired at home but used alongside a dominant community language.
First language: The language acquired naturally in early childhood, typically before the age of five, also called L1 or mother tongue.
Second language: A language acquired after the first language, through formal instruction, immersion, or extended contact, also called L2.
Interlanguage: The developing linguistic system of a second language learner, incorporating features of both the L1 and L2.
Fossilization: The apparent halt in second language development where certain errors or non-target forms become fixed in a learner's interlanguage.
Transfer: The influence of one language on the learning or use of another, either from L1 to L2 or between L2 languages.
Negative transfer: The interference caused when features of the first language or a previously learned language lead to errors in the target language.
Positive transfer: The facilitation of second language learning when features of the first language or a previously learned language are similar to the target language.
Contrastive analysis: A method of second language study that compares the learner's L1 and L2 to predict areas of difficulty or error.
Error analysis: The systematic study of errors made by language learners to understand the processes of language acquisition.
Acquisition: The natural, implicit process of learning a language, typically referring to first language learning but also applied to second language learning.
Learning: The conscious, explicit process of studying a language, often through formal instruction, as opposed to natural acquisition.
Second language acquisition: The field studying the processes and conditions under which learners acquire a language other than their first.
Psycholinguistics: The interdisciplinary study of the psychological and neurobiological processes involved in language acquisition, production, comprehension, and representation.
First language acquisition: The process by which children naturally and implicitly learn their native language during early development.
Language faculty: The hypothesized innate cognitive system dedicated to language, central to the nativist approach in linguistics.
Poverty of the stimulus: The argument that children acquire knowledge of language that cannot be fully derived from the linguistic input they receive.
Critical period: A hypothesized time window, often associated with puberty, after which the ability to acquire language to native-like levels is significantly reduced.
Sensitive period: A time window during which language acquisition is particularly easy and efficient, less rigid than the critical period hypothesis.
Phonological acquisition: The stage of first language development in which children master the sound system of their language.
Morphological acquisition: The stage of first language development in which children learn to form and use grammatical morphemes.
Syntactic acquisition: The stage of first language development in which children learn the rules of sentence structure.
Semantic acquisition: The process by which children learn the meanings of words and the ways words combine to express meaning.
Pragmatic development: The stage of language development in which children learn the social and contextual rules governing language use.
Telegraphic speech: The stage of child language in which utterances consist of content words with little or no morphology, as in "Daddy go store."
Holophrase: A single word used by a toddler to express a complete meaning or request, as in "milk" meaning "I want milk."
Two-word stage: A stage in child language development characterized by utterances of two words, such as "more milk" or "daddy fall."
Overregularization: A child's tendency to apply a regular grammatical rule to irregular forms, as in "goed" for "went" or "mouses" for "mice."
Underregularization: A child's tendency to avoid applying a general rule where it should be used, the opposite of overgeneralization.
Overgeneralization: The application of a general rule or pattern to cases where it does not strictly apply, common in child language development.
Morphological development: The progression of a child's use of grammatical morphemes from first to full adult-like use.
Critical period hypothesis: The claim that there is a biologically determined window during which language must be acquired for full native-like proficiency.
Language deprivation: The condition of insufficient linguistic input, such as in cases of severe neglect, leading to impaired language development.
Sign language: A natural language expressed through manual gestures, facial expressions, and body movements, used by deaf communities.
Fingerspelling: A manual system in which each letter of the alphabet is represented by a specific handshape, used in sign language for proper names and loanwords.
Phonological loop: A component of the working memory model that temporarily holds and rehearses verbal and auditory information.
Semantic network: A model of lexical knowledge in which words are connected by various types of relationships such as similarity, category, and association.
Lexical access: The process by which a speaker retrieves a word from the mental lexicon during speech production.
Tip of the tongue: A state in which a speaker can partially access a word's meaning and phonological form but cannot retrieve the full word.
Word retrieval: The process of accessing and selecting the appropriate word from the mental lexicon during language production.
Speech production: The cognitive and motor process by which a speaker plans and executes an utterance.
Speech perception: The cognitive process by which a listener identifies and interprets the sounds of speech.
Comprehension: The process of understanding spoken or written language, involving decoding, parsing, and interpreting meaning.
Parsing: The process of assigning syntactic structure to a sentence as it is being processed in real time.
Garden path sentence: A sentence that leads the reader down an initial, incorrect interpretation that must be revised, as in "The horse raced past the barn fell."
Garden path effect: The processing difficulty experienced when encountering a garden path sentence and needing to reanalyze the structure.
Reanalysis: The process of reinterpreting a sentence structure after an initial parse has been found to be incorrect.
Forward referencing: The process of predicting upcoming linguistic structure based on the initial input during real-time comprehension.
Backward referencing: The process of interpreting the current input in relation to previously processed information.
Prosodic word boundary: A pause or intonational break that signals the boundary between words or phrases in spoken language.
Word segmentation: The process of identifying word boundaries in a continuous stream of speech, particularly important in languages without space-marking.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Morphological parsing: The process of identifying and interpreting the morphological structure of a word during comprehension.
Sentence processing: The cognitive processes involved in understanding the structure and meaning of a sentence in real time.
Discourse processing: The cognitive processes involved in understanding extended text or conversation, including tracking topics, managing referents, and building a mental model.
Mental model: A cognitive representation of a situation described in a text or conversation, used in discourse comprehension theory.
Situational model: A dynamic mental representation that integrates information from a text with the reader's prior knowledge to simulate a described situation.
Coherence: The property of a discourse in which ideas are logically and semantically connected, forming a unified whole.
Cohesion: The use of linguistic devices such as reference, conjunction, and lexical repetition to link elements within a text.
Topic continuity: The maintenance of a consistent topic across discourse, guiding the flow of information.
Information structure: The organization of discourse into given (old) and new information, guiding the arrangement of sentence elements.
Given-new structure: The principle that discourse typically moves from given information to new information within and across sentences.
Given information: Information that is already established in the discourse context or is mutually known by the participants.
New information: Information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse, typically receiving prominent syntactic or prosodic position.
Focus: The part of an utterance that introduces new or contrastive information, often marked by stress or syntactic position.
Topic: The entity or proposition about which a clause or discourse segment is predicated.
Theme: The point of departure of a clause, typically corresponding to the topic or given information.
Rheme: The part of a clause that provides new information about the theme, corresponding to the focus.
End-weight principle: A principle of information structure stating that more complex or informationally heavy elements tend to be placed at the end of a clause.
End-focus principle: A principle stating that the most important or new information in a sentence tends to be placed at the end.
Givenness: The degree to which an entity is accessible or activated in the hearer's mind, influencing the choice of referring expression.
Discourse referent: An entity in the discourse world to which linguistic expressions in a text refer.
Anaphoric resolution: The process of linking a pronoun or other anaphoric expression to its antecedent in discourse.
Discourse deixis: Deixis that refers to elements within the discourse itself, such as "this chapter" or "the following argument."
Narrative: A discourse form that presents a sequence of events, often with characters, a temporal structure, and a point of view.
Exposition: A discourse form that explains or informs, presenting information in an organized manner without a narrative sequence.
Argumentation: A discourse form that presents claims supported by evidence and reasoning, aiming to persuade the audience.
Procedural text: A discourse form that describes a sequence of steps or actions, such as a recipe or set of instructions.
Conversational structure: The organization of spoken interaction into turns, adjacency pairs, and topic sequences.
Turn-taking: The system by which speakers and listeners alternate in a conversation, governed by social and linguistic rules.
Adjacency pair: A two-part sequence in conversation in which the first part (first pair part) elicits a specific second part, such as question-answer or greeting-greeting.
Repair: The process by which a speaker or listener identifies and corrects a problem in an utterance during conversation.
Self-repair: A repair initiated by the speaker who made the error or produced a problematic utterance.
Other-repair: A repair initiated by the listener in response to a problematic utterance by the speaker.
Mention-verb structure: A discourse pattern in which an entity is first mentioned and then described by a verb, as in "There was a dog. It was barking."
C-left: A cleft construction used in discourse to shift or emphasize the topic of a conversation.
Topic shift: A change in the subject of a discourse, often marked by a new topic introduction or a discourse marker.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse and signals the speaker's attitude or the relation between utterances, such as "well," "so," or "however."
Connective: A word or phrase that explicitly links clauses or sentences, indicating logical relations such as cause, contrast, or sequence.
Discourse function: The role a linguistic element plays in organizing or managing the flow of discourse, beyond its local grammatical or semantic contribution.
Text linguistics: The study of the structure and properties of texts as units of language, including cohesion, coherence, and genre.
Genre: A category of text or discourse characterized by a particular communicative purpose, structure, and linguistic features, such as a recipe, legal document, or news report.
Text type: A classification of texts based on their communicative function, such as narrative, expository, argumentative, or procedural.
Register analysis: The study of how language varies according to the field, tenor, and mode of a communicative situation.
Field: The subject matter or topic of a communicative event, a component of Halliday's register model.
Tenor: The social relationship between participants in a communicative event, another component of Halliday's register model.
Mode: The role language plays in a communicative event, such as spoken or written, formal or informal, a third component of Halliday's register model.
Systemic functional linguistics: A linguistic framework developed by M.A.K. Halliday that analyzes language in terms of its social functions and the systems of choices available to speakers.
Metafunction: The major functional roles of language in Systemic Functional Linguistics: ideational, interpersonal, and textual.
Ideational metafunction: The function of language for representing experience and constructing a model of the world.
Interpersonal metafunction: The function of language for establishing and maintaining social relationships and expressing attitudes.
Textual metafunction: The function of language for organizing information into a coherent text.
Thematic structure: The organization of a clause into theme and rheme, determining the point of departure and the new information.
Transitivity: The systemic functional analysis of clause structure into participant and process types, such as material, relational, or mental processes.
Process type: In Systemic Functional Linguistics, the type of event or relation expressed in a clause, such as material, mental, relational, verbal, behavioral, or existential.
Participant: The entity involved in a process in Systemic Functional Linguistics clause analysis, such as actor, goal, or carrier.
Circumstance: The additional information in a clause that provides context such as time, place, manner, or cause.
Modality: In Systemic Functional Linguistics, the system of expressing degree of certainty, obligation, or inclination, such as "must," "might," or "probably."
Appraisal: The systemic functional analysis of how language expresses attitudes, emotions, and judgments, encompassing attitude, engagement, and graduation.
Interpretation: The process of assigning meaning to linguistic forms, involving both semantic and pragmatic contributions.
Ambiguity resolution: The process by which a reader or listener selects the correct interpretation from among multiple possible meanings.
Pragmatic inference: A reasoning process in which the hearer goes beyond the literal meaning of an utterance to derive intended meaning from context.
Speech act theory: A framework in pragmatics, developed by J.L. Austin and S.E. Searle, analyzing utterances as actions performed by speakers.
Locution: The literal utterance of words with a particular propositional content, the first level of a speech act.
Illocution: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as asserting, requesting, or promising, the second level of a speech act.
Perlocution: The effect of an utterance on the hearer, such as persuading or frightening, the third level of a speech act.
Performative verb: A verb that, when used in the first person present indicative, performs the action it names, such as "promise," "apologize," or "declare."
Constative: A statement that describes a state of affairs and can be evaluated as true or false, as opposed to a performative.
Felicity conditions: The conditions that must be met for a performative utterance to be valid and effective, such as the authority of the speaker.
Hearer's perspective: The interpretation of a speech act from the standpoint of the listener, including how the hearer identifies the illocutionary force.
Speaker's meaning: The intended meaning of an utterance as determined by the speaker's intentions, a central concept in Gricean pragmatics.
Intentionality: The property of linguistic communication in which the hearer must recognize the speaker's intentions to derive the intended meaning.
Communicative intention: The higher-order intention of a speaker to be understood by a hearer, beyond merely producing a signal.
Mutual knowledge: Information that is shared and known to be shared between all participants in a conversation, forming the basis of pragmatic interpretation.
Common ground: The set of assumptions, beliefs, and information that are mutually known and accepted by the participants in a conversation.
Presupposition accommodation: The process by which a hearer accepts and incorporates a presupposition into the common ground even if it was not previously accepted.
Gricean analysis: The interpretation of an utterance in terms of the speaker's adherence to or violation of the conversational maxims.
Flouting: Deliberate overt violation of a conversational maxim to generate an implicature, as in using understatement or irony.
Optimization: In relevance theory, the process by which a hearer processes an utterance up to the point of achieving optimal relevance, balancing cognitive effort and effect.
Explicature: In relevance theory, the fully developed propositional content of an utterance, including disambiguation and reference resolution.
Implicature in relevance theory: The additional assumptions a hearer derives beyond the explicature, guided by the principle of optimal relevance.
Cognitive pragmatics: The study of the cognitive processes involved in pragmatic interpretation, including inference, memory, and attention.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural basis of language, including brain structures and processes involved in language production and comprehension.
Broca's area: A region in the left frontal lobe associated with speech production and grammatical processing.
Wernicke's area: A region in the left temporal lobe associated with language comprehension and the integration of meaning.
Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage, affecting various aspects of language production and comprehension.
Broca's aphasia: A non-fluent aphasia characterized by halting, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, associated with damage to Broca's area.
Wernicke's aphasia: A fluent aphasia characterized by grammatical but meaningless or nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension, associated with Wernicke's area.
Conduction aphasia: An aphasia characterized by impaired repetition with relatively preserved spontaneous speech and comprehension.
Global aphasia: A severe aphasia affecting all aspects of language, including production, comprehension, and repetition.
Anomic aphasia: An aphasia characterized primarily by word-finding difficulties with relatively preserved grammar and comprehension.
Transcortical sensory aphasia: An aphasia characterized by fluent, paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension but preserved repetition.
Transcortical motor aphasia: An aphasia characterized by non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension and repetition.
Split hemispheres: The condition resulting from a commissurotomy, in which the corpus callosum is severed, studied to understand lateralization of language.
Lateralization: The specialization of one hemisphere of the brain for particular functions, with language typically dominant in the left hemisphere.
Language dominance: The tendency for language functions to be concentrated in one cerebral hemisphere, most commonly the left.
Neuroimaging: Techniques such as fMRI and PET used to observe brain activity during language tasks.
Event-related potential: An EEG technique that measures the brain's electrical response to specific linguistic stimuli, such as the N400 and P600 components.
N400: A negative deflection in the event-related potential associated with semantic processing difficulties, such as encountering an incongruent word.
P600: A positive deflection in the event-related potential associated with syntactic processing difficulties, such as encountering a grammatical violation.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, structured collections of real-world text and speech, known as corpora.
Corpus: A large, systematic collection of texts or recordings used for linguistic analysis.
Frequency analysis: The study of how often words, phrases, or patterns occur in a corpus to inform questions of usage, productivity, and salience.
Collocational analysis: The examination of the distributional patterns of words in a corpus to identify habitual co-occurrences and usage preferences.
Concordance: A display of all instances of a word or phrase in a corpus, showing the immediate context of each occurrence.
N-gram: A sequence of N consecutive words, such as a bigram (two words) or trigram (three words), used in corpus and computational linguistics.
Lexical frequency list: A ranked list of words in a corpus ordered by frequency of occurrence.
Corpus-based: Pertaining to linguistic research or description that is grounded in or derived from corpus data.
Text analysis: The systematic examination of a text's linguistic features, structure, and properties, often within corpus linguistics.
Lemmatization: The process of reducing word forms to their base or dictionary form, such as reducing "running" to "run."
Token: A single instance of a word or symbol in a text, as opposed to a type.
Type: A unique word form or symbol in a text, regardless of how many times it appears.
Type-token ratio: The ratio of unique words to total words in a text, used as a measure of lexical diversity.
Subcorpus: A subset of a larger corpus selected based on specific criteria, such as register, period, or author.
Parallel corpus: A corpus containing texts in two or more languages that are translations of each other, used for contrastive and translation studies.
Aligned corpus: A corpus in which corresponding segments in two or more languages are explicitly marked, facilitating cross-linguistic analysis.
Computational linguistics: The interdisciplinary field that applies computational methods to the analysis and processing of natural language.
Natural language processing: The subfield of computer science and AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Part-of-speech tagging: The computational process of labeling each word in a text with its grammatical category, such as noun, verb, or adjective.
Syntactic parsing: The computational process of determining the grammatical structure of a sentence.
Named entity recognition: The computational task of identifying and classifying proper names in text, such as persons, organizations, and locations.
Word sense disambiguation: The computational task of determining the correct meaning of a polysemous word in a given context.
Language model: A statistical or neural model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words, used in speech recognition and machine translation.
Speech recognition: The computational conversion of spoken language into written text.
Speech synthesis: The computational generation of natural-sounding speech from written text, also called text-to-speech.
Machine translation: The computational translation of text from one language to another.
Morphological analysis: The computational process of identifying the morphological structure of a word, including its root, affixes, and grammatical features.
Syntactic parsing algorithm: A computational method for determining the grammatical structure of a sentence, such as chart parsing or recursive descent.
Probabilistic grammar: A grammar that assigns probabilities to its rules or structures, enabling the ranking of possible parses.
Stochastic parser: A parsing algorithm that uses probabilistic models to select the most likely syntactic structure for a sentence.
Finite state transducer: A computational model used in morphology and phonology to represent systematic mappings between input and output strings.
Hidden Markov model: A statistical model used in speech recognition and other NLP tasks to model sequential data with unobserved states.
Neural network: A computational model inspired by biological neural networks, widely used in modern NLP for tasks like translation and parsing.
Transformer model: A neural network architecture, introduced in 2017, that uses self-attention mechanisms and has become the basis for large language models.
Large language model: A neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict and generate natural language, capable of performing a wide range of language tasks.
Tokenization: The process of splitting a text into individual tokens, such as words, subwords, or characters, for computational processing.
Subword tokenization: A tokenization method that splits words into smaller units, such as BPE or WordPiece, to handle unknown words.
Vector space model: A representation of words or documents as vectors in a high-dimensional space, used in information retrieval and NLP.
Word embedding: A dense vector representation of a word that captures its semantic and syntactic properties, such as Word2Vec or GloVe.
Distributional semantics: The theory that the meaning of a word is determined by the distribution of its co-occurrences in a corpus.
Semantic vector: A numerical vector representing the meaning of a word or phrase in a distributional or neural model.
Information retrieval: The field of finding relevant documents or information from a large collection, often using natural language queries.
Query expansion: A technique in information retrieval that augments a user's query with additional relevant terms to improve recall.
Text mining: The process of extracting patterns, insights, and knowledge from large text corpora using computational methods.
Text classification: The task of automatically assigning a text to one or more predefined categories, such as spam detection or topic labeling.
Sentiment analysis: The computational task of determining the emotional tone or attitude expressed in a piece of text.
Topic modeling: A set of computational techniques for discovering hidden thematic structures in a collection of documents, such as LDA.
Latent Dirichlet Allocation: A probabilistic topic model that represents documents as mixtures of topics and topics as distributions over words.
Dependency parsing: A syntactic parsing approach that identifies the grammatical dependencies between words in a sentence.
Constituency parsing: A syntactic parsing approach that groups words into nested constituents, represented in a tree structure.
Universal Dependencies: A project providing consistent syntactic annotation of texts in many languages, using a unified set of dependency relations and POS tags.
Grammatical relation: The syntactic or semantic role a word plays with respect to another word, such as subject, object, or modifier.
Head-dependent relation: A syntactic relationship in which one word (the head) governs another (the dependent), fundamental to dependency grammar.
Dependency grammar: A framework in syntax that analyzes sentences as sets of pairwise head-dependent relations rather than nested constituents.
Word order: The linear arrangement of words and their constituents in a sentence, varying across languages (e.g., SVO, SOV, VSO).
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English "The cat ate the fish."
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese "The cat the fish ate."
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in Classical Arabic and modern Irish.
V2: A word order constraint in which the finite verb appears in the second position in a clause, as in German and Dutch.
Scrambling: The syntactic process in which arguments of a verb appear in a different order than the canonical or unmarked order, common in Japanese and Hindi.
Pro-drop: The omission of a subject pronoun when it is recoverable from context, common in Italian, Spanish, and Mandarin.
Null subject: The absence of an overt subject pronoun in a clause, allowed in pro-drop languages.
Subject-verb agreement: The grammatical requirement that the form of the verb matches the subject in person, number, and sometimes gender.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker (first person), the addressee (second person), and others (third person).
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular and plural (and sometimes dual, trial, etc.) forms of nouns, pronouns, and verbs.
Gender: A grammatical category that classifies nouns and associated words into sets such as masculine, feminine, and neuter.
Animacy: A grammatical or semantic hierarchy distinguishing living from non-living entities, often influencing case marking and verb agreement.
Inclusivity: The distinction in some languages between first-person plural pronouns that include the addressee (inclusive "we") and those that exclude them (exclusive "we").
Trial: A grammatical number category distinguishing exactly two participants, found in some Australian and Oceanian languages.
Quadrality: A grammatical number category distinguishing exactly four participants, found in a small number of Australian languages.
Plural: A grammatical number category indicating more than one entity, typically marked by suffixes, vowels, or other morphological means.
Singular: A grammatical number category indicating exactly one entity, often the unmarked or default form.
Suppletive plural: A plural form that is not derivable by regular morphological means, as in "men" from "man" or "feet" from "foot."
Irregular plural: A plural form that does not follow the regular productive pattern of a language, such as "children" in English.
Collective noun: A noun that denotes a group or collection of entities as a single unit, such as "flock," "herd," or "jury."
Mass noun: A noun that refers to a substance or concept not naturally divided into discrete countable units, such as "water," "furniture," or "information."
Count noun: A noun that refers to discrete, countable entities, such as "apple," "car," or "person."
Uncountable noun: A noun that cannot be used with a numeral or plural morphology in its default form, such as "money" or "advice."
Lexical class: A grammatical category of words sharing common syntactic and semantic properties, such as noun, verb, adjective, and adverb.
Open class: A word class that is open to the addition of new members, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
Closed class: A word class that is relatively fixed in size and rarely admits new members, such as pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, and determiners.
Content word: A word that carries significant lexical meaning, such as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Function word: A word that primarily serves a grammatical or structural role, such as a preposition, article, conjunction, or auxiliary.
Auxiliary: A verb that supports a main verb in expressing tense, mood, or aspect, such as "will," "have," or "be."
Modal verb: A type of auxiliary expressing modality, such as "can," "must," "should," or "may."
Copula: A verb that links a subject to a complement, as in "be" in English or "est" in Spanish.
Linking verb: A verb that connects a subject to a subject complement, such as "seem," "appear," or "become."
Pseudo-cleft sentence: A sentence beginning with a "what" clause, as in "What I want is a break."
Cleft sentence: A construction that divides a clause into two parts, one containing the focused element, as in "It was John who did it."
Extraposition: The syntactic movement of a constituent, typically a heavy or complex one, to the end of a clause, as in "What I said surprised him" from "That I said what I said surprised him."
Heavy NP shift: A syntactic process in which a long or complex noun phrase is moved to a position later in the sentence for processing ease.
Left dislocation: A discourse structure in which a constituent is fronted and followed by a pronoun or gap, as in "John, I saw him yesterday."
Right dislocation: A discourse structure in which a pronoun or subject is followed by a postposed constituent, as in "I saw him, John."
Topicalization: The fronting of a non-subject constituent to the beginning of a clause for topical or discourse purposes.
Subject extraction: The syntactic process of moving or referring to the subject of a clause, as in questions or relative clauses.
Object extraction: The syntactic process of moving or referring to the object of a clause, as in questions or relative clauses.
Gap: An empty position in a sentence structure where a constituent has been moved or is understood by context, as in "What did you see ___?"
Antecedent government: A syntactic principle stating that a pronoun's antecedent must be in a position that governs it.
Local antecedent: The closest potential antecedent for a pronoun or reflexive in a given clause.
Long-distance dependency: A syntactic relationship between elements that are separated by one or more clause boundaries, as in "the man that I think that left."
Island constraint: A syntactic constraint that prohibits extraction of a constituent from certain complex structures, such as relative clauses or subject islands.
Subject island: A syntactic constraint preventing extraction from a subject clause, as in "*the man that [that he left] surprised me."
Complex NP island: A syntactic constraint preventing extraction from within a complex noun phrase, as in "*the book that [the man who wrote ___] impressed me."
Wh-island: A syntactic constraint preventing extraction from within a wh-question or relative clause, as in "*the man that [which book did he buy ___] left."
Economy principle: A principle in syntactic theory stating that derivations should be as short and simple as possible.
Prolixity: The use of more words than necessary, the opposite of economy, sometimes discussed in syntactic theory and style.
Markedness: The relative complexity or unusualness of a linguistic form compared to its alternatives in a language.
Unmarked: The default, regular, or simplest form in a pair or set of alternatives, as in the singular versus plural.
Marked: The non-default, irregular, or more complex form in a pair or set of alternatives, as in the plural versus singular.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, such as all the tenses of a verb or all the cases of a noun.
Morphosyntax: The interaction between morphology and syntax, studying how word formation interacts with sentence structure.
Morphosyntactic alignment: The system by which a language marks the grammatical roles of arguments, such as nominative-accusative or ergative-absolutive.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A grammatical alignment in which the subject of transitive and intransitive verbs is treated the same (nominative) and differs from the object (accusative).
Ergative-absolutive alignment: A grammatical alignment in which the subject of transitive verbs is marked differently (ergative) from the object and the intransitive subject (absolutive).
Split ergativity: A system in which a language uses ergative-absolutive alignment in some contexts and nominative-accusative alignment in others.
Noun class: A grammatical category in some languages that groups nouns into classes, often based on animacy, shape, or semantic properties, as in Bantu languages.
Class agreement: The process by which verbs, adjectives, and other modifiers agree with the noun class of their subject or object.
Nominal class: The system of noun classification in a language, whether based on gender, animacy, shape, or other criteria.
Cliticization: The process by which a morpheme attaches to a host word for phonological purposes while remaining syntactically independent.
Clitic cluster: A sequence of multiple clitics attached to a host word, common in Balkan and Romance languages.
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that combines the functions of two or more separate morphemes, as in Latin "-us" combining nominative, singular, and masculine.
Polysynthesis: A morphological type in which a single word can express the meaning of an entire clause, as in many Native American languages.
Polysynthetic verb: A verb that incorporates multiple morphemes, including nominal elements, to express a complete proposition.
Verb incorporation: A process in which a noun is incorporated into a verb, as in the English "sunburn" or the Mohawk "tsi-nahkwe'kwak" (I-eat-it).
Noun incorporation: The process of attaching a noun stem to a verb to form a compound verb, common in polysynthetic languages.
Incorporation: The general process of combining two or more lexical elements into a single morphological word.
Serial verb construction: A syntactic structure in which two or more verbs appear in sequence without a connecting element, as in "I go take a look."
Light verb: A verb that carries little semantic content on its own and relies on a complement for meaning, such as "give" in "give a
