# Glossary of Linguistics Terms

Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Allophone: A contextual variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning.
Phonology: The branch of linguistics studying the systematic organization of sounds in a language.
Phonetics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the physical properties and production of speech sounds.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are produced by the vocal organs.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical and measurable properties of speech sounds.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived by the listener.
Segmental phonology: The study of discrete speech sounds (consonants and vowels) and their organization.
Suprasegmental phonology: The study of phonological features that extend across more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
Manner of articulation: The type of constriction or airflow pattern used to produce a consonant.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a partial or complete closure in the vocal tract.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release of air.
Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that causes turbulent airflow.
Affricate: A consonant produced as a stop immediately followed by a fricative at the same place of articulation.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip raised while allowing air to flow around the sides of the tongue.
Rhotic: A consonant produced with the tongue tip raised or bunched, as in English /r/.
Glottal: Pertaining to the glottis, the space between the vocal folds.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during speech sound production.
Voicelessness: The absence of vocal fold vibration during speech sound production.
Aspiration: A burst of airflow that accompanies the release of a voiceless stop.
Breathy voice: A phonation type in which the vocal folds are slightly apart, producing a whispery quality.
Creaky voice: A phonation type in which the vocal folds are tightly adducted and vibrate slowly.
Syllable: A unit of pronunciation typically consisting of a vowel nucleus and optional consonants.
Syllable nucleus: The core of a syllable, most commonly a vowel.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster at the beginning of a syllable.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster at the end of a syllable.
Rime: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and coda.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the vowel and any following consonants.
Stress: The relative prominence given to a syllable within a word or phrase.
Tone: The use of pitch variation to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning.
Intonation: The melodic contour of pitch across a phrase or sentence.
Prosody: The study of suprasegmental features including stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Rhythm: The pattern of timing and stress in speech.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable.
Triphthong: A complex vowel sequence involving three vowel qualities within a single syllable.
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, the most common vowel in many languages.
IPA: The International Phonetic Alphabet, a standardized system for transcribing speech sounds.
Minimal pair: Two words in a language that differ by exactly one phoneme and have different meanings.
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two sounds never occur in the same phonological environment.
Contrastive distribution: A relationship in which two sounds can occur in the same environment and distinguish meaning.
Allophonic variation: Non-contrastive variation in the realization of a phoneme.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permitted in a language.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a string of sounds into syllables.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound (typically a vowel) between consonants to break up an illegal sequence.
Elision: The deletion or omission of a sound in certain phonological environments.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less like a neighboring sound.
Metathesis: The transposition or reversal of two adjacent sounds.
Lenition: The weakening of a consonant, such as a stop becoming a fricative.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant, such as a fricative becoming a stop.
Sandhi: A phonological change that occurs at the boundary between morphemes or words.
Umlaut: A historical or synchronic vowel mutation triggered by the sound of a following syllable.
Palatalization: A sound change in which a consonant becomes more front and palatal in articulation.
Labialization: A sound change in which a consonant acquires lip rounding.
Velarization: A sound change in which a consonant acquires a velar secondary articulation.
Grimm's Law: The systematic consonant shift in Proto-Germanic, such as Proto-Indo-European *p becoming Germanic *f.
Verner's Law: A sound change in Proto-Germanic that conditioned voicing based on stress position.
Sound change: A systematic, regular shift in the pronunciation of a sound or set of sounds.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or a grammatical function.
Morphology: The branch of linguistics studying the internal structure of words and the rules for word formation.
Morph: A physical, observable form that realizes a morpheme.
Allomorph: A variant phonological form of a single morpheme, such as /k/ and /kʃ/ for English plural.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning.
Stem: The base form of a word to which inflectional affixes are added.
Base: The form to which a morpheme is attached in a given derivation.
Affix: A morpheme that must be attached to a stem or root to form a word.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before the stem or root.
Suffix: An affix that is attached after the stem or root.
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the internal structure of a root.
Circumfix: A pair of affixes that appear on both sides of a stem to form a single morpheme.
Suprafix: An affix realized as a suprasegmental feature, such as stress or tone change.
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new lexeme, often changing the word class.
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical categories without creating a new lexeme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone and must be attached to another morpheme.
Compounding: A word-formation process combining two or more free morphemes into a new word.
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a word is shortened, such as "advertisement" to "ad."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing a perceived affix.
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes class without any morphological change, such as "to walk" from "walk."
Portmanteau: A word formed by blending the sounds and meanings of two or more words, such as "brunch."
Reduplication: A word-formation process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated.
Suppletion: An irregular alternation between two unrelated forms, such as "go" and "went."
Neologism: A newly coined or recently adopted word or expression.
Loanword: A word borrowed directly from another language.
Calque: A phrase or word translated literally from another language, such as "skyscraper" from French "gratte-ciel."
Lexeme: An abstract unit of vocabulary representing all the inflected forms of a word.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word in a particular grammatical category.
Agglutinative: A language type in which each morpheme carries a single grammatical meaning and boundaries are clear.
Fusional: A language type in which morphemes combine multiple grammatical meanings in a single form.
Isolating: A language type in which morphemes are typically monomorphemic and words are uninflected.
Polysynthetic: A language type in which words can incorporate multiple morphemes to express what other languages express in a full sentence.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent word but syntactically independent.
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the beginning of the following word.
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the end of the preceding word.
Interfix: A morpheme inserted between two roots in a compound to ease pronunciation.
Morphophonology: The branch of linguistics studying the interaction between morphology and phonology.
Morphological alternation: A systematic variation in form triggered by morphological context.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Word: The smallest free form that can stand alone in a sentence.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and expressions in a language.
Syntax: The branch of linguistics studying the rules and principles that govern the structure of sentences.
Phrase: A group of one or more words that functions as a single unit within a sentence.
Clause: A group of words containing at least a subject and a predicate.
Sentence: A grammatical unit expressing a complete proposition.
Constituent: A structural unit of a sentence that functions as a single entity in syntactic operations.
Immediate constituent: A direct component of a larger constituent in a hierarchical structure.
Constituency test: A syntactic test used to determine whether a string of words forms a constituent.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of constituents within a sentence.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence.
Bracketing: A linear method of representing hierarchical syntactic structure using paired brackets.
X-bar theory: A generative syntactic theory that generalizes phrase structure using an abstract X-bar schema.
Head: The core lexical element of a phrase that determines the phrase category.
Specifier: The element that precedes the head in a phrase, often providing additional information.
Complement: The element that follows the head in a phrase and is required by the head's subcategorization frame.
Adjunct: An optional modifier that is not required by the head of a phrase.
Projection: The syntactic node built around a head, forming a phrase.
Phrase marker: A node in a tree diagram representing a syntactic category.
Subcategorization: The specification by a lexical item of the syntactic categories of its required arguments and complements.
Theta role: A semantic or thematic role assigned to an argument, such as Agent, Patient, or Goal.
Agent: The thematic role of a voluntary doer of an action.
Patient: The thematic role of the entity affected by an action.
Experiencer: The thematic role of the entity that perceives or feels a state.
Goal: The thematic role of the endpoint or target of a directed action.
Source: The thematic role of the origin or starting point of a directed action.
Instrument: The thematic role of the means or tool used to carry out an action.
Beneficiary: The thematic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Reciprocals: Thematic roles involving mutual action between participants.
Argument: A required participant in a predicate, typically realized as a noun phrase.
Valency: The number of arguments that a predicate requires.
Subjacency: A condition restricting movement to a maximum of two boundaries per step.
C-command: A structural relation in which a node dominates another and no intermediate node dominates the second.
Government: A structural relation in which a head assigns Case or checks features on a complement.
Binding: The syntactic relationship between a pronoun, anaphor, or name and its antecedent.
Anaphor: A reflexive or reciprocal element that must be bound within a local domain.
Antecedent: The element to which a pronoun, anaphor, or name refers.
Binding Condition A: Reflexive anaphors must be bound within their governing category.
Binding Condition B: Pronouns must be free in their governing category.
Binding Condition C: R-expressions (names) must be free everywhere.
Movement: A syntactic operation that relocates a constituent from one position to another.
Trace: The empty category left behind in the original position when an element undergoes movement.
A-movement: The movement of an argument, such as passive or raising.
A-movement-bar: The movement of a non-argument, such as wh-movement or topicalization.
Wh-movement: The movement of an interrogative or relative operator to a clause-initial position.
Topicalization: The fronting of a non-subject constituent to a topic position.
Clefting: A construction that splits a sentence into a focusing and a relative clause.
Passive: A construction in which the object of an active verb becomes the subject.
Causative: A construction in which a cause is added to the subject of a transitive verb.
Intransitive: A verb that takes one argument.
Transitive: A verb that takes two arguments.
Ditransitive: A verb that takes three arguments.
Reciprocal: A verb or construction expressing mutual action between participants.
Reflexive: A verb or construction in which the subject and object are co-referent.
Coordination: The syntactic process of joining two or more elements of the same category.
Subordination: The syntactic process of embedding one clause within another.
Embedding: The inclusion of one clause or phrase within another.
Recursion: The syntactic process by which a rule applies to the output of itself, allowing unbounded structure.
Island constraint: A syntactic restriction that blocks movement out of certain constituent types.
Subject island: A clause in which extraction from the subject position is prohibited.
Complex NP island: A noun phrase containing a complement clause from which extraction is blocked.
Wh-island: A wh-clause from which a second wh-element cannot be extracted.
Left Branch Condition: A constraint preventing the extraction of a non-complement from a phrase.
Case Filter: A principle requiring all noun phrases to receive Case from a governing head.
Theta Criterion: A principle requiring each theta role to be assigned to exactly one argument and each argument to receive exactly one theta role.
Extended Projection Principle: A principle requiring clauses to have a subject.
Government and Binding: A theoretical framework in syntax based on a set of universal principles.
Principles and Parameters: A theoretical framework positing universal principles with language-specific parametric variation.
Minimalism: A syntactic framework that seeks to explain grammar using the simplest possible operations and structures.
Merge: The fundamental operation in Minimalism that combines two syntactic objects into a set.
Agree: The operation in Minimalism by which a probe establishes a feature-sharing relation with a goal.
Phase: A domain in Minimalist syntax that serves as an interface between the computational system and the external systems.
Derivation: The step-by-step process of building a syntactic structure.
Ungrammatical: A construction that violates the grammatical rules of a language.
Periphrasis: The use of a multi-word construction to express what another language expresses with a single morpheme.
Periphrastic: Describing a grammatical form that is realized as a multi-word expression rather than a single morpheme.
Construction: A form-meaning pairing that constitutes a unit of linguistic knowledge.
Frame: A cognitive structure describing a typical situation involving a set of participants and relations.
Lexicalization: The process by which a multi-word expression becomes fixed and stored as a single lexical item.
Semantics: The branch of linguistics concerned with meaning in language.
Sense: The specific meaning of a word in a particular context or usage.
Denotation: The literal, encyclopedic meaning of a word, independent of context.
Connotation: The set of associated, emotional, or cultural meanings attached to a word beyond its denotation.
Referent: The real-world entity or concept to which a linguistic expression points.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and its referent in the world.
Sign: A linguistic unit consisting of a form and a meaning.
Signifier: The phonological or graphic form of a linguistic sign.
Signified: The concept or meaning component of a linguistic sign.
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word having multiple related meanings.
Homonymy: The phenomenon of two or more distinct words sharing the same form.
Synonymy: The relationship between two or more words that have the same or very similar meanings.
Antonymy: The relationship between words with opposite or contrasting meanings.
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is a subset of a more general word.
Hypernym: A word whose meaning is a superset of a more specific word.
Meronym: A word denoting a part of a whole.
Holonym: A word denoting the whole of a part.
Prototype: The most typical or central member of a conceptual category.
Prototype theory: The theory that category membership is graded and organized around typical exemplars.
Frame semantics: A theory of meaning that analyzes words in terms of the conceptual frames or situations they evoke.
Role and Reference Grammar: A semantic framework that analyzes meaning in terms of thematic roles and referential properties.
Generative Lexicon: A semantic framework in which lexical items have complex internal structure and can be modified at the semantic level.
Predicate: A linguistic expression expressing a property or relation.
Proposition: The truth-conditional content expressed by a sentence.
Truth value: The property of a proposition being true or false.
Quantifier: A linguistic expression that specifies quantity or scope, such as "all," "some," or "no."
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or logical operator is interpreted.
Ambiguity: The property of having more than one possible interpretation.
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from alternative syntactic parse trees.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple meanings.
Presupposition: A proposition assumed to be true as a background for an utterance to be interpretable.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Implicature: A meaning that is communicated but not explicitly encoded in the literal content of an utterance.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred from the assumption that speakers follow Grice's maxims.
Conventional implicature: A meaning triggered by specific lexical items, independent of context.
Metaphor: A figurative expression that maps meaning from one conceptual domain onto another.
Metonymy: A figurative expression in which one entity is used to refer to another based on contiguity or association.
Synecdoche: A type of metonymy in which a part is used to refer to the whole or vice versa.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression substituted for one considered harsh or blunt.
Litotes: An understatement formed by negating the opposite of the intended meaning.
Hyperbole: A deliberate and obvious exaggeration for emphasis or effect.
Tautology: The unnecessary repetition of the same meaning in different words.
Oxymoron: A figure of speech joining two seemingly contradictory terms.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics studying how context contributes to meaning in language use.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action beyond merely conveying information.
Locutionary act: The act of producing an utterance with a specific propositional content.
Illocutionary act: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as requesting or promising.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the hearer.
Assertive: A speech act that commits the speaker to the truth of a proposition.
Directive: A speech act that attempts to get the hearer to perform an action.
Commissive: A speech act that commits the speaker to a future course of action.
Expressive: A speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state toward a state of affairs.
Declarative: A speech act that brings about the state of affairs it describes, such as "I hereby declare you married."
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose literal form performs a different act from its intended illocutionary force.
Illocutionary force: The intended communicative function of a speech act.
Felicity conditions: The conditions that must be met for a speech act to be successfully performed.
Grice's maxims: Four principles of cooperative communication: Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner.
Cooperative principle: Grice's general assumption that participants in a conversation are cooperative.
Deixis: A linguistic phenomenon in which reference depends on the context of the utterance.
Anaphora: A linguistic element that refers back to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphora: A linguistic element that refers forward to a subsequently mentioned entity.
Exophora: A linguistic element that refers to something outside the discourse, such as the physical environment.
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose referent depends on the context of use, such as "I," "here," or "now."
Demonstrative: A word or phrase used to point to a specific referent, such as "this" or "that."
Givenness: The status of information as already known or accessible to the interlocutors.
Topic: The entity or subject under discussion in a discourse segment.
Focus: The new, contrasted, or highlighted information in an utterance.
Topic-comment structure: A discourse organization in which the topic introduces the entity and the comment provides new information.
Salience: The degree to which a discourse entity is cognitively accessible to the interlocutors.
Discourse: Language use above the level of the individual sentence, including coherence and organization.
Discourse marker: A word or expression that organizes or connects discourse units, such as "however" or "meanwhile."
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that create surface-level connectedness in a text.
Coherence: The logical and semantic unity of a discourse, independent of explicit linguistic markers.
Reference: A cohesive device in which one expression points to the same entity as another.
Conjunction: A cohesive device in which connecting words or phrases link discourse units.
Ellipsis: A cohesive device in which material is omitted because it is recoverable from context.
Lexical cohesion: Cohesion achieved through the use of repeated, synonymous, or related words.
Narrative: A discourse structure organized around a sequence of events.
Exposition: A discourse structure organized around the presentation or explanation of information.
Argumentation: A discourse structure organized around presenting and defending a claim.
Script: A cognitive framework representing the typical sequence of events in a familiar situation.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic theory positing that communication is guided by the principle of optimal relevance.
Optimal relevance: The principle that an utterance is interpreted to provide maximal cognitive effects for minimal processing effort.
Common ground: The shared knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions among interlocutors in a conversation.
Mutual knowledge: Information known by all participants in a communicative interaction.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category marking the source or reliability of information.
Reportative: An evidential marking that indicates the information is based on someone else's report.
Hearsay: An evidential marking indicating secondhand or unverified information.
Inferential: An evidential marking indicating the information is a conclusion drawn by the speaker.
Sarcasm: The use of language to express the opposite of the literal meaning, typically with a mocking tone.
Irony: A rhetorical device in which there is a contrast between expectation and reality, or between literal and intended meaning.
Antiphrasis: The use of a word or phrase in a sense opposite to its literal meaning.
Sociolinguistics: The branch of linguistics studying the relationship between language and society.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region or social group.
Accent: The phonological or phonetic variety of speech associated with a particular region or group.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Sociolect: A language variety associated with a particular social group.
Register: A language variety associated with a particular communicative context or purpose.
Standard variety: The prestigious, codified form of a language used in formal institutions.
Prestige: The positive social value associated with a particular language variety.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety.
Language ideology: The set of beliefs and attitudes a community holds about its own and others' languages.
Linguistic relativism: The hypothesis that language influences or shapes the way speakers perceive and think about the world.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The hypothesis that the structure of a language determines or influences the structure of its speakers' thought.
Ethnography of communication: The study of communicative practices within their cultural context.
Communicative competence: The ability to use language appropriately and effectively in social contexts.
Linguistic competence: The internalized knowledge of a language's grammatical system.
Performance: The actual production or processing of language in real-time conditions.
Speech community: A group of individuals who share a set of communicative norms and conventions.
Dialect continuum: A chain of geographically adjacent dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary separating areas that differ in a particular linguistic feature.
Dialectometry: The quantitative measurement of dialectal differences.
Vernacular: The everyday, uncodified language variety used in informal settings.
Lingua franca: A language adopted as a common means of communication among speakers of different native languages.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language, typically without native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that arises from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two languages.
Multilingualism: The ability to use three or more languages.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages within a single discourse.
Code-mixing: The blending of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages that leads to mutual influence.
Language death: The event in which the last native speaker of a language dies.
Language endangerment: The state in which a language is at risk of ceasing to be spoken.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers or the domains of use of a declining language.
Language policy: The set of regulations and decisions made by institutions regarding the use of languages.
Language planning: The deliberate, organized effort to influence the structure, acquisition, or use of a language.
First language acquisition: The process by which children acquire their native language.
Second language acquisition: The process by which individuals acquire a language after their first.
Interlanguage: The evolving linguistic system of a second language learner.
Fossilization: The permanent stabilization of non-native linguistic features in a second language learner's system.
Critical period hypothesis: The hypothesis that there is a biologically determined window for optimal first language acquisition.
Input: The language that a learner is exposed to and receives.
Intake: The portion of input that a learner successfully processes and stores.
Output: The language that a learner produces.
Child-directed speech: Speech produced by adults or older children that is adapted for a younger audience.
Telegraphic speech: A stage in first language acquisition in which children produce short utterances omitting function words.
Overregularization: A child's application of a regular morphological rule to an irregular form, such as "goed" for "went."
Overextension: A child's use of a word in a broader range of contexts than is appropriate, such as calling all four-legged animals "dog."
Phonological development: The process by which children acquire the sound system of their language.
Morphological development: The process by which children acquire word structure and grammatical morphemes.
Syntactic development: The process by which children acquire sentence structure.
Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics studying how languages change over time.
Comparative method: The method of identifying systematic sound correspondences to reconstruct proto-languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed through the comparative method.
Cognate: A word in two or more languages that has a common etymological origin.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.
Onomatopoeia: The formation of a word that imitates or suggests the sound it represents.
Sound correspondence: A regular, systematic relationship between sounds in related languages.
Regular sound change: A phonological shift that applies uniformly to all relevant contexts.
Analogy: A morphological or phonological process in which a form is altered to match other forms in the paradigm.
Leveling: The reduction of allomorphy or irregularity through the spread of a regular form.
Divergence: The process by which a single language splits into multiple distinct varieties.
Convergence: The process by which different languages or dialects become more similar through contact.
Substrate: A language variety that influences a more dominant language from below, often leaving traces in phonology or vocabulary.
Superstrate: A language variety that influences a more dominant language from above, typically contributing vocabulary.
Adstrate: A language variety that influences a neighboring language through sustained contact.
Sprachbund: A group of geographically adjacent languages that share structural features due to prolonged contact.
Areal feature: A linguistic feature shared by languages in a particular geographic region due to contact rather than common ancestry.
Diffusion: The spread of a linguistic feature from one language to another through contact.
Interference: The influence of one language on the speech of a speaker of another language.
Loan translation: The translation of the constituent elements of a foreign word into the native language.
Lexical borrowing: The adoption of words from one language into another.
Morphological borrowing: The adoption of grammatical structures or affixes from one language into another.
Syntactic borrowing: The adoption of word order or clause structure from one language into another.
Phonological borrowing: The adoption of sound patterns or phonemic distinctions from one language into another.
Language family: A group of languages that share a common ancestral proto-language.
Language branch: A subgroup within a language family, such as the Germanic branch of Indo-European.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language.
Language stock: A proposed grouping of language families of uncertain but possibly related status.
Glottochronology: A method of estimating the time of language divergence based on the rate of lexical replacement.
Lexicostatistics: The use of the percentage of shared basic vocabulary to estimate the relationship and age of language splits.
Phylogenetic tree: A diagram representing the hypothesized genetic relationships among languages.
Mass migration: A hypothesis in historical linguistics proposing that wholesale population movement explains large-scale language replacement.
Diachronic: Pertaining to the study of language across time.
Synchronic: Pertaining to the study of a language at a single point in time.
Descriptive linguistics: The study and documentation of how a language is actually used by its speakers.
Prescriptive linguistics: The attempt to establish and enforce rules for "correct" language use.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, structured collections of real-world text and speech.
Computational linguistics: The study of language using computational models and algorithms.
Cognitive linguistics: An approach to linguistics that views language as rooted in general cognitive processes.
Typology: The study of the typological patterns and universals across the world's languages.
Language universal: A property shared by all or most of the world's languages.
Parametric typology: The classification of languages according to the values of a finite set of structural parameters.
Greenbergian typology: A typological framework based on a list of proposed linguistic universals.
Word order typology: The classification of languages according to their basic constituent order.
Typological scale: An ordering of linguistic elements by a structural or functional criterion.
Morphosyntax: The interface between morphology and syntax.
Morphosyntactic alignment: The classification of languages according to how they mark grammatical relations.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A system in which intransitive subjects are aligned with transitive agents.
Ergative-absolutive alignment: A system in which intransitive subjects are aligned with transitive patients.
Ergative: The grammatical case marking the agent of a transitive verb in an ergative system.
Absolutive: The grammatical case marking the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb in an ergative system.
Split-ergativity: A system in which ergative and accusative alignments coexist, conditioned by aspect, tense, or transitivity.
Nominative: The grammatical case typically marking the subject of an intransitive verb or the agent of a transitive verb.
Accusative: The grammatical case typically marking the direct object or patient of a transitive verb.
Dative: The grammatical case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive: The grammatical case typically marking possession, origin, or association.
Instrumental: The grammatical case typically marking the means or tool by which an action is performed.
Locative: The grammatical case typically marking location or place.
Ablative: The grammatical case typically marking separation or source.
Allative: The grammatical case typically marking direction or goal.
Vocative: The grammatical case used in direct address.
Oblique: A case that is neither nominative nor accusative.
Case marking: The morphological marking of grammatical relations on nouns, adjectives, or determiners.
Case assignment: The syntactic process by which a governing head assigns Case to a noun phrase.
Internal Case: Case marked on the noun or noun phrase itself.
External Case: Case assigned to a noun phrase by a functional head such as T or v.
Nominal: A word or phrase that functions as a noun or noun phrase.
Verbal: A word or phrase that functions as a verb or verb phrase.
Adjectival: A word or phrase that functions as an adjective.
Adverbial: A word or phrase that functions as an adverb.
Adjective: A word that modifies a noun and expresses a property or quality.
Adverb: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb, expressing manner, time, place, or degree.
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase.
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its definiteness or quantity.
Article: A type of determiner indicating definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" or "a."
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used to introduce a question, such as "who," "what," or "which."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause, such as "who," "which," or "that."
Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," or "or."
Preposition: A word that precedes a noun phrase to express a spatial, temporal, or abstract relation.
Postposition: A word that follows a noun phrase to express a spatial, temporal, or abstract relation.
Circumposition: A pair of words that together frame a noun phrase to express a relation.
Case marker: A morpheme that indicates the grammatical role of a noun in a sentence.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Voice: A grammatical category expressing the relationship between the participants in an event and the syntactic structure, such as active or passive.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker, the addressee, and others.
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, plural, or other quantity categories.
Gender: A grammatical category classifying nouns into sets, often correlated with natural sex or other properties.
Animacy: A grammatical category distinguishing living from non-living entities.
Definiteness: A grammatical category distinguishing specific, identifiable referents from non-specific ones.
Plural: A number category indicating more than one referent.
Singular: A number category indicating exactly one referent.
Dual: A number category indicating exactly two referents.
Triangular: A number category indicating exactly three referents.
Augmentative: A diminutive or augmentative morpheme indicating larger size.
Diminutive: A morpheme indicating smaller size, often with a connotation of affection or contempt.
Diminutive: A form expressing smallness or endearment through morphological means.
Aspectual class: The classification of verbs according to the internal temporal structure of the events they denote, such as stative, punctual, or durative.
Aktionsart: The inherent aspect of a verb, describing the temporal profile of the event.
Perfective aspect: An aspectual value presenting an event as a complete whole.
Imperfective aspect: An aspectual value presenting an event as ongoing, habitual, or internal.
Progressive aspect: An aspectual value emphasizing the ongoing, in-progress nature of an event.
Perfect aspect: An aspectual value linking a past event to the present moment.
Pluperfect aspect: An aspectual value linking an event to a point prior to the speech time.
Anteriority: The property of an event occurring before the reference time.
Posteriority: The property of an event occurring after the reference time.
Simultaneity: The property of an event occurring at the same time as the reference time.
Durative: An aspectual or Aktionsart value indicating an event that extends over a period of time.
Punctual: An aspectual or Aktionsart value indicating an event that occurs at a single point in time.
Momentaneous: An aspectual value indicating an event with no perceptible duration.
Semelfactive: An Aktionsart value indicating a single, bounded occurrence.
Iterative: An aspectual value indicating repeated or habitual action.
Habitual: An aspectual value indicating regular, customary, or repeated action.
Completive: An aspectual value marking the completion or result of an event.
Inchoative: An aspectual or Aktionsart value marking the beginning of a state or process.
Cessative: An aspectual value marking the end or cessation of a state or process.
Resultative: An aspectual value marking the resulting state after the completion of an event.
Stative: An Aktionsart value describing a verb that denotes a state rather than an event.
Dynamic: An Aktionsart value describing a verb that denotes an event or process.
Telic: An event or verb with an inherent endpoint or goal.
Atelic: An event or verb without an inherent endpoint.
Punctual Aktionsart: A verb type denoting a point event with no duration.
Inchoative verb: A verb that means "to begin" or "to enter a state."
Causative verb: A verb that adds a causer argument to the base event.
Anti-causative verb: A verb that removes a causer argument, converting a transitive into an intransitive.
Middle voice: A grammatical voice in which the subject is affected by the action without an explicit agent.
Reflexive verb: A verb in which the subject and object are the same entity.
Reciprocal verb: A verb expressing mutual action between the participants.
Applicative: A grammatical process that adds an argument, typically a recipient or beneficiary.
Incorporation: A morphological process in which a noun is incorporated into a verb to form a single word.
Noun incorporation: The process of embedding a noun stem within a verbal complex.
Verb serialization: A construction in which two or more verbs appear in sequence to express a complex event.
Serial verb construction: A syntactic construction using a sequence of verbs to express aspect, direction, or manner.
Light verb: A verb that contributes little semantic content and relies on a complement for its meaning.
Heavy verb: A verb that carries substantial semantic content.
Auxiliary verb: A verb that provides grammatical information such as tense, aspect, modality, or voice.
Modal auxiliary: An auxiliary verb expressing necessity, possibility, or permission.
Copula: A verb that links the subject to a predicate noun or adjective without expressing an action.
Linking verb: A verb that connects the subject to a subject complement, such as "seem" or "appear."
Finite verb: A verb form that is marked for person, number, and tense and can serve as the main predicate.
Non-finite verb: A verb form that is unmarked for tense and person, such as an infinitive, participle, or gerund.
Infinitive: A non-finite verb form typically marked by a particle, such as English "to walk."
Participle: A non-finite verb form used to form adjectives or perfect and progressive constructions.
Gerund: A non-finite verb form ending in -ing in English that functions as a noun.
Past participle: A verb form used in perfect constructions and as an adjective, such as "gone" or "broken."
Present participle: A verb form used in progressive constructions, such as "walking" or "running."
Inflectional morphology: The set of morphological processes that mark grammatical categories without creating new lexemes.
Derivational morphology: The set of morphological processes that create new lexemes or change word class.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonological realization, such as the absence of a suffix for plural in some languages.
Suppletive form: A word form that is etymologically unrelated to other forms in its paradigm.
Allomorphic: Having more than one allomorph.
Morphophonemic rule: A rule describing the phonological alternations triggered by morphological processes.
Morpheme order: The linear sequence of morphemes within a word.
Morphotactic: The rules governing the order and selection of affixes.
Affix order: The linear arrangement of affixes in a word.
Affixal: Pertaining to affixes.
Cliticization: The process by which a clitic attaches to a host word.
Host word: The word to which a clitic attaches.
Pro-drop: The grammatical omission of subject or object pronouns, as in Italian or Japanese.
Null subject: The absence of an overt subject in a clause.
Null object: The absence of an overt object in a clause.
Empty category: A syntactic position that has no overt phonological realization.
Pro: An unpronounced pronoun or empty category in syntactic theory.
Prole: An unpronounced operator, often associated with focus or relativization.
Zero anaphora: The omission of a pronominal element that is recoverable from context.
Bound variable: A variable in formal semantics whose value is determined by a quantifier.
Free variable: A variable in formal semantics whose value is not determined by a quantifier.
Bound pronoun: A pronoun whose reference is determined by a quantifier or operator.
Coreference: The relation between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
Co-indexing: The notation in formal syntax indicating that two elements are coreferential.
Discourse representation: A formal model of how discourse elements are related.
Discourse referent: An entity introduced or referenced in a discourse.
File card: In Discourse Representation Theory, a structure representing an entity introduced in discourse.
Discourse Representation Theory: A semantic and pragmatic framework for modeling the interpretation of discourse.
Situation semantics: A semantic framework that interprets meaning in terms of possible situations.
Possible world: A complete way the world could be, used as a model in formal semantics.
Intension: The set of possible worlds in which a proposition is true.
Extension: The set of real-world entities to which a term refers.
Denotational semantics: A formal semantic framework that maps linguistic expressions to their referents and truth values.
Model-theoretic semantics: A semantic framework using mathematical models to assign meaning.
Montague grammar: A formal semantic framework developed by Richard Montague that maps natural language to logic.
Intensional logic: A logical framework that distinguishes between intension and extension.
Truth-conditional semantics: A semantic framework that defines meaning in terms of truth conditions.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and their mode of combination.
Frege's principle: The principle that substituting co-referring expressions preserves truth value.
Russell's theory of descriptions: A semantic theory for definite descriptions that avoids presupposition problems.
Definite description: A noun phrase of the form "the N" that presupposes a unique referent.
Indefinite description: A noun phrase of the form "a N" that does not presuppose a unique referent.
Quantifier domain: The set of entities over which a quantifier ranges.
Scope ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the different possible scopes of quantifiers or logical operators.
Quantifier raising: A syntactic operation in which a quantifier moves to a higher position to take scope.
Variable binding: The semantic operation by which a quantifier binds a variable in its scope.
Lifting: The operation of raising a quantifier above a propositional operator.
Modal logic: A logical framework extending classical logic with operators for necessity and possibility.
Epistemic modality: Modality expressing knowledge or belief, such as "probably" or "necessarily."
Deontic modality: Modality expressing obligation or permission, such as "must" or "may."
Bouletic modality: Modality expressing desire or wish.
Dynamic modality: Modality expressing physical possibility or necessity.
Modal verb: A verb expressing modality, such as "can," "must," or "should."
Counterfactual: A proposition about a situation that is contrary to fact, typically expressed with the subjunctive mood.
Counterfactual conditional: A conditional with a false antecedent, such as "If I had studied, I would have passed."
Subjunctive mood: A grammatical mood expressing doubt, possibility, or counterfactual situations.
Indicative mood: A grammatical mood expressing factual statements.
Imperative mood: A grammatical mood expressing commands or requests.
Optative mood: A grammatical mood expressing wishes or hopes.
Jussive: A mood or particle expressing commands, requests, or wishes.
Mood particle: A word that marks the mood of a clause.
Sentence mood: The illocutionary type of a sentence, such as declarative, interrogative, or imperative.
Interrogative: A sentence type that poses a question.
Declarative: A sentence type that states a proposition.
Imperative: A sentence type that issues a command or request.
Exclamative: A sentence type that expresses strong emotion.
Question type: The classification of questions into yes-no, wh-, tag, and echo questions.

Phonetics:
1. Phonetics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds as they are produced, transmitted, and perceived.
2. Articulation: The physiological process by which speech sounds are produced by the movement of the articulators.
3. Articulator: Any part of the vocal tract (tongue, lips, velum, etc.) that moves to produce speech sounds.
4. Larynx: The portion of the vocal tract containing the vocal folds (vocal cords).
5. Vocal fold: Paired tissue in the larynx that vibrates to produce phonation.
6. Pharynx: The region of the vocal tract between the mouth and the larynx.
7. Alveolar ridge: The bony ridge behind the upper front teeth.
8. Palate: The roof of the mouth, divided into the hard palate and soft palate.
9. Hard palate: The bony anterior portion of the roof of the mouth.
10. Soft palate: The muscular posterior portion of the roof of the mouth (velum).
11. Velum: The soft palate; its raising or lowering controls the nasal cavity.
12. Uvula: The fleshy projection hanging from the rear of the soft palate.
13. Epiglottis: The flap of tissue above the larynx that prevents food from entering the windpipe.
14. Glottis: The opening between the vocal folds in the larynx.
15. Trachea: The windpipe, the tube connecting the larynx to the lungs.
16. Oral cavity: The space enclosed by the lips, teeth, tongue, and palate.
17. Nasal cavity: The space above the oral cavity, connected via the choanae.
18. Choanae: The openings connecting the nasal cavity to the pharynx.
19. Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth.
20. Labial: A place of articulation involving the lips.
21. Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips.
22. Interdental: A place of articulation involving the tongue between the upper and lower teeth.
23. Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue and upper teeth.
24. Alveolar: A place of articulation involving the tongue and the alveolar ridge.
25. Postalveolar: A place of articulation just behind the alveolar ridge.
26. Retroflex: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip curled back toward the palate.
27. Palatal: A place of articulation involving the front of the tongue and the hard palate.
28. Palatal-alveolar: A place of articulation between alveolar and palatal.
29. Velar: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the soft palate.
30. Uvular: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the uvula.
31. Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the pharyngeal wall.
32. Epiglottal: A place of articulation involving the epiglottis.
33. Glottal: A place of articulation at the glottis.
34. Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure in the vocal tract followed by a release of air.
35. Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction causing turbulent airflow.
36. Affricate: A consonant combining a plosive closure with a fricative release.
37. Nasal: A consonant produced with a complete oral closure and nasal airflow.
38. Lateral: A consonant produced with a central closure and lateral airflow.
39. Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid vibrations of an articulator against another.
40. Tap: A single brief vibration of an articulator against another (flap).
41. Approximant: A consonant produced with a close but not turbulent constriction.
42. Semivowel: A consonant that has vowel-like articulation (e.g., /j/, /w/).
43. Glide: Another term for semivowel.
44. Manner of articulation: The classification of consonants by how the airflow is obstructed.
45. Voicing: The presence or absence of vocal fold vibration during sound production.
46. Voiceless: Produced without vocal fold vibration.
47. Voiced: Produced with vocal fold vibration.
48. Aspiration: A burst of airflow accompanying the release of a plosive.
49. Nasalization: The lowering of the velum during sound production, allowing nasal airflow.
50. Pharyngealization: Constriction in the pharynx accompanying a segment.

# Glossary of Linguistics Terms

Phonetics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds as they are produced, transmitted, and perceived.
Articulation: The physiological process by which speech sounds are produced through the movement of the articulators in the vocal tract.
Articulator: Any part of the vocal tract (tongue, lips, velum, etc.) that moves or is moved to produce a speech sound.
Larynx: The portion of the vocal tract containing the vocal folds, where phonation occurs.
Vocal fold: Paired tissue in the larynx that vibrates to produce voiced sound; also called vocal cords.
Pharynx: The region of the vocal tract situated between the oral cavity and the larynx.
Alveolar ridge: The bony ridge of tissue located just behind the upper front teeth.
Hard palate: The bony anterior portion of the roof of the mouth.
Soft palate: The muscular posterior portion of the roof of the mouth, also known as the velum.
Velum: The soft palate; its raising or lowering directs airflow through the oral or nasal cavity.
Uvula: The fleshy projection hanging from the posterior end of the soft palate.
Epiglottis: The flap of cartilage above the larynx that helps prevent food from entering the airway during swallowing.
Glottis: The slit-like opening between the vocal folds within the larynx.
Trachea: The windpipe, the tube connecting the larynx to the lungs.
Oral cavity: The space enclosed by the lips, teeth, tongue, palate, and floor of the mouth.
Nasal cavity: The air space above the oral cavity, connected to the pharynx through the choanae.
Choanae: The paired openings connecting the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx.
Labiodental: A place of articulation involving the lower lip and the upper teeth.
Labial: A place of articulation involving the lips.
Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both the upper and lower lips.
Interdental: A place of articulation involving the tongue blade positioned between the upper and lower teeth.
Dental: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth.
Alveolar: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge.
Postalveolar: A place of articulation on the blade of the tongue just behind the alveolar ridge.
Retroflex: A place of articulation involving the tongue tip curled back toward the mid-palate.
Palatal: A place of articulation involving the front of the tongue body against the hard palate.
Palatal-alveolar: A place of articulation between the alveolar ridge and the palatal region.
Velar: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue against the soft palate.
Uvular: A place of articulation involving the back of the tongue against the uvula.
Pharyngeal: A place of articulation involving the pharyngeal wall.
Epiglottal: A place of articulation involving the epiglottis.
Glottal: A place of articulation at the level of the glottis.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure in the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air.
Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that creates turbulent airflow.
Affricate: A consonant that combines a plosive closure with a fricative release at the same place of articulation.
Nasal: A consonant produced with a complete oral closure and simultaneous lowering of the velum, directing airflow through the nasal cavity.
Lateral: A consonant produced with a central closure in the vocal tract and airflow directed around the sides of the tongue.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid vibrations of an articulator against a passive articulator.
Tap: A single, brief vibration of a mobile articulator against a passive one; also called a flap.
Approximant: A consonant produced with a close but non-turbulent constriction in the vocal tract.
Semivowel: A consonant with vowel-like articulation, typically a glide such as /j/ or /w/.
Glide: Another term for semivowel; a consonant produced with a constriction approaching vowel-like quality.
Manner of articulation: The classification of consonants according to the degree and type of airflow obstruction.
Voicing: The presence or absence of vocal fold vibration during the production of a speech sound.
Voiceless: Produced without vocal fold vibration, as in English /p/, /t/, /s/.
Voiced: Produced with vocal fold vibration, as in English /b/, /d/, /z/.
Aspiration: A prominent burst of pulmonic outflow accompanying the release of a plosive.
Nasalization: The lowering of the velum during the production of an oral sound, permitting simultaneous nasal airflow.
Pharyngealization: A secondary articulation involving constriction in the pharynx accompanying a primary segment.
Uvularization: A secondary articulation involving constriction at the uvular region accompanying a primary segment.
Palatalization: A secondary articulation involving the raising of the tongue body toward the hard palate.
Velarization: A secondary articulation involving the raising of the tongue back toward the velum.
Labialization: A secondary articulation involving the rounding of the lips accompanying a segment.
Secondary articulation: An additional place of articulation that accompanies the primary articulation of a segment.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction to the airflow.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
Monophthong: A single, steady-state vowel sound without a noticeable glide.
Diphthong: A vowel that glides from one target to another within a single syllable, e.g., English /aɪ/.
Triphthong: A vowel sequence combining three distinct qualities within a single syllable.
Formant: A band of concentrated acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum, produced by resonances of the vocal tract.
First formant: The lowest resonant frequency of the vocal tract, primarily correlated with vowel height.
Second formant: The next higher resonant frequency, primarily correlated with vowel frontness.
Fundamental frequency: The rate of vocal fold vibration in cycles per second, perceived as pitch.
Pitch: The perceptual correlate of fundamental frequency, the perceived "highness" or "lowness" of a tone.
Loudness: The perceptual correlate of acoustic amplitude or intensity.
Duration: The length of time a speech segment or prosodic event is produced.
Spectrogram: A visual representation of the frequency content of a sound signal plotted against time.
Waveform: A visual display of the amplitude of a sound signal as it varies over time.
Acoustic phonetics: The subfield of phonetics that studies the physical and measurable properties of speech sounds.
Articulatory phonetics: The subfield of phonetics that studies how speech sounds are produced by the vocal tract.
Auditory phonetics: The subfield of phonetics that studies how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the listener.
International Phonetic Alphabet: A standardized system of symbols and diacritics for representing the sounds of all human languages.
Broad transcription: A level of IPA notation that records only phonemically relevant distinctions, typically within square brackets without diacritics.
Narrow transcription: A level of IPA notation that records fine-grained phonetic detail, often using diacritics.
Diacritic: A small additional symbol attached to a main IPA character to indicate a phonetic modification.
Homorganic: Two sounds that share the same place of articulation.
Heterorganic: Two sounds that differ in their place of articulation.
Phonology: The study of the systematic organization of sounds in a language, including the patterns, units, and rules governing their use.
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can serve to distinguish meaning, e.g., /p/ and /b/ in English.
Allophone: A phonetically distinct variant of a phoneme that does not change lexical meaning, e.g., the aspirated and unaspirated /p/ in English.
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, often indicating they are allophones of one phoneme.
Contrastive distribution: A relationship in which two sounds can occur in the same environment and distinguish word meanings, indicating separate phonemes.
Free variation: A relationship in which two sounds may occur interchangeably in the same environment without altering meaning.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in exactly one phoneme in the same phonetic environment, e.g., "pat" and "bat."
Minimal set: A set of words identical in all positions except one, used to demonstrate a phonemic contrast.
Near minimal pair: Two words that differ in more than one segment but are used to establish a phonemic contrast where a true minimal pair does not exist.
Phonemic contrast: A distinction between two phonemes that is functionally meaningful in a particular language.
Neutralization: The cancellation of a phonemic contrast in a specific phonological environment, such as final obstruent devoicing in German.
Phonemic: Pertaining to phonemes; a distinction or relation that is functionally meaningful.
Phonotactics: The system of rules governing which sound sequences are permissible or prohibited in a language.
Syllable: A basic unit of phonological organization, typically organized around a vowel or syllabic consonant.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster preceding the nucleus in a syllable.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable following the onset, comprising the nucleus and any coda.
Nucleus: The most sonorous element of a syllable, typically a vowel or syllabic consonant.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster following the nucleus within a syllable.
Syllable structure: The hierarchical organization of segments into syllabic units such as onset, nucleus, and coda.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a string of segments into syllables according to a language's rules.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a segment into a word, often to break up a disallowed cluster.
Elision: The deletion or dropping of a segment from a word, especially in connected speech.
Metathesis: The transposition or swapping of the order of two adjacent segments within a word.
Assimilation: The process by which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound in one or more features.
Dissimilation: The process by which two similar sounds in close proximity become less similar over time or within a word.
Lenition: The progressive weakening of a consonant, often involving a change from plosive to fricative to approximant.
Fortition: The progressive strengthening of a consonant, the reverse of lenition.
Sandhi: A phonological change that occurs at the boundary between words or morphemes.
Haplogy: The reduction of a geminate or long consonant to a single short consonant.
Gemination: The lengthening or doubling of a consonant, producing a long consonant segment.
Degemination: The shortening of a geminate consonant to a single consonant.
Vowel harmony: A phonological pattern in which vowels within a word must share a particular feature, such as frontness, backness, or height.
Front vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body advanced toward the front of the oral cavity.
Back vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body retracted toward the back of the oral cavity.
Central vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in a mid-front to mid-back position.
High vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the hard palate.
Mid vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in an intermediate vertical position.
Low vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body lowered toward the floor of the mouth.
Tense vowel: A vowel produced with relatively high muscular tension in the tongue.
Lax vowel: A vowel produced with relatively low muscular tension in the tongue.
Rounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips rounded.
Unrounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral.
Vowel length: A phonological contrast based on the relative duration of a vowel.
Long vowel: A vowel that is phonemically longer than its short counterpart in a language.
Short vowel: A vowel that is phonemically shorter than its long counterpart in a language.
Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property used in phonological theory to characterize and distinguish segments, e.g., [±voice], [±nasal].
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which features are organized in a hierarchical tree structure.
Autosegment: A phonological segment (e.g., tone, register) that is not tied to a single consonantal or vocalic position but spans a string of segments.
Suprasegmental: A property of speech that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or utterance, realized through pitch, duration, and loudness.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch at the syllable or word level to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation over a phrase or sentence, encoding grammatical and discourse information.
Prosody: The study of suprasegmental features including stress, rhythm, tone, and intonation.
Contour tone: A tone in which the pitch moves (rises, falls, or peaks) over the duration of the syllable.
Level tone: A tone in which the pitch remains approximately constant over the duration of the syllable.
Register: A suprasegmental feature involving a change in the configuration of the larynx, producing a contrast such as creaky vs. modal voice.
Juncture: A boundary or pause in the phonological structure that distinguishes phrases or words in connected speech.
Prosodic word: A unit of prosodic organization roughly corresponding to a word, serving as the domain for certain phonological processes.
Phonological word: A unit of phonological analysis that serves as the domain for rules of stress, tone, or other prosodic properties.
Phonological rule: A rule in a phonological grammar that transforms an underlying representation into a surface form.
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word or morpheme in a generative grammar.
Surface form: The phonetic or phonological output after all phonological rules have been applied.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has two or more phonologically distinct realizations.
Morphology: The branch of linguistics concerned with the structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language, which may or may not be freely producible on its own.
Allomorph: A phonologically distinct variant form of a morpheme, e.g., the plural morpheme realized as /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/ in English.
Root: The core, usually unanalyzable morpheme that carries the primary lexical meaning of a word.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: An affix attached to the beginning of a word or stem, e.g., "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix attached to the end of a word or stem, e.g., "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: An affix inserted within the body of a root, as in certain Austronesian languages.
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds a stem, consisting of two parts, e.g., German "ge-…-t."
Suprefix: An affix added to the top of another prefix, creating a multi-layered prefixal structure.
Subfix: An affix added to the bottom of a root, a rare but attested morphological process.
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the lexical category, e.g., "-ness" turning "happy" into "happiness."
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without creating a new lexeme.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a complete word.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is morphologically present but phonetically empty, e.g., the zero plural in "sheep."
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses two or more grammatical or semantic functions.
Agglutination: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each typically expressing one grammatical category.
Inflection: The modification of a word's form to express grammatical relationships, such as tense or case.
Conjugation: The paradigm of a verb's inflected forms, varying by person, number, tense, aspect, and mood.
Declension: The paradigm of a noun, adjective, or pronoun's inflected forms, varying by case, number, and gender.
Compounding: The formation of a new word by combining two or more free morphemes or roots, e.g., "blackboard."
Backformation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparently affixal element from an existing word, e.g., "editor" from "edit."
Conversion: The formation of a new word by changing the grammatical category without any overt affixation, e.g., "to google."
Suppletion: The replacement of one form with an entirely unrelated form in a paradigm, e.g., "go" → "went."
Isomorphism: A one-to-one correspondence between morphemes and affixes in a language's morphology.
Morphological analysis: The process of identifying the morphemes and their structural relationships within a word.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, organized by grammatical categories.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of inflected forms, e.g., the lexeme RUN encompassing "run," "runs," "ran," "running."
Word form: A specific phonological or orthographic realization of a lexeme, e.g., "runs" is a word form of the lexeme RUN.
Stem: The base form to which inflectional morphemes are attached.
Theme: A morphological element that marks a lexical category or grammatical class, often a vowel.
Radical: The core semantic element of a morpheme or word, particularly in Semitic languages.
Morph: An actual occurrence of a morpheme in speech or writing.
Morphotactics: The rules governing the permissible order and combination of morphemes within a word.
Morpher: The physical or orthographic string that instantiates a morpheme in a particular word.
Morphological productivity: The degree to which a particular affix or morphological process is actively used to form new words.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a morpheme depending on its morphological environment.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical meaning.
Iteration: A type of reduplication in which the repeated element is identical to the original.
Portmanteau: A word formed by blending two or more words, e.g., "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Bound root: A root morpheme that must be attached to other morphemes and cannot stand alone.
Free root: A root morpheme that can function independently as a word.
Grammatical morpheme: A morpheme that carries grammatical rather than lexical meaning, such as a case ending or tense marker.
Zero derivation: The formation of a new word through conversion without any overt morphological marking.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent, e.g., the contracted "n't" in English.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Paradigmatic: Relating to the vertical axis of linguistic choice, where one element is selected from a set of alternatives.
Syntagmatic: Relating to the horizontal axis of linguistic combination, where elements are strung together in sequence.
Isomorph: A morpheme with only one allomorph.
Allomorph set: The collection of all phonologically distinct variants of a single morpheme.
Morphophonemics: The study of the systematic relationship between morphemes and their phonological realizations.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages according to their predominant morphological structure (isolating, agglutinative, fusional, polysynthetic).
Isolating language: A language in which words typically consist of a single morpheme, e.g., Mandarin Chinese.
Agglutinative language: A language in which words are formed by concatenating morphemes, each expressing one grammatical category.
Fusional language: A language in which a single affix may express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin.
Polysynthetic language: A language in which a single word can incorporate numerous morphemes, often corresponding to an entire sentence.
Morphological head: The morpheme that determines the grammatical category of the word to which it is attached.
Morphological complexity: The degree to which a language's words contain multiple morphemes and irregular forms.
Morphological irregularity: A word form that does not follow the regular morphological patterns of a language.
Morphological rule: A rule that governs the combination or transformation of morphemes in a language.
Morphological product: The word or word form produced by a morphological process.
Morphological input: The set of morphemes or lexical items that serve as the starting point for a morphological process.
Morphological output: The resulting word or word form after a morphological process has been applied.
Morphological economy: The principle that languages tend to use the simplest possible morphological forms.
Morphological ambiguity: A situation in which a word form can be parsed in more than one morphological way.
Morphological parsing: The process of identifying the constituent morphemes within a word.
Morphological constraint: A restriction on the permissible combination or order of morphemes.
Morphological innovation: A new morphological process or pattern that emerges in a language.
Morphological change: The diachronic alteration of morphological patterns over time.
Morphological leveling: The regularization of irregular paradigmatic forms to match the regular pattern.
Morphological analogical change: The extension of a regular morphological pattern to irregular forms.
Morphological erosion: The gradual reduction or loss of overt morphological marking.
Morphological enrichment: The addition of new morphological distinctions to a language's system.
Morphological productivity scale: A ranking of morphological processes by their active use in forming new words.
Morphological salience: The degree to which a morphological element is perceptually or cognitively prominent.
Morphological default: A form that is used in the absence of specific morphological marking.
Morphological marking: The overt expression of a grammatical category through affixation, inflection, or other means.
Morphological unmarking: The absence of overt morphological marking for a grammatical category.
Morphological symmetry: A balanced or parallel pattern in the morphological system of a language.
Morphological asymmetry: An unbalanced or irregular pattern in the morphological system of a language.
Syntax: The branch of linguistics concerned with the structure of sentences and the rules governing the combination of words into phrases and clauses.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of constituents within a sentence, typically represented as a tree diagram.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the syntactic structure of a sentence, showing constituent relationships.
Constituent: A syntactic unit that functions as a single element within a larger structure, e.g., a noun phrase within a clause.
Complement: A constituent that completes the meaning of a head, e.g., the object in a transitive clause.
Head: The central element of a phrase that determines its category and subcategorization properties.
Specifier: A constituent that precedes the head within a phrase, e.g., the determiner in a DP.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a single category, e.g., NP, VP, PP.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be finite or non-finite.
Sentence: A complete syntactic and prosodic unit expressing a proposition.
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or determiner, e.g., "the tall building."
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, e.g., "ate an apple."
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, e.g., "in the garden."
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, e.g., "very happy."
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb, e.g., "quite slowly."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, e.g., "the," "a," "this."
Determiner phrase: A phrase headed by a determiner, encompassing the determiner and the noun phrase it modifies.
X-bar: A theoretical framework in syntax that posits three levels of projection (X, X-bar, XP) for each phrase.
Projection: The syntactic operation by which a head extends into a phrase of the same category.
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply within its own output, enabling the generation of arbitrarily complex structures.
Subordination: A syntactic relationship in which one clause is embedded within or depends on another.
Coordination: A syntactic relationship in which two or more elements of equal status are joined, e.g., "and," "or."
Embedding: The inclusion of one clause or phrase within another, creating a hierarchical structure.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from its base-generated position to another position in the tree.
Trace: An empty category left behind in the base position when a constituent undergoes movement.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned by a verb to its arguments, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic role of a noun phrase, e.g., nominative, accusative, genitive.
Nominative case: The case typically marking the subject of a clause.
Accusative case: The case typically marking the direct object of a clause.
Dative case: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive case: The case typically marking possession or association.
Subject: The noun phrase that typically agrees with the verb and occupies the nominative or ergative position.
Object: The noun phrase that is the target or patient of the action expressed by the verb.
Indirect object: The noun phrase denoting the recipient or beneficiary of the action.
Agent: The semantic role of the initiator or causer of an event.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity directly affected by an event.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that perceives or feels a state or event.
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes a change of state or is moved.
Goal: The semantic role of the destination or endpoint of a motion or transfer.
Source: The semantic role of the origin or starting point of a motion or transfer.
Locative: The semantic role of the location or position of an event.
Instrument: The semantic role of the tool or means used to perform an action.
Comitative: The semantic role of an entity accompanying the agent in an event.
Instrumental case: The grammatical case marking the instrument or means of an action.
Ablative: The grammatical case marking the source or separation.
Locative case: The grammatical case marking the location of an event.
Vocative: The grammatical case used to address a person or entity directly.
Ergative: A case marking the agent of a transitive verb, contrasting with the absolutive.
