Absolutive: A case marking the patient of a transitive verb or the sole argument of an intransitive verb.
Ergative-absolutive alignment: A case alignment system in which the agent of a transitive verb is marked differently from the patient and the intransitive subject.
Nominative-accusative alignment: A case alignment system in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is marked the same.
Topicalization: A syntactic process that moves a constituent to the beginning of a sentence to mark it as the topic.
Cleft: A sentence construction that splits a clause into two parts, one of which highlights a specific constituent, e.g., "It was John who did it."
Pseudocleft: A cleft construction containing a wh-clause, e.g., "What John did was leave."
Passivization: A syntactic process that demotes the agent and promotes the patient to subject position.
Nominalization: A syntactic or morphological process that converts a verb or clause into a noun-like form.
Raising: A syntactic process in which a subject of an embedded clause is promoted to the subject position of the main clause.
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject of an embedded non-finite clause is semantically coreferential with an argument in the matrix clause.
Binding: The syntactic relationship that governs the reference of anaphoric expressions such as pronouns and reflexives.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression whose referent is determined by another expression in the same discourse.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression whose referent is determined by a subsequent expression in the discourse.
Coreference: The relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
Antecedent: The expression that determines the referent of a pronoun or anaphoric expression.
Pronominalization: The replacement of a full noun phrase with a pronoun.
Binding theory: A component of syntactic theory governing the distribution of pronouns, reflexives, and noun phrases.
C-command: A structural relationship in which a node dominates all sister nodes of its mother and commands all elements within those sisters.
Government: A structural relationship in which a head c-commands a constituent and is not separated from it by a clause boundary.
Empty Category Principle: A syntactic principle requiring that certain empty categories (traces) be properly governed.
Theta criterion: A syntactic principle requiring that each theta role be assigned to exactly one argument, and each argument receive exactly one theta role.
Extended Projection Principle: A syntactic principle requiring that every clause have a subject.
Case filter: A syntactic principle requiring that every phonologically overt noun phrase receive case.
Government and Binding: A theoretical framework in syntax developed by Noam Chomsky in the 1980s.
X-bar theory: A component of syntactic theory describing the internal structure of phrases at three levels.
Phrase structure grammar: A type of generative grammar that uses rewrite rules to generate sentences.
Transformational grammar: A type of generative grammar that maps deep structure to surface structure through transformational rules.
Generative grammar: A theoretical framework in which the set of grammatical sentences of a language is derived from a finite set of rules.
Minimalist Program: The most recent version of Chomsky's generative framework, emphasizing economic operations and interface conditions.
Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation before movement operations are applied.
Surface structure: The final syntactic representation after all movement operations have been applied.
D-structure: The level of representation at which lexical items are inserted into syntactic positions.
S-structure: The level of representation after all syntactic movement has been completed.
Logical form: The level of representation encoding semantic and pragmatic properties of a sentence.
Phonetic form: The level of representation encoding the phonological and phonetic properties of a sentence.
Subcategorization: The specification of the type and number of complements that a head can take.
Subcategorization frame: The set of argument and adjunct requirements of a particular lexical item.
Selection: The requirement that a particular head imposes a specific category on its complement, e.g., a verb requiring a DP object.
Valency: The number of arguments a verb or predicate requires.
Transitive verb: A verb that requires a direct object.
Intransitive verb: A verb that does not take a direct object.
Ditransitive verb: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object.
Copula: A linking verb such as "be" that connects a subject to a predicate nominal or adjective.
Auxiliary: A verb that supports the main verb in expressing tense, aspect, mood, or voice.
Modal: A type of auxiliary expressing necessity, possibility, obligation, or permission.
Light verb: A verb with little inherent semantic content that relies on a complement for meaning, e.g., "have a look."
Heavy NP shift: A syntactic movement in which a long noun phrase is postposed to the end of the sentence.
Subject-object asymmetry: The set of syntactic differences between the treatment of subjects and objects in a language.
Scrambling: The free reordering of arguments in a language, as in Japanese or German.
Word order: The linear arrangement of syntactic constituents in a sentence.
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb.
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object.
OVS: A word order in which the object precedes the verb, which precedes the subject.
OSV: A word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb.
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object.
VOS: A word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject.
Head-initial: A language or phrase type in which the head precedes its complements.
Head-final: A language or phrase type in which the head follows its complements.
Specified subjecthood: A syntactic principle requiring that a finite clause have an overt subject.
Pro: The null pronoun in non-finite clauses, as in "Pro tried to leave."
PRO: The null pronoun in subject position of non-finite clauses, required by the EPP in certain frameworks.
Empty operator: A null element that undergoes movement in A'-dependencies, as in relative clauses.
Operator-variable binding: The relationship between an operator (moved element) and its trace or variable.
A-movement: Movement to an argument position (theta role or case position).
A-bar movement: Movement to a non-argument position, such as topic or focus positions.
Wh-movement: The movement of a wh-element from its base position to the complementizer position.
Expletive: A phonologically overt but semantically empty element, e.g., "it" in "It is raining."
Dummy subject: An expletive that occupies the subject position to satisfy syntactic requirements.
There-insertion: The process of inserting the expletive "there" in an existential construction.
Expletive subject: A subject position filled by a non-referential element such as "it" or "there."
Predicate: The part of a clause that states something about the subject, typically headed by a verb.
Predicative: A position or function expressing a property or state of the subject, e.g., the complement of a copula.
Attributive: A position or function modifying a noun, as in an adjective preceding a noun.
Appositive: A noun phrase that renames or further identifies another noun phrase.
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun phrase, introduced by a relative pronoun or complementizer.
Relative pronoun: A word that introduces a relative clause and serves as an argument within it.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a subordinate clause, e.g., "that," "whether," "for."
Wh-word: An interrogative or relative word such as "what," "who," "where," "when," "why," "how."
Interrogative: A sentence or clause that functions to ask a question.
Declarative: A sentence or clause that asserts a proposition.
Imperative: A sentence or clause that issues a command or request.
Exclamative: A sentence or clause that expresses an emotion or surprise.
Fragment: A discourse unit that lacks a full clausal structure, e.g., "Really?"
Coordination: The joining of two or more syntactic elements of equal status by a coordinating conjunction.
Conjunction: A word that joins words, phrases, or clauses, e.g., "and," "but," "or."
Correlative conjunction: A pair of conjunctions that coordinate two elements, e.g., "both…and," "either…or."
Ellipsis: The omission of a constituent that is recoverable from context.
Gapping: A type of ellipsis in which a verb is omitted from one conjunct of a coordination, e.g., "John ate an apple and Mary a pear."
Right node raising: A type of ellipsis in which a shared final constituent is omitted from both conjuncts.
Stripping: A type of ellipsis in which an entire clause is reduced to a single constituent, e.g., "Yes, he did" / "No, he didn't."
Sluicing: A type of ellipsis in which a clause is reduced to a wh-element, e.g., "He left, but I don't remember where."
VP ellipsis: The omission of a verb phrase whose content is recoverable from a previous clause.
Noun phrase ellipsis: The omission of a noun phrase whose content is recoverable from context.
Clause ellipsis: The omission of an entire clause.
Heavy VP shift: The postposition of a long verb phrase to the end of a sentence for processing ease.
Dangling modifier: A modifier whose intended target is not syntactically available in its base position.
Garden path sentence: A sentence that leads the parser to an initial interpretation that must be revised upon encountering later material.
Center embedding: The embedding of a clause within another clause within a further clause, creating high processing complexity.
Coordination of complements: The coordination of elements that are complements of the same head.
Parallel structure: A syntactic construction in which coordinated elements share the same grammatical form.
Asymmetric coordination: A coordination in which the conjuncts are not of the same syntactic category.
Conjunct: One of the elements joined in a coordination.
Coordination site: The structural position at which a coordinating conjunction is attached.
Right association: The tendency to group coordinated elements with the closest preceding head.
Left association: The grouping of coordinated elements with a preceding head to the left.
Semantics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Lexical semantics: The study of the meaning of individual words and the relationships between them.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules of combination.
Sense: A distinct meaning or interpretation of a word or expression.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it denotes in the world.
Denotation: The set of entities in the world to which an expression applies.
Connotation: The associative or cultural meanings attached to a word beyond its literal definition.
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word having multiple related senses.
Homonymy: The phenomenon of two or more unrelated words sharing the same form.
Synonymy: The relationship between two or more words that have the same or very similar meanings.
Antonymy: The relationship between two words that have opposite meanings.
Hyponymy: The relationship in which the meaning of one term is included within the meaning of another, e.g., "rose" is a hyponym of "flower."
Hypernymy: The inverse of hyponymy; the relationship in which one term's meaning subsumes that of another.
Meronymy: The relationship in which one entity is a part of another, e.g., "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Holonymy: The inverse of meronymy; the relationship in which one entity is a whole composed of parts.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: A semantic or pragmatic assumption that must be true for a sentence to be meaningful or interpretable.
Implicature: A pragmatic inference drawn from an utterance that is not part of its literal semantic content.
Converse implicature: An implicature that arises from the failure to use a more informative expression.
Gricean maxims: Four principles of cooperative communication (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner) proposed by H. P. Grice.
Cooperative principle: Grice's overarching principle that participants in a conversation generally aim to be cooperative.
Maxim of quantity: The principle that one should provide as much information as is required, but no more.
Maxim of quality: The principle that one should make contributions that are true and supported by evidence.
Maxim of relation: The principle that one should be relevant.
Maxim of manner: The principle that one should be clear, brief, and orderly.
Flouting: The deliberate and recognizable violation of a conversational maxim to generate an implicature.
Violating: The open or undisguised violation of a maxim.
Obscuring: The attempt to violate a maxim while avoiding detection.
Truth value: The classification of a proposition as true or false in a given state of the world.
Proposition: The abstract, context-independent content expressed by a declarative sentence.
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines meaning in terms of conditions under which an expression is true.
Montague semantics: A formal semantic framework developed by Richard Montague that uses lambda calculus and higher-order logic.
Lambda calculus: A formal system of functions and variables used in formal semantics to represent meaning composition.
Intension: The function from possible worlds to extensions, capturing the sense or mode of presentation of a term.
Extension: The set of entities to which an expression applies in a particular possible world.
Modal semantics: A semantic framework that incorporates modality (necessity, possibility) through the use of possible worlds.
Possible world: A complete and consistent way the world could be, used as a model in formal semantics.
Lexical field: The set of words related to a particular topic or domain, e.g., words related to "family."
Semantic field: A network of related meanings organized around a central concept.
Semantic role: A function an argument plays in the event or state described by a predicate.
Thematic role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer.
Event semantics: A semantic framework that represents propositions in terms of events, states, and processes.
State: A semantic representation of a situation that persists over time without change.
Change of state: A semantic representation of a situation in which an entity transitions from one state to another.
Inchoative: A verb that expresses the beginning of a state or the entry into a state.
Inchoativity: The semantic property of a verb that denotes the onset of a state.
Transitivity: A semantic or syntactic property of a verb that takes a direct object.
Intransitivity: A semantic or syntactic property of a verb that does not take a direct object.
Diathesis: A syntactic framework for expressing the semantic relations of a predicate, such as active, passive, or middle.
Causative: A construction in which an external agent is added to cause an event.
Anticausative: A construction in which the external cause is removed from a causative event.
Applicative: A construction that adds an extra argument, typically a recipient or beneficiary, to a verb.
Reflexive: A construction in which the subject and object of a verb are the same entity.
Reciprocal: A construction in which the subject and object of a verb act on each other mutually.
Aspect: A grammatical category expressing the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, progressive, or habitual.
Perfective: An aspect marking an event as a complete whole.
Imperfective: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, incomplete, or habitual.
Progressive: An aspect marking an event as in progress at a particular time.
Habitual: An aspect marking a regularly recurring event or state.
Perfect: An aspect marking an event as completed with relevance to a subsequent point in time.
Pluperfect: An aspect marking an event as completed before another past event.
Tense: A grammatical category expressing the time of an event relative to the moment of utterance.
Present tense: The tense marking an event as simultaneous with the moment of utterance.
Past tense: The tense marking an event as preceding the moment of utterance.
Future tense: The tense marking an event as following the moment of utterance.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, e.g., indicative, subjunctive, imperative.
Indicative mood: The mood used for statements of fact or reality.
Subjunctive mood: The mood used for hypothetical, wished-for, or uncertain situations.
Imperative mood: The mood used for commands or requests.
Optative mood: The mood used for expressions of wish or hope.
Counterfactual: A statement that describes a situation contrary to fact.
Modal verb: A verb expressing modality, such as "can," "must," "should," "might."
Epistemic modality: Modality expressing degrees of certainty or knowledge.
Deontic modality: Modality expressing obligation, permission, or prohibition.
Dynamic modality: Modality expressing ability, capacity, or willingness.
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies the quantity or degree of something, e.g., "all," "some," "every."
Universal quantifier: A quantifier that applies to all members of a domain, e.g., "every," "all."
Existential quantifier: A quantifier that asserts the existence of at least one member in a domain, e.g., "some," "there is."
Definite description: A noun phrase beginning with the definite article that picks out a unique entity, e.g., "the king of France."
Indefinite description: A noun phrase with an indefinite article or no article, not picking out a specific entity, e.g., "a king."
Scope: The range of elements over which a quantifier or operator takes effect.
Quantifier scope: The domain over which a quantifier's restriction applies.
Scope ambiguity: A situation in which the relative scope of two quantifiers is unclear, yielding different interpretations.
Binding scope: The syntactic domain within which a variable can be bound by a quantifier.
Free variable: A variable not bound by any quantifier or operator.
Bound variable: A variable that falls within the scope of a quantifier or operator.
Donkey sentence: A sentence with a donkey pronoun whose interpretation resists standard quantificational analysis, e.g., "Every farmer who has a donkey beats it."
Donkey anaphora: The use of a pronoun that is anaphoric to an indefinite noun phrase within a quantificational context.
Presupposition projection: The mechanism by which presuppositions of embedded sentences are projected to the level of the whole sentence.
Presupposition accommodation: The process of adding a presupposed proposition to the common ground to make an utterance felicitous.
Context change: The update of the common ground as a result of an utterance.
Common ground: The set of assumptions and information shared by participants in a conversation.
Context: The linguistic, situational, and cognitive information that contributes to the interpretation of an utterance.
Contextual restriction: The narrowing of a word's denotation based on the context of use.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics concerned with the interpretation of meaning in context, beyond the literal content of words and sentences.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying information, e.g., "I now pronounce you married."
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance, encompassing the phonetic, syntactic, and semantic content.
Illocutionary act: The intended function of an utterance, such as asserting, commanding, promising, or questioning.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Performative: A verb that names the speech act being performed, e.g., "declare," "promise," "apologize."
Declarative speech act: A speech act in which the utterance itself brings about the state of affairs it describes, e.g., "I name this ship."
Directive speech act: A speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something, e.g., a request or command.
Commissive speech act: A speech act in which the speaker commits to a future action, e.g., a promise or threat.
Expressive speech act: A speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state, e.g., thanking, apologizing.
Representational speech act: A speech act that states a proposition, e.g., asserting, denying, reporting.
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose literal meaning differs from its intended illocutionary force, e.g., "Can you pass the salt?" as a request.
Felicitous: A speech act that meets the necessary conditions for its successful performance.
Infelicitous: A speech act that fails to meet one or more of the necessary conditions.
Deixis: The linguistic expression of meaning that depends on the context of utterance, such as person, place, and time expressions.
Anaphoric deixis: Deixis that refers to an element previously mentioned in the discourse.
Cataphoric deixis: Deixis that refers to an element to be mentioned later in the discourse.
Phenotypic deixis: Deixis that points to an entity in the physical or social context of the utterance.
Person deixis: The use of pronouns and person-marking to refer to participants in the conversation.
Spatial deixis: The use of demonstratives and spatial adverbs to refer to locations relative to the speaker or hearer.
Temporal deixis: The use of adverbs and tense to refer to times relative to the moment of utterance.
Discourse: The study of language as it is used in extended stretches of communication beyond the sentence level.
Discourse marker: A word or expression that organizes discourse and signals the speaker's attitude, e.g., "well," "so," "you know."
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that create surface-level connections between elements in a text.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a text, giving it a unified meaning.
Topic: The entity or proposition that a discourse segment is about.
Focus: The new or emphasized information in an utterance or discourse segment.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) and new information.
Given-new: A principle of information flow in which given information is mentioned before new information.
Old-new: Another term for the given-new principle of discourse organization.
Topic chain: A sequence of discourse segments in which the topic is maintained or shifted in a connected way.
Discourse referent: An entity in the discourse model that is referred to by linguistic expressions.
Discourse model: The mental representation of the entities, events, and relationships constructed during discourse comprehension.
Register: A variety of language used for a particular social or communicative context.
Genre: A type of discourse characterized by a particular communicative purpose and structural conventions.
Politeness: A pragmatic strategy for managing face and maintaining social harmony in interaction.
Face: The public self-image or social worth that a person claims in social interaction.
Positive face: The desire to be liked, approved of, and accepted by others.
Negative face: The desire to be unimpeded and free from imposition by others.
Face-threatening act: An act that endangers the positive or negative face of a participant.
Face-saving act: An act that protects or restores the face of a participant.
Mitigation: A pragmatic strategy of softening a face-threatening act.
Hedges: Words or expressions that reduce the strength or commitment of an utterance, e.g., "perhaps," "kind of."
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh or blunt one.
Dysphemism: A harsh or blunt expression used where a euphemism might be expected.
Taboo: A word or expression that is avoided or considered inappropriate in a particular social context.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single discourse.
Code-mixing: The insertion of elements from one language into the grammar of another within a single utterance.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops as a means of communication between groups with different native languages.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that evolves from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular region or social group.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group or class.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Standard language: A variety of a language that has been codified and used for formal, educational, and governmental purposes.
Vernacular: The everyday, informal variety of a language used by a community in casual communication.
Jargon: The specialized vocabulary of a particular profession, occupation, or activity.
Slang: Informal, often transient vocabulary used by particular social groups.
Argot: A specialized vocabulary used by a particular social group, often to exclude outsiders.
Formality: The degree of conventionality and rule-governedness in a variety of language.
Tact: The social sensitivity and consideration shown in linguistic choices.
Rapport: The positive social relationship established through linguistic interaction.
Solidarity: The social bond or sense of closeness expressed through shared language use.
Dominance: The social power or status expressed through language use.
Social distance: The perceived social gap between speakers, which influences language choices.
Power: The social status or authority of a speaker, which influences language variety and form.
Imposition: An act that places a demand or request on another person, threatening their negative face.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and social stratification.
Language variety: A particular form of a language used by a specific group, distinguished from other forms.
Accent: The phonological or phonetic features of a speaker's language that mark their regional or social origin.
Stigma: A negative social evaluation associated with a particular language variety or feature.
Prestige: A positive social evaluation associated with a particular language variety or feature.
Standardization: The process by which a language variety is selected, codified, and promoted as the standard.
Language policy: The set of decisions and actions taken by governments or institutions regarding the use and status of languages.
Language planning: The deliberate effort to influence the structure, function, or acquisition of a language.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be used.
Language revival: The effort to re-establish a moribund or dormant language as a living language.
Language maintenance: The efforts to preserve and continue the use of a language in the face of external pressures.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two or more languages.
Multilingualism: The ability to use more than two languages.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, leading to mutual influence.
Language interference: The influence of one language on another, often manifesting as errors in a second language.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually replaces its native language with another.
Language extinction: The complete loss of a language when its last speaker dies.
Endangered language: A language at risk of losing all its native speakers in the near future.
Linguistic vitality: The degree of health and sustainability of a language within its speech community.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language or two different languages are used in complementary social domains.
Polyglossia: A situation in which multiple languages or varieties coexist within a community.
Ethnolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language, culture, and social organization.
Linguistic anthropology: The study of language in its cultural and social context.
Language ideology: The beliefs and attitudes held by speakers about language varieties, use, and function.
Linguistic relativity: The hypothesis that the language one speaks influences or determines the way one perceives and thinks about the world.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The hypothesis, associated with Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, that language shapes thought.
Strong linguistic relativity: The claim that language determines thought, such that speakers of different languages cannot think about certain concepts.
Weak linguistic relativity: The claim that language influences thought, making certain cognitive tasks easier or harder.
Linguistic determinism: The claim that the structure of a language determines the possible thoughts of its speakers.
Universal: A property or principle that holds across all human languages.
Parameter: A binary choice in the grammar of a language that varies across languages but is limited to a set of options.
Language typology: The classification of languages according to their structural properties.
Language family: A group of languages that share a common ancestral language.
Language isolate: A language with no proven genetic relationship to any other language.
Proto-language: The reconstructed ancestral language from which a family of related languages descends.
Comparative method: A method of historical linguistics that reconstructs a proto-language by comparing related languages.
Sound law: A regular and systematic correspondence between sounds in related languages.
Correspondence: A regular phonetic relationship between sounds in related languages.
Cognate: A word in one language that has a common etymological origin with a word in another related language.
Loanword: A word borrowed from another language and adapted into the borrowing language.
Borrowing: The process of adopting a word or grammatical element from another language.
Historical linguistics: The study of the origins and development of languages over time.
Diachronic linguistics: The study of language change over time.
Synchronic linguistics: The study of a language at a single point in time.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.
Onomastics: The study of proper names and their origins.
Lexicography: The compilation and editing of dictionaries.
Lexicology: The study of the vocabulary and lexical structure of a language.
Vocabulary: The set of words known or used by a speaker or in a language.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word, often in a different grammatical category.
Inflectional morphology: The part of morphology dealing with grammatical word forms.
Derivational morphology: The part of morphology dealing with the formation of new lexemes.
Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created in a language.
Compounding: A word-formation process combining two or more roots into a single word.
Clipping: A word-formation process that shortens a longer word, e.g., "ad" from "advertisement."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words, e.g., "brunch."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, e.g., "NASA."
Initialism: A sequence of initial letters of a phrase that is pronounced letter by letter, e.g., "FBI."
Back-formation: A word-formation process that creates a new word by removing an apparent affix.
Conversion: A word-formation process that changes the grammatical category of a word without adding an affix.
Coinage: The creation of a new word from existing materials.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression that has not yet become established in the language.
Lexical borrowing: The adoption of a word from one language into another.
Calque: A word or phrase formed by translating the components of a foreign word or phrase into the native language.
Semantic change: The diachronic shift in the meaning of a word.
Semantic broadening: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more general.
Semantic narrowing: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific.
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more positive.
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more negative.
Metaphor: A figurative expression that maps meaning from a source domain to a target domain.
Metonymy: A figurative expression that refers to one entity by the name of another with which it is associated.
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, e.g., "he," "she," "it," "they."
Personal pronoun: A pronoun that refers to the participants in the discourse: first, second, and third person.
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, e.g., "himself," "herself."
Reciprocal pronoun: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship, e.g., "each other," "one another."
Demonstrative: A word that points to a specific entity, e.g., "this," "that," "these," "those."
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used in questions, e.g., "who," "what," "which."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause, e.g., "who," "which," "that."
Indefinite pronoun: A pronoun that refers to a non-specific entity, e.g., "someone," "anything," "none."
Pronominal paradigm: The set of pronominal forms in a language, organized by person, number, gender, and case.
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker (first), the addressee (second), and others (third).
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular and plural (and sometimes dual or trial) forms.
Gender: A grammatical category that classifies nouns and pronouns, often into masculine, feminine, and neuter.
Case marking: The morphological marking of a noun phrase's syntactic role.
Inflectional ending: A suffix or other morphological element that marks grammatical categories on a word.
Concord: Agreement between a noun and its modifiers in number, gender, or case.
Agreement: The morphological matching of a verb or adjective with the grammatical features of a noun.
Subject-verb agreement: The morphological matching of the verb's person and number with the subject.
Number agreement: The matching of singular or plural morphology between related elements.
Gender agreement: The matching of masculine, feminine, or neuter morphology between related elements.
Case agreement: The matching of case morphology between a noun and its modifiers.
Complementizer agreement: The agreement between a complementizer and an embedded clause.
Tense agreement: The matching of tense morphology between related elements in a clause.
Aspect agreement: The matching of aspect morphology between related elements.
Mood agreement: The matching of mood morphology between related elements.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category expressing the source of information, e.g., direct experience, hearsay, inference.
Evidential marker: A grammatical element that encodes the source of a speaker's knowledge.
Evidential: A grammatical or lexical element that marks the source of information.
Illocutionary force: The communicative intent of an utterance, such as asserting, questioning, or commanding.
Speech-act theory: A framework in pragmatics that analyzes utterances as actions, developed by J. L. Austin and S. E. Searle.
Performativity: The property of certain utterances that bring about the state of affairs they describe.
Performative verb: A verb that names the speech act being performed, e.g., "declare," "promise," "warn."
Conventional meaning: The literal, context-independent meaning of a word or expression.
Conversational meaning: The context-dependent meaning of an utterance, including implicatures and presuppositions.
Utterance meaning: The total meaning of a specific utterance in a specific context.
Sentence meaning: The abstract, context-independent meaning of a sentence as a grammatical structure.
Propositional meaning: The truth-conditional content of a sentence.
Illocutionary point: The primary function of a speech act, such as representing, directing, or committing.
Sincerity condition: The condition that the speaker must genuinely hold the attitude or belief expressed in a speech act.
Essential condition: A condition that must be met for a speech act to be performed, such as the addressee being present.
Happy conditions: Conditions under which a speech act is performed successfully.
Unhappy conditions: Conditions under which a speech act is performed but is not successful or valid.
Misfire: A speech act that fails to perform its intended function due to unmet conditions.
Abuse: A speech act that is performed but is insincere or in bad faith.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse and signals the speaker's stance, e.g., "well," "now," "anyway."
Discourse particle: A word that does not carry propositional content but signals the speaker's attitude, e.g., "oh," "hmm."
Interjection: A word or expression that expresses a sudden emotion or reaction, e.g., "wow," "oh no," "ah."
Expletive: A word or phrase expressing strong emotion, often vulgar, e.g., "damn," "bloody."
Interjection: A word expressing an emotion or reaction without fitting into the syntactic structure of a sentence.
Filler: A word or sound used to hold a pause in conversation, e.g., "um," "uh," "well."
Discourse strategy: A deliberate pattern of linguistic choices used to achieve a communicative goal.
Rhetorical device: A figure of speech or stylistic technique used to achieve a persuasive or artistic effect.
Metaphor: A figurative expression that implies a similarity between two unlike things.
Simile: A figurative expression that explicitly compares two things using "like" or "as."
Personification: A figurative expression that attributes human qualities to non-human entities.
Hyperbole: A figurative expression that involves deliberate exaggeration for emphasis.
Understatement: A figurative expression that presents something as less significant than it is.
Irony: A figurative expression in which the intended meaning is the opposite of the literal meaning.
Sarcasm: A form of irony that is sharp or cutting in tone.
Litotes: A form of understatement using a double negative, e.g., "not bad" meaning "good."
Oxymoron: A combination of contradictory terms, e.g., "bittersweet," "deafening silence."
Antithesis: A rhetorical device that presents contrasting ideas in parallel structure.
Chiasmus: A rhetorical device in which the second part of a phrase parallels the first but reverses the order.
Anaphora: The repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses.
Epistrophe: The repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
Alliteration: The repetition of initial consonant sounds in adjacent or closely connected words.
Assonance: The repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words.
Consonance: The repetition of consonant sounds in nearby words.
Onomatopoeia: A word that imitates or suggests the sound it represents, e.g., "buzz," "sizzle."
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression substituted for one considered harsh or blunt.
Dysphemism: A harsh or unpleasant word or expression used where a neutral or positive one might be expected.
Malapropism: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, often with humorous effect.
Soliloquy: A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud, typically in a play.
Aside: A dramatic convention in which a character speaks directly to the audience, unheard by other characters.
Colloquialism: An informal word or expression typical of everyday spoken language.
Archaism: A word or expression that was once common but is now obsolete or rare.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
Technical term: A word or expression specific to a particular field of knowledge or profession.
Trade term: A word or expression specific to a particular trade or occupation.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression that has not yet been established in the language.
Dialectology: The study of dialects and their geographic and social distribution.
Geolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and geographic location.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but distant varieties may not be.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary separating areas with different linguistic features.
Dialect survey: A systematic collection of linguistic data from speakers across a geographic region.
Atlas of languages: A collection of maps showing the geographic distribution of linguistic features.
Creolistics: The study of creole languages.
Pidgin and creole studies: The academic field concerned with the development, structure, and use of pidgins and creoles.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn a language.
First language acquisition: The process by which children acquire their native language.
Second language acquisition: The process by which learners acquire a language other than their native language.
Critical period: A hypothesized period during which language acquisition is most efficient, especially for phonology.
Universal Grammar: A theoretical framework proposing that all human languages share a common underlying structure.
Language faculty: The innate cognitive capacity for language acquisition and use.
Language organ: The theoretical neural substrate underlying language capacity.
Modularity: The hypothesis that language is processed by a dedicated cognitive module.
Competence: A speaker's internalized knowledge of the rules and structure of a language.
Performance: The actual use of language in real communicative situations.
Competence-performance distinction: Chomsky's distinction between abstract linguistic knowledge and actual language use.
I-language: An individual's internalized linguistic knowledge.
E-language: The externalized, observable language of a community.
G-rules: The rules of a generative grammar that generate the set of grammatical sentences.
A-language: An individual speaker's particular grammar, including all personal idiosyncrasies.
I-language: An idealized abstract linguistic system.
E-language: The empirical, observable language of a community.
Language instinct: The innate cognitive predisposition for language acquisition.
Poverty of the stimulus: The argument that children acquire grammatical knowledge that cannot be derived from the input they receive.
Critical period hypothesis: The hypothesis that there is a biologically determined window for optimal language acquisition.
Sensitive period: A period during which a cognitive ability is most readily acquired.
Language deprivation: The lack of adequate linguistic input, which can impair language development.
Sign language: A natural language expressed through manual gestures, facial expressions, and body movements.
Sign language typology: The classification of sign languages according to their structural properties.
Manual alphabets: Systems of handshapes used to spell out letters in sign language.
Fingerspelling: The practice of representing letters of the spoken language alphabet with handshapes in sign language.
Deaf culture: The shared social, cultural, and linguistic identity of the Deaf community.
Oralism: A method of teaching Deaf individuals to use spoken and written language.
Manualism: A method of teaching Deaf individuals using sign language.
Total communication: An approach to Deaf education that combines sign language, spoken language, and other modes.
Cognitively oriented phonology: A phonological framework that links phonological representations to perceptual and articulatory knowledge.
Autosegmental phonology: A phonological framework in which suprasegmental features are represented on separate tiers.
Metrical phonology: A framework that represents stress and rhythm in terms of binary metrical trees.
Optimality Theory: A phonological framework that evaluates output forms against a ranked set of constraints.
Candidate: A potential output form in Optimality Theory that is evaluated against constraints.
Constraint: A well-formedness condition in Optimality Theory that candidates are evaluated against.
Constraint ranking: The ordering of constraints by relative importance in a language's grammar.
Harmonic ordering: A constraint ranking in which no constraint is violated in the optimal output.
Faithfulness constraint: A constraint in Optimality Theory that requires the output to match the input.
Markedness constraint: A constraint in Optimality Theory that penalizes structurally complex or marked forms.
Correspondence theory: A framework in which phonological relationships are defined between underlying and surface forms.
Nonlinear phonology: A framework in which phonological representation is organized in multiple tiers.
Phonological tier: A level of phonological representation, such as a segmental tier or an autosegmental tier.
Feature tier: A tier in autosegmental phonology representing a particular distinctive feature.
Tone tier: A tier in autosegmental phonology representing tonal elements.
Stress tier: A tier in autosegmental phonology representing stress elements.
Melody: A sequence of suprasegmental features, such as tones, in a prosodic representation.
Contour: A sequence of two or more tone elements within a single syllable.
Tone melody: The pattern of tonal elements over a string of syllables.
Tone accent: The combination of a lexical tone with a specific tonal contour.
Tone sandhi: A change in tone at the boundary between syllables or words.
Tone neutralization: The loss of a tonal contrast in a particular phonological environment.
Tone spreading: The extension of a tone over additional syllables.
Tone copying: The copying of a tone from one syllable to another.
Tone deletion: The loss of a tone in a particular phonological environment.
Tone insertion: The addition of a tone in a particular phonological environment.
Lexical tone: A tone that is part of the lexical entry of a word.
Prosodic tone: A tone that is part of the prosodic structure of a phrase or sentence.
Contour tone: A tone in which the pitch moves over the duration of the syllable.
Plateau tone: A tone in which the pitch remains at a constant level.
Rising tone: A tone in which the pitch moves upward.
Falling tone: A tone in which the pitch moves downward.
Dipping tone: A tone in which the pitch falls and then rises.
Peaking tone: A tone in which the pitch rises and then falls.
Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which a single syllable in a word or phrase is marked by a pitch change.
Accental: Relating to or characteristic of a pitch accent system.
Accentual: Another term for relating to pitch accent.
Accentual stress: A type of stress in which the primary stress falls on a fixed syllable relative to the accented syllable.
Tonic stress: The primary stress in a word or phrase, often corresponding to the syllable bearing the pitch accent.
Tonic: The syllable or mora bearing the primary stress or pitch accent.
Pretonic: A syllable preceding the tonic syllable.
Posttonic: A syllable following the tonic syllable.
Stress shift: The movement of primary stress to a different syllable in a word or phrase.
Stress assignment: The phonological process of determining which syllable bears primary stress.
Stress rule: A phonological rule that determines the location of stress in a word or phrase.
Stress pattern: The regular distribution of stress in a language or word class.
Alternating stress: A stress pattern in which the stressed syllable alternates in position.
Non-alternating stress: A stress pattern in which the stressed syllable remains in a fixed position.
Fixed stress: A stress pattern in which the primary stress falls on a specific syllable in all words.
Mobile stress: A stress pattern in which the primary stress can fall on different syllables depending on the word.
Free stress: A stress pattern in which the position of primary stress is lexical and unpredictable.
Stress timing: A prosodic rhythm in which stressed syllables occur at regular intervals, as in English.
Syllable timing: A prosodic rhythm in which each syllable is approximately equal in duration, as in Spanish.
Iambic: A metrical pattern in which an unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed syllable.
Trochaic: A metrical pattern in which a stressed syllable is followed by an unstressed syllable.
Mora: A unit of prosodic timing, roughly equivalent to the duration of a short vowel.
Moraic: Relating to or measured in morae.
Moraic segment: A segment that carries a mora in the prosodic representation.
Non-moraic segment: A segment that does not carry a mora in the prosodic representation.
Light syllable: A syllable containing a short vowel or a single mora.
Heavy syllable: A syllable containing a long vowel, a diphthong, or a closed coda, bearing two morae.
Syllable weight: The prosodic weight of a syllable, determined by its moraic content.
Weight-to-stress principle: A phonological principle stating that heavy syllables are preferred as stress bearing.
Prominence: The relative salience of a syllable or prosodic unit, realized through stress, pitch, and duration.
Nuclear stress: The primary stress on a phrase, typically falling on the last content word.
Initial stress: The primary stress falling on the first syllable or word of a phrase.
Medial stress: The primary stress falling on a syllable in the middle of a phrase.
Final stress: The primary stress falling on the last syllable or word of a phrase.
Secondary stress: A level of stress between primary stress and unstressed.
Phrasal stress: The pattern of stress distribution across a phrase.
Sentence stress: The pattern of stress distribution across a sentence.
Intonational phrase: A prosodic unit corresponding to a clause or phrase, marked by a specific intonational pattern.
Intonational contour: The overall shape of the pitch pattern over an intonational phrase.
Falling intonation: A pitch contour that moves downward, typically marking declaratives.
Rising intonation: A pitch contour that moves upward, typically marking yes-no questions.
Rise-fall intonation: A pitch contour that rises and then falls, often marking emphasis or surprise.
Fall-rise intonation: A pitch contour that falls and then rises, often marking uncertainty or indirectness.
Declarative intonation: The intonational pattern typically associated with statements.
Interrogative intonation: The intonational pattern typically associated with questions.
Imperative intonation: The intonational pattern typically associated with commands or requests.
Contour intonation: An intonational pattern that involves a change in pitch direction.
Flat intonation: An intonational pattern in which the pitch remains relatively constant.
Terminal pitch: The pitch level at the end of an intonational phrase.
Initial pitch: The pitch level at the beginning of an intonational phrase.
Pitch range: The span of pitch levels within an intonational phrase.
Pitch reset: A sudden shift in the baseline pitch level during an utterance.
Pitch track: The continuous path of fundamental frequency over time.
Fundamental frequency: The rate of vocal fold vibration, perceived as pitch.
F0: The symbol for fundamental frequency.
Loudness: The perceptual correlate of acoustic amplitude or intensity.
Amplitude: The magnitude of the pressure variation in a sound wave.
Frequency: The number of cycles of a wave per unit time, measured in Hertz.
Hertz: The unit of frequency, equivalent to one cycle per second.
Decibel: A logarithmic unit used to measure the intensity or loudness of a sound.
Wavelength: The distance between successive peaks of a sound wave.
Period: The duration of one complete cycle of a sound wave.
Phase: The position of a point in a periodic cycle of a sound wave.
Waveform: A visual display of the amplitude of a sound signal over time.
Spectrum: A visual display of the frequency content of a sound signal.
Harmonic: A frequency that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum, produced by resonances of the vocal tract.
Anti-formant: A frequency at which energy is absent or reduced in the spectrum.
Spectral tilt: The slope of the overall energy distribution across the frequency spectrum.
Spectral envelope: The overall shape of the frequency spectrum of a sound.
Spectral peak: A local maximum in the frequency spectrum.
Spectral zero: A local minimum in the frequency spectrum.
Spectral centroid: The center of gravity of the frequency spectrum, perceived as brightness.
Spectral flux: The rate of change of the spectral energy over time.
Vocal tract model: A physical or mathematical model of the vocal tract used to predict formant frequencies.
Tube model: A simplified model of the vocal tract as a series of coupled tubes.
Acoustic impedance: The opposition to the flow of acoustic energy at a point in the vocal tract.
Radiance: The acoustic output at the lips of the vocal tract.
Glottal source: The acoustic signal generated at the glottis, serving as the input to the vocal tract filter.
Source-filter model: A model of speech production in which the glottal source is filtered by the vocal tract.
Laryngeal source: The acoustic signal generated by the larynx, including the glottal flow and its harmonics.
Glottal flow: The pattern of airflow through the glottis during voicing.
Glottal area: The cross-sectional area of the glottis during phonation.
Glottal resistance: The opposition to airflow through the glottis.
Glottal inductance: The inertial component of glottal airflow.
Glottal compliance: The elastic component of glottal airflow.
Junction: A boundary between two segments in a phonological or prosodic representation.
Syllabification: The process of assigning segments to syllabic positions.
Bisyllabic: Having two syllables.
Trisyllabic: Having three syllables.
Polysyllabic: Having multiple syllables.
Monosyllabic: Having one syllable.
Aphonic: Not producing sound; silent.
Phonetic transcription: The representation of speech sounds using phonetic symbols, typically IPA.
Phonological representation: The abstract representation of sound patterns in a phonological grammar.
Phonetic detail: The fine-grained articulatory or acoustic properties of a speech sound.
Phonemic contrast: A contrast between two phonemes in a language.
Phonemic neutrality: The absence of a phonemic contrast in a particular environment.
Phonemic distinction: A contrast between two phonemes that is meaningful in a language.
Phonemic equivalence: The relationship between two segments that can serve as alternatives in the same environment.
