Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, such as /p/ vs. /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A context-dependent variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English.
Phone: Any distinct speech sound regardless of whether it constitutes a phoneme in a particular language.
Phonology: The study of the sound systems of languages, including the organization and rules governing how sounds combine and change.
Phonetics: The study of the physical production, acoustic properties, and auditory perception of speech sounds.
Suprasegmental: A prosodic property that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Segment: A discrete unit of sound, typically a consonant or vowel, as opposed to a suprasegmental property.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a word consisting of a vowel nucleus optionally preceded and/or followed by consonants.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the syllable nucleus.
Nucleus: The central, most sonorant part of a syllable, typically a vowel.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the syllable nucleus.
Causality: A phonological constraint in some theories requiring that consonants precede vowels in certain structural positions.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound, distinguishing voiced from voiceless consonants.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed or modified to produce a consonant, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Aspiration: A burst of strong airflow following the release of a plosive consonant, as in the English /p/ in "pin."
Nasalization: The production of a sound with airflow directed through the nasal cavity, as in nasal consonants or nasal vowels.
Palatalization: The modification of a sound toward the palatal place of articulation, as in Russian /t/ becoming /tʲ/.
Velarization: The secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue approaches the velum, as in some [l] sounds.
Labialization: The rounding of the lips during the production of a sound, often as a secondary articulation.
Glottalization: The production of a sound with the vocal folds constricted or closed in the glottis, as in creaky voice.
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking airflow and then releasing it in a burst, such as /p/, /t/, /k/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow, such as /s/, /f/, /ʃ/.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and ends as a fricative at the same place of articulation, such as /tʃ/ or /dʒ/.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the oral cavity blocked and the velum lowered, directing air through the nose, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue blocking the center of the oral cavity while allowing air to flow around the sides, as in /l/.
Trill: A consonant produced by the rapid vibration of a consonant articulator, such as the Spanish /r/.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of an articulator, such as the American English /t/ in "butter."
Approximant: A consonant produced with a narrowing that does not create turbulent airflow, including glides and rhotics.
Glide: A vowel-like segment that functions as a consonant, produced by moving from one vowel position to another, as in /w/ and /j/.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one point of articulation and glides to another within the same syllable, such as /aɪ/.
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound produced with a single, stable point of articulation throughout the syllable.
Tone: A prosodic feature in which the pitch contour of a syllable or word carries lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, determined by the frequency of vocal fold vibration.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable or word, involving greater loudness, length, and pitch.
Intonation: The melodic pattern of pitch variation across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical or pragmatic meaning.
Prosody: The study of the suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing which sequences of sounds are permitted or prohibited in a language's phonological system.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating a phonemic contrast, such as "cat" and "bat."
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two phonetic variants never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of one phoneme.
Contrastive distribution: A relationship in which two sounds occur in the same phonetic environment and can distinguish word meaning.
Free variant: An allophonic variant that can be substituted for another in the same environment without changing meaning or social perception.
Archiphoneme: A theoretical phoneme unit that represents a neutralized contrast at a particular position in a phonological rule.
Phonological rule: A formalized description of how underlying representations are transformed into surface forms in a language.
Underlying form: The abstract mental representation of a word or morpheme before any phonological rules are applied.
Surface form: The actual phonetic or phonological realization of a word as it is spoken or written.
Distinctive feature: A binary or scalar property used to phonologically distinguish phonemes, such as [±voice], [±nasal], [±continuant].
Feature geometry: A hierarchical model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized into subgroups or tiers.
Autosegment: A segment on a separate phonological tier (such as tone or vowel) that is linked to one or more segments on the main consonant-vowel tier.
Optimality Theory: A framework in phonology and morphology where outputs are selected by ranking and evaluating constraints rather than applying ordered rules.
Constraint: A universal requirement or preference in Optimality Theory that candidates must satisfy, such as faithfulness or markedness constraints.
Markedness: A property of a linguistic form indicating it is more complex, less frequent, or more restricted than its unmarked counterpart.
Neutralization: A phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is eliminated in a particular environment.
Chain shift: A systematic, sequential change in which one sound shifts to the position of another, causing a cascade of changes throughout the system.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound, as in "input" pronounced [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less similar to a neighboring sound to reduce redundancy.
Metathesis: A phonological or morphological process in which two adjacent segments swap positions, as in "ask" from Latin "quaerere."
Deletion: The omission of a segment that is present in the underlying form, as in the schwa deletion in "going to" becoming "gonna."
Epenthesis: The insertion of a segment not present in the underlying form to break up an illicit phonological sequence.
Elision: The omission of a vowel or syllable, particularly in rapid or informal speech, as in "comfortable" pronounced "comftable."
Coalescence: A phonological process in which two adjacent sounds merge into a single sound, as in /tj/ becoming /tʃ/ in "church."
Lenition: A diachronic sound change in which a consonant weakens, such as /p/ becoming /f/ or /v/.
Fortition: A diachronic sound change in which a consonant becomes stronger or more marked, the opposite of lenition.
Sandhi: The phonological changes that occur at the boundary between words or morphemes in connected speech.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which all vowels in a word or phonological phrase share a particular feature, such as backness or ATR.
Tone sandhi: A rule-governed change in tone that occurs when tones are adjacent, as in many Chinese and Vietnamese dialects.
Contour tone: A tone whose pitch moves over the course of the syllable, such as rising or falling tones, as opposed to level tones.
Register: A social or communicative variety of language appropriate to a particular setting, audience, or purpose.
Morphology: The branch of linguistics concerned with the internal structure of words and the rules governing word formation.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further decomposed without loss of meaning, such as "un-" or "-ed."
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that appears in different phonological or morphological environments, such as /s/, /z/, /ɪz/ for English plural.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning and to which other morphemes may be attached.
Stem: A root or root-plus-affix combination to which inflectional affixes are attached.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to form a new word or word form, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: A bound morpheme attached before a root or stem, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: A bound morpheme attached after a root or stem, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: A bound morpheme inserted within a root or stem, as in the Tagalog -in- in "gumawa."
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that surrounds a stem, consisting of both a prefix and a suffix, as in the German ge-…-t in "gehabt."
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a neighboring word but syntactically independent, such as English "n't" or French "je."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to other morphemes, such as "-ness" or "un-."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word, such as "cat" or "run."
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the part of speech, such as "-er" in "teach-er."
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that indicates grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person, such as "-s" in "cats."
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which each morpheme expresses a single grammatical category and morpheme boundaries are clear, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single morpheme may express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words tend to be monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by separate words, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which words can incorporate multiple morphemes, often including arguments, into a single complex form, as in many Native American languages.
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories without changing the core meaning, such as "walk" to "walks."
Derivation: The process of creating a new word or lexeme by adding derivational morphemes, such as "happy" to "happiness."
Conjugation: The paradigm of inflected forms of a verb showing person, number, tense, aspect, and mood.
Declension: The paradigm of inflected forms of a noun, adjective, or other non-verbal word showing case, number, and gender.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word organized by grammatical category.
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word under which its various inflected and derived forms are listed.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of related word forms sharing a core meaning, such as the lexeme "run."
Word form: A particular phonological or orthographic realization of a word, such as "ran" as a word form of the lexeme "run."
Compound: A word formed by combining two or more free morphemes (roots) to create a new meaning, such as "blackboard."
Concatenative: A morphological process in which morphemes are added to or within a stem by linear sequence, as opposed to non-concatenative processes.
Non-concatenative: A morphological process in which morphemes are expressed by internal modification of the stem, such as Arabic root-and-pattern morphology.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which part or all of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical or lexical meaning, such as "bi-bi" or "see-see."
Suppletion: A morphological process in which an irregular, historically unrelated form replaces a regular one, such as "go" → "went."
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonological or orthographic content but is inferred from its position in a paradigm, as in the plural "sheep."
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that fuses the meaning of multiple morphemes, as in English "-ings" encoding both plural and possessive.
Morphological alternation: A change in the form of a morpheme or stem depending on its morphological or phonological environment.
Opaque derivation: A derived word in which the relationship between the base and the derivation is not transparent to speakers.
Productive: A morphological or phonological process that is still actively used by speakers to create new forms.
Unproductive: A morphological or phonological process that is no longer used productively and is limited to existing lexical items.
Affixation: The process of adding an affix (prefix, suffix, infix, or circumfix) to a stem to form a new word or word form.
Internal change: A morphological or phonological process in which the form of a stem changes internally, such as Germanic vowel gradation (ablaut).
Ablaut: The historical Germanic process of vowel alternation used to express grammatical or lexical distinctions, as in "sing-sang-sung."
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the structure of sentences and the arrangement of words.
Clause: A unit of syntax containing a subject and a predicate, which may be finite or non-finite.
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a single word of a particular category, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Constituent: A unit within a sentence that functions as a single element in the hierarchical structure, such as "the old man" in "the old man walked."
Constituency: The property of being a constituent, often tested by operations like substitution, fronting, or coordination.
Immediate constituent: A constituent that is directly dominated by another constituent in a phrase structure tree without intervening nodes.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical arrangement of constituents in a sentence, often represented by a tree diagram or bracketed notation.
Tree diagram: A graphical representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence, showing dominance and constituent relationships.
Binary branching: A property of a syntactic structure in which each node dominates exactly two daughters.
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply within its own output, allowing sentences of potentially unlimited length and complexity.
Embedding: The syntactic process of placing one clause or phrase within another, creating a hierarchical structure.
Dominance: A structural relation in which a node in a tree governs or contains another node as its descendant.
Government: A syntactic relation in which a head (typically a verb, noun, or preposition) determines the category or case of its complement.
c-command: A structural relation in which a node dominates a sister node's descendants, relevant to binding and movement theories.
Theta role: A semantic or thematic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, or Goal.
Theta Criterion: A syntactic principle stating that each theta role must be assigned to exactly one argument and each argument must receive exactly one theta role.
Trace: A theoretical empty category left behind at the original position of a moved constituent, such as the gap in "who did you see __?"
A-movement: Syntactic movement that does not cross a subject position and typically assigns or checks Case, such as passivization.
A-bar movement: Syntactic movement that crosses a subject position, such as wh-movement, topicalization, or focus movement.
Wh-movement: The displacement of a wh-word to the clause-initial position to form a question, as in "Where did you go?"
Extraposition: The movement of a constituent, typically a clause, to a later position in the sentence, as in "It is likely that he left."
Topicalization: The fronting of a constituent to the left periphery of a sentence to mark it as the topic of discourse.
Scrambling: The syntactic process by which languages allow relatively free word order, particularly observed in Japanese and German.
Word order: The linear sequence of grammatical categories in a clause, classified by the relative order of Subject, Object, and Verb.
SVO: A word order in which the Subject precedes the Verb, which precedes the Object, as in English.
SOV: A word order in which the Subject precedes the Object, which precedes the Verb, as in Japanese.
VSO: A word order in which the Verb precedes the Subject, which precedes the Object, as in Arabic and Irish.
Subject: The argument that typically agrees with the verb and is the default topic of the clause.
Object: The argument that is acted upon by the verb, typically the internal or patient argument.
Predicate: The part of a clause that contains the verb and provides information about the subject.
Argument: A participant in the event or state described by a predicate, typically a noun phrase that receives a theta role.
Adjunct: An optional, peripheral element of a clause that modifies the proposition, such as a time or place adverbial.
Complement: An obligatory constituent required by a head to complete its subcategorization frame.
Specifier: The constituent in the outermost position of a phrase, typically before the head, such as the determiner in a DP.
Head: The central word of a phrase that determines the category of the phrase and its subcategorization requirements.
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, including its determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts.
Determiner phrase: A phrase headed by a determiner or a noun, proposed in some frameworks to replace the traditional noun phrase.
Complementizer phrase: A phrase headed by a complementizer (such as "that" or "if") that introduces an embedded clause.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object as an obligatory argument, as in "She ate the apple."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, as in "She slept."
Valency: The number and type of arguments required or permitted by a predicate.
Argument structure: The mapping between the syntactic positions of a clause and the semantic roles of the predicate.
Thematic role: The semantic role an argument plays in the event described by the predicate, such as Agent, Patient, or Experiencer.
Agent: The semantic role of the voluntary initiator or causer of an action.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity most affected by the action, typically the direct object of a transitive verb.
Goal: The semantic role of the endpoint or recipient toward which motion or transfer is directed.
Source: The semantic role of the starting point of motion or the origin of transfer.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that perceives or feels a state, as in "She felt happy."
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that is moved, transferred, or whose position changes.
Passive: A voice construction in which the patient argument is promoted to subject and the agent is demoted or omitted.
Active: The default voice in which the agent argument appears as the subject of the clause.
Middle voice: A voice construction that lies between active and passive, often indicating a self-directed or general action.
Causative: A construction or derivation in which a transitive clause is created from an intransitive one, adding a causer argument.
Anticausative: A construction or derivation in which an intransitive clause is created from a transitive one, removing the causer.
Antipassive: A valence-reducing construction that demotes the object to an oblique or adjunct while promoting or retaining the subject.
Applicative: A derivation that adds an additional argument to a verb, typically an indirect object, as in Bantu languages.
Noun incorporation: The syntactic process in which a noun is incorporated into the verb, common in polysynthetic languages.
Serial verb construction: A construction in which multiple verbs appear in a single clause to describe a sequence or composite event.
Light verb: A verb with little lexical content that combines with a nominal or adjectival complement to express a complete predicate, as in "take a walk."
Copula: A verb that links a subject to its predicate, such as "be" in English or "to be" in many languages.
Existential: A construction expressing the existence or presence of an entity, typically using a copula or a special verb.
Negation: The grammatical expression of the falsity or non-occurrence of a proposition, realized by particles, affixes, or special verb forms.
Interrogation: The grammatical construction of questions, typically involving word order change, special particles, or intonation.
Subjunctive: A mood that expresses hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations, as in "I wish he were here."
Optative: A mood expressing wishes or desires, often overlapping with the subjunctive.
Imperative: A mood used to issue commands or requests, as in "Go away!"
Indicative: The mood used to state facts or express what the speaker considers real or certain.
Conditional: A mood or construction expressing a situation dependent on a condition, as in "If it rains, we will stay home."
Finite: A verb form that is fully inflected for person, number, tense, and mood and can serve as the main verb of a clause.
Non-finite: A verb form that lacks full inflection and cannot serve as the main predicate, such as infinitives, participles, and gerunds.
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure of an event, such as whether it is completed, ongoing, or habitual.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates the event time relative to the time of utterance, such as past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the reality or desirability of the proposition.
Perfective: An aspect marking that presents an event as a whole, bounded, or completed unit.
Imperfective: An aspect marking that presents an event as ongoing, habitual, or internally unbounded.
Progressive: An aspect marking that emphasizes the ongoing, in-progress nature of an event, as in "She is running."
Stative: An aspect or class of verbs that describes a state rather than an event, typically incompatible with the progressive.
Aorist: A tense or aspect form in some languages (e.g., Ancient Greek) that presents an action as a simple, undifferentiated event.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of the speaker's information, such as direct perception, hearsay, or inference.
Evidential: A grammatical marker indicating how the speaker acquired knowledge of the proposition.
Epistemic: Relating to knowledge or belief, as in epistemic modality expressing the speaker's degree of certainty.
Deontic: Relating to obligation, permission, or necessity, as in deontic modality expressed by modals like "must" or "should."
Realis: A grammatical category marking a situation as factual, completed, or actualized.
Irrealis: A grammatical category marking a situation as non-factual, hypothetical, future, or desired.
Determiner: A word that precedes and specifies the reference of a noun, including articles, demonstratives, and quantifiers.
Article: A determiner that expresses definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" or "a" in English.
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to a referent in space or discourse, such as "this," "that," or "these."
Indefinite: A determiner or quantifier that does not specify a particular referent, such as "a," "some," or "any."
Quantifier: A word or phrase that expresses the quantity or degree of a noun phrase's referent, such as "every," "few," or "most."
Numeral: A word that expresses a number, whether cardinal, ordinal, or fractional.
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, including personal, reflexive, demonstrative, and interrogative types.
Reflexive: A pronoun or morpheme that indicates the subject and object of a verb are the same entity, as in "She sees herself."
Reciprocal: A morpheme or construction expressing a mutual relationship between two or more participants, as in "They met each other."
Conjunction: A function word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "or," "but," or "because."
Coordinating conjunction: A conjunction that joins elements of equal grammatical status, such as "and" or "or."
Subordinating conjunction: A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because," "although," or "if."
Preposition: A function word that precedes a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or spatial relation, such as "in," "on," or "under."
Postposition: A function word that follows a noun phrase to indicate a relation, common in Japanese, Korean, and many indigenous languages.
Circumposition: A grammatical relation expressed by a pair of markers, one before and one after the complement, as in "between...and."
Particle: A small, often unstressed word that modifies a clause or verb, such as the English "up" in "give up" or the Japanese "-ka" for questions.
Auxiliary: A verb that provides grammatical information (tense, aspect, mood, voice) and supports a main verb.
Modal: An auxiliary expressing modality, such as ability, obligation, or possibility, as in "can," "must," or "may."
Agreement: A syntactic process in which one word changes form to match a grammatical property (person, number, gender, case) of another.
Concord: A term synonymous with or overlapping with agreement, referring to the matching of grammatical features between related words.
Control: A syntactic relation in which the subject of an embedded clause is determined by an argument in the matrix clause, as in "John tried to leave."
Raising: A syntactic process in which an argument from an embedded clause moves to a subject position in the matrix clause, as in "John seems to be happy."
Binding: The syntactic-semantic relation between an anaphoric element (pronoun, reflexive, or name) and its antecedent.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to an antecedent in the discourse, such as a pronoun referring to a previously mentioned noun.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an antecedent that appears later in the discourse.
Coreference: The relation between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity, even if they are not anaphoric.
Binding theory: A component of syntactic theory that accounts for the distribution of anaphors, pronouns, and R-expressions.
Antecedent: The expression to which a pronominal or anaphoric element refers.
Island constraint: A syntactic restriction that prevents certain movements or dependencies from extracting elements out of particular syntactic domains.
Subjacency: A locality constraint on movement stating that a constituent may not cross more than one bounding node at a time.
Relativized Minimality: A constraint on movement and agreement stating that a probe cannot target a goal if an intervening element of the same type is closer.
Minimal Link Condition: A constraint in Minimalist Theory requiring that the closest potential goal for a probe be selected.
Phase: A domain of syntactic derivation (typically vP and CP) at the end of which certain elements become inaccessible to subsequent computation.
Phase Theory: A framework in Minimalist syntax proposing that derivation proceeds in chunks called phases.
Vocabulary Insertion: The process in Minimalist syntax by which phonological forms are associated with abstract syntactic features.
Feature checking: The process by which syntactic features (such as Case or agreement) are matched and valued between a probe and a goal.
Agree: The syntactic operation in Minimalist Theory by which a probe searches for and matches features with a goal.
Probe: The syntactic element (typically a head) that searches for a goal to establish an Agree relation.
Goal: The syntactic element (typically a phrase) whose features are matched by a probe in an Agree relation.
Edge feature: A feature that causes material to move to the edge of a phase, making it accessible for further movement.
EPP: The Extended Projection Principle, a syntactic principle requiring that clauses have a subject.
Projection: The syntactic principle that a phrase's structure is determined by its head.
Successive-cyclic movement: The process by which a constituent moves through intermediate positions (edges of phases) on its way to a final position.
Remnant: The material left behind in a syntactic structure after a constituent has been moved or extracted.
Garden path: A sentence structure that initially leads the parser to an incorrect interpretation, requiring reanalysis, as in "The horse raced past the barn fell."
Ambiguity: The property of a sentence or expression having more than one possible interpretation.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple senses, as in "bank" (financial institution vs. river edge).
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from more than one possible syntactic parse, as in "I saw the man with the telescope."
Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to the interpretation of utterances beyond their literal meaning.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a word or expression.
Reference: The relation between a linguistic expression and the entity in the world it denotes or picks out.
Referent: The entity in the world to which a linguistic expression refers.
Denotation: The set of entities in the world to which a word or phrase applies.
Connotation: The additional, associative, or emotional meaning of a word beyond its core denotational meaning.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or form has multiple related senses, such as "head" of a person, of a company, or of a pin.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form, such as "bank" (river) and "bank" (financial).
Synonymy: The relation between words or expressions that have the same or very similar meanings, such as "buy" and "purchase."
Antonymy: The relation between words with opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "up" and "down."
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one word is included within the meaning of another, as "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird."
Hypernymy: The inverse of hyponymy; the relation of a more general term to a more specific one, as "bird" is a hypernym of "sparrow."
Merenymy: A part-whole semantic relation, as "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Holonymy: The inverse of meronymy; the whole-to-part relation, as "car" is a holonym of "wheel."
Troponymy: A semantic relation in which one word denotes a way of doing what another denotes, as "to waltz" is a troponym of "to dance."
Lexicon: The inventory of words and their associated meanings, forms, and grammatical properties in a language.
Word sense: A distinct meaning of a polysemous word, as in the different senses of "run" (to jog, to operate, to flow).
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for an utterance to be felicitous, such as the presupposition of "John stopped smoking" that John used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning that is conveyed by an utterance but is not part of its literal semantic content, derived by pragmatic inference.
Conversational implicature: A pragmatic inference based on the assumption that a speaker is following Grice's Cooperative Principle.
Generalized conversational implicature: An implicature that arises in virtually any context in which the relevant maxim is flouted.
Particularized conversational implicature: An implicature that depends on the specific context in which the utterance is made.
Gricean maxims: The four categories of conversational principles (quantity, quality, relation, manner) proposed by Paul Grice.
Maxim of quantity: The pragmatic principle to be as informative as required but no more than required.
Maxim of quality: The pragmatic principle to say what one believes to be true and do not assert what lacks adequate evidence.
Maxim of relation: The pragmatic principle to be relevant to the ongoing conversation.
Maxim of manner: The pragmatic principle to be clear, brief, and orderly in one's expression.
Cooperative principle: Grice's overarching assumption that participants in a conversation generally cooperate in being informative, truthful, relevant, and clear.
Flouting: Deliberately violating a maxim in an obvious way to generate a conversational implicature.
Inference: The cognitive process of deriving information that is not explicitly stated from available linguistic and contextual evidence.
Deixis: The phenomenon in which the interpretation of a linguistic expression depends on the context of utterance, such as "here," "now," "I," or "this."
Exophoric: An anaphoric relation in which the referent is found in the physical or situational context rather than in the discourse.
Endophoric: An anaphoric relation in which the referent is found within the discourse itself.
Discourse: Language as it is used in extended stretches of communication, encompassing text, conversation, and the organization of meaning.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse structure or signals a speaker's stance, such as "well," "actually," or "by the way."
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of a text or discourse, ensuring that ideas flow and make sense together.
Cohesion: The linguistic devices (reference, conjunction, lexical choice, etc.) that create surface-level connections in a text.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance or clause into given (old) and new information, often realized through topic and focus.
End-focus: A discourse-pragmatic principle that places new or important information toward the end of an utterance.
End-weight: A discourse-pragmatic principle that places heavier (longer or more complex) constituents toward the end of a clause.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and language use in social contexts.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular geographic region or social group.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Sociolect: A language variety associated with a particular social group, such as a class, profession, or ethnic community.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The interweaving of elements (words, phrases, morphemes) from two or more languages within a single utterance.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages.
Multilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use more than two languages.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages that can lead to borrowing, interference, or new varieties.
Loanword: A word borrowed from another language and integrated into the borrowing language's vocabulary.
Calque: A word or phrase translated literally from another language, such as "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speakers and is no longer used.
Language endangerment: The condition of a language that is at risk of losing its speaker community and falling out of use.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers of an endangered or dormant language and promote its use.
Language planning: The deliberate efforts by governments or communities to influence the development, use, or standardization of a language.
Language policy: The set of decisions, laws, and regulations governing the status and use of languages in a society.
Language standardization: The process by which a particular variety of a language is selected and promoted as the normative form.
Language prestige: The social value and positive regard accorded to a particular language variety by a community.
Stigmatized variety: A language variety that is negatively evaluated by the speech community, often associated with lower social status.
Accent: The particular pronunciation features of a speaker that indicate regional or social origin without changing word meaning.
Dialectology: The study of the geographic and social distribution of dialects and the relationships among them.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a linguistic map that marks the extent of a particular linguistic feature.
Linguistic map: A geographic representation showing the distribution of specific linguistic features or dialect boundaries.
Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestral proto-language, such as the Indo-European family.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language, such as Basque.
Language area: A geographic region in which languages of different families share features due to prolonged contact, as in the South Asian or Balkan areas.
Sprachbund: A group of languages in a geographic area that share structural features due to contact, regardless of genetic relationship.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but the extremes may not be.
Patois: A non-standard dialect or mixed variety, often associated with informal or rural speech.
Creole: A stable, natural language that develops from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language, not spoken as a native language.
Vernacular: The everyday, native language of a community, as opposed to a formal or literary register.
Jargon: A specialized vocabulary used by a particular professional or interest group.
Slang: Informal, often short-lived words and expressions used by particular social groups, especially young people.
Argot: A specialized, often secretive vocabulary used by a particular group, historically associated with criminal or subcultural speech.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one considered harsh, blunt, or taboo.
Dysphemism: A deliberately harsh or offensive word or expression used in place of a neutral or polite one.
Taboo: A social or cultural prohibition on the use of a particular word or reference, often replaced by euphemisms.
Politeness: A pragmatic strategy in which speakers mitigate the imposition of their utterances to preserve the face of participants.
Face: The positive or negative public self-image that a speaker or hearer wants to maintain in communication.
Face-threatening act: An utterance that potentially undermines the positive or negative face of a participant, such as a request or criticism.
Historical linguistics: The study of how languages change over time, reconstructing proto-languages, and tracing the history of linguistic features.
Comparative method: The systematic method of reconstructing proto-languages by comparing regular correspondences among related languages.
Proto-language: The hypothetical ancestral language from which a group of related languages is descended, often marked with an asterisk.
Cognate: A word in one language that is etymologically related to a word in another language through a common ancestor.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words and their meanings.
Sound law: A regular, systematic rule of sound change that applies across the vocabulary of a language, such as Grimm's Law.
Grimm's Law: The systematic shift of Proto-Indo-European stop consonants in Proto-Germanic, such as /p/ → /f/, /t/ → /θ/, /k/ → /x/.
Verner's Law: A follow-up to Grimm's Law explaining the voicing of certain Germanic fricatives based on Proto-Indo-European accent.
Regular change: A sound change that applies uniformly across the lexicon, as opposed to irregular or analogical change.
Analogy: A language change in which a form is altered to conform to a pattern observed elsewhere in the language, as in "mouses" for "mice."
Leveling: A change in which morphological or phonological distinctions are reduced or eliminated, as in the loss of strong verb alternations.
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word over time, such as "awful" shifting from "awe-inspiring" to "very bad."
Pejoration: A semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more negative over time, as in "silly" shifting from "blessed" to "foolish."
Amelioration: A semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more positive over time, as in "nice" shifting from "foolish" to "pleasant."
Narrowing: A semantic shift in which a word's range of meaning becomes more restricted, as in "meat" shifting from "food" to "animal flesh."
Broadening: A semantic shift in which a word's range of meaning becomes more general, as in "bird" potentially broadening beyond its original referent.
Metaphor: A semantic shift or figurative expression in which meaning is transferred based on similarity, as in "the leg of a table."
Metonymy: A semantic shift or figurative expression in which meaning is transferred based on contiguity or association, as in "the Crown" for "the monarchy."
Diachronic: Pertaining to the study of language across time, as opposed to synchronic.
Synchronic: Pertaining to the study of language at a single point in time, without reference to its historical development.
Diffusion: The spread of a linguistic feature from one language or dialect to another through contact rather than common descent.
Substrate: The language of a conquered or displaced population that influences the grammar or vocabulary of the conquering language.
Superstrate: The language of a conquering or dominant group that influences the language of the conquered population.
Adstrate: A language that influences another through prolonged contact between communities of roughly equal social standing.
Creolization: The process by which a pidgin develops into a full, complex natural language with native speakers.
Lexicalization: The process by which a multi-word expression or construction becomes a single lexical item, as in "iceberg" from "ice-berg."
Grammaticalization: The diachronic process by which lexical items or constructions develop into grammatical morphemes or structures, as in "going to" → "gonna."
Reanalysis: A change in the way speakers parse or interpret the structural boundaries of a linguistic form.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological processes that underlie language production, comprehension, and acquisition.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn to perceive, produce, and understand a language.
First language acquisition: The process by which infants and children learn their native language in the first few years of life.
Second language acquisition: The process by which individuals learn an additional language after having acquired a first language.
Critical period: A hypothesized window of early development during which language acquisition is especially rapid and complete.
Sensitive period: A period of heightened neural plasticity for language learning, after which acquisition becomes more effortful but not impossible.
Universal Grammar: A theoretical framework in generative linguistics proposing that all human languages share an innate structural blueprint.
Competence: A speaker's underlying knowledge of the grammatical rules and structures of a language, as opposed to actual performance.
Performance: The actual use of language in real-time communication, which may be affected by memory, attention, and other non-linguistic factors.
Interlanguage: The developing linguistic system of a second language learner that is distinct from both the L1 and the L2.
Fossilization: The stabilization of an erroneous or non-native linguistic feature in a second language learner's interlanguage.
Transfer: The influence of a speaker's first language on the production or comprehension of a second language.
Positive transfer: The beneficial effect of L1 knowledge on L2 learning, occurring when the two languages share features.
Negative transfer: The detrimental effect of L1 interference on L2 learning, occurring when the two languages differ.
Comprehensible input: Language input that is slightly above the learner's current level of competence, making it understandable with context.
Overgeneralization: A developmental error in which a learner applies a regular pattern to an irregular form, as in "goed" for "went."
Telegraphic speech: A stage in child language development in which utterances consist of content words with function words omitted, as in "Daddy go park."
Holophrastic stage: An early stage in child language development in which a single word conveys the meaning of an entire sentence.
Babbling: A stage in prelinguistic development in which infants produce consonant-vowel combinations not yet tied to specific meanings.
Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage, affecting one or more aspects of language production or comprehension.
Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
Global aphasia: A severe form of aphasia affecting both production and comprehension, typically resulting from extensive left-hemisphere damage.
Conduction aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by impaired repetition with relatively preserved comprehension and spontaneous speech.
Anomic aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by difficulty in word retrieval, with fluent speech and preserved comprehension.
Apraxia of speech: A motor speech disorder in which the planning and programming of speech movements is impaired despite intact muscle strength.
Dyslexia: A specific learning disorder characterized by difficulty in accurate and fluent word recognition and spelling.
Dysgraphia: A specific learning disorder characterized by difficulty in writing, including spelling, grammar, and handwriting.
Parsing: The real-time process by which a language user assigns syntactic structure to a sentence as it is heard or read.
Word segmentation: The process of identifying word boundaries in a continuous stream of speech or text.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word's meaning, form, and grammatical properties from the mental lexicon.
Mental lexicon: The cognitive representation of a speaker's word knowledge, including forms, meanings, and grammatical properties.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural mechanisms and brain structures underlying language processing, production, and comprehension.
Broca's area: A region in the left inferior frontal gyrus associated with speech production, syntactic processing, and motor planning.
Wernicke's area: A region in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus associated with language comprehension and semantic processing.
Arcuate fasciculus: A white-matter tract connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas, involved in linking comprehension and production.
Language lateralization: The specialization of one cerebral hemisphere, typically the left, for language functions.
Hemispheric specialization: The division of labor between the left and right hemispheres for different aspects of language and other cognitive functions.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, structured collections of real-world text and speech data.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts or transcriptions used for linguistic research.
Collocation: A statistically significant co-occurrence of words or phrases, such as "strong tea" or "make a decision."
N-gram: A sequence of n words or tokens from a corpus, used in statistical and computational linguistics.
Concordance: A list of all occurrences of a word or phrase in a corpus, showing the surrounding context.
KWIC: Key Word In Context, a format for presenting concordance lines with the search term centered.
Computational linguistics: The interdisciplinary field that develops computational models and algorithms for analyzing and generating natural language.
Natural language processing: The application of computer algorithms to process, analyze, and generate human language.
Tokenization: The process of dividing a stream of text into individual words, punctuation marks, or other tokens.
Lemmatization: The process of reducing inflected or derived word forms to their base dictionary form (lemma).
Part-of-speech tagging: The process of assigning grammatical category labels (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to each word in a text.
Named entity recognition: The process of identifying and classifying named entities (persons, organizations, locations) in text.
Coreference resolution: The process of identifying expressions in a text that refer to the same entity.
Machine translation: The use of computer systems to translate text from one natural language to another.
Speech recognition: The process of converting spoken language into written text using computational models.
Speech synthesis: The process of generating spoken language from text using computational models and signal processing.
Typology: The comparative study of linguistic structures across languages to identify universals, patterns, and typological parameters.
Universal: A generalization that holds across all or most of the world's languages, such as the existence of nouns and verbs.
Parameter: A binary or limited set of options in a grammatical feature for which languages can make different choices, as in the Head-Final/Head-Initial parameter.
Greenbergian universal: A linguistic generalization proposed by Joseph Greenberg based on typological evidence across a sample of languages.
Distinctive feature: A binary property (such as [±voice], [±nasal]) used to represent the contrastive properties of phonemes in a phonological system.
Tier: A separate representational level in autosegmental phonology, such as a tone tier or a vowel tier, linked to the consonant-vowel tier.
Faithfulness: A type of constraint in Optimality Theory requiring that the surface form remain identical to the underlying form.
Merge: The fundamental operation in Minimalist syntax by which two syntactic objects are combined to form a larger constituent.
Tone melody: The sequence or pattern of tones across a prosodic domain, such as a word, phrase, or sentence.
Morphological: Pertaining to the structure, classification, or formation of words.
Phonemic: Relating to or characterized by a phoneme or phonemic contrast.
Phonotactic: Relating to the permitted or prohibited sequences and combinations of sounds in a language.
Phrasal: Relating to a phrase or occurring at the phrase level of syntax.
Clause-mate: Describing two elements that appear within the same clause.
Head-final: A structural or word-order property in which the head of a phrase or clause follows its complements, as in Japanese.
Head-initial: A structural or word-order property in which the head of a phrase or clause precedes its complements, as in English.
Pro-drop: A syntactic property in which null subjects are permitted, as in Italian, Spanish, and Japanese.
Null subject: A syntactically empty subject position permitted in pro-drop languages.
Wh- in situ: A property of languages in which wh-words remain in their base position rather than moving to the clause-initial position, as in Chinese or Japanese.
Embedded question: A question clause that is embedded within a larger declarative or interrogative clause, as in "I wonder where she went."
Cleft: A construction that splits a clause into two parts to highlight a particular constituent, as in "It was John who left."
Pseudo-cleft: A type of cleft construction using a wh-clause as the subject, as in "What I need is a nap."
Split ergativity: A case-marking system in which the alignment of argument roles (ergative vs. accusative) varies by tense, aspect, or definiteness.
Absolutive: The unmarked case for intransitive subjects and transitive objects in an ergative language.
Ergative: The case marking the agent of a transitive verb in an ergative language.
Split case: A system in which different cases are used for different syntactic or discourse functions, as in some ergative languages.
Nominative-accusative: The default case alignment system in which intransitive subjects and transitive agents share one case (nominative), distinct from the transitive object (accusative).
Overt: A linguistic element that is phonologically or orthographically realized, as opposed to covert or null.
Covert: A linguistic element that is syntactically present but not phonologically realized, such as a null subject or trace.
Prosodic: Relating to the suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Prosodic word: The prosodic unit corresponding roughly to a phonological word, often defined by stress and edge tones.
Intonational phrase: A prosodic unit corresponding roughly to an intonational clause, marked by boundary tones and pauses.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of a stressed syllable and any adjacent unstressed syllables, serving as a node between the syllable and the prosodic word.
Prominence: The relative perceptual salience of a syllable or segment, often associated with stress or accent.
Duration: The length of time a segment, syllable, or phrase is produced, a key parameter in prosody and speech timing.
Amplitude: The magnitude of a signal, relevant to the acoustic realization of loudness in speech.
F0: The fundamental frequency of a sound, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration and perceived as pitch.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the speech signal resulting from resonances of the vocal tract.
Vocal tract: The cavity from the larynx through the pharynx and mouth (and optionally the nasal cavity) that shapes the sound of speech.
Larynx: The region of the throat containing the vocal folds, which vibrate to produce the source signal for voiced speech.
Vocal folds: The paired folds of tissue in the larynx that vibrate to produce voiced sounds.
Glottis: The space between the vocal folds in the larynx.
Uvula: The fleshy pendant hanging from the soft palate, involved in the production of uvular consonants.
Alveolar ridge: The bony ridge behind the upper front teeth where alveolar consonants are produced.
Palate: The roof of the mouth, divided into the hard palate (anterior) and soft palate (posterior).
Hard palate: The bony, anterior portion of the palate, the place of articulation for palatal consonants.
Soft palate: The muscular, posterior portion of the palate (velum), which can be raised or lowered.
Velum: The soft palate, whose elevation or lowering controls the nasal passage.
Denture: The area of the alveolar ridge immediately behind the upper front teeth, a place of articulation for some consonants.
Dental: Pertaining to sounds produced with the tongue against the back of the upper front teeth.
Retroflex: Pertaining to consonants produced with the tongue tip curled back toward the palate.
Approximant: A consonant produced with a constriction that is not tight enough to create turbulent airflow, including glides, rhotics, and laterals.
Semivowel: A vowel-like segment that functions as a consonant, such as /w/ and /j/ in English.
Central vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue neither front nor back, such as /ə/ or /ɨ/.
Front vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the front of the vocal tract, such as /i/ or /e/.
Back vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the back of the vocal tract, such as /u/ or /ɑ/.
Tense vowel: A vowel produced with greater muscular tension in the tongue, often associated with a higher or more peripheral position.
Lax vowel: A vowel produced with less muscular tension, often associated with a lower or more centralized position.
Rounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips rounded, as in /u/ or /o/.
Unrounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral, as in /i/ or /e/.
ATR: Advanced Tongue Root, a laryngeal feature that distinguishes vowel pairs in many African and other languages.
Laryngeal feature: A phonological feature related to the state of the larynx, such as [±constricted glottis], [±spread glottis], or [±advanced tongue root].
Creaky voice: A phonation type characterized by low, irregular vocal fold vibration, also called vocal fry.
Whispered voice: A phonation type in which the vocal folds are adducted but not vibrating, producing a breathy sound.
Breathy voice: A phonation type in which the vocal folds are not fully adducted, allowing extra air to pass through.
Phonation: The mode of vocal fold vibration that characterizes a particular voice quality.
Articulatory phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the physiological production of speech sounds.
Acoustic phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the physical and measurable properties of speech sounds.
Auditory phonetics: The branch of phonetics concerned with the perception and processing of speech sounds by the listener.
Diphoneme: A vowel phoneme in some languages whose allophones include both a monophthong and a diphthong.
Monosyllable: A word consisting of a single syllable.
Polysyllable: A word consisting of more than one syllable.
Syllable weight: A prosodic property of a syllable, typically light (CV) or heavy (CVV, CVC), relevant to stress assignment and meter.
Stress-timed: A rhythmic pattern in which stressed syllables occur at approximately regular intervals, as in English.
Syllable-timed: A rhythmic pattern in which syllables occur at approximately regular intervals, as in Spanish or French.
Mora: A unit of prosodic weight in some languages, where syllables are measured in morae for the purposes of stress, meter, or prosodic structure.
Prominent: Having greater perceptual salience or acoustic energy relative to surrounding elements, often used to describe stressed syllables or accented words.
Unstressed: A syllable that lacks full stress, often reduced in vowel quality.
Reduced vowel: A weakened vowel quality, typically a schwa /ə/, that occurs in unstressed syllables in many languages.
Schwa: The mid-central vowel /ə/, often the most common vowel in English, typically occurring in unstressed syllables.
Linking r: An /r/ sound inserted between a word-final consonant and a word-initial vowel in some English dialects, as in "car" + "and" → [kɑːrˈænd].
Intrusive r: An /r/ inserted before a vowel in a following word where no underlying /r/ is present, as in some British English varieties.
Linking vowel: A vowel, typically schwa, inserted between two consonants to facilitate pronunciation, as in "film" + "it" → [fɪləmˈɪt].
H-dropping: The deletion of an initial /h/ in some dialects of English, as in "house" pronounced [aʊs].
Th-fronting: The pronunciation of /θ/ as /f/ in some British English dialects, as in "think" pronounced [fɪŋk].
Glottal replacement: The replacement of /t/ by a glottal stop [ʔ] in some English dialects, as in "butter" pronounced [bʌʔə].
Flapping: The pronunciation of /t/ or /d/ as a rapid alveolar tap [ɾ] in certain environments, as in American English "butter" and "ladder."
Yod coalescence: The merger of /j/ with a preceding alveolar consonant to form an affricate, as in "duke" from "do + yerk" → /dʌk/.
Yod deletion: The loss of /j/ in certain environments, as in "music" pronounced [ˈmʊzɪk] rather than [ˈmjuːzɪk].
R-colored vowel: A vowel whose articulation is modified by the presence of a following /r/, as in American English /ɝ/ in "bird."
Long vowel: A vowel of extended duration, often contrastive with a short vowel, as in the phonemic contrast in English /iː/ vs. /ɪ/.
Short vowel: A vowel of reduced duration, contrasted with a long vowel in some languages.
Vowel length: The durational distinction between long and short vowels that is phonemic in some languages, as in Japanese or Latin.
Consonant cluster: A sequence of two or more consonants without an intervening vowel, such as "str" in "street."
Onset cluster: The consonant cluster in the onset of a syllable.
Coda cluster: The consonant cluster in the coda of a syllable.
Syllable boundary: The point at which one syllable ends and another begins, relevant to stress, phonotactics, and morphophonology.
Prominence boundary: A prosodic boundary marked by a particular intonational contour or pause.
Phrase boundary: A prosodic or intonational boundary marking the edge of a phrase.
Intonational boundary: A prosodic boundary at the end of an intonational phrase, often marked by a final pitch contour.
Declarative intonation: The falling pitch pattern typically associated with statements in English and many other languages.
Interrogative intonation: The rising or distinctive pitch pattern associated with yes-no questions in many languages.
List intonation: The pitch pattern used to mark the items in a list, often with a rising contour on all but the last item.
Falling intonation: A pitch contour that moves from high to low, typically marking statement-final intonation.
Rising intonation: A pitch contour that moves from low to high, typically marking yes-no question intonation in English.
Contour: The overall shape of the pitch movement across a phrase or sentence.
Nuclear stress: The primary or most prominent stress in a phrase or sentence, typically on the final content word.
Pre-nuclear stress: Secondary stress that may occur before the nuclear stress in a phrase.
Stress window: A fixed position in a word where primary stress falls, as in the trochaic iamb pattern in some languages.
Trochee: A metrical or prosodic foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.
Iamb: A metrical or prosodic foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
Meter: The patterned alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables in poetry or in the prosodic structure of language.
Prosodic hierarchy: The hierarchical organization of prosodic units from the syllable up through the foot, prosodic word, phrase, and intonational phrase.
Prosodic word: The prosodic unit roughly corresponding to a phonological word, often containing a single stress peak.
Phonological word: The unit of phonology that is roughly coextensive with a lexical word, serving as the domain for stress and tone rules.
Phonological phrase: A prosodic domain larger than a word, often corresponding to a phrase boundary.
Phonological domain: A span of speech over which a particular phonological rule or constraint applies.
Rule ordering: The linear sequence in which phonological rules apply in a serial rule-based model of phonology.
Structure conservation: A constraint in some rule models requiring that rules apply only at the level of the underlying structure.
Naturalness: The cross-linguistic tendency for certain phonological processes or patterns to be more common or easier to produce and perceive.
Articulatory naturalness: The tendency for sounds and sound changes that are easier to produce to be more frequent or stable across languages.
Perceptual naturalness: The tendency for sounds and contrasts that are easier to perceive to be more common or stable across languages.
Markedness hierarchy: A cross-linguistic ranking of linguistic elements from unmarked (more frequent, earlier acquired) to marked (less frequent, later acquired).
Frequency: The number of times a linguistic form or pattern occurs in a corpus or language.
Corpus-based frequency: The frequency of a form measured in a large body of text or speech data.
Collocational frequency: The frequency with which two or more words co-occur in a given context.
Bigram: A two-word sequence in a corpus, the simplest form of n-gram.
Trigram: A three-word sequence in a corpus.
N-gram model: A statistical model of language that predicts the next word based on the previous n-1 words.
Perplexity: A measure of how well a language model predicts a new sample, lower indicating better prediction.
Cross-entropy: A measure of the difference between predicted and actual probability distributions, used in language modeling.
Entropy: A measure of the uncertainty or information content in a set of possible outcomes.
Information: In information theory, the reduction in uncertainty associated with receiving a particular message or symbol.
Mutual information: A measure of the amount of information obtained about one random variable through another, used in collocation analysis.
Log likelihood ratio: A statistical test used to determine the strength of association between words in a corpus.
Pointwise mutual information: A measure of the association between two specific words, calculated from their joint and marginal frequencies.
Chi-square: A statistical test used to assess the significance of differences in frequency distributions.
Zipf's law: The empirical observation that the frequency of a word is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table.
Hapax legomenon: A word that occurs only once in a given corpus or text.
Type-token ratio: The ratio of unique words (types) to total word occurrences (tokens) in a text, a measure of vocabulary richness.
Lexical diversity: The variety and richness of vocabulary in a text, measured by type-token ratio or related indices.
Function word: A word with primarily grammatical rather than lexical meaning, such as articles, prepositions, and auxiliaries.
Content word: A word that carries substantive lexical meaning, such as nouns, main verbs, adjectives, and adverbs.
Closed class: A small, relatively stable set of words, typically function words, to which new members are rarely added.
Open class: A large, relatively productive set of words, typically content words, to which new members are regularly added.
Grammatical word: A word that primarily expresses grammatical relations rather than lexical content, overlapping with function words.
Lexical word: A word that carries core lexical meaning, overlapping with content words.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be predicted from the literal meanings of its components, as in "kick the bucket."
Phrasal verb: A verb combined with one or more particles (prepositions or adverbs) to create a meaning distinct from the individual parts, as in "give up."
Collocation: A habitual or statistically significant pairing of words, such as "heavy rain" or "strong coffee."
Lexical gap: A situation in which a language lacks a single word for a concept that other languages express with one word, requiring a multi-word expression.
Semantic field: A set of words that share a related area of meaning, such as words for types of food or emotions.
Prototype theory: A cognitive linguistic theory proposing that category members are organized around central, prototypical examples rather than strict necessary and sufficient conditions.
Radial category: A category organized around a central prototype with extensions along different dimensions, as in the word "bird" or "cup."
Fuzzy boundary: A category boundary that is not sharp or absolute, with some members more peripheral than others.
Metonymic extension: The semantic process by which a word's meaning is extended through a contiguity-based association, such as "The White House announced" for the administration.
Dead metaphor: A metaphor that has become so conventionalized that its figurative nature is no longer perceived, as in "the leg of a table."
Live metaphor: A metaphor that is still perceived as figurative and creative by its hearers.
Conceptual metaphor: A cross-domain mapping in which one conceptual domain is understood in terms of another, as in "ARGUMENT IS WAR."
Image schema: A basic, pre-linguistic pattern of embodied experience, such as CONTAINER, PATH, FORCE, or CENTER-PERIPHERY, that structures metaphorical thought.
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework developed by Ronald Langacker that emphasizes the role of conceptualization and usage-based categorization in grammar.
Usage-based model: A framework in which grammatical knowledge is viewed as an emergent property of stored word forms and constructions rather than an innate rule system.
Construction grammar: A framework in which linguistic knowledge is a set of form-meaning pairings (constructions) ranging from fully general to highly specific.
Construction: A form-meaning pair of any level of complexity, from a single word to a multi-word pattern, in construction grammar.
Slot and frame: A construction with a fixed structure (frame) and variable positions (slots) for arguments or modifiers, as in "More the X, the more the Y."
Lexical construction: A construction in which specific lexical items are fixed in the frame, as in "I don't give a damn."
Schematic construction: A construction with fully abstract or variable slots, such as the transitive "X V Y" pattern.
Frame semantics: A semantic approach in which the meaning of a word is understood in terms of a larger cognitive frame or scenario, as in the BUYING frame involving a Buyer, Seller, Goods, and Money.
Frame: A structured network of concepts, roles, and relations that provides the background for interpreting a linguistic expression.
Frame element: A role or participant in a cognitive frame, such as Buyer, Seller, or Goods in a commercial transaction frame.
Thematic role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, also called a theta role or case role.
Semantic role: A general term for the role an argument plays in the event or state described by a predicate.
Predication: The semantic relation between a predicate and its arguments in a proposition.
Proposition: A declarative content or meaning that can be true or false, the basic unit of semantic content.
Predicative: Relating to a predicate or its arguments in a proposition.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another, as in "John killed the bird" entails "The bird is dead."
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be held true for an utterance to be felicitous, surviving under negation.
Scalar implicature: A pragmatic inference based on the violation of the principle of scalar strength, as in "Some of the students passed" implicating "Not all passed."
Horn scale: A natural ordering of scalar terms such as <all, most, many, some, few, none>.
Gricean scale: An artificial or conventional ordering of terms used to generate scalar implicatures in specific contexts.
Hedging: A pragmatic strategy of softening or qualifying a statement to reduce its commitment, as in "I think that..." or "It might be the case that..."
Mitigation: A politeness strategy in which the speaker reduces the strength or directness of a face-threatening act.
Directness: The degree to which an utterance explicitly states the speaker's intention, contrasted with indirectness.
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose literal form does not match its intended speech act function, as in "Can you pass the salt?" as a request.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action (requesting, promising, warning, etc.) in addition to conveying a propositional content.
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific propositional content.
Illocutionary act: The act of performing an intended function (requesting, declaring, promising) in uttering a sentence.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Performative: A sentence that performs the action it describes when uttered under appropriate conditions, as in "I hereby pronounce you married."
Declarative: A speech act that brings about a change in the world simply by being uttered, such as "I now declare this meeting open."
Directive: A speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something, such as requests, commands, and suggestions.
Commissive: A speech act in which the speaker commits to a future course of action, such as promises, offers, and threats.
Expressive: A speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state, such as thanking, apologizing, or congratulating.
Representative: A speech act that states or describes a state of affairs, such as asserting, reporting, or claiming.
Felicitous: A speech act that satisfies all the necessary conditions for its successful performance.
Malapropism: The accidental misuse of a word that sounds similar to the intended word, as in "a nice derangement of epitaphs."
Malaphor: A blending of a malapropism and a metaphor, in which an unintended but meaningful metaphorical expression is produced.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "edit" from "editor."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a word is shortened without changing its meaning, as in "ad" from "advertisement."
Blend: A word-formation process in which parts of two words are combined to create a new word, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced as a word, such as "laser" or "radar."
Initialism: An abbreviation formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "NATO."
Morphological: Pertaining to the structure, classification, or formation of words.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins in a word.
Morphophonemic: Pertaining to the interaction between morphological structure and phonological form.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon of a morpheme having multiple phonological forms (allomorphs) in different contexts.
Suppletive allomorph: An allomorph that is historically unrelated to the other forms of the same morpheme, as in "go" and "went."
Paradigmatic: Pertaining to the set of possible alternatives in a particular structural position, as opposed to syntagmatic relations.
Syntagmatic: Pertaining to the linear combination of elements in a particular context, as opposed to paradigmatic relations.
Langue: The abstract, shared system of rules and conventions in a language, as opposed to the individual act of speaking (parole).
Parole: The individual, concrete act of speaking or a particular utterance, as opposed to the abstract language system (langue).
Competence: The idealized, underlying knowledge of a language held by a native speaker.
Performance: The actual use of language in specific situations, which may deviate from competence due to non-linguistic factors.
Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence in transformational grammar before surface transformations are applied.
Surface structure: The final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied, corresponding to the linear word order.
Transformation: An operation in transformational grammar that maps a deep structure to a surface structure.
Deep grammar: The set of rules and principles underlying the competence of a language.
Surface grammar: The set of rules describing the surface forms of a language.
X-bar theory: A framework in phrase structure that posits a uniform hierarchical structure for all phrases, with X (head), X' (intermediate projection), and XP (maximal projection).
Head complement: The constituent immediately dominated by the head in X-bar theory, also called the specifier in some frameworks.
Complement: In X-bar theory, the constituent merged with the head to form X', typically following the head in head-initial languages.
Specifier: In X-bar theory, the constituent merged with X' to form XP, typically preceding the head in head-initial languages.
Maximal projection: The largest phrase in a given category, traditionally labeled XP (e.g., NP, VP).
Intermediate projection: The node in X-bar theory between the head and the maximal projection, labeled X'.
Bare phrase: A phrase that lacks a determiner or other specifier, as in "cats" vs. "the cats."
Light noun: A noun with little semantic content that serves as a syntactic head, as in "a decision" in "make a decision."
Heavy noun: A noun with substantial semantic content, as opposed to a light noun.
Light verb construction: A construction in which a semantically empty verb combines with a nominal or adjectival complement, as in "take a walk" or "make a decision."
Complex predicate: A predicate in which a noun or adjective combines with a verb to form a single semantic unit, as in Japanese "gomi o harau" (garbage-O sweep).
Resultative: A construction expressing the result or state resulting from an action, as in "He painted the wall green."
Causative verb: A verb that expresses causing an event, as in "break" (transitive) vs. "break" (intransitive) or "kill" vs. "die."
Inchoative: A verb form or construction expressing the beginning of a state or change, as in "The door opened."
Factitive: A causative construction in which the causee is brought into a state, as in "They made him king."
Applicative construction: A grammatical process that adds an argument to a verb, typically an indirect object, as in Bantu and other language families.
Evidential marker: A grammatical morpheme indicating the source of the speaker's information.
Direct evidential: A marker indicating the speaker has direct perceptual knowledge of the event.
Reportative: A marker indicating the speaker's information comes from hearsay or report.
Conjectural: A marker indicating the speaker's information is based on inference or speculation.
Mirative: A marker expressing surprise or unexpectedness, often with an evidential or epistemic component.
Irrealis marker: A grammatical marker indicating a non-actualized, hypothetical, or future event.
Realis marker: A grammatical marker indicating an actualized, completed, or factual event.
Perfect: A grammatical category linking a past event to the present, as in "I have eaten."
Pluperfect: A tense or aspect indicating an event that was completed before another past event, as in "I had left before she arrived."
